West Kowloon arts hub deficit widens to HK$998 million as operating costs rise
‘We will have more revenue in the coming months such as from the upfront fees from the tender of the residential project,’ authority CEO Betty Fung says
The authority managing Hong Kong’s arts hub in West Kowloon recorded a wider deficit in the 2025-26 financial year but expects to generate more income next year by putting a residential development project out to tender.
The West Kowloon Cultural District Authority’s deficit ballooned to HK$998 million (U$127 million) in the year to March 30, from HK$769 million in the same period a year earlier. The increase was mainly due to higher operating costs as it prepared to open the new WestK Performing Arts Centre, which is due to open in autumn 2027.
Revenue jumped 19 per cent to HK$768 million in 2025-26, driven by growth in ticket sales, sponsorship, and sales of intellectual property and creative products, according to a document submitted to the Legislative Council on Tuesday.
“The deficit is still within control, below the HK$1 billion level,” the authority’s CEO Betty Fung Ching Suk-yee said. “We will have more revenue in the coming months such as from the upfront fees from the tender of the residential project.”

OpenAI vows to rebuild trust in Australia after its models breached government websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:13:13 UTC
17:13:13 KST

Muhammed Yasin Gungor
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI pledged Tuesday to restore public confidence in Australia following disclosures that its automated models accessed official government portals without authorization during internal testing, Australian media reported.
“I want to begin with an apology,” OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon told Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney, News24 reported. “During internal training and evaluation, our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to. That should not have happened. We also should have handled our response better.”
Acknowledging the reputational damage caused by the incident, Kwon told lawmakers that the company recognized it had “work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people” and remained committed to carrying out corrective measures.
Kwon pledged that the firm would alert Australian agencies “promptly and directly” if future security anomalies occurred across its systems. He said Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman was not aware of the intrusions when he met Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles last month, explaining that technical personnel were still assessing the incidents.
The hearing followed disclosures made last month after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed during the UN General Assembly in New York that automated models had interacted with the country’s Medicare network.
OpenAI’s internal review identified unauthorized access involving Services Australia, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. The company detected the activity in mid-August following an earlier breach involving machine learning platform Hugging Face, though internal assessments found no evidence that individual patient or client records were compromised.
To address security concerns, OpenAI plans to create a specialized Australian task force comprising independent experts to formulate cybersecurity recommendations and improve cooperation between artificial intelligence firms and government institutions.

Sovereigntist party wins Quebec vote without parliamentary majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:12:07 UTC
17:12:07 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The sovereigntist Parti Quebecois has won the general election in the Canadian province of Quebec, securing a return to power without capturing an outright legislative majority.
"Being elected Premier of Quebec is an immense privilege and a huge responsibility -- one I accept with great humility," party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Monday on US social media platform X, declaring that his administration will "reach out to others" to serve all residents regardless of political background.
The party advocates national sovereignty to establish Quebec as an independent state from Canada.
With 99.98% of polling stations reporting, the Parti Quebecois garnered 28.02% of the popular vote and led in 59 districts, according to Elections Quebec data. The tally leaves the party five seats short of the 64-seat threshold needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly of Quebec, prompting CBC News to project a minority government.
The Quebec Liberal Party finished second with 40 seats and 24.22% of ballots, while the Conservative Party of Quebec secured 19 seats. Quebec solidaire captured nine seats, with co-leader Ruba Ghazal, who was born in Lebanon to a Palestinian refugee family, winning reelection.
The outgoing Coalition Avenir Quebec, led by Premier Christine Frechette, failed to secure any seats despite capturing 13.35% of the popular vote. Voter turnout reached 66.90% among more than 6.4 million registered voters.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney congratulated Premier-designate Plamondon, emphasizing federal cooperation on regional priorities.
"Building a stronger Quebec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," Carney said, adding that Ottawa seeks to collaborate with the incoming provincial government to support local enterprises affected by trade tariffs, generate employment, and expand housing construction across the province.
Carney also thanked Frechette for her service to Quebec and Canada.

Police and Border Guard Board step up checks in Valga after migrant surge

Police and Border Guard Board step up checks in Valga after migrant surge
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) has stepped up its border checks, and not only at the eastern border, but also in Valga, on the Latvian border.
As 41 people who had entered Estonia illegally across the Latvian border were apprehended over the past week, authorities are increasingly checking people and vehicles arriving from Latvia at the border.
The checks were boosted more than usual in Valga on Monday when "Aktuaalne kaamera visited".
"This is migration pressure that may have been initiated by the Belarusian state, but if we are talking about the countries of origin of these migrants, we have apprehended Somali citizens as the largest number, followed by people from other East African countries, including Ethiopia, as well as more distant countries such as India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. There are actually many countries of origin," said Igor Bogdanov, head of the patrol service at the PPA's southeastern police station.
Valga, twinned with Valka on the Latvian side of the border, also has a rail station and PPA personnel have been checking trains arriving from Latvia, which has included walking through the carriages and checking passengers' documents where necessary.
"We are checking transport hubs — railways — and on the roads we are trying to check people and vehicles. We have also informed accommodation providers and others, such as bus companies, that if anything raises questions or suspicions, they should let us know as well," Bogdanov said.
Estonia has detained close to 200 foreign nationals who entered illegally since July, most via Belarus and Latvia, with 72 handed back to Latvia. Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) has described the entries as organized waves orchestrated by another state. The strain has fallen hardest on the court system, particularly the Tallinn Administrative Court, which has to green-light PPA detention requests. Just outside Tallinn, Rae municipality's child protection services, has struggled with a surge of migrants claiming to be minors. Estonia has extended its border-guard rotation on Latvia's border with Belarus, whose regime is aligned with the Kremlin. Estonia has also asked Finland for assistance with patrols and returns.

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. Two people were killed and nine others were injured as a result of an overnight Ukrainian drone attack in the Moscow Region, Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported on his Max channel.
One person was injured in a drone attack on a private house in Russia’s western Smolensk Region, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on his Max channel.
TASS has compiled the key details on the aftermath.
Scale
- From 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on October 5 to 9:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 6 (from 5:00 p.m. GMT on October 5 to 6:00 a.m. GMT on October 6), on-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 868 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to its statement, the drones were downed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tver, Tula and Moscow Regions, Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
- According to TASS calculations based on Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin’s reports on his Max channel, air defenses shot down 161 drones approaching the capital since the start of the day.
- Sobyanin noted that between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time on October 5 and 5:00 a.m. Moscow time (between 5:30 p.m. GMT on October 5 and 2:00 a.m. GMT on October 6), 650 drones flew toward the Moscow Region.
- Air defenses destroyed most of them at long range.
- A total of 105 drones were destroyed as they approached Moscow.
- The attempted enemy attack on Moscow was one of the largest in the past two years.
- Air defensee and electronic warfare systems shot down 185 drones over the Moscow Region, Governor Andrey Vorobyov stated.
- Air defenses downed 46 Ukrainian drones over Russia’s central Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on his Max channel.
- Air defenses destroyed 32 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region overnight, Governor Dmitry Milyaev reported on his Max channel.
- Nineteen Ukrainian drones were shot down over the Smolensk Region overnight, Governor Vasily Anokhin stressed.
Consequences in Moscow Region
- Two people were killed in an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow Region, Vorobyov reported.
- He specified that one of the victims was a 20-year-old man in the village of Radumlya in the Solnechnogorsk district near Moscow.
- In Domodedovo’s Barybin, rescue workers found the body of a 71-year-old man under the rubble of a destroyed private home.
- In addition, according to the governor, a total of nine people were injured as a result of the attack.
- In Pokrovskoye, a man with shrapnel wounds was taken to the hospital.
- In Istra, two residents of Yadromino and Gorok were hospitalized.
- One of them is scheduled for surgery.
- In addition, three people in the village of Lyakhovo in the Domodedovo district required medical attention.
- According to Vorobyov, ten private houses were damaged in Istra, as well as outbuildings and two cars in Safontiyevo, Torlopovo, Gorki, and Yadromino.
- In the village of Pokrovskoye in the Volokolamsk district, the facade and windows of a house were damaged.
- In Domodedovo’s Lobanovo, a fire broke out in a private home.
- Another house was destroyed in Barybin.
- The governor added that emergency services are working in all affected areas.
- In the village of Litvinovo in the Solnechnogorsk district, a drone crashed onto the roof of a store’s warehouse, district head Konstantin Mikhalkov specified, noting that a fire broke out as a result.
- A cargo truck was also damaged.
- A total of 46 employees were quickly evacuated to a safe location.
- According to Mikhalkov, two private homes and a car were also damaged in the district, and nine other cars were burned.
- In turn, Vorobyov later reported that the fire on the warehouse premises has now been extinguished.
- In total, according to him, 47 private homes were damaged across seven districts of the Moscow Region.
- The governor added that four apartments in an apartment building in the village of Lobanovo in Domodedovo were damaged, with shattered windows and balcony glass.
- No one was injured, and no evacuation was necessary.
- Windows at a nearby boiler room were also damaged.
- In addition, three vehicles were damaged: two in Istra and one in Stupino.
Other regions

- The individual declined hospitalization.

Faster returns and stricter border controls: How the EU plans to tighten migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:07:05 UTC
17:07:05 KST

The EU is cracking down on migration two months after launching the Migration and Asylum Pact. Migrants with no right to stay must leave and may be transferred to “return hubs”. A new European Return Order will include key elements of return decisions. But is the EU prepared?
On 1 October, EU interior ministers and Commissioner for Justice and Home Affairs Magnus Brunner approved faster returns at the Justice and Home Affairs Council, a few days after meeting at the Munich Migration Conference on 26 September.
Member states agreed to transfer migrants to detention facilities and include all details of return decisions in a European Return Order to accelerate procedures and facilitate cross-border cooperation. A stronger European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) will take part in return processes, while a European Emergency Response Framework will strengthen the bloc's readiness for mass influxes.
Human rights groups and NGOs are sceptical of the new measure, as Frontex reports that detections of irregular border crossings at the EU’s external borders fell by almost 40% in the first half of 2026, compared with the same period in 2025.
It's "difficult to justify these measures as a proportionate response to current migratory pressure and raises the question of whether they are instead being pursued for other political reasons”, said Marta Welander, EU advocacy director at the International Rescue Committee (IRC).
The EU’s migration status today
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) reports that, as of mid-September 2026, illegal arrivals by sea have fallen to 60,000, down from 98,040 in 2025.
The central Mediterranean route to Italy recorded the steepest drop, with arrivals down by 55%, from 48,231 in 2025 to 21,393 in 2026. Arrivals on the Atlantic and Western Mediterranean routes reached 16,794 from 22,855 in 2025. Fatalities rose from 284 in 2025 to at least 2,292 in 2026. From January to mid-September, the Libyan Coast Guard tracked 17,067 migrants and returned them to Libya.
First-time asylum applications are at their lowest level since 2022, according to Eurobarometer. In June 2026, 37,075 people requested for international protection, compared with 53,025 in January 2022 and nearly 115,000 in October 2023, when requests peaked. Italy (9,660), France (9,165), Germany (4,265) and Greece (3,955) received the most applications, accounting for 73% of all first-time applicants. The number of unaccompanied minors decreased too, from 1,775 in 2025 to 1,105 in 2026.
The EU also issued fewer positive asylum decisions this year. In the second quarter of 2026, positive decisions totalled 74,780, down from 89,850 in the third quarter of 2025 and 90,535 in the third quarter of 2024.
Yet returns are not catching up. Compared with the second quarter of 2025, orders for non-EU citizens to leave fell 12.0% in the second quarter of 2026. Returns to third countries rose 9.7%, but of 110,335 orders issued, only 36,825 were carried out this year so far.
What has the EU done so far?
In the last decade, the EU had to tighten how it handles migrants who enter without authorisation. Since 12 June 2026, the New Pact on Migration and Asylum requires countries to follow a common system for registering arrivals, checking identities and quickly deciding what happens next.
Border authorities must carry out security, health and vulnerability checks, while governments must decide whether a person should enter the asylum system, face a faster border procedure or return.
The new rules place much of this process at the external borders. People who arrive irregularly must undergo mandatory screenings before they formally enter the normal asylum procedure. The system also expands the use of Eurodac, the EU database that records information on asylum seekers and irregular migrants.
The Pact changes how EU governments divide responsibility, since countries like Italy, Greece, Spain and Cyprus have long argued that their geography gives them a disproportionate share of arrivals.
The new system creates a permanent solidarity mechanism under which other member states must contribute. They can help in three ways, first in relocations, physically transferring asylum seekers into their own territories. Second, by paying €20,000 per non-relocated person into a centralised EU fund, to finance border infrastructure or migration management. And the third, by deploying staff, equipment, or other infrastructure elements to frontline states.
This system is now in force, but implementation remains uneven. In its first assessment after the Pact took effect, the Commission saw progress in Spain, Cyprus, Greece and Italy, especially in preparing authorities to handle responsibility transfers. It also said that some countries still needed to take further practical steps.
The EU is also trying to reduce irregular migration before people reach its borders by working with countries in North Africa, the Middle East and elsewhere on border management, migrant smuggling, returns and readmission.
Faster returns
The new rules mainly tighten the Return Regulation, included in the June pact, to make returns faster and simpler.
Migrants without the right to remain must leave the member state where they are located. They must always cooperate with national authorities, or they can face sanctions, including reduced benefits and allowances or even criminal sanctions.
Member states can send migrants to so-called “return hubs”, detention facilities outside the EU to await deportation, modelled on Italy’s detention centres in Albania. Front-runners, including Denmark, Germany, Greece, Austria, and the Netherlands, which make up the “Group of Five”, are pushing to establish the first hubs in 2027. Uzbekistan, Rwanda, and Uganda are potential locations. Migrants who pose security threats can be banned indefinitely from entering the EU or detained for longer than 24 months.
The IRC warns that return hubs are "counterproductive” as they "risk compounding the dangers people face", Welander explained. "Those sent to a third country with no durable legal status or protection could be pushed to attempt re-entry through irregular and more dangerous routes or fall back into the hands of smugglers and traffickers”, she added.
National authorities must include details of return decisions in a new standardised form, the European Return Order. It facilitates cross-border cooperation by providing national authorities with information on return decisions issued by other member states. For now, mutual recognition of these decisions remains voluntary, though it may be reassessed three years after the new rules take effect.
The proposals are a “sticking plaster, not a sustainable solution”, Welander said.
“Outsourcing migration management responsibility puts the EU in a position of dependency on third countries, which gain leverage to use migration cooperation as a bargaining chip […] this is not simply a technical fix for slow deportations, it reflects a political choice to place migration management outside the reach of EU law and courts”.
What happens to migrants' rights?
From the start, return hubs have been the most contentious issue in the reform crunch. NGOs and human rights advocates across Europe call them “deportation facilities” and warn of rights violations, despite the EU’s guarantee to build these facilities in safe third countries and to carry out returns under international law.
“The notion of "safe" third country doesn't mean a lot. A country could be considered safe by the EU and still be unsafe for certain people, depending on their individual circumstances […] Amnesty International has specifically documented rights violations both in Uganda and Rwanda, including arbitrary detention and other repressive measures”, warned Chiara Catelli, advocacy officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants.
Detention facilities can’t be built in a human rights-compliant manner, she added. “No safeguard can make deportation centres a legitimate tool to manage migration. The very fact of sending people to places they don't even know, far from the life they were trying to build, goes against the right to private and family life”.
Catelli also warned of the inhumane living conditions migrants might face and the lack of safeguards to respect migrants’ rights. “Already in Europe, people in immigration detention face appalling conditions […] - how will this be different in places where civil society or other independent bodies' oversight will be even more difficult or outright impossible?”, she said.
Stronger border controls and response capacity
The new rules also include a stronger protection of the EU's external border. Member states proposed boosting Frontex's mandate and transform it from a protection agency into a repatriation agency with an own task force.
For Welander, “handing Frontex a bigger operational role in returns, including potentially in third countries and at ‘return hubs’”, does not solve underlying diplomatic and legal bottlenecks. “It does, however, raise important accountability questions. Frontex is already under scrutiny over its involvement in pushbacks and fundamental rights violations, including an ongoing investigation into Greece”, she added.
The EU plans to add €130 million to the €250 million Drone Action Plan to develop new technologies for border security and to deepen “migration diplomacy” with third countries to halt migration flows at their source.
Ministers also discussed the European Emergency Response Framework, proposed by the EU Commission in September, to strengthen the EU’s emergency response to sudden large-scale arrivals or "engineered and weaponised" migration, as President von der Leyen called it.

Global oil stocks are alarmingly low and could take two years to rebuild, Aramco warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:06:23 UTC
17:06:23 KST

The CEO of the world's biggest oil company warned at a conference that the global oil supply system is reaching its limit and that replenishing global oil stockpiles could take two years.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser has warned that the world’s oil supply cushion is shrinking. The head of the world’s largest oil company said the Iran war has drained stocks that could help offset further supply disruptions.
The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that typically handles around 20% of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, led to major supply disruptions and higher prices, hitting the global economy.
Seven months into the war, the global oil stockpile system is "already straining," said Nasser, speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
"And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin," he told the two-day conference attended by leaders from across the energy sector.
G7 countries, in coordination with the International Energy Agency (IEA), agreed on Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by the US-Iran war.
But Nasser explained that total oil inventories do not reflect the amount of oil that can actually be supplied to the market. "That's why you find they're struggling with 100 million barrels."
But Nasser warned Monday against looking at headline figures for commercial reserves, noting that "less than 10%" were available for use. A large portion of the reserves reported by countries represent the minimum volume required to keep infrastructure operational, he said.
According to Nasser, global oil inventories stood at around 10 billion barrels at the start of the crisis. Since then, nearly 3 billion barrels of oil supply have been lost, or roughly half the crude and refined products that would normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz during that time. More than 1 billion barrels have been withdrawn from global inventories to help offset those losses, with most drawn from onshore commercial inventories.
Nasser described these inventories as "the last major tool in the box", adding that much of the remaining stock, estimated at less than 6 billion barrels, is “not practically available.”
Nasser said tapping reserves buys the market time but does not fix long-term supply and demand imbalances. He added that these volumes could help the world through one winter, but do not amount to a lasting solution.
He pointed out that rebuilding inventories after the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens could take up to two years.
Regional exports recover as producers use alternative routes
Despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil exports from the Middle East Gulf region, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler.
"At least 16.5 mbd (million barrels a day) left the region between 1 and 28 September, matching the pre-war average excluding Iran. That is 10.5 mbd above March's monthly average," said the firm.
The recovery followed changes to the region’s export routes.
Some 40% of those exports now bypass the Strait of Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, with pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates providing key alternative routes. Most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore.
Nasser said Aramco was meeting its customers' requirements, citing the company's use of international storage facilities and the speed with which it has repaired infrastructure damaged during the conflict.
Aramco is also seeking additional routes for crude exports and new storage facilities abroad, in order to reduce its reliance on a single channel to reach buyers in global markets.
Saudi oil facilities have been hit by several attacks launched by the Houthis in Yemen since fighting resumed between the Saudi-led military coalition and the Iran-backed Houthi fighters.

The UN Human Rights Office verified some 15,280 civilian casualties in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, 55% more than in the same period last year, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on 2 October.
Türk's statement comes as Russia has begun its Winter 2026-2027 campaign of long-range strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said Russian forces began the campaign in late September. Damage to energy infrastructure disrupt electricity, heating, and water supplies during the winter, increasing the risks to civilians.
Russian glide bombs killed and injured nearly 2,500 civilians in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts during the first eight months of the year, 62% more than in the same period last year, according to UN figures.
"As winter approaches, Ukrainians fear the worst is yet to come," Türk said.
On 4 October, Russia's Defense Ministry announced that it was intensifying strikes on infrastructure in Kyiv City and Oblast and across Ukraine, according to ISW.
Why Russia is turning to long-range strikes
ISW said Ukraine's 2026 battlefield successes "appear to be forcing" Russian President Vladimir Putin to shift focus from advances on the battlefield toward a winter campaign intended to compel Ukraine to surrender.
A week earlier, ISW assessed that Putin was likely attempting to force Ukraine to capitulate before spring 2027, with his theory of victory heavily relying on cheap, jet-powered Geran-type drones.
A toll rising all year
The 15,280 figure extends a trend the UN has tracked all year. Over the first seven months of 2026, its monitoring mission verified 1,839 civilians killed and 10,638 injured. In September, UN Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council that more civilians were killed or injured in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of 2025.

Trump orders firing squad for Hasan, 2009 Fort Hood attacker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:04:54 UTC
17:04:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump orders firing squad for Nidal Malik Hasan who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas
President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad to execute the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree the gunman later described as retaliation for US wars in the Muslim world, the Pentagon said on Monday.
Putting former US Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by Army firing squad was approved by Trump at the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X.
Parnell noted that Hasan shouted "God is greatest" in Arabic during the attack, which killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.
The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution, Parnell said, adding, "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come."
Death by firing squad was one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.
The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.
Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but unconscious and hospitalized on life support.
Pike's lawyers had previously urged that the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners faced in establishing a sound intravenous line.
A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police upon his arrest.
In a statement responding to Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill."
Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president."
If Hasan is put to death, it would mark the first military execution since 1961, the group said. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out "by musketry" in November 1945, the center reported.
At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

Lithuanians revive the debate on ending the practice of seasonal time change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:04:22 UTC
17:04:22 KST

As the next switch to winter time approaches, the question of why Europe continues to "adjust the clocks" twice a year has returned to the agenda.
In the Lithuanian capital, Vilnius, a large video screen displays cities from other parts of the world in real time. While one city enjoys the early afternoon, another is already shrouded in evening twilight. At the end of October, Lithuania and the rest of the European Union will once again turn their clocks back by an hour, reverting to standard—or winter—time.
For some Lithuanians, this annual transition has long been a source of annoyance. One woman told LRT that she dislikes changing the clock. She noted that while it feels like gaining an extra hour, just as one gets used to it, things have to change again; she would really like a definitive decision to be made on which time system to keep. Another passerby agreed, stating that a choice simply needs to be made. He argued that there is no need to switch the clock back and forth—a permanent time setting is needed, whether it be winter or summer time.
Lithuania's Minister of Transport, Juras Taminskas, shares this view. Since the beginning of the year, he has been trying to persuade the Baltic and Nordic states to end this practice. The minister joked that even his dog is confused by the changing of the clocks. He recalled the old saying that cows do not understand the time shift, noting that his dog doesn't understand it either—when the time changes, the dog ends up being taken for a walk at a different hour.
Taminskas hopes to get the issue on the agenda when Lithuania takes over the Presidency of the Council of the EU in January.
 The minister acknowledged that reaching an agreement would not be easy, particularly with Southern European countries. However, he added that given the current political climate—with so many important issues and challenges—the inability to agree on something so simple, yet something that has affected citizens emotionally, physiologically, and physically for decades, is, to put it mildly, embarrassing.
Meanwhile, Luminor chief economist Žygimantas Mauricas takes a more pessimistic view. He stated that, given the general difficulty of reaching agreements on other matters, success on this issue is unlikely. The biggest obstacle is reportedly not the lack of consensus on ending time changes, but rather the disagreement over which time—winter or summer—to keep.
For Lithuania, the choice is complex. Summer time would provide more light in the evenings and be more beneficial for public health, as people would receive more sunlight. However, there are also economic considerations. Like Latvia, Estonia, and Finland, Lithuania is in the Eastern European time zone, whereas parts of the rest of Europe are an hour behind. Sharing the same time zone as major trading partners can simplify cross-border transactions; Mauricas noted that Germany is particularly important to Lithuania.
At the same time, geography is a fixed factor. Spain and Poland are separated by nearly 3,000 kilometers yet share the same time zone. Mauricas described this as essentially absurd, noting that it means Spain sacrifices morning daylight hours, while Poland loses daylight in the evenings. 
If Lithuania were to adopt winter time to align with Poland, evenings would be darker; while this would be economically advantageous, it would also spark public dissatisfaction.
 Mauricas stated that sticking to winter time would generate even more complaints than the practice of changing the clocks. His calculations indicate that by remaining on winter time, Lithuania would lose about 40 minutes of evening daylight.
Taminskas stated that a decision should be reached through a joint vote, with the majority view prevailing. The minister noted that Lithuania has already held initial discussions with Latvia, Estonia, and the Nordic countries regarding the retention of summer time. Public opinion polls in Lithuania consistently show support for keeping summer time.

Hungary to open Communist-era informer files in reckoning with Cold War past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:03:57 UTC
17:03:57 KST

Hungary to open Communist-era informer files in reckoning with Cold War past
BUDAPEST, Oct 6 - In a historic move, Hungary will soon start releasing tens of thousands of Communist-era police files in an online public database, giving people access to lists of informers and collaborators used by the former state security services.
The release, timed for the 70th anniversary of Hungary's 1956 anti-Soviet uprising, is part of Prime Minister Peter Magyar's pledge to make the records, stored in a vast basement of archives in Budapest, public and allow Hungarians to come to terms with their totalitarian past.
Although Communist rule ended in 1989, Hungary delayed fully opening the files due to a lack of strong political will from successive governments. So far, apart from researchers, ordinary people could only request access to their own records or those of close family members but now anybody will be able to conduct searches in the online database.
During the Cold War, secret police agencies in eastern Europe such as East Germany's Stasi or Hungary's security services relied on collaborators drawn from the public, often via blackmail, threats or rewards. Between 1956 and 1989 some 55,000 secret collaborators were recorded in Hungary.
They monitored friends, family members, neighbours and co-workers to detect signs of dissent and Western influence -- and their reports often led to arrests and interrogation.
Many flats in downtown Budapest -- called K-flats or conspiracy flats -- served as locations for meetings between secret police officials and civilian collaborators.
MUSIC BANDS TARGETED
In the 1980s, informants attended concerts in Budapest's underground rock scene that attracted youthful crowds and were seen by the authorities as potentially subversive.
Peter Muller "Sziami", still an iconic figure in today's music scene, recalls his band Kontroll Csoport (group) performing in 1983 a song he had written titled "Informers and Provocateurs".
"In our own way," the lyrics read, "we keep watch too: the one standing in front of you is our man -- you’ve blushed, you’ve been exposed, informers and provocateurs."
"And then we turned spotlights on the crowd and we saw the audience of around 1,000 people spinning around, looking to see who could be the informers," Muller, 74, said in his studio, smiling mischievously.
Muller was almost thrown out of college for his music, and police banned some of his concerts and interrogated him. His first punk-rock band called "URH" in 1980, legendary in the underground culture, was named after the radio frequency band used by the state police and was often targeted.
Despite those memories, however, Muller has mixed feelings about the opening of the files after such a long time.
"I do not feel entirely comfortable with the idea that society needs such a cleansing or catharsis after all this time — that people must be singled out, humiliated, shamed, and punished when they have either already died or moved on to a different stage of life," he told Reuters.
CONFRONTING OUR PAST 'MORE DEEPLY'
The Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security (ABTL) manages the former state security services' records, with files comprising the names of 50,000 to 60,000 collaborators.
Its director, Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, hailed the release of the Communist-era files, based on a law passed by parliament in September, as a "historic step" and said it went further than elsewhere in the former eastern bloc.
Poland opened its archives much earlier but does not allow open, unrestricted searches, as will be the case now in Hungary.
Germany also took a more restrictive approach in its 1991 act to open the Stasi files, while in the Czech Republic not all files have been uploaded to an online database.
The Hungarian law says understanding the past and the transparency of public institutions are "essential prerequisites" for the functioning of a democratic state.
The release of four types of files will come in two stages, starting on November 4. On that day in 1956 Soviet tanks entered Budapest to crush a pro-democracy uprising that had begun on October 23.
Some details of the files will be redacted to protect sensitive personal information, including health records, addictions and sexual orientation.
"As both an archivist and a historian, I believe that passing judgment based on this information is inappropriate," Cseh told Reuters.
"However, I do think it is possible to gain insight into life stories and confront our past more deeply — not only at an individual level but also at a societal one." REUTERS

Outgoing president: My chances to serve Estonia will be even better as ex-head of state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
08:03:00 UTC
17:03:00 KST

Outgoing president: My chances to serve Estonia will be even better as ex-head of state
President Alar Karis tells ERR in an interview that while he plans to take some time to reflect after leaving office, his calendar is already beginning to fill up and he intends to continue working on issues related to AI and technology.
One more week and you'll be at your country home by the Piusa River where Sirje Karis is already waiting for you and you'll start working your way through all the books you left unfinished or didn't get around to reading at all over the past five years. What can the president still accomplish in these final seven days?
The final days are a time to thank the people you've worked and traveled alongside. I've also recently completed my farewell visits to neighboring countries, the last of which was to see the king of Sweden. That's part of leaving office. A portrait has also been completed and I'll be shown it during my final week. It will be hung in Kadriorg.
So this is a big week of giving thanks for you?
In many ways, yes. You should thank people all the time, not just during your final week, but it's part of being an outgoing president — looking back a little and remembering the people you worked with.
From the outside, it seems that you grew increasingly comfortable in the presidency and that you grew into the role organically. Your most recent Independence Day speech this year was certainly one of your most memorable and could even be read as something of a testament. Are you a little sorry to leave, especially considering it was your own idea that a president could serve a single seven-year term? Perhaps the best years would only be starting now.
It's hard to say whether they would have been the best years because routine sets in whether the term is five years or seven. A lot of things repeat themselves. But yes, you look back a little and also think about what you could have done differently. The time isn't really ripe for that yet, though.
I've often held positions that I've left voluntarily rather than because I was forced to, so this isn't particularly painful. It's simply one chapter coming to an end and time will tell what the next one brings.
The arrival and departure of presidents always attracts a lot of interest. When did you actually know that you wouldn't seek another term? You said when you took office that it would be a one-time thing. Did you never reconsider, with your Victory Day speech simply making the decision official?
I left the door open a little. I said that a small miracle would have to happen for me to agree to run again. In the spring, political parties also started coming to see me and suggesting that I continue. So I gave it one more thought.
You have to announce that you're not running at the right time: You can't say it too early, but you can't say it too late either because the new president needs enough time to prepare for the job. Announcing it too early can also cause problems. I think Tony Blair said about a year in advance that he would no longer be party leader and after that nobody talked to him anymore. Everyone started looking around him to see where the new jobs would be.
So the miracle didn't happen?
I wouldn't want to make too much of that miracle; it was more of a metaphor. But I really did reconsider one more time before announcing my final decision in an understated way at the parade.
There's an old saying: lose an illusion, gain an experience. What illusions have been shattered for you over these five years and what have you personally learned from the experience?
I'll pick up on the word "experience." The biggest thing — I wouldn't call it a disappointment — was discovering that experience isn't really needed much in this job. You can share it with people who aren't directly involved in politics or who don't affect your day-to-day life as president. But generally, everyone has their own ideas and perhaps someday it will be possible to talk about how much that experience was put to use and how much it wasn't.
Why, then, is nobody interested in what a person has been through in life and the experience they have accumulated? Is everyone playing their own tune?
Everyone is in their own bubble with their own ideas and everyone wants to put those ideas forward. In my view, the biggest problem today is that no one has time to think and, unfortunately, no time to listen either. Put those two things together and no one knows what to do with experience.
Who's taking that time away from us? Weren't you able to set aside Mondays or Tuesdays when the president could read in his office without being disturbed?
I was, but then someone walks through the door and says, "I see you've got a gap in your calendar today." Everyone makes the case that their issue is important and in fact it is important — the president doesn't really deal with trivial matters. But there are so many of them and I have to say that I wasn't always able to create those gaps for myself.
I stole a few days here and there, for example in the summer when everything is quiet. But as for the president having a week or two of vacation, the Estonian president doesn't get that, although our neighbors do.
It seems to me that this came as a surprise to you: It's a job where you get into the carriage and it just keeps hurtling along with no other option. A university rector, at least, has somewhere he can reflect on things, gaze at the stars and listen to his heart.
A rector is still the master of his own time. He makes his own decisions, takes responsibility for them and knows what he's going to say and where. A president doesn't have that freedom. He serves the country in the most literal sense and has to do what the president of Estonia does. That's inherent in the office. Whether getting into a carriage is the right metaphor is another question, but you certainly have to keep moving all the time.
Despite having no time and everyone waiting at your door, Toomas Mattson undertook the task of compiling your writings from quite a long period into a major volume for the "History of Estonian Thought" series. It's a very substantial book, perhaps the largest ever published in the series.
Among Estonia's presidents, only Lennart Meri has previously been represented in the series, with several volumes of his speeches and his political testament. Now you're in it as well. When you looked through the series during your spare moments at Kadriorg, did you ever wonder why it doesn't include the statesmen and politicians who have been given a mandate by the people to exercise public authority?
I did. I have a bookshelf in the Blue Room. It doesn't contain every volume, but there's a very long row of them. I look them over from time to time and there are historical figures from the Estonian state represented there. I wasn't particularly keen on doing this myself because it's a very serious series and the thickness of a book alone isn't enough to warrant inclusion. Since people thought I should be included, I agreed, but I said I wouldn't interfere: Go ahead and do it and make the selections yourselves. Even in 1,000 pages, it doesn't contain everything I've ever written or said. It's a selection.
More volumes can always be added. Historically speaking, the series does indeed include a lot of people, but I'm thinking about the present day — the people who are active now and determining the country's future. We don't see them publishing books or thinking about these issues on a somewhat higher intellectual level.
Siim Kallas just had a book published in the same series, so perhaps we'll start seeing more now. Maybe I wasn't self-critical enough — although I'm relatively self-critical — to say that I don't belong in this series yet. Let someone compile a volume after I've passed into eternity. But this is how it turned out. The book has been done a little differently. We live in the age of artificial intelligence, so AI-generated summaries have also been included. It's simply a sign of the times. Since Toomas Mattson wanted to do it this way, I gave him free rein.
Your colleague Alexander Stubb in Finland published a very substantial book-length essay at the beginning of the year. Its title could perhaps be translated into Estonian as "The Triangle of Power" or "The New World Balance." What I have in mind is that an active politician is also participating in intellectual debate and contributing new ideas. What would we need to reach that level here as well?
That brings us back to the fact that before Stubb became president, he had time. He made the time to write and put his thoughts down on paper, producing material that could be published as books. He gave me an autographed copy of his book, with a rather large inscription and I leafed through it. It contains many interesting ideas that, as an active politician and president, he might not express quite so openly and boldly. In that sense, it's an interesting book to read.
Was this cleared with Hando Runnel — publishing AI-generated material in the "History of Estonian Thought" series? There's actually quite a substantial amount of AI-generated text in it. What did the poet say?
The poet didn't say anything to me, but I assume he gave his approval. You can always debate whether an AI-generated summary needed to be included after every article; perhaps one at the end would have been enough. But as I said, I gave the editor free rein, so I assume he obtained the necessary approvals.
Have you ever derived any profound literary or intellectual pleasure from an AI-generated text — thinking, "Now that was a good piece of writing"?
In a negative sense, yes. You look at it and see just how ridiculous a text can be. I used AI myself a couple of years ago for a speech marking the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' anniversary: I had AI write the first part and watched to see how the audience reacted. During speeches, people usually just sit and listen, but then I told them that part had been written by AI and that now my own text would begin. Everyone is experimenting with it, including with music. This is a period of experimentation when everyone is trying to figure out what the downsides are and how it can be put to positive use.
What's your overall sense of it? Have your five years in office also been characterized, in some sense, by the explosive emergence of AI? It's everywhere now. You've always been optimistic about progress — new opportunities in science and technology, grabbing the bull by the horns and forging ahead. Are you still an optimist?
I am. We know from history that the Luddites, the machine breakers, didn't get very far. I've had a similar experience in my own fields of developmental biology and molecular genetics. In the 1970s and 1980s, the fear was so great that scientists even gathered in California and asked: What are we doing? We're capable of playing God — where will all this lead? Scientists and politicians then came together, regulations and laws were introduced and ethical issues were examined because technology makes far more possible than what is actually put into practice. Technologies generally have limits; they don't develop endlessly.
What's frightening today is that everyone has this new technology in their pocket. It's precisely the speed of it that creates a certain amount of anxiety.
In your 2025 Independence Day speech, you called for a major leap forward in education: bringing AI into schools and having all students and teachers experiment with it. That has nevertheless drawn considerable criticism. It hasn't all gone smoothly and there are many questions surrounding it. Does AI actually help anyone learn or become more knowledgeable or does it end up doing the work itself and put an end to learning?
I believe there are many different sides to it when it comes to teaching children and training teachers as well. But what can we do? We can ignore it, we can switch it off or we can try to find as many positive uses for the technology as possible because it isn't going anywhere. There may be a stock market crash in the business world, but the technology itself will remain. We have to determine what it can do and — most importantly — where it doesn't need to be used. AI doesn't have to be used in schools either.
Is there anywhere it shouldn't be used? Is there anything you would consider off-limits? There's been discussion here that AI thinks better, solves math problems better and will build our houses for us — and in the end, it'll be a better lawyer too.
In some ways, perhaps the fine arts. But we know from history that electronic music has been made before as well. We're seeing the strongest backlash from people in creative fields because they see soulless music, soulless poetry and soulless works of art being produced. Today, even speeches are being written using AI.
But a presidential speech is still the real thing?
It's still the real thing. AI hasn't been used in them. Even if you do use it, you still have to go over the result using your own brain. It's very difficult to say because everything is developing so quickly. A year earlier, I had already said in a presidential speech: Look at what's in your pocket and learn how to use it. There wasn't much reaction at the time, so I had to get more hands-on myself and get something started.
You were recently in New York and gave a speech at the U.N. I understand that you also briefly crossed paths there with Jaan Tallinn who has prominently warned us about the risks and dangers, including fears that the world could soon come to an end. Did you ask Mr. Tallinn what he's afraid of?
Everyone has fears, Jaan Tallinn especially, because he has been involved in this himself and knows how it works. But as with genetic engineering, those fears may not come to pass. I spoke about AI at several events and this particular one brought together some of the more pessimistic voices. I tried to bring some positive light into the room. That's how it is: There are views on both sides and eventually we'll find a middle ground where AI is used sensibly. And as I said, it doesn't always have to be used.
I could talk at length about my past laboratory work where expensive machines were purchased and people tried to run scientific hypotheses through a particular machine. A great deal depends on the teacher, just as it did before AI and just as it does in the age of AI. That's why we started with teachers: to give them an understanding of what AI is today.
We all value our teachers and the work they do is extremely important. As president, your primary tool is your voice; the president's office doesn't have a large budget. But teachers have faced serious financial difficulties and they've made those concerns very clear over the past five years.
Looking at it from the outside, it's difficult to understand how, on the one hand, there isn't a cent to spare, while on the other, tens of millions go somewhere and nobody quite understands where the money went. How do those proportions look from Kadriorg? There's never enough money for teachers, cultural workers and others, while somewhere else the amount of money being spent just keeps growing.
With large sums of money, there are often strings attached: The money can only be used for the purpose for which it was allocated. What often happens is that the goal becomes spending the money no matter what and the result is that it isn't spent very wisely.
When it comes to teachers, I may be somewhat biased because my daughter is a teacher and I hear about their concerns. Salary is understandably important, but I see the real problems as lying elsewhere. The workload is enormous, especially for a young teacher and it isn't just about preparing lessons. There are also parents whose expectations for their children are extremely high and all of that gets channeled through the teacher. I think workload is the primary issue and should be addressed first and then salaries need to be reviewed. In reality, salaries are never quite enough because our desires and aspirations grow even when our salaries aren't particularly low.
Thinking about teachers and your idea of a "wise nation," which you've championed from the very beginning, you've said that you know only one path forward in life and that's the path of education. On the other hand, in your last major speech you said that, from the outside, Estonians may appear energetic and capable and the country may seem to be functioning well, but our souls are cold and there is a great deal of hidden loneliness and isolation. People don't feel included in society. Leaving the numbers aside, where does this profound sense of loneliness come from?
There is a sense of being left behind in Estonia, but not only in Estonia; it's the same in other countries. Perhaps it comes from the fact that somewhere we have people making decisions about the country who march to their own beat and forget that our people are out there and that our people aren't all alike. It's biodiversity — people are very different. If you move forward only with those who are at the forefront, who think ahead and love technology, then they'll do well in life. But there are people who aren't doing well, not because they can't be bothered to do anything, but because they've been caught in life's gears. We see this regionally as well. There's always someone who will pick them up and start influencing them, including through social media.
Focusing on just one segment of society isn't always the best approach, although I see politicians saying that of course they're engaging with everyone, going here, there and everywhere. Unfortunately, this indicator has continued to decline.
Perhaps this is the president's role: When it comes to foreign policy and standing up for Estonia, we aren't alone. We have many friendly countries and their presidents who do a great deal for us. But domestic issues in Estonia are something only the Estonian president deals with and I've tried to hold the pieces together as much as possible so that it doesn't all fall apart.
What gives us inner strength and restores us? Do you have your own prescription for coping with the sadness that can sometimes overcome us, especially now, with fall approaching?
November is probably the bleakest month when it's dark and there isn't any snow yet. But I think people actually tend to have these problems in the spring when everything is beautiful but they may not feel like doing anything. Everyone should find something to do. Sometimes our relationship with time seems paradoxical: A person feels lonely, yet has no time. The worst thing is to feel lonely among other people. But being on your own, taking that time and thinking — I find that restorative. Or reading a book and putting on some music. That certainly lifts my spirits.
Although I do let things affect me and take them to heart. I don't show it, but sometimes even the smallest thing can bring a tear to my eye.
Here's another trend from these five years: Thousands of children who might otherwise have been born haven't been, the numbers keep falling and people are sounding the alarm. The trend remains negative and we know this is a broader phenomenon. But looking specifically at Estonia, what do you think is the best explanation for why this is happening?
People have tried to explain it in all sorts of ways, but I don't have a particularly good answer either. Estonians might take some comfort from the fact that things are even worse in Latvia, but the problem is actually serious: The population keeps shrinking. It's easy for me to talk — I have three children and six grandchildren — but you can't force anyone to have children. The desire has to come from within and the broader environment should encourage that inner desire. One thing I definitely don't want to do is blame everything on the war in Ukraine. It's a combination of many things: anxiety about the future and perhaps the future of AI affects some people as well. These kinds of troubling factors always tend to coincide.
Another reason is that we want to live well at last. We want a life free of worries where we don't have to worry about what will happen to our child or whether they'll get into the right school or kindergarten. Perhaps it's easier to get a cat and a dog and then life is a little less stressful. This is a feature of an affluent society and it's a general problem in the Western world: We want to live better and better and we don't want to worry anymore. We're even talking now about how students shouldn't have to work all that hard at school. But learning requires effort and you have to make that effort because at some point you encounter real life and the rules there are entirely different. You have to be prepared for that.
You're a grandfather several times over yourself and your youngest grandchild was born just this spring. It's important for parents to have a support network — someone they can call and someone who will come and look after the baby. As grandparents, have you and your wife had a chance to bounce the little one on your knee? Have you had time to babysit so the parents can go to a concert or spend a little time reading?
There will probably be more time for that now because both my children and my grandchildren have largely grown up relatively independently. In one sense, that's good for children: They enter the world early and have to learn to manage on their own. Their mother and father have always had a lot of work. But this spring, my daughter — the same one who's a teacher — had a baby who turned seven months old yesterday. We've been to see them and perhaps now we'll have more time to worry as well.
As you get older, you start worrying more about your children and grandchildren. Life experience teaches you everything that can go wrong: When you're watching a small child, you notice a sharp corner over there, something else over here. It wears you out and you don't quite know how to play with them in the same way. I had my children when I was young and back then there wasn't time to think about those kinds of fears.
Let me return to the subject of books. I don't know whether you even managed to visit the National Library of Estonia as president. I think its doors had only been open for a matter of months when you took office and they've been closed (for renovation — ed.) ever since. I mean as a user. Aren't you the first president since Estonia regained independence who hasn't been able to set foot in it?
I've been there several times. The building isn't completely finished yet, but events are being held there. I've been given several tours and the archives are there as well. It's an impressive building. When I used to go there in the past, it somehow felt depressing and dark; even the ceiling was dark. Now everything is white and bright and the atmosphere is completely different.
It was supposed to reopen several years ago, so we should all be using it by now. I remember asking you five years ago whether we would celebrate the Estonian National Symphony Orchestra's centenary in a new concert hall. The Tallinn-Tartu rail project is dragging on just as it was five years ago. When you put all of that together, doesn't it seem to you that things have ground to a halt? Everything gets started and then it drags on and gets bogged down, the doors stay closed and people have to go somewhere else.
The comforting thing is that it's like this everywhere. Look at the Sydney Opera House: That project dragged on, too, ended up costing several times more than planned and the architect, who actually designed a magnificent building, even fell out of favor. Now we look at it as a great wonder. That's how these things go. As for the railway, I said back in 2016 that it wouldn't be completed on schedule, that it would end up costing several times more and that we should think about where the money would come from. Now 10 years have passed. I'm not trying to play oracle; you only have to look around to see that things aren't moving. We tend to argue over many things, we can't agree on anything and eventually people get tired and projects are put on hold. That's especially true of the concert hall, the opera house and the library as well.
I believe the library will eventually open and all the books will be brought together there nicely. I'm the kind of person who buys a book if I want it. I'm not much of a library person. I have sometimes used online libraries for specialist literature, but if I really want to read something, I want to have it on my shelf at home.
That's a privilege you have; not everyone can afford that. Books, incidentally, are becoming increasingly expensive. Even the book I have here now is from the library because its retail price is fairly steep. That's not to say it isn't worth paying for.
I certainly don't want to come across as being against libraries — quite the opposite. I've visited many small communities that have small libraries. They're wonderful places and people don't just read books there; they discuss books and do all sorts of other things. They're extremely important institutions.
Speaking about the Estonian National Symphony Orchestra five years ago, you said something along the lines of, "I'll try to make the case for that hall as well." Nothing has come of it and apparently nothing will for some time yet. More broadly, over these five years we've moved toward a world of power politics; it's been a time of war. It feels as though noble ideals and faith in the power of words get pushed aside when the strongmen arrive and start carving up the world. What's your own sense of it? How much can words actually accomplish in today's world when, generally speaking, power seems to be what counts?
I believe power has always mattered. Perhaps it simply wasn't as visible before as it is today. It's inevitable that the big countries lead the world, even though most of the world's countries are smaller states. The question is how that power is exercised. This isn't the best of times. It's more of a confused period in which the old world order no longer really applies and a new one hasn't yet been devised. That means countries the size of Estonia have to be extremely vigilant. But that doesn't mean you always have to speak loudly and forcefully everywhere. Diplomacy can also be conducted differently and sometimes more effectively than going on CNN every other week and repeating the same message. We have to combine all the options available to us.
As I understand it, you've even turned down some CNN interviews recently, believing or proceeding on the assumption that your words wouldn't carry much weight anyway?
No, I didn't say that my words don't carry weight. It probably comes from my scientific background: I want to say something new each time rather than repeat what's already been said. Although I know that in politics, constant repetition is itself a source of power.
But I'm not alone. In foreign policy, the balance of responsibility actually lies with the prime minister. The prime minister attends NATO meetings and European Council meetings, especially now, since the war in Ukraine began. So I've tried to find another kind of policy, another way of making Estonia bigger.
That alternative policy remained somewhat mysterious to the public. It was never entirely clear what it was supposed to mean. Is there something about your presidency that still weighs on you — that you tried, as president, to establish yourself and find your place on the foreign policy stage, but that effort ultimately failed?
I don't believe anything failed. This is where education comes into play again: You can say the same thing in very different words. The music is the same, the melody is the same, only the lyrics are different. I never got the sense that this was understood. But I wouldn't call it a failure. What I did — taking people from the cultural sector out into the wider world together with businesspeople, for example — created an entirely new way of thinking. They met abroad and wondered why they hadn't met more often back in Estonia because bringing them together generates so many good ideas.
This kind of soft diplomacy has somehow been pushed into the background, even though, to be fair, its impact can sometimes be considerably greater.
So during those visits, you were able to make connections behind the scenes and advance Estonia's interests in ways the public perhaps never fully saw?
The public does see it, but the public isn't particularly interested. When the president travels to other countries with people from the cultural and business sectors, opens doors for them or helps open those doors — something they're all grateful for afterward — it doesn't make headlines. Journalists aren't interested because there's no conflict and you have to accept that. It wouldn't be difficult to go abroad and start squabbling in public — with our prime minister and foreign minister, for example — but then you have to ask what that would mean for Estonia. There are plenty of countries where the prime minister and president don't get along in public.
Instead, we should look at countries whose systems are structured similarly to ours, such as Germany and many others. Nobody would say that Steinmeier, who has served twice as foreign minister, knows nothing about foreign policy, yet he conducts himself in a way relatively similar to the president of Estonia.
These five years also saw the unveiling of a monument to Konstantin Päts behind the Estonia Theater where you also gave a speech. The 150th anniversary of Päts' birth also fell during this period, but you didn't attend the Bank of Estonia's major event commemorating Päts. Peep Jahilo, then head of the Office of the President, attended to represent you.
I won't go into what kind of figure Päts was, but how much have you thought about Päts and Tõnisson and all those other names who were here in Estonia on the eve of World War II? When the war in Ukraine began — and it did come as a major shock — how much did you think about what could actually happen and have you ever felt fear in your heart during this period?
Not fear as such, but understandably, as head of state, you find yourself thinking about these things and looking at the parallels with the past and with the war in Ukraine today. We cannot afford a war like the one in Ukraine. I've often said: Take a pair of scissors, cut out the areas that are currently under Russian control and place them over a map of Estonia. Then you'll see that we cannot fight a war like that because Estonia would simply cease to exist. So we have to be a little more clever and think about how to prevent such a war.
As for Päts' era, my mother was born during Päts' time and there was plenty of talk about Päts at home, including idealized stories. But every president belongs to his own time and Päts belonged to his, with his own flaws and virtues. He was the president of our country. You can't simply ignore him, but nor can you accuse him of selling Estonia to Soviet Russia. These things aren't that simple.
Estonia's presidents have maintained a certain distance from Päts. I'm thinking again of that major ceremonial event at the Bank of Estonia: Was it preferable to send the head of the president's office rather than attend yourself?
I wouldn't say that's how it was. I only just read in the newspaper that I had avoided attending the opening of a factory. These things aren't that simple. It's easy to write a headline, but there are other obligations that require you to be somewhere else and do other things. I haven't avoided anything. I'm not afraid of uncomfortable meetings or events and an event at the central bank isn't an uncomfortable event.
That brings us briefly back to foreign policy. In foreign affairs, we like engaging with like-minded countries. It's pleasant company; we all think alike. But in my view, we need to pay more attention to those with whom we have some disagreements as well. Things may look different from their perspective, but we need to listen and then explain how we see the world.
In the spring, you said we'd heated the sauna too hot. Now that you're about to hand over the presidency, how would you assess the situation? Has the temperature in the sauna come down or are all our backs still red?
It's more like a smoke sauna: You keep heating it for quite a while and it stays warm for a long time too. But I think things will heat up again when we have the Riigikogu election in spring 2027. I've called for civility, although I know civility isn't much of a match for aggressive politics. But if you're taught at home to be polite, that should stay with you.
What comes next for you? Looking at Estonia's recent presidents, they've all sought, in one way or another, some kind of international role, without much success. Will you head to the Piusa River, reflect on your experiences by the Härma sandstone outcrop and write your memoirs? Or might there still be someone interested in all the experience you've now accumulated?
I think there will be. I also need time to sit and think and that's precisely what I've been missing in this job. I'll certainly make use of that time, but my calendar is already filling up. This summer, I joined the U.N.'s "AI for Good" commission, which brings together all the giants who are concerned about the future right now, whether Microsoft, OpenAI, Google and so on. I'll try to bring to it the experience we're gaining here from our AI Leap initiative and, in turn, bring international experience back here. Technology and innovation in general continue to interest me, as does their intersection with politics.
I'm fairly convinced that as a former president, I may actually have better opportunities to serve Estonia than I do now as president.
Your painted portrait will also be unveiled at the presidential palace this week. This isn't the first time you've had this kind of official portrait painted; you've long had one at the University of Tartu from your time as rector. You won't be staying to look at this portrait — the people who come after you will. In what situations might they look at it and what advice might your portrait offer them?
I haven't seen the portrait myself yet. Just as I didn't interfere with the book, I didn't interfere with the portrait either. I don't like interfering with the work of professionals: They do their job and ultimately it's their name on it. This is the third painting of me and they're probably all very different. I expect this one will be different as well. Since all of this is, so to speak, for after I'm gone and I'll probably visit Kadriorg very rarely in the future, I imagine some tour groups will look at it. The portraits of the presidents at Kadriorg are also very different from one another.
We're coming to the end of our conversation and you'll soon be able to get on with your week, but we still have Alar Karis' cultural recommendation to hear.
That's always the hardest question: what book to recommend or what work to suggest listening to. I've always said that you should try to seek out variety, especially in today's world where so much of what we read and listen to is presented to us. Don't assume that because you've finished one book, you should pick up another one just like it. Find opportunities to read very different things. The same applies to music. It will be better for us and for our peace of mind and we'll gain a better sense of the world around us.
We should listen to young people who are only just beginning their cultural journeys as artists, composers or performers. We've seen the caliber of artists Estonia has produced; some have already become internationally renowned.
--
