The FBI tracked US First Lady Melania Trump and her son Barron as part of preparations for the 2022 search of President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate, and later monitored the phone activity of Susie Wiles, now the White House chief of staff, for months, according to documents released by the White House transparency team early Tuesday.
According to the documents, the surveillance of members of the Trump family was intended, among other things, to help the bureau determine the right time the search the former president's Palm Beach estate as part of the investigation into classified documents he retained after leaving office following his first term. The investigation carried the code name "Plasmic Echo."
Correspondence between FBI agents from late May 2022 listed among the tasks ahead of the search a requirement to complete a picture of the travel plans of Trump, his wife and his minor son, including the type of aircraft they used and their precise schedules.
Another document explicitly stated that search warrants would be executed only after the former president had left Mar-a-Lago. The FBI ultimately carried out the search on August 8, 2022. As part of the operation, agents searched Trump's office as well as the couple's bedrooms.
According to the released documents, then-Attorney General Merrick Garland approved the investigative steps after a recommendation from then-FBI Director Christopher Wray.
Wray warned Trump investigation could affect democratic process before election
In a May 2022 memorandum, Wray warned that the investigation was sensitive and could involve senior officials from Trump's first administration, and that if it became public before an election it "could be disruptive to the democratic process."
At the bottom of the memorandum, Wray wrote to Garland by hand: "Merrick, I recommend you approve. CW."
One month before the search, an unidentified special agent raised doubts about the FBI's legal authority to search the office and bedroom of a former president and even suggested holding additional discussions with Trump's attorneys.
Wiles surveillance included calls with Trump, lawyers, advisers and journalists
The documents also reveal that between February and May 2023, FBI personnel monitored the call records of Wiles, who at the time was running Trump's political operation ahead of the 2024 election.
According to the records, the FBI tracked her calls with nearly two dozen attorneys connected to Trump, as well as campaign staffers, political advisers and journalists.
The identities in the documents were almost entirely redacted, with the exception of Kash Patel, who now serves as FBI director and at the time held no government position.
The records also include calls between Wiles and Trump himself. One entry dated May 19, 2023, states that a phone number identified as the "FPOTUS Vanity Number," belonging to the former president, called Wiles at 2:05 p.m. The call lasted 16 minutes and 11 seconds.
On one day in March 2023, the documents show Wiles made or received 39 calls. The records include precise call times and the duration of each call.
Another internal email noted that an ABC News reporter called Wiles for a two-minute, 36-second conversation. Other records also listed calls with reporters from The Washington Post and Politico.
After FBI agents questioned Wiles in Florida in April 2023, investigators also examined her phone activity before and after the interview.
Special counsel Jack Smith probe focused on possible obstruction, classified documents
At the time, special counsel Jack Smith was already focusing on suspicions of obstruction of the investigation and on whether Trump had wrongly claimed that all classified documents had been returned to the National Archives.
A federal judge dismissed the case against Trump in July 2024, ruling that Garland's appointment of Smith was unlawful.
The White House sharply criticized the investigative actions. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bies told the New York Post that "Jack Smith's surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power," adding that "Spying on political opponents is the politicization of law enforcement. Those responsible must be held accountable."

Jerusalem unveils unity mural honoring Hersh Goldberg-Polin and Ori Danino at Teddy Stadium

15:30:29 KST

The Jerusalem Municipality dedicated a new “unity” mural at Teddy Stadium on Monday honoring Hersh Goldberg-Polin and Ori Danino, two Jerusalem residents and supporters of rival football clubs who became close friends during 328 days in Hamas captivity.
The mural, created by Jerusalem-born artist Tomer Peretz, depicts Goldberg-Polin and Danino together at a packed Teddy Stadium, a place both had known since childhood. Danino was a devoted Beitar Jerusalem supporter, while Goldberg-Polin supported Hapoel Jerusalem.
Their backgrounds also reflected different parts of the city. Danino grew up in a Haredi family in Jerusalem’s Ramot neighborhood, while Goldberg-Polin was raised in an Anglo religious family in Talpiot.
Rival football fans became close friends in Hamas captivity
Both were abducted separately during Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack and were ultimately held together in Gaza. According to testimony from hostages who later returned, the two developed an exceptionally close relationship during their 328 days in captivity, caring for and sustaining one another under extreme conditions.
In the days following the attack, when Goldberg-Polin was severely wounded after his left arm was blown off, Danino reportedly argued with their captors and pushed them to provide him with medical treatment, which helped save his life at the time.
Their friendship has since become a symbol of unity in Jerusalem, particularly given their loyalty to rival football clubs whose fan bases can represent very different parts of the city.
The municipality said the mural seeks to reflect the idea that people with different backgrounds, identities and worldviews can still stand together.
Rachel Goldberg-Polin honors the bond between the two
“In our beautiful, complex, diverse, beloved, frustrating, dynamic and holy city, we have two teams that can seem completely different,” Rachel Goldberg-Polin, Hersh’s mother, said at the dedication.
“And then there were two boys, brought together in fire,” she said. “They became symbols of love for the fans of each team, and they ended up bound together – protecting, defending, advocating and breathing for each other.”
“At the end of the day, all there is, is love. Two hearts. One city. Jerusalem. Together.”
Teddy Stadium mural offers a permanent tribute
The artwork imagines an ending they were denied: Goldberg-Polin and Danino alive and laughing together in Teddy Stadium, surrounded by the teams, supporters and city they loved.
The municipality said the mural is intended to remain at the stadium as a permanent symbol of hope and brotherhood, and as a reminder that Jerusalemites with different opinions, identities and loyalties can still find common ground.
For Danino and Goldberg-Polin, even football rivalry became part of that story: “Only Beitar” and “Only Hapoel,” the municipality said, ultimately gave way to something they shared.
“Two fans. Two teams. One city. Jerusalem.”

US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dead at 86
Unknown

US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dead at 86
American televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, fraud conviction for bilking followers and divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Oct 5 at age 86.
The death of Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media by his second wife, Lori Bakker.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband’s latest television ministry.
She paid tribute to Bakker as a “pioneer of Christian television”, but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.
Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of US President Donald Trump, who was known for his own brand of right-wing populism.
Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on US television in the 1980s, achieving fame on the show The PTL Club. PTL stood for “Praise The Lord” and “People That Love”.
Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should have stood for “pass the loot”.
Bakker spent 4½ years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.
Prosecutors painted him as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power.
“Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests,” Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing him.
Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent US$265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 930-hectare Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers on 200 TV stations and raked in US$129 million a year.
With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk.
He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was larded with requests for money donations.
Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy make-up smeared on her face.
‘I have sinned’
Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on all 24 fraud and conspiracy charges brought against him.
Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of US$158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide.
They said he siphoned US$3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house.
The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. 
“I have sinned,” Bakker told the court. “I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone.”
Bakker’s chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.
Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the “prosperity gospel” he once preached and writing a book titled I Was Wrong.
“I’ve had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me,” Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, whom he married in 1998.
They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping The Jim Bakker Show at a 240-hectare development called Morningside near the tourism city of Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities to Heritage USA.
Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.
In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for Covid-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic.
Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first US president to be impeached twice.
James Orson Bakker was born on Jan 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who maintained a strict fundamentalist Christian household.
He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostalist Assemblies of God denomination.
Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children’s religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network.
Setting out on his own in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire. REUTERS

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,544,260 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022

Russia has lost around 1,544,260 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 6.
The number includes 1,540 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,396 tanks, 25,494 armored combat vehicles, 158,551 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,785 artillery systems, 2,184 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,688 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,866 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Joana Vasconcelos blends art and haute couture in exhibition for Valentino Garavani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:24:49 UTC
15:24:49 KST

Lisbon is hosting an exhibition where works by sculptor Joana Vasconcelos converse with dresses by a renowned Italian designer, fusing domestic life and haute couture.
MAAT – the Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology in Lisbon – is hosting until 22 February the exhibition "VENUS – Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelos" (source in Portuguese), inspired by the world of the renowned Italian fashion designer.
The project stems from a partnership between the Valentino Garavani and Giancarlo Giammetti Foundation – Giammetti being the designer's life and business partner – and Portuguese sculptor and artist Joana Vasconcelos, who has devised a visitor journey in which her own work enters into dialogue with the pieces created over the years by the designer.
"I wanted to show the diversity and the wonder of Valentino's work, the way he worked with embroidery, all the fabrics he used, completely different from one another. But also how, from these materials, he created this idyllic woman, this goddess-like woman," the Portuguese artist told Euronews, recalling how the designer "transformed, through his dresses, women's identities".
Drawing on the designer's archive, to which Joana Vasconcelos had access in order to shape this exhibition, the sculptor revealed that she had sought "to choose dresses that weren't the cliché of 'Valentino Red'", a colour strongly associated with the ideals of power, passion and sensuality. Even so, the show includes a particularly emblematic example of what has become one of the Italian creator's trademarks.
At the press presentation of "VENUS – Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelos", the Portuguese artist explained to Euronews that it was from this "idea of luxury" that Valkyrie Venus emerged, a textile sculpture that occupies the central place in the entire show.
"And it was from this work that the exhibition was born, in which we play on the paradox between the domestic and luxury. The woman at home, the woman in intimacy, the woman who is not seen; and the woman in public space, the woman who becomes a goddess because she wears a Valentino dress," Joana Vasconcelos explained. The Valkyrie Venus itself incorporates the "textures" and colours of the garments chosen as the source of inspiration for its creation.
It was with this apparently contradictory relationship "between the private and the public" in mind that the sculptor has designed, within MAAT's spaces, a route where visitors can see some of her most emblematic works, as well as new creations, in symbiosis with garments bearing the signature of the acclaimed Italian fashion designer.
Speaking about the whole process of selecting the dresses to be included in the exhibition and their interconnection with her own sculptures, Joana Vasconcelos confided to Euronews that "it was not a challenge", but rather something "very dynamic and fun". One example is the "Ironing Room", as she calls it, for which she chose "dresses that cannot be ironed", displayed flanking an artistic composition in which that household appliance is the main protagonist.
"So it was this strange way of life that led me to create this exhibition," a true "game between dresses that are worn only on certain occasions of perfection and luxury" and life "in the domestic sphere, which does not include that kind of elements". This second dimension appears throughout the route through the "presence of feather dusters, pots and cutlery", among other utensils that are highly characteristic of life at home.
The show at MAAT is an adapted version of a project originally on display in the Italian city of Rome, more specifically at PM23, the cultural space founded by Valentino and Giancarlo Giammetti, where it ran until 19 July 2026.
"VENUS – Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelos" (source in Portuguese), which aims to be a meeting point between art and haute couture, is being held as part of the celebrations marking MAAT's 10th anniversary, at a time when the museum itself is also hosting three other new exhibitions.

Pacific leaders watch Tuvalu reclamation effort ahead of UN climate meet
FUNAFUTI, Tuvalu – Representatives of 30 nations watched on Oct 6 as white sand dredged from an atoll lagoon was used to reclaim land from the ocean in a fight by the tiny Pacific nation of Tuvalu to keep its main island from being lost to rising waves.
A group of coral island clusters with about 10,000 inhabitants whose land is on average just 2m above sea level, Tuvalu is one of the nations most vulnerable to climate change.
“You are standing on front-line soil,” Foreign Minister Paulson Panapa told the leaders gathered ahead of pre-COP, a preparatory conference for the United Nations COP31 climate forum in Turkey in November.
“Promises will not hold back rising tides... what this moment requires is decisive delivery.”
The reclamation effort on Oct 6, spread over 6ha, is part of work costing about US$50 million (S$64 million) of donor funds that also built sea walls and barriers to protect land.
“We are sinking,” said Faiva Namoliki, a 39-year-old architect huddled in a sodden jacket in pouring rain outside the event.
“Here they see the reality,” he said of the visitors. “We hope they will carry the message away with them, and it will make a difference.”
Rising sea levels
Sea levels around Tuvalu have risen about 15cm in the three decades to 2023, say NASA researchers, or twice as fast as the global average.
“Small amounts of sea level rise make a very big difference in making flood events bigger and more damaging,” Jamie Ovia, the head of Tuvalu’s climate change department, told the leaders.
“If we add just 30cm of sea level rise – expected by 2050 – this supercharges the flooding and makes it drastically bigger than floods we would have seen every 100 years in the past.”
Such inundations would be economically crippling, he added.
Pre-COP events are typically technocratic meetings of climate negotiators, but Australia, which is leading the talks in 2026, aims with its Pacific partners to highlight the issue of rising sea levels through the Tuvalu gathering.
It also seeks to bolster ties in the region and counter growing Chinese influence.
But attendance fell short, with 11 of the Australian government’s tally of 14 attending presidents and prime ministers hailing from Pacific islands. The rest came from Australia, Mauritius and East Timor.
Dignitaries arrived amid heavy rain to be handed umbrellas as they descended from aircraft in matching bright blue patterned shirts, before a traditional song performance by dancers, drummers and singers with flower headbands.
Significant additions to land mass
The project highlighted on Oct 6 is the third in a series that will soon have added about 21ha to Tuvalu’s main island, project manager Alan Resture told the visitors.
The additions are significant in a nation with a total land mass of around 26 sq km, about twice the size of a large airport.
Pacific nations have been at the forefront of efforts to limit global warming to 1.5 deg C to avoid its worst effects – a threshold the world is set to exceed in the coming years.
“Every fraction of a degree matters,” Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the visiting leaders.
Australia is bankrolling pre-COP, but has drawn fire as a major exporter of coal and gas that continues to approve fossil fuel projects.
“Here in Tuvalu, we are seeing what action can look like,” said Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. “It’s about people.” REUTERS

The EU is considering tightening restrictions on Russian diplomats amid escalating hybrid threats - media

Unknown Publisher

The EU is considering tightening restrictions on Russian diplomats amid escalating hybrid threats - media
Kyiv • UNN
The EU is discussing increased scrutiny of Russian diplomats due to hybrid attacks. So far, only two countries have introduced a strict transit permit requirement.
A recent wave of hybrid attacks across Europe has raised questions about the possible involvement of Russian diplomats, prompting member states to consider imposing stricter restrictions and checks. Euronews reports, UNN writes.
Details
The movements and activities of Russian diplomats have come under close scrutiny as the European Union faces a series of hybrid attacks, some of which are directly linked to Moscow and have shaken its collective security.
According to senior diplomats familiar with the course of the negotiations, the issue is being considered as a possible next step in the bloc’s sanctions regime.
As the publication notes, Brussels seeks to turn the page after the controversial exclusion of two influential oligarchs last month, which put the EU’s united front under strain. Countries are now looking for ways to unite and counter interference by the Kremlin.
Among the options under consideration is tightening restrictions and checks on Russian diplomats to counter hybrid warfare and state-organized sabotage.
Last month, Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats accused of "unacceptable" conduct under the 1961 Vienna Convention. Moscow responded with mirror measures.
Other alarming incidents, including the suspected arson attack at a defense facility in Estonia and the discovery of an unexploded drone at Leipzig Airport in Germany, both of which have been linked to Russia, have further heightened concerns.
This discussion, which is still at an early stage, is a continuation of the mechanism introduced by the EU last year as part of its 19th package of sanctions.
The system requires Russian diplomats working in the bloc’s countries to notify authorities of their intention to travel to another member state or transit through its territory outside their country of residence "no later than 24 hours" before the planned entry.
This rule applies to diplomatic and consular representatives of all ranks, including ambassadors, administrative, technical and service staff, as well as their family members.
Although this system has given European authorities more opportunities to monitor the movements of Russian diplomats, it does not restrict them in itself.
Member states may apply a stricter procedure requiring Russian diplomats to obtain permission for transit. If permission is denied, the diplomat may not cross the country concerned. However, this procedure is optional. So far, only two countries have introduced it.
As the system has been in operation only since January 2026, experience with its application remains limited
The notification system was based on the assumption that Russian diplomats are "often involved" in activities aimed at spreading pro-war narratives and manipulating public opinion. The focus is now shifting to their possible direct or indirect role in hybrid attacks.
In Brussels, the discussions will have to take into account the Vienna Convention, which grants diplomatic representatives broad rights and guarantees in their daily work. This document is considered one of the greatest achievements of international law.

Here's how Labor, the Coalition and One Nation's migration cuts compare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:22:26 UTC
15:22:26 KST

How do Labor, the Coalition and One Nation's migration cuts compare?
The Coalition's long-awaited migration plan has been revealed, completing the set of competing policies being offered by the government, the opposition and One Nation, who have risen in the polls in particular due to the party's promise to drive immigration to its lowest levels in Australia's history.
Migration rates to Australia since 2019 have been much higher than many comparable countries, with more than double the growth in population from migration compared to the United Kingdom, and three times Germany.
One Nation has vowed to cut migration to negative levels in its first years, the Coalition has promised to temporarily halve migration to 100,000, and Labor wants migration rates to return to the longer-term trend of 225,000 — but it quickly gets more complicated.
Every attempt to lower migration removes workers from some sector, risks hitting already slow economic growth, and potentially puts already in-need industries like health and aged care into deeper workforce shortages.
One Nation, the Coalition and the federal government have each sought to strike a different balance — with One Nation also explicitly stating its intentions to up-end migration to Australia as part of its policy to end multiculturalism.
What does each party want to do with migration levels?
The federal government, the Coalition and One Nation have all proposed net migration rates lower than today, though their plans differ significantly.
One Nation has promised net negative migration for the first three years, before settling to a longer-term net migration ceiling of below 130,000.
The party has vowed to cut net migration by 750,000 in its first three years in order to reach its goal of more people leaving the country than arriving, providing "breathing space" for housing construction to catch up. Spread evenly, it would amount to a net migration rate of negative 25,000 based on Treasury's migration forecasts for those years.
The Coalition has proposed to more than halve net migration for two years to 100,000, 130,000 in its third year and 160,000 in its fourth year. After that, net migration would be tied to the pace of housing completions.
Meanwhile, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has announced measures to achieve a net migration rate of 225,000 a year by 2028, though there are no further cuts proposed in the future years when One Nation and the Coalition have both promised serious reductions.
That 225,000 a year figure was already forecast in the federal budget, but actual migration to Australia has repeatedly come in higher than forecast, and the politics around net overseas migration has changed.
Once considered more of an indicator, the government itself has now acknowledged that net overseas migration figure as a hard target it is committed to reaching.
How do the parties plan to cut migration?
One Nation promises to achieve deep cuts by severely restricting international student visa places to just over 100,000 a year. That compares to about 290,000 visas granted to students last financial year.
Additionally, visas for families of international students and skilled migrants would be ended almost entirely.
There were just shy of 46,000 visas granted to family and dependents of students last financial year — all of those would have been refused except for roughly 6,500 partners and children attached to postgraduate researchers, who are exempt from the plan.
That commitment was effectively made by the federal government last month.
In relation to skilled migrants, the most recent migration trend data showed fewer than half of the visas being granted under Australia's skilled worker program were actually for the workers Australia is seeking, like nurses and builders.
Out of about 132,000 skilled worker visas issued in the 2025 financial year, 71,650 were actually granted to partners and children of those workers. That would be cut to zero under One Nation.
The rest of the party's migration cuts would be achieved by deporting visa overstayers and other unlawful non-citizens, and clearing the backlog of people on bridging visas — generally people awaiting a decision on an application, or challenging a decision to refuse or cancel a visa.
With migration playing a significant role in maintaining Australia's economy in recent years, critics warned migration cuts of that magnitude would drive the country into recession.
Senator Hanson responded that "a larger economic pie doesn't mean anything if individual Australians' slice of it is getting smaller".
The Coalition will also target international student visa places, cutting commencements down from their current planning level of 295,000 a year to 240,000, and abolishing temporary graduate visas.
More than 100,000 temporary graduate visas are issued every year, which typically allow people to live and work in Australia for up to three years after graduation depending on the qualification. That would be ended by the Coalition with some limited exceptions.
The visas are meant to keep in-demand graduates in Australia while they search for work, but the Coalition says they are instead being used as a pathway to citizenship, with some people never working in the field they graduated from.
Like One Nation, the Coalition says it will clear the caseload of more than 400,000 people on bridging visas, mainly by requiring subsequent visa applications to be made offshore (except for working holiday-makers), which it says will "virtually eliminate" bridging visas.
The permanent humanitarian visa program would also be halved from 20,000 to 10,000, with the ability to temporarily lift that amount to respond to major incidents, like the Coalition did following the civil war in Syria in 2015.
Its reductions in international students, temporary graduates and bridging visa holders would make space for more skilled workers, with construction workers to be "heavily prioritised" although net migration overall would still be at some of the lowest levels in Australia's history.
The Coalition says its plan is focused on reducing migration while improving the skills mix, rather than "simply cutting numbers without regard to the economic consequences".
The federal government has promised to end the practice of international students "visa hopping" to stay in Australia longer by requiring that students can only be granted a visa for further qualifications that are a higher level of study, such as moving from a bachelor degree to a masters.
It is also limiting family visas for international students, except those from Pacific and South-East Asian nations, as well as dependents of students studying PhDs.
But it will not do the same for families of skilled workers, as promised by One Nation, warning that doing so could make it harder for Australia to get workers already in short supply.
While One Nation and the Coalition have promised not to touch working holiday-maker visa levels, which are heavily depended on by farmers and regional communities, the federal government says it is tightening the second and third years of the scheme, reducing year-two visas by 12,000 places to 45,000, and year-three places by 31,000 places to just 5,000, with a ballot system to determine who can extend their stay.
Finally, the government is establishing a team of 100 Border Force officials to assist in the removal of the roughly 77,000 visa overstayers in the country, as well as adding more facilities to hold overstayers awaiting deportation.
What does each party want to do with who comes to Australia?
One Nation's proposal would cut the number of people coming to Australia who do not have a work-related purpose for migrating.
But the party is also campaigning on a platform of much higher standards for visa holders, with stricter punishments for those who breach visa conditions or Australia's laws.
It would toughen rules that currently require the mandatory cancellation of a visa if a person is sentenced to a prison term of more than a year to deport anyone who commits a crime at all, regardless of the length of sentence. People deported from Australia would be banned from ever returning.
A blanket visa refusal would be enacted on people from certain countries, with the party saying people from countries "known to foster extremist ideologies" would not be allowed to enter.
That list of countries would be determined using the Foreign Affairs Department's "do not travel" advice where it relates to security concerns.
The Coalition also wants to lift the standards for visa holders, including stricter adherence to an Australian values test and more enforcement to ensure people on student visas are not working beyond permitted hours.
The party would remove appeal rights for people whose visas are cancelled on character grounds, including those facing deportation due to criminal offences.
The federal government already legislated new powers to deport people inciting hate in the wake of the Bondi terror attack.
Mr Burke's address last month did not detail any further changes related to safety or national values.
But the minister did say directions to the Home Affairs department would be tweaked to add construction, agriculture, fisheries and teaching to the priority list, encouraging more workers in those sectors, after temporarily forcing a slowdown in processing of visa applications.

U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order allowing drivers to use tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, a fuel normally reserved for farm machinery and other off-road equipment, on public roads.

Diesel prices in the United States have hit record highs above $6 a gallon in recent weeks, with export restrictions imposed by major supplier Russia after Ukrainian attacks on its fuel facilities adding to pressure on global markets.

What to know about plague after suspected Siberian lab worker case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:21:00 UTC
15:21:00 KST

What to know about plague after suspected Siberian lab worker case
- A suspected pneumonic plague case in Siberia involved a laboratory worker who died of severe pneumonia; Russian authorities found no evidence of plague or lab accidents, but nearly 200 contacts are monitored.
- Plague is a serious bacterial infection with three forms; pneumonic plague spreads between people via respiratory particles and requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent death.
- The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute monitors plague and other infections in Siberia; the WHO is closely watching the situation, though the risk to the public remains low pending further information.
AI generated
SIBERIA – Plague is one of history’s most feared diseases, responsible for pandemics that killed tens of millions of people. Today, human cases are rare and can usually be treated with antibiotics.
A suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia has renewed attention on the disease after a young worker at a Russian institute that studies plague and other dangerous infections died of severe pneumonia.
The Russian authorities have not confirmed that she had plague and say tests found no micro-organisms associated with her work.
Still, the circumstances of her death and the extensive precautions taken afterward have prompted scrutiny from health authorities in the US, Europe and the World Health Organization.
What happened in Siberia?
A 28-year-old laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East died overnight between Oct 1 and Oct 2 after developing severe pneumonia.
Independent Russian media reported that she may have been exposed to the bacterium that causes plague after breaking a test tube at the institute.
That account has not been verified, and Russia’s public health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, says an investigation found no laboratory accident involving dangerous microorganisms.
It also said that extensive testing of samples from the woman found no microorganisms associated with her work.
The official cause of her illness remains pneumonia of “unknown” origin.
Almost 200 people who may have had contact with the woman have reportedly been placed under medical observation, while the hospital where she was treated was quarantined.
Other restrictions have also reportedly been imposed at medical facilities in the region.
No plague infections have been confirmed among her contacts, and the Russian authorities say the epidemiological situation is stable.
The media reports have, however, raised questions about how any possible exposure to plague could have occurred.
Work with dangerous pathogens normally involves multiple layers of protection designed to prevent a spill or broken container from exposing laboratory staff.
The WHO is monitoring the situation and says the risk to the general population appears to be low, based on the unofficial information available.
It is seeking information from Russian authorities about what happened, the laboratory tests being conducted and their results, why contacts are being traced, whether any have become ill and whether there could be any international public-health implications.
What exactly is plague?
Plague is a bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis, which normally circulates among rodents and other small mammals and the fleas that live on them.
People usually become infected after being bitten by an infected flea or through contact with an infected animal.
The bacteria can also be inhaled, and people with pneumonic plague can spread the infection to others through respiratory particles.
There are three main forms of plague, all caused by the same bacterium but primarily affecting different parts of the body.
Bubonic plague, the most common, typically causes fever, chills and painful, swollen lymph nodes known as buboes. It is the form most closely associated with the Black Death of the Middle Ages.
Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria multiply in the bloodstream. It can cause bleeding, tissue damage, organ failure and shock.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria infect the lungs. It can develop when another form of plague spreads to the lungs or when a person inhales the bacteria directly.
Symptoms can develop rapidly and include fever, weakness, chest pain, shortness of breath and coughing, sometimes with bloody sputum.
Does plague still exist today?
Yes. The bacteria persist in wild animal populations in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas, meaning plague cannot realistically be eradicated.
The WHO recorded 3,847 human cases and 423 deaths in 10 countries from 2019 through 2025. Most occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.
Cases also occur occasionally in wealthier countries.
The US typically records several infections a year, mostly in western states where the bacteria circulate naturally among wild rodents and their fleas.
How dangerous is pneumonic plague?
Antibiotics, modern sanitation and disease surveillance mean plague no longer poses anything like the threat it did centuries ago.
Still, it is very dangerous if it is not recognised and treated quickly.
Pneumonic plague is the most rapidly progressing form of the disease. Symptoms can appear within one to three days of exposure.
Without effective antibiotics, the infection can kill within about a day of severe symptoms developing.
That makes early treatment critical.
The WHO says common antibiotics are effective against Yersinia pestis and the chances of recovery are high when pneumonic plague is detected and treated promptly.
People known to have been exposed can also be given antibiotics before they become sick.
The short incubation period also means infections typically become apparent relatively quickly.
Several days after the Russian worker died, there was still no confirmation that she had plague and the authorities had reported no plague-like illness among the almost 200 contacts being monitored – easing some concerns that the disease, if present, had spread.
How easily does pneumonic plague spread?
Pneumonic plague is the only major form of plague that can spread directly between people.
An infected person can release bacteria in respiratory particles when coughing.
Transmission generally requires close exposure to somebody who is sick, particularly when the patient is coughing.
Unlike Covid-19 or influenza, plague is not known for sustained transmission through communities by people with mild or no symptoms.
People with pneumonic plague usually become severely ill within a short period, which can help health authorities identify cases and trace their contacts.
However, because the disease progresses rapidly and can spread between people, even a single suspected case requires an urgent public-health response.
When pneumonic plague is suspected, health authorities generally act before waiting for laboratory confirmation.
The WHO recommends starting appropriate antibiotics, as well as identifying and monitoring close contacts and generally giving them preventive antibiotics for seven days.
Why does Russia have an “anti-plague” institute?
Anti-plague institutes have a long history in Russia and other parts of the former Soviet Union.
Plague occurs naturally in wild rodents across parts of Central and northern Asia, including Siberia, Mongolia and northern China.
Russia has long operated a network of specialist laboratories and monitoring stations to detect plague in animals, investigate human infections and prevent outbreaks.
The Irkutsk institute was established in 1934 specifically to combat plague in Siberia and the Russian Far East.
Its responsibilities later expanded to other dangerous infections including cholera, anthrax and brucellosis, as well as other diseases that can spread from animals to people.
Today, the institute says it monitors areas where plague circulates naturally across Siberia and the Far East, conducts disease surveillance and diagnostic testing, advises regional health authorities and helps respond to outbreaks of dangerous infections.
Until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, it also operated a secret biological weapons programme that included research on Yersinia pestis.
That history has contributed to international scrutiny of the Siberian incident, although there is no public evidence linking the Irkutsk worker’s death to any biological weapons research. BLOOMBERG

Germany news: Saxony-Anhalt parliament sits after AfD win

Here is a look round at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
German Economy: Recovery faces setback as factory orders plunge
In August, orders from German factories fell faster than expected, marking the first decline in four months. Orders were down 10.6% compared to July.
According to the statistics agency Destatis, the decline in orders from large German manufacturers highlights the fragility of the recovery in Europe's largest economy.
Germany's economy has been stagnant for an extended period and has only been recovering slowly, supported by massive public spending. However, recent data have shown signs of strengthening.
The German Economy Ministry said that August's orders data represented a "significant setback." It also noted that, excluding the drop in large orders, the overall situation was virtually unchanged from July.
The August decline was driven by weaker domestic demand. Orders fell by more than 60% in the category that includes military vehicles, aircraft, ships, and trains.
Germany raises military spending
Orders in this sector have increased as Germany spends vast sums on its military to confront an increasingly hostile Russia and amid concerns about US security guarantees for Europe.
The ministry stressed that the growing importance of public procurement has made orders "highly volatile."
By comparison, new orders from June to August were 1.3% higher than in the previous three-month period.
The energy crisis stemming from the conflict in the Middle East has created additional challenges for Germany's economic recovery, but the economy has weathered the impact better than initially feared.
Experts recently doubled their growth forecast for this year to 1.3%.
IN DEPTH: Ex-spy chief August Hanning arrested for espionage — reports
August Hanning, who served as the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005, has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, according to various media sources.
DW will keep you up to date with the latest developments in the case in this article: Germany: Ex-spy chief arrested for espionage — reports
BREAKING: Police rush to Lower Saxony school after rampage alarm sounded
Police in Lower Saxony have been deployed to a high school in the town of Langwedel after being alerted to a possible rampage attack by an alarm, according various German media.
It remains unclear whether there are any casualties.
More to follow ...
German-Russian man jailed over helping Russian military
A German-Russian man has been sentenced in Latvia to seven years in prison and one year on probation after being found guilty of collecting and supplying money and goods to Russian military personnel.
The man was detained by Latvian authorities while on one of his car trips allegedly transporting the goods across the Latvian-Russian border.
The man denied supplying sanctioned goods, saying he was transporting humanitarian aid such as wheelchairs, crutches and nappies.
The Latvian news agency LETA cited the responsible court in Riga as having said he was in fact carrying goods including night-vision devices and telescopes.
Prosecutors used correspondence, photographs and videos found on the man's mobile phone to back their case against him.
The verdict against the man, who holds both German and Russian citizenship, is not yet final and can be appealed.
Wadephul warns of climate change as security risk
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has highlighted the consequences of climate change for global security as the Berlin Climate and Security Conference kicks off in the capital.
"Particularly in fragile states, climate change exacerbates poverty and hunger — and can thus also become a fertile ground for extremism and terrorism or lead to waves of migration," he said.
Wadephul also emphasized the importance of climate protection in enhancing national security.
"When Russia once more deliberately attacks the energy infrastructure in Ukraine, decentralized, renewable energy sources could become a form of life insurance," he said.
"Investment in climate protection is also investment in our security," he added.
The Berlin Climate and Security Conference, which has been held annually since 2019, brings together some 250 international actors in the fields of climate, peace and security.
Participants include representatives from countries particularly affected by climate change and from the UN, EU and scientific and civil society organizations.
New Saxony-Anhalt parliament sits to choose speaker
The newly elected state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt is poised to hold its first session on Tuesday, over four weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won elections there with almost 44% of the vote.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the legislature, the same number of seats as the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) together.
During the session, parliamentarians are to vote for a speaker, with the AfD, as the strongest force, empowered to nominate the first candidate.
The AfD has put forward long-serving parliamentarian Tobias Rausch, 35, for the post, a choice that the populist BSW, which holds 5 seats, has pledged to back.
All the other parties refuse to work with the AfD under a policy known as the "firewall," and the CDU chairman in the state has advised members of his party to abstain from the vote.
If Rausch is elected, he will become the first AfD speaker of a state parliament in Germany.
However, if he fails to be elected in a first round of voting, all the other parties can put forward their own candidates.
There will be no vote on who will lead the state.
The session will be accompanied by protests by civil society groups who see the AfD, which has been classified as a "confirmed extremist" organization by domestic intelligence in the state, as a danger to Germany's democracy.
Welcome to our coverage

The new parliament in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt is poised to sit for the first time after elections in September handed a landslide victory to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
The session is being watched closely to see whether the AfD succeeds in installing its first speaker in a state parliament in Germany, with the populist BSW party pledging to back the AfD's nomination for the post.
One of Germany's top cultural events, the Frankfurt Book Fair, is also getting underway with preliminary events, including a press conference, before its doors open on Wednesday for specialist visitors.
And Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that the climate crisis could undermine security and fuel new waves of migration as the Berlin Climate and Security Conference kicks off in the capital.

Australia opposition pledges ‘biggest cut to immigration’ in history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:18:14 UTC
15:18:14 KST

Australia’s opposition coalition has pledged what it calls the “biggest cut to immigration” in the country’s history, proposing to reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 a year during its first two years in government.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor unveiled the plan on Tuesday as the Liberal-National Coalition seeks to link immigration levels to housing availability and pressure on public services.
The proposal would reduce the number of temporary visa holders by about 650,000 over four years, while permanent skilled migration would remain capped at 185,000 places a year.
Students might face restrictions
International students would face tighter restrictions, including a cap of 240,000 new student commencements. The coalition also plans to abolish most Temporary Graduate Visas, with exemptions for PhD students and those studying health and education or attending regional universities.
The coalition would also halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places a year and require most applicants for second or subsequent temporary visas to apply from outside the country.
‘Australia is not a hotel’
“A temporary visa should mean temporary. Australia is a home, not a hotel,” the coalition said.
Under the plan, net migration would gradually increase after the initial cuts, reaching 160,000 in the fourth year.
Migration has become a major political issue in Australia amid housing and cost-of-living pressures.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's Labor government has also tightened migration rules, including for international students, while arguing that migration remains important for addressing critical skills shortages.

Jim Bakker, TV preacher felled by scandals, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:12:45 UTC
15:12:45 KST

US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, a fraud conviction for bilking followers, and a divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86.
The death of Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media by his second wife, Lori Bakker.
"It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband's latest television ministry.
She paid tribute to Bakker as a "pioneer of Christian television," but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.
Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and a new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, known for his own brand of right-wing populism.
Bakker rose to fame through ‘The PTL Club’
Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on US television in the 1980s, achieving fame on the show "The PTL Club." PTL stood for "Praise The Lord" and "People That Love."
Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should have stood for "pass the loot."
Bakker spent 4-1/2 years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.
Prosecutors painted him as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power.
"Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests," Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing him.
Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers on 200 TV stations and raked in $129 million a year.
With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk.
He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was larded with requests for money donations.
Tammy Faye was much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.
Fraud conviction brings Bakker’s empire crashing down
Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on all 24 fraud and conspiracy charges brought against him.
Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide.
They said he siphoned $3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house.
The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. "I have sinned," Bakker told the court. "I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone."
Bakker's chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.
Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the "prosperity gospel" he once preached and writing a book titled "I Was Wrong."
"I've had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me," Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, who he married in 1998.
They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping "The Jim Bakker Show" at a 600-acre (240-hectare) development called Morningside near the tourist city of Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities to Heritage USA.
Bakker faced scrutiny for promoting false COVID remedy
Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.
In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for COVID-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic.
Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first US president to be impeached twice.
James Orson Bakker was born on January 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who maintained a strict fundamentalist Christian household.
He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostal Assemblies of God denomination.
Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children's religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network.
Setting out on his own in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire.

Somaliland seeks deeper security ties with Israel, sees Turkey as growing threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:12:35 UTC
15:12:35 KST

Somaliland is seeking to deepen security cooperation with Israel, including by obtaining air-defense systems, amid Turkey's growing military presence in Somalia, senior Somaliland presidential foreign affairs adviser Mohamed Osman Fadal said in an interview with Middle East Eye published this week.
"We need air-defense systems," Fadal said. "We want Israel to support us against Turkey."
According to Fadal, the deployment of Turkish F-16 fighter jets in Somalia and Ankara's expanding drone capabilities are among the reasons officials in Hargeisa want to strengthen Somaliland's defenses. Turkey deployed military aircraft to Somalia this year, and three Turkish F-16s participated in an April flyover over Mogadishu as part of celebrations marking Somali Armed Forces Day.
The remarks offered a rare glimpse into how Somaliland views its developing relationship with Israel. In recent months, reports have also increased regarding the possibility of an Israeli military presence at the port of Berbera.
Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud claimed on Friday that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in the city and also use its airport.
Somaliland denied that such an agreement exists. Its defense minister said in June that there was no Israeli military presence and no negotiations over establishing a base. He did, however, confirm that Israel provides training to Somaliland's military and police.
Somaliland sees Israel as counterweight to Turkey, Somalia ties
Officials in Hargeisa have described Israel as a potential counterweight to the increasingly close cooperation between Somalia and Turkey.
Mohamed Abdirahman Hassan, director-general of Somaliland's Foreign Ministry, told Middle East Eye that officials in Hargeisa fear the Somali government is considering military action against Somaliland and that Turkey could assist it.
The claim has not been independently verified, however, and Somalia's federal government has not announced any plan to invade Somaliland.
Turkey is considered one of Somalia's main strategic allies. In 2017, Ankara opened its largest overseas military training facility in Mogadishu and has since trained thousands of Somali security personnel.
In 2024, Turkey and Somalia signed a 10-year defense and economic cooperation agreement that includes assistance in building, training, and equipping Somalia's navy and strengthening maritime security. Turkey has also expanded its involvement in the energy sector, including oil and gas exploration off Somalia's coast.
Analysts question Somaliland's warnings over Turkey
Not everyone is convinced by Somaliland's warnings.
Mogadishu-based analyst Ahmed Abdi told Somalia Today that, in his view, Turkey does not pose a significant threat to Somaliland and that the statements are largely aimed at audiences outside the region.
According to Abdi, Somaliland is seeking to position itself alongside Western actors that criticize Turkey or support Israel, hoping the secure greater international support and further recognition.
Abdi assessed that the strategy was unlikely to succeed, in part because Turkey is a NATO member and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan maintains ties with US President Donald Trump.
He said Somaliland would have a stronger case if it based its demand for recognition on its own achievements and status rather than on opposition to other countries.
The reports also challenge the assumption that closer security ties between Israel and Somaliland are driven primarily by the Houthi threat across the Gulf of Aden.
Hassan told Middle East Eye that Somaliland does not support confrontation with the Houthis and instead prefers direct political dialogue.
Somaliland, Israel differ over approach to Houthi threat
That position differs significantly from Israel's approach, after the Houthis have attacked Israel and shipping routes in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden over the years.
The gap may indicate that, from Somaliland's perspective, Turkey and its relationship with the Somali government currently represent a more central security concern than the Houthis.
Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and has since maintained its own governing and security institutions. According to the report, Israel is currently the only country to have formally recognized it as a sovereign state.

EU discusses tighter restrictions on Russian diplomats amid hybrid attacks – Euronews
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
09:12:00 EEST

EU discusses tighter restrictions on Russian diplomats amid hybrid attacks – Euronews
EU countries are discussing tighter restrictions and additional checks for Russian diplomats amid a wave of hybrid attacks in Europe.
Source: European Pravda, citing Euronews
Details: The movements and activities of Russian diplomats have come under closer scrutiny as the European Union tackles a series of hybrid attacks, some of which have been directly linked to Moscow and which have shaken its collective security. Euronews reported that this issue could be the next step in the EU's sanctions regime.
Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats last month, accusing them of "unacceptable" conduct under the 1961 Vienna Convention. Moscow responded in kind.
Other worrying incidents, including a suspected arson attack on a defence company facility in Estonia and the discovery of an unexploded drone at Leipzig Airport in Germany, both linked to Russia, have further increased concerns.
The discussions, which are still at an early stage, are a continuation of the mechanism introduced by the EU last year as part of its 19th sanctions package. This requires Russian diplomats working in the EU to notify the authorities of their intention to travel to another member state or transit through one outside their host country at least 24 hours before their planned entry.
This applies to diplomatic and consular representatives of all ranks, including ambassadors, as well as administrative, technical and service staff and their family members.
Although the system has given European authorities greater powers to monitor the movements of Russian diplomats, it does not in itself restrict their movements.
Member states can introduce a stricter procedure requiring Russian diplomats to apply for permission to transit. If permission is refused, the diplomat may not cross the border. However, this procedure is optional. So far, only two countries have introduced it.
"As the system has only been in place since January 2026, experience is limited," a European Commission spokesperson said.
According to Euronews, discussions in Brussels will have to strike a balance with the Vienna Convention, which grants diplomatic representatives broad rights and protections in their day-to-day work. This document is considered one of the most significant achievements of international law.
Background:
- The Estonian Internal Security Service established that an arson attack on the building of the defence company Milrem Robotics in Tallinn on the night of 14-15 August was an act of sabotage ordered by Russian intelligence services.
- Germany directly accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig Airport in early August and announced retaliatory measures, including the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House Russian Houses are cultural centres established in other countries to promote Russia's language and culture and Russian education. They also serve as platforms for Russian state propaganda and soft power in Berlin.

New mass protest by thousands of school students is expected in Paris after clashes with police

Up to 40,000 demonstrators are expected in Paris on October 6 over problems in education. Since the protests began, 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured.
In France, tens of thousands of demonstrators are expected to take to the streets of Paris on October 6 for protests at schools demanding improved learning conditions. This comes as influential French trade unions join high school students amid a wave of protests that have already seen clashes with police. UNN reports this with reference to AFP.
Details
The authorities expect between 20,000 and 40,000 demonstrators in Paris.
New protests are expected on Tuesday after classes were disrupted at 589 of the country’s 3,700 lycées and 32 universities, according to the education ministry and the student union.
The protests have been ongoing since late September. Students then began blocking the entrances to hundreds of secondary schools for 15- to 17-year-olds, complaining about a lack of teachers, overloaded schedules, run-down classrooms, and buildings unable to cope with rising temperatures.
Many of the protests were peaceful. But some students set fire to garbage bins and bus stops or clashed with police, who responded with batons, tear gas, and riot-control projectiles, the publication writes.
Since the movement began, 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured, according to the authorities, while a 15-year-old teenager lost an arm on Monday, October 5, when he picked up a grenade fired by officers.
Several trade unions accused police of using disproportionate force against protesters. Police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests began, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday.
The government has tried to address these complaints while accusing left-wing activists of hijacking the protest movement.
According to the education minister, 24 schools have been burned or looted since the movement began. More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been detained. Lecornu’s office reported that 85 teachers were also injured.
The unrest erupted just months before the 2027 elections, in which the successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron will be elected after his maximum two terms in office.

Anger has been building since former president Hashim Thaci, viewed by many as a hero of the independence struggle, was sentenced last month over crimes committed during the 1990s war against Serbia.
Riot police used tear gas and a water cannon on protesters outside Kosovo's parliament on Monday night, after lawmakers ended their session without passing a bill to limit the powers of the country's war crimes court.
Several hundred demonstrators had spent most of the day outside the building, vowing to blockade it until the law was approved. When the session closed in the evening, they moved towards police lines to try to stop lawmakers from leaving.
Tear gas was aimed at the crowd, while some protesters threw firecrackers at officers. Bins were set alight near the parliament and projectiles were hurled at police, who responded with a water cannon and armoured vehicles.
During the hours-long stand-off, demonstrators denounced the sentencing last month of former president Hashim Thaci for war crimes committed during the 1990s war of independence against Serbia.
Thaci and three other senior guerrilla figures received heavy sentences after being found criminally responsible for murders, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment carried out by Kosovo Liberation Army fighters.
The verdict prompted outrage and rallies in the Balkan country, where the four men are widely seen as heroes of the independence struggle.
The bill cleared its first reading on Monday but was not passed into law. It would strip the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) of the power to try war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the war between ethnic Albanian guerrillas and Serb armed forces. Its jurisdiction would instead be limited to crimes committed inside Kosovo in the immediate aftermath of the war.
The KSC is established under Kosovo law but based in The Hague. Opposition parties and war veterans' organisations have long criticised it.

Imre Kaas: Save the rescuers!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
06:08:00 UTC
15:08:00 KST

Imre Kaas: Save the rescuers!
Estonia relies heavily on volunteers to bolster its internal security, but low pay for professional rescue workers risks making that reliance increasingly necessary.
Estonia has done very well so far because there are so many kindhearted people around us. One is a neighbor with a knack for fixing things who goes around clearing clogged sewer pipes in the neighborhood or comes over to help stack firewood, another serves as an assistant police officer, a third spends every weekend training with the Estonian Defense League and a fourth volunteers at the local rescue station.
Of course, it is entirely possible that all these activities are undertaken by the same person, simply because they cannot sit around doing nothing.
For a volunteer, what matters is the act itself — giving society something it would otherwise lack. Even if that something is security. And internal security matters, even if greater emphasis has been placed on ensuring external security in recent years and in light of Russia's military activity.
The defense budget, artillery shells, hybrid attacks, the threat posed by drones. All of these might seem like matters of external security, but in reality they are domestic issues, too. When you insure your home, you are bound to wonder whether your policy covers damage caused by a stray drone.
Everyone in Estonia expects that if something happens to them or their home, help will already be on its way. The swift arrival of rescue workers, paramedics or police officers is taken for granted and whenever the pay of those responsible for internal security comes up again in public debate, many people are surprised to learn just how meager their incomes still are.
Of course, people can and should complain about such pay, even if doing so incurs Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi's displeasure. After all, the minister said on ETV's "Esimene stuudio" that rescue workers' salaries would rise faster than inflation, or by roughly the same amount, and that those receiving such favorable treatment should not complain. The remark quite rightly provoked a storm of indignation because complaining is just about the only thing that is still free.
Even the host had to remind the minister that rescue workers' pay is among the furthest behind and that it is difficult to make ends meet on it. Ligi nevertheless described it as a matter of choices, adding that, to put it mildly, he disliked the tone rescue workers used when asking for money.
Having listened to and read the comments made by those asking for higher pay, I see nothing behind them but concern about making ends meet. There is nothing inappropriate about their tone. I am also reminded of a telling sign from a past demonstration demanding higher pay: "Save the rescuers!" And we are still in the same situation.
Of course, there is little point in comparing Jürgen Ligi's own €7,800 salary with that of rescue workers, but the figures are worth setting out nonetheless. Among Estonia's 1,668 professional rescue workers, 112 earn the minimum salary of €1,606 a month. A rescue worker's average base salary is €1,758. In the new year, they will receive a pay increase of just under €50 a month. That will at least allow a rescue worker to afford one more basket of groceries, although the finance minister himself acknowledged that, in the worst-case scenario, wages will rise only in line with inflation and such an increase will bring no measurable improvement in quality of life.
The Rescue Board and trade unions have said that a fair level of pay for rescue workers would be 1.2 times Estonia's average salary or about €2,700 a month. Reaching that level would require an additional €25 million or so a year for the payroll budget and that calculation concerns average pay. That is, of course, a large sum and not one that can simply be taken from somebody else's budget line. As an election promise, however, it would sound impressive.
Despite their poor pay, professional rescue workers do a good job and there is no indication that water flows through their hoses any more slowly because of it. On the other hand, motivation is a complicated thing and pay an important part of it. Salary is among the first things mentioned in employee satisfaction surveys and there is probably no one whose pay clearly exceeds their expectations. In the case of rescue workers, the situation is even more prosaic: Even outsiders can see that this level of income buys only enough food to stave off starvation a little longer.
So I fear that the role of volunteers will grow even further simply because there will not be enough professionals. Estonia already has 119 volunteer rescue stations alongside 71 professional ones. This gives the country an enormous amount of additional capacity for ensuring internal security, but that capacity depends on people's free time and motivation. Nor can those 3,241 volunteer rescue workers and assistant explosive ordnance disposal specialists be expected to sit on a tree stump armed with nothing but a bucket and an ax.
For example, volunteer rescue worker Hendrik Tali wrote in Delfi that they scrape together every cent needed to keep operating. They, too, are affected by the cost of electricity and fuel because without them the lights at rescue stations do not stay on and the vehicles do not move. And when you hear that some volunteers respond to emergencies in vehicles built 50 years ago, your arms almost drop helplessly to your sides.
Volunteers — assistant police officers — also provide the police with a significant amount of additional manpower. Estonia currently has 1,300 assistant police officers who have performed a total of 111,616 hours of police work this year. Eighty-eight percent of assistant police officers are active, meaning they serve regularly. Fortunately, assistant police officers do not have to buy their own handcuffs or batons and their vehicles are somewhat more modern than those used by volunteer rescue workers.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski
