Vietnamese President To Lam and his spouse, Ngo Phuong Ly, will make a state visit to Denmark from October 19 to October 21.
King Frederik and Queen Mary will host a gala dinner for the Vietnamese presidential couple at Christiansborg Palace on October 19.
To Lam and Ngo Phuong Ly will be accompanied by ministers, senior officials and a business delegation, the Danish Royal House said.
The visit marks 55 years of diplomatic relations between Denmark and Vietnam. It will focus on shared interests including green solutions, health, food and trade.
It will be the third state visit hosted by King Frederik since he became king, following visits from Iceland and Egypt. The Danish royal couple has made eight state visits abroad.
The Royal House, the organization supporting Denmark’s monarch and royal family, also highlighted the family’s connection to Vietnam.
Prince Henrik, King Frederik’s father, spent the first five years of his life in Vietnam when the country was part of French Indochina. His family returned to France in 1939. Henrik spoke Vietnamese, Chinese, French and Danish. He died in 2018.
Frederik and Mary last visited Vietnam officially in 2022, when they were crown prince and crown princess.
Vietnam is a socialist republic led by the Communist Party. To Lam serves as both president and the party’s general secretary, considered the country’s most powerful position.
Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.
Royal Run 2027 sells out more than 100,000 spots in under three hours
All 102,500 spots for Royal Run 2027 have sold out less than three hours after ticket sales opened on Wednesday.
The races in Vordingborg, Silkeborg, Thisted, Haderslev and Copenhagen/Frederiksberg will take place on Whit Monday in 2027.
According to the Danish Sports Confederation, Danmarks Idrætsforbund, and sports organization DGI, this was the fastest sellout in the event’s history.
Thisted was the first host city to sell out, with all 10,000 available spots taken in just under two hours.
Royal Run will have fewer participants in 2027 than this year, when 112,450 people took part. The 2026 edition sold out in four hours, which was also a record at the time.
Copenhagen/Frederiksberg has hosted Royal Run every year since the event began in 2018. Thisted, Silkeborg, Haderslev and Vordingborg will host it for the first time in 2027.
“That all start numbers are once again snapped up in such a short time says something about the place Royal Run has gained among Danes,” DGI chief executive Jens Otto Størup said.
Royal Run was first held in 2018 to mark King Frederik’s 50th birthday, with 70,938 people registered.
Participants can choose between three distances: one mile, five kilometers and 10 kilometers.
Thousands of Home Guard soldiers to take part in major exercise across Jutland and Funen
Military vehicles and armed Home Guard soldiers will be visible in several towns across Jutland and Funen from Thursday to Sunday as part of a large planned exercise.
Police in South and Southern Jutland, Southeast Jutland and East Jutland said residents should not be concerned by the increased military presence.
The exercise, called Blåtand, is expected to involve several thousand Home Guard soldiers, according to Colonel Peter Fausing, regional commander for the Home Guard in Regional Command West.
“It is one of the largest exercises in recent times here in Denmark,” he told Ritzau.
The exact number of participants is uncertain because the Home Guard is made up of volunteers. Around 6,500 active Home Guard soldiers are based in Jutland, on Funen and on nearby islands.
The exercise will focus on cooperation between the Armed Forces and other emergency authorities. Soldiers will practice tasks including guarding areas and setting up cordons in support of the police.
Training will take place in both towns and rural areas.
Military activity is expected in places including Odense, Middelfart, Aabenraa, Kolding, Vejle, Aarhus, Grenaa, Frederikshavn and Samsø.
The Home Guard is Denmark’s voluntary military emergency preparedness organization.
Green groups challenge government claim that 2035 climate target is on track
Environmental groups and climate experts are challenging the Danish government’s claim that it has demonstrated a path to meeting its 2035 climate target.
Climate Minister Samira Nawa has said the government considers the path to an 85% emissions reduction by 2035 to be demonstrated, even though current measures are projected to deliver only an 80% reduction.
“It is demonstrated because there is enough time to make the decisions, and because there is enough time to handle the risks that may arise on the way towards 2035,” Nawa said.
Greenpeace and green think tank Concito argue that this differs from how the term has previously been used in Danish climate policy.
“That is stretching the definition of demonstrated,” Concito chief economist Torsten Hasforth said.
Greenpeace political campaign lead Christian Fromberg said additional policy would be needed before the target could be considered demonstrated.
“Of course, that target has not been demonstrated yet. That will require new policy,” he said.
The Climate Council has previously assessed possible pathways toward an 85% reduction target, while stressing that reaching a higher target would require additional measures beyond policies already adopted.
The government has proposed an 85% target for 2035, which would go beyond Denmark’s current 2030 target of a 70% reduction.
Enhedslisten climate spokesperson Rasmus Vestergaard Madsen also said the final 5 percentage points still needed to be backed by concrete measures.
4 years on, Danish-Greenland history projects unveiled
More than four years after Denmark and Greenland agreed to examine their historical relationship, researchers have presented the first four subprojects in the investigation.
The projects will focus on adoptions, people who were legally registered without a father, school and language policies, and settlement and working conditions, Greenlandic broadcaster KNR reported.
“We are beginning with four important projects, which each shed light on concrete decisions and their consequences,” research leader Tenna Jensen said in a press release cited by KNR.
The Danish government and Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, agreed to launch the investigation in June 2022.
The decision came after reporting by Danish broadcaster DR on the so-called IUD case, in which thousands of Greenlandic women and girls had contraceptive devices fitted without their knowledge or consent.
The investigation will examine major decisions and events since World War II and their consequences for Greenland’s population. Its stated purpose is to provide a basis for reconciliation with the past.
Possible areas of research mentioned earlier included the closure of Greenlandic settlements, adoptions and Greenlandic children sent to Denmark.
The investigation is based at Ilisimatusarfik, the University of Greenland, and citizens are expected to be involved in the work.
Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.
Danish economy grew 0.9% in second quarter after sharp upward revision
Denmark’s economy grew by 0.9% in the second quarter of the year, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
The estimate was revised upward by 0.6 percentage points compared with the previous calculation for the quarter, published in August. Statistics Denmark said the change followed an update to the data used in the calculation.
Gross domestic product, or GDP, measures the size of a country’s economy. Denmark’s GDP was 5.7% higher in the second quarter than a year earlier.
Las Olsen, chief economist at Danske Bank, said the revision puts Denmark’s annual growth rate at the high end compared with other countries.
“This largely reflects a strongly increasing production among Danish companies abroad, and this is of course not least Novo, which is producing significantly more medicine than previously,” he wrote in a comment.
Erik Bjørsted, chief economist at Dansk Metal, a Danish trade union representing workers in industry and related sectors, also pointed to strong economic activity but said employment is a better measure of the economy’s health.
“The GDP figures can fluctuate a lot from quarter to quarter and are subject to considerable uncertainty,” he wrote.
“But when companies continue to hire more employees, it is a clear sign that the Danish economy continues to do well.”
Employment increased by 0.2% in the second quarter, according to Statistics Denmark.
Severed cable disrupts train traffic between Odense and Fredericia
Several trains between Odense and Fredericia were cancelled Wednesday morning after a cable was severed on western Funen, causing delays and signal problems.
The disruption affected regional train services, while other trains operating in the area could also face delays, according to P4 Trafik.
DSB, Denmark’s national passenger rail operator, deployed replacement buses for the cancelled regional trains.
It remains unclear when normal train services will resume.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
At around 9:15 a.m. Wednesday, Banedanmark told Ritzau that repair work was relatively far along, but problems with the railway signals remained.
As a result, authorities could not yet say when train traffic between Odense and Fredericia would return to normal.
Danish prisons reach record overcrowding as inmate numbers exceed capacity
Danish prisons are more overcrowded than ever, with 4,650 inmates currently held in facilities designed for 4,300 people, according to Fængselsforbundet, the Danish prison officers’ union.
The average occupancy rate has reached a record 105.4%, up from 102.7% last year.
Overcrowding means prisons have to create additional capacity by installing bunk beds in cells or converting hobby rooms, visiting rooms and offices into accommodation.
Vejle Arrest, a remand prison, has recorded an average occupancy rate of 135% this year.
Jan Bruun, a union representative at the prison, said the situation is putting pressure on the facility as cells fall increasingly into disrepair.
“We spend a lot of time finding room for inmates, swapping around when a double cell does not work between two inmates, and moving again when some have letter and visiting controls lifted,” he said in the union’s statement.
Hillerød Arrest has had an occupancy rate of 140% in recent months, placing additional demands on staff. At Randers Arrest, occupancy has averaged 115% this year, with the local union representative reporting more conflicts among inmates.
The pressure could increase further as tougher sentences introduced under Denmark’s penal reform take effect.
Half of the increased penalties for violence and rape came into force in February, while further increases are due to take effect in January.

Danish cyber hotline extends hours after breach exposes 8.8 million personal records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:20:45 UTC
13:20:45 KST

Denmark’s cyber hotline will remain open until midnight in the coming days following unauthorized access to 8.8 million records in the national CPR system.
The hotline will operate from 8 a.m. to midnight. It normally closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays, the Agency for Societal Security said.
The hotline advises residents and businesses on digital security, fraud and cyberattacks. It can also help people whose identities have been misused.
Residents with a specific suspicion that their CPR number is being used fraudulently can receive help creating a credit warning.
A credit warning alerts companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving loans or credit, making financial identity theft more difficult.
Authorities detected irregular activity in the CPR system on October 2.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information during September.
The records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority, said automated searches appeared intended to identify valid CPR numbers.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating. Authorities have not identified those responsible.
Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates urged residents to remain vigilant.
Authorities advised people never to provide passwords or other confidential information to unsolicited callers or message senders.

Denmark says it is too early to decide whether breach victims need new CPR numbers
Denmark has not decided whether people affected by unauthorized access to 8.8 million personal records will need new CPR numbers, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said.
Egelund spoke after briefing two Folketing committees about the breach of Denmark’s national personal information register.
“I have requested a security review of the entire CPR system,” Egelund of the Moderates said.
She said the findings would determine what changes were needed to restore trust and security. No deadline has been set for the review.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.
The affected records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.
Egelund said authorities were focused on preventing the stolen information from being used for identity theft, phishing and other digital fraud.
A website and telephone hotline have been established to advise residents about protecting themselves.
The breach has been reported to Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating.
Authorities have not identified who was responsible. Egelund said investigators had not ruled out any possibilities, including international involvement.
Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow
More than 2,000 owner-occupied apartments are for sale in Copenhagen for the first time since early 2024, according to housing website Boligsiden.
At the beginning of October, 2,057 apartments were listed in Copenhagen Municipality.
That was more than five percent higher than one month earlier and almost twice the number available one year ago.
The increase gives buyers more choice and could reduce competition for individual apartments, said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Sellers must now compete with more properties for buyers’ attention, she added.
Daetz said the changing balance had also led to larger price reductions on Copenhagen apartments.
Every district recorded an increase in listings over the past year.
Copenhagen S, which includes parts of Amager, had 530 apartments for sale at the beginning of October. That was an increase of more than 150 percent from one year earlier.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, said the figures showed that Copenhagen’s housing market was losing speed.
He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.
German spy chief warns Russia is waging a ‘shadow war’
The head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has warned that Russia is intensifying what he described as a “shadow war” against the country, saying Germany risks being drawn into a violent conflict.
“No other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany,” Martin Jäger said during a public hearing in the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, according to AFP.
The hearing took place before the parliamentary committee responsible for overseeing Germany’s intelligence services.
Jäger pointed to a case in August in which a drone carrying an explosive charge was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig. Agents with Russian connections are suspected of being behind the incident.
Germany has repeatedly accused Russia of conducting hybrid operations involving sabotage, espionage and other attempts to disrupt public order. Moscow has rejected such accusations.
Jäger said Russian intelligence services were acting “highly professionally and ruthlessly.”
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war does not fit into traditional military and legal categories,” he said, according to German broadcaster Tagesschau.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.

The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Cars powered only by petrol now account for less than half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet, according to figures from bilstatistik.dk.

Lego Foundation invests 200 million DKK to strengthen Danish teacher training
The Lego Foundation will invest 200 million DKK over five years in efforts to attract and retain more teachers and educators in Denmark.
The funding expands a partnership with Danske Professionshøjskoler, the association representing Denmark’s six university colleges.
The colleges will develop an action plan explaining how the money will be used to increase enrollment in teacher and educator training programs and help graduates remain in those professions.
“It is not a task for the Lego Foundation to define the concrete efforts,” foundation CEO Sidsel Marie Kristensen said. “They know much better than us what it takes to solve it.”
The initiative builds on cooperation that began in 2018.
The foundation cited shortages of qualified teachers and educators, falling academic performance in public schools and an increasing number of children excluded from school communities.
“Skilled teachers and educators are completely crucial for children’s well-being and learning,” Kristensen said.
A recent study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found that teacher shortages remain a problem in Denmark.
The latest PISA study also showed historically weak results among Danish 15-year-old students.
The foundation’s total support for Danske Professionshøjskoler has now reached 565 million DKK since 2018.
The Lego Foundation is a Danish commercial foundation that owns 25 percent of the Lego Group.
Danish justice minister wants prosecutors barred from wearing religious and political symbols in court
Danish prosecutors should follow the same rules as judges and be barred from wearing visible religious or political symbols during court hearings, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said.
“Neither Muslim nor other visible religious symbols must be allowed to weaken the public’s confidence that what takes place in Danish courtrooms is objective,” Wammen of the Social Democrats told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Since 2009, Denmark’s Administration of Justice Act has prohibited judges and lay judges from wearing religious or political symbols during hearings. The rule does not currently apply to prosecutors.
The debate began after Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor with the State Prosecutor in Viborg, wrote on LinkedIn that she was proud to be Denmark’s first prosecutor to wear a headscarf.
Dennis Flydtkjær, immigration spokesperson for the Denmark Democrats, said wearing a headscarf did not necessarily make a prosecutor biased. However, he said there should be no doubt about objectivity in court.
The Danish People’s Party has also criticized the different rules for judges and prosecutors.
The Association of Public Prosecutors said it did not understand the attention directed at Sediqi and supported her unconditionally.
The association said she had followed all current rules.
Denmark’s prosecution service confirmed that it has no internal rule preventing employees from wearing a hijab at work.
Sediqi has not commented.
Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”
EU countries to discuss coordinated response to rising fuel prices after US pressure
European Union countries will meet Friday to discuss a coordinated response to rising fuel prices, a European Commission spokesperson said, according to AFP.
The meeting follows pressure from the United States for Europe to help increase diesel supplies and lower prices.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News he was “very confident” that Europe would cooperate.
“Now is the time for a coordinated release of diesel stocks,” Wright said, citing the coming harvest and winter seasons.
The US government particularly wants France and Germany to release diesel from strategic reserves, AFP reported.
Washington has also threatened to ban diesel exports if European countries do not act, three unnamed sources told Reuters.
Europe has become more dependent on fuel imports from the United States since it banned Russian fuel following the invasion of Ukraine. The war involving the United States, Israel and Iran has also disrupted supplies from the Middle East.
US President Donald Trump has considered an export ban to reduce American fuel prices before the November midterm elections.
However, Trump said Wednesday that such a ban could instead push prices higher.
The average US diesel price has reached $6.39 per gallon, equal to about 42.52 DKK. A gallon is approximately 3.7 liters.
Diesel cost an average of $3.70 per gallon one year ago, according to AFP.
Denmark loses 4-2 to Portugal despite twice equalizing in Nations League match
Denmark lost 4-2 to Portugal in the Nations League on Thursday after twice equalizing before 35,951 spectators at Parken in Copenhagen.
Portugal played without Cristiano Ronaldo, who left the national team camp Wednesday and traveled to Madrid.
Joao Cancelo opened the scoring after 13 minutes, moving through the Danish defense and lifting the ball over goalkeeper Mads Hermansen.
Mikkel Damsgaard equalized for Denmark in the 24th minute, finishing a team move at the far post.
Two minutes later, Goncalo Ramos restored Portugal’s lead after receiving a through ball from Bruno Fernandes.
Rasmus Højlund made it 2-2 seven minutes into the second half. Damsgaard supplied the pass, and Højlund chipped the ball over Portuguese goalkeeper Diogo Costa.
Højlund then performed Ronaldo’s well-known goal celebration, prompting spectators to respond with its familiar “Siiuuu” chant.
Portugal went ahead again 12 minutes later when Vitinha headed in another assist from Fernandes.
Substitute Joao Felix scored Portugal’s fourth and final goal.
Denmark competed closely in general play but could not match Portugal’s finishing.
Brian Riemer’s team now has three points from its opening three Nations League matches, following one victory and two defeats.
Denmark will next play Wales away on Sunday.
Nearly 189,000 people enter lottery for 45,000 Copenhagen Half Marathon places
A total of 188,522 people have entered a lottery for 45,000 places in the 2027 Copenhagen Half Marathon, organizer Sparta Atletik & Løb said Thursday.
“This shows how effectively Copenhagen and the city’s dedicated spectators draw in running enthusiasts from all over the world,” CEO Dorte Vibjerg said.
Sparta Atletik & Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, began drawing names after registration closed overnight. The first successful applicants will receive emails on October 5.
The race had 35,000 registered participants this year. Organizers increased capacity to a record 45,000 for 2027 but said they could not accept every applicant without affecting safety and quality.
“We would so like to invite everyone to the party,” Vibjerg said. “But we do not want to compromise on quality.”
Entrants could register alone or in groups of up to three. Groups will either receive places together or not be selected.
Successful applicants will have 48 hours to buy a ticket, which costs 795 DKK plus an administration fee.
Tickets were previously sold on a first-come, first-served basis. Organizers introduced the lottery to give all applicants an equal chance.
Similar systems are used for major European running events, including the Berlin and London marathons.
The Copenhagen Half Marathon, also called CPH Half, will take place September 19, 2027.
Electric cars reach record 88.8 percent of Danish new-car registrations
Denmark registered 20,206 new passenger cars during the past month, an increase of 13 percent from the same month last year, according to bilstatistik.dk.
Electric vehicles accounted for a record 88.8 percent of registrations. Excluding commercial vehicles, their share reached 97.5 percent.
Tesla’s Model Y was the best-selling car with 1,226 registrations, followed by the Model 3 with 1,073. The Skoda Elroq placed third, while Toyota’s bZ4X and C-HR+ completed the top five.
Ilyas Dogru, chief consultant at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, said Tesla traditionally registers imported Model 3 vehicles at the end of a quarter.
He said Tesla’s offer of zero-percent financing also increased demand by giving buyers savings worth tens of thousands of kroner.
Mobility Denmark, the Danish automotive industry association, criticized government plans to raise taxes on some electric cars in 2027.
Electric cars currently face tax above a price of 419,300 DKK. The proposed threshold is 366,200 DKK.
Under the proposed budget, a car costing 400,000 DKK would face a tax of almost 25,000 DKK from New Year.
FDM expects some buyers to complete purchases before the higher tax takes effect, potentially increasing sales during the final three months of the year.
Danish woman fined 200,000 DKK and restricted from keeping dogs over animal mistreatment
A 59-year-old woman from South Funen has been fined 200,000 DKK for irresponsible treatment of dogs and puppies.
The Court in Svendborg also barred her from handling dogs in the future, with an exception allowing her to own and care for one dog.
Authorities inspected the woman’s property five times between spring 2024 and spring 2025, Funen Police prosecutor Frederik Bendixen said.
“It has been established that there was irresponsible treatment during each of these five visits,” Bendixen said.
The case involved Pomeranian dogs that were kept in cages that were too small, among other problems.
During one inspection, authorities found 29 dogs at the property. The woman also lacked permission to operate a commercial dog business.
Authorities removed all the dogs during their final inspection.
Some were euthanized, while others were transferred to animal shelters or sold, according to the prosecutor.
The woman was also convicted of selling a puppy before it was eight weeks old.
Prosecutors had requested a fine of 250,000 DKK.
The court considered that the woman had previously been convicted of irresponsible treatment of animals when deciding her sentence.
The woman pleaded not guilty. It is not known whether she will appeal the verdict. The ruling was delivered last week, but the court’s written record was completed Thursday.
Legislation for departure centers outside the EU is now in place, says Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov
European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.
Bødskov said the five countries had made progress during talks Thursday morning.
EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.
Bødskov said Spain partly contributed to the situation by offering legal residence to undocumented migrants. Spain originally expected about 500,000 applications, but more than 1.1 million people applied by the June 30 deadline, according to Euronews.
He said the EU remained vulnerable to sudden large arrivals and needed stronger external borders.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.
Prosecutors seek prison sentence and nightlife ban for Danish man over fatal punch at World Cup event
Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.
The incident occurred around 8:45 p.m. on June 30 during a public screening of the football World Cup at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen.
According to the indictment, the defendant stood on a bench and threw two beer cans toward a group, hitting one person. He then allegedly punched the Swedish man on the left side of his head or neck.
The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.
Vietnamese president to visit Denmark for talks on green solutions, health and trade
Vietnamese President To Lam and his spouse, Ngo Phuong Ly, will make a state visit to Denmark from October 19 to October 21.
King Frederik and Queen Mary will host a gala dinner for the Vietnamese presidential couple at Christiansborg Palace on October 19.
To Lam and Ngo Phuong Ly will be accompanied by ministers, senior officials and a business delegation, the Danish Royal House said.
The visit marks 55 years of diplomatic relations between Denmark and Vietnam. It will focus on shared interests including green solutions, health, food and trade.
It will be the third state visit hosted by King Frederik since he became king, following visits from Iceland and Egypt. The Danish royal couple has made eight state visits abroad.
The Royal House, the organization supporting Denmark’s monarch and royal family, also highlighted the family’s connection to Vietnam.
Prince Henrik, King Frederik’s father, spent the first five years of his life in Vietnam when the country was part of French Indochina. His family returned to France in 1939. Henrik spoke Vietnamese, Chinese, French and Danish. He died in 2018.
Frederik and Mary last visited Vietnam officially in 2022, when they were crown prince and crown princess.
Vietnam is a socialist republic led by the Communist Party. To Lam serves as both president and the party’s general secretary, considered the country’s most powerful position.
Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.
Royal Run 2027 sells out more than 100,000 spots in under three hours
All 102,500 spots for Royal Run 2027 have sold out less than three hours after ticket sales opened on Wednesday.
The races in Vordingborg, Silkeborg, Thisted, Haderslev and Copenhagen/Frederiksberg will take place on Whit Monday in 2027.
According to the Danish Sports Confederation, Danmarks Idrætsforbund, and sports organization DGI, this was the fastest sellout in the event’s history.
Thisted was the first host city to sell out, with all 10,000 available spots taken in just under two hours.
Royal Run will have fewer participants in 2027 than this year, when 112,450 people took part. The 2026 edition sold out in four hours, which was also a record at the time.
Copenhagen/Frederiksberg has hosted Royal Run every year since the event began in 2018. Thisted, Silkeborg, Haderslev and Vordingborg will host it for the first time in 2027.
“That all start numbers are once again snapped up in such a short time says something about the place Royal Run has gained among Danes,” DGI chief executive Jens Otto Størup said.
Royal Run was first held in 2018 to mark King Frederik’s 50th birthday, with 70,938 people registered.
Participants can choose between three distances: one mile, five kilometers and 10 kilometers.
Thousands of Home Guard soldiers to take part in major exercise across Jutland and Funen
Military vehicles and armed Home Guard soldiers will be visible in several towns across Jutland and Funen from Thursday to Sunday as part of a large planned exercise.
Police in South and Southern Jutland, Southeast Jutland and East Jutland said residents should not be concerned by the increased military presence.
The exercise, called Blåtand, is expected to involve several thousand Home Guard soldiers, according to Colonel Peter Fausing, regional commander for the Home Guard in Regional Command West.
“It is one of the largest exercises in recent times here in Denmark,” he told Ritzau.
The exact number of participants is uncertain because the Home Guard is made up of volunteers. Around 6,500 active Home Guard soldiers are based in Jutland, on Funen and on nearby islands.
The exercise will focus on cooperation between the Armed Forces and other emergency authorities. Soldiers will practice tasks including guarding areas and setting up cordons in support of the police.
Training will take place in both towns and rural areas.
Military activity is expected in places including Odense, Middelfart, Aabenraa, Kolding, Vejle, Aarhus, Grenaa, Frederikshavn and Samsø.
The Home Guard is Denmark’s voluntary military emergency preparedness organization.
Green groups challenge government claim that 2035 climate target is on track
Environmental groups and climate experts are challenging the Danish government’s claim that it has demonstrated a path to meeting its 2035 climate target.
Climate Minister Samira Nawa has said the government considers the path to an 85% emissions reduction by 2035 to be demonstrated, even though current measures are projected to deliver only an 80% reduction.
“It is demonstrated because there is enough time to make the decisions, and because there is enough time to handle the risks that may arise on the way towards 2035,” Nawa said.
Greenpeace and green think tank Concito argue that this differs from how the term has previously been used in Danish climate policy.
“That is stretching the definition of demonstrated,” Concito chief economist Torsten Hasforth said.
Greenpeace political campaign lead Christian Fromberg said additional policy would be needed before the target could be considered demonstrated.
“Of course, that target has not been demonstrated yet. That will require new policy,” he said.
The Climate Council has previously assessed possible pathways toward an 85% reduction target, while stressing that reaching a higher target would require additional measures beyond policies already adopted.
The government has proposed an 85% target for 2035, which would go beyond Denmark’s current 2030 target of a 70% reduction.
Enhedslisten climate spokesperson Rasmus Vestergaard Madsen also said the final 5 percentage points still needed to be backed by concrete measures.
4 years on, Danish-Greenland history projects unveiled
More than four years after Denmark and Greenland agreed to examine their historical relationship, researchers have presented the first four subprojects in the investigation.
The projects will focus on adoptions, people who were legally registered without a father, school and language policies, and settlement and working conditions, Greenlandic broadcaster KNR reported.
“We are beginning with four important projects, which each shed light on concrete decisions and their consequences,” research leader Tenna Jensen said in a press release cited by KNR.
The Danish government and Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, agreed to launch the investigation in June 2022.
The decision came after reporting by Danish broadcaster DR on the so-called IUD case, in which thousands of Greenlandic women and girls had contraceptive devices fitted without their knowledge or consent.
The investigation will examine major decisions and events since World War II and their consequences for Greenland’s population. Its stated purpose is to provide a basis for reconciliation with the past.
Possible areas of research mentioned earlier included the closure of Greenlandic settlements, adoptions and Greenlandic children sent to Denmark.
The investigation is based at Ilisimatusarfik, the University of Greenland, and citizens are expected to be involved in the work.
Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.
Danish economy grew 0.9% in second quarter after sharp upward revision
Denmark’s economy grew by 0.9% in the second quarter of the year, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
The estimate was revised upward by 0.6 percentage points compared with the previous calculation for the quarter, published in August. Statistics Denmark said the change followed an update to the data used in the calculation.
Gross domestic product, or GDP, measures the size of a country’s economy. Denmark’s GDP was 5.7% higher in the second quarter than a year earlier.
Las Olsen, chief economist at Danske Bank, said the revision puts Denmark’s annual growth rate at the high end compared with other countries.
“This largely reflects a strongly increasing production among Danish companies abroad, and this is of course not least Novo, which is producing significantly more medicine than previously,” he wrote in a comment.
Erik Bjørsted, chief economist at Dansk Metal, a Danish trade union representing workers in industry and related sectors, also pointed to strong economic activity but said employment is a better measure of the economy’s health.
“The GDP figures can fluctuate a lot from quarter to quarter and are subject to considerable uncertainty,” he wrote.
“But when companies continue to hire more employees, it is a clear sign that the Danish economy continues to do well.”
Employment increased by 0.2% in the second quarter, according to Statistics Denmark.
Severed cable disrupts train traffic between Odense and Fredericia
Several trains between Odense and Fredericia were cancelled Wednesday morning after a cable was severed on western Funen, causing delays and signal problems.
The disruption affected regional train services, while other trains operating in the area could also face delays, according to P4 Trafik.
DSB, Denmark’s national passenger rail operator, deployed replacement buses for the cancelled regional trains.
It remains unclear when normal train services will resume.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
At around 9:15 a.m. Wednesday, Banedanmark told Ritzau that repair work was relatively far along, but problems with the railway signals remained.
As a result, authorities could not yet say when train traffic between Odense and Fredericia would return to normal.
Danish prisons reach record overcrowding as inmate numbers exceed capacity
Danish prisons are more overcrowded than ever, with 4,650 inmates currently held in facilities designed for 4,300 people, according to Fængselsforbundet, the Danish prison officers’ union.
The average occupancy rate has reached a record 105.4%, up from 102.7% last year.
Overcrowding means prisons have to create additional capacity by installing bunk beds in cells or converting hobby rooms, visiting rooms and offices into accommodation.
Vejle Arrest, a remand prison, has recorded an average occupancy rate of 135% this year.
Jan Bruun, a union representative at the prison, said the situation is putting pressure on the facility as cells fall increasingly into disrepair.
“We spend a lot of time finding room for inmates, swapping around when a double cell does not work between two inmates, and moving again when some have letter and visiting controls lifted,” he said in the union’s statement.
Hillerød Arrest has had an occupancy rate of 140% in recent months, placing additional demands on staff. At Randers Arrest, occupancy has averaged 115% this year, with the local union representative reporting more conflicts among inmates.
The pressure could increase further as tougher sentences introduced under Denmark’s penal reform take effect.
Half of the increased penalties for violence and rape came into force in February, while further increases are due to take effect in January.

Denmark says it is too early to decide whether breach victims need new CPR numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:20:40 UTC
13:20:40 KST

Denmark has not decided whether people affected by unauthorized access to 8.8 million personal records will need new CPR numbers, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said.
Egelund spoke after briefing two Folketing committees about the breach of Denmark’s national personal information register.
“I have requested a security review of the entire CPR system,” Egelund of the Moderates said.
She said the findings would determine what changes were needed to restore trust and security. No deadline has been set for the review.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.
The affected records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.
Egelund said authorities were focused on preventing the stolen information from being used for identity theft, phishing and other digital fraud.
A website and telephone hotline have been established to advise residents about protecting themselves.
The breach has been reported to Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating.
Authorities have not identified who was responsible. Egelund said investigators had not ruled out any possibilities, including international involvement.
Danish government to propose restoring Great Prayer Day as public holiday in 2030
Denmark’s cyber hotline will remain open until midnight in the coming days following unauthorized access to 8.8 million records in the national CPR system.
The hotline will operate from 8 a.m. to midnight. It normally closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays, the Agency for Societal Security said.
The hotline advises residents and businesses on digital security, fraud and cyberattacks. It can also help people whose identities have been misused.
Residents with a specific suspicion that their CPR number is being used fraudulently can receive help creating a credit warning.
A credit warning alerts companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving loans or credit, making financial identity theft more difficult.
Authorities detected irregular activity in the CPR system on October 2.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information during September.
The records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority, said automated searches appeared intended to identify valid CPR numbers.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating. Authorities have not identified those responsible.
Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates urged residents to remain vigilant.
Authorities advised people never to provide passwords or other confidential information to unsolicited callers or message senders.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.
