“I don’t think I’m happy in the happiest country in the world”: The question that took an international from being a student to opening a restaurant chains in Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Bruce Kim’s first months in Denmark left him with a question. He had moved from South Korea to a country repeatedly described as one of the happiest in the world, but after living there for six months, he was not convinced. “I don’t think I’m happy,” he remembers thinking.
Kim, now 40, had arrived in Denmark in 2010 as an exchange student at DTU, the Technical University of Denmark. He was studying transportation, and Denmark had not been some long-held ambition. In fact, it had been the only exchange option available through his university in South Korea. “If there had been more choices, I don’t think I would have chosen Denmark,” he said. To him, Denmark was an “unknown country,” associated with agriculture, cheese, milk, high prices and cold weather. He had also heard it was difficult to make friends. “Denmark wouldn’t have been my first choice.”
Today, Kim runs the restaurant chain Kopan, with four restaurants and a food truck and employs around 40 people. He never trained as a chef and did not come to Denmark to become an entrepreneur. Food was not even the original point. What eventually became a business started as an attempt to understand the country he had unexpectedly landed in, and Kim still does not see what he is doing today as entirely separate from that first experiment. “I think I’m still doing the same thing,” he said. “I’m still curious about Denmark as a society and about the happiness index.”
A reason to stay
Kim’s exchange semester at DTU was also the final semester of his bachelor’s degree in South Korea. “When I finished my exchange program at DTU, I automatically graduated from my university,” he said. Suddenly, he had several possible directions: return to South Korea to look for work, continue studying there or apply for a master’s degree elsewhere in Europe.
A professor at DTU encouraged him to stay after seeing how seriously he had approached his studies. Kim also applied to universities in Sweden and the United Kingdom, but Denmark had started to present him with a puzzle he wanted to solve.
Around the time he finished his exchange, Denmark was again receiving international attention for its place in global happiness rankings. Kim struggled to reconcile that reputation with his own experience. “Even though I had stayed in Denmark for six months, I didn’t think I was happy,” he said. Friends in South Korea were also asking him about it. They were seeing Denmark presented as an exceptionally happy country while South Korea was performing poorly in the same comparisons.
“My curiosity about the happiness index made me stay in Denmark for my master’s,” Kim said.
That curiosity deepened when a Korean broadcaster asked him to help with a documentary about happiness in Denmark. The subject was already on his mind, so he agreed. After the program aired in South Korea, he began receiving more questions from Korean viewers. “They asked me a lot of questions about what makes Denmark happy and how I felt about living in Denmark,” he said.
Kim did not feel he could simply answer them.
“I needed to find answers to those questions from the Korean audience,” he said.
By then he had completed his master’s degree. The obvious options were familiar ones: find a job, pursue a Ph.D. or return to South Korea. Instead, Kim decided to use part of the time he was allowed to remain in Denmark for something else. He gave himself a year and called the project “Delivering Happiness.”
“I wanted to know more about happiness from local people,” he said. But before he could ask Danes what made them happy, he needed a way to meet them.
Eight minutes with a stranger
Kim needed what he called a “tool” to make strangers stop and talk to him. At the time, he said, Korea was still unfamiliar to many of the people he met in Denmark. “A lot of people asked me, ‘Are you from North Korea or South Korea?’”
That gave him an idea. He could introduce a small part of Korean culture and, at the same time, ask Danes about their own society.
“I thought food might be a good way to meet people,” he said.
With permission from Copenhagen Municipality, Kim went onto the streets with a bicycle and began making Korean pancakes. The food itself was simple, but one detail made it particularly useful for his experiment: a pancake took around eight minutes to prepare.
“I thought eight minutes might be a good amount of time to have a small interview,” he said.
So while people waited for their food, Kim asked them about happiness. He spoke with students and other people he met on the street about education, satisfaction and what they believed made life in Denmark work. He then shared their stories online for the Korean audience that had been asking him those same questions.
The project gradually became known beyond the people who happened to encounter his bicycle. Kim said some Danes started approaching him specifically because they had heard about what he was doing and wanted to contribute. “They came to my bicycle and talked about their stories,” he said. “Not because they were interested in my pancakes, but because they were interested in my project.”
The idea, as Kim understood it, was that their experiences might offer something useful to people in South Korea. “They thought their interviews and their stories could also contribute to Korean society and maybe help increase happiness in Korea,” he said.
As a social experiment, Kim felt it was working.
As a food business, less so.
“I didn’t make much money,” he said. The pancake itself, he admitted, was not necessarily the main attraction. But that did not bother him. The calculation was different. More pancakes meant more conversations.
“If I sold 10 pancakes, that meant I had interviewed 10 people,” he said.
For a year, that was enough.
‘I kept it secret’
There was one group of people Kim was not interviewing about the project: his parents.
They knew their son had completed his studies in Denmark and was trying to establish his career abroad. They did not know that instead of working in transportation, he was cycling through Copenhagen and selling pancakes to strangers.
“I kept it secret,” Kim said. “I didn’t tell my parents about the project for a year.”
When he spoke with them, he presented a different version of his life. “I told them, ‘I’m looking for a job. I haven’t found one yet, but don’t worry about me. I still have two more years.’”
Eventually, the secret did not hold. His parents discovered what he had been doing through an interview Kim had given to a Korean broadcaster. They were disappointed that he had not told them the truth, and his father was also disappointed by the choice itself.
“My father was disappointed that I was selling pancakes on the street,” Kim said.
He understood the reaction. His parents had expectations for what would follow after their son went abroad and completed a master’s degree. Selling pancakes on the streets of Copenhagen was not the obvious next step.
Kim himself was still far from certain that it was.
After the first year of the project, he returned to South Korea. He told his family that he had enjoyed the experiment, but he would take a more conventional route when he went back to Denmark. “Maybe I’ll just find a job when I go back to Denmark,” he told them.
But when he returned, he still did not know what that job would be. “I only had two years left, and I hadn’t found a job,” he said. “I didn’t know what to do.”
Then something happened that changed the way he thought about the project.
A conversation after tragedy
During Kim’s journey back to Denmark in 2014, a passenger ferry sank in South Korea with many students on board. Kim first heard information suggesting the students had been rescued. “I felt relieved. I thought there was nothing to worry about,” he said.
When he reached Copenhagen Airport, he learned that many had died.
“The news caused me a lot of stress and worry,” he said.
In Copenhagen, Kim gathered with other Koreans at a church. “I shared how I was feeling,” he said. The people there had different lives and professions, and they began talking about their experiences in Denmark. Their conversations included the way Denmark approached safety, work and education.
“Those stories touched me,” Kim said.
He had spent a year collecting stories from Danes and sending them toward South Korea. Now he was listening to Koreans in Denmark describe what they themselves had experienced in the country.
The conversation gave Kim another idea. “I believed that if I wanted to bring more good stories from Denmark to Korea, I needed to bring more Koreans to Denmark so they could have their own experiences.”
That created a practical problem.
“In order to do that, I needed to create jobs.”
The pancake project went back onto the street.
When people started coming for the food
Starting again was not much easier. “It was a hard time for me,” Kim said. “The winter was long, very cold and rainy.”
There was another problem: the original pancake still was not particularly suited to Danish customers.
Kim’s Danish friends began telling him why they thought it was not working. The pancake was sweet, used sugar and was fried in oil. They suggested adapting it, including by adding kimchi.
Kim rejected the idea.
“In Korea, we don’t eat kimchi with bread,” he said. “We eat kimchi with rice.”
His friends kept insisting.
“Bruce, in Denmark people eat bread, not rice,” Kim remembers them telling him. “Maybe you can try.”
Eventually he did. Kim began making versions with fillings such as kimchi and bulgogi.
“Suddenly, we got a lot of attention from local people,” he said.
For perhaps the first time, people were not only interested in the social experiment. They also wanted the food.
The project eventually received a fixed spot at a Copenhagen food market. Kim said the opportunity was connected not only to what he was selling but also to the social purpose behind it. His project shared stories from Denmark with people in South Korea, and Kim also provided pancakes to homeless people in Denmark based on his sales.
“We were helping both Denmark and Korea,” he said.
The experiment had started to become a business, even if Kim had not set out to build one.
Four restaurants, almost by accident
A fixed location solved one problem but created another. During the summer, outdoor sales were strong enough for Kim to employ people. In winter, customers moved indoors and sales dropped.
That left him with a choice he did not like.
“In winter, people went inside, so we couldn’t sell many pancakes,” he said. “That meant I would have to fire my employees.”
Instead, he opened a restaurant nearby.
“To keep my employees and my staff, I needed to open a restaurant next door,” he said.
The first restaurant, then, was not simply an attempt to expand. It was a way to keep the people already working for him employed through the winter. The outdoor operation and restaurant could support each other across different parts of the year.
From there, the operation continued growing.
By the time of the interview, Kim said he had four restaurants as well as the food truck, with around 40 employees.
It is a long way from studying transportation at DTU, and an even longer way from the eight-minute conversations beside a bicycle. But when asked how it feels to have ended up in an entirely different career, Kim pushes back slightly against the premise.
“Denmark gave me the chance to choose something different,” he said. He had not been trained in food and had not entered Denmark planning to work in restaurants. “But my curiosity about Denmark and happiness brought me to this project and eventually to this business.”
To Kim, the method has changed much more than the purpose.
“I’m still curious about Denmark as a society and about the happiness index,” he said. “I still want to share what we have experienced in Denmark with Korea, and I want to bring more Korean people to Denmark.”
“If someone asks me why I run these restaurants, I still tell them I’m curious about Denmark,” he added. “I still want to bring more Danes to Korea too.”
‘I need to knock on many doors’
Turning the experiment into a company also exposed Kim to another side of being a foreigner in Denmark.
“The first thing was that there wasn’t much information,” he said.
Starting a business meant figuring out how to create a company, handle taxes and employ people. Kim said more information is available in English today, but when he started, finding those answers was difficult.
“I had to knock on many people’s doors,” he said. “‘Could you tell me how to open a company? How do I pay taxes?’”
His Danish friends became part of the process. “A lot of my Danish friends helped me with the project,” he said. “Otherwise, it would have been impossible to start a business or a project as a foreigner.”
That reliance on other people also shaped the way Kim sees the broader challenge of making a life in Denmark. He believes foreigners often arrive without knowing much about the country, while Danes may also have limited knowledge of the places newcomers come from. “There is an imbalance of information because people don’t know each other,” he said.
For people moving to Denmark, his advice is not to expect closeness to happen immediately. He believes newcomers need to make an effort to learn about Danish culture, study the language and build relationships.
“They’re not open in the beginning,” he said. “But if you make an effort to get closer to Danes and learn about Denmark, they open up slowly.”
“It takes some time.” Kim found his own shortcut, or at least his own starting point. “I feed them a lot of Korean food,” he said.
He would invite Danish friends home and offer them Korean barbecue. For someone who had once needed an excuse to spend eight minutes talking to strangers, sharing food became a way of getting past the distance he initially felt in Denmark.
“That’s why they really trust me through food,” Kim said.
Four restaurants and around 40 employees later, that part of the experiment has not changed very much. “That’s why I chose food for my project.”

The Pentagon confirmed earlier that the bombers had left the RAF Fairford airbase – used by the United States to launch ‘defensive’ strikes on Tehran – even as the British government insisted the site was safe.
"There were some threats," Trump told reporters at the White House.
"And rather than tempting the enemy – we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far."

Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, five suspects arrested at the time and a British-Iranian national detained afterwards have all since been released on bail.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counter-terrorism police.
Trump would not comment on a report that the threat involved attack drones, saying: "I can't tell you that but if they did they'll suffer greatly."
"We actually know the people that made the threat," said Trump, adding: "They would be linked to Iran."
Two US officials told US media outlets that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot.
One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours.
Asked whether the base was safe however, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official spokesman replied "yes."
"We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," he told reporters.
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel theft, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.
Burnham previously said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Trump had previously rebuked British authorities for releasing the arrested men, all in their mid-20s, on bail – pending further investigation.
Iran's embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.

‘Remember 7.10.23’: Hostage Square bears few remnants of a national crisis – but trauma lingers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:48:28 UTC
12:48:28 KST

In the days following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, the families of the hostages held in Gaza turned the plaza next to the Tel Aviv Museum of Art into what became known as Hostage Square.
Filled with “Bring Them Home” signs and hostage posters, yellow ribbons, and yellow balloons, the square hosted demonstrations and press conferences.
It was here that the families created a replica of a Hamas tunnel and established the Empty Shabbat Table, a haunting art installation to remind visitors – and especially the Israeli government – that their loved ones still languished in Gaza. And it was here, two years later, that the families and thousands of other Israelis gathered to watch the last of the living hostages return to Israel.
Three years after the attack on Simchat Torah, there are few remnants of the hostage families’ encampment: the tunnel replica, a few yellow ribbons and a sign bearing the words “Remember 7.10.23.” During the days leading up to the third anniversary, some paid respects to the few hostage families who set up a sukkah on the square, but the plaza was nearly empty.
By all outward appearances, Israelis have moved on.
Yet beneath the surface, many are still grappling with the trauma of October 7 and the multifront war the attack triggered.
In an N12 news site poll in June, 74% of respondents said they fear that terrorists will carry out another large-scale attack, and 66% said they want the October 7 attack to be investigated by a state commission of inquiry.
Last month, in an Israel Democracy Institute survey, 68% of Jewish Israelis and 32% of Arab Israelis said the October 7 attack is a “central factor” in deciding which party to vote for, behind security and the high cost of living.
October 7 trauma persists among Israelis
In the café at the edge of Hostage Square, Isaac Badra, a 33-year-old realtor, recalled how he and his wife opened their home to their upstairs neighbors because the Badras live on the “safer” ground floor and their Tel Aviv building has no bomb shelter. The trauma persists, he said.
He vividly remembered the air-raid sirens, reserve soldiers rushing to base on Simchat Torah, and the frantic phone calls with his wife’s family near the Gaza border as Hamas attacked Sderot, where they live.
“My wife’s mother said she saw terrorists in the street, but I couldn’t grasp what she was saying,” he recalled. When he turned on the TV, he realized the scale of the attack. “I locked all of our doors and our windows and prayed.”
Three years later, Badra said, “When I hear noises outside, I jump. When Arab construction workers shout out to each other, I jump. And now I doubt whether my friends abroad really have our back.”
Roni Shoval, a defense industry worker from northern Israel not far from the Lebanon border, said the trauma of the past three years “is still inside me.” He called the attacks “a modern Holocaust for Israel.”
Even three years later, “I’m not ready to visit Nova,” he said, referring to the memorial at the site of the music festival where Hamas murdered 378 people and abducted dozens more. “Look, I’m getting goosebumps now just talking about it.”
Shoval, 54, is still doing IDF reserve duty, years beyond the maximum age because the IDF needs his expertise. He doesn’t want the same for his children.
“My son will be drafted soon,” he said. “Back in the day, I served in Gaza and Lebanon. I don’t want him sent to Gaza and Lebanon.”
Trust in government gone after October 7
At a nearby table, 24-year-old Yael Meyer sat with classmates from Tel Aviv University. The attack the previous day aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, they said, only reinforced the trauma of October 7 and the war that followed.
“I’m always aware that there could be another terror attack. But I always had the sense that the security services would protect us.” Since October 7, that trust in the government is gone, she said.
Her friend Talia Zecler, also 24, said she felt “helpless” after the attack. “I was angry at my country. Entire families were killed or kidnapped,” she added. “It feels like we’re living in an endless war.”
Her heart races when the sound of a passing motorcycle resembles an air-raid siren. But at the same time, she still marvels at the bravery and solidarity of ordinary Israelis in the months after the attack.
“People became more connected after October 7. They volunteered everywhere, including at Hostage Square,” she said. “There was a sense of unity, that we’re in this together, and we saw it on the flydubai flight.
“This is the Israeli spirit.”
Sitting in the café with her parents, S., a 19-year-old IDF soldier, said the trauma she experienced on October 7 at her home in Jerusalem “is minuscule” compared to the experience of those whose families were directly harmed by the attacks on the Gaza border and, later, attacks by Hezbollah, Iran, and the Houthis.
“Sure, when I hear a plane flying in the sky, I think, will there be another war with Iran? I immediately go there,” said S., whose name could not be published due to military protocol.
But as the country prepares to vote for the next government on October 27, she plans to channel her hopes and dreams in the voting booth.
“The most important things for me right now are to have a national investigation of what happened on October 7 and to repair our relations not only with our immediate neighbors but everywhere. We don’t live in a vacuum,” she said.

Laos Replaces Prime Minister in Major Leadership Reshuffle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:45:00 UTC
12:45:00 KST

Laos’ National Assembly yesterday approved a major leadership change that included the removal of Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone.
In what the state-run Vientiane Times described as “a significant change in senior state leadership,” lawmakers yesterday voted unanimously to appoint Sonexay’s deputy Saleumxay Kommasith as the country’s new prime minister. Sonexay was appointed president of the National Assembly, succeeding the late Xaysomphone Phomvihane.
The position has been vacant since Xaysomphone, the son of revered communist leader Kaysone Phomvihane, died in August at the age of 70. The Central Committee of the ruling Lao People’s Revolutionary Party described his passing as “an immense loss for the Party, the State and the Lao people of all ethnic groups.”
According to the Laotian Times, 57-year-old Saleumxay has a background in diplomacy, having spent much of his career in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He has previously served as Laos’ representative to the United Nations and as foreign minister between 2016 and 2024, and was also appointed as a deputy prime minister in 2022.
Beyond the need to fill the vacant National Assembly position, Lao media reports were reticent about the reasons for Sonexay’s removal, and in Laos it is often hard to separate performance-based from patronage-based appointments. Nonetheless, the fact that he was kept on as prime minister at the last national congress of the LPRP in January, presumably with the expectation that he would serve for a full five-year term, suggests that the reasons for his removal are probably more short-term.
Indeed, his successor’s address to the National Assembly after yesterday’s vote may offer some clues as to the change. In his remarks to lawmakers, Saleumxay praised the country’s current economic trajectory, stating that the economy grew by 4.8 percent in the first nine months of 2026, up from 4.6 percent over the same period last year. But according to the Vientiane Times, he also noted that agriculture “continues to face difficulties. Floods, pest outbreaks, and African swine fever have affected production, while fuel price volatility has increased production and transport costs.”
Laos’ economy has been under severe strain in recent years. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the country was hit by a debt-driven economic crisis that was marked by spiraling inflation, a rapid depreciation of the kip, and, for a period in mid-2022, fuel shortages that threatened the country’s food security. While Laos has since managed to stabilize its economy somewhat, the impact of the energy supply shock emanating from the U.S.-Iran war has threatened to disturb this progress, as the new prime minister’s remarks yesterday suggest.
Whatever the drivers, yesterday’s leadership shake-up is just the latest in a number of reshuffles that have broken the historically placid surface of Lao political life. The most recent of these was in late 2022, when Phankham Viphavanh was removed as prime minister, in a move that was widely recognized as a response to the economic crisis. On that occasion, the beneficiary was none other than Sonexay.
According to the Laotian Times, Laos also reshuffled nine senior government officials in June 2025, including the governor of the central bank and ministers responsible for finance, education, health, labor, agriculture, and industry and commerce.

US President Donald Trump called Russia’s suspected pneumonic plague case a “big problem” on Monday as unofficial reports indicated that nearly 200 people were under observation following the death of a researcher at a Siberian infectious-disease laboratory.
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “It’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter, like an army.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Asked about the risk of the disease spreading internationally through travel, Trump appeared to play down the immediate threat, saying there was little travel headed toward the affected area.
The White House has said it is monitoring the situation in Russia and beyond after the researcher died days after being diagnosed with pneumonia of “unknown origin,” according to a Russian health agency.
Speaking on CNN, Dr. Ashish Jha, a former White House COVID-19 response coordinator and infectious-disease expert, said the circumstances surrounding the death raised “a lot of red flags.”
Jha pointed to reports that nearly 200 people were under observation, that several hospitals had been locked down and that Russia’s FSB security service had become involved in the response.
“That is not what you would expect from a simple lab accident,” Jha told CNN.
He also raised concerns about the history of the laboratory itself, saying it is officially described as a civilian facility but has longstanding links to military biological research.
Trump Blames Ukrainian Strikes on Russian Refineries for High Gas Prices
Jha further said Russia has been expanding its biological-weapons capabilities, arguing that the combination of the laboratory’s history, the scale of the quarantine measures and the limited information released by Russian authorities warranted closer scrutiny.
“Take those two facts, take the facts that you just mentioned, it is hard not to be concerned that there is something more going on,” Jha said.
He stressed, however, that there was no confirmed evidence the researcher had been exposed to a weaponized pathogen.
Russian opposition figure and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, also speaking to CNN, argued that the Kremlin’s lack of transparency made official Russian accounts difficult to trust.
Kasparov said Russia was operating on a war footing and suggested the laboratory could have been involved in military biological research, though he offered no direct evidence that the researcher’s death was connected to a weapons program.
“Whatever they said, they lied,” Kasparov said of Russian authorities, arguing that official statements from Moscow should be treated with deep skepticism.
Dr. Jonathan Reiner, a CNN medical analyst, urged caution, saying there was still no independent confirmation that the researcher had died from plague or clarity about how she became infected.
“It’s hard to know until we have more information,” Reiner said, adding that early reports during disease outbreaks are often “wrong, or incomplete, or misleading.”
He cautioned against jumping to either extreme – assuming the incident marked the beginning of another pandemic or dismissing it as nothing to worry about.
Reiner also stressed that pneumonic plague is very different from COVID-19. The disease has been known for centuries and can be treated effectively with antibiotics when detected early.
CNN separately reported that roughly 200 people were under quarantine or medical observation, while hospitals in the area had imposed restrictions and Russian officials said the woman died from severe pneumonia of unknown origin.
Russian authorities quarantined people connected to the Siberian research facility after the researcher’s death, while health officials stopped short of confirming pneumonic plague as the cause.
Officials in the Irkutsk region said the woman had died from severe pneumonia of “unknown origin,” even as restrictions around the facility expanded and questions grew over the circumstances of her illness. Russian authorities also publicly denied reports that pneumonic plague had been confirmed.

- Meloni faces ongoing deepfake abuses, has taken legal action, but the trademark may only add legal hurdles, not fully prevent misuse.
AI generated
ROME - Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has applied to the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) to trademark her voice in a new move to protect herself against AI-generated deepfakes, records showed on Oct 5.
Her application, dated Oct 5 on the EUIPO website and confirmed by her office, includes a four-second audio recording of herself twice repeating the phrase, in Italian, “I am Giorgia Meloni”.
Io Sono Giorgia (I Am Giorgia) was the title of her 2021 autobiography that echoed a famous declaration Meloni made at a political rally in 2019 and which was even turned into a disco track.
Manipulated images of Meloni have circulated online in recent years and have at times been shared as authentic, including one depicting her sitting on a bed in her underwear.
Meloni has denounced such material as part of efforts to spread falsehoods and target individuals, urging users to verify content before sharing it online. She has said that while she is able to defend herself, many others are not.
The EUIPO application is still under examination.
Italian media have reported that even if approved, the application would not by itself prevent the use of her voice in AI-generated deepfakes, though it could create additional legal obstacles for those seeking to replicate it.
In 2024, Meloni launched a civil action against a man from Sardinia accused of creating and posting online deepfake pornographic images using her face. The case remains pending before an Italian court. REUTERS

Women's stars call on Cricket Australia to fix scheduling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:32:27 UTC
12:32:27 KST

Australian women's cricketers are urging Cricket Australia to look at fixturing to give the national team visibility for its young fans amid a big gap in the schedule.
After upcoming white-ball matches against Bangladesh and New Zealand, the Australian team will not play on home soil until March 2027.
Under current schedules, there will be no WBBL or international women's cricket during the school holidays in Australia for at least the next three years.
Senior women's players have called on Cricket Australia to push to return some of their games to the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule will hurt the sport's growth among girls.
Australia begin their home summer against Bangladesh on Friday, marking the first of three ODIs in Brisbane before three T20s against New Zealand in Sydney.
All three of the Sydney matches fall on school nights.
They will then not play on home soil until they host New Zealand for ODIs in March, in what looms as a sign of things to come for the world's number one-ranked team.
Under the current ICC schedule, there will be no WBBL or international women's cricket during the school holidays in Australia for at least the next three years, with all fixtures in the shoulder seasons.
"We don't want to be the sport that falls behind because we're just getting it wrong," veteran wicketkeeper-bat Beth Mooney told AAP.
"We're just pushing it uphill, because we're in a bad timeslot and it's a bad time of year for parents.
"They're not dragging their kid out to watch a 7pm T20 on a Tuesday night or whatever it is.
"That's going to stop girls getting into the game, because parents aren't going to take them."
Mooney's comments come after Australia's most-capped player Ellyse Perry expressed similar concerns earlier last month.
Australian players have for a long time had some frustrations over the schedule, particularly around the same consistency in men's cricket.
This summer has been impacted by the ICC moving the Champions' Trophy to India, leaving no international women's games at all in Perth.
But multiple players have also expressed concerns to AAP over India being able to claim the January window for its lucrative WPL, fearing it will only expand into a larger window. This year it runs January 14 to February 7.
They are concerned the national team is at risk of being out of sight and out of mind, stunting momentum after another T20 World Cup win.
One push is for more home matches to be scheduled in December around the Christmas window, with Australia to tour Sri Lanka through that period this year.
"We're not getting crowds, it's not marketed well. There is no big-ticket item where people go, 'The Australian women's team play here [at this time] every year,'" Mooney said.
"We want to be relatable athletes. And if we're not front and centre of the summer it makes it pretty difficult when it's meant to be a summer sport.
"We don't need to compete with the men. They play the day-night Test at some point. We can have T20s before that.
"Or we can play night T20s when there is a men's Test on."
Australia's coach Shelley Nitschke said it was "obviously disappointing" not to play at home in December or January, while captain Sophie Molineux argued home games in December would be "really special" for her team.
"It would also help see fans come through," Molineux said.
"I completely understand that the schedules are getting bigger and busier."

Taiwan civil groups oppose barring certain suspects from receiving legal aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:29:19 UTC
12:29:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nine civil society groups issued a joint statement Monday opposing KMT lawmaker Lin Pei-hsiang’s (林沛祥) proposed amendment to the Legal Aid Act and calling for greater investment in legal aid services.
Lin proposed freezing NT$50 million (US$1.58 million) and eliminating NT$5 million from the Judicial Yuan’s 2026 budget, per Tai Sounds. He also called on the Judicial Yuan to bar the Legal Aid Foundation from providing services to suspects in murder, fatal drug-driving, fraud, sexual assault and child abuse cases. The proposal is reportedly backed by Judicial Yuan Secretary-General Kao Chin-chih (高金枝).
Lin said roughly 90% of the foundation’s work involves providing legal counsel to suspects. He also alleged that the foundation’s finances are rife with falsehoods and called for government intervention.
The Judicial Reform Foundation, Amnesty International Taiwan, Taiwan Association for Human Rights, Environmental Rights Foundation and five other civil society groups rejected Lin’s proposal and his characterization of the foundation’s work, per UDN.
Citing the foundation’s 2025 data, the groups said its lawyers handled 29,931 criminal cases, accounting for 51.58% of all lawsuits handled by the foundation. When legal counseling services are included, the foundation received 233,000 applications, more than 123,000 of which were for legal counseling.
The groups further explained that among the foundation’s regular cases, 6,353, or 10.95%, involved criminal defense, while 32,421 involved people who were underage or had mental disabilities, and 22,699 involved people facing financial difficulties. The groups warned that directing criminal defense cases back to the public defender system could further overburden an already strained legal system, per Newtalk.
The civil society groups argued that if the government believes victims are not receiving sufficient resources, it should invest more in the legal aid system rather than limit its services and force it to choose between protecting victims and upholding suspects’ right to counsel.
Taiwan Association for Victims of Occupational Injuries Commissioner He Kuang-wan (賀光卍) cautioned against pitting victim protection against suspects’ right to counsel, per UP Media. He said providing legal counsel does not mean identifying with the accused, and that upholding procedural justice does not equate to easing victims’ pain.

Google, Constellation Energy near billion-dollar deal for nuclear power

- Nuclear power is gaining renewed interest due to its reliable, emissions-free electricity, crucial for the AI boom and tech companies' rising energy demands.
- Other tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft have similar agreements with nuclear operators, reflecting a broader industry trend towards nuclear energy for clean, constant power.
AI generated
MARYLAND – Google parent Alphabet is close to an agreement to buy nuclear energy from Constellation Energy as technology companies race to line up power for the data centre boom.
The tech giant is nearing a deal to pay Constellation US$1 billion (S$1.28 billion) or more over the course of a multi-year agreement that is expected to be announced as soon as this week, according to people familiar with the discussions, who asked not to be named because the information is private.
Constellation, the biggest US reactor operator, and Google declined to comment on Oct 5. The exact scale and location of the nuclear capacity could not be determined.
The immense amount of electricity required for the artificial intelligence boom is helping to revive interest in nuclear energy, which offers round-the-clock power that is also emissions-free. Recent deals have focused on existing facilities as new reactors can take a decade or more to obtain permits and build, and the next wave of fission technology is still likely years from widespread deployment.
Amazon struck a similar deal last week with Constellation. The cloud and e-commerce company agreed to buy 690MW of power, including capacity from upgrading the Calvert Cliffs nuclear facility in Maryland.
Google already has multiple agreements with atomic power producers. It agreed in 2025 to buy electricity from NextEra Energy, a deal that will support the power company’s plans to restart its Duane Arnold reactor in Iowa that has been shuttered since 2020. And in September, the tech company lined up new capacity from Southern by funding upgrades at two atomic plants.
Microsoft agreed to buy electricity from the shuttered Three Mile Island nuclear plant in 2024, and Constellation is planning to restart its reactor at the site in Pennsylvania in 2027.
While safety risks and heavy cost overruns saw the world sour on atomic energy early last decade, it has been undergoing a global revival over the last few years. As well as surging demand from the tech sector for data centres, nuclear power is being embraced by many nations as a way to cope with a jump in electricity consumption while cutting emissions. The meeting will build on discussions from other Apec financial meetings and cover topics including global and regional macroeconomic conditions, fiscal policies to support people's livelihoods and digital infrastructure financing.
The ministry will arrange hotel accommodation, transport and reception services in line with Apec guidelines, Lee said, adding that the SAR government would assist delegations with their registration procedures and work closely with the ministry throughout the process.
The chief executive thanked the central government for its trust in the SAR government in hosting the event.

South Korea shipped fuel to Russia via sanctioned vessels, media reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:13:48 UTC
12:13:48 KST

In several instances in July and August 2026, fuel was shipped from South Korea to Russia, according to the Guardian on Oct. 6.
Potentially undermining sanctions, over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, from South Korean ports were loaded onto sanctioned Russian tankers, the Guardian reported. The findings were based on an analysis of port records and ship-tracking data.
Seven Russian tankers, including three sanctioned by the UK and EU, made 14 voyages from the nation's far-eastern ports to South Korean ports, where they were loaded with fuel before returning. In one instance, fuel was loaded onto a Russian tanker via ship-to-ship transfer, avoiding South Korean ports.
The transfer of fuel does not appear to violate South Korean law, the Guardian reported, despite involving vessels sanctioned by Seoul's western partners. South Korean export controls against Russia currently focus on electronics, machinery, and vehicles.
While Moscow is known to use its shadow fleet of aging, poorly insured tankers to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil infrastructure have sent it scrambling for fuel.
Ukraine has systematically targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure in long-range strikes, dramatically increasing its campaign against oil refineries in the past two years. Kyiv considers refineries valid military targets, as they supply both fuel and funds to the Russian armed forces.
On Oct. 4, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks.
Since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, South Korea has stood as an ally to Ukraine, sending 630 million euros ($706 million) in bilateral aid as of February 2026, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.
However, in recent weeks, relations between Seoul and Kyiv have been strained.
President Volodymyr Zelensky angered Seoul after providing details of a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea during a Sept. 23 U.N. General Assembly speech. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Oct. 2 warned of "additional measures" against Ukraine if its government refuses to take responsibility for a downward spiral in Kyiv-Seoul relations.
While the South Korean foreign ministry did not comment on the findings directly, it told the Guardian in a statement that as “a responsible member of the international community, the [South Korean] government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”

Secessionist party wins Quebec election in Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:11:44 UTC
12:11:44 KST

Secessionist party wins Quebec election in Canada
Parti Quebecois returns to power, promising a third referendum on Quebec’s independence from Canada.
The secessionist Parti Quebecois has won the most seats in Quebec’s election and will form the next government in the predominantly French-speaking Canadian province, according to media reports.
The result on Monday revives the question of whether the province should leave Canada, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity.
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the party’s leader, is set to become premier.
During the campaign, he promised a third referendum on leaving Canada during his first term, although he said he would wait until US President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029.
It was not yet clear whether the party had reached the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly.
If it falls short, it would lead a minority government and need support from opposition lawmakers to pass major legislation and survive confidence votes.
The Parti Quebecois, or PQ, last governed the province from 2012 to 2014.
Monday’s victory marks a sharp recovery for the PQ, which won just three seats in the 2022 provincial election.
Its return also ends eight years in power for the Coalition Avenir Quebec, or CAQ, a centre-right Quebec nationalist party that does not support independence.
Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, told The Associated Press news agency that the victory reflects Quebec’s multiparty system, where support is divided among several parties, rather than a surge in secessionist sentiment.
Support for independence remains at about 30 percent, low by historical standards, he said.
Still, Beland said a secessionist government in Quebec represents a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching in Alberta.
“Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Beland said.
Quebec held two previous referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995, and voters rejected secession both times.
The second vote was decided by a narrow margin, but there has been no further referendum in the three decades since.

Israel continues to face major mental health struggles in wake of October 7, ERAN data show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:11:33 UTC
12:11:33 KST

Three years after October 7, 2023, the Israeli public still faces substantial mental health struggles in a variety of categories, the ERAN organization revealed on Tuesday.
In the three years since the war began, over 928,000 people have been aided by ERAN's professional mental health teams, assisted by 1,850 volunteers.
Over 150,000 people also used ERAN's digital mental health services during this time, in addition to over 770,000 who called one of ERAN's hotlines.
"The three years of war have confronted us with a harsh and enduring reality," David Koren, CEO of ERAN, said. "Behind every person who reaches out to us lies a story of coping with pain, loss, anxiety, loneliness, or burnout - and often, a combination of these. Amidst this reality, we work tirelessly to provide a safe space where individuals can share their experiences, find a listening ear, and know that they do not have to bear their burdens alone."
Out of all those whom ERAN aided, 21,829 suffered from an issue related in some way to suicidality or suicidal ideation.
The percentage of youths turning to ERAN for assistance in cases related to suicidality, the organization reported, had nearly doubled since October 7, going from 2.6% during the first year of the war to 4.4%.
"ERAN’s data reminds us that, precisely amidst the illusion of normalcy, it is crucial to notice those who are struggling, recognize signs of distress, ask directly about suicidality when concerns arise, listen, and ensure that help is accessible before the distress deepens," Dr. Shiri Daniels, National Director of Counseling at ERAN, said.
ERAN also reported that the percentage of requests related to loneliness had sharply risen, from 28% at the start of the war to 41% by its third year.
Violence, sexual harm doubles for soldiers calling ERAN since Oct. 7
Among soldiers, calls related to violence and sexual harm doubled from 5% to 10% between the first and second years of the war, lowering to 8% in the third year.
However, the proportion of soldiers who brought up an issue related to suicidality throughout the three years since October 7 has remained at 1%, without any rise.

Human Rights Council adopts China-proposed resolution on accessibility for all
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
11:11:04 CST
12:11:04 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- The 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) on Monday adopted by consensus the draft resolution titled "Promoting accessibility for the full enjoyment of all human rights by all" proposed by China on behalf of 47 countries.
Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, said during his introductory remarks that building an accessible environment provides important safeguards for people of all groups to participate equally and conveniently in social life and to fully enjoy their human rights.
This draft resolution seeks to promote accessibility and an age-friendly environment in the context of population ageing. It also focuses on the opportunities and challenges arising from emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, and calls upon all countries to prioritize innovation, inclusiveness, openness, fairness, safety and security in the development and use of emerging digital technologies, with a view to enhancing the accessibility of information and communications, Jia said.
Representatives of Cuba and Egypt, among others, spoke in support of the resolution, commending China for actively promoting the concept of "accessibility for all" and moving forward the accessibility cause.
They believed that the resolution calls for providing technical assistance for developing countries and promoting international cooperation in relevant fields, in line with the needs of developing countries.
In 2024, the UNHRC adopted, for the first time, a resolution under the same title proposed by China, marking the first thematic resolution on accessibility in UN history. ■

====================================================================================================

Israel must be ready for any threat, no matter how unthinkable it may seem - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:10:56 UTC
12:10:56 KST

Tomorrow, Israel marks three years since the October 7 massacre, the darkest day in the state’s history.
The anniversaries are occasions for mourning, remembrance, and, unfortunately, argument over who bears accountability and responsibility. But they must also remain moments for examining whether the lessons of that catastrophe have actually been absorbed.
Following the military’s investigations into October 7, the IDF intends to base its readiness on what Israel’s enemies are capable of doing, rather than on assessments of what they intend to do.
“It is our duty to investigate and ensure that the lessons are implemented so that we may be more worthy of the trust the people have placed in us,” IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Zamir said at the memorial ceremony held at Zikim military base early Monday.
That idea should extend well beyond the physical battlefield on which IDF soldiers fight and die.
The next strategic surprise will not necessarily resemble the last one. Israel has spent three years trying to strengthen or reinforce its borders, fighting a war on multiple fronts, and reconsidering intelligence assumptions.
Last week Israel came close to another disaster
But adversaries adapt, and a threat to Israelis may emerge through a border fence, a cyberattack, a shipping route, or, as last week demonstrated, from inside the cockpit of a commercial aircraft.
The story is well known and does not need to be repeated here in detail. Indian pilot Capt. Smit Machchhar’s bravery, and the courage of the Israeli passengers, have rightly received enormous praise. But it should not obscure how close Israel came to another disaster, born of the assumption that an extraordinary scenario was too unlikely to demand adequate preparation.
Officials in Oman reportedly removed the terrorist copilot, Hamam al-Hammami, from flying duties over concerns about extremism. The Jerusalem Post has reported on how flydubai hired him without conducting a background check with the Omani government.
Australian authorities had information about his activities during his years there as a student. Royal Air Maroc trained him for three months in 2025 and then declined to employ him.
Meanwhile, in Israel, the usual void of accountability exists: In this case, who is responsible for the security vetting of pilots for airlines flying to Israel?
According to an Israeli source, Hammami told investigators he had researched airlines operating routes to Tel Aviv and deliberately chose flydubai.
This doesn’t necessarily mean every warning would necessarily have reached Israeli authorities, or that every foreign pilot flying to Ben-Gurion Airport can realistically undergo an Israeli intelligence investigation.
But it does mean that the security system must ask whether its assumptions about civil aviation have kept pace with the threats confronting Israel.
October 7 demonstrated the danger of confusing an assessment with a guarantee.
For years, Israel knew that Hamas possessed the capability to breach the border, attack communities, fire rockets, and take hostages. What failed was the assessment of intent. Hamas was believed to be deterred, interested in preserving its rule in Gaza, and unlikely to risk the devastating Israeli response that a major assault would invite.
That assumption collapsed at 6:29 a.m. on October 7, 2023.
The Flydubai incident is obviously different in scale and circumstance – more of a lone-wolf than a pack attack – and it would be unfair to equate the two. But the intellectual warning is familiar.
A trusted airline from a friendly state, operating a routine commercial route to Israel, does not stop presenting security risks simply because the relationship is peaceful and the flight has become ordinary. Nor does the possibility of a radicalized crew member disappear because such a scenario sounds improbable.
Security is partly about preparing for events one hopes never occur.
Israel cannot investigate every imaginable danger with equal intensity. Resources are finite, intelligence is not perfect, and there is always the element of surprise. But October 7 should have permanently lowered Israel’s tolerance for vulnerabilities whose consequences could be catastrophic.
The passengers aboard flight FZ1073 were extraordinarily fortunate and brave. Their ability to improvise under terrifying circumstances saved lives. But Israel’s security doctrine cannot rest on civilian improvisation.
October 7 showed the balance and cost of judging likelihood versus capability. Israel will never be able to anticipate every threat, but it can no longer afford to treat dangerous possibilities as remote simply because they are difficult to imagine. The unthinkable has already happened once.

CIA warns deepening internal fractures put Israel at risk of civil war — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:10:29 UTC
12:10:29 KST

A classified United States intelligence assessment has warned that deepening political, economic, and social fractures could place Israel at risk of civil war or state collapse, according to an investigative report.
The analysis, titled "Fracture From Within", was prepared in August by the CIA's Red Cell— a specialist unit mandated to challenge prevailing intelligence consensus and provide alternative strategic perspectives — independent investigative outlet Drop Site News reported, citing two US sources familiar with its contents.
The assessment outlines a volatile convergence of domestic pressures confronting the country ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27.
Key friction points include severe economic contraction, soaring defence expenditure, escalating settler violence across the occupied West Bank, and deep societal resentment over compulsory military service exemptions granted to ultra-Orthodox men.
Combat trauma, political survival, and isolation
The report singles out Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's battle to retain power as a primary driver of constitutional and political instability.
Years of genocide in Gaza and continuous warfare across Lebanon and Iran have exacerbated existing social divisions, with significant numbers of returning reservists suffering severe psychological trauma following protracted deployments.
The military draft has developed into one of the country's most acute domestic fault lines, as repeated reserve mobilisations fuel anger over blanket exemptions maintained for the ultra-Orthodox community.
Compounding these domestic stresses, the CIA document warns that growing international diplomatic isolation—characterised by eroding support within the United States—threatens to accelerate internal destabilisation.

Coalition promises deep cuts in migration fight with One Nation, Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:09:55 UTC
12:09:55 KST

Coalition promises deep cuts as it enters migration fight with One Nation and Labor
In short:
The Coalition has unveiled a plan to drive net overseas migration down to 100,000 for two years through major changes to graduate, humanitarian and other visa programs.
It would go further than Labor's migration targets while increasing skilled migration, but the Coalition has not released modelling of the broader economic impact.
What's next?
The Coalition has promised to release costings for its migration policy closer to the 2028 federal election.
The Coalition would slash Australia's temporary migration intake by about 650,000 over four years through deep cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas that go further than Labor's plan.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has unveiled what he described as the "biggest cut to immigration in this country's history", declaring he was "confident" the changes would be budget "neutral" but without offering modelling on the broader economic impact of the policy.
Under a future Coalition government, net overseas migration (NOM) would be slashed to 100,000 for the first two years, followed by 130,000 in the third and 160,000 in the fourth year.
Australia's NOM fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, with Labor pursuing a target of 245,000 for this financial year and 225,000 the year after.
Mr Taylor said Australia needed "breathing space" after several record years of migration post-pandemic, arguing this was best achieved by slashing temporary migrants and prioritising high-skilled workers, including in construction.
"Australia should be a home, not a hotel," he said.
One Nation has announced it would cut 750,000 temporary visas, resulting in a negative NOM for three years and then an intake of 130,000 people in the fourth year.
Mr Taylor announced the Coalition's alternative proposal on Tuesday, which includes a cap on student visas and halving Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 annually.
The biggest cut is to bridging visas, which would go from about 414,00 to 20,000 by forcing temporary visa holders to leave Australia if they want to apply for a new visa.
The Coalition would also impose a 30-day limit for anyone wanting to make an onshore claim for asylum in Australia.
What are each party's migration targets?
Read more
Labor:
The government is aiming for 245,000 net overseas migration (NOM) by June next year, and 225,000 by the middle of 2028. Those figures were forecast in the budget and are now a target.
In March, the NOM was 292,100, according to figures released last month by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Coalition:
The Coalition has announced an annual NOM target of 100,000 for the first two years if it wins the election.
It will aim for 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in the fourth year.
One Nation:
The minor party unveiled a policy to slash immigration by 750,000 over three years, pushing the NOM into negative territory.
After that, they would aim for a "ceiling" of 130,000, to be reviewed every year.
Which visas would be affected?
Temporary graduate visas would be scrapped except for some limited post-study pathways for PhD, health and education graduates, as well as those studying at regional universities.
The Coalition would cap international student commencements at 240,000, restrict most dependents from accompanying them and link each student visa to the institution they enrolled with.
Mr Taylor said he would increase the share of skilled migrants, including about 60,000 more temporary skilled visa holders and 15,000 new skilled project visas a year for major projects.
The talent and innovation allocation would double to 7,000 through a new AUKUS and Five Eyes visa, while permanent applicants would be prioritised based on factors like age, income, English language proficiency and skilled partners.
The temporary skilled priority list would be changed to fast track construction and prioritise employer-sponsored migration in regional Australia.
Broadly, anyone making a second or subsequent temporary visa application would have to leave Australia and lodge the paperwork offshore.
The Coalition would scrap Labor's caps for second and third-year working holiday maker visa extensions and instead increase fees with exemptions for those who completed required regional work.
Loading...
Economic knock-on effects
The cuts would initially bring Australia's migration levels down to the lowest outside the pandemic since 2004.
Mr Taylor said the Coalition had been working with the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) and the policy would be "neutral" on the federal budget.
He did not release any costings but implied this would be achieved by an increase in skilled migrants at the expense of other visa classes.
Mr Taylor said the economics were "simple" because a student or temporary graduate visa holder contributed on average $7,000 to $14,000 in taxes compared to a temporary skilled visa holder contributing more than $30,000.
"If you bring people in who can make a … significant contribution and they're going to work hard, then it's better for the budget and the economy,"
he said.
Mr Taylor accused Labor of using population growth to prop up Australia's broader economic prosperity but did not release modelling showing what such a large reduction in migration would mean for the economy.
The Coalition has promised to release costing closer to the federal election in 2028.
One Nation reacts to Coalition policy
Nationals leader Matt Canavan described the measures as a plan to "take back our country" from temporary migrants, who he accused of undercutting Australians' wages.
"We are a country, not a campground," he said.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who unveiled her own policy to dramatically reduce temporary migration last month, said the Coalition had turned up "late to the grand final" with a policy after "both teams have headed back to the changerooms".
She said Labor and the Coalition had both been "dragged kicking and screaming" into the debate by One Nation.
"It might sound like Liberal and Labor are saying the right thing, but actions speak louder than words," Ms Hanson said.
Labor's limits on visas
Last month, the federal government unveiled several changes aimed at reducing Australia's migration intake, with measures largely targeting students and their families as well as working holiday-makers.
Under changes that came into effect on Friday, international students would largely be barred from bringing family, would need a new visa to change courses and could only move to a higher-level qualification after graduating.
Limits imposed on the working holiday-maker program included the introduction of a ballot system for visa holders hoping to stay in Australia beyond one year.
The ballot would be capped at 45,000 second-year places and 5,000 third-year places, down from about 57,000 and 31,000 respectively last year.
Labor also redesigned the skilled migration points test to give greater recognition to construction trades, with those regulatory changes made about two weeks ago.

EU suspends some meat imports from Namibia over foot and mouth disease outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
03:04:58 UTC
12:04:58 KST

James Kunda
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The European Union temporarily suspended imports of fresh beef, sheep and goat meat as well as some processed meat products from Namibia on Monday following an outbreak of the highly contagious foot-and-mouth livestock disease.
In a statement issued in the capital Windhoek, EU ambassador to Namibia Ana Beatriz Martins said the suspension also covered certain farmed and wild hoofed animals as well as products such as biltong and jerky.
“The measures are aimed at protecting animal health while Namibia works to contain the outbreak. However, processed meat that has undergone the EU’s prescribed high-level treatment to reduce foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) risks can still enter the European market,” Martins said.
FMD was confirmed on a commercial farm in the Karasburg State Veterinary District in the southern African nation in late September. Following the outbreak, Namibian authorities notified the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and introduced restrictions on the movement and export of cloven-hoofed animals and their products.
WOAH subsequently suspended Namibia’s FMD-free status for the affected zone with effect from Sept. 26.
“Namibia has responded with speed and transparency, and we commend its veterinary services for their professional response,” Martins added.

Assange created the ‘fifth estate’ – ex-CIA analyst (VIDEO)
Julian Assange is a key figure in the creation of alternative media, former CIA analyst Ray McGovern has said, expressing hope that the Australian journalist and activist is preparing to get back to work.
McGovern spoke to RT as WikiLeaks marks its 20th anniversary. The website, co-founded by Assange in 2006, has published some of the most explosive leaks of the past two decades, exposing CIA hacking tools, classified US war records, illegal mass surveillance, and other closely guarded secrets.
The platform became a global phenomenon, making Assange one of the most prominent contemporary publishers, while also embroiling him in more than a decade of conflict with the US and other governments. Ahead of the anniversary, Assange suggested that he will return to public life two years after striking a deal for his freedom with the US and securing his release from British custody.
Assange is a key figure in the creation of the alternative media, the “fifth estate,” McGovern said, adding that traditional media has lost its intended purpose, becoming closely controlled instruments for governments worldwide.
“The media in our country, and I dare say in many countries, the UK, Germany, is very tightly controlled. And so that’s the fourth estate, as Edmund Burke said, more important than Parliament itself. The fourth estate is co-opted now, it has been for decades,” he said.
“It’s very clear that the intelligence services have a lot of influence over what goes out into the media. And so you need an alternative. That’s why we placed great hope in what we call the ‘fifth estate,’ namely WikiLeaks and outfits like it that would encourage people to blow the whistle in a secure way and not endanger themselves.”
McGovern welcomed the prospect of Assange’s return to active work, calling it “salvation” for people willing to blow the whistle on dirty government secrets.
“He will find ways to make it possible for people like me and my colleagues, if we come upon information that needs to be spread out into the media or out into the public, to have a secure way of doing that. That was his success. He’s bright enough to do that again, I am convinced.”

War-weary northern Israelis rethink loyalty to Netanyahu before election

War-weary northern Israelis rethink loyalty to Netanyahu before election
- Northern Israelis, once strong supporters of Netanyahu, are reconsidering their votes due to dissatisfaction with his government's handling of ongoing conflicts with Hezbollah.
- The 2023-2024 war caused severe disruption, trauma, and displacement, shaking community trust and increasing calls for change amid prolonged violence and high living costs.
- Despite anger, some residents still back Netanyahu’s hawkish coalition, believing it offers the best protection against attacks and regional threats.
AI generated
Nahariya, Israel – On Israel’s border with Lebanon where Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets and drones, previous backers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu say they are rethinking how they will vote in the first election since the war.
“Many I know were right-wing and were Bibi supporters, and today they’re not,” said plant nursery owner Sigal Malachi, using a nickname for Israel’s longest-serving premier.
In traditional strongholds of Netanyahu support, many told AFP they could no longer back his right-wing government in the Oct 27 vote, accusing it of failing to secure a lasting quiet with the militants.
Hezbollah, an Iran-backed Lebanese militant group, began firing into Israel in October 2023 in support of Hamas following the deadliest-ever attack on the country.
The barrages altered life in northern communities, displacing tens of thousands of Israelis and forcing people like Malachi to close shop for several years.
Northern Israelis are accustomed to incoming fire from the Lebanese side of the border, but they say that round of conflict was more intense.
“We grew up with Katyushas (rockets) and bombs,” said Malachi, whose plant nursery reopened in March. “This war was different.”
She described that “if you went outside, within a second you’d be running” for shelter.
The war was halted with a fragile ceasefire in November 2024, but evacuees were not allowed home until early 2025.
Life began slowly returning to normal, until the northern front reopened after the outbreak of the Iran war.
Maxim Zarbaylov, who was born in the former Soviet Union but has long lived in Nahariya, the northern-most Israeli town on the Mediterranean, is among those wavering.
“All my life I voted for (Likud), for Bibi Netanyahu... But this year I want to vote for (Gadi) Eisenkot,” he said, referring to the former military chief who is Netanyahu’s main election rival.
Hezbollah has repeatedly dragged Lebanon into conflicts with Israel, most recently in March with rocket fire at Israel in support of Iran.
Israel has in turn seized what it calls a “security zone” in Lebanon, where authorities say Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people.
At least 48 Israeli civilians and 30 soldiers have died on the Lebanese front since 2023.
‘Psychological catastrophe’
The prolonged violence has left border residents in limbo.
“After Oct 7, we don’t sleep well anymore,” Malachi said. “I’ve thought about leaving. But the roots are so deep that I’m staying.”
In Shlomi, an Israeli border town, the enemy is a tangible presence behind a hill.
Shadi Tuma, who owns a supermarket there, prides himself on running the only one that remained open.
“This area is under a trauma we haven’t seen before. There’s anger. The government is unable to provide a comprehensive response,” he said. “It’s a huge psychological catastrophe. Not everyone is able to cope with a war that lasts three years.”
The war has cracked the local support base for Netanyahu, Tuma said.
In the last elections in 2022, the premier’s Likud party won 43% of the vote in Shlomi, compared with 23% nationwide.
Residents who backed Netanyahu “now want change because they no longer trust this government”, Tuma said.
He said the high cost of living was a major complaint.
“Many people I see are struggling to make it to the end of the month.”
For Tuma, the conflict is also personal.
He was born in Lebanon, the son of a fighter with the South Lebanon Army, a militia that fought alongside Israel in the 1980s and that had many fighters granted Israeli citizenship.
‘Feel protected’
The war could have shifted longstanding political loyalties in towns like Nahariya, a sleepy resort of about 70,000 people.
In 2022, 38% of voters there chose Likud.
But Zarbaylov says there is anger over the failure to stop Hamas’ unprecedented assault on the country.
“What happened on Oct 7, Bibi could have prevented it, but he didn’t,” he said. “The army, the top commanders, the chief of staff, could have prevented it.”
Others believe only the current hawkish coalition can protect them.
Patrice Haddad retired to Nahariya from Paris a year ago, drawn by the town’s “charm”.
Israel’s “Law of Return” allows any Jew anywhere in the world to immigrate and automatically receive citizenship.
Adjusting to life under the rockets was not simple at first.
“We were told we had 30 seconds to find shelter” after sirens blared, he said. “In reality, sometimes we only had 15, sometimes less.”
For his first election as an Israeli, he has made his choice.
“The left in Israel has done a lot of harm, it wanted to give up territories,” he said. “It’s important to vote for the right, because for me, with a government like Netanyahu’s, we will feel protected.” AFP

How Christian Networks in Asia Are Shaping Support for Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
02:59:00 UTC
11:59:00 KST

With much of the international discourse, specifically in North America and Europe, focused on criticizing Israel, a large group of international Christian leaders congregated in Jerusalem to show support. One of the key participants was senior Filipino pastor Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña who leads a large evangelical community across the Philippine islands. Bishop Sobrepeña is the founder of Word of Hope Christian Ministries which includes 43 satellite churches and hosts 70 services on any given Sunday across Manila. Partaking in this year’s event, Bishop Sobrepeña stated, “For Christians in the Philippines, the opportunity to come here and pray in Jerusalem is deeply meaningful. We also come to listen to the people of Israel and to carry their stories back to the churches and communities we serve.”
The Bishop was one of more than 550 prominent Christian leaders with vast followings who recently participated in a 10-day Eagles’ Wings delegation organized in conjunction with Bishop Sterns and Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Attendees hailed from 51 different nations and congregated around the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) in Jerusalem, commemorating the third anniversary of the October 7th attack. The gathering offers a window into a less frequently discussed dimension of the Israel debate: the continued mobilization of Christian communities in parts of Asia and the wider Global South around Israel.
Taking a closer look at Israel sentiment in Western countries, antisemitism interwoven with anti-Israel sentiment is on the rise. In 2025 the Anti Defamation League (ADL) recorded 6,274 antisemitic events in North America alone. The Hillel organization reported 2,334 incidents across U.S. campuses in the 2024-2025 academic year, stating that, “Antisemitic incidents on campus are at a record high in the past school year.”
In Western Europe the Community Security Trust (CST) recorded a staggering 3,700 antisemitic incidents across Britain over the course of 2025, the second highest annual total of such events ever recorded. French authorities cited 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025, with France’s Interior Ministry calling it a “historically high” figure.
As sentiment over Israel grows increasingly polarized in the West, there are a number of well-educated Asian evangelical Christian communities who unequivocally support Israel, comprising the backbone of its support in the region. South Korea is home to nearly 9 million evangelical and Pentecostal Protestants who display the Israeli flag during rallies and prayers. Roughly 8 percent of Singapore’s population run a network of influential evangelical megachurches while boasting an active Christian Zionist movement that mobilizes fundraising initiatives, educational tours and pro-Israel forums.
The Philippines is a particularly heavy hitter on the East Asian evangelical pro-Zionist front with an estimated 13 million evangelical adherents within a predominantly Catholic milieu. A Pew study surveying Pentecostals across 10 nations highlighted that 67 percent of Filipino Pentecostals surveyed said they sympathized with Israel.
In this context, Eagles’ Wings has been working for the last three decades to bring tens of thousands of evangelical Christians from around the globe to Israel. The organization was founded by Bishop Robert Stearns who is a staunch supporter of Israel and an outspoken supporter of moving the United States Embassy to Jerusalem. In Stephen Spector’s 2008 book Evangelicals and Israel: The Story of American Christian Zionism, Bishop Stearns discusses Israel’s regional threat profile while declaring himself willing to “die defending Israel.” He has spoken on Israel’s behalf both at the House of Lords in London and the Israeli Knesset.
Stearns founded Eagles’ Wings with a clear mission in mind: Firsthand encounters with Israel can be utilized to strongly shape how large Christian networks around the world understand Israel and antisemitism. They have been working to achieve this goal by having brought 25,000+ Christians to the Holy Land, organizing Nexus Leadership Missions which offer intensive educational tours to global pastoral leaders, as well as spearheading the Christian answer to Birthright, dubbed the ‘Israel Experience’, bringing college-age Christian students to Israel.
One of the key events as part of this year’s Eagles’ Wings 10-day delegation was “Awake Jerusalem at the Tower of David.” The event took place on October 3 at Jerusalem’s iconic Tower of David with hundreds of Christian leaders from 51 different countries in attendance. The event showcased international Christian artists while also including communal worship being covered and broadcasted by Daystar Television Network, a media partner of Eagles’ Wings.
For Israel, the challenges that lie ahead are not merely diplomatic. As the international stage becomes increasingly harder to navigate the relationships that Israel fosters with Asia and the Global South may become of increasing strategic importance. This gathering of 550 Christian leaders from 51 nation-states demonstrates merely one aspect of this shifting climate. Prominent religious communities from the Philippines to Korea and Brazil to Kenya will be able to shape the conversation about Israel within their respective societies. The mobilization of these groups shows the potential benefits that Israel stands to reap from fostering non-traditional alliances and that vis-à-vis culture, religion and interpersonal connections a new path to diplomacy may emerge.
