‘Microbes have gotten smarter’: Trump reacts to mysterious Siberia plague lab death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:08:54 UTC
08:08:54 KST

The death of Daria Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Irkutsk Oblast in Siberia, continues to reverberate around the world and reached the White House on Monday evening. President Donald Trump was asked by reporters what Washington planned to do in light of the risk that pneumonic plague could reach the United States from Russia.
We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it,” he replied. “We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can.”
Trump spoke to reporters on the South Lawn before boarding the presidential helicopter on his way to a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska. He described the incident as “a big problem for Russia,” adding: “Well, I hate to see them having it. It's a rough disease”
The president also offered his own explanation for the danger: “We used to be able to control [the disease], but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. The germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well anymore.”
The U.S. State Department, however, said earlier in a statement that “plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland before departing for Iceland: “I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it.”
Based on information provided by the Russians, he said, it appears that a laboratory employee was infected.
“There’s very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia, obviously.  But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” Rubio added.
The State Department said it was closely monitoring the situation together with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It noted that many details remain unverified and called on Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and transparently.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), plague has a high fatality rate but can be readily treated with antibiotics when diagnosed early.
WHO said it was in contact with Russian health authorities to verify the incident and its circumstances and to determine what laboratory tests were being conducted and their results. The organization said it was aware of reports that the employee died of severe pneumonia, but that the cause of death had not yet been officially confirmed and, according to the information provided, laboratory testing was still underway.
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” WHO said, adding that it would update its risk assessment as more information became available.
The European Commission also said it was monitoring the case closely and was in contact with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
Kremlin: ‘Don’t listen to rumors’
Publicly, Moscow is seeking to present a relatively calm picture. In the Kremlin’s only response to the case, spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday: “We should rely on the official statements from Rospotrebnadzor and not listen to various rumors and speculation.”
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s public health authority, said samples taken from Shipilova contained no microorganisms connected to her work. It said no accident involving pathogens had occurred at the institute and that the epidemiological situation in the region was stable.
Irkutsk Oblast Gov. Igor Kobzev said a special expert commission had determined the cause of death to be “pneumonia of unknown origin,” adding: “The situation remains under our control and the control of specialists.”
“Things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well as they used to.” U.S. President Donald Trump
On the ground, however, restrictions remain in place. More than 60 institute employees have been isolated inside the building since Friday. In Irkutsk, three municipal hospitals, the Ivano-Matreninskaya Children’s Hospital and the city maternity hospital are under quarantine, with no explanation given.
Maxim Modin, head of the Shelekhov district in Irkutsk Oblast, where the institute is located, said no infectious diseases had been reported among institute employees over the past 10 days and that everyone who recently came into contact with Shipilova was being tested.
The institute itself declined to respond to a request for comment from CNN. At the Irkutsk aluminum plant in Shelekhov, near the laboratory, employees were instructed to wear masks. Plant director Artyom Fominikh said “conflicting reports” were circulating and urged people to remain calm.
Central Asian countries also did not wait for further clarification. Kazakhstan’s Health Ministry assessed the risk as “very low” but introduced sanitary and quarantine controls at border crossings. Uzbekistan said it had increased authorities’ preparedness to deal with particularly dangerous infectious diseases.
Kyrgyzstan, which has no land border with Russia and lies about 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from Irkutsk, announced Monday that it was introducing quarantine controls at its border crossings.
Prof. Tal Brosh-Nissimov is the Head of the Infectious Diseases Unit at Samson Assuta Ashdod University Hospital, spoke with ynet this week about the possibility that Shipilova was infected in a laboratory accident.
“Let’s assume what’s being reported is true. I have no idea what the safety level is there or what their procedures are. When people work in laboratories with dangerous bacteria, accidents happen and people are exposed. The description of what happened to this woman is consistent with exposure to the plague bacterium,” he said.
According to Brosh, the key to understanding this scenario is how the bacterium entered the body.
“If a test tube containing the plague bacterium broke and an aerosol was released from the tube — meaning droplets were dispersed into the air — you can develop pneumonic plague if you inhale the bacterium,” he explained.
“There are several forms of plague. The most severe, the deadliest and the most contagious is pneumonic plague. It is an extremely fast-moving and aggressive disease, and the description of her condition deteriorating within days is consistent with it. It’s not certain, but it fits. It progresses very quickly and causes extremely severe pneumonia.
“Plague can be treated, but treatment has to begin very quickly. It does not respond well to late treatment.”

NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh government informed Supreme Court on Monday that it has decided to replace the public prosecutor in the 2021 case of farmers being mowed down in Lakhimpur Kheri, but said allegations against the outgoing PP by the witness were unfounded. Former minister Ajay Mishra's son Ashish is an accused in the case.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also forwarded the vigilance report on the trial judge, placed before it in a sealed cover, to the Allahabad HC chief justice for appropriate decision. The witness had accused the judge of improperly withdrawing to himself cases under NDPS and SC/ST Act and acquitting the accused.UP standing counsel Ruchira Goel said the earlier PP was a seasoned prosecutor of 16 years and had not given up key witnesses as alleged.
If doubts cast, better to replace PP: UP counsel
She said there were certain witnesses who had died and others had turned hostile, which he had given up. The bench said it understood the predicament but said whenever doubts were cast on the PP which would affect a free and fair trial, it was better to replace him.“We are not casting any aspersion on the professional ability of the earlier PP,” the bench said.Appearing for Mishra, senior advocate Siddharth Dave accused the witness of attempting to prejudice the trial, the PP and the trial judge by making wild allegations and trying to coerce them to record a conviction.
“Every now and then, the witness threatens the trial judge and the PP by stating that he will complain to SC,” he said.The bench said the state had done a commendable job by replacing the PP but clarified, “We are not saying anything against anyone. Our only concern is that the trial should proceed smoothly in a free and fair manner.” The bench, which is monitoring progress of the trial, was informed that 86 of 131 witnesses in the case had been examined.
The SC posted further hearing after two weeks.The case relates to an Oct 2021 incident when Ashish Mishra allegedly ran over protesting farmers with his SUV, killing four of them. A mob of farmers then lynched the driver of the vehicle and two BJP workers. A journalist was also killed in the violence. Ashish is on bail and is barred from residing in his hometown Lakhimpur Kheri.UP standing counsel Ruchira Goel said the earlier PP was a seasoned prosecutor of 16 years and had not given up key witnesses as alleged.

Russia says Ukraine hit two facilities at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia says Ukraine hit two facilities at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
MOSCOW, Oct 5 - Ukrainian drones attacked two facilities at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine overnight on Monday, but there is no threat to nuclear safety, the head of Russia's state nuclear corporation said.
Alexei Likhachev, director general of Rosatom, said a driver delivering food for plant employees was killed in the drone attack.
According to Likhachev, a laboratory building and a radioactive waste processing plant were the targets. Ukraine has not commented on the incident.
On Saturday, the plant's management said Ukrainian shelling over recent weeks had damaged external power supply equipment at the plant, with electricity currently being provided by emergency diesel generators.
The plant produces no electricity but needs power supplied by two external links to keep nuclear fuel cool.
Russia seized the plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of the war that began with Moscow's February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Moscow and Kyiv have since regularly accused each other of military action that compromises nuclear safety.
The International Atomic Energy Agency, the UN's nuclear watchdog, has repeatedly acted to secure a ceasefire around the plant to have repairs carried out to lines connecting the plant to the main power grid.
UN monitors are stationed at the Zaporizhzhia plant and three others operating in Ukraine.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, writing on her ministry's website, accused the West of enabling Ukrainian attacks by failing to condemn them publicly.
"Kyiv's intensification of shelling the Zaporizhzhia plant has been made possible by the lack of an appropriate response to such actions from Western countries, which are effectively facilitating new attacks," Zakharova wrote.
"Such an attitude towards strikes by the Ukrainian military demonstrates the true value of statements by representatives of these countries about nuclear and physical nuclear safety at various international forums." REUTERS

Spain’s Leader Is Betting His Government on the Housing Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:02:23 UTC
08:02:23 KST

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain called for early elections on Monday after Parliament last week rejected two key housing decrees amid widespread protests over rising rents and housing scarcity. The elections, originally scheduled to take place next summer, will now be held on Nov. 29.
One of the decrees was a relief package aiming to extend eviction protections for vulnerable households, regulate rentals, and offer tax relief and assistance for renters, landlords, and first-time homebuyers, while the other aimed to offer greater stability for renters by establishing automatic renewals.
The rejected measures came from Sánchez’s governing coalition, comprising his Socialist Party, PSOE, and the left-wing alliance Sumar. The coalition lacks a majority in Parliament and must rely on other parties to pass legislation. That dependence leaves the government vulnerable when those parties withhold their support—which is what played out with the two housing measures on Oct. 2.
In calling early elections, Sánchez is hoping voters will give his coalition enough support in Parliament to advance its housing agenda—but risks handing his opponents the majority instead.
“To do more, we need to renew and expand the people’s support,” Sánchez said in a statement on Monday.
But he faces a central challenge: persuading voters to blame the parties that blocked his proposals, rather than his government, for the lack of relief.
Various parties have offered differing explanations for why they rejected the decrees.
Junts—a Catalan pro-independence party—said in a statement Oct. 1 that many of the proposed measures would reduce the supply of rental homes and drive up prices, making housing even harder to access for people with lower incomes. Juan Bravo, housing spokesman for the conservative PP party, said on Oct. 2 that the government was proposing significant market interventions without adequately addressing the shortage of homes through construction.
Sergio Nasarre Aznar, a professor of civil law at Universitat Rovira i Virgili, agrees with some of the points the parties have made in opposing the decrees, telling TIME that “what Pedro Sánchez is proposing will cause a serious breakdown of the housing market”—making it even more difficult to access housing.
He also argues that the measures could make housing harder to access by increasing legal uncertainty. He warns of “the threat of future court rulings annulling some of the measures.”
Sánchez’s opponents are also choosing to emphasize other issues, including immigration: Vox leader Santiago Abascal, for instance, has made tougher migration policies a condition of supporting a future government with the conservative PP.
The move is also a gamble because Sánchez’s party may need to overcome blowback over corruption scandals, its handling of migration, and repeated difficulty securing support in Parliament.
Pablo Simón, a political scientist with the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, tells TIME that focusing on housing could help Sánchez move beyond those difficulties and engage progressive voters.
“After months dominated by corruption scandals, parliamentary weakness, and government fatigue, housing gives Sánchez an issue around which he believes he may be able to mobilize key parts of the progressive electorate again,” he says, “particularly younger voters, renters and voters in large cities.”
How did housing become the breaking point?
Spain’s housing supply has struggled to keep pace with demand in recent years, and an increasingly unaffordable market has become a growing pressure point, with the Bank of Spain showing an estimated housing shortfall of 750,000 homes accumulating from 2021 to 2025.
The Spanish Youth Council’s 2025 report showed an average monthly rent of €1,176, the equivalent of roughly $1,317, which then represented 98.7% of a young person’s average salary in Spain.
But public outrage came to a head in September when an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid after occupying the unit for decades. Thousands of protestors took to the streets.
Simón believes that the Prime Minister sees their fury as an opportunity.
“Sánchez is taking advantage of what is probably the best window of opportunity available to minimize PSOE losses,” he says. “If he manages to make the campaign revolve around this issue, he could hope to close the gap with the PP and, in the most favourable scenario for him, even compete to finish as the largest party.”
That does not mean Sánchez expects to win an outright majority, Simón cautions.
And he further questions if housing can become a decisive voting issue.
“It is clearly one of Spain's most important social problems and has a strong capacity to generate political mobilization, but that does not necessarily mean it will determine how people vote,” he says.
What is at stake in the election?
With a snap election, Sánchez is gambling that the housing issue will remobilize the left and give his coalition more seats in Parliament to advance its proposals.
But even if the Prime Minister succeeds in putting housing at the center of the campaign, Simón says, “that does not automatically mean that the PSOE will be the party that benefits electorally from it.”
The PP, Vox and Junts could still hold enough seats between them to block Sánchez’s housing proposals, he says, noting that far-right Vox is “growing strongly.”
Politico polling from Sept. 26 shows Sánchez entering the election campaign at a disadvantage, with PP at 34% of the vote share next to PSOE’s 26%. Vox follows at 18%, while Sumar holds some 5%. Those figures predate the election announcement and do not directly predict parliamentary seats.
“It is widely assumed that the right-wing bloc will secure an absolute majority,” Simón says, “so the main question is not whether Sánchez can remain in government, but how much he can limit the scale of the defeat.”
A defeat for Sánchez could have consequences beyond its borders. A government led by the conservative PP, potentially with far-right Vox, would reinforce Europe’s shift to the right, alongside conservative-led Germany and far-right-led Italy. It could also remove a prominent progressive voice from European debates over immigration, defense spending, and relations with Israel.
If Sánchez secures the greater parliamentary support he’s seeking, meanwhile, it would not guarantee relief from rising housing costs.
Previous efforts illustrate the difficulties. Spain’s 2023 housing law enabled rent limits in designated high-pressure areas, but implementation has varied by region. Attempts to tighten rules on temporary rentals have also encountered parliamentary resistance. A subsequent rental-regulation proposal advanced in December 2024, showing that negotiations could overcome some divisions. But support for debating the legislation did not mean agreement on its substance.
At the same time, expanding public housing requires years of investment and cooperation between national and regional authorities. A new parliamentary majority would not, on its own, remove those obstacles. And Simón says it remains unclear which party can claim ownership of the housing issue.
“Voters assign responsibility to different levels of government, and there is no broad consensus on the appropriate solutions,” he explains.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative PP, said on Monday that he believes Sánchez called the election out of fear—but he supports the decision.
"These are not elections like the previous ones: This is about Spain defeating Sánchez and what he represents,” he said.
He acknowledged the housing crisis has yet to be addressed, claiming that “the cost of living is unbearable” in Spain and that “housing is out of reach.”
Vox leader Abascal commented on Monday that focusing on “national priority, deregulation, and remigration” would be the conditions for a potential governing alliance with the PP.
What is the process of calling for a snap election in Spain?
Following Sánchez’s announcement, elections are set to take place Nov. 29. The call for early elections is fairly common and reflects a core element of Spain’s electoral process.
Spain’s Constitution allows the prime minister, after consulting the Cabinet, to seek the early dissolution of Parliament and a new election. The king formally issues the decree; however, this action is a formality.
Sánchez’s office said Monday that King Felipe VI’s election decree would be published Tuesday.
The previous election was July 23, 2023, and parliamentary terms normally last four years, meaning that the latest possible date to hold elections would have been Aug. 22, 2027.
No official date had been set when Sánchez called to move up the timeline by as many as nine months.
Sánchez has called early elections before: in 2019, after Parliament rejected his budget, and in 2023, after his party suffered losses in local and regional elections. The PP won the most seats in the July 2023 vote, but Sánchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to remain Prime Minister.

Details

I do not remember the Hungarian national team taking even a single shot in the first half. Yemen’s Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites

Unknown Publisher

Yemen’s Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
TAIZ, Yemen – Iran-backed Houthis on Oct 5 said that they had struck Riyadh’s international airport, an Aramco refinery and several other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.
Pakistan and Turkey meanwhile pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.
The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on social media platform X that its naval forces had hit “military targets” belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
They “destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines” and had “thwarted a planned attack” targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.
Loud explosions rattled Riyadh on the evening of Oct 5 as the fighting escalated, and a Houthi spokesman said the group had hit the Saudi capital’s King Khalid International Airport as well as an Aramco refinery and other targets in the kingdom’s south.
The government announced on Oct 4 the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of Yemen’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
In September, the Iran-backed group seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping, in Yemen’s deadliest fighting in years.
The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life, and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
On Oct 5, representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event of any attack.
They also agreed “to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”, and condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia.
Global oil system ‘straining’
Houthi attacks have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.
A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack on Oct 4 had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom’s exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.
Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war, before the Houthis began targeting the world’s largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Oct 5 that global oil stockpiles were “scarily thin” owing to the war.
“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
Mokha fighting
Yemeni military sources said on Oct 5 that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the Houthi-held city of Mokha, but stopped short of confirming an official announcement of the port’s recapture.
While the war in Yemen predates the broader Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become its most active front in recent weeks. According to UN figures, the fighting has displaced more than 184,000 people.
Yemen’s civil war began broke out in 2014, with the Saudis intervening the following March, but fighting was paused by a 2022 ceasefire that held until July 2026. AFP

NEW YORK, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- New York State on Monday declared a statewide disaster emergency over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a U.S. state since cases began surging in 2025.
New York State Governor Kathy Hochul issued an executive order declaring a "State Disaster Emergency" in response to an increase in measles cases across the state.
According to the executive order, 108 cases of measles have been reported among New York State residents this year through Saturday. Of those, 92 were reported since July 15, largely in under-immunized, rural communities in 18 counties.
There have been seven confirmed cases in New York City.
The outbreak comes as measles cases rise across rural areas of New York and neighboring states. The Pennsylvania Department of Health announced on Monday that 1,004 measles cases have been confirmed across 39 counties in Pennsylvania so far in 2026, with five confirmed measles-associated deaths.
The order expands the pool of healthcare professionals authorized to administer measles vaccines. The state has launched a "Measles Dashboard" to help the public and health officials track local risks and raise awareness.
The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through Nov. 4, according to a release by the New York State government.
As of Oct. 1, the United States had reported 3,887 confirmed measles cases in 2026. Of those, 3,869 were reported by 47 jurisdictions, while a total of 18 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States, according to the latest data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The agency recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as the best protection against measles.
The vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners has declined in recent years and fell to 92.4 percent in the 2025-2026 school year, below the 95 percent coverage target, with lower coverage in some communities, the CDC said. Enditem.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday called for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks.
The horrors of those attacks must never be repeated, and the ensuing hostilities in Gaza must end, Guterres said in a message marking the third anniversary.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Palestinian militant group Hamas attacked Israel from Gaza, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage. Israel responded with a war on Hamas in Gaza that killed at least 74,000 Palestinians.
"The devastating hostilities that followed (the attacks) have inflicted untold suffering on Palestinians in Gaza, including massive loss of life, displacement, and destruction. Civilians continue to endure intolerable conditions. Their suffering, too, demands an end, now," said the UN chief.
The ceasefire reached last year has brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace, he noted.
"I urge all parties to implement their commitments in full and advance to the next phase of the ceasefire," said Guterres. "It is time for the ceasefire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law."
He said that there is a need to build the political path to lasting peace across the whole region, adding that the United Nations remains unwavering in its commitment to these imperatives.
"Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity, and aspirations fulfilled," said Guterres. ■

Visa doesn't create absolute right to enter India, says Delhi High Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:59:29 UTC
07:59:29 KST

NEW DELHI: Delhi High Court has stressed that a foreign national does not have an inherent or legally enforceable right to seek entry into India even if granted a visa. It added the statutory framework does not treat the possession of a visa as creating an absolute and unconditional right of admission into India.
Justice Amit Mahajan observed: "The statutory scheme expressly contemplates circumstances in which, notwithstanding possession of requisite travel documents, a foreigner may not be permitted to enter India on grounds, including considerations relating to national security, sovereignty and integrity of India, relations with a foreign State and public health, besides others specified by central govt."
"The claim is destined to fail because there is no inherent or legally enforceable right of a foreign national to seek entry," he added. High Court's observations came while dismissing a plea by a Turkmenistan woman, seeking a direction to Centre to furnish a written speaking order giving the reasons for refusing her entry on March 25.

Ex-hostage Avinatan Or attempted escape during time in Hamas captivity

22:58:41 UTC
07:58:41 KST

Ex-hostage Avinatan Or planned an escape attempt during his time isolated in captivity in Gaza after October 7, 2023, he told N12's Uvda in an interview on Monday.
"In the army they always told us, there's no such thing as a 100% perfect defense, there will always be some weak point," he explained.
Or was kept in darkness in a below-ground cell, but according to him he was able to feel around and locate part of a wall of sandbags though which he could feel airflow.
"That doesn't happen in a tunnel," Or said.
For the next six months, approximately, Or dug his way through the sandbags. He used a garbage bag to conceal himself from the security camera, he explained, and used a 60 meter extension cable to dig.
Or also described a bag he'd prepared with clothing he'd found and a sack on which he'd written the word "Hostage." He also wrote a will and letters to his parents, in the event that he was killed after his escape.
However, when he finally broke through the wall, Or was instead discovered and re-captured. Afterwards, he said, he faced torture and much harsher conditions, including starvation and beatings.
Hamas terrorist pushes hostage to leave for Europe
Another year later, Or was released from captivity.
Before his release, Or said, he was confronted by one of the Hamas terrorists who had kept him hostage.
"Say goodbye to Dad and Mom, meet up with your friends - two, three, four days, a week - then grab a bag, pack, and head to Europe," he said the terrorist told him. "You know why? Because we will carry out another October 7th. As long as there is a single Jew in the Land of Israel, we will slaughter you again and again."
"I looked at him and said, 'I’m not leaving,'" Or recounted. "He asked, 'Why?' and I said, 'Look at the Gaza Strip - everything here is ruin, everything here is death. When the war ends and the crossings open, will you leave for Egypt?' He said, 'No.' I asked, 'Why not?' He replied, 'Because this is my home.' I told him, 'Excellent - this is my home, too.'"

Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:55:00 UTC
07:55:00 KST

Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces staged a lightning advance on Oct 5 to retake the coast around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait up to the city of Mokha, the government said, pushing the Iran-backed Houthis out of most of the areas they seized in September.
In response, the Houthis said they had attacked key locations in Saudi Arabia, including the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, the Abha international airport and the Khamis Mushait military base.
The claims could not be immediately verified. Saudi Arabia and Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Yemeni forces of the internationally recognised government, backed by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha late on Oct 5 and Houthi fighters were retreating into the highlands, four government sources said. The Defence Ministry said the city had fallen.
The advance, if confirmed, would loosen the Houthis’ grip on a vital Red Sea oil route already roiling energy markets alongside Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, though the group could still strike vessels with drones from other positions.
Fighting has raged along several front lines in Yemen for weeks since a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said late on Oct 5 that naval forces carried out a military operation in Yemen’s Red Sea governorate of Hodeidah.
The government forces had already taken key positions including an airstrip in the Dhubab district at the mouth of the strait, whose seizure by the Houthis last month sent shock waves through energy markets.
Reuters could not independently verify the extent of the government gains. 
The Houthis, who have controlled many of Yemen’s more populous areas including the capital Sanaa since 2014, said the Saudi-backed government’s claims were baseless.
Meanwhile, the Houthis themselves made important advances near the third-largest city of Taiz, gaining sections of a mountain road to leave government forces besieged, according to five military sources with the Yemeni government. One government source denied the road had been cut.
The group also threatened to attack traffic in Saudi airspace.
The escalating conflict has prompted Riyadh’s allies to act. 
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia under their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement.
The fighting has worsened a humanitarian crisis in Yemen, the poorest state in the Arab region. The UN migration agency said on Oct 5 that 184,000 people had been displaced since the war resumed.
Yemen’s internationally recognised president, Rashad al-Alimi, swore on Oct 4 to fight “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia”.
Saudi Arabia said on Oct 5 that it had attacked hundreds of targets to provide air cover for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces. The Yemeni government said it had launched attacks on several fronts including in Sanaa province.
The Houthi-run health ministry said two people had been killed and seven wounded in strikes on the province’s Sanhan and Sa’wan districts.
Heaviest fighting in south-west Yemen
While the war has raged on several fronts, the heaviest fighting has been in the south-west, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz.
The Houthis damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable, and on Oct 4, their fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, five government military sources said, though another government source denied this.
A Houthi-run news agency on Oct 5 cited a military source as saying the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen’s interim presidential council.
The advances left Taiz,a city with a population of over half a million and a garrison of thousands of government fighters, surrounded by Houthi forces, the government military sources said.
In al-Mudhaffar area, just outside Taiz but within the area besieged by the Houthis, a long queue formed outside a petrol station as people waited for fuel and cooking gas canisters.
“This is the daily state in Taiz,” said Shehab Hazaa.
Mecca alliance agrees to deploy military forces in Saudi
In a statement following their meeting, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan accused the Houthis of attempting to target Islam’s holiest sites, Mecca and Medina.
“The parties also condemned in the strongest terms the attempted targeting of Mecca and Medina, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom, reaffirming their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity,” the statement said.
The “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, signed in August, is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all. REUTERS

Emirati firm plans two mega property development projects in Syria
Syria on Monday signed a framework agreement with an Emirati company for two huge property development projects as the country boosts efforts to attract foreign investment to finance reconstruction after years of war.
Dubai real estate tycoon Mohamed Alabbar, chairman of Emirati developer Eagle Hills Properties, signed the accord at the presidential palace in Damascus, in the presence of Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa.
"We believe that Syria deserves the return of its people and the pursuit of the reconstruction process," said Alabbar, who is also chairman of the UAE's Emaar Properties.
Authorities did not specify the value of the two projects or an expected completion date.
According to state media and videos shown during the event, one project near Damascus is to include apartments, villas, hotels and shops, while the other is a residential and tourism development involving a marina around the coastal city of Latakia.
In July, Bloomberg reported that Alabbar was planning two major housing and tourism projects, worth at least $20 billion, in the capital and Latakia.
Syria is trying to recover after more than 13 years of civil war that fractured the country and ravaged its industry and infrastructure, with most of the population living in poverty.
The new authorities are seeking to modernise the country's infrastructure, attract investment and boost development, particularly after the lifting of economic sanctions.
The World Bank has estimated that rebuilding Syria will cost more than $216 billion.
Syria's Public Works and Housing Minister Mustafa Abdul Razzaq said during the ceremony that "without an immediate response, the housing deficit in Syria could surpass two million housing units by 2030".
Tourism Minister Mazen al-Salhani said the projects could create "more than 40,000 direct and indirect job opportunities".
In June, authorities announced a project with a Saudi company that aims to create around 20,000 housing units near Damascus.
Since 2025, Syria has signed several agreements and memoranda of understanding with foreign firms, including in the transport and energy sectors.

France, Germany call for new EU trade tools to protect European industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:45:46 UTC
07:45:46 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
France and Germany called Monday for new European Union trade instruments, arguing that the bloc’s existing measures are no longer sufficient to address challenges facing its trade system.
In a joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the EU as facing “unprecedented challenges.”
They said the rules-based trade system was “massively affected” by the “weaponization of trade,” market-distorting practices and global macroeconomic imbalances.
“All this undermines the level playing field for our companies, our position as a sovereign key industrial producer and our ability to innovate, leading to increased dependencies and geoeconomic risks,” the letter said.
“For all these reasons, we need urgent action to address these threats, to diversify and to derisk,” it added.
Macron and Merz welcomed efforts to strengthen the EU’s resilience and competitiveness and called for the full use of the bloc’s existing trade defense measures.
“But this does not suffice anymore,” they said, calling for a “comprehensive framework” to complement the existing toolbox with new legal instruments “in a lean and non-bureaucratic way.”
The first proposed instrument would aim to reduce European dependencies, resolve existing supply-chain concentration and prevent emerging concentration risks.
A second instrument would address cases in which third countries “deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions by political or economic means.”
Such actions could result in what the letter described as “severe and systematic distortions” of the EU’s internal market.
The proposed mechanism would give the European Commission the ability to take “decisive and systemic reaction,” including through “powerful measures, up to an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed.”
“This instrument has to be country-agnostic,” the letter said.
Macron and Merz also pointed to “significant non-tariff barriers” facing EU exporters.
They also highlighted the presence in the EU market of products with “record levels of non-compliance to EU regulations,” including consumer safety rules.
They cited “misalignment and under-evaluation of real exchange rates” as contributing to price competitiveness advantages over European companies and “growing imbalances with the EU.”
The letter also called for strengthening the European industrial base through “industrial policy, simplification as well as public and private investment.”
The proposals follow discussions at the June European Council and the Franco-German Council of Ministers in July.
Macron and Merz said their ideas had been detailed in an accompanying Franco-German non-paper.
They said they looked forward to advancing discussions at the European Council meeting in October.

US monitoring suspected pneumonic plague in Russia, Trump says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:44:07 UTC
07:44:07 KST

US President Donald Trump has announced that Washington is closely monitoring a reported fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Russia and stands ready to provide assistance to Moscow.
"We're looking at it very strongly. We just heard about it," Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday.
Calling the fatality a "big problem for Russia", Trump added: "Years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger. But we'll help them. We'll help them. Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help."
The US State Department confirmed that American authorities, alongside the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), are actively reviewing reports emerging from Russia's Irkutsk region.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also affirmed that Washington is tracking developments closely.
Quarantine in Siberia
The alert follows the death of 28-year-old laboratory worker Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
Her death prompted authorities to place dozens of contacts into quarantine and dispatch the head of Russia's consumer health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, directly to the Siberian region.
While the incident triggered widespread concern across social media, Russian officials maintained the situation remains under control, attributing the death to pneumonia of unestablished origin and denying claims that a vial containing pathogens was dropped.
The World Health Organisation stated that the general public health risk appears low, noting that updated assessments will follow further disclosures.
Plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, is endemic to Siberian wildlife, though human transmission remains rare.
Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous airborne form and can be fatal within one to six days if untreated with antibiotics.

2026-10-05
22:37:35 UTC
07:37:35 KST

Britain has failed in its attempt to prevent the closure of its consulate in East Jerusalem, while Israel has responded to the possibility of the mass expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London in retaliation for the closure.
Following ynet’s revelation that Britain is considering expelling 27 Israeli diplomats from the embassy in London, Israeli diplomatic officials said: “There is no reason for us to address speculation about decisions other countries may or may not make in the future. We have already demonstrated that every move against Israel will be answered accordingly, and that will continue to be the case.”
The British message regarding the possible expulsion of the diplomats if Israel does not reverse its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem was conveyed to Israeli officials amid deteriorating relations between the two countries. Tensions reached a peak with Britain’s decision to impose economic sanctions on settlements in the West Bank, prompting Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to announce retaliatory measures, including the closure of the consulate, which serves the Palestinian population and where 27 British diplomats work.
The Guardian reported that Britain’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, visited Jerusalem last week in an attempt to persuade the government to cancel or postpone the consulate’s closure, but the talks failed. Powell opposed British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s decision to move forward with a ban on trade with settlements, fearing that it could play into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hands in the upcoming election.
The decision to close the British Consulate and revoke the diplomatic credentials of its staff is due to take effect Thursday. As a result, dozens of local employees have been dismissed and the British diplomats are preparing to leave. Officials familiar with the matter said the British were particularly angered by the short notice Israel gave their diplomats — 30 days to leave Israel. By comparison, Russia gave Britain four months to close its consulate in St. Petersburg in response to an espionage dispute between the two countries.
Britain has not publicly announced how it will respond to Israel’s measures because officials believed they could persuade Jerusalem to reverse course through quiet, behind-the-scenes contacts. However, as previously reported, ynet has learned that Britain has already conveyed a message to Israeli officials through Ambassador Simon Walters that if the decision remains in place, it will be forced to take a severe step of its own and expel 27 diplomats serving at the Israeli Embassy in London.
In other words, one Israeli diplomat would be expelled for every British diplomat whose work in East Jerusalem has been terminated.
If Britain does take such a step, it would severely impair the Israeli Embassy’s ability to function. The embassy’s diplomatic staff numbers more than 27, but not by much. The ambassador’s post has also been vacant for more than a year, since Tzipi Hotovely returned to Israel in September 2025. The embassy is currently headed by chargé d’affaires Christian Cantor.
The British Embassy declined to comment on the report.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid, No. 2 on the Beyachad ("Together") party list, responded to the British step being considered following Sa’ar’s decision: “Creating crises is not a policy. Picking fights with the entire world is not a policy. What this means in practice is shutting down the Israeli Embassy in London. How exactly does that benefit the State of Israel?”

Egyptian journalists allege torture after arrest, NGO says
An NGO representing six staff members of an Egyptian fact-checking platform arrested last week said on Monday that the journalists reported being tortured after they were detained.
The detained journalists made up the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, an independent media platform known for fact-checking and investigative reporting.
Egypt has long faced criticism from press freedom organisations over restrictions on media activity.
Lawyers for the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), which is defending the journalists, said most of them testified before the Supreme State Security Prosecution that they were subjected to "various forms of torture and mistreatment".
The SSSP is a special branch of the public prosecution that oversees the prosecution of crimes linked to the state's security.
"The journalists described being bound with their hands behind their backs and blindfolded while being held and interrogated at National Security facilities," EIPR said in a statement.
"They also reported beatings, forced stripping, electric shocks and threats to harm them or their families."
They also alleged that officers "forced them to record fabricated 'confessions'" that could be used to convict them, according to the statement.
The journalists' location wasn't disclosed for five days until their interrogation began on Sunday.
Only one journalist, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Omeira, has been detained for 15 days pending investigation, facing charges of "joining a 'terrorist' group, spreading false news, and using a social media platform for that purpose", said EIPR.
The other journalists' investigations remain ongoing.
Egyptian authorities have defended the arrests, accusing the journalists of belonging to a platform linked to the banned Muslim Brotherhood and of "publishing false news".
Matsadaash, whose name means "Don't Believe It" in Arabic, rejected the allegations.
Dozens of Egyptian journalists staged a sit-in in Cairo on Saturday, calling for their release.
According to EIPR, the latest arrests bring the number of journalists in Egypt detained in connection with their work to 26.

Only 15% going to work use public transport: NSO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:32:32 UTC
07:32:32 KST

Walking is the 2nd most common mode of work commute
NEW DELHI: Long traffic snarls, a common feature on roads across the country, may be linked to how people commute to work. Only 15% of workers use public transport such as buses, trains, trams or auto-rickshaws, while 46% rely on two-wheelers or cars, according to the first-ever National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) by the National Statistics Office (NSO).Two-wheelers account for 43% of workers' commute nationally and cars for 3%. In urban areas, reliance on these vehicles is higher, with 53% of workers using two-wheelers and 5.7% travelling by car.
28.3% of people reach workplace on foot: NSO
Walking is the second most common mode of work commute in the country, accounting for 28.3% of workers, 10.7% use bicycles. More than a third of rural workers (36%) walk to work, compared with just 14% in urban areas, as per the data. The survey was conducted between July 2025 and June 2026 and included trips which are longer than 1 km. Travelling to and fro has been counted as two trips in the survey.The survey showed a worker takes an average of 25 minutes to reach the workplace. In urban areas, the commute takes 27 minutes, compared with 23 minutes in rural areas. The morning commute remains heavily concentrated before 10 am, with nearly 95% of workers leaving home for work then.
In terms of cost, workers spend an average of Rs 785 a month on commuting, with men spending substantially more (Rs 835) than women (Rs 533). The gap widens further in rural areas, where men spend more than twice as much as women — Rs 674 against Rs 307.
In contrast, student mobility shows a markedly different pattern. Walking is the single largest mode, accounting for 37% of students travelling to educational institutions, followed by buses at 29.5% and bicycles at 15.8%. Around 88% reach their institutions within 30 minutes, while the average journey takes 23 minutes. Nearly four in five students leave for school between 7 am and 10 am.Besides meeting the railway ministry’s specific data requirements, the survey is expected to provide insights into how, when and why people travel. “Information on travel patterns and public transport use will help identify gaps in existing transport systems, assess accessibility, optimise routes and improve service frequency and scheduling,” said NSO in a statement.

Five other men were injured in the incident, two of whom are still in Royal Darwin Hospital.
At a press conference in Perth, Chief of Army Susan Coyle confirmed Corporal Hannam was a junior non-commissioned officer who had served in Afghanistan and trained soldiers in Ukraine.
"It is with deep and profound sadness that I can confirm that we lost one of our soldiers yesterday," she said.
"Brendan is survived by a partner and two young children.
"He is a much-beloved junior leader in our army, he has served and sacrificed on two operational tours.

General Coyle said Corporal Hannam had aspirations to be a medical technician in the army.
"And I know that he would've been superb," she said.
The Mount Bundey Training Area, about 100 kilometres south-east of Darwin, is used by the Australian Army and its allies for live-fire training.
NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro confirmed the five injured soldiers were flown to Royal Darwin Hospital.
"The Northern Territory supported two injured evacuations by helicopter to Royal Darwin Hospital at about 7:30 last night and another three by plane at about 9:30 last night," she said.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with the family who are obviously devastated by this loss and of course, the support of our entire community is there for all of our service personnel who will be feeling this loss immensely."
General Coyle said the death of a member of the army brought profound sadness.
"My heart goes out to his family, as well as to his mates, the unit, across the broader army as well," she told 102.5 ABC Perth earlier today.
"[This is] always a difficult time for anybody, but it hits home, it's like they're your own kids."
General Coyle said further details would not be released until after an investigation was completed.
"The site gets secured at the incident, it gets handed over to our military police," she said.
"We have a land accident investigation board team that will then undertake an investigation as well.
"We've got to give them the time and space to truly understand what has happened so that we can make informed decisions on what to do next and what steps to take to try and mitigate this so it doesn't happen again."
NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole said he had sent resources to the training facility to assist the Defence Department's investigation.
"We can't comment on the cause of the injury to the defence personnel but we are assisting and we're helping to investigate on behalf of the coroner," he said.
Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment.

He was 28 years old when he died.
General Coyle says when the time is right for the family, she and other key governmental and department figures will meet with them personally to express their condolences.
"Chief of the defence force, the deputy prime minister and the governor-general have all reached out to have that conversation and when it's the right time for the family," she says.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the nation's thoughts were with the family, friends and colleagues of all of the soldiers involved.
"There are no safe or easy days for those who serve in our country's name," Mr Albanese said.
"This sad incident is a terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation's uniform.
"Every loss and every incident is felt deeply by the broader Defence family, but by none more so than their mates who served alongside them. We think of them today and every day."
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles said the incident was "a tragic loss of one of our finest soldiers".
"Australia's servicemen and women do an exceptional job training and fighting for our country," he said.
"This work in the defence of our nation carries risk."
Mr Marles said Defence was working with and supporting all the families involved and that further information would be provided "in due course".
Federal Minister for Veterans' Affairs Matthew Keogh extended his condolences to the family of Corporal Hannam and the broader Australian Defence Force family.
"No matter how someone in our Australian Defence Force passes away, it's tragic and we want to make sure that their families and the people who work with them are supported whenever that occurs," he said.
Mr Keogh said the army had already been looking into the force's training systems and ensuring "everyone is as safe as possible".
Federal Opposition Leader and Shadow Minister for Defence Angus Taylor offered condolences to the soldier's family, loved ones and unit mates.

"We wish them a full and swift recovery, and our thoughts are with their families who will be supporting them through this very challenging time."
The latest incident is the second death of an Australian soldier this year, after Warrant Officer Class Two Lachlan Muddle from the Special Air Service Regiment died during a training exercise in Jervis Bay in May.
Warrant Officer Muddle fell to the ground after a midair collision with another paratrooper.
The other paratrooper, a sergeant from the Australian Defence Force Parachute School, survived the fall with minor injuries.
The Mount Bundey incident is not the first death at the Northern Territory training ground.
In 2017, Australian Army Private Jason Challis was killed there during a live-fire training exercise.
An inquest into his death in 2019 heard Private Challis was shot while standing behind a plywood wall in an urban attack exercise, in a setting meant to resemble a village.
The NT coroner described the Victorian soldier's death as being part of a "shambolic" live-fire exercise and partly the result of a "long-held mindset" against rehearsals for combat-like operations.
The Department of Defence later pleaded guilty in the Darwin Local Court to one charge of failing to comply with a health and safety duty.

In a record, over 10,000 women clear JEE-Advanced

NEW DELHI: Women's success rate in JEE-Advanced reached a record high in 2026 despite fewer registrations, with over 10,000 qualifying for the first time during this period. Yet their share of IIT seat allotments barely changed, from 20.15% to 20.22%. Of the top 100 rankers, 97 were allotted seats at just three IITs - Bombay, Delhi and Madras - with Bombay alone taking 68.This time, a total 18,861 admissions were made in IITs, with 20% being female candidates. Among the top 25 rankers, 8 candidates each took admission in IIT Delhi and IIT Madras, while six toppers took admission in IIT Bombay.The Joint Implementation Committee report, prepared by IIT Roorkee, shows sharp gains for SC and ST candidates. Including candidates with disabilities in both years, their qualification rates among registered candidates rose by 9.9 and 8.3 percentage points, respectively, to 50.2% and 42.1%.SC qualifiers increased from 12,528 to 15,856, while the ST count rose from 5,017 to 6,379. Both increases were around 27%, faster than the 4.6% rise in the number of qualifiers, from 54,378 to 56,880.
JEE(A): Women accountfor 23% of registrations but 17.8% of qualifiers
Of 43,112 registered women, 10,107 qualified, taking their success rate to 23.4%, against 21.7% last year.
In 2025, 9,404 women qualified from 43,413 registrations. Among women who appeared in both papers, the success rate was 24.9%.Women accounted for 23% of registrations but 17.8% of qualifiers, showing that their improved success rate has yet to close the gap with male candidates.Women received 3,814 seat allotments, up from 3,664, out of 18,861 overall. Their qualifying count grew 7.5%.IITs have added seats exclusively for women to ensure they make up at least one in five new undergraduate students. Their share of allotments is only slightly above that level. The report records 3,777 allotments in seats set aside for women and 37 in seats open to all genders. Women are considered first for women-only seats within the relevant category.
The small number allotted seats open to all therefore does not show how many could have secured them on rank alone.The qualifying total also includes students eligible for a one-year preparatory course before starting an IIT degree. Their number rose from 9,644 to 13,127, nearly a quarter of all qualifiers. This route is available to eligible SC and ST candidates and those with disabilities against unfilled reserved seats. Those admitted must pass the course before entering allotted degree programme.Excluding this group, SC and ST qualifiers still increased by about 17% and 19%. However, the overall number qualifying directly for degree programmes fell from 44,734 to 43,753. The report records 189 seat allotments for this course. Qualifying for either of these routes does not guarantee an IIT seat; admission also depends on rank, eligibility and available seats.

Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed a direct missile strike on Riyadh’s main international airport as part of a large-scale barrage targeting airports, military bases, and oil infrastructure across Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Monday night that the group, officially known as Ansar Allah, carried out three operations using “a large number” of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in response to intensified Saudi-backed strikes on Yemen.
The first attack targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and achieved a “direct and precise hit,” Saree claimed, saying air traffic was disrupted. The second targeted Saudi Aramco’s refinery in Rabigh, where the group claimed a direct hit started fires. The third operation reportedly targeted Abha Airport, Khamis Mushait air base, the Aqeefah military camp, and other “sensitive sites” in Najran and Jizan.
The Saudi authorities have not addressed the specific claims of direct hits on the airport and refinery or said whether Houthi strikes caused disruption at King Khalid. The Foreign Ministry issued a broader statement condemning continued Houthi attacks on Riyadh and several other Saudi cities and “civilian and economic facilities,” while reiterating the kingdom’s right to respond.
#Statement | The Foreign Ministry expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s strongest condemnation and denunciation of the terrorist Houthi militia’s continued targeting of civilians and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom; its blatant and repeated attacks against the holiest sites on earth—Makkah and Madinah— the capital Riyadh, and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, Najran, Taif, and Yanbu; and its targeting of Saudi vessels in the southern Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
— Foreign Ministry 🇸🇦 (@KSAmofaEN) October 5, 2026
Loud explosions were reportedly heard in northern Riyadh near King Khalid airport. An AFP journalist reported hearing a “powerful explosion,” and residents said blasts shook windows in the area.
Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry has renewed a warning that photographing, publishing, or circulating information about missile and drone interception operations or impact sites could result in legal action. The same warning was issued earlier in the war. Saudi media republished it shortly after midnight amid the latest attacks.
The Houthis warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace, declaring it a theater of military operations, while exempting the airspace over Mecca and Medina. King Khalid airport remains operational, but Flightradar24 data shows substantial delays, with average delays reaching 38 minutes.
The group said the barrage was retaliation for 60 Saudi air and missile strikes on Sanaa and the provinces of Al-Jawf, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada, and Marib over the previous 24 hours, which it said caused civilian casualties. Saree claimed that Saudi forces conducted 1,576 strikes since the latest escalation began.
The exchange comes as Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies intensify a major counteroffensive against the Houthis. The Saudi-led coalition says around 100 fighter jets are providing round-the-clock air support as government forces attempt to retake territory lost along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The coalition claims it destroyed 324 “high-value” Houthi targets.
Saudi-backed forces said on Monday that they recaptured Dhubab and the nearby towns of Bab and Hadeid, with witnesses telling AP they saw government tanks and troops entering the towns. The Houthis have denied reports of a broader retreat, while fighting has also intensified around Taiz.
The US is also assisting the Saudi campaign with intelligence sharing, target identification, and operational planning, American and regional officials told AP. The US Embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans to remain vigilant for missile and drone attacks.

They call &quot;from the police&quot; and ask for money for a relative: the Cyber Police warned about a scam scheme
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
01:20:51 EEST
07:20:51 KST

They call "from the police" and ask for money for a relative: the Cyber Police warned about a scam scheme
Kyiv • UNN
Fraudsters report an alleged detention of a relative and demand money. The Cyber Police identified the typical signs of the scam and offered advice.
A widespread "relative in trouble" scam scheme has become more active in Ukraine. In this scheme, criminals call citizens, pose as police officers, and report the alleged detention of their relative. The Cyber Police Department of the National Police of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
Details
It is noted that during the conversation, scammers may claim that the relative allegedly ended up in police custody because of a traffic accident, a fight, or another fabricated situation, and that money is needed to "resolve the matter" without criminal liability.
The criminals may then demand that the money be urgently transferred to an account they specify, that cash be handed over through a courier or taxi driver, or that the victim meet a person posing as someone else in person
It is noted that scammers may also use another scenario: telling a person that they themselves allegedly face criminal liability because of certain actions, purchases, or other fabricated circumstances. In this case, they demand that the victim transfer money or follow other instructions "to avoid liability."
In fact, there may have been no detention or initiation of criminal proceedings whatsoever. The purpose of such calls is to frighten people and force them to act hastily without verifying the information they have received
They emphasize that, in order to increase trust, scammers may give the relative’s first and last name, address, or other personal data—either fabricated or genuine. They may also pose as police officers and name fictitious or real department names, addresses, or other details intended to confirm the truthfulness of their story. At the same time, possessing such information by itself does not confirm that the caller is a genuine law enforcement officer.
If you are told that a relative has allegedly been detained, do not rush to hand over or transfer money. End the conversation and contact the relative or other family members yourself to verify the information. If necessary, contact the police at 102 and report the suspicious call
They urge people not to give strangers bank card details, SMS codes, passwords, or other confidential information. If you have already given money to scammers or disclosed your banking information, contact your bank and the Cyber Police as soon as possible, or call 102 or 112.

New York declares first US measles disaster emergency since 2025 surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:19:04 UTC
07:19:04 KST

New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a US state since cases began surging in 2025.
The state also expanded the pool of health professionals allowed to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines as cases rise in rural communities.
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement.
New York has reported 108 measles cases this year through October 3, including 92 since July 15 in under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties, well above typical annual levels, according to the executive order.
Seven of the cases are in New York City, and 101 are elsewhere in the state, the governor's office said. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15.
Outbreak spreading in Pennsylvania
Neighboring Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading outbreak, with 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the order said.
Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state's total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The US is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults' consent for such reporting.
Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4.

Employee of Russian plague institute dies of suspected pneumonic infection, Trump offers help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:18:52 UTC
07:18:52 KST

Almost 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia after a worker at an anti-plague research institute in eastern Siberia died of what many have been reporting as a form of plague on Thursday.
The employee was hospitalized with severe pneumonia last Tuesday before dying in the hospital on Thursday, according to local news, which wrote on Friday that the 28-year-old Darya Shipilova was suspected to have fallen ill with the plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia.
Early Russian reports wrote that Shipilova had contracted the pneumonia after breaking a vial of plague bacteria.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, where the woman had reportedly visited, stated that she had died from an unspecified form of plague.
Tsydenov later modified his statement to say she had possibly died from the plague.
Employee diagnosed with 'pneumonia of unspecified etiology', Russian watchdog says
Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor said on Sunday that the employee had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology," in a statement on Sunday, adding that no microorganisms linked to her work had been found.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, extensive anti-epidemic measures were put in place, including "identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing."
Aside from two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection (the most frequent cause of the common cold), no other infectious agents were found, according to the official watchdog agency.
However, many still suspect, as initial reports indicated, that Shipilova contracted pneumonic plague, one of the three kinds of plague caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, the same one behind the infamous Black Death that affected Europe in the mid 1300s.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria attacks the lungs, resulting in severe respiratory symptoms, including shortness of breath and coughing, which can turn bloody.
Pneumonic plague is also the only form that can be transmitted between humans through inhaling respiratory particles from someone who is sick.
While pneumonic plague can be fatal if left untreated, if detected and treated within 24 hours of symptom onset, recovery rates are high, according to the World Health Organization.
Trump 'concerned' about plague while Kremlin warns against rumors
US President Donald Trump said that he was concerned about the suspected plague outbreak when asked by reporters on Monday, saying that it was "a big problem for Russia."
"Well, I hate to see them having it," Trump said. "It's a rough disease."
Trump also said that the US would be willing to provide help if needed.
"We'll help," Trump said. "Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also told reporters that US authorities were monitoring the situation on Monday, warning that "if something like that gets out it could quickly spread."
"We're watching and monitoring it closely," he said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged Russians to listen to Rospotrebnadzor's report rather than "various rumors and speculation."

The six-day survey, completed on Monday, found that just 32 percent of US voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president.
While that low rate has held steady since September, the latest Reuters-Ipsos poll suggests his support among Latino voters is continuing to slide.
Trump’s approval rating shrunk this month to 24 percent among Hispanic voters, its lowest point in either of his two terms in office.
The Republican leader had previously made substantial inroads with that constituency.
The Pew Research Center estimated that Trump and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were within three percentage points of each other in the 2024 presidential race, earning 48 percent and 51 percent of the Hispanic vote, respectively.
That rate marked a significant jump for Trump over the 2020 election, when he only earned 36 percent of the Hispanic vote.
Experts have credited the boost in Hispanic support with helping Trump win the 2024 race. His 2020 bid, by contrast, ended in defeat to Democrat Joe Biden.
The Monday poll found that Trump’s gains among Hispanics have largely evaporated.
About 52 percent plan to vote for the Democrats in the November midterms, compared to 26 percent for Republicans.
The upcoming midterm is largely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second term and will decide whether the Republicans maintain their majorities in the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Democrats have seized on Trump’s low approval ratings, hoping to translate frustration with the president into voter momentum for their party.
A Democratic majority in one or both houses of Congress would place substantial constraints on Trump’s agenda for the remainder of his time in office.
But Trump has also faced rumblings from within his Republican Party as the November 3 midterms approach.
One Republican incumbent, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, released a campaign advertisement last month that addressed Trump directly, saying, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
She cited Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown as a source of tension. “Some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said, pointing to the detention and deportation of immigrants with no criminal record.
Experts have also warned that the president’s shrinking popularity, driven in part by concerns about the cost of living and his decision to launch a war on Iran, could weigh down Republican candidates in key races across the country.
Still, Trump has continued to express confidence about the prospects of his Republican Party in the upcoming midterms.
He has also defended his decision to place himself at the centre of the Republican election campaign strategy. Trump recently launched a 32-day blitz of cross-country rallies ahead of the November 3 midterms.
“Just so you understand, they all want me to go,” Trump said, denying that some Republicans would prefer he keep his distance. “They all want me to go campaign.”

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 6, 2026
Dozens quarantined in Siberia after plague institute lab worker dies
A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting the authorities to quarantine dozens of people and the head of Russia’s health watchdog to fly to the Irkutsk region.
The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said on Oct 5 the situation was under control.

New York declares state of emergency over measles outbreak
New York Governor Kathy Hochul issued an executive order declaring a state of emergency in response to rising measles cases on Oct 5, as infections skyrocket nationwide.
The order allows the state to respond more quickly to the outbreak and speed testing and vaccination, Hochul said in a statement. As of Oct 3, New York has recorded 108 total cases, including seven in New York City. A majority of the infections were recorded since mid-July.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” she said.
NATO drafts plan to defeat Russian attack with drones and AI
NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defence technologies like drones and AI into traditional power.
The so-called theory of victory document, which Bloomberg has seen in an unclassified form, will be presented by Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, in Poland on Oct 12 amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia.
It is meant to clarify how the alliance would handle a possible incursion into NATO territory, according to senior officials and diplomats familiar with the matter. There have been numerous recent reports that Moscow is considering such action.
Turkey, Pakistan agree rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said on Oct 5, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
The three countries in August signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event one were attacked.
The pact unites NATO’s second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Nigerian military aircraft crashes, killing 32
A Nigerian Air Force plane crashed on Oct 5 in the country’s south-west, killing all 32 people on board, President Bola Tinubu said, declaring three days of national mourning.
It is one of the worst air disasters in recent years in Africa’s most populous country.
The passenger aircraft was on a “routine mission” from Benin City in southern Nigeria to the economic hub of Lagos when it went down at Igbokoda in south-western Ondo state shortly after 9am (4pm Singapore time), the president and the air force said.
