04:47:53 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Iceland late on Monday to begin a three-nation European tour to advance US influence in the Arctic after Washington sealed a pact on Greenland.
Rubio will meet with officials in Reykjavik "to discuss economic and security collaboration," the US State Department said in a statement announcing the trip.
The lightning visit, as symbolic as it is political, comes after the US signed a security pact with Denmark and Greenland in late September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The agreement has apparently put an end to President Donald Trump's threats to buy or even annex Greenland, which soured relations with the European Union.
Before taking off, Rubio described Iceland as "a good friend of the United States."
"So it's an opportunity to stop there and meet with them... it really is a result of a conversation I had with their leaders at the NATO summit with the leaders earlier this year, and with their foreign minister, so I'm looking forward to it," he said.
Under the pact, Washington plans to establish two new military bases on Greenland, drawing the autonomous Danish territory further into US orbit.
Trump’s Arctic ambitions
With competition on the rise in the Arctic, Iceland has regained status as a strategic player, even as the island continues to rely heavily on the United States for security.
At the start of September, Trump sparked new controversy by sharing an AI-generated map that appeared to show all of North America, the Caribbean, Greenland and Iceland as "the United States of America."
In response, Reykjavik summoned the US ambassador "to convey a clear message that the image was wholly inappropriate," Iceland's foreign ministry said in a statement to AFP.
Icelanders had voted in late August 52.8 percent to 47.2 percent against resuming negotiations on joining the EU, which have been frozen since 2013.
The last US secretary of state to visit Iceland was Antony Blinken in 2021.
Since gaining independence in 1944, Iceland has never had a military. It relies on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) for its security and on a bilateral defence pact signed with the United States in 1951.
Washington does not have a permanent base in Iceland, but is looking to consolidate its control over Arctic access routes coveted by Russia and China.
Trump again signaled his obsession with Greenland on Sunday, posting on his Truth Social platform an AI-generated image of his face looming over what appears to be its landscape, accompanied by the words "Hello, Greenland!"
Greece, Portugal
After Iceland, Rubio continues to Athens to participate in a "strategic dialogue" with NATO member Greece on regional and energy security, the State Department said.
The visit follows media reports about possible conflicts of interest involving the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr. and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom.
In a letter addressed to Rubio, Congressman Gregory Meeks sought clarification of a Wall Street Journal report alleging she had stated the United States could create "political change" in European countries.
Rubio will later wrap up his European tour with a brief stop in Lisbon.

Pro-Israel Samoa prime minister apologizes after Nazi salute video resurfaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:46:54 UTC
04:46:54 KST

The prime minister of Samoa, a remote island nation in the heart of the Pacific Ocean, was forced to apologize Monday over a 19-year-old video showing him shouting “Heil Hitler” and giving a Nazi salute during a family gathering. The embarrassing footage of Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt is particularly striking given that he and his country are regarded as staunch supporters of Israel.
The Samoa Observer revealed Sunday the existence and contents of the seven-second video, which reports said was filmed at a Schmidt family gathering in Samoa in July 2007. A screenshot from the video shows Schmidt holding a microphone in one hand while raising the other, surrounded by others making the same gesture. The newspaper reported that Schmidt can be heard saying into the microphone: “Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!”
Schmidt, who served as deputy speaker of Samoa’s parliament in 2007 and has led the island nation since his election victory in August 2025, did not deny the report. In a statement posted on social media Monday, he said: “I acknowledge that these words and the gesture were inappropriate and could have caused hurt and offense, and I apologize for using them.”
He added that the video was filmed “at a private family gathering — not intended for public viewing.” In the statement, he stressed that his conduct in the video did not reflect his personal beliefs or the views of the Samoan government or people, and said he rejected “Nazism, antisemitism, racism and every form of political extremism.”
According to the newspaper, it is not known what happened immediately before or after the clip, and Schmidt’s statement offered no further explanation.
The controversy erupted as news organizations across the Pacific region have condemned Schmidt’s continuing treatment of the Observer. The newspaper has been barred since November from covering news conferences and government events involving Schmidt and other officials after the prime minister accused it of misleading coverage.
On Friday, Schmidt confirmed allegations that photographs of him taken by an Observer reporter outside government buildings during an official event had been deleted from the reporter’s camera by an aide. He defended the move, arguing that the Observer, Samoa’s largest media group, had violated the ban imposed on it.
The Observer called Schmidt’s boycott “an authoritarian act,” while news organizations across the region have urged the prime minister to reverse course. The Journalists Association of Samoa said it was “deeply concerned” by the incident involving the deletion of the photographs.
Like several other leaders of small South Pacific island nations, Schmidt has previously voiced strong support for Israel. Since September 2023, three Pacific island nations, including Samoa, have been among the handful of countries to follow the United States in opening embassies in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv. Analysts attribute the support Israel enjoys in the region to deeply rooted Christian traditions woven into public life.
When Schmidt was sworn into office in September 2025, he even wore a Jewish prayer shawl during a ceremony that also included the blowing of a shofar. “Samoa will not retreat from its support for Israel as the nation of God’s people,” he told reporters after the event, according to local media reports.
Samoa is a tiny nation of about 220,000 people, located near Fiji and west of American Samoa, a U.S. territory in the eastern part of the Samoan island chain.
In the early 20th century, Samoa was under German rule and was a German colony, which is why many residents have German ancestry and German surnames. In 1914, New Zealand seized what was then known as Western Samoa from Germany and retained control until 1962, when the country gained independence.

Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said that Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.
He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.
The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.

Mexico seeks evidence of border shooting that prompted US troop deployment

Mexico seeks evidence of border shooting that prompted US troop deployment
Mexico’s Sheinbaum has expressed concern about US officials overstepping norms on security cooperation.
Mexico has asked the United States for evidence of a cross-border shooting that allegedly targeted US security personnel.
In her daily news conference on Monday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum explained that the US had reported “shots from the Mexican border”.
“We asked for all the evidence because we have no evidence,” Sheinbaum said. She added that Mexico’s National Guard, Army and Navy had not detected any shots being fired from Mexican territory towards the US.
Sheinbaum made her remarks a day after the US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wrote on the social media platform X about the shooting, which allegedly took place in Texas across from the Mexican state of Tamaulipas in late September.
Johnson said the targets were members of the US Coast Guard, and that the threat would be “swiftly addressed”.
“The U.S. Embassy in Mexico is helping coordinate with Mexican forces deploying to the border area where U.S. Coast Guardsmen were fired upon,” Johnson wrote.
“Together, we intend to patrol both sides of our shared border, protect our communities, and make it more difficult for criminal and terrorist organizations to operate.”
Some 500 US troops, along with helicopters, drones and anti-drone equipment, have been sent to the border since the alleged shooting.
Mexico has sent its own deployment in the border area, as part of a joint operation called Operation Mirror between the two countries to secure the frontier.
In Monday’s news conference, Sheinbaum confirmed that the Mexican deployment was designed “to forestall any issues” that may arise.
During their time working together, Johnson and Sheinbaum have repeatedly been at odds over questions of border security and national sovereignty.
A former US Army Green Beret who later served in the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), Johnson has served as ambassador to Mexico since May 2025, under US President Donald Trump.
Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has sought to increase US influence over Latin America, as part of a policy informally dubbed the Donroe Doctrine — a twist on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine.
His administration has also taken a more active role in the region’s security, on the premise of combatting narcotics trafficking and criminal organisations.
Trump has repeatedly said he may carry out military strikes inside Mexico to attack the cartels he said are “running Mexico”, framing their presence as a threat to US security. Sheinbaum, however, has warned that such an operation would violate her country’s sovereignty.
Mexico’s tensions with the Trump administration have strained relations with Johnson. Sheinbaum has accused the ambassador of overstepping diplomatic norms, while Johnson has sought to push the Mexican government to cooperate with Trump’s demands.
In June, Johnson criticised Sheinbaum’s government on social media for turning the “fight against cartels” into a “political dispute”.
Sheinbaum responded the next day with a warning for Johnson, saying, “Ambassadors must respect the internal political affairs of their countries.”
Law enforcement agencies in the US and Mexico have long cooperated in counter-narcotics operations, but Trump’s militaristic approach has created friction with left-wing governments including Mexico.
On Monday, Sheinbaum took issue with Johnson for announcing the opening of an international police academy in the central state of Queretaro without her government’s knowledge.
“How can a groundbreaking ceremony take place with a US ambassador and a Mexican governor, but not with the federal security cabinet?” she said.
Under the Mexican constitution, the federal government must approve the activities of foreign forces on Mexican soil.
But that law was tested earlier this year, when two CIA agents were reportedly killed in an April car accident in the northern Mexican state of Chihuahua, alongside members of the state’s law enforcement.
What the CIA agents were doing in Chihuahua remains unclear. Reports emerged that the CIA agents may have been participating in a state-led raid on a local drug lab without federal authorisation.
One state official publicly denied that report, saying the agents were conducting an unrelated training on drone usage.
Sheinbaum said neither she nor her cabinet were informed of any CIA activities, and her government pledged to investigate the incident.

Turkey, Pakistan agree on rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
RIYADH – Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said on Oct 5, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
The three countries in August signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event one were attacked.
The pact unites NATO’s second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular ones targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Iran-backed Houthis by name.
The trio “reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed “to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which on Oct 5 launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh’s support seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade. AFP

Russian Attack Destroys KUSUM Pharmaceutical Plant in Sumy, Killing Employee and Halting Production
A Russian attack destroyed the KUSUM pharmaceutical plant in Sumy on October 4, killing one employee and halting production at the facility.
KUSUM reported the destruction in a statement published on Instagram on October 4. The company identified the killed employee as Yevhen Volodymyrovych Miroshnychenko, who had worked in the plant’s engineering department since 2009.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The plant in Sumy has been destroyed. But KUSUM continues to work for the people who need our medicines every day,” the company stated.
The Sumy facility produced medicines that the company described as essential for Ukrainian patients. KUSUM is assessing the extent of the destruction and working to maintain uninterrupted supplies of its products in Ukraine.
The plant produced cardiovascular, gastroenterological, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, antihypertensive, mucolytic, and pediatric medicines, including tablets, capsules, granules, suspensions, and syrups.
The company also operates manufacturing facilities in Indore and Bhiwadi, India, which it plans to use to reorganize production and sustain deliveries. KUSUM noted that the transition would depend partly on avoiding regulatory obstacles.
The attack follows an earlier major loss for the pharmaceutical producer, when one of its warehouses was destroyed. KUSUM emphasized that it continued operations after that incident and now intends to maintain medicine supplies despite the destruction of its Sumy plant.
The destruction of the KUSUM plant fits a broader pattern of Russian strikes on foreign-owned industrial facilities in Ukraine.
On September 3, a Russian drone strike caused a major fire at a Coca-Cola production plant in Velyka Dymerka, Kyiv region, one of Europe's largest beverage manufacturing sites.
Earlier, a drone attack on Dnipro damaged an oil processing facility owned by US agribusiness Bunge, spilling about 300 tons of oil onto roads and leaving the city's embankment routes impassable for two to three days.

Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:30:50 BST
04:30:50 KST

Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election
- Published
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat.
On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.
That parliamentary result confirmed that Sánchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority.
But as has so often been the case throughout Sánchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.
His government has been struggling in recent months.
His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos Cerdán and José Luis Ábalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.
In addition, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that Gómez and Sánchez vehemently deny.
Meanwhile, Sánchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.
Although Sánchez had insisted until recently that he would see out the legislature and not call elections until next summer, his government had looked increasingly unlikely to make it that far.
The wave of outrage which has exploded in recent days over housing has provided him with the ideal reason to call elections early - and a welcome issue away from Ceuta and the allegations of corruption.
Appealing to his own party's voters and those further to the left on Monday, he called for voters to "mobilise and ensure that parliament gives us a much bigger, progressive majority with which to defeat the elites, conquer social rights and keep transforming Spain".
On the upcoming campaign trail, Sánchez can point to the fact that his adversaries on the right - such as the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox - voted against his government's housing measures, which sought to prevent the eviction of tenants, improving the conditions of their contracts and preventing investors from buying residential property.
The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the Sánchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists.
However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that Sánchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.
Earlier this year, when Sánchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then.
However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.
Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides Sánchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

From making interceptors to guarding sky: Ukrainian drone maker gets its own private air defense unit and will pay for it from weapon sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:28:53 UTC
04:28:53 KST

A Ukrainian drone maker just got its own air defense unit, and says it has already downed Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has issued an order granting the Night Hornets, the anti-Shahed unit of interceptor maker Wild Hornets, the status of a private air defense, and the company announced it is starting to build its own network of remotely launched interceptor drones.
Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-powered Shahed drones, which cuts the reaction time of Ukraine's mobile fire groups from about a minute to as little as six seconds. Now, a private company joins the air defense line, while Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia is producing up to 500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month.
The planned network will combine remote-control centers, a grid of remote interceptor launches built on the company's Hornet Vision Ctrl technology, and field positions. Wild Hornets will not sell protection for individual sites and will pay for the unit from drone sales profit.
"The unit has more than 50 downed Shaheds to its name, including jet-powered ones. We create technologies that work. We use them ourselves to protect our country," the company says.
Air Force commanders will direct the crews
The crews already go on daily combat duty alongside the military and will take orders from the Air Force command. The unit draws on Wild Hornets instructors and test pilots, including veterans of the war and pilots who rose from beginners to instructors. The company wants to fold private air defense into the country's overall system, including over Kyiv.
Air alerts now swallow nearly a third of mall hours
Due to Russia's jet-powered drones, air-raid alerts covered 30.8 percent of shopping-center operating hours across Ukraine in September, a record, up from 22 percent in August and 14.1 percent a year earlier, the Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers reports. The average mall has now lost 176.5 working days since the full-scale invasion, including 9.6 in September alone.
Kyiv shows the sharpest jump. The share of alert time during mall hours in the capital rose from 11.6 percent in August to 32.7 percent in September, the council said.
The damage reaches well beyond the malls. Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.

St. Petersburg’s Nevsky District Court has sentenced animator Oleg Kuvayev, creator of the animated series “Masyanya,” in absentia to four years and one month in a penal colony, Mediazona reported.
Kuvayev was charged with failing to meet his obligations as a “foreign agent” (Article 330.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code) and calling for activities directed against state security (Article 280.4).
Prosecutors had requested a prison sentence of five years and 11 months.
News of a criminal investigation into Kuvayev for calling for activities directed against state security emerged in October 2023. The investigation stemmed from an episode of “Masyanya” in which the main character urges Russian soldiers to surrender.
Russia’s Justice Ministry designated Kuvayev a “foreign agent” in December 2023. Authorities launched a criminal investigation into him under the “foreign agent” law after he failed to submit reports to the ministry on three occasions.
Kuvayev has lived in Israel since 2006. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he has released several antiwar episodes of “Masyanya.”

Australia's migrant policy offers lessons for EU and US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:26:00 UTC
04:26:00 KST

Australia's migrant policy offers lessons for EU and US
October 5, 2026
Nations that send asylum seekers to third countries for offshore processing and holding could spend billions, only to face accusations of human rights abuses and financial mismanagement, as in Australia.
The European Union has nevertheless been considering the idea, and the United States has already made similar third-country deals, but Australia has been processing or relocating people outside the country where they seek protection for more than two decades.
Former Australian Prime Minister John Howard introduced the so-called Pacific Solution in 2001, targeting immigrants who arrived by boat, and establishing Australian migration processing centers with the help from governments in Papua New Guinea (PNG) and the tiny island nation of Nauru .
Thousands sent to islands under Australia's 'Pacific Solution'
Center-left and center-right governments described the policy as a deterrent, saying people were less likely to attempt dangerous ocean crossings or pay smugglers if arriving by boat did not provide a route to Australia. In his 2001 election policy speech, Howard said the famous line, frequently quoted since: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."
In 2008, a newly elected Labor Party government phased out the practice, saying it was a cynical, costly, and ultimately unsuccessful exercise.
But faced with more deaths at sea, a Labor government under Prime Minister Julia Gillard started sending maritime arrivals to Nauru and Manus again in 2012, after an expert panel recommended reopening the centers.
"I'm not going to play politics or look at political scoreboards when too many lives have been lost," Gillard said at the time.
Between 2013 and 2014, the number of people transferred offshore peaked to more than 3,000.
Journalists have been mostly barred from the centers on Nauru and Manus Island. Graham Thom, Advocacy Coordinator for the Refugee Council of Australia (RCOA), told DW that this lack of access and independent oversight meant many Australians accepted the narrative that the policy was working.
EU considers offshore arrangements
People without a legal right to remain in the EU could face deportation to third countries as soon as 2027, with Rwanda and Uzbekistan reportedly under consideration as third-party countries, as well as Uganda.
The European Parliament in June approved new rules that would pave the way for so-called "return hubs" outside the EU's borders.
Denmark's Minister for Immigration and Integration, Morten Bodskov, told reporters last month the hubs would not be detention and deportation centers.
"We are not talking about camps," Bodskov said, describing the scheme instead as "a new chance to have a life in a partner country."
Denmark, alongside Germany, Austria, Greece, and the Netherlands, known collectively as the Group of Five, said in September they had agreed on steps towards a deal with a non-EU country, without naming it.
The group was to speak with the United Nations , the International Organization for Migration and the UN Refugee Agency about their next steps.
The proposal allows for harsh penalties for those who refuse to be removed to the hubs, including detention for up to 30 months pending deportation from the EU and entry bans.
US already has a third-country migration scheme
The US government has already made deals with at least 30 third countries in Africa and Latin America. In June, Amnesty International said some agreements had been revealed through the US Freedom of Information Act, while others "remain secret."
The US Supreme Court ruled late last month that the second Trump administration could resume deportations under the third-country scheme, after a US appeals court ruled that immigrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture.
The first deportations from the US under the third-country removal scheme were of immigrants convicted of crimes, but more recently, foreign nationals not accused of any crime have also been deported. 
Accusations of human rights abuse
Asylum seekers and human rights advocates have repeatedly alleged human rights abuses in Australia's offshore migration processing program, with Thom describing the policy as a "medieval idea."
A group of asylum seekers formerly detained on Manus Island reached a AU$70 million (€43.47 million/$48.47 million) settlement in 2017 after filing charges for abuse and unlawful detention.
In February, an Australian Senate inquiry heard first-hand witness accounts of neglect, untreated health conditions, and serious concerns for the safety and dignity of camp inhabitants — especially of women being kept on Nauru. Prior to the hearing, 73 UN member states had publicly raised concerns about Australia's migration policies.
Brazil, China, Finland, Germany, Serbia, Switzerland and Turkey called for an end to offshore processing of asylum claims.
Australia has yet to officially comment on the recommendations, but successive governments have said offshore processing helps deter dangerous boat journeys, with former Prime Minister Tony Abbott describing the policy during his term as "decent, humane and compassionate."
The effect of offshore processing is difficult to isolate from other policy measures, especially the practice of turning back asylum boats. This "turnback" policy was introduced and reintroduced under conservative governments in 2001 and 2013 respectively, but with inconsistent data on incidents.
As in the US, offshore migration processing for Australia has expanded beyond its original scope, with Nauru recently agreeing to accept convicted foreign nationals from Australia who can't legally be returned to their countries of origin, for AU$2.5 billion over the next 30 years. Australia had already spent more than AU$13 billion on offshore detention since 2012.
Measuring the success of Australia's model is difficult, but its high long-term costs and legal and human rights concerns may serve as a warning for other countries considering similar policies.

Türkiye’s Aselsan reveals homegrown communications satellite constellation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:25:25 UTC
04:25:25 KST

Zeynep Duyar
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Turkish defense firm Aselsan unveiled its new low Earth orbit communications satellite constellation on Monday at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026), held in the southwestern province of Antalya. 
The Gokbagi (Astralink) dual-use satellite network provides efficient and quick communications services for military, public and civilian sectors.
Aselsan CEO Ahmet Akyol told Anadolu that the firm plans to begin launching the first satellites of the constellation within the next few years.
“At the congress, we’re displaying our Gokbagi project for the first time, which we designed from the chip level up,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of IAC 2026, co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and the SAHA Istanbul defense cluster and organized by the Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.
“We use the name ‘Astralink’ globally, but it continues to be called Gokbagi in Türkiye,” he said.
The project is expected to mark a new milestone in Türkiye’s efforts to secure its space technology independence.
“We’ve also developed satellite receivers based on active electronically scanned array (AESA) technology for ground services, allowing us to digitally track satellites without adjusting antennas for more effective and efficient communication, made possible through our long-standing expertise in design technology, starting from the chip up,” he said.
Aselsan is also displaying its Gokturk-3 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite, which is able to capture high-resolution images of the terrestrial surface through dense cloud cover.
Akyol stated that the firm also invested in new space manufacturing infrastructure at its newly constructed campus.
“Today, we’re talking about artificial intelligence (AI) in space, entering a new era where all these surveillance, communications and navigation systems are built and processed in orbit and transmitted back to Earth — we came to this event from TEKNOFEST, where thousands of young enthusiasts competed in satellite competitions, and the fact that the topics they competed on at the event come to life here is a source of value for our country, as we take pride in building and launching our systems,” he added.

Ukrainian Vulcan Assault Rifles Spotted with Indonesian Special Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:21:30 UTC
04:21:30 KST

Soldiers from the Indonesian Rapid Response Force (Kopasgat) were spotted carrying Ukrainian Vulcan special assault rifles in a bullpup configuration.
Photos of the soldiers with Ukrainian assault rifles were published by the Indonesian defense website KERIS Reborn. The soldiers’ affiliation with Kopasgat is indicated by their corresponding sleeve insignia.
In the published photo, the Ukrainian Vulcan can be identified by its distinctive layout, receiver shape, and controls. Judging by the photo, the version is chambered in 7.62×39 mm.
It is currently unknown how many Ukrainian assault rifles the Indonesian unit received or what their status is, whether they are part of the standard issue or in a trial phase. There is also no publicly available information regarding Indonesia signing a production contract for the purchase of Vulcan rifles.
Kopasgat (Korps Pasukan Gerak Cepat) is a special corps of the Indonesian Air Force. Its units are tasked, in particular, with protecting air bases and other Air Force facilities, conducting special operations, and supporting aviation operations.
The Vulcan is a Ukrainian special-purpose assault rifle designed in a bullpup configuration. In this layout, the magazine and the main components of the firing mechanism are located behind the pistol grip.
This design allowed the weapon to be made compact without significantly shortening the barrel. With an overall length of approximately 712 mm, the rifle has a barrel length of 415 mm.
The weapon is based on the Kalashnikov family of assault rifles, featuring a gas-operated system and a rotating bolt that locks the barrel bore. At the same time, the design was significantly modified to accommodate the bullpup configuration.
The rifle features a new receiver, modified controls, and Picatinny rails for mounting optical, red-dot, and other sighting devices. The design also allows for the use of magazines from Kalashnikov assault rifles of the corresponding caliber.
The Vulcan is available in 5.45×39 mm, 7.62×39 mm, and 5.56×45 mm calibers.
The history of the assault rifle began with the Malyuk project, work on which started in 2005 following the signing of a contract with the Scientific and Technical Directorate of the SSU.
The developers were tasked with creating a bullpup-style assault rifle, making maximum use of existing Kalashnikov components. In late 2006, prototype models were handed over to members of the SSU’s Alpha special forces unit for testing.
Subsequently, the project attracted the interest of the Ministry of Defense, but further development of the design dragged on for several years.
A new phase began in 2014, when representatives of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine contacted the developers. They proposed refining the assault rifle in accordance with military requirements and experience in the combat use of small arms.
It was this refined design that was given the code name Vulcan. According to Serhiy Lugovskyi, chief designer at InterProInvest, the assault rifle underwent such significant changes during development that only about 20% of the design elements from the original Malyuk version remained.
Therefore, it is more accurate to view Malyuk and Vulcan not simply as two names for the same unchanging assault rifle, but as different stages in the development of a single design. Malyuk became the initial project, while the model refined for military needs received the official designation Vulcan Special Assault Rifle.
At the same time, the name Malyuk has not disappeared and continues to be used by the manufacturer and in open sources regarding this family of weapons.
The common designation Vulcan-M is not the official name of the assault rifle. According to Lugovskyi’s explanation, it appeared in the industrial design documentation as one of the proposed names for the product’s appearance, after which it spread among journalists and in open sources.
According to the documentation, the military model is named the Special ‘Vulcan’ Assault Rifle.
Separately, based on this design, the civilian self-loading hunting carbines Malyuk K-01 and K-02 were developed. Unlike the military Vulcan, they do not have an automatic fire mode: a single pull of the trigger fires a single shot.
The first prototype Malyuk rifles were handed over to the SSU’s Alpha special forces unit for testing as early as 2006.
After the start of the Russian-Ukrainian war, testing of the rifle continued, now incorporating lessons learned from combat operations. Representatives of military intelligence joined the effort to refine the design.
In the mid-2010s, Ukrainian special forces tested the weapon, particularly in combat conditions in the Donbas. The assault rifles also underwent trial use in units of the Special Operations Forces.
In 2017, the Armed Forces of Ukraine adopted the 5.45×39 mm and 7.62×39 mm versions under the official designation Vulcan Special Assault Rifle.
Subsequently, this weapon was spotted in the hands of service members of the Main Intelligence Directorate, Special Operations Forces, Airborne Assault Troops, and the Marine Corps. Vulcans were also supplied to certain special-purpose units of the Military Law Enforcement Service.
Thus, the assault rifle primarily spread among units for which the weapon’s compact size, while retaining a full-length barrel, could be advantageous when operating in vehicles, buildings, and other confined spaces.

Trump approval at record low; Hispanic voters sour on US Republicans, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:18:54 UTC
04:18:54 KST

Trump approval at record low; Hispanic voters sour on US Republicans: Poll
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s approval rating held at a record low in recent days, as many Hispanic voters panned his job performance and planned to spurn his Republican Party in next month’s midterm elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Oct 5.
The six-day poll showed 32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump’s presidency, unchanged from a September Reuters/Ipsos survey that saw the leader’s rating at the lowest of his political career.
Hispanic voters helped propel Trump to victory in the 2024 presidential contest, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote compared with roughly one-third in the 2020 election.
But support for the President has waned in recent months as Americans struggle with high inflation triggered by Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran.
Just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance in the White House, the lowest share in either of Trump’s two presidential terms.
Many independents still undecided
The poll gave numerous signs that Trump’s low popularity was weighing heavily on his Republican Party, with registered voters preferring Democrats to Republicans by 44% to 37% less than a month before the Nov 3 election.
Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% of independent registered voters still undecided.
Just 26% of Hispanic registered voters plan to vote Republican in the contest, which will determine control of both chambers of Congress during the last two years of Trump’s current term.
Some 52% of Hispanic voters plan to vote for Democrats, about double the level of support for Republicans and the largest Democratic advantage since Trump took office.
Republicans are bracing themselves for a rough performance in the congressional elections.
Many analysts have predicted Democrats will take a majority in the House of Representatives, with control of the Senate also increasingly seen as up for grabs.
Cost of living is the top issue on Americans’ minds as they decide how they will vote in November, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Consumer inflation has spiked following a surge in gasoline and diesel prices brought on by the war with Iran that Trump launched in February.
Republicans’ advantage among older Americans has dwindled in 2026.
Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump’s party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points – 44% to 42% – compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December.
The 50-and-older demographic is particularly important for midterm elections when older Americans historically have made up large shares of the electorate. Among voters under age 50, Democrats led by 18 points.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, surveyed 4,506 US adults and had a margin of error of about two percentage points. REUTERS

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, surveyed 4,506 US adults and had a margin of error of about two percentage points. REUTERS

Russia says it’s fighting scammers. Its latest proposals would push VPN services off Russian servers, tie eSIMs to devices, and expand telecom data retention.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:17:15 UTC
04:17:15 KST

Russia says it’s fighting scammers. Its latest proposals would push VPN services off Russian servers, tie eSIMs to devices, and expand telecom data retention.
Fighting fraud has been a major focus of Russian lawmaking in recent years. The country has already adopted two sweeping packages of anti-fraud measures, and the authorities often use the fight against fraud as a pretext to push through repressive measures. This was their justification, for example, for banning voice and video calls on Telegram and WhatsApp. This week, Russia’s Digital Development Ministry published provisions from a third package aimed at telephone and online fraud. It includes another set of major proposals that could impose much tighter restrictions on internet use in Russia. Meduza reviewed the document and breaks down its key proposals.
VPN services would find it harder to use Russian hosting providers
Roskomnadzor, Russia’s communications regulator, would create a separate registry of Russian hosting providers’ customers who use rented computing resources to run proxy or VPN services that help circumvent internet censorship. Individuals or companies found to be circumventing blocks would be barred from signing new contracts with any hosting provider in the country for a full year.
The government would have to establish a procedure for Roskomnadzor and hosting providers to exchange this information.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 10²⁻¹. Special rules governing hosting providers
5³. The federal executive authority responsible for regulating and overseeing the media, mass communications, information technology, and telecommunications shall maintain, under a procedure established by the Government of the Russian Federation, a registry of persons who use hosting providers’ computing resources to host information and telecommunications networks or information resources (a website and/or webpage on the Internet, an information system, or a computer program) that provide access to information resources or information and telecommunications networks blocked within the Russian Federation under this Federal Law, and whose owners have failed to comply with the requirements of paragraph 1 of part 7 of Article 15⁸ of this Federal Law. The Government of the Russian Federation shall determine what information must be included in this registry.
5⁴. A hosting provider may not supply computing resources for hosting information in an information system permanently connected to the Internet to persons listed in the registry provided for in part 5³ of this Article who apply to the hosting provider within one year of being added to the registry.
Russian hosting providers would have to disconnect customers at the FSB’s request
It is unclear whether, in practice, the security service, which oversees internet blocking, would use this power solely to combat cyberattacks or also against VPNs. The amendment reads:
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 10²⁻¹. Special rules governing hosting providers
12. A hosting provider must cease supplying computing resources upon receiving a request to that effect from an agency conducting criminal intelligence operations or from the organization specified in paragraph 2 of part 2 of Article 5 of Federal Law No. 187-FZ of July 26, 2017, “On the Security of the Russian Federation’s Critical Information Infrastructure,” where necessary to counter cyberattacks.
Related reading
Companies would have to report their VPN use to Roskomnadzor
The authorities currently allow companies to use VPNs capable of circumventing Russian blocks, provided they meet two conditions:
The company needs the VPN “for technical purposes necessary to its operations”
The company determines in advance which employees will use the VPN
Under the proposal, companies would have to notify Roskomnadzor that they are using VPNs to circumvent blocks, though the notification process remains unspecified. There would also be unspecified requirements for employees with VPN access, along with rules governing its use. The government would draw up these requirements and rules subject to the FSB’s approval.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 15.8. Measures to counter the use within the Russian Federation of information and telecommunications networks and information resources that provide access to information resources and information and telecommunications networks blocked within the Russian Federation
17. The provisions of this Article shall not apply to operators of state information systems, government bodies, or local government bodies, or to the use of software and hardware that provide access to blocked information resources and information and telecommunications networks, provided that the owners of that software and hardware determine its users in advance and that it is used for technical purposes necessary to the operations of the person using it.
18. The Government of the Russian Federation, with the agreement of the federal executive authority responsible for security, shall establish requirements and rules governing the use of software and hardware that provide access to blocked information resources and information and telecommunications networks in the circumstances specified in part 17 of this Article and by the persons specified in that part. These shall include the procedure for notifying the federal executive authority responsible for regulating and overseeing the media, mass communications, information technology, and telecommunications of the use of such software and hardware, and the content and format of the information to be submitted.
All websites and apps would have to give the FSB users’ registration and login data
The proposed requirement would apply to both Russian and foreign services. They would have to keep records of users’ registrations and every account login for three years. They would also have to give this information to the FSB, with “the information to be supplied and the procedure” still to be determined by the government:
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 8. The right of access to information
10. The owner of a website and/or webpage on the Internet, and/or an information system, and/or a computer program, operating on the Internet within the Russian Federation, where access to information on that website and/or webpage, and/or in that information system, and/or computer program is provided to users who have logged in, must:
2) retain information on users’ account registrations, logins, and account closures for three years after those actions have been completed, and provide that information to authorized government agencies conducting criminal intelligence operations or ensuring the security of the Russian Federation, with the information to be supplied and the procedure determined by the Government of the Russian Federation.
Related reading
Foreign websites and apps would have to authenticate Russian users exclusively by phone number
Currently, authentication requirements apply only to websites, information systems, and programs owned by Russian citizens or legal entities. They can choose how to authenticate users: by phone number, through the Gosuslugi government services portal, through the Unified Biometric System, or through another Russian system.
Article 13.55 of the Code of Administrative Offenses already allows fines of 500,000 to 700,000 rubles for companies that violate this requirement.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 8. The right of access to information
10¹⁻¹. A person specified in part 10 of this Article who is neither a Russian legal entity nor a citizen of the Russian Federation must authenticate users located within the Russian Federation using a mobile phone number.
Sole proprietors and private individuals would no longer be able to sell SIM cards on telecom operators’ behalf
Currently, private individuals, sole proprietors, and legal entities can all sell SIM cards if they have an agency agreement with a telecom operator.
The bill proposes removing that right from the first two groups. Only employees of those legal entities, working under employment contracts, would be allowed to sell the cards. Telecom operators would have to verify the information provided about those employees.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
7. Legal entities that are not telecom operators may enter into mobile telephone service contracts and process subscribers’ payments for those services only if they have written agency agreements authorizing them to act on a telecom operator’s behalf. The powers granted under those agency agreements may not be delegated to third parties. Such agency agreements may not be concluded with sole proprietors or private individuals.
For legal entities that are not telecom operators, employees working under employment contracts with those entities shall enter into mobile telephone service contracts and process subscribers’ payments for those services.
A telecom operator must verify the accuracy of information about an employee of the telecom operator or a person acting on its behalf who arranged the signing of a mobile telephone service contract, using the procedure and methods established in paragraph 6 of this Article.
Telecom operators would have to store additional information alongside the traffic data and metadata required by the Yarovaya law
Operators would have to store information “on network addresses and ports” used by a customer when signing a contract for communications services. They would have to keep it for three years. The government has yet to determine “the procedure for storage and the amount of information to be stored.”
It is hard to say exactly why the authorities want this information. Most likely, it would allow them to determine after the fact whether a subscriber had masked their IP addresses with a VPN or proxy servers when signing a contract.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 64. Telecom operators’ obligations and restrictions on communications service users’ rights during criminal intelligence operations, measures to ensure the security of the Russian Federation, investigative actions, the detention of criminal suspects and defendants, and the enforcement of prison sentences
1. Telecom operators must store the following within the Russian Federation:
3) information on network addresses and ports used by the subscriber and the telecom operator when concluding a communications service contract over the Internet, including the time the contract was concluded — for three years after those actions have been completed. The Government of the Russian Federation shall establish the procedure for storage and the amount of information specified in this subparagraph to be stored.
Embedded SIM cards would be tied to specific devices
When someone buys an eSIM, their contract with the telecom operator would include the identifier (IMEI) of the specific phone, tablet, or smartwatch they use. When an eSIM is reissued for another device, the contract would apparently be amended at the same time. Most likely, this is intended to deter fraudsters from even attempting to clone their victims’ eSIMs (which is no easy task).
Roskomnadzor would monitor telecom operators’ compliance with this requirement.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
1.1. To conclude mobile telephone service contracts, a telecom operator or a person acting on its behalf must use the following, which must meet requirements established by the Government of the Russian Federation:
Where user equipment (terminal equipment) has an embedded identification module whose information can be modified through software, and that information is needed to identify an individual subscriber and/or user equipment (terminal equipment) on a mobile carrier’s network, the mobile telephone service contract must include information about the user equipment (terminal equipment) in which that identification module will be used, including its identifier.
Where user equipment (terminal equipment) has an embedded identification module whose information can be modified through software, and that information is needed to identify a person using communications services under a subscription held by a legal entity or sole proprietor, and/or user equipment (terminal equipment) on a mobile carrier’s network, information about that equipment’s identifier must be entered into the Unified Identification and Authentication System by the subscriber that is a legal entity or sole proprietor, or, at that subscriber’s discretion, by the communications service user. Before providing communications services using that equipment, the telecom operator must verify that the information is present and accurate by submitting a query to the Unified Identification and Authentication System through the Unified System of Interagency Electronic Interaction.
Max would let users lift self-imposed restrictions and buy a new eSIM
Russians can currently bar themselves from obtaining a new phone number by visiting a telecom operator’s office in person or applying remotely through Gosuslugi. Beginning March 1, 2027, they will be able to block calls from abroad in the same way.
For now, the only way to lift these self-imposed restrictions is to visit a government services center in person. The Digital Development Ministry proposes allowing people to lift them remotely, including through the Max messaging app.
Users would also be able to buy a new eSIM through Max.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
1. Within the Russian Federation, telecom operators provide communications services to subscribers under communications service contracts concluded in accordance with civil law, this Federal Law, and the rules governing the provision of communications services.
Communications service contracts may be concluded over the Internet, except in the circumstance specified in the fifth paragraph of paragraph 1.1 of this Article, provided that an individual, including a sole proprietor, or a legal entity expresses consent through one of the following methods:
[…]
using an enhanced unqualified electronic signature and, in accordance with paragraph 4 of part 3 of Article 1 of Federal Law No. 156-FZ of June 24, 2025, “On the Creation of a Multifunctional Information Exchange Service and Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Russian Federation,” providing information contained in documents establishing a Russian citizen’s identity through the multifunctional information exchange service, provided that, to enable the submission of that information through the multifunctional information exchange service, a photograph of the citizen submitting the information has previously been matched to that citizen’s biometric personal data held in the Unified Biometric System
Article 45. Special rules for providing communications services to citizens
7². The restrictions specified in paragraph 7¹ of this Article on concluding mobile telephone service contracts and on allowing user equipment (terminal equipment) to receive telephone calls originating from a foreign telecom operator’s network and bearing numbers corresponding to a foreign numbering system and plan may be lifted through one of the following methods:
3) using an enhanced unqualified electronic signature and, in accordance with paragraph 4 of part 3 of Article 1 of Federal Law No. 156-FZ of June 24, 2025, “On the Creation of a Multifunctional Information Exchange Service and Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Russian Federation,” providing information contained in documents establishing a Russian citizen’s identity through the multifunctional information exchange service, provided that, to enable the submission of that information through the multifunctional information exchange service, a photograph of the citizen submitting the information has previously been matched to that citizen’s biometric personal data held in the Unified Biometric System;
Foreigners would be able to buy SIM cards online in some cases
Foreigners can currently buy a SIM card only in person at an operator’s office. Since January 1, 2025, they have been subject to a blanket ban on signing contracts remotely. The Digital Development Ministry proposes some exceptions, but it is not yet clear how this provision would work.
The exceptions would be set out in a separate document: the rules governing the provision of communications services, approved by a Russian government decree.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 45.1. Special rules for providing mobile telephone services to foreign citizens or stateless persons
2. Mobile telephone service contracts may not be concluded with a foreign citizen or stateless person over the Internet, except in circumstances specified in the rules governing the provision of communications services.

Türkiye says Mecca Defense Alliance discussed support for Saudi Arabia amid developments over Yemen

Esra Tekin
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Türkiye and its Mecca Alliance partners discussed possible support for Saudi Arabia’s defense as well as diplomatic steps to resolve tensions involving Yemen through peaceful means and dialogue, said the Turkish foreign minister on Monday.
Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the Mecca Alliance – formed by Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan – Hakan Fidan said the gathering had been convened in light of recent developments in the context of Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
“We discussed in detail what kind of support could be provided for Saudi Arabia’s defense and, on the other hand, what could be done to resolve the issue peacefully and through dialogue,” Fidan said.
He said Saudi Arabia had taken a “very constructive approach” toward resolving the issue and that participants had an opportunity to hear Riyadh’s position during the meeting.
“We shared some of our views,” he said, adding that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has “put forward a clear will on this issue, and as a reflection of that will, we took a number of decisions here.” 
Work on alliance's institutional structure in final stages
Fidan said the extraordinary session was held alongside a previously planned meeting focusing on efforts to institutionalize the alliance agreement, which was reached this August.
He said work on the alliance’s institutional structure had reached its final stages, with the meeting addressing issues including the structure of the secretariat and the appointment of a new secretary-general.
A candidate proposed by Pakistan for the secretary-general post was approved during the meeting, Fidan said, later confirmed as Pakistan’s Nauman Mahmood, a retired lieutenant general, set to serve a three-year term.
The participants also discussed technical issues related to the alliance and its future institutional framework.
Türkiye’s national defense minister and senior military officials also attended the meeting, Fidan said, adding that they particularly contributed to discussions concerning military, operational, and technical matters.
Fidan said the talks focused both on strengthening the institutional structure of the Mecca Defense Alliance and on possible steps that could be taken in response to the current situation involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
He described the meeting as productive.
The pact forming the new alliance was signed on Aug. 7, followed by a series of steps by its three member states to institutionalize the agreement.

Estúdio Módulo releases designs for Itaú Cultural headquarters in São Paulo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Estúdio Módulo releases designs for Itaú Cultural headquarters in São Paulo
Brazilian architecture practice Estúdio Módulo has released its competition-winning designs for the headquarters of Itaú Cultural, which feature a tall, slender building wrapped in glass and white louvres.
The São Paulo-based architectural studio's design for Itaú Cultural, an arts research institute, was selected through a competition involving six firms.
The design is meant to "establish an intense relationship with the city, both visually and through its use, almost as a continuation of the urban space," said Estúdio Módulo.
"The composition seeks to articulate the legacy of Brazilian concrete art, high-tech solutions with a sustainable character, and references to popular art," the team added.
The design by Estúdio Módulo consists of a slender, rectangular building with 19 levels, eight of which are below ground.
The upper levels are enveloped in a semi-transparent white screen. A terracotta-coloured staircase – meant to evoke "the artisanal character of Brazilian folk art" – is visible through floor-to-ceiling glass walls.
"A skin of white louvres filters the light and gradually reveals the presence of colour in the interior planes, activated by the observer's movement," the team said.
"In oblique and lateral views, the facade surprises with the chromatic dynamism that manifests itself behind the brise-soleil, making the building a kind of kinetic work of art."
The tower rises from a low podium, where a large central cutout will be the primary entrance. The podium's rooftop will have a terrace ringed by glass balconies, with onlookers able to view the street activity below.
"Terraces overlooking the avenue create moments of pause and strengthen the relationship between the institution and the city," the team said.
Totalling 12,275 square metres, the tower will contain spaces for exhibitions, performances and educational offerings, along with studios and public gathering areas.
The below-grade levels – envisioned as a performance hub – will hold an auditorium with 100-plus seats and a theatre with over 400 seats.
The headquarters building is proposed for a site along Paulista Avenue, described as "one of the city's most vibrant and symbolic urban axes".
Nearby are two major cultural institutions, the São Paulo Museum of Art (MASP) and Centro Cultural FIESP.
Itaú Cultural currently occupies a building on the same avenue. Its new headquarters is designed to be a major contribution to the urban landscape.
"The project is expected to become a significant addition to São Paulo's skyline and public space," said the team.
Slated to open in 2031, the building will serve as the headquarters for Itaú Cultural, which promotes of artistic and intellectual work in Brazil.
Other projects in São Paulo include a mixed-use building by FGMF that consists of irregularly stacked boxes and a pair of skyscrapers linked by a glass skybridge, a project designed by Königsberger Vannucchi,
The renderings are by Estúdio Módulo.

'Huge gap' between employers and abuse survivors over workplace support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:15:02 UTC
04:15:02 KST

'Huge gap' between employers and abuse survivors over workplace support
In short:
Research by the Humans for Purpose Academy has found the vast majority of survivors felt inadequately supported by their workplaces as they escaped domestic and family violence (DFV).
The report found major gaps that employers can address to help women, including better informing women about access to DFV leave.
It found that women in migrant and minority communities faced bigger challenges in getting support.
Just 8 per cent of domestic violence (DV) survivors said their employer helped them manage the impact on their work, a new study finds, while 71 per cent of employers felt confident they would know what to do.
Research by the Humans for Purpose Academy, published today, also found that despite 85 per cent of employers recognising their duty to support staff experiencing abuse, some 89 per cent of survivors had deep concerns about revealing their situation to their boss, or did not disclose at all.
The report, which highlights the gap between survivors' experience at work and how employers view workplace culture, also found that just 34 per cent of victims were aware of their entitlement to 10 days paid family and domestic violence leave.
Report author and chief executive Melanie Greblo, who is herself a survivor of DV, said the research demonstrated a need for governments and businesses to play a role in helping women through such periods.
The organisation recommended a new national employer compact, expanded reporting and further government-backed incentives.
"Most employers feel confident that they know what to do if a staff member was experiencing domestic violence, but only one in 12 survivors say their workplace actually stepped in to help them manage the impact of their experience on their work," she said.
Ms Greblo said one "huge gap" was that only a third of survivors surveyed knew that Australian employees were entitled to 10 days of leave, while more than 70 per cent of employers were aware of it.
"So the report really calls on business, government and the community at large to come together to really focus on employment as that lever for recovery," she said.
Employment 'a part of recovery' for survivors
The Humans of Purpose Academy report made five recommendations in total:
- Dedicated research funding to map employment opportunities for women escaping DV
- Industry to lead and communicate good employer practice, with expanded government reporting
- Establish a national employer compact for DV-safe employment
- A pilot scheme incentivising small and medium businesses to complete DV workplace training
- Scale up existing, proven recovery-to-employment programs that support women to access safe, secure and sustainable employment
Ms Greblo said the research showed that ongoing employment was "a part of recovery" from DV, rather than "an outcome of recovery".
"We know that employment is critical because of the income it provides to workers, but for survivors of domestic violence, it also supports them in rebuilding a lot of other things like their self-confidence," she said.
"It gives them a social connection and a whole lot of other benefits of being employed that many of us take for granted."
Minorities more vulnerable
Ms Greblo said DV survivors were often juggling legal proceedings, counselling and supporting children who had experienced trauma while trying to gain or maintain work.
"I think what we have is a misconception in Australia that leaving a violent relationship is the finishing line, and sadly, it's not,"
she said.
"But reaching that point of safety doesn't restore your income, it doesn't restore your confidence, your career or your financial independence overnight.
"So we really need to start treating safe, sustainable employment as part of domestic violence recovery."
She said women from minority communities were more vulnerable to a lack of support from employers and were less knowledgeable about ways to find help.
"Those barriers are compounded if you are a migrant woman who's newly arrived in Australia or has arrived in Australia and since left the partner who she came with," Ms Greblo said.
"There can be all sorts of other added barriers around that for women with visas."

'There is so much more that unites than divides' Nigerian king tells 'Post' - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

04:14:37 KST

“The sooner we all heal and allow things to flow from a healed heart, the world can only be a better place,” His Majesty Ogiame Atuwatse III, 21st Olu of the Warri Kingdom of Nigeria, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday in an interview in Jerusalem's Tower of David.
The king's visit to Israel - his first - was organized by Bishop Robert Stearns of Eagles' Wings, a global Christian movement dedicated to strengthening Jewish-Christian relations, supporting Israel, and fighting antisemitism.
The current delegation brought 550 Christian leaders from 51 nations to Israel, where they met leaders, soldiers, and attended the annual international Christian worship festival Awake Jerusalem.
Taking place during Sukkot and the week of the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, one of the purposes of the visit is to "reveal the truth about the region."
Reflecting on this, the king told the Post that peace in the region means "Hearts. Vision. Perception. And once the heart is at peace, at equilibrium, everything stems from the heart."
He said peace is not "simply the absence of conflict," but is about "what flows from being connected to the creator of the world, the source of our being."
The last three years in Israel have been shaped by the terror attack that took place on October 7th, 2023, and the ensuing multi-front war.
At the same time, Nigeria has been experiencing several overlapping conflicts, including the Boko Haram/ISWAP insurgency in the northeast of the country, mass kidnappings, and banditry in the northwest and north-central regions, and militancy (especially in relation to oil) in the Niger Delta region.
What can Israel, Nigeria learn from each other?
Given the conflict-ridden realities of both nations, what does Atuwatse think Israel and Nigeria can learn from each other?
"Too often, we've seen in history where lenses, because of emotions and experiences, are not at equilibrium," he said. "The sooner we all heal and really allow things to flow from that place, that healed heart, the world can only be a better place."
Atuwatse said that beyond the spiritual connection, the relationship between African nations and Israel can be developmental, such as partnering in education, in technology, in infrastructure, in security, and more.
"Israel has always interacted well with Africa, and by Africa I put Ethiopia at the front of that, obviously due to historical ties. Roughly half of the African continent is Christian, and of course Christianity comes out of Judaism because of Jesus Christ, so even for spiritual and religious reasons, our hearts are always in this direction."
"Things are first spiritual before they're physical, so that's why I believe there are so many opportunities for partnership between Israel and the African continent," he continued.
Atuwatse said his key takeaway from his visit has been that "there is so much more that unites than divides."
"Obviously Nigeria is a very diverse nation: there are many tribes, many cultures, a couple of religions, but sometimes people are very focused on the division."
"But if we all yield ourselves, we can produce a really beautiful tapestry. That's the appeal that Jerusalem has."
'Jews, Christians are walking together in solidarity, friendship'
Stearns echoed the words of the king, adding, "When we take the time to humanize the other, when we understand one another's journey, one another's perspective, this begins to bring a place of equilibrium and openness, and from that place, real progress can occur."
He cited Isaiah 60:3, "Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn," as a prophecy being fulfilled given the visit of kings such as the Olu to Israel.
"We live in a day of miracles. Israel has been reborn after 2,000 years of exile. The exiles have returned home from 106 nations of the earth. And now, another miracle. After 2,000 years of division, Jews and Christians are walking together in solidarity and friendship."
While this delegation has been taking place for 24 years, this year takes on special meaning because it is "a tipping point in human history," Stearns told the Post.
"We live in a time where people are more led by emotion than they are by reason. We see tragic photos, TikTok videos, Instagram, and emotions are stirred up."
"That's different than being here and engaging deeply and understanding the layer after layer of the situation here. So our focus at Eagles Wings is the next generation. We are completely focused on bringing the next generation of Christian leaders here."
"It's a domino effect. It's a force multiplier effect that makes an impact in the next generation."
