Alireza Sepahi survived the gallows once, but the Islamic Republic came back for him - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:14:33 UTC
04:14:33 KST

In case you have somehow been living in ignorant bliss, the crimes of the Islamic Republic of Iran are there for everybody to see.
They are visible in the bodies of protesters killed on Iran's streets, when lorries were filled with protesters and driven away to be dumped outside morgues or other locations after January’s massacres, in the prisons filled after successive uprisings, in the testimony of those who say they were beaten, tortured or forced to confess, and increasingly in the gallows erected for those who dared to challenge the state.
The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission reported last month that between March and the end of August alone, Iranian authorities had executed at least 29 men in connection with the protests, five of them publicly, while more than 70 people remained at imminent risk of a death sentence or execution. The mission also detailed trials plagued by forced confessions, denial of access to lawyers, and violations of basic due process, among other legal transgressions.
All of those stories deserve to be told, but among them, one of the most heartbreaking is that of Alireza Sepahi, because in July, when the Islamic Republic came to kill him, his own heart stopped them.
Sepahi was born in 2001 and was arrested following the January uprising in Isfahan. He became one of the defendants in what is known as the Alikhani Square case, built around events on January 8, when, according to the Iranian judiciary, four members of the security forces were killed during clashes with protesters. The state accused defendants in the case of crimes including moharebeh, or "waging war against God," efsad-fil-arz, "corruption on earth," armed rebellion, carrying weapons, and involvement in the deaths of the four men. On Monday, when announcing Sepahi's execution alongside that of Alireza Raeisi, the judiciary's Mizan news agency stated the convictions had been upheld by the Supreme Court.
The circumstances under which those convictions were secured are another matter entirely.
Sepahi's arrest was violent from the beginning, former cellmate said
Human Rights Watch reported that at least 12 defendants in the Alikhani Square case were sentenced to death in mass proceedings and has documented the broader Iranian judiciary's systematic use of statements extracted under torture and reports supplied by security agencies. Amnesty International separately warned during the summer that defendants in the case faced execution following proceedings it regarded as grossly unfair. IranWire reported that dozens were arrested in connection with the case and that the defendants were given only a handful of short court sessions in which to defend themselves.
Sepahi's own arrest was, according to accounts subsequently given by a former cellmate, violent from the beginning. Iran International reported that security forces entered his family's home and shot him four times in the legs during his arrest. The former prisoner said he had personally seen the pellet wounds and recounted Sepahi's description of what happened: when the judge later suggested that he might have been shot while trying to escape, Sepahi replied that he had been shot inside his room. One pellet was reportedly lodged deeply enough in his thigh to require surgery.
What followed, according to the same former prisoner and Iranian civil rights activists, was approximately 26 days of interrogation and torture. Sepahi was allegedly struck in the face and beaten on his already wounded legs until they began bleeding again. His mother, Somayeh Afshar, was reportedly brought close enough to hear or witness some of what was happening to her son. The former cellmate recalled Sepahi eventually crying out that he would sign whatever his interrogators wanted him to sign. Other defendants later told the court that statements they had given implicating Sepahi and others had been obtained through torture, sexual assault, or threats of rape. Those allegations have not been independently adjudicated, but they are part of a larger pattern of forced confessions documented by international human rights organizations in Iranian capital cases.
His mother was arrested too. Afshar is herself serving a five-year prison sentence at Dowlatabad Prison on charges including assembly and collusion and acting against national security. Sepahi's brother and teenage sister were also detained following his arrest, according to reporting based on accounts from people familiar with the family.
By July, the Islamic Republic’s machinery of execution began moving.
Two defendants in the Alikhani Square case, Erfan Esfandiari and Gol-Mohammad Mohammadi, were executed on July 19. Days later, authorities prepared to execute Sepahi alongside his cousin Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi. On the evening of July 27, an iron scaffold appeared in Alikhani Square itself - meant as a clear signal to protesters of the fate that awaited them. Residents understood what it meant too and turned out in force to protest the public execution. The regime was forced to deploy its security forces to disperse the crowd.
Sepahi never reached the gallows
At dawn on July 28, Abolfazl Sepahi and Amirhossein Safari were publicly hanged. Alireza Sepahi was supposed to die with them, but he never reached the gallows.
Shortly before the execution, under the extraordinary psychological pressure of knowing that he was about to be hanged, Sepahi suffered what Human Rights Watch and Iran Human Rights described as a heart attack, while other reports called it a stroke or severe medical emergency. Whatever the exact medical specifics, he collapsed and was rushed to Al-Zahra Hospital in Isfahan, where he was resuscitated. His cousin and Safari were executed without him.
His heart had saved him this time, but only for two days. Then they returned him to Dastgerd Prison.
It is nearly impossible for anyone who lives in the West, who has grown up with freedom of speech, or any of the basic freedoms that we take for granted, to understand exactly how the regime treats its own citizens. Here, a man who was protesting for a better life was being taken by the state to be executed. His body failed him before the state could complete the task; doctors treated him and brought him back to life. Not for a second chance, though - but just so the Islamic Republic would be the ones to carry out the sentence.
Sepahi’s mother and sister, according to reports, wrote on Instagram that they wished he would not recover from his medical collapse, or even that he had died during the January uprising, because they could not bear the prospect of watching him eventually be hanged.
Imagine what kind of a regime you have to live under for a mother to wish that about her own son. But her son had survived, and when Sepahi was well enough to be executed, the regime had no second thoughts.
In early September, he was transferred once more to solitary confinement, raising fears that the execution was imminent. By then, his lawyer, Shahrzad Shahbazi, had secured a judicial review through Branch 39 of Iran's Supreme Court. Shahbazi said she expected the case to be examined while respecting the defendant's right to a proper defense.
Instead, according to Shahbazi, the parallel branch of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court rejected the request without even convening a hearing and sent the file directly to the sentence-enforcement department. She continued trying to pursue another review.
Sepahi was still in solitary confinement, but by Sunday, things were not looking up.
He and Alireza Raeisi were again moved into solitary confinement at Dastgerd Prison, and their families were summoned for what prisoners and their relatives know as the "final visit." Sepahi's mother was brought from the prison where she herself is serving her sentence so that she could see her son one last time.
That same day, another heartbreaking chapter was added to an already painful story.
Before their arrests, Sepahi had been engaged to a young woman named Mahshad Kashani. She too was imprisoned after the January protests and is serving a five-year sentence. They were both incarcerated, separated from one another, and apparently denied the ordinary life they had once expected to have together. But on Sunday, the two were wed, married over the telephone from their respective prisons.
Human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi recited their marriage vows. Nobel laureate Shirin Ebadi summed up what followed in a single sentence: "He became a groom yesterday, and today they executed him."
At dawn on Monday, Alireza Sepahi was hanged at Dastgerd Prison. Raeisi was executed with him. With their deaths, seven defendants from the Alikhani Square case have now been executed.
Even then, the pain for Sepahi's family was not over when they were reportedly denied access to his body for burial.
IranWire reported that the family asked to bury him in Isfahan but was refused permission and told that his body would instead be transferred to Kashan. Iran International subsequently reported that he had been buried there. Similar restrictions on funerals and the return of bodies have repeatedly been reported after Iranian protest crackdowns, in part because funerals themselves can become centers of protest. Hundreds of relatives of protesters have reported since January how they have been denied any access to their loved ones’ bodies for burial. It is among the mounting crimes of the Islamic Republic against its own people.
There is a temptation when writing about the Islamic Republic regime to use increasingly elaborate adjectives: brutal, barbaric, medieval, monstrous. After more than four decades of domestic repression, perhaps the vocabulary begins to fail because every word has been used so many times before. It is simply evil.
Sepahi's story needs no drama or embellishment. He was arrested after a protest, shot during that arrest; he and other defendants alleged torture and coerced testimony, before being condemned to death in a mass case whose proceedings have been challenged by Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and UN experts. He watched co-defendants, including his cousin, go to the gallows. When his own execution came, his heart gave out. So he was resuscitated, returned to prison, and put through the process again. His Supreme Court review was accepted and then rejected by another court without a hearing, according to his lawyer. His imprisoned mother came to say goodbye, while he married his imprisoned fiancée by telephone. Hours later, he was dead.
Another window into the regime we are fighting against
Public executions and the accelerating use of capital punishment against protesters inside Iran are a means of political repression intended to instill fear and deter further dissent. The UN Fact-Finding Mission reached a likewise grave conclusion about Iran's intensified use of the death penalty following January’s protests.
For those of us in Israel who spend so much time trying to understand the Islamic Republic as a military and geopolitical adversary, Sepahi's story offers yet another window into the regime we are fighting against. Its conduct abroad cannot be separated from the methods it uses to maintain power at home.
Through the many heartbreaking stories that have emerged from Iran over the past nine months, Alireza Sepahi’s is among the most painful. His heart saved him once from execution, so the Islamic Republic simply bided its time until it could carry out its punishment.

At least 22 people have died after two boats collided on the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of Congo, an official said.
The incident occurred near the town of Ngombe in Lukolela territory in western Equateur province at around 2 a.m. local time on Saturday, Crispin Mputu, the provincial interior minister, told Reuters.
The collision involved two vessels traveling on the river. One was a commercial boat operating between Kinshasa and Mbandaka, while the other was a passenger riverboat traveling from Mongala province to Kinshasa, Mputu said.
The impact caused the passenger boat to sink. A security source told Reuters it had 163 passengers on board.
Twenty-two bodies have been recovered and buried, while 59 people were rescued, Mputu said. He added that other victims might have been buried elsewhere.
River transport is the main form of travel and trade in much of western Congo
The sunken vessel remains submerged at a depth of 12 meters, and recovery efforts were continuing on Monday evening, Mputu said.
River transport is the main form of travel and trade in much of western Congo, where towns and cities are located along the Congo River, but accidents are common because vessels are often overcrowded and poorly maintained.

New mural in Tel Aviv shows Bart Simpson as a Hamas terrorist, Netanyahu, Eisenkot chasing him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:14:29 UTC
04:14:29 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yashar politician Gadi Eisenkot, wearing bulletproof vests and carrying batons, chase Bart Simpson, who has been transformed into a Hamas terrorist in a new Tel Aviv mural titled RUN.
The latest intervention of the Italian pop artist who goes by the name ‘aleXsandro Palombo’ appeared on September 29 as a new mural located on Yeven Metsula Street, Tel Aviv.
The mural was painted less than a month before Israel's October 27 Knesset election and days before the anniversary of October 7.
The scene turned a cartoon chase into what Vanessa Esteban describes as “an immediate and provocative image.” Simpson was reinvented as a young Hamas fighter pursued through the street by Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Although Netanyahu and Eisenkot sit on opposite sides of the political aisle, Palombo’s mural places the two pursuing the same target amid the campaign.
Bart as a child soldier
Palombo’s intention to politicize Bart’s character in his new work signifies the indoctrination of minors, jihadist propaganda, and the transmission of violence to new generations, the artist explained in a statement.
“Hamas becomes a reference within the mural to an ideological system in which propaganda, the glorification of armed struggle and radicalization also reach children,” Esteban pointed out.
RUN is part of a series of new interventions that Palombo is currently creating in Israel. An Italian artist, Palombo is known for a visual language that combines pop culture, street art and striking imagery to address memory, diversity, ethics, antisemitism, violence, human rights, discrimination and the relationship between power and society.
This work was done despite graffiti being illegal in Tel Aviv, as the city has allowed most graffiti relating to October 7 to stay up.
A familiar cast
Palombo has repeatedly reworked Simpsons characters in past works, including a mural that appeared outside the Holocaust memorial in Milan depicting Simpsons characters in Auschwitz and an image elsewhere of Marge Simpson cutting her hair in solidarity with Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman who died as a result of police brutality in custody in September 2022.
This particular image was “erased several times, and after each removal I recreated it, recontextualizing it, so that attempts at censorship and silence would not be the final answer,” Palombo told Bet Magazine Mosaico during an earlier interview.
In a 2025 interview about the vandalism of his Holocaust mural in Milan, Palombo told The Jerusalem Post that using the unmistakable style of the Simpsons allowed him to speak directly to younger generations.
The art of resilience
“I won’t give up,” Palombo asserted to Bet Magazine. “With my murals, I engage in civil resistance. I tell the story of our wounded times.”
The magazine describes Palombo’s art as “painful images inspired by current events” and “uncomfortable works that are periodically vandalized and erased by fanatical extremists.”
While his anonymity is similar to that of the artist Banksy (another well-known “hidden” urban artist), the Jüdische Allgemeine has reportedly dubbed him “the anti-Banksy,” according to Bet Magazine Mosaico, because of his opposing views on issues such as antisemitism, terrorism, and memory.
The contemporary pop artist and political activist describes himself as an "authentic outsider" but, in recent years, has had numerous works of his dedicated to combating antisemitism, preserving Jewish memory, and addressing October 7, repeatedly vandalized.
While vandalism significantly undermines an artist’s integrity, Palombo stated that “sometimes, recreating a vandalized work is an act of responsibility and resistance: I don’t give up, and I continue because those faces and those stories must not be left alone.”
Palombo did not discover his predominant themes after October 7. As early as 2014, in the series "Stop Hamas Terrorism" and "Once Upon a Time the Children of Palestine," he depicted Aladdin and Jasmine as armed terrorists threatening bound Disney princesses, alongside child characters such as Bart Simpson, Pinocchio, and Peter Pan, shown as child soldiers.

Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:10:43 UTC
04:10:43 KST

The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens.
The co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”, running contrary to its belief in the right of Israel to exist.
The binding policy motion passed in a vote at the Greens’ conference in Brighton on Sunday. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.
The policy says Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, should be “treated as any other form of racism”, and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine “with equal rights for all”.
The European Green party, which represents 47 parties, including the Green party of England and Wales (GPEW), said it supported a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, and the new motion went against this.
The alliance “will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW, to understand the official party policy of GPEW, how they position themselves towards the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people and members in the party”, it said in a statement.
Felix Banaszak, the leader of the German Greens, known formally as Alliance 90/the Greens, told a press conference the motion was “intolerable and unacceptable”.
“It runs counter to everything that Alliance 90/the Greens stands for in Germany, and it also runs counter to what the European Green party stands for,” he added.
Banaszak said: “There is a widely held view within the European Green party that Israel has a right to exist and that this right must not be undermined.” His party would “approach our partner parties in Europe to clarify how to deal with this”.
Sandy Ruthven, the chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust and a longstanding Green member, resigned over the motion and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism.
The fallout from Sunday’s vote has also intensified a debate over whether the Greens’ highly decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly.
Policy is made at the party’s two annual conferences, which generally involve a small proportion of members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.
Ellie Chowns, a former co-leader, said the party’s governance and policymaking “urgently need to be modernised”.
“As a party we pride ourselves on our democratic member-led policymaking process, but I do think we need to ask ourselves some searching questions when less than 1% of our members actually participate,” Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, told the Guardian. “This is long overdue and has become even more urgent with the huge expansion of our membership.”
Chowns said she understood the concerns of European Greens, which she shared, but stressed: “There is still much more that unites us than divides us.”
One source in the party said the criticism from European Greens, especially those in Germany, was understandable given their differing stances on Gaza and Israel.
They said: “The German Greens support arming Israel, opposed a ceasefire to Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, backed the suspension of funding to Unrwa and co-sponsored a Bundestag resolution describing the arguments and methods of the peaceful, Palestinian-led BDS campaign as antisemitic.”
Any change to internal party structures would be hard to implement. One Green insider said that to give MPs greater authority over members would undermine the party’s commitment to grassroots democracy. However, they said the existing model could produce a lack of coherence and strategic direction, while giving a disproportionate influence to members with the most time to participate in policymaking.
They suggested members could determine broad strategic priorities, with smaller bodies developing detailed policy while remaining accountable to the membership.
Another senior Green defended the party’s model of direct democracy, arguing that allowing members to determine policy was fundamental to the party’s character.
Daniel Schuster, the regional director of the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s European office, said: “The British Green party’s decision to formally classify Zionism as a form of racism is absurd, not based on any logical basis and is itself racist. And timing, just days before the third anniversary of the 7 October terrorist Hamas attacks, is designed to inflict pain on a deeply solemn occasion.
“Branding Zionism itself as racism crosses a profoundly consequential line. It takes a movement for Jewish national self-determination and transforms it into something for which Jews are expected to apologise. We will not.”
In a statement, the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, said: “Antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct – blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe. It’s our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK. As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of.”
He added: “Through the Green party’s unified stance and dedicated pressure, we have begun to shift this government away from its complicity with the Israeli government’s atrocities in Gaza, with the foreign secretary now taking the long overdue step of ending trade with illegal settlements.”

Boeing to triple production of guidance heads for Patriot missiles — secures major contract

Boeing to triple production of guidance heads for Patriot missiles — secures major contract
Kyiv • UNN
Boeing has received a seven-year, $14.7 billion contract from Lockheed Martin to expand production of PAC-3 MSE guidance heads. Capacity\r\nwill triple.
On Monday, Boeing announced that it had received a seven-year contract from Lockheed Martin worth approximately $14.7 billion to expand the production and supply of guidance seekers for PAC-3 MSE (Missile Segment Enhancement) missiles, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
According to media reports, the PAC-3 MSE is a kinetic-hit-to-kill interceptor used in the Patriot air defense system to intercept ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as aircraft.
This contract will allow Boeing to triple production of guidance seekers for the PAC-3 MSE—a key component of the missile's guidance system that detects and tracks targets and ensures their interception.
In January, Lockheed announced that it had concluded a seven-year framework agreement with the U.S. Department of Defense aimed at increasing annual production capacity for PAC-3 interceptor missiles from approximately 600 to 2,000 units.
These production agreements are intended to encourage contractors to accelerate the expansion of production volumes.
They are part of a broader initiative by the Trump administration aimed at giving priority to weapons production over payments to shareholders.
Industry representatives warn that Congress has not yet allocated funding for these agreements, meaning that contractors may be unable to make large-scale investments in components and production capacity until lawmakers make the relevant decision.
The publication emphasizes that demand for these interceptors has surged as conflicts in Iran and Ukraine deplete U.S. weapons stockpiles; this prompted the U.S. Army in July to sign a contract worth up to $58.6 billion with Lockheed Martin to increase PAC-3 missile production.

Meet the 2026 Nobel Prize Winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:09:23 UTC
04:09:23 KST

The Nobel committees announced the year’s first winners on Monday, awarding the prize for physiology or medicine to a trio of scientists who the committees said have “laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience.”
The news kicks off a week of announcements for the prestigious prizes, which are awarded each October to individuals or groups for outstanding contributions across six fields: physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, peace, and economic sciences.
The committee will continue revealing the winner or winners of one category every weekday until the final laureate is announced. The physics award will be given on Tuesday; chemistry on Wednesday; literature on Thursday; peace on Friday; and economic sciences next Monday, Oct. 12.
Winners will receive a diploma, a medal, and 12 million Swedish kroner—the equivalent of roughly $1.2 million—during the award ceremonies in Stockholm and Oslo in December.
The peace prize, often the most closely watched of the awards, will be given to one of 287 candidates who were nominated this year, the Nobel committee said.
Last year, the honor was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado to honor her work fighting against dictatorship and promoting democracy in her country for nearly 25 years. Machado later gave her medal to President Donald Trump, who has long coveted and publicly campaigned for the prize, after the U.S. ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a military raid in January.
Read More: Meet the 2025 Nobel Prize Winners
The committee, however, issued a statement in the wake of the gesture declaring that laureates cannot share or transfer prizes.
“The decision is final and applies for all time,” the committee wrote.
Trump has again been nominated for the peace prize this year, but is not expected to win the award amid the U.S.’s ongoing war with Iran.
Here’s what to know about the 2026 winners who have been announced.
Physiology or medicine
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were awarded the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine for their pioneering discoveries in optogenetics, a method that uses light to determine how cells operate in the brain or even to exert control over those processes.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for physiology or medicine.
Hegemann is a professor of biophysics at Humboldt University in Berlin. Nagel teaches plant physiology at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. And Deisseroth is a professor of behavioral sciences at Stanford University.
The laureates' use of optogenetics will allow researchers to “discover exactly which of the nerve cells in a complicated bundle control different brain functions,” such as those related to pain, social behavior, thirst and hunger, and reward and attention, the committee wrote.
Nagel said in an interview with the Nobel Institute that he was “very surprised” upon receiving the news and that he thought it was “too early to get this prize in medicine optogenetics,” given his belief that other medical discoveries have benefited a greater number of people. Hegemann said to the institute that he was “overwhelmed” upon receiving the news.
Deisseroth, who has similarly said he was “quite surprised” to receive the honor, told Stanford Medicine that he “couldn’t be happier,” noting that “the trio that the committee picked spans the progression from the early algal explorations all the way to advanced neuroscience experiments.”
“So this prize really captures the full journey of discovery,” he said.

Christa Pike survived two lethal injections. Could Tennessee try to execute her again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:02:44 UTC
04:02:44 KST

Nearly five days after a failed attempt to execute her with two lethal injections, convicted murderer Christa Pike remained unconscious Monday in a Tennessee hospital, with her lawyers saying it could be several more days before her fate becomes clear.
Little information has been released about Pike’s condition since the failed execution. She is known to be hospitalized under guard while doctors try to clear the massive dose of the lethal drug pentobarbital from her body.
In an interview with CNN on Sunday, Pike’s attorney Stephen Ferrell was asked whether she had regained consciousness at any point since the execution attempt. “Not to my knowledge,” he said.
Ferrell said that before the execution, Pike had granted medical power of attorney to another person, who is now protecting her privacy. “I’m not sure exactly what that person has been told,” he said.
Speaking about what Pike experienced before she was rushed to the hospital, Ferrell said: “We don’t know right now, and we may never know, what kind of torture she went through during this process, where her consciousness was, what physical pain she experienced and what psychological torture she endured.”
Pike, whose case has received extensive international media coverage in recent days, was just 18 when she murdered her classmate Colleen Slemmer on Jan. 12, 1995.
Slemmer was studying with Pike and Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, in a vocational training program in Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was interested in Shipp and, in a fit of jealousy and rage, lured her to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee campus, where Pike and Shipp tortured and brutally murdered her.
Pike slashed Slemmer more than 100 times with a box cutter and struck her with a large piece of asphalt. Shipp carved a pentagram into her body, a star-like symbol associated with Satanism.
The crime scene caused widespread alarm at the time amid the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s in the United States, when rumors circulated about supposed satanic cults abducting people, including children, and subjecting them to ritual abuse.
Pike’s 1996 death sentence made her one of the youngest women ever sent to death row in the United States.
Her attorneys and supporters later argued that capital punishment was excessive given her very young age when she committed the crime and untreated mental illness, following a childhood marked by neglect and severe sexual abuse, including rapes at ages 11 and 17. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Ferrell has stressed that during the sentencing phase of Pike’s trial, her defense lawyers did not present jurors with critical information about her background or argue that her young age should be taken into account.
He has also pointed to advances in understanding adolescent brain development and argued that Pike’s death sentence was unusually severe. Pike’s boyfriend, Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the murder, was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole because of his age.
Prison chief resigns, Trump asks: ‘How does that happen?’
Last week, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee rejected Pike’s clemency request, while the Supreme Court also declined to stop the execution.
Just an hour before the originally scheduled execution time on Wednesday, another court unexpectedly issued an order temporarily blocking the sentence while it considered several of Pike’s claims. Hours later, the execution was allowed to proceed.
Pike was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. The procedure began Wednesday evening local time. The execution team first administered one dose of pentobarbital intended to kill her.
When the drug failed to produce the expected result, the team administered a second dose, as required by the protocol. Pike still survived. Witnesses who attended the execution, as well as her attorneys, said that during the procedure she complained: “I feel like my arm is going to explode.” At another point, she asked: “Is it supposed to happen like this?”
Witnesses said she could be heard crying, whimpering and breathing heavily throughout the procedure. Even when they were removed from the viewing room more than two hours after entering, they said they could still hear Pike snoring loudly behind the closed curtains.
Pike was taken to a hospital unconscious, with her arms swollen and blistered from the injected drug, but still alive. She was intubated and placed on a ventilator.
Following the failed execution, Lee announced that executions in Tennessee would be suspended through the end of the year and ordered an independent investigation into the state’s capital punishment system, led by former federal prosecutor Ed Stanton.
Tennessee Correction Commissioner Frank Strada announced his resignation Saturday following the failure.
The botched execution became a national controversy and also drew a reaction from U.S. President Donald Trump.
“How does that happen?” Trump said the following day. “It should be easy to do. It shouldn’t be particularly difficult.”
If Christa wakes up: ‘She may not be legally competent’
It remains unclear what will happen to Pike’s death sentence. Her attorneys have already asked Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison, but Ferrell said Tennessee has not yet announced whether it intends to try to execute Pike again.
“If she recovers, she may not recover fully, and there may be questions about her legal competency,” he said.
Pike’s lawyers believe problems with the intravenous lines may have caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body tissue rather than properly entering her bloodstream.
“Apparently, at no point did anyone on the execution team realize that the IV lines were not properly placed or that the veins had blown, and that the pentobarbital was entering, in whole or in part, into Ms. Pike’s tissue,” her attorneys wrote in a court filing.
The filing noted that Pike had previously argued that executing her would constitute cruel and unusual punishment because of her particular physical conditions, including thrombocytosis, post-traumatic stress disorder and small veins.
Meanwhile, as they prepare for future legal proceedings, Pike’s attorneys asked a court over the weekend to order Tennessee correction officials to preserve all written records, correspondence, photographs and video footage from the attempted execution.
Officials from the Tennessee Department of Correction and the state attorney general’s office have remained almost completely silent since Pike was taken to the hospital.
Like many other states that use capital punishment, Tennessee maintains strict secrecy around many details of its executions, from the identities of those involved in the procedure to how the drugs are manufactured and obtained and what quality-control testing they undergo.
“The state of Tennessee needs to start telling its citizens exactly what it is doing, so that through the democratic process the people of Tennessee can decide whether this is what they want done in their name,” Ferrell told CNN.

Trump blames Democrats and Ukraine for soaring US fuel prices, not Iran war
Trump shifts blame for fuel price hikes to Democratic-led states such as California and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
With the United States midterm elections approaching, President Donald Trump has attempted to shift blame for high fuel prices from the US-Israel war on Iran to Democrats and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries.
“What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘Refineries,’ where Russia’s are being blown up by Ukraine, and where ours are being closed up, in Blue States, like California, by the Dumocrats,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Monday.
While Trump claims domestic refinery closures are driving the spike, daily exports through the Strait of Hormuz have actually plunged 97 percent since the war began, choking global supplies.
Petrol prices are continuing to climb for consumers. The average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) is $4.36, up from $4.14 a month ago and up from $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices.
“The ongoing conflicts with Iran and Russia’s war with Ukraine are reinforcing each other, impairing oil product markets, but Middle Eastern flows are far from normal,” Rachel Ziemba, senior adjunct fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
On Friday, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves amid pressure from the White House. Meanwhile, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve hits its lowest level since 1982.
“US tells some [European Union] members to release ‘strategic reserves’ or face a potential US diesel export ban, pushing France and Germany to do so, oil prices, along with gasoline and diesel futures strongly lower as a result,” Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X.
Global pressures
Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure have also driven up prices, particularly diesel fuel. On Sunday, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence claimed that it has disabled more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity.
“The damage to Russia’s refineries – and risk of more US sanctions on those who process Russian oil – are exacerbating the situation, but the underlying issue is still the volatile flows from the Middle East, the greater difficulty getting oil products out and the lower buffers in place,” Ziemba added.
The latest strikes come amid ongoing attacks since the war between Russia and Ukraine began in 2022. In June, Russian refinery throughput hit its lowest level in two decades, according to an analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA). The analysis also found that diesel production has fallen 30 percent over the past 18 months.
Trump has also blamed price increases on refining cuts in Democratic-led states such as California, where two refineries have shut down over the past year. The closures reduced the state’s refining capacity by 17 percent, creating some supply gaps, according to an analysis by S&P Global.
However, Trump’s effort to shift blame to Democrats comes ahead of consequential midterm elections that could shape the balance of power in Washington. At the same time, most Americans appear to blame Trump for rising prices. A recent AP-NORC poll found that 65 percent of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for higher prices, while 61 percent said the US economy is worse off than when Trump returned to office.

'I'm not a terrorist, I'm just a journalist', how to carry on reporting for Russia and Belarus from exile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
19:00:37 UTC
04:00:37 KST

Alina Koushyk and Maxim Katz, two opposition journalists living in exile who fled Belarus and Russia respectively, on how they pursue their work from abroad.
"Journalism is not a crime," Alina Koushyk, Editor-in-chief of Belsat, a TV station founded in Poland in 2007 and broadcasting independent news to neighbouring Belarus, tells Euronews.
The Lukashenka regime, which has been cracking down on opposition and the press, labelled the Belarusian journalist a "terrorist" and an "extremist" and Moscow added her to its list of wanted individuals.
"I'm not a terrorist, I'm just a journalist. For many years, I've been working just to say the truth, an alternative point of view. And this is not a crime".
A dozen of journalists working for Belsat have been imprisoned in Belarus. The regime released most of them last year.
In addition, Minsk released 250 political prisoners in March, including Belsat TV journalist Katsyaryna Andreeva, in a deal brokered by the United States, and in exchange for US sanctions relief.
But former Belsat employee Ihar Ilyash, along with other prominent Belarusian journalists such as Denis Ivashin, remain behind bars.
Meanwhile, Russian opponent and YouTuber Maxim Katz had left Russia three days before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine per chance, to record part of his documentary series on World War II in London.
When the war broke out, he says he understood he couldn't go back to Russia, anticipating Moscow's crackdown on dissident voices.
He was right, of course. A few weeks after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Moscow introduced war censorship laws banning people from calling it a "war" instead of a "special military operation", with dissidents facing up to 15 years in prison.
Russia designated Katz a "foreign agent" and "wanted person" and sentenced him in absentia to eight years in jail.
Katz is now based in Israel with his family.
"This gives me an opportunity to feel free about what I am doing", he says.
For her part, Koushyk says although she feels safe in Europe, she adds she always keeps her eyes open, stressing cybersecurity and media literacy are essential for journalists protection.
"Belarusian and Russian secret services are working here. There are agents, there are spies, and this is not a cinema. This is our reality".
'Satellite is important'
Koushyk says she thinks daily about how to report about her home country despite the distance.
"We try to keep close contact with Belarus and with the ground as much as possible, but of course, yes, we are in exile", Koushyk says.
So the journalist scans legal sources, authorities websites but also Telegram channels and TikTok: "Ordinary people inform [us] a lot about what is going on in the country".
But she cannot interview Belarusians in the street or even call them over the phone, because they would immediately be jailed, she says.
Belarusian authorities labelled the Poland-based channel an "extremist" organisation in 2021 - as it did Euronews in 2026 - with Belsat TV employees and viewers facing up to seven years in jail.
Hence, satellite networks are crucial to reach audiences in countries facing censorship, Koushyk says.
"Satellite is important, especially for Belarus, because if you watch satellite, you don't have digital threats. They cannot trace you".
Reporters without Borders has launched the Svoboda satellite in 2024 to broadcast independent and reliable information in Russian to countries affected by censorship.
In addition, Belsat TV relies on several platforms including Instagram and YouTube to reach its audience.
Koushyk says, unlike in Russia, it is possible to access their digital content in Belarus without a VPN.
And Katz says the best way to reach audiences in Russia is YouTube, followed by Telegram.
Although Russian authorities have blocked access to YouTube since February, it remains accessible with a VPN.
Katz' YouTube channel has a daily reach of one million people, which is comparable to some Russian TV channels, he says.
How to deconstruct propaganda
According to Koushyk, the best way to deconstruct Minsk's propaganda is by informing the audience based on facts, by providing an alternative point of view.
"I don't believe that you have to say that they are wrong and we are right".
Katz adds journalists have to adapt their language if they want to reach the Russian audience, by talking about problems people "see from their window" and issues "from their daily life".
"Obviously, I'm anti-war and anti-Putin. But the question is, how do you tell it?"
"If you want to talk with the Russian audience, you should talk as you would talk in a kitchen in St. Petersburg and not at a protest action in Riga."
Although she criticises Lukashenka's regime, Koushyk says she is "very patriotic".
"Journalism is a mission. It's much more than just information because we are not only informing our audience, we are also promoting Belarusian language, Belarusian culture. That makes our society more resistant to Russian propaganda".
Katz considers returning to Russia after a possible fall of the Putin's regime.
He hopes the next Russian government will be pro-European, stressing there is a higher pro-European sentiment among the population than people think.
But he fears the atrocities the Russian army is committing in its war against Ukraine will prevent Moscow from coming back to the European table of discussion any time soon.
For her part, Koushyk is confident she will one day return to Belarus.
"Everything we are doing is [aimed for us] to be back to our country".

He was given clearance to join the Roosters earlier than scheduled, and made his NRL debut in the final round of the 2024 premiership.
To suggest Nawaqanitawase made an impact in rugby league is an understatement.
He took the NRL by storm in his first full season, which was capped off when he debuted for Australia in last year's Ashes series in England.
Nawaqanitawase was selected in NSW's successful State of Origin squad this year and played a crucial role in helping the Roosters capture their first NRL premiership since 2019.
His athleticism and aerial skills on the wing contributed to an astonishing strike rate of 47 tries in as many NRL matches.
Nawaqanitawase has hit the pause button on his NRL career for now, having signed with Japanese rugby club Saitama Wild Knights on a two-year deal.

Kiss is justified in declaring Nawaqanitawase will not walk straight back into the Wallabies squad.
But his presence will create competitive pressure among candidates for the Wallabies' wing spots ahead of the Rugby World Cup, which Australia is hosting.

Shin Bet joins UAE probe of flydubai co-pilot accused of crash plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:57:16 UTC
03:57:16 KST

Israeli Shin Bet security officials have arrived in the United Arab Emirates and are taking part in the interrogation of the Omani co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flydubai passenger jet bound for Tel Aviv, as investigators widen their inquiry into his travels, possible contacts and motive.
Five days after the attack aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073, investigators are examining whether Hamam al-Hammami acted alone or had been recruited or directed by a terrorist organization. The current assessment is that he acted independently, according to Israeli officials familiar with the investigation. UAE authorities have formally described the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.
Al-Hammami has told investigators that he was motivated by a desire to take revenge on Israel over its actions in the Gaza Strip, according to information from the investigation obtained by ynet.
Investigators have also ruled out the involvement of the flight attendants in the attempted hijacking and crash, according to the findings so far. The cabin crew were extremely frightened during the incident, although some Israeli passengers initially suspected that crew members might have been cooperating with the co-pilot.
The suspicions arose in part from passengers' accounts that some crew members demanded that they release al-Hammami after he had been overpowered and restrained. There is no indication, however, that any flight attendant participated in the attack.
Investigators examine travel to hostile countries
Israeli officials say al-Hammami told interrogators that his primary plan was to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport, Israel's main international airport near Tel Aviv. If he could not reach Israel, investigators believe he had a backup plan to crash the plane into a U.S. military installation in Jordan.
The alleged plot was not conceived shortly before last week's flight. Israeli officials say al-Hammami had been planning an attack for months and had initially intended to carry it out in July, but abandoned that attempt because of a personal connection with one of the crew members aboard that flight. Investigators say he had flown to Israel as early as June and was preparing himself to become a "martyr." Other reporting citing officials briefed on the investigation has also said he had previously intended to attack an Israel-bound flight but called off the plan.
At a meeting of the Security Cabinet, a Mossad representative told ministers that investigators had established that al-Hammami had visited several countries Israel considers hostile or enemy states in recent years, not only Syria, as previously reported.
Apart from an extended stay in Syria, the visits were brief. Investigators are examining whether he met anyone during those trips who may have recruited, directed or otherwise influenced him.
For now, however, investigators have found no evidence that al-Hammami was acting on behalf of a terrorist group or foreign government, and the working assessment remains that he acted alone. International investigations are also examining his background and movements in countries where he previously lived or studied.
Authorities in Australia and New Zealand are investigating his time in those countries about a decade ago. Australian authorities have confirmed that a joint counterterrorism team involving federal police, Victoria Police and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation is examining his links to the country. He held an Australian student visa and studied there between 2015 and 2017, according to Australian authorities.
Captain's struggle thwarted alleged plot
The alleged plan was ultimately thwarted by the actions of Indian captain Smit Machchhar, Israeli passengers who helped overpower al-Hammami and off-duty pilots who stabilized and later landed the aircraft.
The Sept. 30 flight was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers, most of them Israelis, when al-Hammami attacked Machchhar inside the cockpit with an emergency crash axe, according to UAE authorities and Israeli officials.
Investigators believe al-Hammami intended to beat Machchhar unconscious, seize the controls and crash the aircraft.
Despite being seriously wounded, Machchhar fought back and managed to open the cockpit door, allowing others to enter and overpower the co-pilot. A reserve flydubai pilot traveling aboard the aircraft later took control and landed it safely at Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia.
The aircraft plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds during the struggle. 
According to an investigation by the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, al-Hammami disconnected the autopilot, took control of the aircraft, shut down the engines in flight and pushed the controls forward, causing the plane to lose about 16,000 feet in less than a minute.
After al-Hammami was subdued and the aircraft stabilized, the replacement pilots initially sought permission to land in Jordan, according to the Israeli account. Jordanian authorities refused once they learned that a suspected hijacking was underway, and the aircraft ultimately diverted to Saudi Arabia.
Al-Hammami was detained after the landing and later transferred from Saudi Arabia to the UAE, where he remains under investigation.
‘That’s why I chose flydubai’
The investigation has increasingly focused on evidence that the attack was planned before al-Hammami joined flydubai.
Channel 13 reported that al-Hammami told investigators: “I searched and checked which company flies to Tel Aviv, and that’s why I chose flydubai. I tried to get accepted by all the airlines. I planned the operation even before I was hired by the company.”
Two Israeli officials with knowledge of the investigation have separately said he told UAE interrogators that he had planned the attack before joining the airline.
The disclosure has intensified scrutiny of how al-Hammami was hired and how he was cleared to operate flights to Israel.
Al-Hammami had previously worked for Oman Air and was reportedly removed from flying duties after concerns arose about extremist views. Yet no international warning appears to have prevented him from subsequently obtaining a cockpit position with flydubai.
The case has also raised questions in Israel because al-Hammami is a citizen of Oman, which does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. Israeli officials have said pilots from countries without such relations were not supposed to operate flights to Israel, but it remains unclear how that restriction was applied and why al-Hammami was permitted to serve on the route.
Security failures under scrutiny
The attack has exposed broader gaps in the security system governing foreign airlines flying to Israel, including questions over which Israeli agency was responsible for receiving and vetting foreign crew lists.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday acknowledged that there had been a security "loophole" and ordered National Security Council chief Shmuel Ben Ezra to appoint an examiner to conduct what his office described as a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel.
The review comes amid scrutiny of longstanding warnings about fragmented responsibility for foreign aviation security. The state comptroller warned in 2024 of deficiencies in the system and recommended a broader government review of the division of responsibility among agencies. Recent reporting has found continued uncertainty over whether the Transportation Ministry or Israel's intelligence and security agencies were responsible for screening foreign crews.
Netanyahu's review will be internal, however. The person appointed to lead it will not have independent investigative or enforcement powers.
The National Security Council, now headed by Ben Ezra, has itself been involved in efforts to address aviation security arrangements, raising questions over how quickly the review will identify the failures that allowed al-Hammami into the cockpit of an Israel-bound aircraft and whether any resulting recommendations will close the gaps exposed by the attack.

Tories are united behind Badenoch, but MPs want focus on economy over culture wars to win back voters

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:57:10 UTC
03:57:10 KST

During a quick-fire Q&A at the Conservative party conference this weekend, Kemi Badenoch was asked who she would pick between Robert Jenrick or Suella Braverman.
“Why do you keep offering me these? It’s like asking if I’d rather be shot or drowned,” the Tory leader responded with her trademark directness.
The Tories appear more united than they have done in years. Part of that is because they have a common enemy to unite against: Tory defectors to Reform.
It is not lost on Badenoch’s team that this time last year, it was a matter of when, not if, Jenrick, her erstwhile leadership rival, would try to oust her.
Mutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting her demise. But after a successful conference, Badenoch limped on – and Jenrick emerged a diminished figure who weeks later would be kicked out of the party.
His presence, however, lives on, with shadow ministers openly sharing their relief that he is no longer among their number.
“Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left,” said one shadow cabinet member. Others were less polite. “Rob going was like pulling out a splinter,” one said. “I miss him like I miss an abscess in my molar,” another added.
But while the unity comes, in part, from a mutual dislike, there are of course other factors: Badenoch’s strength as a leader; the country’s yearning for stability; the constant threat of Reform UK to the party’s right.
Badenoch has been running the show for almost two years – the longest serving Tory leader since Boris Johnson – and has begun to set out her principles, writing a 30,000 word pamphlet titled The Right Way before the conference.
Tory MPs also seem to have finally realised that voters take a dim view of the party cycling through leaders at such breakneck speed, with five in the past eight years.
Nigel Farage’s woes have also given them reason for hope: while the Reform leader believes his party will recover from a difficult summer, some Tory MPs are confident that his party has peaked.
Other party insiders – possibly more plugged into what is going on in their constituencies – concede that Farage still represents a huge threat. They are among those concerned about Badenoch pitching to the right.
Instead, they say that she needs to do more to win over centrist voters for the party to stand a chance of winning another election. Part of that is by focusing more on the economy and less on culture wars.
“There’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything. But we do have to be careful with our language,” one MP said. Another added: “That’s not Kemi’s instinct. But she does finally seem to understand it all has to be about the economy. That’s where we win.”
Badenoch believes she can “shrug off” the Liz Truss anchor and beat Reform and Labour on the economy, MPs say. Andrew Griffith, her shadow chancellor who has previously worked in business, helps the party’s credibility, they add, and Badenoch will speak more about the topic this week.
The Tory leader also polls ahead of her party, which insulates her from much internal criticism. One adviser said the Tories do better when their leader is in that position – citing David Cameron and Boris Johnson – but worse when they’re behind, as Rishi Sunak was.
Badenoch has told her top team that they have to work “day by day” to restore the party’s fortunes. Yet there is no escaping that almost two years after she was elected as leader, the Tories are still polling lower than they did in 2024 with their catastrophic general election defeat.
“You won’t hear much from us on that,” one senior aide said. “The qualitative stuff is good but it’s not backed up yet by the numbers. We need to put on three or four points in the polls. If we do that and gain momentum we’re back.”
Others are hopeful that the exposure of their conference week can give them enough of a lift in the polls to help them maintain the narrative that they’re on the march.
The spectre hanging over the whole affair, however, is the prospect of a snap general election. Andy Burnham’s political away day at Chequers on Monday has got many Tories spooked, even though the prime minister has ruled out calling an early election.
Perhaps more in hope than expectation, shadow cabinet ministers said they did not believe Burnham would call an election. “He said it would be irresponsible and it’s hard to walk that back,” said one.
However, Badenoch told a bash for Tory MPs on Sunday night the party was getting ready for an election regardless. But while she sounded bullish, her closest lieutenants are anything but. “If there is one, we’re all fucked,” they said.

NATO drafts plan to defeat Russian attack with drones and AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:56:09 UTC
03:56:09 KST

NATO drafts plan to defeat Russian attack with drones and AI
NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defence technologies like drones and AI into traditional power.
The so-called theory of victory document, which Bloomberg has seen in an unclassified form, will be presented by Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, in Poland on Oct 12 amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia.
It is meant to clarify how the alliance would handle a possible incursion into NATO territory, according to senior officials and diplomats familiar with the matter. There have been numerous recent reports that Moscow is considering such action.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said recently that there were no indications that Russia was preparing for a conventional attack on the alliance but that Europe should be prepared for enduring hybrid attacks.
Grynkewich spokesman Colonel Martin O’Donnell declined to discuss details of the plan, but emphasised that the alliance was “purely defensive”.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage,” O’Donnell said.
“Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked.”
Although the broad strokes of NATO’s warfighting principles are known, open communication about them is rare.
The initiative is meant to reassure the public about NATO’s readiness while showing a more concrete picture of what is behind the heightened defence spending.
The document is also meant to illustrate to allies how NATO would integrate traditional weapons with the new capabilities that have emerged since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and to urge more defence investment and better preparations, the people said, asking for anonymity to discuss private matters.
The strategy insists on the defensive nature of NATO and on avoiding involuntary provocations, while explicitly mentioning the need to collectively counter hybrid threats – aggressive actions below the threshold of a conflict – as part of deterrence.
By demonstrating readiness, NATO wants the enemy to conclude that it cannot win, the strategy says.
But if NATO were attacked, it would block an incursion with a mix of land forces and other assets from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a concept relying on low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting.
After gaining freedom of manoeuvre, it would seek to destroy enemy command and control with the goal of defeating Russian forces quickly and overwhelmingly.
NATO allies, especially in Europe, have massively ramped up defence spending, with tensions emerging about how to prioritise between traditional weapons such as tanks, and alternative technology that has come to the forefront in the Ukraine conflict.
On Oct 5, Germany’s foreign intelligence chief warned lawmakers that Russian President Vladimir Putin has passed the point where he could end attacks on Ukraine “without jeopardising his power base at home,” increasing risk around the continent.
The US sent a questionnaire to NATO allies this summer gauging their defence spending and support for President Donald Trump’s policies to inform decisionmaking on planned cuts of US military assets committed to defending Europe.
As part of this questionnaire, the US asked whether allies had any more forces to commit to NATO for Grynkewich’s defence plans. BLOOMBERG

Northrop’s Talon Blue Collaborative Combat Aircraft Makes First Flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:54:43 UTC
03:54:43 KST

Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue YFQ-48A Collaborative Combat Aircraft took its first flight Oct. 3, heightening the competition for the Air Force’s future combat fleet.
Talon Blue is Northrop’s so-called “loyal wingman” drone, an autonomous aircraft designed to pair with crewed fighters. The Oct. 3 flight was an important milestone for the firm as it looks to break into the Air Force’s CCA program—thus far, the service has awarded production contracts to General Atomics and Anduril Industries, but more “increments” are expected in the coming years.
Northrop said the drone completed a fully autonomous flight, including taxi, takeoff, “in-flight maneuvers,” and landing from its Mojave, Calif., facilities.
Air Force leadership say they plans to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. While the service has not selected Talon Blue for production yet, the company has been bullish that the service could be a customer in the future. The Air Force also gave Talon Blue an official Department of Defense Mission Design Series designation, YFQ-48A, last December, signaling that it sees the aircraft as a competitor for future CCAs.
“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness,” Craig Woolston, Northrop Grumman’s vice president and general manager for research and advanced design, said in a statement. “We listened. Talon Blue’s first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities. Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next.”
The company’s CCA is a unique offering. It was first unveiled last December to a small group of reporters, including Air & Space Forces Magazine, as a self-funded effort. The company’s Scaled Composites subsidiary, known for its history of innovative aircraft, built it, and the company has touted how quickly it developed the aircraft. The time between when the aircraft was conceived and when it had “weight on wheels” was roughly 15 months, company officials said. When Northrop announced the aircraft, it said it expected the aircraft to fly around fall 2026, a milestone the company has now met.
Talon Blue falls under the company’s broader Project Talon. The project also includes the Talon IQ, an autonomous testbed for using Scaled Composites Model 437 aircraft. Talon IQ uses Northrop’s Prism mission autonomy software. So far, the Air Force has pursued a “software sold separately” approach to CCAs, running separate competitions for the mission autonomy software and the aircraft themselves.
While General Atomics’ FQ-42 Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ Fury FQ-44 have been awarded production contracts from the Air Force and are undergoing ongoing testing with the service as part of the Increment 1 of the service’s first autonomous wingman, Northrop Grumman is hoping to market Talon Blue for future Air Force purchases and to U.S. allies.
Northrop’s original CCA offering lost out on the Increment 1 contracts due to its cost, president of the company’s aeronautics division Tom Jones said, leading to what became Talon Blue.
“The idea was to see if we could build an aircraft that had all the same capability of our original offering, and do it faster,” Jones said at the unveiling last year. “So the outcome was an aircraft, but the outcome we’re shooting for was the process: How do we design and build things that perform at a high level, but that we can build quickly now and can do affordably?”
The Air Force has yet to spell out the requirements for Increment 2 of the CCA program.
“It’s getting defined as every day goes by,” Gen. Dale White, the Pentagon’s director of critical major weapon systems, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference when asked by Air & Space Forces Magazine about the status of Increment 2.
“The challenges I may have in the Indo-Pacific theater could be very different [from those] in the [U.S. Central Command] theater and different again in the [European Command] theater,” White said. “So how do we take all of those different requirements and make sure we have a [CCA] capability that can address many different mission sets across many different requirement centers?”
Whether Northrop’s Talon Blue fits into that picture is still unknown. But the YFQ-48A could also be appealing to U.S. allies, some of which have started rolling out their own CCAs, such as the U.K. government-backed, British-designed Brontanax CCA from BAE Systems. U.S. Air Forces in Europe and NATO Allied Air Command boss Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds said other European nations were watching the U.S.’s work on CCAs.
“You’re going to see a lot more interest from other nations inside Europe,” Hinds said at Air, Space & Cyber when asked about CCAs.
When the Talon Blue aircraft was unveiled last December, Jones said multiple U.S. military services and international partners are interested in the drone, and some had visited Mojave to see it.
“We’re still extremely good at making something very complex,” Jones said at the time. “This was really about broadening that paradigm to what it means to be a high-performing engineering, aviation, development, and manufacturing organization to encompass all aspects of it.
Talon Blue is important for Northrop’s future tactical aircraft efforts, as the company recently lost out to Boeing to build the Navy’s future F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter jet. The company is still building major weapons systems for the Air Force: the B-21 Raider stealth bomber, set to enter service next year and a project that will likely be expanded beyond the original program of record of 100 aircraft, and the LGM-35A Sentinel, the next-generation intercontinental ballistic missile.
The CCA market Talon Blue is competing for is crowded, not just by the FQ-42 and F-44, but also by Lockheed Martin’s new Vectis offering. Other possible competitors, such as Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat and Kratos’s XQ-58 Valkyrie, have been used by the U.S. military in tests and exercises alongside crewed aircraft.
The Air Force sees CCAs as a critical part of the future force.
“I can imagine a day in the future, 10 years [from now], maybe more, where a CCA autonomy algorithm does a better job flying a fighter airplane than I did as a captain,” Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s Chief Modernization Officer, said last month. “That hurts my ego a little bit. But at the same time, I see that this trend is happening, and we’ve got to find a way to do that.”

The Fossil Fuel Turning Point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:45:08 UTC
03:45:08 KST

The world has spent decades debating how to transition away from fossil fuels. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, 195 countries reached, by consensus, an unprecedented agreement to do so. Since then, we have seen both the cost of waiting and the opportunity to act.
From Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) warnings to the recent confirmation by the United Nations Environment Programme that the world is set to overshoot limits needed to prevent some of the worst of global warming's harms, change is imperative. Extreme weather events are becoming more lethal, frequent, and intense.
It is crystal clear to us that fossil fuel dependence is a liability, threatening energy security and economic development across the planet.
Yet the past year has also brought significant progress, showing how the transition away from fossil fuels is becoming a reality. After leaders gathered in New York for Climate Week and the UN General Assembly, there are several lessons we must carry into COP31—and reasons to accelerate action.
An emphasis on implementation
At COP30’s closing plenary, we announced a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels by 2050. It examines the barriers societies face, the finance and policies they need, and the different pathways available to them, recognizing that countries start this transition from very different points.
Our agenda was also restructured to accelerate implementation of the Paris Agreement, uniting the world around solutions. A new two-tier multilateralism is already in motion. One speed is anchored in countries and consensus. The second, which does not require consensus, focuses on implementing the decisions of the COPs.
In that spirit, COP30 stimulated coalitions under the Global Climate Action Agenda, such as the one that organized the Santa Marta Conference, convened by Colombia and the Netherlands. The subsequent report set out options for national planning, investment, and international cooperation.
These efforts are building the foundations for our future beyond oil, gas, and coal. The test now is whether they help countries turn commitments into action.
An early answer came last month when Germany became the third country, after France and the Netherlands, to publish a national roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. At the UN General Assembly in New York, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider presented the roadmap to phase out oil, coal and gas by 2045, framing fossil fuel dependence as a costly vulnerability.
Our fossil fuel dependence laid bare
When the war against Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the consequences reached far beyond the region. Brent crude prices rose above $100 a barrel, putting pressure on fuel costs worldwide, squeezing government and household budgets alike. Since the start of the crisis, inflated prices for oil and gas have cost an extra $1.83 billion per day to importers with no additional benefit.
Spain and Brazil show that this vulnerability can be reduced. By late April, benchmark wholesale electricity prices had risen more than 20% in some European countries. In Spain, where renewables supplied nearly 60% of electricity, prices had fallen. Its investment in renewable power helped cushion the shock, showing how the choices countries make about their energy systems can protect them from fossil fuel volatility. In Brazil, the country with the largest proportion of renewables in the energy mix in the G20, the impact of prices has also been far less severe, as most drivers have the option to choose sustainable ethanol instead of gasoline at pumps nationwide.
Our overreliance on fossil fuels has become unavoidable, undeniable, and unsustainable.
Renewables are the world’s leading source of electricity
The clearest evidence yet that we have reached a positive tipping point for our power systems arrived in April, when the global energy think tank, Ember, released an annual review confirming that renewables overtook coal as the world’s leading source of electricity in 2025.
Renewable energy truly is the growth story of our time: powering economies, creating jobs, and strengthening competitiveness. Countries that build abundant, affordable renewable power, and the networks to deliver it, can attract the industries and investment of the electric age. And produce at scale the non-fossil fuels to decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors such as air and maritime transport.
Momentum is continuing to build: Southeast Asian countries have released four times more long-term renewable energy and electrification policies than fossil fuel policies since the Iran war.
According to the United Nations, every dollar invested in renewable energy creates up to three times as many jobs as a dollar invested in fossil fuels—making the transition an opportunity to build livelihoods as well as energy security.
The challenge ahead
In 2025, the world added more renewable electricity capacity than in any previous year, but deployment must accelerate. To meet this global imperative, we must double the amount of renewable power currently deployed on our grids in the next four years.
We must also scale the electrification of energy, transport and industry to strengthen energy security, improve efficiency and boost competitiveness. Earlier this year, we launched the Electrify Now campaign to advance this effort. The incoming COP31 Presidency has also proposed increasing electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035. The challenge now is to turn this momentum into improvements people can see: electric buses on city streets, cleaner heat for homes and factories, reliable electricity for communities still without it, sustainable fuels replacing fossil ones in sectors where electrification is challenging.
Delivering those benefits requires renewable energy as well as stronger grids, storage, and institutions able to coordinate their development. Without effective planning, projects can wait years for connections, and renewable resources fail to reach the people who need them.
At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, we shall strengthen credible plans, or commitments to develop them, for clean electrification within wider energy and economic strategies. Those plans must reflect national circumstances, be built in dialogue with society, and set out how national and subnational governments, together with business and many other actors, will expand infrastructure and stimulate investment.
Business must match those commitments with capital, technology, and training. International financial institutions must help countries facing high borrowing costs secure affordable finance. Workers and communities affected by the transition need support to share in its benefits.
What matters is what changes beyond the negotiating halls: more secure, affordable energy, better livelihoods, and less exposure to the next fossil fuel crisis. The task ahead is vast and calls for systemic change, but the direction is set, and the tools are at hand.

Türkiye, Pakistan activate collective deterrence of Mecca Pact against Houthi attacks on S Arabia

Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan moved to strengthen their joint defence framework on Monday as senior political and military officials met in Riyadh for an emergency session of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee established under the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defence.
Türkiye was represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, National Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu. The meeting comes amid renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and wider concerns over regional security.
Fidan said the three countries discussed steps to support Saudi Arabia's defence while also examining ways to resolve regional issues peacefully through dialogue.
The alliance was established in August by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, with the three countries subsequently agreeing to build permanent institutions and strengthen collective deterrence and defence capabilities.
Allies seek stronger collective defence
According to Pakistan's Foreign Ministry, the three countries agreed that military forces and capabilities could be rapidly deployed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance's framework.
The sides also condemned attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Madinah and reaffirmed their commitment to confronting attacks against Saudi Arabia and Islamic holy sites.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said the alliance remains committed to confronting attacks and protecting the kingdom, while collective deterrence measures would be used against threats and those responsible.
Pakistan's Foreign Ministry also announced that Nauman Mahmood would serve as the Mecca Alliance's first secretary-general for a three-year term, reflecting the effort to establish a permanent institutional structure.
Focus on dialogue alongside deterrence
The Riyadh meeting also highlighted diplomacy as part of the alliance's approach to regional crises.
At the alliance's first Strategic Political and Defense Committee meeting in Istanbul on August 31, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan agreed to support de-escalation and restraint and encourage peaceful solutions to regional disputes.
They also agreed to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia and expand cooperation in defence industries, joint technology development and production.
The latest meeting comes as Saudi Arabia faces renewed attacks by Yemen's Houthis and as discussions continue over possible political engagement to reduce tensions.
The three countries are seeking to develop the Mecca Agreement into a more institutionalised security framework while combining collective defence measures with diplomatic efforts aimed at regional stability.

Russian Strikes Damage 533 Ukrainian Rail Locomotives, Forcing Kyiv to Seek Replacements
