- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Strikes Damage 533 Ukrainian Rail Locomotives, Forcing Kyiv to Seek Replacements
Ukraine is seeking replacement locomotives from European partners after repeated Russian strikes nearly exhausted its reserves and threatened rail deliveries supporting Black Sea exports, the Financial Times reported on October 5.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi told the Financial Times that Kyiv is negotiating with countries that use the same 1,520-millimeter railway gauge to secure locomotives compatible with the Ukrainian network.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In 2026, Russian forces increasingly targeted locomotives, passenger trains, and stations, repeatedly disrupting services and forcing temporary evacuations of passengers.
The shortage is already affecting logistics around Ukraine’s port of Pivdennyi. Mykyta Hrubov, chief executive of port operator TIS , told the FT that three locomotives had been lost near the company’s terminal, creating a bottleneck for cargo deliveries.
Russian forces have intensified attacks on trains carrying grain and iron ore in recent weeks, putting additional pressure on the rail system that connects Ukrainian producers with Black Sea ports.
Radio Liberty reported on October 1 that Russian attacks had damaged 533 Ukrzaliznytsia locomotives and another 75 belonging to private industrial companies since the start of the full-scale invasion, citing Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry.
Ukraine is working with the European Commission and international railway organizations to identify locomotives available abroad, First Deputy Infrastructure Minister Serhii Derkach told Radio Liberty. Negotiations include Azerbaijan, neighboring countries, and private operators.
Slovakia has offered three locomotives, while Lithuania has agreed to provide another three. Derkach added that Lithuania has 27 broad-gauge locomotives that could potentially be purchased for Ukraine.
“We see that the number of locomotives currently available and that can be delivered to Ukraine can, in principle, ensure the normal operation of Ukrzaliznytsia for now,” Derkach stated.
He cautioned that the outlook would depend on the intensity of further Russian strikes and Ukraine’s ability to protect its rolling stock.
Ukraine has also secured $100 million through the World Bank’s RELINC program to purchase locomotives, Derkach noted, according to Radio Liberty.
Partners are additionally helping Kyiv explore purchases of used rolling stock as the fastest replacement option.
“The first priority, of course, is finding used locomotives that are in working condition, so they can be acquired, brought to Ukraine, and immediately put into service,” he explained.
The pressure on Ukraine’s locomotive fleet is part of a broader Russian campaign against the country’s railway system. In 2026, Russian forces intensified strikes not only on locomotives but also on passenger trains and stations, forcing regular service disruptions and temporary passenger evacuations.
Days earlier, a Russian overnight attack damaged the Kyiv-Pasazhyrskyi railway depot, along with data centers, business centers, and residential buildings in the capital. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the strikes as attacks and stated that emergency crews were working almost continuously to deal with the aftermath.

Now Is the Best Time to Get Your Flu Shot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:40:08 UTC
03:40:08 KST

Doctors often use the phrase “flu before boo” to remind people to get their flu vaccine before Halloween. But this flu season, you might not want to wait until Oct. 31 to get vaccinated.
“We might be seeing an early flu wave this year,” says Emily Martin, professor of epidemiology at the University of Michigan’s School of Public Health, pointing to national clinical surveillance data collected by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) that shows an uptick of flu cases in the U.S. in recent weeks.
“It's not unusual to have a little bit of flu show up when college students return to campus and when kids go back to school. However, we've been seeing some flu activity in the last few weeks that seems to be sticking around,” says Martin, who studies the spread of respiratory viruses and vaccine effectiveness.
Getting the flu shot now is a good idea, Martin says, as it takes about two weeks for the vaccine to become fully effective. She adds that October is generally an ideal time to get the flu vaccine because it not only offers protection from early waves of the virus, but also gives continued coverage through January and February when flu cases are typically at their peak.
“The flu shot’s effectiveness does wane over time, so if you get it in June or July, it could be weaker by the time you get to February,” she says. “Still, it’s important to remember that the flu shot—whenever you get it—is more effective than not getting a flu shot at all. So if you have an opportunity to get it, don't overthink the timing.” Martin says she plans on getting the flu shot next week.
What are the different types of flu shots?
The flu vaccine is available as a shot or nasal spray. For the first time, a flu shot using mRNA technology is available this year. In a study published in May 2026, the mRNA-based flu shot, produced by Moderna and called mFlusiva, was up to 27% more effective in preventing flu than any of four currently available flu shots. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved mFlusiva for people ages 50 and older.
You need to get a flu vaccine every year to stay protected against the virus as flu strains are constantly evolving, and immune protection against the flu decreases over time. (That is also true if you get sick from the flu, Martin says. Natural immunity also wears off.)
Is the flu shot effective?
Flu vaccination helps prevent infection and significantly reduces the risk of severe disease and death. The CDC estimates that flu vaccination prevented 10 million flu-related illnesses, 180,000 flu-related hospitalizations, and 12,000 flu-related deaths in the U.S. during the 2024–2025 flu season.
But flu vaccination rates have been declining across the U.S. in recent years. Flu vaccination among children fell from 63% in the 2019–2020 flu season to 50% in 2024–2025—a drop of 13 percentage points. About 300 children died in 2024-2025 because of complications related to the flu. Most of them were unvaccinated, the CDC says.
Who should get a flu shot?
The Trump Administration has attempted in recent months to weaken flu vaccine recommendations, but official vaccine guidance remains unchanged: The CDC continues to urge everyone aged 6 months and older to get the flu vaccine, a recommendation affirmed by other medical organizations such as the American Medical Association (AMA) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).
Earlier this year, the CDC, under direction from the U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., tried to reduce the number of routinely recommended childhood vaccinations from 17 to 11. Seasonal flu was one of the six vaccines no longer recommended to all children. A federal judge blocked the move.
In August, President Trump signed an executive order that called for the same overhaul to the childhood immunization schedule, but the order doesn’t? have legal power, legal experts say, and official vaccine recommendations haven’t been impacted.
Doctors and vaccine scientists say the Trump Administration’s moves have sown confusion and skepticism about vaccines.
“Vaccines shouldn’t be a political discussion. They are scientific tools that have done a great job at preventing infections and deaths,” says Dr. Ashlesha Kaushik, a pediatric infectious diseases specialist and AAP spokesperson. “There has been no change in the scientific evidence to inform the [Trump Administration’s] announcements. It’s just confusing to medical professionals and to parents.”
If people have questions about vaccines, they should speak to their doctor, Kaushik says. “I encourage parents and patients to ask their clinicians any questions they have. Clinicians are on their side.”
Kaushik says she and her children have already received their flu shots this year.
The flu vaccine remains “our best bet” at preventing hospitalization and serious complications from the flu in both adults and children, Kaushik says. It reduces the risk of dying from the flu by 80% for children.

According to initial reports from the investigation, which is taking place in the United Arab Emirates, Hammami is said to have stabbed the flight’s captain with a cockpit emergency axe and attempted to seize a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, with the intent of harming some 166 Israelis on board.
Israel is still working to establish a final profile of Hammami to determine whether he acted as a ‘lone wolf,’ was affiliated with any organization, or was sent directly by Iran.
His interrogation revealed that he sought revenge for what he described as the “genocide in Gaza,” sources say.
Following reports that his intent was to crash the aircraft into Ben-Gurion Airport, sources from the interrogation also said he had prepared a backup plan to crash the plane into the US military base in Jordan, which has been targeted by Iran on multiple occasions over the past year.
IAF officer: 'I couldn't be calm' until incident ended

America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:36:17 UTC
03:36:17 KST

America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
The Pentagon’s decision to relocate B-1 bombers from the British air base comes after months of frustration in the Trump administration over Britain’s defense spending.
LONDON — Britain and the U.S. sought to ease friction Monday after American bombers were suddenly moved amid major security concerns at the base that hosted U.S. aircraft used to strike Iran.
The U.S. move is the latest stumbling block in the special relationship between the allies and underscores reservations in Donald Trump’s administration about how the U.K. is handling its defense and security commitments.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday that it had removed all B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford air base — where they were deployed to conduct what have been termed as "defensive" strikes against Iran — and sent them back to their home stations in America.
Advertisement
Trump went further, telling journalists Monday evening: "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? ... If we're going to be threatened we're just going to move them, and that sort of alleviates that."
It comes as Britain's counter-terrorism agencies investigate a suspected terror plot against the air base, which the U.K. government believes involves Tehran.
Trump on Monday added: "We actually know the people that made the threat, and they've got themselves a big problem," adding in response to a follow-up question: "They would be linked to Iran."
He later said that he believes the U.K. is still a safe place for U.S. forces.
Downing Street had earlier insisted that the base was safe, but refused to comment directly on America’s decision to remove the bombers from the area.
The move comes as the Trump administration has grown increasingly frustrated with the U.K.’s defense spending and the White House's continuing anger that the U.K. didn’t send warships to the Middle East to help with the American blockade of Iranian shipping.
Advertisement
Something deeper is wrong
London has yet to outline a path to meet the NATO standard of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035 — up from its current level of around 2.7%. It has also been shut out of a subgroup within the alliance convened by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby. The group is slated to meet again in Poland some time later this month.
Late last month, Colby hinted at that frustration with London, saying the countries' long history will continue to bind them, but the British government needs to make the case to its people for spending more on defense.
“There's this incredible legacy, and that's what we want to rekindle,” Colby said. “Exactly how you convince the British people [to spend more on defense] I would not presume to say, but … there's probably sort of a degree of reconciliation between what the U.K. wants to be doing, what it spends, and what it spends on, because you know a modern military is not cheap.”
The U.S. is also conducting a sweeping review of its posture in European NATO countries — including the U.K. — which will determine the number of American troops and military assets on the continent.
Sophia Gaston, a senior national security researcher at King’s College London, said: “The Trump administration is undeniably sensitive to the costs of the Iran conflict as they head into the midterms next month, so their caution is understandable.
An armored vehicle is seen at RAF Fairford on Sept. 28, 2026. | Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images
“It’s also hard not to, at some level, perceive a degree of uncertainty about the capacity of the British services to currently prevent such an attack. That partly reflects the innate challenge drones and other aspects of modern warfare pose to the sitting ducks of expensive kit.
Advertisement
“But it also speaks to the American wariness towards the pressured state of Britain’s military capabilities. Not only does Washington no longer wish to be solely responsible for allies’ protection, its expectations for the security allies offer its bases has also increased.”
Trump on Monday praised his relationship with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He said: "He's liberal, very liberal, but I hear he's going to open up North Sea oil if he does that in Aberdeen. If he does that, you're going to have a rich country. If he doesn't, you're going to have a bankrupt country."
Britain’s security concerns
In May, the U.K. raised its terrorism threat level to “severe” — meaning a terrorist attack is highly likely — after its MI5 security service said the U.K. had been “experiencing a gradual increase in terrorist threats for some time” including from hostile states like Iran.
In Britain, police and the security services are dealing with a three-fold threat from Iran-backed groups: attacks against Iranian dissidents, attacks against the country’s Jewish population, and the targeting of U.S. assets such as those used for strikes against Tehran.
Counter Terrorism Policing is currently investigating potential Iranian state involvement in a major incident at RAF Fairford on Sept. 27, when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base.
Six men — including a British-Iranian national — have so far been arrested on suspicion of terror offenses. All have subsequently been released on bail while police continue their investigation.
Advertisement
US strike capability
Though the Pentagon stressed that bombers remain “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities” — including from the U.S. mainland — removing them would make any further American strikes on Iran more complex, since the bombers would have to double their flight path from the continental U.S. to the Middle East.
There is a fresh U.S. buildup in the region, with a third aircraft carrier currently steaming across the Pacific along with several large amphibious ships carrying 2,500 Marines, joining the 2,500 already at sea in the Middle East, giving President Donald Trump more options should he restart the bombing campaign after the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
Christoph Bergs, a research analyst at the RUSI defense think tank, said: “The basing of US B-1 bombers at RAF Fairford for operational employment against Iran was based on the UK stipulation that these were only used for defensive strikes. This likely included a more modest targeting list. Their withdrawal reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat.”
The Pentagon declined to comment on whether it will, or is considering, the removal of other aircraft from British bases used to support operations against Iran.
This article has been updated with comments from Donald Trump.

Summer heatwave cost France at least €16 bln, lawmaker says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:35:57 UTC
03:35:57 KST

PARIS, October 5. /TASS/. The economic toll of this summer’s record-breaking heatwave in France has reached approximately €16 billion, a figure that surpasses official government forecasts, Eric Coquerel, Chairman of the National Assembly’s Finance Committee, announced during a parliamentary hearing.
"I would like to note that some parties--specifically representatives of ministries and state agencies--find it difficult to provide figures and estimates. <...> Personally, I arrive at a minimum figure of €16 billion," the lawmaker said.
Coquerel, representing the opposition left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party, based his estimate on macroeconomic costs and the impact on living and working conditions. Citing data from France's National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE), he noted that the extreme weather slashed economic growth by €3 billion and widened the budget deficit by €1.5 billion.
Regarding living and working standards, state agencies spent €2.5 billion, while private households suffered about €500 million in damages. Households also faced an additional €800 million in expenses, driven in part by surging electricity bills from increased air conditioning and fan usage. In the business sector, Coquerel highlighted the agricultural industry, where professional associations estimate losses at no less than €10 billion.
According to Meteo-France, the summer of 2026 was the hottest in France since records began in 1900, eclipsing the extreme summers of 2003 and 2022. On September 16, AFP reported, citing the national public health agency, that approximately 8,000 excess deaths had been recorded nationwide since late May across three distinct heatwaves.
In early August, Minister for the Ecological Transition Monique Barbut projected that the recurring heatwaves could cost the country "approximately €10-15 billion." In early September, French Minister of Economy and Finance Roland Lescure announced that his ministry had downgraded its 2026 GDP growth forecast from 0.7% to 0.5%, noting that the prolonged heatwaves alone shaved 0.1 percentage points off GDP growth.

====================================================================================================

The 100 million-year-old reason this part of Australia has more earthquakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:34:55 UTC
03:34:55 KST

In brief
- The Gippsland region of Victoria has heightened seismic activity relative to most other places in Australia.
- More than 100 million years ago, Earth's crust stretched and fractured along faults, helping form the Gippsland Basin.
At just after 2am on Saturday morning, a magnitude 4.8 earthquake occurred at Arawata, about 6km northeast of Korumburra and 100km southeast of Melbourne.
Residents closest to the epicentre described a loud bang — a phenomenon which occurs only in the epicentral region of an earthquake, when seismic energy reaches the surface.
They also described houses and windows rattling, and trees swaying back and forth as a result of the strong shake.
The earthquake was also experienced across the state of Victoria, waking many people from their sleep even as far away as Shepparton, Ballarat and Warrnambool.
Geoscience Australia received more than 21,000 reports within hours.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The earthquake was followed by hundreds of aftershocks, the majority too small to be felt. The largest so far was a magnitude 3.1 less than an hour after the main shock.
These aftershocks, which by definition only occur near the epicentre, are still happening several days later.
Although earthquakes can and do happen anywhere in Australia, the Gippsland region of Victoria has heightened seismic activity relative to most other places.
But why is this the case?
Gippsland's shaky history
In the last 100 years, there have been about ten earthquakes in Gippsland of about the same size or larger than the one at Arawata last weekend; on average, that's about one every decade, though they haven't always been equally spaced through time.
In 1969, there were two moderate earthquakes of magnitude 5.0 and 5.3 near Boolara, over a period of a few days. This location also produced a magnitude 5.0 in 2000.
In 2012, there was a magnitude 5.4 quake near Moe. Although there were no reported serious injuries resulting from this earthquake, it was the same magnitude as the 1989 Newcastle earthquake, where tragically 13 lives were lost when a building collapsed.
The Korumburra–Arawata region has also experienced a number of earthquakes prior to those that occurred on the weekend.
In 2009, a magnitude 4.6 event was followed by a similar magnitude earthquake about two weeks later.
Since that time, locals have felt around two earthquakes every year, including a widely felt magnitude 4.4 in 2011. There have been many more recorded earthquakes during this time, but they have been too small to be felt.
All this is to show that the region is quite prone to shaking — but not for the same reason as earthquake-prone places like Aotearoa New Zealand.
What makes earthquakes happen
Most of the world's earthquakes happen near tectonic plate boundaries — places such as New Zealand, Japan and the western United States. Here, earthquakes are frequent because of the immense forces where tectonic plates meet.
Even though Australia is well within a tectonic plate and far from its edges, the continent is still stressed by the large forces at our distant plate boundaries — for example, through New Zealand to our east, and Indonesia and Papua New Guinea to our north.
These stresses travel through the plate and build up. When the stress becomes too great, it's suddenly released along zones of weakness in the crust, called faults. That release, and rupture of a fault, is what we feel as an earthquake.
The Korumburra–Arawata region and indeed the whole Gippsland region is known for several geological faults. Here, more than 100 million years ago, the Earth's crust extended to form the Gippsland Basin, and these faults accommodated it.
In more recent times, the last five to 10 million years, these faults were reactivated to accommodate a reverse force: compression of the crust. This has resulted in uplift (Earth's surface rising) and mountain building.
Earthquakes like the one on Saturday morning are a release of stress associated with all these forces.
Young faults
Faults like some of those in Gippsland that have accommodated recent crustal deformation are called "neotectonic", meaning they are geologically young.
We haven't investigated the majority of the neotectonic faults in the Gippsland Basin, so we don't yet know much about them.
One fault that has been studied is the Waratah Fault — a northeast-oriented fault which is about 37km long, extending from Foster to off the coast near Walkerville.
There is geological evidence this fault has hosted an earthquake which was large enough to rupture the surface in the last 125,000 years.
This evidence also suggests that rupture along the full length of this fault could produce earthquakes as large as about magnitude 7.0.
Earthquakes of this size are rare in Australia, and smaller earthquakes are much more likely.
Aftershocks associated with Saturday's earthquake so far appear to align in the same orientation as many of the known neotectonic faults in the Gippsland region, but we don't yet know which fault is producing these latest quakes.
It may even be that they're from a previously unknown fault; this was the case with the 2021 magnitude 5.9 Woods Point earthquake 120km northeast of Melbourne.
Earthquake geologists are looking to investigate additional Gippsland Basin faults in the coming years to better understand earthquake hazard in the region.
Aftershocks of Saturday morning's earthquake are expected to continue over the next few days to weeks. Generally, these earthquakes will decrease in magnitude and will become less frequent with time.
However, as with all aftershock sequences, there's still a chance that an earthquake of similar magnitude or larger may happen.
Dee Ninis is an earthquake scientist at Monash University. She works at the Seismology Research Centre, is president of the Australian Earthquake Engineering Society, and a committee member for the Geological Society of Australia — Victoria Division.
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

Jen's mother died waiting for a visa. Now she fears the same future for her father
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:34:38 UTC
03:34:38 KST

In Brief:
- Families say new visitor visa rules will make it harder to reunite with ageing parents.
- Parent visa applicants face waits of up to 18 years, and more than 40 years in some cases.
Jen's mother died waiting for her Australian visa to be approved.
Now, eight years after first lodging an application, she fears her widowed father could be left in limbo too.
Jen moved from South Africa in 2008 as an international student. Since then, she's built a life in Australia, married, had children and became a citizen.
Thinking about the future, she applied for a Contributory Parent visa in 2018 so her parents could eventually join her in Australia.
Her mother died in 2022 before the visa was processed — and eight years on, her father is still waiting.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In the meantime, he's travelled regularly between South Africa and Australia to spend time with Jen and his grandchildren. But changes to visitor rules mean even that may soon become harder.
"It really impacts our family because we don't have multi-generational care and family around, and my parents don't know my kids as intimately as we wish they would," Jen told SBS News.
The changes were announced in September as part of the federal government's efforts to reduce net overseas migration.
Among them was a new "no further stay" condition that will be applied to visitor visas, preventing holders from applying for another visa while in Australia.
For Australians with ageing parents living overseas, advocates say it removes one of the few practical pathways that allowed families to stay together while waiting for parent visas that can take decades to process.
Now, Jen faces a choice she never expected to make.
"Our whole life is here," she said.
"So if we want to reunite with my dad, I have to move the whole family over either back to South Africa with my Australian kids and my Australian husband and then restart our lives there, or we do this long-distance family thing."
'No further stay'
The "no further stay" condition requires visitor visa holders to leave Australia before applying for another visa.
The government says the measure will ensure visitor visas "are only used by genuine visitors and not as a pathway to extending a stay in Australia" and is aimed at curbing so-called visa hopping.
But Melbourne-based registered migration agent Gary Grewal says the change is affecting families who were never the target.
Until now, parents who met the age requirements could enter Australia on a visitor visa, apply for a parent visa from within Australia and remain in the country on a bridging visa while waiting for a decision.
"Now with the no further stay condition, they cannot apply for these visas," he said. "So the reality is they need to go back and wait overseas."
Grewal said visitor visas granted to parents have also become more restrictive in recent years.
Where parents were previously able to spend extended periods in Australia, more recent visas have often been granted for significantly shorter stays, further reducing the time families can spend together.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said in July that the parent visa backlog was something the government was working to address, but there were no easy answers.
In the 2024-25 financial year, there were 157,000 parent visas in the backlog, an increase of 52,000 compared to six years ago, according to Department of Home Affairs data.
Waits that outlast the applicants
The changes come against a backdrop of lengthy parent visa queues.
The Contributory Parent visa, which costs about $49,000, has an estimated processing time of 18 years.
The much cheaper Aged Parent visa, available to eligible parents who have reached pension age, has an estimated processing time of more than 42 years.
For Jen, those figures have become painfully personal as her father ages.
"Even though we're in the queue, we can't have my dad stay here and just wait it out until the visa's granted," she said.
"If you do the maths, your parent has to be 109 years old to get that visa.
"There's no human filter to these policies that they're putting in place."
Almost half of Australians have at least one parent born overseas, according to 2021 Census data.
Grewal said annual caps on parent visas have contributed to growing queues, leaving families separated for years or even decades.
"It's a big toll on the family for what you want to do, which is spend time with your ageing parents," Jen said.
An impossible choice
For Sandhya, the problem isn't immediate, but she's worried it soon could be.
She moved from the United States to Western Australia about a decade ago. She and her partner are now Australian citizens and have built their lives here with their children.
Her parents, who live in India and are aged in their 70s and 80s, are healthy and active.
But she always assumed that if one of them became seriously ill, lost their partner or could no longer live independently, there would be a pathway to bring them to Australia.
Now she is no longer sure.
"It only takes a fall or an illness or a loss of one of them for the situation to become really urgent and for me to want to bring them here permanently," she said.
"The only option is for us to apply for an aged parent visa, but that's going to take decades.
"One or two years is a reasonable time, but what is with 10 to 20 years? If you're applying for your parents, are you expecting them to live to 150?"
Sandhya said she and her partner have paid almost $2 million in taxes since arriving in Australia and would happily support their parents financially if they came.
"For us to not have any pathway to bring our parents here, that's a very worrying prospect," she said. "So what is the solution for me?"
"I would have to move back to India, but my kids are building their lives here."
The cost to families
Grewal said the loss of bridging visa pathways means family reunification is increasingly becoming dependent on wealth and circumstance.
He points to one Perth family who withdrew a parent visa application because they could not afford the costs involved.
When the father later suffered a serious accident in India, his son had to leave Australia to care for him.
Another couple, a GP and a psychiatrist who had lived in Australia for 15 years, ultimately relocated to India permanently to be with their ageing parents.
"It is very difficult," he said. "Families are going to be split for at least a decade."
"Grandparents can't see their grandchildren. They can't help with their children's families."
Grewal believes Australia risks losing skilled migrants to countries that provide faster and more practical options for family reunification.
Sandhya wants the government to look more closely at the human impact of migration policy and rejects the narrative that immigrants are "resource-hungry".
"People from other countries are legitimate contributors to society here, and we have to find pathways for when they're in a vulnerable state and need support."

Jobseekers exploited by recruitment scammers on LinkedIn
Tony Young is one of many Australians who have applied for work using websites like LinkedIn, only to realise afterwards it was a scam.
The former tech executive has sent out applications for more than 400 jobs over the past three years.
While responding to a job advertisement on LinkedIn, Tony was contacted by someone claiming to be a consultant who could help improve his resume.
"That quickly turned into a conversation where the person was saying 'your resume is not quite a good fit for this but I can do this for you and it's going to cost $1,000'."
When he refused, the "consultant" quickly lowered their offer and asked Tony whether he would "do it for $50".
The ABC has observed an uptick in fraud targeting jobseekers as soon as they update their online status to indicate they are looking for work.
It includes fake job ads, fraudsters posing as recruiters with "cloned" profiles and people taking advantage of desperate jobseekers by offering to help with CV writing for significant sums of money.
Australian jobseekers are being warned about this pervasive, sophisticated employment fraud as recruiters voiced concerns to the ABC and in online forums about fake advertisements flooding recruitment websites.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said in just two months, July and August 2026, it received 138 scam reports relating to LinkedIn with reported losses of up to $254,449.
Fake ads and recruiters
Tony said he often received emails or comments on his online posts that seemed to be from companies purporting to be "hiring" on LinkedIn.
In June, he received an email from a so-called "career and talent leader" at engineering consultancy Aurecon who wanted to have a "senior leadership discussion" with him.
The ABC can confirm that no-one from Aurecon actually contacted Tony.
In addition, the person who emailed Tony had cloned a LinkedIn profile belonging to a real employee from the engineering firm.
Aurecon said it was aware that fraudsters sometimes misused its brand name to deceive jobseekers through fake job emails, fraudulent websites or unsolicited job offers.
The company stressed that it conducts formal virtual or in-person interviews before making offers and would never ask candidates to make any up-front payments.
Is this 'actually real'?
LinkedIn's latest Job Search Safety Pulse report has found Australians are more vulnerable to recruitment scams than ever.
Nearly half of the people surveyed for that report said they would take risks when applying for jobs due to ongoing cost-of-living pressures.
More than a third said they would be more likely to let their guard down.
Questioning whether a job is "actually real" has also become a routine part of the job search, according to the LinkedIn report.
The same report found 61 per cent of Australians had seen a job ad that they suspected was fraudulent and 27 per cent have come close to falling for one.
Around 16 per cent of the respondents said they had fallen victim to job scams.
For younger gen Z jobseekers, born between 1997 and 2012, employment scam victim percentages rose to 25 per cent.
'Designed to exploit' jobseekers
"Recruitment scammers often pretend to represent large companies or recruitment firms and will contact people either directly through LinkedIn or via email with a job opportunity that is tailored to the information on their LinkedIn profile," an ACCC spokesperson said.
They said "job scams may ask people to pay money to start a job" or participate in a "course or training".
Tech recruiter Trevor Churchley said scam activities on LinkedIn had become more noticeable in the past two years.
Mr Churchley said he was personally aware of several real profiles being "taken over or cloned".
He said the fake profiles were then used to target jobseekers who publicly disclosed they were unemployed.
"They're the perfect target to approach because … all of a sudden, they gain the attention of recruiters … hopefully leading to jobs," Mr Churchley said.
"This is a scam designed to exploit jobseekers."
Many applicants place the #opentowork banner on their LinkedIn profiles, hoping to become more visible to recruiters.
But these jobseekers have also been attracting attention from scammers pretending to be recruiters, Mr Churchley said.
Hard to spot a fake
Mr Churchley warned of red flags including recruiters based in unusual locations and having no followers or connections.
He said they were not easy for genuine jobseekers to spot as they are often desperate for work.
He has also warned that no legitimate companies would contact their candidates with @gmail.com, @outlook.com, or @hotmail.com email addresses.
A spokesperson from LinkedIn said "scams of any kind are against our policies" and the company takes "proactive action to detect and remove" the majority of spam and scam content on its website automatically.
"We're continuing our investment in free verifications for identities, jobs, recruiters and company pages to provide trust signals about the people and opportunities on LinkedIn," the spokesperson said.
"More than 115 million members are now verified, with 75 members verifying every minute, and over 81 per cent of all job views on LinkedIn are for verified jobs."
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) noted there are many social media and online networking platforms "where criminals circulate fake job advertisements and attempt to engage potential victims", without providing any specific company names.
"The AFP is aware of employment scams being promoted across a range of online platforms, including professional networking sites," its spokesperson said.
The secret uses of CVs
A resume often contained far more personal information than people realised, said Ryan Ko, director of the Cyber Research Centre at the University of Queensland.
"Beyond names, phone numbers and email addresses, it can reveal employment history, education, professional networks, locations, certifications and even government security clearances," he said.
"Scammers can use this information to build detailed profiles of individuals, making phishing emails, fake job offers and identity fraud attempts far more convincing.
"In some cases, the information may also be used to answer security questions or support account takeover attempts."
Professor Ko said scammers could harvest information on resumes for both direct and indirect benefits.
"Scammers may use it for identity theft, financial fraud, or selling personal data to other criminal groups," he said, adding that this helped scammers conduct "more targeted social engineering attacks" that are more likely to succeed than generic scam messages.
"The more they know about a victim, the easier it is to manipulate them or befriend them."
After securing a six-month full-time contract, Tony is finally able to wrap up his job hunting journey — for now.
"It is a relief to at least be able to close out the calendar year in role and get back to actually contributing,"
he said.

Bruising lead-up to inquiry as OpenAI executive set to take stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:32:15 UTC
03:32:15 KST

analysis
OpenAI hoped for a warm welcome. Instead it's going to face a tough crowd
It is a bruised OpenAI that is set to limp into the Australian political spotlight today at the Joint Select Committee hearing on Artificial Intelligence being held in Sydney.
The company had been pencilled in for a centrestage performance, tapping into a bit of Silicon Valley star power, to convince Australians they should want the AI company to make our nation its second home.
But it is hard to imagine a worse warm-up act than Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's announcement that OpenAI's agents had "hacked" into a Medicare statistics website making global headlines.
It wasn't exactly a digital Armageddon, given the incident was neither particularly sophisticated nor revealed anything of importance. Even though it was quite novel and a taste of things to come.
But you wouldn't have known from the whack Albanese gave the company amid his global push for AI regulation.
He used an international stage to shame the company, revealing it had sent a 2:42am email to a government inbox advising of the hack.
The situation was made worse after subsequent reporting that OpenAI's agents had also tried to hack other federal government agencies and, dropping late on Friday afternoon before the long weekend, the NSW government's news of another hacking.
The Australian government hack was the tip of the iceberg as OpenAI disclosed similar incidents to more than 100 other organisations.
The company has tried to stem the bleeding with a formal apology and sent out a US-based top-level executive, chief strategy officer Jason Kwon, to show they're taking it seriously.
Last time Kwon was here he was wining and dining top public servants. This time he might feel like he's on the menu.
OpenAI isn't the only AI company appearing before the committee, with Anthropic, Google and Microsoft representatives also set to appear, but it has, for better or for worse, been given the top billing.
AI doom predictions not helping
Outside those snafus the preceding weeks weren't much kinder.
Last month was dominated with headlines of researchers at AI companies leaving or, weirdly, not leaving, because of their stated belief there was a good chance they were building a technology that would kill all of humanity.
Now, there's a lot of scepticism around this point of view given it seems to "yada yada" the fairly consequential steps between "AI gets very good" and "the global population goes to zero".
Regardless of your views of the likelihood of AI annihilation there's no doubt the gloomy predictions became part of the global zeitgeist.
In September, Democratic pollster David Shor found that the importance of AI as an issue for American voters had increased "dramatically" in just a week, amid the controversy.
These existential fears only reinforce existing concerns with 70 per cent of Australians saying they think AI is moving too fast, according to polling put out in September by the Minderoo Foundation.
Overall, the hacks, AI doomerism and the barrage of coverage about data centre proposals and the backlash against them has hardly been an ideal warm-up act.
Bipartisan reform and maybe political cover
To understand what we should expect from today it's worth looking at the origins of this hearing.
The creation of a Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence was in fact initiated by the Coalition, with both Andrew Hastie and Aaron Violi speaking in favour of it, moved by Tony Burke, and passed on voices.
In other words: this political examination of AI is a bipartisan expedition.
Contrast that with its duelling federal inquiry, the data centres and artificial intelligence inquiry led by Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, which struck a notably sceptical tone about the social license of AI infrastructure and the companies using it.
Instead, we've gotten a snap inquiry with terms of reference so long and broad you almost need AI to summarise it.
There are some serious and important questions that OpenAI will hopefully face, including but not limited to why it lets its AI have access to the open internet without safeguards or close monitoring.
This is an industry that simultaneously claims to take safety seriously while letting its unmuzzled creations loose into the world.
However, the speculation among the AI industry and its watchers is that the main purpose of the inquiry is in setting the stage for bipartisan-backed reforms that would pave the way for AI companies to train in Australia.
No doubt the Albanese government would like some political cover for any tough decision. Some in the opposition have signalled they're happy to work with the government, even if they wouldn't mind seeing some political pain first.
The copyright problem
Out of everything the government has flagged as an area that needs reform, copyright looms large as the issue that feels the furthest from an solution.
AI companies say they need some kind of deal that would let them train their AI in Australia legally and without fear of repercussions for what is assuredly mass copyright infringement under Australian law.
Creatives and rights-holder groups accuse the AI companies of stealing their work and now refusing to even try to operate legally by signing deals.
They will make that case when they appear at the hearings today, before AI companies get a chance to defend themselves.
Some in the government think this will show the status quo isn't working for anyone and something needs to change.
Last month, we got a glimpse of what the government has been working on behind the scenes with two proposals to change the law to pave the way for AI training on copyrighted material.
Now it's the companies' turn to convince us that it's all worth it.
But after the last few months it's going to take quite a virtuoso performance for OpenAI to get this audience onside.

Ukraine Signs Survivor-Centered Guidelines for Investigating Wartime Sexual Violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:32:05 UTC
03:32:05 KST

Ukraine’s law enforcement agencies have adopted new rules for investigating conflict-related sexual violence that place survivors at the center of the process, with Russia’s full-scale war now in its fifth year and the number of documented cases still rising.
The interagency document will guide investigators from the National Police and the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), as well as prosecutors, in handling such cases. Ivan Vyhivskyi, minister of internal affairs, announced the decision in a statement on Monday, Oct. 5.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today, we took an important step in this direction,” Vyhivskyi said, adding that its key principle is the survivor-centered approach.
“When interacting with the justice system, a person must receive safety, respect for their dignity and the necessary support,” he continued.
‘One of the gravest crimes,’ Vyhivskyi says
Conflict-related sexual violence remains one of the most serious, but also the most common, crime of the war.
The new rules – whose signing ceremony took place in the presence of British Ambassador to Ukraine, Neil Crompton – comply with international and European standards for protecting the victims, including those set out in directives of the European Parliament and the European Council.
According to the minister, the next stage is “coordinated and practical implementation” of the signed document.
This includes systematic training of investigators and prosecutors, unified procedures and proper interagency cooperation.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Guided Bombs Killing 6, Wounding 59, Including Children
UN documents nearly 900 cases by Russian forces
The new instructions for Ukraine’s law enforcement comes less than three weeks after a UN report found that Russian authorities were responsible for the vast majority of documented sexual violence cases linked to the war.
Between Feb. 24, 2022 and July 31, 2026, the UN Human Rights Office recorded 1,004 cases of conflict-related sexual violence, of which 892, or 89%, were atributted to Russian authorities, including the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and the Federal Security Service (FSB).
Most of the victims of Russian abuses were men, primarily Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) and civilian detainees. The report documented 725 male victims, 151 women and 16 children, with female victims ranging in age from 4 to 82.
The documented abuses included rape, gang rape, genital mutilation, electric shocks and forced nudity, as well as threats of sexual violence.
One of the most frequently reported methods involved a Soviet-era military field telephone, known as a “tapik,” used to deliver electric shocks to victims’ genitals. At least 155 Ukrainian POWs and retained medical personnel were subjected to the practice.
Russia refused to give UN unrestricted access to POW camps
Of the report, the remaining 112 cases were attributed to Ukrainian authorities, mostly involving the mistreatment of Russian POWs, with threats of sexual violence accounting for nearly half of them.
According to Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, such violations had been documented on both sides of the front line. However, there was a sharp difference “in scope and scale.”
She said Ukraine has taken “concrete steps to prevent and address such violations,” while also granting UN investigators unrestricted access to POW camps and other detention facilities under its control.
Russia has failed to do the same.
Responding to the findings, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of using rape and sexual violence as a weapon of war. He said the documented cases likely represent only a fraction of the true scale, as many survivors stay silent because of trauma, fear or social stigma.
The UN has also warned that its figures substantially understate the extent of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine, citing underreporting, fear of reprisals and restricted access to Russian-occupied areas.

Mecca alliance agrees to activate collective deterrence measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:32:04 UTC
03:32:04 KST

Turkiye, Pakistan agree Saudi Arabia military deployment under Mecca pact
The three countries agree to trigger collective deterrence measures in response to ‘heinous attacks’ by Yemen’s Houthis.
Turkiye, Pakistan agree to military deployment to Saudi Arabia
Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
The decision was announced on Monday after the three countries’ defence and foreign ministers held an emergency meeting in Riyadh. It marked the first time the alliance – known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence – has been invoked since it was signed on August 7.
The agreement declares that an attack on any of the three nations will be treated as an attack on all, mirroring a central provision of NATO’s founding treaty.
“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures, within the framework of the Alliance, in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, said in a social media post.
He said the alliance had “reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries, in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom, and holy sites”.
A separate joint statement published by Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said the three countries would “provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment” to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments, the joint statement said, would be carried out under “approved arrangements” and in accordance with each country’s laws.
The announcements came hours after forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a counteroffensive to retake territory the Iran-aligned Houthis captured last month. The Yemeni forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia, said they have retaken the port city of Mocha on the Red Sea and are now in control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Saudi-led coalition has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support.
The Houthis, meanwhile, claimed an attack on the King Khalid International airport in Riyadh and the Aramco refinery in coastal Rabigh.
The group also said it hit a series of sites, including an airport, an airbase and other critical locations.
There was no confirmation from Riyadh on the Houthi claim.
Mecca defence pact
The Mecca Defence Alliance emerged as a response to intensifying conflicts in the region, triggered by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
The defence pact was signed in August, shortly before the Houthis launched their offensive in Yemen, which has included attacks against Saudi targets.
The three members of the alliance combined have nearly 1.4 million active troops, about 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets, according to the 2026 Global Firepower Index.
The agreement initially offered few details about each country’s military obligations, though steps to formalise the alliance followed.
After the Houthis fired a barrage of missiles towards Saudi Arabia in early September, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said an attack on the kingdom could set the pact in motion.
“If there is unprovoked aggression, or a spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely the Mecca agreement will become operational,” Asif told Geo News, a Pakistani outlet.
Until Monday, however, the alliance had taken no action. Analysts had said that Pakistan and Turkiye were reluctant to abandon their roles as mediators in the US-Israel war on Iran.
Abdulaziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said the decision to activate the Mecca defence pact will have a major impact on security in the region.
“The Houthi attacks and provocations in recent weeks and months really hastened the Mecca alliance, inspired it, even,” Alghashian told Al Jazeera. They “helped” push forward its structure, he said.
Alghashian said the episode also offered a glimpse of a regional security architecture taking shape.
“A lot of the times we keep talking about regional security architecture, it’s one of these very fancy words,” he said. “A lot of the times, it’s hollow, and not many people know what it means in detail. But I think now, we’re beginning to see how this is fleshed out. It’s a critical juncture in the history of the region.”

objects out of place: a collective art exhibition set inside former zurich washroom

objects out of place: a collective art exhibition set inside former zurich washroom
the original washroom’s cabins, washing areas, tiles, and fixtures form an integral part of the exhibition.
former workers’ washroom in Zurich frames group exhibition
What happens when contemporary design is taken out of its usual setting? Dislocated Utility_Objects out of Place is a site-specific group exhibition curated by Paulina Reséndiz and Natascha Madeiski and presented during Zurich Design Weeks 2026 in a former SBB workers’ washroom in Zurich. The exhibition brings together 25 artists, designers, and craft-oriented practitioners, exploring the space between design, art, and craft through a range of material practices.
The former washroom was originally built for SBB workers and their families whose homes did not have private bathrooms. Its original spatial structure remains visible, including individual cabins, washing areas, tiles, and fixtures, and forms an integral part of the exhibition. Instead of creating a neutral display environment, the works are positioned directly within the existing architecture, allowing the building’s history, original function, and traces of use to shape how they are presented.
Furniture, ceramics, glass, and textiles shape Dislocated Utility
The exhibition brings together furniture, lighting, ceramics, glass, textiles, and other object-based practices. Placed within the same setting, works with different relationships to function, making, and materiality create connections across established design categories.
By removing objects from their expected contexts, Dislocated Utility_Objects out of Place examines how setting influences the perception of utility, material, and form. The former washroom becomes both the exhibition space and part of its visual and material framework, placing contemporary objects in direct relation to an architecture shaped by everyday use.

Tracey Moffatt is known to be 'controlling' but now she's letting go of all her work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Tracey Moffatt's complete works find a home at Chau Chak Wing Museum
When Tracey Moffatt was five years old, she won a children's art competition and was asked to donate her winning entry to the local children's hospital.
The problem was, it wasn't Moffatt's work.
"I stole the painting from a boy who was a better artist than I was," the award-winning artist tells ABC Radio National's Awaye!.
"In those days we'd make our paintings and put them outside on the concrete to dry in the sun," she says, thinking back to her childhood in the outer suburbs of Brisbane in the 1960s.
"I picked up Johnny's [painting] because he had run home. [My teacher] was so delighted with the picture. The next thing I know, it's entered in a child's painting competition and it won."
Moffatt is not proud of her "childhood shenanigans". In fact, she calls the request to donate the painting her "letter of shame".
Still, it proves even from a young age she had an eye for art.
"I knew what was good," Moffatt says.
And in time, she learned how to make good art herself, turning to photography and filmmaking due to what she describes as her "complete and total lack of the ability to paint or draw".
Sixty years after that painting escapade, Moffatt is being honoured with the acquisition of her entire archive by the Chau Chak Wing Museum in Sydney, gifted by an anonymous donor. It includes an edition of every photographic work, film and video produced by Moffatt since 1985.
Creation not documentation
In photography and filmmaking, Moffatt found a true affinity for creating narratives through movement, sound, light and colour.
It resulted in some of the most recognisable and acclaimed works of contemporary Australian art, including the films Night Cries — A Rural Tragedy (1989) and BeDevil (1993), and the episodic photo series Something More (1989), Scarred for Life (1994) and Up in the Sky (1997).
Over her four-decade career, Moffatt's work has been recognised in acquisitions and exhibitions by major art institutions including the Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney, the Tate Modern in London, the Guggenheim and Dia Center for the Arts in New York. Her films screened at Cannes Film Festival and in 2017 Moffatt represented Australia at the Venice Biennale, the first Aboriginal person to do so as a solo artist.
Moffatt's sustained focus on creating highly staged images is a deliberate rejection of the notion of capturing or documenting reality. Instead, she uses her extensive knowledge of early printing processes and cinematic history to create something entirely new.
"I know that [a piece] is working when I feel I haven't seen such an image before. If an image suddenly resonates with me, that's when I know. There's no formula," she says.
Sometimes the line between creativity and documentary feels razor thin, as in Moffatt's photographic series Up in the Sky (1997).
The collection of 25 stills invites viewers into a non-linear story set in an Australian outback town, where a young white woman and an Aboriginal baby appear to be separated by nuns.
While Moffatt is undoubtedly emulating a documentary look, the black and white stills from Up in the Sky are just as staged as technicolour vignettes in her best-known series, Something More (1989).
"What's common in all of my work in film and video is storytelling and narrative. I've never been one to take the camera out on the street and capture. I'm not into capturing, I'm into creating," Moffatt says.
A rare assembly
The donation of Moffatt's archive to Chau Chak Wing Museum is the first of its kind in Australia, and will see an edition of every photograph, film and video she has put her hand to since 1985 housed "neat as a pin" in the museum's newly appointed Tracey Moffatt Archive room.
"I'm so honoured by the idea of my archive being held by Chau Chak Wing Museum for safekeeping and eventual display. An artist couldn't want for anything better," Moffatt says.
Moffatt also contributed a donation of her own, in the form of Andy Warhol-inspired "time capsules" of ephemera, test prints, newspaper clippings, old scripts and costumes, as well as personal photographs.
Coupled with the artworks, they create a rare assembly of an artist's creative output. Moffatt suspects the archive will entice the academics who've always been interested in her art.
"Students call me nonstop, and I'm studied not only here, but around the world. So this is a place where students can study if they're interested in my work," she says.
"It's also somewhere scholars that write about my work can come in and drag out framed pieces they might've missed out on previously."
'I'm happy to let it go'
In addition to masterpieces, the museum's Tracey Moffatt Archive is also home to "failed" test prints, including a series of images set in a pioneer village. While she initially thought the series had potential, Moffatt has since changed her mind.
"I wanted an indistinct look, so I moved the camera when I shot this series, but as a result, nothing but blur. So in the end they didn't read well enough," she says.
Another set of photographs were deemed "awful" after she tried to put wax on them.
Moffatt ultimately titled the triptych Art That Does Not Work (2018) and agreed to have the pictures displayed in the Chau Chak Wing Museum's exhibition honouring the donation.
Art That Does Not Work hangs opposite the much more successful series Scarred For Life II (2000), which recreates moments of childhood tragedy and ignominy, such as being the only boy on the rugby team wearing a hand-knitted jersey, or being forced to cut the lawn with a pair of scissors, as a punishment.
"The museum is brilliant at display … I've been known to be quite controlling, but for this sort of thing, I'm happy to leave it to other people," Moffatt says.
Moving forward she has no intention of being involved in any of the curatorial decisions about how or when her archive is displayed, and will instead focus on making new works.
"I have commissions. I've got a big new piece I've made for the National Gallery. And then I have other commissions for next year, and I am working on a new photo series. So I've got a lot on my plate," she says.
There is one small caveat to Moffatt's hands-off approach. She's asked that the museum refrain from "a big Tracey Moffatt show" and instead look for creative ways to incorporate her series into themed exhibitions.
"It's all about letting go. Let it go and let it go. I've always been like this. My work has crossed borders. It's gone out into the world. I just have this thing of 'set it free'.
"I've made it, and I'm happy to let it go."
Tracey Moffatt Sorted is at Chau Chak Wing Museum in Sydney until August 2027.

Greens think tank wants public supermarkets to challenge 'duopoly'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:28:47 UTC
03:28:47 KST

Greens think tank proposes publicly owned supermarkets to challenge Coles-Woolworths 'duopoly'
In short:
The Greens' research institute has called for a publicly owned supermarket chain to challenge Coles and Woolworths.
The $25 billion pitch is inspired by a policy commitment by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
What's next?
Greens leader David Shoebridge says the chain could be a solution to rising food prices.
The Greens' official think tank has called for the forced sale of 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets to be converted into public grocers in a pitch to slash grocery bills by hundreds of dollars a month.
Almost everybody is concerned by rising food prices, according to a YouGov poll of 1,500 voters commissioned by The Green Institute.
Petrol, insurance, healthcare and housing prices were rated as concerns for nearly nine in ten people surveyed, but food and grocery bills were the key cost-of-living issue with 94 per cent rating it a concern.
Three in ten voters said their mental health had suffered due to the cost of food, and four in ten said their household's diet was less nutritious than it was a year ago, or that they had skipped meals or eaten less due to grocery costs.
The Green Institute's executive director Max Chandler-Mather said grocery prices have surged under a Coles and Woolworths "duopoly" raking in billions of dollars in profit.
According to the think tank's analysis of annual reports by the supermarket giants, Coles's supermarket earnings before tax had grown by 58 per cent since 2019, while Woolworths's had grown by 41 per cent.
Meanwhile, essential goods like cooking oils, eggs, beef and milk had risen by 45 per cent and wages had gone backwards.
Coles posted a $1.09 billion net profit for the most recent financial year, while Woolworths reported net profits of $1.14 billion.
A report by the competition watchdog last year found the pair had increased profits in recent years and had little incentive to compete on price.
It stopped short of calling those profits "excessive" and did not conclude that Coles and Woolworths held a duopoly.
Mr Chandler-Mather said a publicly owned grocer could force the supermarkets to be more competitive.
"For half the cost of a single AUKUS submarine we could establish a national network of publicly owned supermarkets that would save families thousands of dollars on their groceries," he said.
"It is abundantly clear that Coles and Woolworths are some of the most profitable supermarkets in the world, and what they have done over the last five to six years is take advantage of an inflation and cost of living crisis."
The think tank proposed a $25.1 billion investment over five years to establish 200 "Fair Go Grocers" by forcibly acquiring stores from Coles and Woolworths, as well as three distribution centres, and to construct another 424 stores and 10 distribution centres across the country.
Stores would be run effectively at cost and would be cost neutral to the budget after the first five years of investment.
The Green Institute said by avoiding the need to turn a profit the cost of essentials could be slashed by 30 per cent and grocery bills cut by hundreds of dollars a month.
"We thought the goal of Fair Go Grocers, our public supermarket, should be to reach 20 per cent of market share," Mr Chandler-Mather said.
"We think at that point that would allow Fair Go Grocers to function as an effective public competitor to drive down grocery and food prices
"We need a much larger public intervention if we are going to fix this issue."
Mr Chandler-Mather said anti-price gouging laws that began in July had done nothing to reduce grocery prices.
Greens leader David Shoebridge said the idea of a publicly-owned supermarket with cheaper food should be considered.
"When I talk to people I hear about the dread they feel heading down the supermarket aisle. The shopping trolley feels like pushing a boulder up to the check-out," Senator Shoebridge said.
"People want politics to be putting solutions on the table, not just saying it's all too hard.
"This is one of the solutions because it makes buying the essentials at the supermarket cheaper."
The Greens and Coalition both supported introducing divestiture powers last term that would allow the supermarket giants to be broken up if they were behaving uncompetitively.
Break-up powers were opposed by Labor, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese describing them as an idea from "the old Soviet Union".
'Laser-like focus' on cost of living needed
The public grocer plan drew inspiration from a recent policy commitment by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani to establish five affordable publicly owned supermarkets in the city that would offer 30 per cent discounts on essentials.
Mr Mamdani has become a blueprint for left-wing political groups after he upset the traditional Democratic establishment in New York City to win the mayoral race.
It was achieved through a grassroots campaign focused on public ownership of assets, universal childcare and free transit funded in part by raising taxes on wealthy residents and corporations.
"Really, the question for not just political parties but our government right now is why aren't they doing the same?" Mr Chandler-Mather said.
"If the New York mayor can take bold action like establishing a chain of publicly-owned supermarkets then the Labor Party could be doing the same here."
The Green Institute pitch is its first major policy intervention since the former Greens MP took over as director.
It also follows a leadership change in the federal Greens last week when Senator Shoebridge became party leader and Steph Hodgins-May his deputy following a contested ballot.
It prompted uncommon public venting by rivals Mehreen Faruqi, who said the choice should have been made by all members, and Sarah Hanson-Young, who said friendships had been "made and lost" in the "brutal" week.
Mr Chandler-Mather said with the leadership resolved the party must make sure its first concern is the cost of living.
"Politics is always going to involve a little bit of argy-bargy. Certainly, I think now the laser-like focus for the Greens has to be on the cost of living and affordability crisis," Mr Chandler-Mather said.

At least 22 dead after two boats collide on Congo river, official says
DAKAR, Oct 5 - At least 22 people have died after two boats collided on the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of Congo, an official said.
The incident occurred near the town of Ngombe in Lukolela territory in western Equateur province at around 2 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on Saturday, Crispin Mputu, the provincial interior minister, told Reuters.
The collision involved two vessels travelling on the river. One was a commercial boat operating between Kinshasa and Mbandaka, while the other was a passenger riverboat travelling from Mongala province to Kinshasa, Mputu said.
The impact caused the passenger boat to sink. A security source told Reuters it had 163 passengers on board.
Twenty-two bodies have been recovered and buried, while 59 people were rescued, Mputu said. He added that other victims might have been buried elsewhere.
The sunken vessel remains submerged at a depth of 12 meters and recovery efforts were continuing on Monday evening, Mputu said.
River transport is the main form of travel and trade in much of western Congo, where towns and cities are located along the Congo River, but accidents are common because vessels are often overcrowded and poorly maintained. REUTERS

Ukraine war latest: Kharkiv devastated by Russian glide bombs, children among victims

- Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
- Ukrainian pilots to soon start training on French Rafale jets, Zelensky says
- Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, including children, injured after Russian forces struck Kharkiv with glide bombs on Oct. 5.
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram.
"As a result of the strikes… warehouse buildings are on fire, and residential buildings have been damaged. There may be people under the rubble of a residential building that was hit in the attack. A search and rescue operation is underway," he added.
Russian glide bombs, often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.

New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
Automated machine gun turrets using artificial intelligence to aim have downed their first Russian jet-powered drones over Ukraine, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Oct. 5.
A day prior, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
"There are already cases of shooting down even jet UAVs, even 'Geran-5' from the those very turrets," Ihnat said on national television.
"The use of innovative technologies — artificial intelligence — has eliminated human error. Machine vision is used in the shooting down. Artificial intelligence allows you to target even jet-powered drones."
Since Russia started using jet-powered drones en masse against Kyiv toward the end of summer this year, they, especially the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, have presented an air defense problem for which Ukraine has not yet found a single solution.

Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.

Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country.
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.

The Middle East war was started in late February by the U.S. and Israel when they launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, even as Washington and Tehran were in the midst of negotiations on Iran's nuclear program.
The warring parties agreed on a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution to the conflict but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz prompted a return to U.S. military operations.

The U.S. and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal it has long denied pursuing – though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Strait of Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The U.S. has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
A tanker was struck while attempting to transit the waterway on Sunday while another turned back on Monday after being threatened with attack by Iranian forces, according to the British maritime agency UKMTO.
