What is ‘Herod’s Pool’, and why is Israel developing it in the West Bank?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:24:06 UTC
03:24:06 KST

What is ‘Herod’s Pool’, and why is Israel developing it in the West Bank?
Israel is developing a reservoir on land in the occupied West Bank, with water syphoned off from Palestinians.
Israel says that work has begun on a development project around an outdoor pool in the occupied West Bank filled after settlers illegally diverted water from a Palestinian village over the summer.
Instead of restoring the water to the village of Fasayil, near Jericho, Israeli authorities are working to formalise what has now been termed “Herod’s Pool”, named after an ancient Jewish king.
On Sunday, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a far-right settler, announced that “development and preservation” of Herod’s Pool had commenced, connecting it to a larger project to “strengthen [Israel’s] hold” on and preserve historical sites.
“The Settlement Revolution continues!” he declared in a social media post that carried an image of workers and wheelbarrows near the site.
The announcement follows Smotrich’s June pledge of more than three million shekels (almost $1m) to develop the site, even though the pool sits on privately-owned Palestinian land belonging to a farmer.
The illegal diversion of water to the pool is part of Israel’s monopolisation of water resources in the occupied West Bank’s fertile Jordan Valley.
It also marks the latest Israeli seizure of Palestinian land in the name of archaeological heritage.
Here’s what we know about the Herod’s Pool project.
What is ‘Herod’s Pool’?
Herod’s Pool is the name Israeli settlers have given an ancient reservoir that lies in the Palestinian village of Fasayil. It is named after Herod the Great, a Jewish king from the first century BC.
The reservoir sits next to a natural spring.
Although settlers claim it once belonged to King Herod, archaeologists have not established when the pool was built. Alon Arad, executive director of Emek Shaveh, an Israeli NGO that defends cultural heritage rights and monitors the political use of archaeology, told the Reuters news agency that the pool’s origins are unclear.
“We see in many cases the use of archaeology … to create this feeling that the West Bank is exclusively Jewish,” he said.
Israeli politicians and settlers have also sought greater Israeli control over “Solomon’s Pools”, three ancient reservoirs in Bethlehem governorate, which have been used by Palestinians for generations.
Palestinians say the targeting of their water sources is part of a comprehensive plan to seize the resources of the occupied West Bank and force them off their land.
Who owns the pool?
The reservoir sits on land belonging to Palestinian farmer Saad Nemer and his family. Nemer says that his grandfather purchased the property more than a century ago. Israeli-issued documentation and older title records reviewed by Reuters support the family’s ownership claim.
Nemer said that settlers had been repeatedly redirecting water from his farm to swim in the pool. He explained that settlers had stolen his irrigation pipeline for the task, and over time the theft had left his farmland scorched and his greenhouses empty.
Nemer also said that settlers had threatened him and beat one of his employees.
The Israeli military body that administers the occupied West Bank, COGAT, has acknowledged that the water was diverted “without authorisation” and said it would investigate, even as Smotrich and other Israeli politicians celebrate the pool.
Nemer told The New York Times that he had been informed by COGAT that his water would be restored, but said it returned for only one day before being cut off again. He is now fearful of approaching the reservoir to reconnect his pipeline due to settler violence.
How have Israeli settlers invoked Herod?
While there is no proven link to Herod, the name features prominently in Israeli heritage projects across the occupied West Bank, which Israel refers to as “Judea and Samaria” in an attempt to separate it from its Palestinian population.
Critics, including archaeological rights groups, say such projects are increasingly being used to extend Israeli control over Palestinian land and heritage sites.
There is Herodium, a sprawling hilltop structure south of Jerusalem, said to be the ruins of a fortress the king erected. It has been under Israeli control for decades and operates as a national park, despite Palestinian protests that it is part of their heritage.
In Sebastia – ancient Samaria – Israel has dedicated large amounts of funding since 2023 to excavate the city’s archaeological park and develop it as an Israeli “national park“, usurping Palestinians who have long showcased the archaeological ruins as part of their history.
Israeli Minister of Heritage Amichai Eliyahu, who himself lives in an illegal West Bank settlement, has said it would be “first and foremost a Jewish heritage site”. His office cited excavation of “the magnificent Roman city built by King Herod” when describing the archaeological periods the project intends to expose.
The Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron – where Israel has repeatedly restricted Muslim access – stands on land considered to be Prophet Abraham’s burial place by Muslims and Jews. Part of it is believed to have been built during the Herodian era.
In 2017, UNESCO recognised Hebron’s Old City as a Palestinian heritage site, and warned that it was endangered by Israeli settler encroachments.
Ahead of UNESCO’s decision, prominent Hebron settler Yishai Fleisher – who has served as an adviser to Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir – objected to the designation on the grounds that it was “built by a Jewish king”, referring to Herod.

Putin authorizes Italian banking group UniCredit to spin off part of its Russian bank and sell the remaining business
Vladimir Putin has signed an order allowing the Italian financial group UniCredit to restructure its Russian subsidiary, UniCredit Bank, and sell all of the subsidiary’s shares. The document was published on Russia’s legal information portal.
The order allows UniCredit Bank to spin off a new company whose shares will go to the bank’s sole shareholder, UniCredit. It also authorizes the purchase of 100% of the bank’s shares.
No further approvals are now required to sell the Russian assets, the order states.

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, UniCredit planned to sell its Russian business. Media reports said a consortium from the UAE was interested in buying the bank. Kommersant reported that the consortium was acting on behalf of Alfa Group.

France, Germany push for EU rapid-response trade tool with likely focus on China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:21:58 UTC
03:21:58 KST

France, Germany push for EU rapid-response trade tool with likely focus on China
BRUSSELS/BERLIN - France and Germany have proposed that the European Union reinforce its economy by enacting a new rapid-action measure to strike back against countries that harm it, with China the most likely focus of their proposal.
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Oct 5, 10 days before EU leaders are to discuss Chinese trade imbalances at a Brussels summit.
They said “systemic market-distorting practices” jeopardise the bloc’s economy and industrial base, requiring urgent action.
The commission said it welcomed the letter that accompanied a document setting out Franco-German proposals, saying it was a valuable contribution to the debate on geoeconomic risks and global imbalances.
It aligned with Von der Leyen’s stance on competitiveness and her approach to trading partners, including China, it added.
The new measure would not target any specific country, but highlights dumping, widespread subsidies and restriction of currency convertibility – market distortions that many EU leaders say China is engaged in.
German officials said the EU needed a tool as powerful as the Section 301 tariffs imposed by the United States or China’s restrictions on exports of critical minerals in a new world where trade is increasingly used as a weapon.
The bloc, said the document, needs to deploy its trade defence tools more swiftly and efficiently, with more investigations and a broader approach to cover whole sectors.
The document added that there was an urgent need for measures to deal with imports of chemicals, PET and hybrid vehicles.
France, Germany push for two new trade tools
France and Germany also said the European Commission should propose two new instruments as soon as possible to focus EU efforts on diversification and securing economic security.
The first, which the Commission has already mentioned, would seek to limit companies’ reliance on single sources for certain critical supplies.
The second would limit access to the EU single market for countries that undermine fair market conditions through political or economic means, without specifying what the trigger for EU reaction would be or what action the EU should take.
The paper said that any proposal by the Commission to activate counter-measures against another country should be adopted unless a qualified majority of EU members opposed – a lower hurdle than for some trade measures.
The paper also said the Commission should be able to activate such new measures swiftly, which German government officials said could mean a matter of days.
Legislation to enact a new instrument would still need approval by EU governments and the European Parliament.
A French presidential adviser said it was urgent for the EU to take action, that the imbalances with some trade partners had become unsustainable, and that France and Germany were keen for the bloc to deploy existing anti-dumping measures as soon as possible.
“France and Germany are very keen to put an end to the naivete on trade,” the adviser told reporters. REUTERS

Türkiye plans to achieve full space independence with satellite constellation, space infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:19:39 UTC
03:19:39 KST

Mert Davut, Emir Yildirim
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Türkiye is investing in its independent space infrastructure with a new domestic positioning satellite constellation of more than 100 craft to secure its sovereignty in orbit, a sector representative said on Monday.
Haluk Bayraktar, chair of the SAHA Istanbul defense cluster, stated that Türkiye transformed from a technology importer in 2002 to a global aerospace producer, with domestic manufacturing rates surging from 20% to 80% in the past two decades.
Bayraktar, speaking at the opening of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in the southwestern city of Antalya, stated that Türkiye’s annual defense and aerospace exports rose from $250 million to a whopping $11 billion over the same period.
“We now achieve in just one week the exports we used to produce in an entire year back in 2002,” he said.
“What started in a small workshop by a handful of young engineers turned into efforts to design and produce the critical components of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) through domestic means, making Türkiye a leader in the field that accounts for 65% of the global UAV export market and a country that exports technology to over 40 countries,” he added.
Bayraktar stated that the agile development philosophy is powering the Turkish industrial ecosystem, which is now extending into orbit to reduce foreign reliance on space technology.
“We’re building a strong space infrastructure with our communications satellites and positioning constellation of 100 satellites to establish an independent navigation system,” he said, noting that the country has already developed capabilities ranging from sounding rockets exceeding 100-kilometer (62.1-mile) altitudes to homegrown hybrid orbital transfer vehicles.
He mentioned that the IAC’s theme this year is “The World Needs More Space,” which he thinks carries two meanings.
“Access, as in more countries reaching orbit at a lower cost, and opening up opportunities, as in more small businesses in the supply chain and young engineers at the table, as well as countries that were once told that space was not for them."
He added that Türkiye is investing in young talent via initiatives like the premier defense and aviation event TEKNOFEST, which recently held its first event in the nation’s southeast, having drawn 1.6 million student applications for its engineering and rocketry competition.

Shin Bet chief threatens return of detention without trial for Jewish extremists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:19:08 UTC
03:19:08 KST

Shin Bet chief David Zini told the Security Cabinet that he would seek to restore the use of administrative detention against Jewish extremists if other measures fail to curb violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, ynet has learned.
Zini made the remarks during a Cabinet meeting Sunday that included a discussion of security in the West Bank and a heated exchange between him and Settlements and National Missions Minister Orit Strock.
Administrative detention allows Israeli authorities to hold suspects without filing criminal charges, based largely on classified intelligence. The measure is used primarily against Palestinians but has also been applied in a limited number of cases against Jewish Israelis suspected of extremist violence.
Defense Minister Israel Katz ended the use of administrative detention orders against Jewish suspects in 2024, shortly after taking office.
Since becoming head of the Shin Bet domestic security agency, Zini has also resisted calls to restore the measure. According to reports, he opposed requests from Shin Bet field officials who favored bringing it back, arguing that violence by Jewish extremists against Palestinians could instead be addressed through electronic monitoring and other measures.
At Sunday’s Cabinet meeting, however, Zini indicated that he could change course if those alternatives proved ineffective.
His comments came during a contentious discussion with ministers over violence in the West Bank. After Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said attacks by Jewish extremists against Palestinians were damaging Israel’s international standing, Zini criticized what he described as insufficient condemnation by Israeli leaders.
“There are not enough condemnations from the leadership, and that harms security and the settlement movement,” Zini said.
Strock challenged his characterization.
“You are presenting it as though the Arabs are sweetness and honey and only the settlers are the problem,” she said. “Palestinians attack shepherds, injure them and endanger their lives. Bring those attacks to the surface as well, deal with them and talk about them.”
Zini responded: “The Palestinians are not burning Jewish homes here. You are disconnected. We need to see condemnation and denunciation from the entire leadership. This harms the settlement movement and harms security.”
Strock said leaders of Jewish communities in the West Bank had repeatedly condemned such violence.
“I don’t understand who else he wants a condemnation from,” she said. “The entire settlement leadership opposes and condemns this kind of violence. All the council heads and rabbis have issued calls against it. I also go to the farms and sit with the young people to explain it to them.”
“Where do you condemn it?” Zini asked.
Strock cited radio appearances and replied: “Everywhere. Just listen.”
Following the exchange, lawmaker Tally Gotliv came to Strock’s defense and called for Zini’s resignation.
“Shin Bet chief, my heart goes out to you,” Gotliv said in a statement. “Maybe if, God forbid, my brother had been arrested and indicted and faced the danger of a lengthy prison sentence, I too would agree to go out of my way and change my skin for him. But with all due respect, you are the head of the Shin Bet, and if they have managed to hold you by the throat as well, then be brave enough to resign.”
She accused Zini of failing to condemn Palestinian terrorism in the West Bank and said his remark that Strock was “disconnected” reminded her of the period before the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel.
Pressure grows over West Bank violence
The Cabinet confrontation comes amid a rise in violent incidents involving Israelis and Palestinians in the West Bank in recent months and mounting international criticism over settler violence.
People familiar with Israel’s relations with Washington have warned that the issue could lead to further U.S. pressure on Israel, including possible sanctions. Measures targeting settlements and settlers have also been advanced in Congress, with two initiatives coming close to passage in the past week.
Any decision to restore administrative detention for Jewish suspects would ultimately rest with Katz, who ordered an end to the practice.
Shin Bet chiefs have traditionally sought the ability to use administrative detention in cases where security officials say they have intelligence indicating an imminent threat but cannot expose the evidence in ordinary criminal proceedings.
Even after Katz ended the practice for Jewish suspects, the Shin Bet on several occasions asked him to approve its targeted use in specific cases, according to people familiar with the matter. Those requests were rejected.
Security officials instead turned in part to electronic monitoring. But officials now say that approach has proved ineffective, with Jewish extremists learning to challenge or circumvent restrictions through legal means.
Olive harvest season raises tensions
Zini’s warning also comes as the annual olive harvest begins, a period that frequently brings heightened tensions between Israeli settlers and Palestinians in the West Bank.
Numerous Jewish communities and agricultural outposts have been established or expanded over the past year, some bordering Palestinian farmland and creating additional potential points of friction.
More than 100 Israeli agricultural farms are now spread across the West Bank, and their number continues to grow. According to data from an association representing the farms, they currently maintain a presence over more than 1.1 million dunams, or about 272,000 acres.
Supporters of the agricultural outposts view them as strategically important to the Israeli settlement movement. Their expansion has also required the IDF to alter its deployment and defense arrangements.
The military’s security concept in those areas has shifted from primarily defending established communities and major roads to providing broader protection across large stretches of open land where the farms are located.
For Palestinians in West Bank towns and villages, meanwhile, the olive harvest is one of the most important periods of the agricultural year and a major source of income for many families.
According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, known as OCHA, there were more than 10 million olive trees in the Palestinian territories in 2019, supporting the livelihoods of about 100,000 Palestinian families.
Palestinian Authority agricultural officials reported that 2022 was a record year for olive oil production in the West Bank, with the harvest yielding about 32,000 metric tons.
Production has since fallen sharply. The 2024 harvest produced about 27,300 metric tons of olive oil, while production dropped to roughly 7,000 metric tons in 2025 — a decline of about 75% from the previous year.
The combination of the approaching harvest, expanding Israeli agricultural outposts and recent violence has placed Israeli security officials on heightened alert as they seek to prevent further clashes between settlers and Palestinians.

'One of most prominent figures in Israeli culture': Singer, theater icon Illy Gorlizki dies at 91
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:18:43 UTC
03:18:43 KST

Israeli actor, singer and theater figure Illy Gorlizki, one of the most recognizable figures in Israeli culture across generations, died at the age of 91, his partner and leading cultural institutions said on Monday.
Born in Tel Aviv in 1935, Gorlizki spent more than seven decades working in theater, film, television and Israeli music, taking part in some of the formative moments of Israeli popular culture.
Gorlizki began his theater career as a teenager. At 17, he was accepted to the drama school affiliated with the Ohel Theater and simultaneously began appearing in small roles. During his military service, he joined the Central Command entertainment troupe, where he sang and performed alongside several young talents who would later become pillars of Israeli entertainment.
He secured his place in Israel’s cultural pantheon in 1964, when he starred as Shlomo in the celebrated musical King Solomon and Shalmai the Shoemaker alongside Yona Atari. The musical, based on a play by Sami Gronemann, translated and adapted by Nathan Alterman with music by Sasha Argov, became a huge success and was performed about 1,000 times.
Gorlizki and Atari became an unforgettable duo as a result and later continued their collaboration in the show Shuk Hametziot.
President Isaac Herzog called Gorlizki a "one of the most prominent figures in Israeli culture, leaving a profound mark on the stage, cinema, and Hebrew song."
"We will always remember his starring role in the play King Solomon and Shoemaker Shlomo and his legacy as a talented artist who nurtured generations of actors," the president said in a statement published on social media.
Seven decades on the Israeli stage
Gorlizki subsequently appeared in a long list of plays, musicals and films, including Three Days and a Child, Scouts, and Tevye and His Seven Daughters. Alongside his work at the Cameri Theater, he appeared in successful entertainment productions including Shuk Hametziot, Zehu Bidur, and Hachamim Balaila, the latter alongside Yossi Banai. He won three Kinor David awards for his work.
Gorlizki did not limit himself to his career as an actor and singer. He devoted a significant portion of his life to fighting for the rights of performing artists. He was the first director of EMI, the Israel Artists Association, and was among the founders of Eshkolot, the organization responsible for managing and distributing royalties to performing artists in Israel.
In 2015, when he celebrated his 80th birthday, Gorlizki spoke to Walla Culture ahead of a tribute evening held in his honor at the Cameri Theater. Asked what he had learned by the age of 80, he replied with the sentence that became the interview’s headline: "I miss tomorrow."
He spoke about the need to keep looking forward and quoted Ludwig Wittgenstein: "Do not always live on the barren heights of cleverness, descend sometimes into the green valleys of foolishness." He later referred to Dante and the line, "It is love that moves the sun and the other stars."
In retrospect, that quotation says much about Gorlizki himself. Even at 80, he did not speak of summing up his life, but of tomorrow. He belonged to a generation that largely created the language of the Israeli stage itself, a generation that connected theater, music, entertainment and Hebrew song and made them part of everyday Israeli culture.
Friends and colleagues pay tribute
Singer-songwriter Hanan Yovel eulogized Gorlizki: "Illy was a wonderful man, head and shoulders above others in every field, and a rare combination of spirit and practicality. He was extraordinarily intelligent, wrote wonderful books, was a light-footed dancer, sang the original ‘Hamsinim Bamishlat,’ and was truly a Renaissance man. King Solomon and Shalmai the Shoemaker, starring him, was a Broadway-level spectacle unlike anything seen in Israel until then, and not much since. He was a huge star, God’s deputy as far as I was concerned, and when he complimented me on melodies such as ‘Kshe-Tzilzalta Ra’ad Kolekh,’ I was beside myself with pride and excitement. He was far ahead of his time in many ways. He was born with his heart on the right side, rare even in his defects, but his heart was always in the right place. I will miss him very much."
Dalia Gutman, a media figure and former program director of Israel Television, said: "Illy was a perfect performer. In one of the programs I produced, he tap-danced, light as a butterfly. It was a pleasure to watch and hear him. Nathan Alterman attended the dress rehearsal of King Solomon and Shalmai the Shoemaker and hated every moment. He was convinced it would be a terrible failure, but Illy calmed him down and promised him he was wrong. Illy, of course, was right. It was a huge hit that audiences could not get enough of, and Illy became the star, with a capital S, of Israeli theater. His connection with Alterman, of course, continued through his collaboration with the wonderful Yona Atari, whom Illy brought back on stage toward the end of her life, when she was not at her best, for a one-time performance, in a moving gesture of love between longtime partners."
Actor and comedian Tuvia Tzafir said: "Illy, my dear friend, our Herzl and Ben-Gurion of Israeli artists, that’s what I always called him. I was so sorry to hear on Monday morning that you had gone. I know that at our age this happens more and more often, and yet it still hurts so much to lose someone like you. How do you eulogize a friend? A friend who accompanied me through so many stations in life: theater, television, and of course my personal life. You were not only a talented actor, but also a gifted singer, a man of knowledge and a philosopher, a good friend and an entrepreneur who thought about the good of everyone."
Eshkolot, the Israeli performers’ rights organization, said: "The Eshkolot family bows its head and painfully bids farewell to Illy Gorlizki, one of the company’s founders and its honorary president, who for decades was one of the central forces in the struggle for the rights of performing artists in Israel. Illy was a man of vision and action. At a time when performers’ rights were barely on the public agenda, he was among the first to identify the need for a strong body that would represent artists, protect their rights and work to ensure that they received appropriate compensation for their work. He did not settle for having a vision, but acted to turn it into reality."
David Krivoshei, chairman of the executive committee of ILAM, the royalties organization for performing musicians in Israel, said: "Illy Gorlizki was one of Israel’s greatest artists, and alongside an illustrious career as an actor, singer and stage performer, he devoted a significant part of his life to advancing the rights and status of performers in Israel. The legacy he left behind continues into the next generation."
The Cameri Theater said: "We bid farewell on Monday with deep sorrow to Illy, who joined the Cameri ensemble in 1956 and played a series of unforgettable roles, but won his place in the hearts of the public with his double role in the immortal musical King Solomon and Shalmai the Shoemaker, alongside the late Yona Atari."
His devoted partner in recent years was Anat Globus, a deputy editor of Channel 12 News’s Ulpan Shishi, who told Walla: "My Illy went on his way this morning. The house is empty. Sad. On Tuesday we will say goodbye to our Illy, to bid farewell and share all the love and memories he left behind."
Gorlizki’s coffin will lie in state at the Cameri Theater in Tel Aviv beginning at noon on Tuesday. His funeral will take place at 2:30 p.m. at the Menucha Nechona Cemetery in Kfar Saba. At Gorlizki’s request, no shiva will be held.

Necva Taştan Sevinç
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Monday unsealed four arrest warrants against Taliban figures over alleged crimes against humanity involving persecution on gender and political grounds in Afghanistan.
The court said its Pre-Trial Chamber II made public warrants against Haibatullah Akhundzada, Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Habibullah Agha and Neda Mohammad Nadim.
The warrants were issued on July 8 and Sept. 9, 2025. The existence of those against Akhundzada and Haqqani had already been announced in July 2025.
Judges found reasonable grounds to believe the suspects were responsible for ordering, inducing or soliciting persecution against girls, women and others who did not conform to Taliban policies on gender, gender identity or expression.
The warrants also concern alleged political persecution against people perceived as “allies of girls and women.”
The alleged crimes occurred from the Taliban’s return to power on Aug. 15, 2021, until at least Jan. 20, 2025.
The chamber found that the suspects implemented a government policy resulting in severe violations of fundamental rights in connection with murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance.
Girls and women were specifically targeted because of their gender and severely deprived of rights to education, privacy and family life, alongside freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion, the court said.
Judges said gender persecution includes direct violence and systemic, institutionalized harm, including discriminatory social norms.
The chamber also found that people perceived as opposing these policies, even passively or through omission, were targeted as political opponents.

Astronomers Confirm Discovery of the Youngest Known Exoplanet Ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:15:16 UTC
03:15:16 KST

How are planets born, and how do they grow? This is an essential question in astronomy, one that researchers try to answer by observing “young planets.” That’s easier said than done. All the planets in our solar system are the same age, 4.6 billion years old. Astronomers therefore need to look elsewhere to find planets that have formed more recently—making exoplanets enticing research grounds.
Still, the vast majority of the approximately 6,000 exoplanets confirmed to date are also billions of years old. That’s not because there aren’t youthful planets out there, but old planets are easier to discover using common techniques such as the transit method, in which astronomers detect the slight dimming of a star’s light as a planet passes in front of it.
Newly formed exoplanets are often buried within disks of gas and dust, the leftover building blocks from a planet's formation, also known as a protoplanetary disk. The difficulty of just locating such a new celestial body is part of what makes the discovery of the exoplanet Elias 2-24b—now the youngest ever confirmed—so exciting.
The research team, led by Andrea Bernardi at Diego Portales University in Chile, identified the exoplanet by focusing on seven protoplanetary disks where there were notable gaps in the dense matter, since it is believed that growing planets carve out such voids. They reanalyzed “coronagraph” data, in which the central star is blocked out, making the dim reflected light from surrounding celestial bodies stand out.
Scientists had known about a gap in the disk surrounding the star Elias 2-24 for nearly a decade. The European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its official name) had detected a point of light within this gap, sparking an ongoing debate over whether it was truly a planet. The researchers used data collected in 2018 and 2020 at the W.M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to compare the dot’s positions over the years. They concluded that this bright spot was not an unrelated background star or noise from the equipment, but rather a celestial object gravitationally bound to Elias 2-24—in other words, a planet.
Elias 2-24b is located approximately 450 light-years from Earth. It orbits its star at a distance of approximately 55 astronomical units (one astronomical unit being the average distance between Earth and the sun). Its mass is estimated to be at most 1.9 to 4.0 times that of Jupiter, though researchers believe its volume is likely to be much smaller than our local gas giant. Since its host star is less than 1 million years old, Elias 2-24b is estimated to be similarly young.
Until now, the youngest exoplanets confirmed through direct observation were those orbiting the stars PDS 70 and WISPIT 2, both of which are over 5 million years old. This new discovery breaks those records by a significant margin.
And Elias 2-24b has a few attributes that require reevaluating some planetary formation models. One of the standard theories is known as the “core accretion model,” which posits that giant planets are formed when a solid core grows more massive and attracts surrounding gas. The time required for formation varies depending on the conditions of the calculation, but according to NASA, it should take about 5 million years for a Jupiter-sized planet to form. That’s also given Jupiter’s distance from the sun, approximately 5 astronomical units. For a planet with a much farther removed orbit like Elias 2-24b, accruing this mass should take even longer.
However, Elias 2-24b doesn’t seem to be following these rules. Despite being 55 astronomical units from its host star, it’s already a giant and behaving like a planet after a remarkably short 1 million years. The research team believes this planet was formed through core accretion, which would mean that this model can produce giant planets much faster than previously assumed.
Lucas Siesa, a professor at Diego Portales University and coauthor of the paper, pointed out in a press release, “Elias 2-24 b shows us that even our best planet-formation models are still missing some important processes.”
What can improve these models is finding more young planets, which may soon be more possible than ever. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched by NASA this past August, is equipped with an even more powerful coronagraph than the one the researchers used to locate Elias 2-24b. Astronomers therefore hope to soon detect more young planets as well as other planets obscured by their bright stars.
“This is just the beginning of a new era of discovery,” Siesa said. “It’s incredible that with modern technology, we are actually able to see planet formation in action, and Roman will take planet hunting to the next level.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

Sam Altman à Decoded : “Le monde devrait accepter que certaines choses négatives se produisent” face aux bénéfices de l’IA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:11:56 UTC
03:11:56 KST

Le PDG d’OpenAI, Sam Altman, a soutenu lors d’un entretien exclusif accordé à Decoded by POLITICO que les bénéfices de l’IA justifient d’en accepter certains risques. | Heather Diehl/Getty Images
Pour le PDG d’OpenAI Sam Altman, il subsiste une différence fondamentale de vision entre son entreprise et son concurrent Anthropic en matière de réglementation de l’intelligence artificielle. Les avantages de cette technologie justifient d’accepter certains risques, a-t-il estimé dans une interview exclusive accordée à Decoded by POLITICO, ajoutant que l’IA devait rester largement accessible au grand public.
“Je pense qu’il y a un réel fossé”, a souligné Sam Altman auprès de Brendan Bordelon, coauteur de Decoded et journaliste senior spécialisé dans la tech chez POLITICO. Interrogé sur ce qu’il différencie plus spécifiquement son entreprise de celle de Dario Amodei, il a répondu : “Nous pensons que le monde devrait accepter que certaines choses négatives se produisent face aux bénéfices de cette technologie.”
Anthropic a longtemps été considérée comme la plus fervente défenseure de la réglementation de l’IA au sein du secteur, une position qui, jusqu’à récemment, contrastait avec l’approche plus souple prônée par OpenAI. Mais les divergences politiques entre ces deux géants de l’intelligence artificielle se sont atténuées ces derniers mois, la maison mère de ChatGPT soutenant désormais des règles plus strictes, alors que ses modèles ont défrayé la chronique pour avoir piraté des sites de manière autonome.
Advertisement
Sam Altman a approuvé l’appel lancé le mois dernier par Dario Amodei à ralentir le développement des modèles d’IA les plus avancés. Son entreprise a même emboîté le pas à Anthropic en soutenant de nouvelles lois d’Etats fédérés américains qui imposent des exigences de sécurité plus strictes que celles qu’OpenAI avait précédemment défendues — ce qui marque un léger revirement par rapport à sa stratégie antérieure en la matière. Par ailleurs, ses lobbyistes ont récemment apporté leur soutien à une proposition bipartisane de la Chambre des représentants qui obligerait les principales entreprises du secteur à accueillir des auditeurs indépendants chargés d’évaluer la sécurité de leurs modèles.
Malgré cette convergence, Sam Altman a tenté de distinguer la position de son entreprise en matière de réglementation de celle de Dario Amodei, rappelant les accusations de capture réglementaires contre Anthropic, formulées par des conseillers tech du président Donald Trump.
“Je ne suis pas d’accord, mais je comprends le point de vue de ceux qui se disent : ‘Cette technologie va devenir tellement puissante, et elle est tellement dangereuse, qu’un seul laboratoire à San Francisco devrait en disposer et veiller à ce qu’il n’arrive rien de grave, tout en trouvant le moyen d’en répartir les bénéfices’”, a exposé Sam Altman. Pour lui, c’est un “compromis totalement inacceptable” qui va à l’encontre de la “position plus souple en matière réglementaire” défendue par OpenAI.
“Je ne ferai pas le compromis de dire : ‘Nous veillerons à ce qu’il n’y ait pas de piratages majeurs, pas d’utilisation abusive de cette technologie, zéro escroquerie [ou] toute autre chose négative qui pourrait se produire’”, a poursuivi le patron de l’éditeur de ChatGPT. “Car je pense que les gens feront énormément plus — d’un ordre de grandeur supérieur — de bonnes choses que de mauvaises.”
Le PDG d’OpenAI a ajouté ne pas croire aux “risques véritablement catastrophiques”, notamment à la possibilité d’“une grave perte de contrôle face à l’IA”.
Interrogé à ce sujet, un porte-parole d’Anthropic a répondu que les “propositions réglementaires [de l’entreprise] ne s’appliquent qu’aux modèles de pointe”. La société a également fait référence à un échange sur les réseaux sociaux en août entre Dario Amodei et un gestionnaire d’investissements, dans lequel il répondait aux critiques concernant la captation réglementaire et les répercussions sur les petites entreprises.
Advertisement
“Anthropic a toujours formulé ses propositions politiques avec beaucoup de prudence”, soulignait Dario Amodei à l’époque. “Nous nous efforçons vraiment de présenter des propositions qui désavantagent (freinent) les entreprises d’IA de pointe tout en *favorisant* leurs concurrents plus petits.”
L’interview de Sam Altman, publiée lundi dans le premier numéro de Decoded et dans le podcast quotidien qui l’accompagne, a également abordé le nouvel accord sur l’IA de Donald Trump avec les géants de la tech, ainsi que son initiative de la rebaptiser “superintelligence” ; la vague d’incidents de piratage autonome perpétrés par des modèles d’OpenAI et la question de savoir si l’entreprise devrait engager sa responsabilité juridique ; l’opinion de Sam Altman sur l’argent du secteur de l’IA qui inonde la politique américaine ; l’influence des “altruistes efficaces” au sein d’OpenAI ; ainsi que son point de vue sur des acteurs politiques de premier plan, notamment le président français Emmanuel Macron et le gouverneur de Californie Gavin Newsom.
Decoded by POLITICO — une émission réalisée par Brendan Bordelon, Christine Mui, Calder McHugh et Sam Sutton — s’appuie sur le travail d’une cinquantaine de journalistes de POLITICO à travers le monde pour traiter non seulement de l’avenir de la tech, mais aussi des personnalités, des débats politiques et des luttes qui la façonne. Formula 1 launches review into software glitch that disrupted Bahrain GP in Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:11:15 UTC
03:11:15 KST

Halis Sünnetci
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Formula 1's governing body, the FIA, said it will conduct a full review of a software-related power loss that disrupted the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with several cars slowing dramatically or stopping during the formation lap.
The FIA said an “unprecedented combination” of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the configuration of the Sepang International Circuit caused a number of cars to lose power.
“As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the Power Unit before the start of the race,” it said.
The governing body said the problem had not been detected by either the FIA or teams during testing or laps to the grid.
“The FIA, together with the teams and Power Unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue,” it added.
Heavy rain delayed Sunday's scheduled start at Sepang by 40 minutes when several drivers, including eventual winner Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, encountered power problems during the formation lap. 
Verstappen likens power loss to 'Lego race'
Verstappen said Formula 1's increasingly complex power units and their reliance on software contributed to the problem.
“That's the problem that we have. You know, these engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented,” the Red Bull driver said.
Verstappen said he was the first driver to encounter the issue before looking in his mirrors and seeing others struggling behind him.
“It was like the Lego race,” he said, referring to the drivers' parade at this year's British Grand Prix in which the drivers raced life-sized Lego cars.
Hamilton replied: “Yeah, we had the same speed.”
Verstappen added: “Same speed. Yeah, it was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on.”
Hamilton said his Ferrari eventually slowed to the point that he had to stop on track.
“I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before,” the seven-time world champion said.
Verstappen went on to win the race ahead of Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, while Hamilton recovered from 18th place following an unsuccessful tire gamble to finish third.

A shadow Conservative Home Office minister has claimed there are “no-go zones” in Luton where “white people won’t go”.
Blake Stephenson, the MP for Mid Bedfordshire who was appointed to the Tory frontbench role two weeks ago, claimed the town was “a very dangerous place” where some communities “live in ghettoes”.
His comments, made at a fringe meeting at the Conservative party conference, mirror claims by far-right activists including from the terrorist mass murderer Anders Breivik, who have also said Luton has “no-go zones”. These claims have been denied by the local police force as well as local Muslim and Christian groups.
Speaking at a Centre for Policy Studies meeting in Birmingham, Stephenson claimed to know Luton well because he lives in a neighbouring constituency. “I know Luton reasonably well because I live 10, 15 minutes away and represent Mid Bedfordshire, I live in a village just over the border.
“I think the town is a shadow of its former self. There are parts of that town – and unfortunately the police will tell you this – it can be a very dangerous place. There are parts where white people won’t go. They are like no-go zones. It is not alone, there are other towns across the country in a similar situation. It is dreadful where we have got to.
“But we can move on from it but it requires deep levels of integration and we need to break apart these, erm … this is where it gets icky, but we need to make sure we don’t have ghettoes where there are no-go zones for anybody. The country is for all of us not just certain communities,” he said.
“It does get icky for some people, but I think there is a consensus, certainly on the right, that mass migration has been an absolute disaster.
“So it’s up to us to put a plan together and deliver. We’ve got the borders plan. You know, some of that may feel a bit icky for some people, but we’ve got to face into it, lean into it,” he said.
In a statement delivered to court in Oslo in 2012, Breivik asked his audience to look at Luton “and the more than 1,000 Islamic no-go zones where police do not dare pass through”. The city was, he said, living in “warlike conditions”.
Bedfordshire police said in a statement at the time that “no-go areas do not exist in Bedfordshire”.
Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, co-founded the far-right English Defence League in Luton in 2009, and claimed there were “no-go zones” for white people in the town.
Stephenson, who was elected as an MP in 2024, studied industrial relations with politics at the University of Kent, followed by law at the University of Law in Guildford. He was called to the bar in 2007.
He was appearing at a fringe meeting entitled From Boriswave to Brain Drain: How Can We Fix Migration?
Earlier in the discussion, Stephenson said the Equalities Act had created a framework where “white young men” were being discriminated against, and claimed the government was reserving internships for racial minorities.
“You know, equality should be equality for all. It’s a fairly, fairly simple concept, but it’s actually become quite a complicated construct. And the people that are losing out are white young men,” he said.
He claimed that some government schemes did not allow young white men to apply. “I’m not surprised that young white men feel like the system is rigged against them, particularly with the government coming out with schemes that won’t allow them to apply for internships. That is state-sponsored racism and it needs to stop,” he said.
The Conservative party has been approached for comment.
Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, said: “It is deeply irresponsible for any politician, let alone a senior Conservative, to peddle the same rightwing nonsense about Luton that we see from the likes of Yaxley-Lennon and Reform.
“It is simply untrue and the shadow Home Office minister should get off social media and get to know the fantastic Lutonians I’m proud to represent and call my neighbours. I’d also call on the new Lib Dem/Tory/Green coalition-run council in Luton to disown these comments from their colleague.”

Russia Tests Balloons Equipped with Cables to Defend Against Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:05:10 UTC
03:05:10 KST

Russia has begun testing balloon barriers against Ukrainian drones.
The tests were shown by the Rossiya 1 TV channel in the VESTI program.
The system consists of balloons with a cable stretched between them, to which Kevlar threads are attached, hanging down.
The idea is that a drone that gets caught in this net will wrap the threads around its propeller and lose control.
According to the designers, the technology is already ready for mass production.
However, protecting a single large facility will require launching at least 10 such balloons into the sky.
Similar balloons were used during World War I and, especially extensively, during World War II to counter enemy aircraft. They forced bombers to fly at higher altitudes, which reduced the accuracy of their strikes.
Presumably, in the case of modern aerostats, the objective will be similar — by posing the threat of collision with cables, to force Ukrainian drones in certain areas to fly at higher altitudes, thereby making it easier for radar to detect them and for air defense systems to engage them.
Earlier, a Russian chemical company announced a tender to purchase airships to protect its facilities from attacks by Ukrainian drones.
In addition to deploying cables against drones, airships are also used for other purposes in modern warfare. In particular, the Russian state-owned holding company Rostec has developed an airship to ensure stable communications.
Unlike mobile base stations, lifting a radio module into the air minimizes the impact of terrain on signal quality. In Ukraine, balloons are viewed as platforms for launching drones and missiles against the enemy.
Missiles can be launched from stratospheric balloons at altitudes ranging from 12 to 18 kilometers.

Russian authorities deny plague outbreak as media delete coverage and Central Asian countries tighten sanitary border controls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:04:38 UTC
03:04:38 KST

Speaking to the press regarding the epidemiological situation in Russia’s Irkutsk Region, Kremlin press secretary Dmitry Peskov demanded that journalists “stick to the official statements,” the state-owned news agency TASS reported earlier today. On Oct. 4, TASS had described the situation in the region as “stable,” assuring readers that an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died not of plague but of “pneumonia of unknown etiology.” Amid these official statements, Russian media have been deleting reports of suspected plague in the Irkutsk Region, while Central Asian countries — Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Kazakhstan — have tightened sanitary controls at the border.
At a briefing for journalists on Oct. 5, Peskov urged participants “to ignore various rumors and speculation” about plague in the Irkutsk Region and instead rely on official statements from the consumer rights watchdog Rospotrebnadzor:
“We have Rospotrebnadzor, where top professionals in this field work — let’s listen to their official statements.”
A few hours earlier, the Russian business outlet Kommersant had cited Axios, writing that the Trump administration was monitoring reports of a possible plague outbreak in Russia. Twenty-five minutes later, the Telegram post and the news item on the Kommersant website were deleted.
In recent days, the REN TV federal network deleted all five of its posts about plague in the Irkutsk Region, as was noted by the independent outlet Lyudi Baikala. Two of them had already been indexed by the TGStat service.
One of the stories reported that Darya Shipilova, a laboratory technician at the Anti-Plague Institute in Irkutsk, had worked with strains of the plague pathogen and studied the body’s immune response to the infection. Another post, citing a source, reported that a patient suspected of having plague had died at a district hospital in the Irkutsk Region.
Rospotrebnadzor denies there is an outbreak in the region. On Oct. 4, the agency said Shipilova had died of “pneumonia of an undetermined type” and assured the public that “the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk Region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is stable.”
Public officials, too, have been deleting or editing statements about the plague. In a Telegram post dated Oct. 3, Baikalsk authorities asked residents to temporarily avoid traveling to Shelekhov and nearby towns because of “unofficial information about a confirmed case of plague infection in a person.” The post was available for almost two hours.
In addition, on Oct. 2 Buryatia Governor Alexey Tsydenov stated on the state-backed messenger Max that a woman in the Irkutsk Region “had died of plague.” He later edited the message, adding the word “possibly.” On his Telegram channel, Tsydenov published the already-edited post with the softened wording.
Despite official statements, hospitals in Irkutsk have begun introducing quarantine measures, as The Insider wrote on Oct. 4. On Oct. 5, the spread of quarantine measures continued. Lyudi Baikala reported, citing hospital patients, that restrictions had been introduced at the Irkutsk Regional Psychoneurological Dispensary.
Amid reports of a plague outbreak in the Irkutsk Region, Central Asian countries have begun tightening sanitary controls at their border with Russia, and Uzbekistan has introduced similar measures despite the fact that it does not share a land border with Russia. Enhanced sanitary and quarantine controls were also introduced by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
This past spring saw reports that Russian authorities had attempted to conceal an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in the country. Officials had announced an outbreak of pasteurellosis and rabies among cattle amid quarantine measures and the mass culling of animals. Additionally, authorities had imposed bans on moving livestock and exporting livestock products from several regions. However, many experts and farmers pointed out that pasteurellosis is a relatively straightforward infection that is treated with antibiotics — combating it does not require the mass killing of animals. Moreover, the government applied a five-kilometer radius for the slaughter of all susceptible livestock, as is prescribed in cases of foot-and-mouth disease.

Ashkan Rahgozar to serve as juror at Festival of Animation Berlin
TEHRAN – Iranian animator Ashkan Rahgozar will serve as a juror at the New Talents section of the 9th Festival of Animation Berlin (FAB), which will be held from October 8 to 11 in Berlin, Germany.
Rahgozar is one of the four members on the jury panel that also includes animation director Antje Heyn, film producer Franka Sachse, and stop motion designer, IRNA reported.
In addition, Rahgozar’s latest animation “Juliet and the King” will be shown during the festival and will be followed by a session titled “Animation Between Art and Challenge,” where the director will speak about the making of a hand-drawn animated film in Iran.
In this case study, Rahgozar offers insights into the making of his animated feature film “Juliet and the King”.
In the 90-minute 2D family animation, Nasser-al-Din Shah, the Iranian king, gets an invitation to visit France. He loves Europe, and he always takes the chance to visit there. While visiting a Romeo and Juliet play in Paris, the actress catches his eye. He falls in love with her so deeply that he asks her to perform the same play in Tehran, so he can impress her and win her heart.
Julie, the actress, decides to take this chance. With the help of her friend Jamal, she goes to perform in Iran, anticipating progress in her career. But she suddenly finds herself among jealous court ladies and the center of the king’s attention.
Blending a traditional Disney-style fairy tale with 19th-century Iran as its backdrop, the result is a compelling examination of cultural contrast. Set in the latter half of that century, this story offers Rahgozar’s interpretation of how Persian society once viewed the world. While times have certainly evolved, the themes explored remain relevant and thought-provoking.
The animated movie premiered at the 43rd Fajr Film Festival last year. It has participated in several international film festivals and has won six prestigious awards so far.
The Festival of Animation Berlin is the first film festival dedicated to animation in Germany's capital. With the festival's focus being on artistic animation of all kinds, FAB annually presents the best animated films in both regional and international categories.
FAB aspires not only to promote numerous filmmakers but also to pay tribute to the art of animation. Filmmakers from Berlin and across the globe get the opportunity to associate with like-minded people and present their work to the public.
Apart from competition categories, the festival comprises a rich side program revolving around animation-related themes. As a platform where inspiration, creative exchange, innovation, and communication come together, it seeks to create a point of connection between both emerging and established filmmakers as well as local audiences.

Amir Naderi’s “The Runner” to screen at Kaohsiung Film Festival

Amir Naderi’s “The Runner” to screen at Kaohsiung Film Festival
TEHRAN- Amir Naderi’s 4K-restored classic “The Runner” will be screened at the 2026 Kaohsiung Film Festival in Taiwan, while the Iranian filmmaker will serve as chair of the jury for the festival’s International Short Film Competition.
The 26th edition of the Kaohsiung Film Festival will be held from October 9 to 26 in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, according to the festival’s official website.
Naderi, a key figure of Iran’s New Wave cinema, will chair the five-member final-stage jury of the International Short Film Competition. The competition features short films from around the world, with works selected across various forms and genres.
Alongside his jury duties, Naderi will return to the festival with “The Runner,” his acclaimed 1984 film produced by the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCYA). The digitally restored 4K version has been selected for the festival’s Special Screenings section and will have its Taiwan premiere.
“The Runner” is scheduled to be screened at the Kaohsiung Film Archive on October 15 and 20. The first screening will be attended by Naderi and Majid Niroumand, who played the lead role of Amiro, and will be followed by a discussion with the filmmakers.
Set in the southern Iranian port city of Abadan, the film follows Amiro, an orphaned boy who lives alone and struggles to make a living by shining shoes, selling water, and collecting empty bottles. His dreams of escaping poverty and building a better future drive the story.
Drawing heavily on Naderi’s own childhood experiences, “The Runner” portrays the boy’s determination to overcome difficult circumstances through education, perseverance, and his desire to discover a wider world. The recurring image of running becomes a central metaphor for survival, freedom, and refusing to surrender to hardship.
The film was selected for the 1985 Venice Film Festival and won the Golden Montgolfiere at the Festival of the Three Continents in Nantes. It has since become one of the internationally recognized works of Iranian cinema and an important example of the country’s New Wave filmmaking.
Naderi, who was born in Abadan in 1946, is regarded as a key figure of the Iranian New Wave. His early films frequently focused on street children, youth and marginalized figures, using spare narratives and a distinctive visual language to explore survival and youthful aspirations. Naderi's films often explored the struggles of working-class people, as seen in his debut film "Goodbye Friend" (1971).
After the Iranian revolution, Naderi continued to make films, including the critically acclaimed "The Runner" and “Harmonica”, which gained international recognition and critical acclaim.
The 2026 Kaohsiung Film Festival has selected 40 international and 20 Taiwanese short films for its Short Film Competition from 2,715 submissions received from 97 countries.

Ansarallah sets Aramco sites ablaze as mercenaries commit war crimes in Yemen

Mercenary war crimes at Dhubab Airport
While Saudi-backed media promoted tactical movements along the western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaked video footage exposed the lawless conduct of foreign-funded proxies.
Verified recordings filmed at Dhubab Airport show members of the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council and UAE-funded Southern Giants Brigades forces committing severe war crimes against captured Ansarallah prisoners of war.

On the ground, claims by Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi regarding gains in Dhubab remain fragile and short-lived.
Historical experience across Taiz, Hodeidah, and Al-Jawf suggests that foreign-backed formations consistently crumble once immediate air support subsides.
Just last month, Yemeni forces demonstrated their tactical agility by liberating Mocha, Dhubab, and Perim Island in an eighteen-hour coastal push. Similar coalition offensives in 2018 stalled completely, and current frontline reports confirm that Ansarallah units have maintained control over essential supply routes while preparing decisive counterattacks to reclaim temporary proxy gains.
Western collusion and strategic failure
This ongoing aggression relies heavily on direct intelligence and logistical support from Washington and Tel Aviv.
American military officials have supplied targeting data for over 200 sites inside Yemen, alongside more than 100 U.S. advisers operating with coalition command.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly offered military backing to support the campaign, following previous Israeli strikes on Sanaa leadership targets.
Yet years of advanced Western weaponry and foreign advice have failed to resolve Saudi Arabia’s core military vulnerabilities or secure its southern border.
The humanitarian cost of the Western-backed campaign continues to climb.
World Health Organization reports confirm over 5,000 casualties since August, alongside a threefold increase in cholera cases across targeted governorates.
Nevertheless, relentless aerial bombardment cannot protect Saudi energy infrastructure from long-range retaliation.
By establishing a direct equation between Saudi aggression and the vulnerability of Aramco facilities in Jeddah and Yanbu, Ansarallah has shattered the coalition’s security guarantees, proving that Riyadh cannot achieve through foreign airpower what it has failed to gain on the battlefield for over a decade.

Plague may have resurfaced in Russia. But this isn’t the Black Death.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:00:48 UTC
03:00:48 KST

On October 1, 2026, the inpatient unit at the district hospital in Shelekhov, in Russia’s Irkutsk region, closed because of a suspected “especially dangerous infection.” Media outlets later reported that 28-year-old Darya Shipilova had died there of pneumonic plague. According to one account, she was a laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute and accidentally broke a test tube containing the bacterium that causes the disease. There has been no official confirmation that she died of plague; the authorities say she had “pneumonia of unknown cause.”
Wasn’t plague eradicated?
No. It became much less common, and it hasn’t caused a pandemic since the mid-20th century. Many factors appear to have contributed to this decline. One was the development of antibiotics that can cure plague. People also began coming into contact with rats and their fleas less often.
Today, people mainly contract plague through contact with wild animals. In Russia in 2016, for example, a 10-year-old boy contracted the infection after helping butcher marmots. In the U.S., an average of seven people contract plague each year — mainly through bites from fleas that have fed on infected rodents. Plague is now most common in African countries, particularly the Democratic Republic of the Congo (where an outbreak of Ebola virus disease is also ongoing) and Madagascar (where more than 2,000 people fell ill in 2017).
Russia officially recognizes 11 areas where plague circulates naturally, but in 2025, the bacterium that causes it was detected in only three of them. Every year, tens of thousands of people living in these areas are vaccinated against plague. There is a caveat, though: very few countries use the vaccine, and a lack of research means its effectiveness is unknown.
Is plague dangerous?
Yes. There are several forms of plague, all caused by the same bacterium but with different symptoms. The most common, bubonic plague, causes severe swelling of the lymph nodes. Pneumonic plague causes flu-like symptoms and lung failure. Other forms of the infection are less common.
Even with prompt antibiotic treatment, bubonic plague is fatal in 14% of cases. The death rate for pneumonic plague is twice as high. Treatment is more likely to succeed if it begins within two days of the onset of symptoms and uses drugs appropriate for that form of plague.
Without treatment, 30% to 60% of people with bubonic plague die. For pneumonic plague, the death rate can reach 100%.
How easily does plague spread from person to person?
Plague can spread through respiratory droplets, but only in its pneumonic form, and transmission requires prolonged contact. Usually, those who become infected live with or care for someone who has the disease. Plague doesn’t spread the way measles does: with measles, someone can walk into a room after an infected person has left and catch the disease.
During the first 24 hours, a patient with pneumonic plague poses no risk to others — the risk arises only when coughing begins. The World Health Organization recommends that anyone who has been within two meters (about 6.5 feet) of someone with plague in the past 10 days take appropriate antibiotics. Although people around the world continue to contract pneumonic plague, there has been no new pandemic. That is precisely because the bacterium spreads so poorly between people and established protocols help identify everyone who has been in contact with a patient, isolate them, and provide care. If the woman in the Irkutsk region did have pneumonic plague, that certainly doesn’t mean another pandemic is imminent.
Again, transmission through respiratory droplets is uncommon, and many other ways plague can spread between people are even rarer. Today, people mainly contract plague through contact with wild animals — specifically, through flea bites. That is why people at risk in Russia are vaccinated. According to Russian vaccine instructions, however, protection fades quickly, so another dose is needed every year (or after just six months if the situation in the region worsens).

How the TikTok algorithm changed political campaigning in 2024
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:00:48 UTC
03:00:48 KST

A recent study shows that political candidates on TikTok garner more views and interactions when they use short, highly emotional, and performance-based videos rather than detailed policy discussions. The research reveals how the structural design of the app encourages political messaging that prioritizes quick entertainment and visual spectacle over traditional campaigning. The findings were published in the Journal of Political Marketing.
Social media has completely changed how politicians reach voters, allowing them to bypass traditional news outlets. On platforms like TikTok, the audience tends to be younger, and the content moves rapidly. Researchers wanted to understand how candidates adapt their communication styles to survive in this specific digital environment.
To explore this, the researchers relied on a concept called Media Ecology Theory. This theory suggests that communication platforms are not just neutral delivery pipes for information. Instead, the specific design tools and rules of a platform shape the actual messages people create.
The investigators also looked at the idea of “affective publics.” This term describes how digital communities often form around shared emotions rather than logical debates. On an app powered by an algorithm that rewards rapid engagement, a shared joke or a burst of outrage might travel much further than a policy white paper. The study was authored by Jenny Bronstein and Tal Eitan, researchers at the Department of Information Science at Bar-Ilan University in Israel.
The researchers analyzed every TikTok video posted by the official accounts of Donald Trump and Kamala Harris during the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign. The data covered the period from when each candidate launched their account in the summer of 2024 until the day after the November election. The final dataset included 276 videos, consisting of 57 posts from Trump and 219 posts from Harris.
The research team watched and coded each video based on its structural style and its content. They looked for stylistic choices like speaking directly to the camera, sharing casual moments, or showing footage of large crowds. They also tracked emotional themes, noting whenever a candidate used humor, criticized their opponent, or featured a celebrity. Finally, the researchers compared these categories against public engagement numbers, such as views, likes, comments, and shares, to see which formats were most visible.
The overall posting habits of the two candidates differed greatly. Trump posted less frequently, but his videos were shorter, averaging 18 seconds. These shorter clips were associated with higher average engagement per post. Harris uploaded videos much more often, and her videos were longer, averaging 37 seconds. Her longer, issue-focused videos were associated with steadier but lower average interaction levels.
Both campaigns relied heavily on visual spectacle to project momentum. Over 80 percent of the videos from both candidates featured campaign stops, motorcades, or rallies. Showing energetic crowd scenes and candidates stepping off airplanes served as symbolic displays of power and territorial reach. For Trump, videos featuring these campaign spectacles were associated with higher share counts.
The candidates took different approaches when speaking directly to the camera. Trump favored an assertive, broadcast-style delivery. He focused on economic themes, border control, and confidence in victory, using forceful language. These direct-to-camera appeals made up about two-thirds of his posts and correlated with higher numbers of plays and likes for his account.
Harris used direct-to-camera appeals less often, featuring them in about a third of her posts. When she did speak directly to the viewer, she adopted a more instructional tone. She prioritized topics like human rights, disaster recovery, and reproductive rights, often encouraging civic participation. Her direct appeals were generally longer and more explanatory than Trump’s punchy statements.
Both candidates dedicated roughly half of their videos to informal, relatable moments. Trump cultivated a populist image by visiting a McDonald’s and riding in a garbage truck. Harris shared personal stories about cooking or caring for family members, trying to project warmth and accessibility. The researchers found no statistically significant differences in engagement for these relatable videos, suggesting that casual moments alone did not guarantee higher algorithmic visibility.
Humor and entertainment proved to be highly effective for capturing attention, even though the candidates used them sparingly. Less than 10 percent of the videos from each candidate relied primarily on jokes, memes, or parody. For Trump, these comedic posts were linked to significantly higher engagement across all metrics.
The candidates also used the platform to attack each other, but they utilized different formats. Harris referenced Trump in about a fifth of her videos. She frequently used split-screen formats to play a clip of her opponent and then offer a detailed rebuttal. In one video, she stated, “As president, I will take on corporate price gouging to lower the cost of groceries. Donald Trump can’t figure out what groceries are.”
Trump referenced Harris in about a third of his videos, but he rarely engaged directly with her specific claims. Instead, he relied on sarcasm, visual exaggeration, and direct mockery. In one video blaming his opponent for job losses, he stated, “In the last month, Kamala Harris has destroyed 24,000 jobs, manufacturing jobs, beautiful jobs.” Ultimately, the researchers found no statistically significant differences in engagement for videos that focused on attacking opponents.
Associating with celebrities and online influencers was another major strategy. Trump featured male figures from competitive sports and podcasting to reinforce a populist, masculine image. Harris collaborated with diverse musicians, actors, and media personalities to emphasize inclusivity and broader cultural relevance. For Trump, videos featuring these cultural figures were correlated with higher share counts, functioning as an effective shortcut for signaling identity.
The researchers noted a few limitations to their work. The study focused entirely on TikTok, meaning these communication patterns might not apply to platforms with different designs, such as Instagram or X. The analysis was also limited to two candidates in a single U.S. election cycle.
Additionally, the study relied on public engagement metrics, which only reflect how widely a video circulated. These numbers do not reveal how audiences actually felt about the videos or whether the content influenced their voting behavior. The coding system also only noted whether a specific feature was present in a video, without measuring the intensity of the emotional appeal.
The study, “Campaigning on TikTok: Platform Affordances, Affective Messaging, and Candidate Communication Styles in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election,” was authored by Jenny Bronstein and Tal Eitan.

Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:00:47 UTC
03:00:47 KST

Investigators believe the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said.
The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai flight FZ1073, experts believe.
Police and security agencies in at least six countries are scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone.
Hammami allegedly used an emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.
Israeli media have quoted from Hammami’s statements to interrogators since being transferred to United Arab Emirates custody on Thursday to report that he planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, or possibly another high-profile target nearby.
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.
In a phone call with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”
Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.
The investigation into Hammami has now spread to more than eight countries. Authorities in New Zealand and Australia are examining reports that the co-pilot studied in both nations about 10 years ago.
Hammami, who has an Omani father and a Syrian mother, is thought to have been employed by Oman Air from 2018 to June 2025, but left the airline after being moved to a desk job out of concerns that he had developed extremist views. He was then hired by Royal Air Maroc, the Moroccan national flag carrier, but did not obtain permission to fly and gave up his job there.
Shortly afterward, Hammami was hired at the state-owned flydubai, which has needed pilots as it expands rapidly. The airline conducted checks for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.
A key question for investigators is when Hammami began to formulate his plan to attack a plane full of Israelis or target Israel.
Netanyahu has claimed Hammami had undergone “radical Islamist indoctrination” and was clearly suicidal, without giving details.
Nine hours after the attack, a post was made to an online social media account in Hammami’s name praising Ayman al-Zawahiri, a former al-Qaida leader, as well as a militant responsible for a lethal suicide attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009. A second post contained religious imagery.
An analysis of Hammami’s X account by a company that uses AI to measure the toxicity of individuals’ social media accounts found dozens of misogynistic posts, including public threats against women. The analysis by Accountability! – which recovered Hammami’s deleted account by scraping internet archives, and reviewed almost 3,000 posts and responses – found repeated use of slurs against women, and a “consistent pattern” of use of terms meaning “whores”, and “filthy feminist”. The researchers also found homophobic slurs directed at men.
“Beyond offensive language, the analysis surfaced explicit conditional threats of physical violence … including repeated imagery of stomping on a woman’s head and making her ‘a lesson for others’,” the analysis found.
“Online toxicity isn’t just corrosive, it’s a warning sign. This pilot was telling the world who he was in his posts. Had anyone in charge been listening, nearly 200 people might never have been put in danger,” said Gur Megiddo, a co-founder and chief executive of Accountability!.
Regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities, with Israel.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the transportation ministry was responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights but the transportation minister, Miri Regev, said on X that the security agencies handled flight security.
Israeli newspapers reported that a key database of foreign pilots had not been checked despite concerns raised by official reports.
The attack occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 which triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks before a fiercely contested general election in which security – and responsibility for failures to keep Israelis safe – has been a central issue.
Opposition politicians have seized on the apparent lapses to attack Netanyahu, who has boasted of his ability to keep Israelis safe.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, the head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”

US scrambles all 12 B-1 bombers out of Britain over unexplained threats
