Finnish workers report better work ability as burnout persists
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:50:48 EEST
02:50:48 KST

Finnish workers are reporting stronger work ability than a year ago, but more than a quarter remain at increased risk of burnout, according to new research from the Finnish Institute of Occupational Health.
The institute’s How is Finland doing? study found that 43% of employed people rated their work ability as excellent in summer 2026, up from 39% a year earlier. Researchers examined five areas of work ability, covering physical, cognitive, social, emotional and skills-related demands.
Physical work ability received the strongest results, with 67% of respondents saying they were fully able to meet physical demands such as standing or lifting. Emotional work ability ranked lowest, with 41% saying they could fully handle demands involving other people’s emotions.
“Work ability is more multidimensional than many people think,” research professor Jari Hakanen said. He said an employee might perform well in one area while needing support in another.
Younger workers reported stronger physical and cognitive work ability than older groups. More than half of workers under 30 rated their overall work ability as excellent.
Their results were weaker on other measures of workplace wellbeing.
28% of workers aged 18 to 29 experienced boredom at work daily or several times a week. The rate was 23% among those aged 30 to 45, 15% among 46 to 55-year-olds and 12% among workers aged 56 to 66.
Fewer than half of workers aged 18 to 29 experienced work engagement daily or several times a week, compared with 65% among workers in their 50s and early 60s.
The institute found that younger workers also reported more loneliness and weaker social work ability, which measures their ability to deal with teamwork and informal workplace interaction.
Senior researcher Janne Kaltiainen said the findings should not be viewed only as characteristics of younger employees. Differences in experience, occupations and the social demands of jobs employing younger people also play a role.
Burnout symptoms showed no difference between age groups. Overall, 26% of employed Finns faced an increased risk of burnout or symptoms consistent with burnout. The level remained above that recorded before the Covid-19 pandemic.
Researchers identified bureaucracy and conflicting workplace roles as factors linked to burnout symptoms.
Researcher Jie Li said rigid procedures, poor tools, slow information flows and conflicting expectations add unnecessary demands and reduce the time employees spend on their main work.
Job insecurity, excessive workloads, repetitive tasks and physical demands were also associated with burnout, though the study found weaker links across the working population.
The amount of remote work had no association with workers’ overall assessment of their ability to work.

What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:48:50 UTC
02:48:50 KST

It is rare to hear a European say "I'm sorry" to the Ukrainians. Dag Øistein Endsjø, who nominated the Ukrainian people and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the Nobel Peace Prize 2026, shared it several times during our interview.
Mr. Endsjø is a professor of religious studies at the University of Oslo in Norway. He comes across as intelligent and reserved. But when he talks about Europe not helping Ukraine as much as it could, his eyes give away deep personal emotions.
"Just thank you for keeping us safe. Thank you for the extreme sacrifice you've been making for all of us. And I'm sorry that my government and the other governments haven't done enough," he said, speaking to me not as a journalist but as one of the Ukrainians.
These words reach cut through, because tens of millions of us live under daily psychological and physical terror, feeling forgotten and betrayed.
At the same time, Professor Endsjø names things as they are, even when it is uncomfortable. When the full-scale invasion began, he says, he doubted Ukraine would hold. And he admits that Norway has profited from the war: by its own Finance Department's calculation, about €106 billion in additional revenue from higher oil and gas prices.
He was honest with us. Our questions were sharp too, even those about US President Donald Trump's chances to win this year's award, and he answered them the way he answers everything: straight.
Do you think people who fight the war can be nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize?
People who defend themselves, yes! Who defends a free and democratic state against unprovoked aggression, yes, I think so.
Many say Ukraine should stop fighting and negotiate. Wouldn't a peace prize reward the war?
It's not a reward for the war, because the war could stop tomorrow if Russia just found out they didn't want to break international rules and could pull out. This is not about continuing the war. On the other hand, the war would stop the moment Ukraine threw out Russia. That, regrettably, seems to take more time.
This is not, in any way, about rewarding or promoting war as such. This is about standing up against war, because not standing up against war has only provoked more war and aggression from Russia.
Russia is attacking free and democratic countries unprovoked. They started in 2008 with Georgia, and then moved on to Ukraine, and as so many others point out, they have their plans.
"Moldova, if Ukraine hadn't been able to resist this invasion, would also have been under Russian rule now for sure. Poland and the Baltics would have been under extreme pressure, maybe also invaded," Mr. Endsjø says.
If there was a moment when you thought that Ukraine might lose the war?
Yes, in the beginning, when I saw those lines of tanks heading for Kyiv, I was afraid that everything was lost. Also noting the lackluster reaction from the free world and how they only came with condemnations and no ammunition, just a flight out.
If Ukraine is defending peace, why is the war getting closer to Europe's borders?
That is because of Russia. If Ukraine hadn't defended itself and just given up, the war would have been even closer to Europe. We would be even more under threat with probably even more degrees of sabotage and terrorist attacks around in Europe.
Does Ukrainian resistance escalate the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia?
No. The other way around. If Ukraine had given up, it would have been a more direct threat to NATO countries.
But some politicians say that in this case, Russia will just negotiate and sell energy as it did in the past
Yes, while sabotaging and even murdering people around in Europe, and acting like a state of terrorism. So, no, it would remain aggressive. You can listen to various prominent Russians on Russian TV. You know, you're not allowed to say anything on Russian TV unless the government approves it...
People are again and again threatening Finland, Poland, Britain, and the Baltic. Just as they made up these fake republics in Luhansk and Donetsk in 2014, they have tried to do the same in Estonia and Latvia already.
So if it hadn't been for Ukraine and Ukraine's resistance, the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia would have been even greater. Because Ukraine keeps Russia at bay.
If Ukraine agrees to a ceasefire, will you consider this a failure or a victory?
I, as a non-Ukrainian but fellow European, like any other European, have no right whatsoever to tell the Ukrainians what to do.
If the Ukrainians themselves find that this most horrible war is too much, and you want a ceasefire and you want to stop, and it's not for me to criticize. It's not for any European to criticize. We cannot tell the Ukrainians what to do after that horrible sacrifice you've made already.
I only hope that Europe and the rest of the free world will assist Ukraine even more, so that you will be even more successful in throwing out the Russian occupation army of the entire of Ukraine, including Crimea.
What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say that Ukraine brought the world to peace?
They will not use nuclear weapons. If they wanted to do it, they would have done that already. China and India are completely clear that they will not accept any use of nuclear weapons, so that would mean that Russia would be completely isolated and completely devastated economically in weeks. So that's not going to happen.
Putin says the war ends if Ukraine gives up Donbas. Why give a Nobel Peace Prize to a country that refuses?
This is just a proposal from Putin and American so-called negotiators. They're supposed to be negotiating, but this is not a negotiation. This is just about trying to make Ukraine give up without even a fight, which Russia is unable to do, and, incredibly, in some way, try to force Ukraine to give up its rightful ownership of its occupied territories.
This is just appeasement, just as what Chamberlain did in 1939 and what Europe has done again and again in 2008 and 2014. This would be a completely terrible mistake.
"Ukraine deserves the Nobel Prize, no matter how long they keep on fighting against this horrible aggression by this dreadful kleptocracy," Mr. Endsjø says.
Europe says Ukraine keeps the peace for everyone. Can it then demand that Ukrainian refugees go back and fight?
I, as a European, think that other Europeans cannot demand anything of the Ukrainians, whoever they are. This must be up to the Ukrainian people and the Ukrainian government.
Do people in Norway still genuinely believe that Ukraine can win this war, dragging on for so long?
I think so. Very many do believe that. But this depends on whether the West keeps on, and the free world continues to support Ukraine. Here in Norway, we are in a particular situation because, as our own Finance Department calculated last year, we have earned an extra 106 billion euros from the war (additional government revenues generated by high energy prices — ed.) due to higher oil and gas prices.
We don't support you as much as we should. We should have given you those 106 billion euros.
Why should someone in Europe care whether Ukraine wins or loses?
That is the point: that this is a war against the free world from a horrible dictatorship. More or less, you can call it a kleptocracy — that's the most, I guess, the most precise definition of Russia today. It's not a democracy whatsoever. It's most of all a kleptocracy where the top leaders just steal whatever they can get their hands on.
If Ukraine had fallen, it's not just that that would be horrible for Ukraine as such, but that would mean also that Russia would have had its hands on all the immense resources Ukraine has. Also, all the million men and women who probably would have been forced into the Russian army, and made it an even more dangerous enemy to the West.
So this is about the survival of all of us. Ukraine is the free world. We belong together. Ukraine should have been in NATO and the EU a long time ago.
If Russia says it only wants Donbas, why not just give it to them and let the war end?
This is like World War II all over again. They say: "If we only get Donbas, we're going to at least have proper negotiations."
Donbas, that is the Ukrainian Sudetenland. That's just what the West forced Czechoslovakia to do in 1938 and 1939. The Sudetenland wasn't just a nice little border region. It was the defense line of Czechoslovakia. So the moment the Germans got that, they were defenseless against the full-scale invasion that followed in the months afterward.
"Donbas, it's not just a small border region. It's the most important line of defense," Mr. Endsjø says.
Forcing Ukraine to give up anything whatsoever is rewarding the Russian aggression.
But I have to give Putin right in one thing when he says: "We are, you know, continuing World War II." That's true, because you have to remember what Russia did in World War II. They started it together with Nazi Germany in 1939. They occupied the Baltic countries, they occupied Moldova, they occupied half of Poland, they split Poland with Nazi Germany, and they tried to occupy Finland.
When Norway was invaded by Nazi Germany, Russia congratulated Germany. They were on Germany's side. The only thing that made Russia shift sides in World War II was the German invasion. What did they do after World War II? They didn't liberate any country - they occupied. They just changed one occupation for another.
"Eastern Europe wasn't liberated before 1990 and 1991. That's the actual end of World War II, when the Russian occupation of Eastern Europe ended," he stresses.
They even talk about the northern parts of Northern Norway. In 1945, they did have designs. They wanted Svalbard and the northern islands. They had plans to take the regions closest to Norway, which were also part of the Soviet Union. They want everything they have ever had, and they want it back.
Trump has made no secret of his desire for the Nobel Peace Prize. Could the Committee deny Ukraine the award simply to avoid provoking him?
Trump has been nominated for the Peace Prize several times, but I don't think he really has a chance. What I did note is that last year's recipient, Mrs. Machado from Venezuela, was probably chosen partly due to it. I don't criticize the prize, as she is a democratically elected leader, a good candidate, and a good recipient.
"But I believe part of the reason she got it was that the Nobel Committee wanted a recipient who would not provoke President Trump," he says.
I consider that they are going to worry about that again, about whether the recipient is going to provoke Trump or not. You never know what his reaction will be anyway. I don't think they really see him as a serious candidate — someone who just started an immense war in Iran, drawing the whole world economy down.
My nomination has gone viral — there are thousands of posts online. I usually don't get 750,000 views on my Facebook posts, but I did with my post about Ukraine. I really do believe that Zelenskyy and Ukraine are the most worthy recipients at this point in time.
If continuing the war means more Ukrainians will die, why not negotiate to stop the killing? Zelenskyy says Ukraine plans to fight further. Does it bring peace, really?
It does. Look at Norway in 1940. It was peace, but it wasn't peace. It was an occupation. It was killing, it was murder, and even worse in other parts of Europe. What happened in Norway was nothing compared to what happened in Poland, the Baltics, Ukraine, and Belarus.
Thank God the current Western leaders understand this: they are not going to force Ukraine to give up, to let millions of people live under horrible occupation, and give up more land. They stand by Ukraine now, and I hope they will support it even more, especially Norway.

From the rent crisis to Trump: 5 things that will shape Spain’s snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:48:14 UTC
02:48:14 KST

From the rent crisis to Trump: 5 things that will shape Spain’s snap election
Shifting attitudes toward the far right, fallout from the Ceuta crisis and the U.S. president’s geopolitical maneuvers could have a major impact on the Nov. 29 vote.
Spaniards have eight weeks to decide whether Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez should extend his eight-year tenure, or make way for a right-wing administration that could dramatically change the national trajectory — not least because it could include the far-right Vox party.
Here, POLITICO breaks down the main factors that will shape the Nov. 29 snap election.
The immediate spark may have been nationwide housing protests, but the race will also be shaped by Spain’s political extremes, the unresolved migrant crisis in Ceuta and geopolitics in the age of Trump.
Advertisement
Here are five things to watch.
Kingmakers on the extremes
Spain’s two largest parties — Sánchez’s center-left Socialist Party and Alberto Núñez Feijóo’s center-right People’s Party — are expected to get roughly the same results as they did when voters went to the polls in 2023, with both falling short of a governing majority. That means the next government will be led by whoever can cobble together the largest parliamentary alliance.
Polls put the People’s Party at around 34 percent, ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists, who are backed by 26% of voters. PP leader Feijóo says he is comfortable governing with the far-right Vox party, which is polling at around 18 percent, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. The PP already governs alongside Vox in several regions.
Sánchez’s hopes of reelection hinge on pulling off the same unlikely feat he achieved three years ago, when he managed to form a parliamentary majority with far-left, regional and separatist forces.
This time around, that option appears to be out of reach as a result of the collapse of the country’s left-wing political forces. Sumar — the junior partner in Sánchez’s coalition government — has plummeted in the polls and is currently leaderless.
Health Minister Mónica García is among the frontrunners to head the new alliance, which plans to present itself as the “Broad Front” later this month. It will be up to its eventual leader to try to forge a viable left-wing electoral alliance with bitter rivals Podemos, as well as big personalities like housing activist and former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau.
Advertisement
Appetite for Vox
Over the past decade, the far-right Vox party has evolved from a fringe group into a major political force — and, now, a plausible coalition partner in a national PP government.
In contrast to when national elections were last held in Spain, Vox has a clear track record of teaming up with the PP at the local and regional levels. The two parties currently govern together in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia, and previously ruled in Valencia and Murcia.
Within those governments, Vox has successfully pressured the PP into adopting tougher migration policies and denouncing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s Green Deal. Some PP-Vox governments have also replaced policies on violence against women with a broader “intra-family” framing that waters down the gender-specific nature of such crimes, and rolled back LGBTQ+ protections.
In 2023, Sánchez used the prospect of a PP-Vox government to spook voters into backing his candidacy, but it looks less likely that strategy can pack such a punch this time. Vox has expanded its political representation in several elections over the past three years, suggesting the party may no longer carry the same electoral stigma.
But the PP will nonetheless have to tread lightly. Although its clearest path to power involves a coalition with Vox, saying so may turn off moderate voters. The worse the center-right party performs, the more power its eventual far-right partners will have to determine policy.
The open wounds
There are two unresolved issues that could shake up the election: the Ceuta migration crisis and the ongoing corruption cases involving members of Sánchez’s inner circle.
Advertisement
Thousands of migrants remain in Ceuta after a mass surge that prompted major questions about Spain’s security readiness and its tense relationship with Morocco. While the recent housing protests have momentarily distracted voters, attention on the crisis could return as judicial investigations produce new findings detailing the government’s handling of the event.
King Felipe VI’s visit to Ceuta and Melilla next week could prompt a major diplomatic clash with Morocco, which claims the exclaves as its own and has warned that the visit would be a “provocation.” Any fresh influx of migrants into Ceuta would also increase focus on the unresolved crisis and reshape the electoral narrative around border security and national defense.
The focus of the campaign could also be derailed by the corruption scandals affecting the prime minister’s inner circle. Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial for alleged influence peddling and embezzlement. The trial date has not yet been set and is not expected to begin before the election.
Fresh revelations involving close Sánchez ally and former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, who is under investigation for alleged influence peddling, criminal organization and document falsification, could prove costly. So, too, could findings linked to the investigation into the Socialist Party’s alleged plot to discredit the judiciary.
Both Gómez and Zapatero maintain their innocence.
The power of the protesters
Sánchez on Monday boasted that, during his time in office, Spain has become “the fastest-growing economy in the entire European Union, leading in job creation.”
Advertisement
But average citizens are not necessarily feeling the impact of Spain’s strong growth and record employment figures. Inflation has outpaced salary gains, leaving many households with little additional purchasing power as prices — and, most crucially, housing costs — surge.
Spain’s housing activists have succeeded in harnessing wider frustration over the cost of living and organizing massive demonstrations and protest encampments in nearly every major city.
The Spanish Tenants’ Union could play a key role in the election by either endorsing a party or undermining turnout by telling supporters to stay home.
Pedro Sánchez addresses the Congress of Deputies on the government’s handling of the situation in Ceuta after a mass influx of migrants, at the lower house of parliament in Madrid on Sept. 3, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images
The union’s spokesperson, Valeria Racu, told POLITICO her group wanted politicians to commit to enacting indefinite rental contracts, legally mandated rent reductions, an end to evictions and speculative purchases, and a major expansion of public housing by reclaiming homes held by banks and investment funds.
Parties that make those commitments stand to benefit from the protesters’ votes. If none do so, however, there could be a substantial drop in turnout as disillusioned voters stay home. Although polls show housing is a top concern for voters across the ideological spectrum, that scenario would likely be felt most among left-wing parties.
The Trump effect
Three decades ago, then-Agriculture Minister Jesús Posada told conservative Prime Minister José María Aznar that his campaign needed to be based “less on Syria, and more on [the Spanish region of] Soria.”
Meanwhile, Trump remains an awkward topic for the People’s Party. Its advocacy of a more traditionally Atlanticist, Washington-friendly foreign policy is hardly a crowd-pleaser in a country where recent POLITICO polling found that a majority of respondents — 51 percent — considered the U.S. to pose a “threat” to Europe.
Vox’s unabashedly pro-MAGA stance has also created tensions with parts of its electorate. The U.S.’s military operations have contributed to soaring fuel and fertilizer costs, hitting the party’s rural voters particularly hard. Trump’s feud with Pope Leo XIV has also raised eyebrows among its conservative Catholic supporters, while the president’s clash with his former ally, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, has irked some far-right supporters.
All politics may be local, but in the world of Trump, developments abroad can have major impact in Spain — and could well play a role in the election.

The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s past | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:46:10 UTC
02:46:10 KST

The Conservative party wants to go back to the future under Kemi Badenoch. In her foundational text, The Right Way, released at the weekend, the Tory party leader makes its intellectual lineage explicit, repeatedly invoking Margaret Thatcher’s 1976 policy statement The Right Approach. The 2026 economic framework is familiar: only private enterprise creates wealth; taxes, regulation and spending can obstruct growth and competition; markets make the country stronger. The speech by her shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, made it clear that Conservative failures over its 14-year spell in charge were the result of the party straying from Thatcherite principles.
One might argue that, on the contrary, errors were because the party slavishly followed such a creed. When Rough, a depleted North Sea gasfield that once provided around 70% of the UK’s gas-storage capacity, was judged uneconomic by its private owner, a Conservative government in 2017 accepted that international markets could provide the UK with adequate energy security. That proved to be a big mistake when Russia invaded Ukraine, sending fossil fuel prices upwards. Britain was particularly exposed as a net energy importer and highly dependent on gas. Tory ministers had to bring back Rough into operation in 2022. Mrs Badenoch puts its closure down to “false economies”. But what was wrong was putting private profitability ahead of the country’s needs.
In his speech to conference, Mr Griffith attempted to distance himself and his party from the chaotic Liz Truss administration, although he was a member of its disastrous Treasury team. But his diagnosis today appears similar. Britain, in his telling, is supposedly more of a command economy than a market‑based one. To kickstart it, he argued, will require lower taxes, welfare reform and deregulation.
The difference, Mr Griffith was keen to stress, is that tax cuts will now come through spending cuts rather than additional borrowing. Why shrinking the state would strengthen growth enough to offset its effect on demand and productive capacity is unanswered. Just how big those cuts might be was revealed by the Guardian. Mr Griffiths admitted when he was the shadow business secretary that the Tories were planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn that the party had announced if it won the next election.
This might be seen as the kind of clear blue water that the Tories need to put between themselves and Labour. But the real enemy is further right. As the pollster John Curtice told a Demos fringe event, the voters most dissatisfied with high rates of immigration, the performance of the economy and the NHS are disproportionately moving to Reform UK. The perceived failures of Labour are not automatically benefiting the Conservatives. Prof Curtice said that either the party was “still getting the blame” for its record in government, or Reform was “simply speaking a language” that appeals more to those voters. It is hard to see how restoring Thatcherite principles will help the party here.
Mrs Badenoch recognises that the world has changed. She acknowledges that insecure supply chains and economic coercion may require the state to step in. But public investment must remain a special case, and, she says, “help to an individual firm should be exceptional and, where possible, temporary”. The real problem with her prospectus is Britain’s future requiring permission from 1976.

Denmark: Data of millions compromised in hack

Denmark: Data of millions compromised in hack
October 5, 2026
Denmark's national registry was hacked in an incident the authorities described as "extremely serious."
Hackers secured access to personal information on millions of people, the country's digital affairs ministry said on Monday. The compromised information included names, addresses and social security numbers, known in Denmark as national registry numbers.
The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised. This figure exceeds Denmark's population size because it includes people who have already died or emigrated, the Danish authorities said in a statement.
The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The hackers have not yet been identified. The means they used to gain access has since been cut off.
The ministry said it was first alerted to an "anomaly" in the system "during September."
Information of deceased, emigrated people included
Denmark has a population of roughly six million people. However, its national registry includes information of eleven million people, which includes the data of those deceased or people who have moved abroad and don't live in Denmark anymore.
Christina Egelund, Denmark's digital affairs minister, said the incident's full extent will investigated by the authorities.
"This is an extremely serious incident," Egelund said. "We are in the process of tracking the exact extent of this incident with all those affected."
Danish news agency Ritzau reported that the register includes information on church membership, details of legal incapacitation and restrictions on legal capacity.

The Guardian view on sexual abuse in schools: teachers cannot deal with this alone | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:45:41 UTC
02:45:41 KST

The Guardian’s findings about the extent of sexual abuse in schools require an urgent, calibrated response. Data revealing multiple rapes committed each year on school premises in England and Wales is hard to comprehend. Yet this is what freedom of information requests to police forces, covering the period from 2021 until last year, have revealed. As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many of the victims is disturbing. More than 8,500 sexual offences at or near schools were committed against under-13s, most of them girls.
Data about perpetrators contains gaps, including their age and sex. While the overwhelming majority of such acts are carried out by boys, we don’t know the exact proportion, nor if there is an age gap between those carrying out abuse and those being targeted. Only 33 out of 43 police forces shared their data, meaning that large areas including Scotland are not represented. But whatever the exact details, and allowing for the fact that these are reports, not convictions, the findings are deeply dismaying.
The suggestion by the acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, that the figures could reflect an increased willingness to report sexual abuse rather than more abuse taking place, must be taken seriously. At the same time, an unknown number of assaults continue to go unreported. Exact comparisons with the past are not possible since there is no equivalent dataset. What can be said, 10 years after a committee of MPs recommended that ministers should make sexual abuse in schools an “immediate policy priority”, is that the problem has not gone away; some experts believe that it is getting worse.
The response to the problem so far has relied on three main tools. One is the promotion of sex and relationships education. The scale of image-based abuse in schools requires further investigation, but Monday’s warning of a huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material globally points to the need for a curriculum that keeps abreast of technological change. The second tool is online safety laws including age verification, tighter restrictions on pornography, and the pledge by Sir Keir Starmer’s government to place smartphones off-limits for under-16s. The third is the criminal justice system, and ongoing efforts to improve the way that police and prosecutors deal with victims.
Ministers will need all these to work if they are to have any chance of meeting their goal of halving violence against women and girls. But acute resource and capacity problems are hampering courts and prisons, while pornography regulation needs to be enforced as well as discussed. While campaigners are hopeful, effects need to be measured. In relationships education, good intentions must not be confused with effects. To make a difference, schools need investment, training and evaluation.
This problem cannot be left to teachers to deal with; parents should also discuss these issues with young people. And politicians will have to be brave. The focus on sexual crimes by rightwing and far-right parties in many countries places liberals in a difficult position, with some fearful that by talking about them, they risk adding to a narrative that sows discord and scapegoats immigrants. The abuse of children by other children is an upsetting subject, but looking away is the worst of all options. As a society, we owe it to young people to deal with it.

Pezeshkian calls for practical, cross-political plans to counter economic pressure
TEHRAN— President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for practical, implementable, and politically inclusive plans to address Iran’s economic and social challenges, saying his administration has adopted a new approach to managing the special circumstances facing the country.
Speaking at a consultative meeting with members of the Parliament on Monday, Pezeshkian said improving people’s livelihoods and economic conditions was the government’s top priority, particularly amid the pressures resulting from war and sanctions.
He said the country’s current circumstances require cooperation and greater synergy among government institutions, lawmakers and different segments of society, stressing that efforts to address economic and social problems should be based on national unity and cooperation rather than confrontation.
Pezeshkian said the pressure on Iran’s economy had increased in recent months, but added that public support and measures taken by government officials had prevented the enemy’s economic war from achieving its objectives.
In a post on X on Sunday night, the president said the administration had adopted a new arrangement for managing the current conditions, adding that the enemy’s plan in recent months had been to cut the country’s vital lifelines in an attempt to place greater pressure on the people.
At Monday’s meeting, Pezeshkian said improving the livelihoods of people in need, female-headed households, low-income families and other vulnerable groups should remain at the center of government policymaking.
He said practical initiatives to improve people’s living conditions could begin at the “neighborhood and community level, including through greater use of neighborhood-based governance and mosque-centered initiatives.”
“Laws cannot be implemented through force and pressure,” Pezeshkian said, emphasizing the importance of increasing public services, interaction and mutual assistance to encourage positive changes in society.
Call for national synergy
The president stressed that overcoming the country’s challenges requires stronger coordination among all institutions and social groups.
“There is no such thing as government and non-government; we are all one nation,” he said, calling for practical and implementable plans to address economic and social problems.
Pezeshkian said that while different views may exist at the theoretical level, proposed solutions must ultimately be capable of implementation.
Energy savings and continued production
Pezeshkian also described energy conservation, consumption management and higher productivity as essential under the current circumstances.
Improved energy consumption patterns could free up resources that could be directed toward supporting livelihoods and improving incomes and wages, he argued.
At the same time, he stressed that energy-saving measures should not disrupt production. The government, he said, is pursuing efforts to ensure that electricity and energy supplies to production units and businesses are not cut, allowing economic activity to continue and helping prevent unemployment.

Making Sense of the Ambiguous Ending of Verity

Warning: This post contains spoilers for Verity.
Under the studio lights of Hot Ones, across the table from host Sean Evans, Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) looks every inch the bestselling novelist with the enviable life. We have seen a sliver of this interview before, playing on a laptop while someone else watched. Now it fills the frame, and for once nothing stands between Verity and the audience: no laptop screen, no manuscript page. The footage comes from before: before the car wreck that left her silent, before a writer moved into her house to take over her work, before the night her husband and that writer carried her body down to the lake. The interview is the film’s final image, and Verity gets the closing line, a remark about certainty. Then cut to black.
Verity’s return to its title character at its very end is a bold way to close a story that declines to say whether she was a sociopathic monster or the ultimate tragedy. It is also, for director Michael Showalter and author Colleen Hoover, the entire idea. Showalter’s Verity adapts Hoover’s 2018 novel, a self-published thriller that became one of the biggest word-of-mouth hits in contemporary publishing. In the book, Lowen, a broke writer grieving her mother, is hired to finish Verity’s series, which the latter can no longer write herself; a car accident has seemingly left her unable to speak or even comprehend what’s going on around her. In Verity’s office, Lowen finds So Be It, an autobiographical manuscript Verity wrote before her accident, in which she confesses to resenting her twin children, Harper and Crew, and to letting Harper drown in the lake behind the house. She also finds Jeremy, Verity’s husband, grieving and attentive, and growing closer to her by the day.
The film keeps the shape of Hoover’s ending, including its refusal to definitively explain what really happened inside that house. What it changes is who speaks last. “There’s something about this story that’s very big,” Showalter tells TIME. “Crazy things happen. It’s scary, it’s sexy, it’s surprising. I wanted to preserve those moments that are like, whoa, that just happened.” Hoover, a producer on the film, had a simpler test. “I was just hoping that readers would walk away with the same feeling they felt when they read the book,” she says.
A love affair with a manuscript
The film opens not on Lowen but on Verity, mid-interview, with Gayle King marveling at one of the best-selling authors on the planet and Verity calling her life “all a miracle.” Some could say, King replies, “it’s a miracle built on villains,” a line that hangs over everything that follows.
On a Manhattan sidewalk outside Grand Central, Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson), headphones on, is spattered with a stranger’s blood when a car strikes a cyclist nearby. The man who walks her to a coffee-shop bathroom and hands her a clean white shirt is Jeremy Crawford (Josh Hartnett), who seems steadier than she is. “I’ve seen worse, unfortunately,” he says. When she asks what happened to him, he tells her he pulled his eight-year-old daughter’s body from a lake last spring. She answers with her own loss: Her mother died last week of cancer.
Minutes later she encounters him again in a meeting with Hachette Book Group, where Verity’s editor asks whether she would finish Verity’s series. Jeremy privately tells Lowen the offer is a lowball; she should ask for $500,000. She does, and gets it.
Lowen heads north to the Crawfords’ home in Vermont, where Verity kept her papers and Jeremy offers her a room. The house, all angles and low ceilings, sits with the lake at its back. There she meets Crew (Brady Wagner), the surviving twin, small and watchful, and Verity herself, propped upright, eyes open but vacant.
Lowen finds the manuscript early, saved on a USB flash drive hidden in a cigarette pack in Verity’s desk. It reads as nothing the publisher asked for: an autobiography of the marriage, opening on the night Verity, in a red dress, first caught Jeremy’s eye. From there, the film alternates between Lowen’s days in the house and the chapters of So Be It, and the way it stages those chapters is its most daring swing.
As Lowen reads, the manuscript takes over the screen: Verity narrates her confession and occasionally turns to address her reader directly, as if she can feel Lowen turning the pages. The author’s note ends on a dare. “Here you are. Human. Curious,” she writes. “Carry on. But know one thing: there is no light where we’re going.” The device breaks the fourth wall of a story that is, underneath the murder plot, really about what reading can do to a person.
Hoover allows that the device gave her pause; it “could either go really well or really badly.” But seeing it on screen settled the question, and she loved it. For Showalter, the reading itself became the film’s real subject. “It’s a relationship. It’s intimate. It’s all-encompassing,” he says. “It’s a love affair.”
The manuscript’s logic is stark. Verity never wanted to share Jeremy with anyone, and once the twins arrive, she finds one far easier to bear than the other. “Crew was fairly quiet, but Harper cried constantly,” she writes. “It was like she was trying to punish me, telling me I was a bad mother.”
Her first attempt to kill Harper comes while the twins are still infants, when she presses a pillow over the baby, believing suffocation could be mistaken for SIDS. But she’s interrupted when Jeremy wakes and finds her, though he doesn’t see what she’s attempting to do. Her second try comes years later. Harper and Crew are painting at the dining table when Jeremy, about to leave for Boston, suggests Verity take them out in the canoe—and she does. Harper sits in the front, Crew in the middle. “None of us were wearing life vests, and I shifted all my weight, and the boat tipped over,” Verity writes. She saves Crew and lets Harper drown. A mother exaggerating ordinary resentment into a monster’s confession is exactly what the letter, when it eventually arrives, will claim Verity was doing.
Readers of the novel will notice the family is smaller. Hoover’s version has three children, two of whom die; the film makes Harper and Crew twins and leaves only one death at its center. The change predates Showalter’s involvement, but he says it “streamlined” the story and lets the film “focus on the one child and the mystery surrounding that.”
Slowly becoming Verity
The more Lowen reads the manuscript, the further she steps into Verity’s life. Between chapters, she watches Verity’s Hot Ones appearance on her laptop. When Jeremy takes her out for a belated birthday dinner, he points her to his wife’s closet to find something special to wear. Lowen chooses a red dress that echoes the one Verity wore the night the couple met. Over wine and Wiener schnitzel at what Jeremy bills as the best Bavarian restaurant in rural Vermont, he confesses he lied earlier: Verity never read Lowen’s book. He did. “Because the thing is, your writing matters to me, Lowen,” he says. Back at the house, they kiss, until Lowen thinks she sees Verity standing in the dark hall behind him. Jeremy tells her his wife can’t walk. Despite Lowen’s unnerving vision, that night they become lovers. In the film’s most delirious sequence, the dread follows Lowen into sleep: She kisses Jeremy in a dream, then pulls back to find Verity beneath her, blood on her lip.
With the dress, the husband, and the dream, Showalter is signaling exactly which tradition he’s drawing from. “Hitchcock does so much in his films with doppelgängers,” he says, citing Vertigo and All About Eve, as well as Brian De Palma’s Body Double, as touchstones for stories about people taking on another person’s identity. “[Lowen] covets the success. She covets the relationship. She covets all of it,” Showalter says. “She’s sort of slowly becoming Verity.”
The house’s last secret comes from Crew. “Mommy said I shouldn’t talk to you if you ask any questions about her,” he tells Lowen, and when she asks whether his mother is pretending she can’t talk, he bites down on a knife. Lowen goes to Verity. “You have this perfect life,” she tells her. “You have everything that anyone could ever want. That I want. And you don’t deserve it. So I’m gonna take it from you. All of it. Your house. Your career. Your husband.” It is the closest the film comes to a confession from Lowen. It’s up to our interpretation whether the words wash over Verity, meaningless, or she hears each and every one.The manuscript ends where Verity’s public story began, with the car. In its final chapter, she recounts the police interviews after Harper’s death and Jeremy’s grief, which she finds tiresome. “He’s become such a drag now that Harper’s dead,” she writes. “I almost wish I hadn’t killed her. If that’s the case, so be it. I’ll just drive my car into a tree.” Lowen reads those lines knowing how the story turned out: there was a tree, a wreck, and a woman upstairs who hasn’t spoken since.
A death by the lake
The turn comes on a stormy night, when Jeremy realizes Lowen planted a camera in Verity’s room to try to catch her in a lie. Confronted, Lowen stops explaining and starts accusing. “Your wife is not who you think she is,” she tells him, handing him a printout of the manuscript. Jeremy finishes reading it looking like a man seeing his wife for the first time. He storms into Verity’s room. “You murdered our daughter, Verity,” he shouts. His wife does the one act that ends the argument over her condition for good: she moves. She has, in fact, been faking her incapacitation the entire time, while hatching a plan of her own.
Jeremy’s hands go to Verity’s throat, and Lowen, watching, stops him, not to save Verity but to save him. “Think about Crew,” she says. “He won’t have a mother or a father if you do this.” She tells him to “make it look like an accident” by covering Verity’s nose and mouth until she stops breathing. “Don’t leave any marks.” So Jeremy smothers his wife in her bed while Lowen stands a few feet away, and Showalter’s camera holds a few feet closer than that, leaving the audience nearer to the killing than Lowen, who called for it. The couple carry the body to the water and let it go, arranging a fiction for whoever finds her: Verity woke from her long absence and walked into the lake that took her daughter. “It was done,” Lowen says in voiceover. “It could not be undone. We were free from Verity.”
For Showalter, Lowen’s suggestion is the crucial moment. Until then, he says, “we are all Lowen going into this haunted house with these larger-than-life characters.” The instant she proposes making it look like an accident, “all of a sudden, it’s like the rug has been pulled out from under us.” He considers it the story’s engine. “The minute you think you’re on solid ground, you’re not.”
Staging Verity’s death in the lake is the film’s own invention, and it works two ways at once. In the novel, the couple make it look as though she choked on her own vomit. Here, her death mirrors Harper’s: another drowning, another death made to look like an accident. And it gives Lowen a physical role in the cover-up; she is no longer advising a murder but helping to hide one. When the police come, Lowen lies as smoothly as she writes. One officer asks whether she was working with Verity on the newest Noble Virtues novel. “Perhaps,” Lowen says, and when he admits he’s a fan, she adds, “It’ll be the best one yet.”
The letter under the floorboard
Seven months later, Lowen is pregnant, and the Crawford house is emptying into a moving truck; she, Jeremy, and Crew are bound for Southport, North Carolina. She hands Jeremy an advance copy of Diligence, the latest book in Verity’s series, which Lowen wrote. Crew has retrieved his pictures from a secret hiding place he won’t reveal. Lowen finds it anyway: a loose floorboard, with several handwritten pages beneath it.
Verity’s letter, written to Jeremy after the crash during the months she spent feigning her condition, insists that So Be It was never a confession but a writing exercise. It came, she writes, from a dinner with her editor, Amanda, who called it “antagonistic journaling”: keep a journal of your life, except flip your inner dialogue to the opposite of what you were thinking, the opposite of who you are. Living inside a villain’s head proved “exhilarating,” the secret behind her “realistic, terrifying characters” and the reason her books sold. After Harper’s death, with her mind in “such a dark space,” she leaned on it harder, pushing the pages to be “more jarring, more disturbing.” Jeremy, finding the file open on her computer, mistook the villain for his wife. “It was just an exercise. It wasn’t real,” she writes. “After all those years of marriage, how could you, even for one second, believe any of that manuscript to be true? I mean, seriously, Jeremy. Do you know me at all?”
The letter then describes what he did about it. Every memory of their family, she writes, was “erased with every new word of the manuscript that you had read.” She remembers his face, “complete and utter misery,” and then very little: “I felt dizzy, and everything became a blur, and I realized that you believed it.” By her account, Jeremy drugged her. He put her behind the wheel of their car, aimed it at the trees, and sent it off, so that the wreck would look like Verity had done what her manuscript promised. She came to as it was happening. “I looked out the windshield; all I saw were trees, and in that moment I knew what you were doing,” Verity writes. “You were going to kill me and make my death look like an accident. I had unknowingly written my own death into the last two sentences of my manuscript.” Those are the last two sentences Lowen read, and the ones that gave the manuscript its title.
If the letter is true, Jeremy staged his wife’s death from her own ending, and the phrase Verity uses for it, “make my death look like an accident,” is the one the audience heard an hour earlier from Lowen, in the bedroom. It also explains the months of silence. “Inconveniently, I was still alive, so I made a plan,” Verity writes. Denying the manuscript would never work, and if Jeremy learned she had recovered, “you can turn me in to the police or finish the job yourself.” So she played the invalid and waited for a chance to take Crew and go. Crew, she writes, was the only one who knew she was still there. Which means Jeremy already knew the pages existed when Lowen handed him the printout, and his shock, like his wife's silence, was an act.
The letter is the most argued-over object in Hoover’s novel, and the one that puts its title to the test. “That was my whole goal with the book, and also the title,” she says. The word verity, after all, means truth. She hadn’t outlined the ending, but once the letter occurred to her, “I got so excited and probably didn’t sleep for three days writing that scene.”
After reading the letter, Lowen chooses not to show it to Jeremy; Hoover sees the silence as practical. “What’s done is done,” she says. Nor, in her view, does Lowen want to believe the letter at all, though Hoover wonders how anyone could move forward, carrying Jeremy’s child, without some fear. But she points to the same consolation the character reaches for: whatever the truth, Jeremy was protecting his children. “Like, oh, he’s going to be the best dad ever,” Hoover says. “He would kill his wife for his kids, which doesn’t really constitute dad of the year.”
Team Manuscript or Team Letter
Hoover’s readers have spent the better part of a decade splitting into camps over which document to trust: Team Manuscript holds that Verity’s manuscript is a confession to take at face value, while Team Letter claims Verity became the victim of her own craft. The film leaves the question fully open: which version of Verity was real?
As a reader of her own book, Hoover leaned toward Team Manuscript in the past. The movie has since complicated that view. “While the movie was being made, I still wanted to be confused,” she says. She got her wish and then some. “I had to go back and reread the book for some annotations recently, and now I feel bad for Verity in a way that I never felt after writing the book—and I think that’s because of the movie.” Showalter, she says, “opened up this possibility for so many different perspectives to be the truth,” and each return to the story has landed her somewhere new. “After writing it, I thought one way. Watching the movie, I thought one way. But then reading the book again, after having all of that, really made me start questioning again.”
Showalter’s thinking on the film shifted, too. He explored multiple endings before landing on the one that made the cut. In many, Lowen ends the film “way more at peace with everything,” her doppelgänger arc complete, having “fully become sort of the dark phoenix rising a little bit.” He stands by the final cut. “We ultimately decided not to go that far, but to leave it in that very ambiguous place,” he says.
Giving Verity the last word
The novel ends inside Lowen’s head, as she weighs which Verity to believe, and the film gives her that moment too, in voiceover that begins during her last sweep of the house and carries into the car ride. “Her manuscript, her letter, her husband. I have no idea what to believe,” she says. “The only thing I know for certain is that Verity was a master at manipulating the truth. The only question that remains is which truth was she manipulating.” Then the film takes the ending away from her.
As the car disappears down the road with Jeremy, Lowen, and Crew, sun dappling through the trees, Showalter cuts back to the Hot Ones interview, the clip Lowen watched on her laptop inside the Crawfords’ house. This time no screen frames it.
Evans asks which of the nine moral themes behind Verity’s book series was the most fun to corrupt. “Truth,” Verity says. “I wanted to see how far you could push it, how certain I could make the audience before showing them that maybe certainty wasn’t the wisest choice.” She’s describing her novels, but she is also describing the movie that just ended, which spent its runtime making its audience certain about her, then handed them a letter threatening to change everything. And she is speaking past every character in the film, straight to the theater, the way her manuscript spoke past Lowen to us. The clip that entered the film as Lowen’s homework exits as Verity’s final address.
For Showalter, the cut is less a twist than a refusal. “We’re not going to let you walk out of here knowing for sure what was real and what was false,” he says. “It was giving her the last word.”
Hoover shares that instinct, and she counts not two Veritys in Hathaway’s performance but really three: the Verity of the manuscript, as Lowen imagines her; the bedridden Verity; and the public Verity from the interviews. “You walk out thinking, which one is the real Verity?” Hoover says. “I love that they decided not to answer that question, and that you leave with that uncertainty.”
Lowen leaves the Crawfords’ home with nearly everything she coveted in the film’s first act: Verity’s husband, Verity’s surviving child, a baby on the way, and a higher-profile writing career attached to Verity’s name. But she will never know whether the man beside her in the car is a grieving father or the villain of Verity’s letter, or whether the woman they carried to the lake wrote a confession or a character. Certainty is the one possession Lowen has to leave behind.
Lowen won’t be the only one left wondering. Readers have argued over Verity since 2018; now anyone with a ticket can join in. Somewhere in the days and weeks ahead, in a lobby or a group chat, one viewer will swear the manuscript was real and another will swear by the letter. Verity, who wrote both, took the answer with her into the lake. That is the ending’s last trade: the living inherit the doubt, and the dead, as ever, hold the truth.

What We Know About Russia Pneumonic 'Plague' After Dozens Quarantined in Siberia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:40:04 UTC
02:40:04 KST

Dozens of people have been quarantined and outbreak control measures are underway after a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia died last week in undisclosed circumstances.
There have been conflicting reports about how the 28-year-old laboratory worker, named by local media as “Darya Shipilova,” had fallen ill and some Russian media reports are no longer available online. A local news source claimed that the lab worker was exposed to plague via a broken test tube, but local authorities have said there was no evidence to support this.
Igor Kobzev, the regional governor of Irkutsk, said Monday the staffer had died from “pneumonia of undetermined” origin. Acknowledging there have been “different interpretations of the events” in the media, he said extensive laboratory tests had determined “no microorganisms related to the girl's professional activities were found in her biological samples.” He also said no new employees from the institute had sought medical attention in the past few days.
Rospotrebnadzor, the government body responsible for public health, similarly told state media the institute had not found signs of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens in the lab.
Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in the Irkutsk region, said “comprehensive anti-epidemic measures are being implemented” in the area in response to the incident and that anyone who had contact with the deceased patient is being tested daily. Dozens of people who had been in contact with the lab worker have now been quarantined and are under observation by medical professionals.
Local media also reported that the inpatient department at the Shelekhov hospital where the lab worker died has been closed due to a suspected “particularly dangerous infection,” with local residents informed they will be unable to visit family at the facility. This has not been confirmed by public officials.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, in remarks carried by Russian state media outlet TASS, told reporters Rospotrebnadzor should be followed for official updates, “rather than listening to various rumors and speculations.”
TIME has reached out to the Russian Health Ministry, the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, and Rospotrebnadzor for further comment.
Amid growing online speculation, some social media users have likened the reports coming out of Russia to those that circulated in the early days of the COVID-19 outbreak in early 2020.
But Dr. Simon Clarke, associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, stressed in a statement that it is “important to remember that pneumonic plague is a very different” disease.
“It is caused by bacteria, Yersinia pestis, famous for causing the Black Death, that remains with us today mostly in animals across parts of Asia, Africa and the Americas,” he said. "Pneumonic plague is particularly serious because it means the infection has reached the lungs and is nearly always fatal if not treated promptly. Unlike the bubonic plague which enters the body via infected flea bites, pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact.”
However, unlike many viral respiratory diseases, he said, “plague is caused by bacteria and is generally treatable with antibiotics, if identified quickly.”
Remarking on the unverified reports that a lab worker was exposed to plague via a broken test tube, Clarke again urged caution. “It is not unheard of for pathogens to escape from labs, but an awful lot must have gone wrong for a lab worker to be infected by a broken test tube,” he said.
Meanwhile, the U.S. is closely monitoring the evolving situation.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told TIME: “The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is monitoring the situation closely with the State Department and our other interagency partners. The safety and security of U.S. citizens is our highest priority.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday said “it seems there was a worker at the lab that was infected” and “there’s concern that could have spread, at least internally, so you’ve seen them do quarantines.”
“There’s very limited travel between the U.S and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out and it could quickly spread,” Rubio continued. “We're watching and monitoring it closely.”
He emphasized that while he doesn’t think the situation, at this point in time, is cause for alarm, he does consider it to be “cause for focus."
As the situation in Siberia continues to unfold, here’s what to know about the plague:
What is the plague?
The bacterium Yersinia pestis has a long, dark history with the human race; it was this pathogen, spread by flea bites, that killed more than 25 million Europeans during the Black Death of the 14th century. There are three different forms, all caused by the same bacterium but affecting different tissues: bubonic, which can cause dark swellings in the groin and armpits; septicemic plague, in which the pathogen enters the bloodstream; and pneumonic plague, which attacks the lungs. The pathogen can be spread by the bites of infected fleas, by contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, or by breathing in airborne particles that contain it.
What is pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague occurs when the pathogen infects the lungs. This can happen when the bacterium spreads to the lungs of someone with another form, or after someone breathes in particles containing the pathogen. It’s the only form that spreads easily between humans.
The symptoms include fever, weakness, rapidly progressing pneumonia, and cough. Pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period—as short as one day. If untreated, this form is almost always fatal. Even with treatment, about 30% of infected people die.
Can you treat plague?
When given early, antibiotics work well against all forms of plague. When a case is suspected, government guidance suggests acting quickly to treat with oral or intravenous antibiotics rather than waiting for a precise identification from a lab result.
Where is plague endemic?
Natural reservoirs of the bacterium exist on all inhabited continents except Oceania, according to the World Health Organization. In the U.S., cases are concentrated in the West; visitors to Yosemite National Park, for instance, are warned against feeding ground squirrels and chipmunks, creatures that can carry fleas containing Yersinia pestis. Every year, a handful of people in the American West, usually campers and hikers who have come into contact with rodents, test positive for plague.
A recent paper records a lethal case of pneumonic plague in Arizona that occurred in 2025. The patient in that case is thought to have acquired the bacterium from professional exposure to two cats with respiratory symptoms that may have been pneumonic plague.
Globally, plague is most common in Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar, according to the WHO.
Could the plague bacteria cause outbreaks?
Yes. In fact, there are often annual outbreaks in Madagascar, from September to April, and some of these outbreaks have been of the particularly dangerous pneumonic form, which can spread through the air.
That’s why public-health monitoring to prevent initial cases from spreading is an important way to guard against wider spread. In its general guidelines for managing plague, the WHO calls pneumonic plague “of particular concern because of the high risk of triggering epidemics.” Any cases of plague, especially pneumonic form, are important to contain quickly, WHO says.

‘Compassion in judging is not favour or leniency’: Supreme Court Justice Vikram Nath
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:39:35 UTC
02:39:35 KST

Justice Nath said the courts must ensure that legal principles do not overshadow the human realities.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court judge Justice Vikram Nath on Monday said compassion in judging should not be mistaken for favour or leniency, but should instead mean understanding the human circumstances behind a legal dispute without compromising fairness or the law.Speaking at the second Prof. (Dr) N R Madhava Menon Memorial Lecture, Justice Nath said the courts must ensure that legal principles do not overshadow the human realities of those involved in a case.The annual lecture was held on the theme "Judging with Compassion: Human Understanding in the Practice of Law"."Let me say what compassion in judging is not. It is not favour and it is not leniency. It is not deciding for a party merely because that party is weak, or allowing emotion to overcome evidence. And it is certainly not abandoning the law. Compassion in adjudication means understanding before judging -- the discipline of seeing the human circumstances in which a legal controversy arose. Its opposite is not strictness, which is sometimes exactly what an institution needs. The opposite of compassion is indifference," Justice Nath said as per news agency PTI.Justice Nath, who is also the executive chairman of the National Legal Services Authority, stressed that being impartial does not mean becoming detached from the human consequences of judicial decisions.
"The blindfold on Lady Justice does not mean she cannot see. It means she does not look at who stands before her before deciding what is right. She still weighs and weighs with care. A judge must be impartial, but never indifferent," he said.He said the justice system must also consider how its procedures are experienced by people who come before the courts, particularly those who may already be vulnerable."For the survivor made to relive her trauma in the witness box or the litigant who cannot follow the language of the proceedings, the process is what justice actually feels like," he said. "We must ask whether, for too many, it has itself become a trauma," he said.Referring specifically to cases involving survivors of sexual violence and child witnesses, Justice Nath said courts could adopt a trauma-informed approach without compromising judicial standards.
"a trauma-informed courtroom is not a softer courtroom," he said.He also warned against allowing public sentiment to influence judicial fairness, particularly at a time when cases can be tried in the media before courts have reached a conclusion."A compassionate court is not a court with a favourite side. It is a court that can understand every side, without becoming captive to any. In an age of trial by television, when the public often decides before we do, that takes the courage to be fair to the person everyone has condemned and the courage to be firm with the person everyone has forgiven," he said.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

Details: Trump also blamed the Democratic Party for US oil refineries closing in blue states. These states are called "blue" because their voters consistently support the Democratic Party in elections.
Background:
- In late September, Trump said he had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to slow down strikes on Russian oil refineries and that Zelenskyy had supposedly agreed.
- On 22 September, Zelenskyy said there were no attempts during closed-door talks with Trump to force Kyiv to unilaterally stop attacks on oil refineries and other facilities of this kind.
- On 13 September, Trump called on Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian diesel fuel facilities, claiming that the attacks were causing shortages.

Vance says US bombers moved from Britain out of ‘abundance of caution’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:38:11 UTC
02:38:11 KST

Trump says US moved bombers from British base after ‘threats’
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said on Oct 5 that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from a British airbase.
The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran.
Last week, five British men were arrested near the base – which Iran’s Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target – on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
“We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them,” Trump told reporters on Oct 5.
“So we had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we just move them, and that sort of alleviates that. And we actually know the people that made the threat.”
When asked if they were linked to Iran, Trump responded: “They would be linked to Iran.”
Earlier on Oct 5, Vice-President J.D. Vance said the US moved the bombers out of an abundance of caution.
“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States (and others), so we are being extremely cautious, and that’s all I’d say about that,” Vance told reporters.
However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of the bombers and the suspected Iranian plot. He said the Pentagon is “constantly reallocating resources where they need to be.”
A NATO military source had said on Oct 5: “It is still believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK.”
While much about the incident remains unexplained, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any plot was likely backed by Iran.
Iran has said accusations that it was involved in any plot are baseless, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X: “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree.”
Key airbase for US strikes
Rubio said on Oct 4 the US had confidence in the security of all its bases.
Fairford, located 145km west of London, is one of the most important European bases for the US, being one of only a few suitable for heavy bombers such as the B-1 aircraft.
It has played a key role in previous US campaigns in the Middle East, although its bombers are not stationed there permanently.
During the current conflict, the US had permission to use Fairford only to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, or so-called defensive strikes.
London had refused permission for the US to use British bases for offensive strikes on Iran.
That approach has strained ties between the US and Britain, typically one of Washington’s closest allies.
A Pentagon official confirmed on Oct 4 that all US bombers that had been deployed to Fairford had headed to their home stations in the US.
The Pentagon said the US bomber force remained ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities “anywhere, anytime”.
The New York Times, citing two US officials, said the US had rushed over the weekend to move the bombers after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot. It said some of the planes had left while aerial refuelling aircraft were still being scrambled.
A US official declined to comment. The British government also declined to comment, although a spokesman for Burnham said the base was safe.
Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, said the redeployment would in the short term reduce US capacity “to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat”.
But he noted that use of Fairford was already limited given London’s stipulation on defensive strikes. The aircraft could now potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for more air-to-air refuelling to cover the additional distance, but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, he added.
Trump said plot was for ‘big damage’
In the early hours of Sept 27, five British men in their 20s were arrested after being seen running into fields from three white vans parked near the base. Police said no explosive devices were found but a quantity of petrol was present.
The men have since been released on bail. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts four days later, has also been released on bail.
Trump said at the time of the first arrests that the plot had planned “big damage” and that it might have been connected to Iran. Trump later said he would not have released the suspects on bail.
A senior NATO military official said the removal of the bombers would have no impact on the alliance. The official said: “NATO’s defensive agility towards any aggression remains unchanged and unmatched thanks to the unity, strength, and combined capabilities of 32 nations.”
The Wall Street Journal first reported the removal of the US bombers. REUTERS
