Kuai Kuai workers set to vote on ending strike today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:11 UTC
01:37:11 KST

The Kuai Kuai union’s strike would likely end today after Kuai Kuai Co agreed to union demands, said the Taoyuan City Government’s Department of Labor yesterday.
Department commissioner Lee Hsien-hsiang (李賢祥) made the remark after holding a negotiations yesterday afternoon between the union and the company, during which he said company chairman Chung Yu-lin (鍾育霖) agreed to the union’s demands.
Under the proposed terms, employees who resign following a job transfer would receive four months’ additional pay on top of the statutory severance package, while those who choose not to relocate with the company two years after the plant move would receive eight months’ additional compensation in addition to statutory severance pay.
Photo courtesy of the Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions via CNA
Union Chairman Liu Neng-hung (劉能宏) said the union would hold a provisional meeting today to vote on the proposal and would call off the strike if it is approved.
Earlier yesterday, the union, whose members work at the company’s Jhongli factory, voiced their concerns during a protest outside the Ministry of Labor in Taipei, four days after workers began a strike that was later extended indefinitely.
The dispute arose after Kuai Kuai workers learned in July through the news that Kuai Kuai, which has been owned by the San-Ti Group since 2019, sold the Jhongli site to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering for NT$5.67 billion (US$178.37 million).
As part of the deal, Kuai Kuai would lease back parts of the site for up to two years while preparing to relocate.
The deal sparked concern among workers that the company would abandon them and force them into resigning by relocating without paying them severance and other layoff benefits.
In response to the strike on Friday, Kuai Kuai said it would not lay off workers for the two years it remains at the Jhongli site, and would provide statutory severance plus two months’ wages for ensuing layoffs.
Peng Kuei-mei (彭桂梅), a union board member, said the no-layoff pledge “provides employees with no protection at all,” saying that the company could still meet that pledge if workers left on their own, in which case they would not receive severance.
Employees who left after the relocation because the new factory was too far away or had unsuitable working conditions could be denied severance because they were not formally laid off, she said.
To deal with the issue, the union is seeking compensation for any relocation, which could impose a heavier burden on the factory’s many middle-aged and older workers, who might struggle to find new jobs or adapt to a new work location, it said.
Peng questioned the company’s uncertain relocation plans, with Pingtung County and then Hsinchu and Taoyuan being considered but no site being secured.
“How can employees be expected to keep working for two years and believe they will still have jobs afterward?” Peng said.
The union said that a labor broker had twice brought migrant workers to the picket line on Friday last week and asked them whether they wanted to enter the factory to work, in what the union said was an attempt to get them to cross the picket line.
The union questioned whether an employer or broker should be allowed to require migrant workers to make such declarations.
In response to the protest, Chin Shih-ping (金士平), a section chief at the labor ministry’s Department of Employment Relations, reiterated that companies must not subject workers participating in union activities or strikes to “adverse treatment.”
Asked specifically about the broker’s actions, Chin described the circumstances as “complicated” and would require further review before the ministry could take a position.
According to the union, the plant has about 160 Taiwanese employees, including 155 union members, and about 60 migrant workers, mainly from Vietnam and Indonesia, none of whom are union members.

TV host Kevin Tsai faces backlash over Shen event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:09 UTC
01:37:09 KST

Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) has faced a backlash in China after he on Sunday attended the opening of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign headquarters.
Shen has been called a “staunch Taiwanese independence separatist” by the Chinese Communist Party, which has threatened to hold him accountable under its anti-secessionist laws.
A livestream showed Tsai, who previously hosted the popular variety show Kangsi Coming (康熙來了), holding a campaign balloon bearing the slogan “Let Taipei Get Back on Track” and waving a cheering stick alongside supporters, drawing widespread attention online.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Asked about his attendance, Tsai reportedly said he had come to “see what it was like” and hear different perspectives, adding that he might attend events for other candidates and would like to interview them all.
His manager said Tsai’s attendance was preliminary research for possible interviews with both candidates.
Tsai’s appearance at Shen’s event became a trending topic on Chinese social media, with posts labeling Tsai a “separatist.”
Chinese electric vehicle maker Leapmotor, which last month announced Tsai as a brand “partner,” removed promotional content related to the entertainer by Sunday evening and issued a statement reaffirming its commitment to Beijing’s “one China” principle, while fashion magazine Harper’s Bazaar China deleted an interview with Tsai published last month.
Shen yesterday called the backlash unfair, saying that Tsai had simply come to the event to learn about the candidates’ policy platform.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is seeking re-election, urged China to respect Taiwan’s free and democratic way of life and not discriminate against people because of their political views.
“I support and respect Tsai’s right to express any views of his own,” Chiang told reporters.
KMT caucus secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said the caucus opposed efforts by Chinese Internet users and businesses to blacklist Tsai, adding that Beijing should respect freedom of speech and democracy.
Taiwan is a democratic and pluralistic society in which everyone has the right to learn about candidates’ policies and ideas, Hsu said.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), deputy executive director of Tunghai University’s Center for Mainland China and Regional Development Research, said the incident illustrated how Beijing uses its market power to influence the politics of Taiwanese entertainers.
As China has already branded Shen a “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatist,” publicly attending his campaign event could carry commercial consequences for entertainers in the Chinese market, Hung said.
Political labeling, online pressure and corporate action are used to enforce Beijing’s political red lines, he said.
Businesses know where the political lines are and take steps to protect their interests without direct government intervention, he added.
The incident sends a warning to entertainers, businesses and others who associate with the DPP or politicians whom the Beijing has threatened to sanction, Hung said.
China is seeking to establish boundaries for political engagement by making political associations carry a price, he said.
Once Chinese market pressure spills into Taiwan’s elections, it threatens the autonomy of the nation’s democracy, Hung said.
Beijing does not need to dictate how Taiwanese people vote if it can raise the cost of supporting certain parties and politicians, he added.
By making Taiwanese weigh the risk of losing jobs, endorsements and other commercial opportunities in China before participating in their own elections, Beijing is extending its political red lines into Taiwan’s democratic system, he said.
China can draw red lines in its own market, but it has no right to impose them on Taiwanese, Hung said.

Streamlining the carbon fee system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

In June of this year, the Ministry of Environment completed its first collection cycle under the carbon fee system, the first phase of which targets close to 500 of Taiwan’s largest emitters. The scheme is to be gradually expanded to encompass small and medium-sized manufacturers and commercial service providers that emit less carbon individually but exist in large numbers, with established carbon pricing mechanisms and the option of voluntary reduction plans that qualify companies for reduced rates.
This climate policy, which has significant implications for the green transformation of Taiwan’s industrial structure and its competitiveness in global supply chains, demonstrates the government’s commitment to implementing the Climate Change Response Act (氣候變遷因應法) and achieving its 2050 net zero emissions target. However, implementation faces a number of challenges, including carbon fee rate disputes, stringent approval requirements for voluntary emissions reduction plans, and a lack of carbon accounting capacity among small and medium-sized enterprises. Striking a balance between carbon pricing incentives, international competitiveness, and the burden of corporate transition has become a pressing public policy issue for central government agencies to confront.
Carbon pricing seeks to internalize the external costs of greenhouse gas emissions, directing investment and technological development toward low-carbon innovation. However, if it is designed primarily as a revenue-raising mechanism while neglecting financial support for companies’ efforts to develop and implement emissions reduction technologies, it risks triggering carbon leakage. This occurs when high carbon fee costs prompt the relocation of operations to other countries with weaker environmental regulations, dealing a blow to global emissions reduction efforts and the domestic economy. If the review process for voluntary emissions reduction plans lacks clarity and objective, quantifiable criteria, it risks leaving excessive room for administrative discretion and bias. This could create unfair competition between industries and infringe on businesses’ property rights and freedom of operation.
Strong governance in the transition to a carbon fee system requires a legal framework built on stable rules, transparent procedures and predictability. Drawing on the examples of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Singapore’s carbon tax system, earmarking carbon fee revenues for specific purposes and introducing phased tax incentives are essential to maintaining resilience throughout the industrial transition.
Central government authorities should establish a legal requirement that 100 percent of carbon fee revenues be allocated to a specific greenhouse gas reduction fund and be earmarked for subsidies that help businesses upgrade low-carbon equipment, develop green energy technologies and conduct carbon capture, utilization and storage trials. Clear funding mechanisms and due process in the provision of technical support are essential to alleviating businesses’ fears about their viability in the face of double taxation and rising transition costs.
To streamline Taiwan’s carbon pricing framework and help industries make a smooth transition, central government authorities should amend the Regulations Governing Self-determined Reduction Plans (自主減量計畫管理辦法) and establish clear statutory criteria for qualifying for preferential carbon fee rates. The ministry should revise regulations to grant substantial carbon fee deductions directly to companies that adopt renewable electricity and meet statutory benchmarks for improving energy efficiency. It should also establish a streamlined online review system to eliminate regulatory uncertainty in administrative procedures.
Most importantly, the government should establish a public-private partnership to help small and medium enterprises measure their carbon emissions and transition to lower-carbon operations. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Ministry of Digital Affairs could jointly assess those enterprises’ digital and green transition needs, develop free, decentralized carbon accounting tools that do not require expensive software, and bring in third-party verification bodies. This would help traditional industries with limited resources establish compliant carbon footprint data and safeguard their ability to compete fairly within supply chains.
The continued rollout of the carbon fee system is key to Taiwan’s transition to net zero emissions and its standing in international green supply chains. The climate crisis demands urgent action, and the path to industrial transition must be grounded in justice, reason and the rule of law. The Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Executive Yuan should respond directly to the concerns of industry and environmental groups and undertake sweeping reforms to climate regulations and industrial incentive programs across government agencies.
The carbon fee system must be an engine for industrial upgrading in Taiwan. It is critical for national competitiveness and environmental justice that this regulatory framework operates with professionalism, rigor and proper legal procedures — and that every review of fee rates and emissions reduction plans withstands practical scrutiny. Only then can Taiwan turn the climate crisis into an opportunity for transformation and secure a more stable and conducive environment for economic development in the global transition toward a sustainable future.
Roger Lo is a freelancer.

What happens when Chinese AI goes rogue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

Covering the recent round of artificial intelligence (AI) apocalypse warnings, I have tried to reject this cult-like deference toward all-powerful computer systems and the inevitability rhetoric: If Silicon Valley does not build them first, someone else — likely China — will.
Yet a recent spate of incidents in the US has spurred a fresh, heated debate on the safety of allowing AI systems to act on their own. A growing number of researchers inside the companies involved are also warning of “existential” dangers, with Anthropic PBC even flagging such concerns to investors in its initial public offering prospectus.
For China, the risks of near-term hazards like labor market threats or the more alarming science-fiction scenarios such as hacks on critical infrastructure are making it harder to write off the furor as a distinctly US obsession.
Beijing has dismissed some of these warnings as “fearmongering,” seeing the calls to slow AI development as an attempt to hold China back. However, voices inside the industry have also suggested that frontier risks simply are not being felt as acutely at home because they are further behind the US.
Huawei Technologies Co’s rotating chairman Eric Xu (徐直軍) wondered whether Chinese AI was advanced enough to encounter the “type of risk” US providers were increasingly debating. AI model makers in China “may need to speed up their pace” to reach the level that they could “also feel the risks,” Xu said, while acknowledging the need for balance, according to Reuters. It shows how global debate has devolved in unhelpful ways.
Accelerating the race is the wrong answer on both sides of the Pacific. There are nearly 1,000 large language models in China, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. Competition on this scale already makes even Silicon Valley’s breakneck pace seem muted.
The Chinese industry has also been plowing significantly more resources into agents, or systems that can act more autonomously. Agent misbehavior, especially the Hugging Face Inc incident in July, when one of OpenAI’s agents broke out of its evaluation environment and broke into Hugging Face’s systems, has kicked off this safety reckoning.
As the short-lived OpenClaw frenzy showed, even China’s nontechnical public is willing to experiment with them. It means if agentic AI is inherently more risky, it is likely only a matter of time before we see concerning behavior from Chinese AI tools.
Companies are aware. A DeepSeek paper that includes founder and chief executive officer Liang Wenfeng (梁文鋒) as a coauthor bluntly warns that agent behavior can be “untrustworthy.” Escaping containment is not a distinctly US risk, either. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 exploited a loophole in a sandbox during cybersecurity testing, US-based Frontier Security said. Some Chinese AI agents have also shown the kind of deceptive and concerning trends that have raised alarm about US tools.
While Beijing has pushed back on some of the “doomerism,” policymakers are paying attention. China last month released AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, a policy document that notably also dropped in English, clearly aimed for Western audiences. It explicitly warns that AI has demonstrated a “self-accelerating trend,” adding that the question of whether this could exceed human control demands attention and vigilance.
Another cornerstone of the latest safety contention is recursive self-improvement, or AI systems that can autonomously advance their own capabilities. It is the development path that spurred an Anthropic researcher to quit and warn that makers of the technology earnestly believe it could “kill us all” within a decade.
As Oxford China Policy Lab research associate Qian Zilan (錢子蘭) has said, China is further along in this regard than many in the West might realize, partly because its researchers describe it in different terms. It all reveals how little visibility each side has into the risks of what the other is building.
In discussing the technology’s risks, Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has warned — most recently in conversation with US President Donald Trump — that “AI must be kept under human control.”
Xi’s self-interest in maintaining order offers a narrowing window for cooperation on risk mitigation dialogue. It also exposes the limits of the safety protocols that did emerge from the Trump-Xi summit, namely a new “channel” for reporting AI-related incidents.
These hotlines have not always been effective. During the 2023 spy-balloon crisis, the Pentagon tried to reach its Chinese counterparts through a crisis line but Beijing declined the call. Such a setup is also inherently retroactive. Preventative risk sharing also does not have to depend solely on government-to-government talks, especially when regulators might struggle to keep pace with the technical knowledge.
It would be more productive to have outlets where companies and researchers can exchange information more directly.
China has burdensome regulations in place surrounding AI; using it as the boogeyman is no longer a convincing excuse for inaction from lawmakers in Washington.
If Chinese AI systems are just months behind, and the country’s all-out push for agents comes to fruition, it is likely a matter of time before more concerning scenarios emerge from the other side of the Pacific. Policymakers should act before the next incident is more than just a warning shot.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Nobel medicine prize goes to US, German scientists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:08 UTC
01:37:08 KST

The Nobel Prize in medicine was yesterday awarded to three scientists who created a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
The Nobel Assembly lauded their work and said the method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.
Photo: AFP
The assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Wurzburg, also in Germany.
Optogenetics opened what the Nobel assembly called a new era in neuroscience, the discovery of a light-controlled switch to turn on and off nerve cells and circuits in the brain to better learn how it works — to start unraveling the pathways that lead to behavior and disease.
It started when Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae can swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.
Photo: AP
Deisseroth then worked with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
“It’s a very precise set of tools for doing experiments about how the brain works that are pretty hard to do any other way,” the University of Pittsburgh’s Jeremy Berg said.
He was at the National Institutes of Health in the early 2000s when it awarded Deisseroff major funding for “this vision of optogenetics that was pretty much spot-on the way it played out.”
Deisseroth, a self-described night owl, said he was up late in his northern California home working on papers and e-mailing his students. He had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly.
“No real sleep was achieved,” he told The Associated Press in a phone call an hour after the announcement.
He said the next task on his to-do list was to pack school lunches for his children, who were still sound asleep.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about US$1.2 million).
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.

Japan is traditionally seen as a reliable host for major sporting events, but an Asian Games dogged by organizational woes has tarnished that image and raised questions over future bids, experts said.

Countries complained of being stranded for up to six hours at the airport on arrival.
Teams were not shy in criticizing the local organizers.
Korean Sport and Olympic Committee president Ryu Seung-min said: “If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F.”
Photo: SNTV via AP

Japan might struggle to escape the shadow of the Asian Games for some time to come, said Hirokazu Arai, a professor specializing in sports psychology.
“If Japan were to bid for the Olympics again, trust in Japan may have fallen, and it might be harder to win a bid,” he said. “And within Japan, people may take the view that if these kinds of things are going to happen, we don’t need the Olympics.”
Many in Japan have questioned the value of hosting major sporting events as they grapple with the fallout from the graft-stained and COVID-19 pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics.
Cost overruns, corruption and COVID-19 all tainted the public’s memory of the Olympic Games, which took place largely behind closed doors in 2021, a year later than planned.

The country subsequently dropped the idea of hosting the Winter Olympics in the northern city of Sapporo because of a lack of public support.

She said the Asian Games had “reaffirmed my belief in the value of hosting international sporting events in our country.”

Asian Games organizers were presented with a headache when the number of athletes and officials that was initially expected ballooned by about 2,000.
Unlike at past Games, there was no traditional athletes’ village, to save money.
Participants instead stayed on a cruise ship, in hotel rooms and in temporary wooden huts.
Some teams complained about the wooden units, saying they were too cramped and the beds were too short.
After a troubled build-up, organizers hoped the attention would switch to sport when the action got under way.
However, still the problems continued, with transport and accommodation difficulties and further mix-ups with anthems and flags.

There were sparse crowds at some events, starting with thousands of empty seats at the opening ceremony.
Organizers blamed the bad weather.
Arai said he believes the Games have damaged Japan’s international reputation as a safe pair of hands.
“The previous [Asian] Games were in China, and I’m sure there were athletes who came here expecting Japan to put on a better event than China,” he said. “But I don’t think you can say that’s how it’s turned out.”
Anger that had faded in the years since the Tokyo Olympics could flare up again, Arai said.
“The people at the top of Japan’s sporting world are moving towards trying to bring the Olympics here again,” he said. “From their perspective, they may have felt that criticism had started to die down, but this situation could cause that criticism to intensify again.”

Will the NHI’s new budget help the staff?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:07 UTC
01:37:07 KST

On Sept. 23, negotiations over next year’s National Health Insurance (NHI) global budget reached a conclusion. The NHI Committee set the growth rate for overall expenditure — encompassing hospitals, primary care clinics, dental services and traditional Chinese medicine — at 5.5 percent for next year. This pushes the total budget just above NT$1 trillion (US$31.46 billion) for the first time. It is the second consecutive year that an agreement has been reached to increase the budget, reflecting a consensus among medical professionals and payers on the need for greater investment in healthcare. The question is whether this additional funding can improve working conditions and help retain staff.
The negotiations included almost NT$5.8 billion in additional funding to improve nurses’ pay, which would be included in next year’s budget. How effectively this is allocated remains to be seen. The overall budget increase accounts for the demands of an aging population and rising medical costs. It cannot be treated as a surplus that hospitals and clinics are free to spend as they see fit. The scale of investment and how the money is used are two separate questions, and they are equally important.
Increased government reimbursements under NHI do not directly translate to higher wages for medical staff; healthcare institutions must first decide how to internally distribute the funds. Payment structures certainly affect institutional income, but it is ultimately management that has control over salaries, hiring and staffing schedules. When discussing staff retention, it is critical to ask not just how much the government is investing, but how employers are using the resources they receive.
When healthcare institutions “raise wages,” are these increases to fixed salaries or available bonuses tied to additional conditions? The Ministry of Health and Welfare has said that the average monthly salaries it publicly reports factor in non-regular payments. These averages alone cannot tell us how compensation has changed; if higher earnings are coming from working more night shifts and overtime, it cannot be claimed that working conditions have materially improved.
There are better ways to assess the effectiveness of retention efforts, such as measuring how much of the additional funding is being spent on personnel; how much fixed salaries have increased; and where the patient care workload per shift decreases after new staff are hired. Comparing salaries, actual working hours, vacancies and turnover rates is the only way to understand how much conditions for frontline workers have actually changed. It is worth examining whether or not improved pay for one professional group affects the salaries and workloads of others.
Clarifying how funds are distributed within institutions requires accounting for the different services provided and financial constraints faced by different facilities. Attributing all staffing shortages to the same cause should be avoided. However, responsible resource allocation can still exist under financial hardship; concrete measures for staff retention must be offered alongside explanations of cost pressures.
The NHI Committee’s consensus in negotiations completes just one stage of budget allocation. For frontline medical workers, the most pressing questions remain: Do salaries reflect the work they put in? Can they actually take time off? Can they see a stable future in the profession? It is the employers who control salaries and working arrangements that must provide answers to these questions.
Lu Chun-wei is a dermatologist and assistant professor at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital.

Tokyo 37-day rain ends
A sunny weekend in Tokyo marked the end of a record-breaking 37 straight days of rain, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said yesterday. Tokyo’s rainy season normally takes place in June, but the city endured regular heavy downpours throughout the summer, as well as heavy flooding across the wider Tokyo metro region. Friday’s showers capped the city’s longest stretch of rainy days since records began in 1886. “The longest streak of rainy days continued from Aug. 27 to Oct. 2, making 37 consecutive days of rain,” JMA official Eri Kawanami said. Since the beginning of last month, Tokyo had been soaked by 696.5mm of rain, more than three times the normal level, JMA said.

Trade deal talks with the US have reached a “plateau,” Minister of Finance Nirmala Sitharaman said yesterday, after negotiations dragged on for months with the two sides struggling to resolve sticking points. The nation’s foreign exchange reserves decreased by US$1.159 billion to US$600.745 billion last month from the previous month, the central bank said in a statement yesterday.
The decline in foreign exchange reserves was mainly due to the strengthening US dollar and the central bank’s intervention in the foreign exchange market by selling US dollars and buying New Taiwan dollars to cap the local currency’s depreciation, it said.
It aligned with the situation in Japan in August, when the nation’s foreign exchange reserves fell below the US$1 trillion mark, down US$94.6 billion month-on-month to US$995 billion, as Japanese authorities intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the yen, the central bank said.
Photo: Reuters
Last month, the US dollar index rose 2.03 percent, while other major non-greenback currencies except the yen declined, weighing on the central bank’s portfolio when the amount was converted into US dollars, an online report by the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the sister newspaper of the Taipei Times) yesterday quoted Department of Foreign Exchange Director-General Eugene Tsai (蔡炯民) as saying.
The euro lost 2.23 percent, the British pound declined 2.34 percent, the Canadian dollar weakened 2.17 percent and the Australian dollar was down 2.76 percent, while the yen advanced 1.87 percent and the yuan appreciated 0.25 percent, central bank data showed.
The NT dollar fell 0.69 percent against the US dollar last month, as foreign investors posted net outflows of about US$2.3 billion, Tsai said.
Looking ahead, foreign fund flows and local exporters’ US dollar holdings, as well as overseas investments by Taiwanese individuals and businesses, all have an impact on the movements of the NT dollar, he said, adding that the central bank would act according to market conditions to avoid excessive fluctuations in the NT dollar.
As for the yen exchange rate, whether the Bank of Japan would raise rates further and if the Japanese authorities would intervene in the market again are key factors to the currency’s future movements, he said.
It also depends on global capital flows and overseas asset allocation by Japanese investors, he added.
Meanwhile, the market value of securities investments and NT dollar-denominated deposits held by foreign institutional investors rose to US$1.927 trillion last month, equivalent to 321 percent of foreign exchange reserves, compared with US$1.861 trillion and a ratio of 309 percent the previous month, central bank data showed.

How an eviction sparked Spain’s housing protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

Tens of thousands of protesters in the past few days have taken to the streets of cities in Spain to demand help for renters, after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman put the government under immense pressure to tackle the nation’s entrenched housing crisis. Those demonstrations were amplified after lawmakers on Friday rejected Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s package of emergency measures to tackle the housing affordability crisis.
Sanchez yesterday announced early general elections to take place on Nov. 29, aiming to seize on his base’s anger over the rejected housing measures.
Large crowds marched in Madrid calling for a general strike and affordable housing. In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse protesters who broke through the security perimeter outside the City of Arts and Sciences, a futuristic complex by famed architect Santiago Calatrava, where a real-estate summit was being held.
Illustration: Yusha
Images showed altercations between police and protesters, with officers using batons to strike demonstrators, who threw barriers.
About 1,000 protesters have spent the past week camped out in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol, one of the capital’s most popular public spaces, after Maria del Carmen Abascal was evicted from her home of seven decades in downtown Madrid on Sept. 23.
The protesters say they will not leave until the government takes real steps to protect tenants. A similar encampment has cropped up in Barcelona’s Plaza Catalunya.
The Sanchez-led government responded with emergency measures aimed at restricting evictions, curbing property speculation and giving renters indefinite leases, among other measures, but conservative opposition parties joined forces to reject the ratification of the measures in parliament.
The housing crunch has been simmering for years in Spain, eating into household budgets and angering voters. While many countries have similar circumstances, Spain’s poorest and its young are being particularly impacted, because they cannot afford to purchase a home and are being squeezed by the country’s small stock of rental properties.
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The price per square meter has risen from 8.20 euros (US$9.19 at the current exchange rate) in 2016 to 15.10 euros this year, according to the real-estate Web site Idealista.
The government said that 26 percent of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40 percent of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the EU average of 18 percent.
Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development for government-owned rental properties, which represent less than 2 percent of its available stock. The EU average is 8 percent.
Tens of thousands of people periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers and blaming real estate speculators as well as tourist apartment platforms like Airbnb for rising rents.
However, a new wave of indignation swept Spain when Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her apartment after police cordoned off the street. Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.
“I haven’t managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what’s theirs,” Abascal said in a video recorded from a hospital bed after the eviction.
The Spanish real-estate company that had insisted on evicting her to rent the property at a much higher price ended up reaching an agreement for her to return to the apartment, her lawyer said, adding that Abascal was “happy.”
She has yet to be discharged from the hospital.
Even with a satisfying resolution for “Maricarmen,” as Abascal is now widely known, she remains the embodiment of the struggle against suffocating rental costs.
Protesters have carried signs with slogans such as “Not even one more Maricarmen,” and demonstrations have been cropping up in cities across the country.

The Flydubai copilot who stabbed his captain in a suspected attempt to crash the plane has told United Arab Emirates (UAE) interrogators he planned the attack before he was hired by the Dubai state-owned airline, two Israeli officials with knowledge of the probe said.
A third source briefed on the UAE probe said the copilot, an Omani national, had planned to crash last Wednesday’s flight into Ben-Gurion airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but opted not to, the source added.
It was not immediately clear why the copilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although the copilot is thought to have known someone onboard, the source said.
Photo: EPA
All of the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did Flydubai.
The copilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073, which had been bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the UAE prosecutor general has said, calling the incident a “terrorist attack.”
Two sources have said the copilot is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. Israeli officials have not named the copilot, but have said he is from Oman. UAE authorities and Flydubai have not publicly disclosed the copilot’s identity.
Reuters has not been able to independently reach al-Hammami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced any formal charges against him and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel.
Oman has not commented on the incident.
The two Israeli officials said the copilot told interrogators that he had applied for a job at Dubai state-owned Flydubai after searching for airlines that fly to Tel Aviv.
The third source said Israel was being continuously updated about the investigation from the UAE.
Disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted after passengers and crew subdued the copilot. The pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, survived the attack and has been hailed as a hero for managing to open the cockpit door. The plane was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israeli.
A reserve Flydubai pilot traveling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the copilot was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred to the UAE on Thursday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said pilots who are citizens of countries that Israel does not have diplomatic relations with, including Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to Israel.
It is not clear how the copilot came to be assigned to the Tel Aviv flight, and Netanyahu has since ordered a security review of foreign airlines flying to Israel.
New Zealand Assistant Police Commissioner Michael Johnson yesterday said that the copilot had spent time in the country and that police were looking into the period. He did not say when the copilot allegedly visited the country or name him.
A multi-agency Australian counterterrorism unit is also investigating links to Australia of the copilot, who was once enrolled at RMIT University in Melbourne, Victoria. A fourth source said the copilot had studied there about a decade ago.
Netanyahu has said the copilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly suicidal, although he has not said when or where that indoctrination allegedly occurred. The copilot completed three months of theoretical training at Royal Air Maroc last year, but his application to work there was later rejected, the Moroccan airline said.

‘Message in blood’: Vienna Jewish sites targeted in alleged Hamas terror plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:36:18 UTC
01:36:18 KST

The Jewish Museum Vienna and the Austrian-Israeli Society were among the possible targets of an alleged Hamas network that investigators say was preparing attacks in Europe around the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to a joint investigation by Germany’s Der Spiegel and Austria’s Der Standard.
The investigation, published this week, provides new details about an alleged plot that European authorities disrupted last year, including the possible involvement of senior Hamas official Basem Naim and communications with his son, Mohammed, whom investigators have identified as a central figure in the network. 
German federal prosecutors last month indicted seven suspected Hamas members, alleging they were involved in acquiring weapons and preparing an attack in Germany or Austria. Prosecutors say the network obtained 13 pistols, a fully automatic rifle and 718 rounds of ammunition as part of preparations for attacks against Israeli representatives, Jews or people considered supportive of Israel. Hamas has denied links to the suspects. tagesschau.de
Senior Hamas official’s son at center of investigation
According to Der Spiegel and Der Standard, Basem Naim, a member of Hamas’ political bureau and a former health minister in Gaza, allegedly discussed plans for attacks in Vienna or Germany with his son behind the scenes.
The two also communicated on Telegram about other matters, including ceasefire negotiations with Israel and U.S. policy, according to the investigation. The alleged conversations are notable because the elder Naim has publicly condemned attacks targeting Jews in Europe and the United States.
Investigators have pointed to another episode as evidence of the close relationship between father and son.
After an Israeli strike targeting Hamas leaders in Qatar in September 2025 put Basem Naim in danger, Mohammed made an unplanned trip to the Gulf state, according to the investigation. The trip came about a month after he had allegedly recorded a video in Vienna claiming responsibility in advance for the planned attack.
Der Standard said the trip indicated the close relationship between the two men, although investigators have not established publicly what they discussed during the meeting. 
Mohammed Naim had previously been linked to weapons recovered in Vienna. The latest investigation provides additional details about the video authorities say he recorded.
Late on Aug. 7, 2025, investigators say, Naim was filmed in a rented room in Vienna’s Favoriten district wearing a hat, covering his face and concealing his eyes behind sunglasses. Two pistols were placed on a table in front of him.
The recording lasted 4 minutes and 32 seconds.
In the video, according to the investigation, Naim spoke of taking revenge against Israel over what he called “genocide” in Gaza and warned that “blood will be spilled.” He also allegedly said the “armed resistance” would send Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “message in blood.”
Investigators later found traces linking Naim to weapons seized in Vienna, according to Der Standard. The two pistols displayed in the video are suspected of having been part of the same weapons shipment. 
Guns hidden in Vienna storage unit
The joint investigation also provides new details about how the weapons were stored.
Five HS-9 pistols were allegedly hidden for weeks in a self-storage facility in Vienna’s seventh district. The unit had been rented under a false name and was located within roughly 1.5 to 2 kilometers of several Jewish and Israeli institutions, according to Der Standard.
The storage facility was also near major public transportation routes, potentially allowing people to arrive and leave quickly without attracting attention.
The pistols were hidden inside a suitcase lined with a thick layer of aluminum foil. Investigators also found gun-cleaning oil and lubricant used to maintain firearms.
Investigators viewed those items as an indication that the cache was not merely an emergency weapons stockpile but contained firearms being maintained for possible use, according to the report. 
It remains unclear precisely what attack was planned for Oct. 7, 2025, who would have carried it out and which location would ultimately have been targeted. But the Jewish Museum Vienna and the Austrian-Israeli Society were among the sites investigators considered possible targets, Der Standard reported.
Mossad tip reportedly helped uncover network
The investigation also sheds new light on intelligence that helped German authorities identify the alleged network.
According to Der Spiegel and Der Standard, Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency provided Germany’s domestic intelligence service in June 2025 with information indicating that terrorism suspects were involved in weapons transactions in Germany.
German authorities subsequently placed members of the network under close surveillance as they traveled across Europe and acquired weapons and ammunition, the outlets reported.
The German government had previously declined to confirm or deny whether Mossad had provided such information, citing restrictions governing intelligence shared by foreign services.
13 pistols, an automatic rifle and seven defendants
The existence of the alleged network and preparations for an attack had previously been disclosed by German authorities.
Federal prosecutors say Hamas’ military wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, had been building weapons stockpiles in Europe before a concrete attack plan began taking shape by July 2025.
The attack was allegedly intended to take place around the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when Hamas-led terrorists killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel and abducted 251 others to Gaza, triggering the war in the enclave.
The potential targets included Israeli representatives, Jewish civilians and people or organizations identified as supportive of Israel, according to prosecutors. German media previously reported that Jewish institutions and pro-Israel demonstrations were also considered.
Prosecutors say the network ultimately acquired 13 pistols, a fully automatic rifle and 718 rounds of ammunition through two separate procurement operations.
In the first, five HS-9 pistols were transported by train from Copenhagen to Berlin in late July 2025. The weapons were then transferred through an intermediary to Mohammed Naim, who allegedly took them by train to Vienna and placed them in the storage unit.
Naim allegedly returned to Berlin in late August to obtain 100 rounds of ammunition for the pistols.
The second procurement effort also led to Denmark. A suspect identified as Borhan El-K., who investigators say had contacts in criminal circles, allegedly traveled to Germany in August 2025 to collect a fully automatic rifle, eight Glock pistols and more than 600 rounds of ammunition.
The weapons were moved through an intermediary to Berlin and were apparently intended to be hidden in Leipzig, according to the investigation.
German police intervened before that could happen.
On Oct. 1, 2025 — six days before the anniversary of the Hamas attack — authorities arrested three suspects during a weapons transfer and seized firearms and ammunition.
Additional arrests followed in Britain, Denmark, Cyprus and elsewhere in Europe. Nine suspects have been arrested in connection with the case, and seven have been indicted before a Berlin higher regional court. They hold German, Danish, Bulgarian and Lebanese citizenship. 
The defendants face allegations including membership in a foreign terrorist organization, preparation of a serious act of violence threatening state security and firearms offenses. Some are also accused of violating German laws governing weapons of war. The court must still decide whether to open a trial on the charges.
German intelligence source among defendants
One of the most unusual aspects of the case involves a defendant identified as Mohammed S., a Lebanon-born Berlin resident who was simultaneously working as a source for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, known by its German initials BfV.
He is accused of helping the network obtain ammunition without telling his intelligence handlers about his own involvement.
According to earlier German reporting, after members of the network lost part of their ammunition, Mohammed S. allegedly helped obtain 300 rounds for about 1,050 euros. He was arrested in January 2026.
The BfV has acknowledged that he was a source but said he was never instructed by the agency to participate in the alleged plot. The disclosure has prompted questions in Germany over how an intelligence source allegedly became involved in supplying ammunition to a suspected terrorist network. 
A network years in the making
European investigators believe the infrastructure uncovered in 2025 grew out of a broader Hamas effort that began years earlier.
Investigations have linked Hamas operatives to a weapons cache established in Bulgaria as early as 2019, with members of another network attempting to locate weapons depots in Europe in 2023.
Four members of that earlier network were convicted in Berlin this year and sentenced to prison.
The latest case represents a potentially significant development in European authorities’ assessment of Hamas activity on the continent. European security officials have historically viewed Europe primarily as a base for fundraising, political activity and logistical support rather than a theater for Hamas attacks.
Recent investigations have raised concerns that this may be changing.
A study by the Combating Terrorism Center at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point concluded that Hamas had spent years developing weapons caches in Europe and preparing capabilities that could potentially support attacks outside Israel and the Palestinian territories. 
In the network uncovered last year, German prosecutors allege those preparations had progressed considerably further: weapons were ready for use, firearms and ammunition were being moved across several European countries, possible targets were being considered and a video claiming responsibility had already been recorded.
For investigators, those elements are central to the case that the alleged network had moved beyond maintaining weapons for possible future use and was preparing for a specific attack.

Muslim outreach or message to Akhilesh? How Imran Masood's 'elevation' will test Congress-SP alliance in UP

NEW DELHI: The new Congress team in Uttar Pradesh has a daunting challenge at hand: to revive the fortunes of the grand-old-party in the 2027 assembly elections. But before the big political test early next year, there is a pressing concern at hand: the alliance dynamics. And to that extent, the Congress appointments send a mixed signal to ally Samajwadi Party.The appointment of MLA Aradhana Misra-Mona, who is perceived close to SP chief Akhilesh Yadav, as the new state chief signals the willingness of the Congress for an amicable seat-sharing discussions. But the simultaneous elevation of Imran Masood, a known critic of Samjawadi Party’s “big brother attitude”, raises obvious questions about the Congress’s intent vis-a-vis its ally.So, how will this contradiction play out when the two parties sit on the table to decide the contours of their alliance? More so, as there is already an open war of words between the leaders of the two parties over the seat share. Congress leaders have insisted that division of seats should be based on “respect and equality.” Aradhana Misra-Mona acknowledges that with the 2027 state elections only a few months away, she would have to hit the ground running as her party seeks to regain political space it has steadily lost in the state since 1989.
Masood's strong remarks
To understand why Imran Masood’s high-profile appointment may have caused some unease, here’s a look at some of the statements he has made in the recent past.June In a video on X Imran Masood said that the Congress will no longer accept the formula that SP had applied in 2024 Lok Sabha polls and that the party was preparing to contest 2027 assembly polls on 200 seats in UP.July "Muslims' mosques are being demolished, madrassas are being razed, injustice is being meted out to Muslims, and atrocities are being committed against Dalits. They ought to speak up on these issues, too. But they (SP leaders) won't do that; instead, they target me. If you genuinely want to fight the BJP, then finalise the alliance... If you don't want to do anything on the ground, then it means you are not honest." "If you are shouting 'gathbandhan', then bring it to the ground. If you don't bring it to the ground and it only exists on TV and in statements, then what is the meaning of that alliance? That is not honesty. If you want to do it honestly, sit down and finalise it."September "If an alliance is to be formed, it should be finalised; otherwise, we must proceed with our own preparations. The political climate, not just here, but across the entire country, is such that one cannot move forward without the Congress; the Congress is essential. A fight against the BJP can only be waged with the Congress; only the Congress can take them on.""Don’t form an alliance. Who is asking for it? Are we begging anyone? Let everyone do what they want. When a wedding procession sets out, there are many drummers, as well as people who dance and sing. Let these people dance and sing. We are focussed on our work.”
SP pushback
Clearly, very strong statements which have led to equally strong reactions from the Samajwadi Party. Akhilesh has led the pushback for the Samajwadi Party, making it clear that winnability will be the only criteria for division of seats.When asked about Masood’s remarks, Akhilesh once said: “I have nothing to do with the statement given by anyone. Our INDIA alliance is intact. If they fight together, they will benefit."Masood and SP leaders have also engaged in open war of words over who, Rahul or Akhilesh, was more capable of leading the fight against the BJP.While a lot of these remarks are posturing for dominance in seat-sharing talks, the fact is that the open fighting between the two allies has the potential to confuse their cadres. The Congress move to give prominence to Masood could be part of its strategy to keep the pressure going on the Samajwadi Party.
'Right message to Muslims in UP'
However, former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha feels Congress and Samajwadi Party are not in competition. He asserts that Masood’s appointment has a much bigger and important messaging for the minorities, something the Congress should have done long ago.“UP has seen a lot of polarisation under the BJP regime. Muslims form 18% of the state’s population. I think Masood’s appointment is a manifestation of Congress actually beginning to do what it should have done a long time ago, to be bold, to embrace the fact that the minorities are vulnerable under the BJP, that the Muslims need representation, and to stand for them by having a representative who is going to be a working president. The message is very clear that we are not scared, we are not fearful of the majority community treating the Congress or the Samajwadi party, as the BJP likes to call it, as the "Miya" party,” says Sanjay Jha.“I think the more the opposition becomes fearless and embraces secularism and stands up for Muslims who have been targeted in a blatant fashion, is good for politics. So I endorse the political standpoint of the Congress,” Sanjay Jha adds.Masood is a first-time MP and a prominent face in western Uttar Pradesh politics. Ahead of the 2022 UP assembly polls, Masood left the Congress and to join the SP. However, left the SP in October that year and joined the BSP, where Mayawati immediately appointed him coordinator for western UP. In August 2023, however, Mayawati expelled Masood from the party, accusing him of indiscipline and “anti-party activities”. He returned to the Congress later that year.
Don’t make public statements
Amid the tussle over seats, Samajwadi Party (SP) MP Dharmendra Yadav has urged Congress leaders to refrain from making public statements on seat-sharing for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls and instead raise the issue directly with SP president Akhilesh Yadav.His remarks came a day after Congress' Uttar Pradesh in-charge, Rajendra Pal Gautam, once again called for "equal share and equal respect" for the grand old party in the state.Dharmendra Yadav, Akhilesh Yadav's cousin, described the former chief minister as a "very large-hearted leader." 2024 template
The Congress-Samajwadi Party (SP) alliance won 43 seats in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 general election, limiting the BJP to 33 in the most populous state. The SP won 37 seats, including the Faizabad Lok Sabha seat that includes Ayodhya, while Congress won six, including Saharanpur, from where Imran Masood was elected.
While the Samajwadi Party wants this record to be the guiding principle for alliance talks and winnability to be the sole criterion, the Congress wants a greater share as it feels the SP’s improved performance was due to gains from the alliance. To prove their point, Congress leaders cite SP’s performance in 2014 and 2019 elections, when it could win only 5 seats each.Clearly, both the allies know that they need each other to take on the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. Little wonder then, Rahul and Akhilesh have managed to keep the bonhomie going despite the confrontation between the state leaders. It will be interesting to see how much of a role will Congress give its new working president Imran Masood in the seat-sharing talks.

Brazil votes: CIA cultivated evangelical churches ‘for decades’ – Pepe Escobar
The US has sought to influence Brazilian politics for decades, including through the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), and has played a role in the country’s current presidential election, independent journalist and geopolitical analyst Pepe Escobar has told RT.

Jewish candidate leads UN race, but path to victory unclear
Rebeca Grynspan has won three of four straw polls and now holds a commanding lead over rivals, but the UN's record of friction with Jewish and Israeli interests makes her path far from guaranteed
Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan, an economist, United Nations executive and daughter of Holocaust survivors, is in the driver’s seat.
The road she’s driving on still isn’t the straightest, but she has the clearest path of anyone to becoming the next UN secretary-general.
The race to fill the post of term-expired Antonio Guterres has been unorthodox. Both Guterres and his predecessor, Ban Ki-moon, were clear frontrunners almost instantly.
This time around, through four straw polls, no one has been able to firmly separate themselves from the pack.
But the numbers still tell a tale. Grynspan has won three of the four secret-ballot straw polls conducted by the UN Security Council, placing second in one.
The most recent straw poll was held shortly after the UN General Assembly’s high-level debate week, which gave candidates a chance to lobby with world leaders, and Grynspan only improved her standing, coming away with 10 “encourage,” three “discourage,” and two “no opinion” votes among the 15 council members.
While it isn’t clear whether any of those three “discourage” votes were placed by the five veto-wielding permanent members of the council, Grynspan’s two closest competitors, Guyana’s UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and International Atomic Energy Agency head Rafael Grossi of Argentina, tallied eight “encourage” votes, but racked up six and seven “discourage” votes, respectively, showing much wider discontent with their candidacies.
Everyone else still left in the race is deep underwater.
So, where does that leave us?
Firstly, it’s important to note that the race is not closed. New candidates could elect to join and inject some fresh ideas. But that window seems to have closed with the passing of the high-level week, and entrants thus far who weren’t there from the beginning of the campaign have fared respectably at best, disastrously at worst. No one, though, has shined.
Beyond that, “discourage” votes, even if held by a veto-holding council member, don’t signal a candidate’s death. They’ve been known on more than one occasion to be used as leverage, in exchange for promises of patronage or other perks for those countries, or for the candidates dropping out to clear a path for the frontrunner.
It’s difficult to see at this point any competitor able to close the necessary ground on Grynspan, and even harder to imagine someone from the outside swooping in to capture the council’s imagination at this late stage.
But then again, it’s hard to fathom the United Nations, antisemitic in so many different areas, elevating a Jew to its highest post.
That’s what the numbers say, though.

Russia plays down reported plague lab death and says, trust us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:32:26 UTC
01:32:26 KST

Russia plays down plague fears and denies lab accident, says scientist died of "pneumonia of unknown origin"
Russia's government played down concerns Monday sparked by media reports that a female scientist in Siberia might have died of exposure to the plague after a lab accident.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that the state health watchdog known as Rospotrebnadzor was the "lead agency with expertise in this area," and he urged Russians to "listen to official information" from its "highly qualified professionals."
The researcher who died has been identified by Russian reports as Darya Shipilova, 28, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute more than 2,500 miles east of Moscow.
Russian media initially reported that she broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and then died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said she died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.
The plague bacterium referred to by the reports is yersinia pestis, the same one that caused the Black Death that swept across Europe in the mid-1300s, killing an estimated 25 million to 50 million people. That pandemic, often referred to as the bubonic plague, was spread by fleas living on rodents and other animals in close proximity to — and in the same grim sanitary conditions as — people.
The pathogen, if untreated, can cause swelling, fever and death.
Shipilova, according to Russian media, died from the pneumonic plague, which is caused by the same bacteria but attacks the lungs and causes a fever and a cough that can turn bloody. Pneumonic plague can be transmitted from person to person, unlike bubonic plague, and can also be fatal.
The head of Russia's eastern Republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, initially said Shipilova died of the plague in a post on the state-backed messaging app MAX. He later edited the post to add the word "possibly," according to an independent regional Russian media outlet that operates in exile, Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal).
He was not the only Russian official to walk back their words on the story.
Local officials initially warned people not to visit the town of Shelekhov, where the scientist was hospitalized and later died, citing "unofficial information" about a human plague case.
The post was deleted less than two hours later, according to both Lyudi Baikala and Astra, another independent news website.
Since then, Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has said it carried out "anti-epidemic measures" that included testing nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova.
The agency said some people had tested positive for colds or COVID, but that no pathogens causing dangerous infections were found. It also said there had been no accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and it attributed the scientist's death to "pneumonia of unknown origin."
A WHO spokesperson said that based on the unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general public appears to be low.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the reports of a suspected plague case in Russia were not cause for alarm, but "for focus."
"We know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided," he said. "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread."
But Rubio said, given "very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia," he did not believe it was "cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus, and a cause to just keep an eye on it, and we're doing that."

US approves US$1 billion arms sale to UAE
WASHINGTON – The United States on Oct 5 announced the approval of a US$1 billion (S$1.3 billion) sale to the United Arab Emirates of up to 10,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance sections for rockets.
“The proposed sale will improve the United Arab Emirates’ capability to meet current and future threats by developing and maintaining a strong and ready self-defence capability and improving interoperability with US forces,” the US State Department said in a statement.
It “will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major defence partner”, the statement added.
The Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System converts unguided rockets into precision munitions that can be employed for purposes including shooting down drones, thereby avoiding the use of costly missiles to shoot down comparatively cheap aircraft.
The UAE and other US-allied Gulf countries have been hard hit by the Iran war, during which Tehran’s forces have repeatedly targeted them with both drones and missiles.
The State Department also announced on Oct 5 the approval of a US$400 million sale to Kuwait – another Gulf state – of “repair and return services” for Patriot missiles, which have played a key role in countering Iranian attacks in the region.
“Kuwait will use the enhanced capability to strengthen its homeland defence” and “will have no difficulty absorbing these article and services into its armed forces”, the department said in a statement. AFP

A Saudi-led coalition says it has reclaimed territory overrun by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:30:34 UTC
01:30:34 KST

A Saudi-led coalition says it has reclaimed territory overrun by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Yemen’s military spokesman said that more than 1,100 attacks had been launched against Houthi positions.
- The Houthis had captured territory overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital waterway for traffic passing through the Suez Canal.
- The Houthis denied Yemeni government claims that they had been driven out of towns near the strait.
BEIRUT — Yemen’s embattled government and a Saudi-led coalition have launched a major campaign aimed at dislodging Iran-backed Houthis who had recently seized vital parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The offensive, which had already reclaimed territory overlooking a key waterway, marks a sharp escalation in what thus far been an ancillary conflict in the wider U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
In a televised address on Sunday evening, Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced a military operation to “extend the authority of the state and its institutions over the entire national territory.”
The operation would continue, he said, “until the country is liberated from the control of terrorist militias.”
The campaign comes almost a month after a blitzkrieg offensive by the Houthis saw Saudi-backed government forces collapse in disarray and give up wide swaths of territory along the Red Sea coast, including the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important maritime chokepoint.
The Houthis also made important gains inland, all but besieging the strategic city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, in a move that augured more Houthi advances.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which links the Mediterranean Sea with the Indian Ocean, is a new tinderbox in the Iran war.
On Sunday, the group said it seized Turbah, a garrison town that lies on the sole supply route linking Taiz to Aden, a key port on the Arabian Sea.
On Monday, Yemen’s military spokesman Majed al-Nuzaily said that “Operation Yemen Dawn” had launched more than 1,100 attacks against Houthi positions. He added that pro-government factions succeeded in clawing back Mokha, the town of Bab el-Mandeb and a nearby airport from the Houthis — claims the group denied.
Video posted on social media by activists accompanying pro-government factions depicted what was said to be the aftermath of attacks on Houthi positions along the Red Sea coast.
“They ran away into the sea. We captured some of them, and the rest were killed,” said one fighter from the Giants Brigade, a pro-government group.
Meanwhile, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a military spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a post on X that 100 warplanes participated in a Monday raid that destroyed 324 “high-value targets.”
Later, he said the warplanes were providing “air protection” over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait as well as “round-the-clock air support for Yemeni armed forces on the ground.”
When it was first formed in 2015, the Saudi-led coalition consisted of nine nations, including the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Bahrain along with Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Sudan and Senegal.
The fighting represents the sharpest escalation since a 2022 ceasefire between the Houthis, Yemen’s government and Saudi Arabia broke down in July.
Officially known as Ansar Allah (“Supporters of God”), the Houthis occupy much of Yemen’s north — its most populated section — and have long clamored for greater control over the rest. Iran has incorporated the rebels as members of its anti-U.S. coalition, the so-called Axis of Resistance, and has provided weapons, training and other aid to the Houthis, which belong to a branch of Shiite Islam.
The Yemeni government is a fragile body that, despite being internationally recognized, has no real foothold in the country it ostensibly rules.
In the days after the ceasefire broke down, the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi shipping, and launched attacks crippling Saudi Arabia’s oil export infrastructure. That included the East-West Pipeline, the main conduit Saudi Arabia has used to circumvent Iranian and American closures of the Strait of Hormuz.
Then in early September, the Houthis scythed through the Red Sea port of Mokha, along with Dhubab, Bab el-Mandeb and Perim Island. The offensive essentially granted the group control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a move that rocked energy markets already made skittish by the U.S. and Israel’s war on Iran.
Vessels using the Suez Canal must pass through the strait to reach the Mediterranean Sea to the north or Arabian Sea to the south.
This week’s offensive is not the first time the Yemeni and Saudi governments have tried to roll back the Houthis.
After the Houthis took over the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and a coalition of Arab nations launched a bombing campaign in support of anti-Houthi forces. That campaign managed to expel the rebels from Aden, but the Houthis — tough mountain fighters who received Iranian training to field and eventually manufacture drones and missiles — proved a difficult adversary.
The war turned into a grinding conflict, killing hundreds of thousands of people and spurring successive health crises and famine. In 2022, after years of stalemate, the government and rebels signed on to a ceasefire.
With front lines frozen, infighting among pro-government factions — which had never been the happiest of allies — broke out into open war, causing a still-unresolved rift between Saudi Arabia and the Emirates.
Experts say those dynamics are likely to bedevil the government’s ambitious plans for a march on Sanaa.
“The government doesn’t have the capabilities, the materiel, nor the cohesion of the forces,” said Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemen advisor at the European Institute of Peace. He added that previous assaults — when the Saudi-led coalition was larger, there was less fragmentation in anti-Houthi forces and the Houthis were less capable — couldn’t achieve the war objectives the government has now placed.
“It would require a lot more investment, not only from Saudi Arabia, but also from the U.S,” he said.
In any case, Al-Omeisy said Saudi Arabia was not looking for a “zero-sum game” involving the Houthis’ defeat, but was likely more interested in rolling back some of the group’s recent gains.
“They want a better hand for when they sit down for negotiations — and inevitably there will be negotiations,” Al-Omeisy said.
Faced with escalating Houthi attacks and a reluctant U.S. administration unwilling to intervene, Saudi Arabia is actively seeking regional defense partnerships.
In recent weeks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia — reached out to President Trump for the U.S. military to attack the Houthis. But Trump demurred, appearing unwilling to provoke a new front in the war of Iran.
In remarks to the press on Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. intended “to live by” the defense and security agreement it has with Saudi Arabia, but would not go into details about any U.S. involvement in the current campaign.
He added that the U.S. was expecting the counteroffensive would happen.
“Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack and see the threat that that poses, and they have a right to defend themselves,” he said.
There have since been reports of some 200 U.S. military advisors stationed at planning centers in Saudi Arabia, along with U.S. tankers providing aerial refueling capabilities for Saudi warplanes. But it all falls short of the military involvement Bin Salman reportedly wants.
With the U.S. on the sidelines, Saudi Arabia has turned to other nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, with which it recently signed a tripartite, NATO-style mutual defense agreement.
On Monday, Turkish officials and Pakistan’s foreign and defense ministers and army chief met with their counterparts in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, to discuss how to “institutionalize” the pact, according to official statements.
But observers expect the participation would be limited to protecting Saudi Arabia’s borders from ground assault by the Houthis or providing air-defense equipment against ballistic missiles and drones.

Exactly two years ago today, I decided to start this challenge. I never thought it would interest so many people, never thought it would last this long, and never thought I would become a "social media personality" or a "content creator"

Merz goes to Kiev to 'escape' low ratings in Germany — Berliner Zeitung
Unknown

01:29:11 KST

BERLIN, October 5. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Ukraine last weekend to escape low ratings in Germany and defeats in regional elections, Harald Neuber, head of the news and international departments at Berliner Zeitung, said.
Merz visited Ukraine for the first time this year last weekend. As Neuber points out, the visit came amid a decline in approval of the chancellor’s performance to a record low - only 10% of the country’s residents rate his performance positively, while 88% view it negatively. In contrast, he is popular in Ukraine - in August, 64% of respondents in one poll said they viewed the chancellor positively.
"A German chancellor who is six times more popular in Kiev than in Berlin is a sociological curiosity and a political diagnosis. Anyone who is popular in Kiev but punished in Magdeburg [the poor showing by Merz’s party in the elections in Saxony-Anhalt - TASS] should ask whether the trip to a war zone was a duty or an escape. The answer is unpleasant: both," Neuber wrote.
He noted that in Kiev, Merz promised new military assistance and called for continued support for the country. And although polls show that slightly more than half of Germany’s residents share the chancellor’s view on policy toward Russia, this does not automatically mean they are ready to send more weapons to Kiev. "Quite the opposite. Poll data show the opposite trend," the journalist wrote. He recalled that a recent Infratest poll showed that 42% of Germans - the highest level since February 2022 - believe the current volume of military assistance to Ukraine is excessive.
Polls also show that Germans do not consider it necessary to resume gas supplies from Russia, in line with Merz’s position, Neuber wrote. "The question is how long a chancellor with a 10% approval rating can credibly speak on behalf of the majority [of the country’s residents]. Will Merz’s rule come to an end together with Ukraine, or will the federal government’s Ukraine policy [come to an end] together with Merz?" the author asks. In his view, Germans are not opposed to helping Ukraine as such, but are against "help without an end goal."

Senior British officials have made it clear to Israel that if the British Consulate in East Jerusalem is closed and British diplomats are expelled, the UK will respond by expelling 27 Israeli diplomats, along with their families, two sources familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
The consulate is expected to close on October 8, following an order issued by Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar.
The move reportedly follows Britain's economic sanctions on the West Bank.
There is no reason for us to address speculation regarding decisions other countries might make in the future, diplomatic sources told the Post.
"We have already demonstrated that any move against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and this will continue to be the case in the future," the sources added.
In addition, Britain's top national security official quietly visited Israel last week in a bid to prevent the closure of the consulate, three sources told Reuters.
UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, whose visit Britain's government has not disclosed, held talks with Israeli officials but failed to reach an agreement to keep the consulate open, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
UK claims Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution
In announcing the sanctions, Britain said that Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution, the idea of a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel. Israel has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood.
Britain cited Israeli government-backed plans to expand settlements and rising extremist settler attacks targeting Palestinians in the West Bank. The British sanctions are to take effect next year.
The British consulate, located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood, handles the country's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
Sa'ar has said that Britain's decision to impose sanctions was "morally distorted," accusing Britain's ruling Labour Party of being hostile towards the country, and of interfering in Israel's upcoming general election on October 27.

Jewish contingent marches separately on 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street
