IAF soldiers reveal air force's initial response to flydubai attempted hijacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:36:54 UTC
00:36:54 KST

An Israel Air Force officer who first identified a distress signal from a flydubai aircraft last week said the situation initially appeared routine, but quickly escalated after a second signal indicated the plane may have been hijacked.
Lt. N., an air force aerial image identification officer, was on duty at 8:30 a.m. when he detected the first distress signal from the aircraft.
He told Walla that the initial alert did not immediately suggest a major emergency.
"It was an emergency signal transmitted by the aircraft. In retrospect, this was already after the drastic descent it had carried out," he said. "First, I was trying to understand why the aircraft was activating it, whether it was some kind of malfunction, perhaps a malfunction in our systems, or whether it was really a genuine signal, and I was trying to understand details about that flight. I wasn't alarmed at first, before I really understood what the incident was."
N. then checked the aircraft type and flight path and passed the information to other air force officials.
He said the situation still appeared consistent with a possible technical problem at that stage.
"When I understand that the aircraft is supposed to arrive in Israel, I alert the management position, and from there they really try to understand more details," said N. "From my perspective, it is a standard flight. There can be malfunctions during the procedures. It can be a procedure and a decision made inside the aircraft in order to make clear that there is something unusual here, but until that point, it was not something I had encountered before."
Second aircraft distress signal indicated possible hijacking
As air force personnel waited for the results of additional checks, a second distress signal arrived from the aircraft. This time, the code indicated a possible hijacking.
N. said the second signal immediately changed the assessment.
"Another emergency signal, but it became the signal for a hijacked aircraft," he emphasized. "I tell myself, this is already something unusual. There is no way this is a malfunction, because it is not a coincidence, and there is a high probability that this really is a hijacked aircraft. And from there, we basically set the incident in motion in the air force."
He said it was the first time he had encountered such a signal during a real incident.
"I'm not alarmed. A little stressed. It is the first time I have experienced a signal like this. I encountered something like this in the past, but it was due to a malfunction. Not a real incident. Since finishing the control course, it crosses your mind, but the chances are low," he continued. "This is not what an air traffic controller thinks about at night when he goes to sleep. Our world thinks more about UAVs and cruise missiles."
Once N. relayed the hijacked-aircraft code and issued the alert, the air force and senior command went on heightened alert.
He said there was no room to dismiss the possibility that the aircraft had been hijacked, particularly with Israelis potentially on board.
"I'm not prepared to take the risk that someone really may have hijacked the aircraft, and there may be Israeli passengers on board, and there is no way we let something like this pass without a response," N. said.
Maj. D., a reservist who serves as head of national airspace defense in the Air Control Array, said the aircraft was first detected between Saudi Arabia and Jordan and appeared to be headed for Tel Aviv.
According to D., the second signal prompted the air force to escalate its response within seconds and scramble fighter jets.
"We first detected the aircraft between Saudi Arabia and Jordan and saw that it was due to land in Tel Aviv," D. noted. "It looked strange. When we received the second signal about a hijacking, we decided within a few seconds to escalate the report and scramble fighter jets. We moved to prepare a response for every scenario, while at the same time we worked to obtain more intelligence and information about the incident.
"Throughout the incident, there was a great deal of uncertainty, D. continued. "It was not always clear to us whether the aircraft was in contact with another party, and during the incident a great deal of information flowed to us, some of it incorrect."
The uncertainty increased further when the aircraft began turning away from Israel.
D. said the team spent roughly half an hour running through possible scenarios as information continued to come in.
"As we are identifying what is happening, the aircraft begins turning around and moving away from the country, which added even more uncertainty for us," he added. "Amid that uncertainty, we sat as a team and spent about half an hour running what were essentially war games. What happens in this situation... One of the scenarios is that it really reaches our territory with the distress signal, under the assumption that it has been hijacked.
"During the incident, you try to disconnect from emotion as much as possible," he continued. "Only after I came out of the incident did I think about the fact that my brother is abroad, and I wondered whether he could have been on the flight. We prepare for the most severe scenario that could happen, and we have very clear procedures for it."
IAF tensions remained high amid Israeli media reports of pilot dispute
As the aircraft turned toward Saudi Arabia and Israeli media reports began circulating about a dispute between the pilots, tension remained high in the air force operations room.
N. said officials did not consider the incident over until they had confirmation that the aircraft had landed safely and that the Israeli passengers were no longer at risk.
"Until we receive information that the aircraft has actually landed safely and that the incident is really over, nothing is fine," N. noted. "We don't listen to rumors. We understand that the aircraft is landing in Saudi Arabia. I'm concerned. Why? A civilian aircraft landing with Israelis in a Muslim country, and not at a civilian airport. Until they announced that the rescue flight had departed, or that the Israeli civilian passengers had boarded the rescue flight, I couldn't be calm."
Capt. A., a reservist and air force air traffic manager, said his unit began clearing Israeli airspace once the incident was formally classified as unusual.
The aircraft was still far from Israel at the time, but the air force needed to prepare the airspace for fighter jets that had been scrambled.
"I go into action after the incident is defined as unusual," said A. "At this stage, the aircraft is still very far from the country, so we act to clear the airspace in a way that meets the needs of the fighter jets being scrambled. The skies are crowded with crop-dusting aircraft, sports aviation, commercial flights to Eilat or eastward, air force training, drones and helicopters, and the clearance we carried out was immediate.
"We call it moving to sterile airspace because it is possible that it will reach us later, and we need to plan ahead and check what other takeoffs and what other flights are planned in the airspace," A continued. "It is very possible that if this incident gets closer to the country, we will have to stop takeoffs completely. I have been an air traffic controller for more than a decade, and I have never had to close the skies because of a significant incident."
Asked about the possibility that the prime minister could soon be receiving updates from the IDF chief of staff and air force commander as officials prepared for the most extreme scenario, shooting down the aircraft, A. said his unit remained focused on its defined responsibility.
"At the end of the day, we come to do the job according to the procedures we know. We are in the air traffic section, and our role is clear and defined: clearing the airspace. All those other things, as they say, are not with us..." the captain concluded.

Talking points from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:36:45 UTC

Breadcrumb
Talking points from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
Tropical storms, software bugs and a bad tyre choice may have delayed them, but in the end the three generational talents of modern Formula One stood on the podium.
After a race weekend that placed a premium on experience, preparation and pure talent, AFP Sport looks at three things we learned from Sunday's delayed, rain-hit Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia:
Verstappen and Red Bull poised for run-in
Having committed himself to a fresh long-term deal with Red Bull, Verstappen has galvanised the team and, with the keen and able support of Isack Hadjar, led them back to the front of the field.
It was Verstappen's first win this year. It was also Red Bull's first with their own power unit, which they developed around a Ford engine. The victory confirmed they have recovered from the implosion that followed Christian Horner's exit and the loss of design genius Adrian Newey and others.
Verstappen also moved level with Michael Schumacher on 72 wins for the same team.
The German set his total with Ferrari between 1996 and 2006. They are behind only Lewis Hamilton, who won 84 for Mercedes between 2013 and 2024.
Verstappen's loyalty and leadership have helped forge a new spirit of unity under Laurent Mekies' soft power as team chief, setting an example in commitment and work ethic that makes Red Bull a threat to Mercedes.
Sepang shines despite storms and bugs
The unprecedented crowds, relishing a spectacular return event after a nine-year gap, were evidence of the success of Formula One's lateral thinking in taking the Bahrain Grand Prix to Malaysia after it was cancelled in April.
A thunderous downpour caused a 100-minute delay to the start, exacerbated by a software failure, in programmes controlled by the International Motoring Federation (FIA). That led to bizarre scenes on an aborted formation lap. What followed was a memorable race.
"It was insane," said Verstappen, who was one of many to lose power. "At some points, we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand it... I saw eight cars crawling, and Lewis stopped... It's not what you want for the sport."
Hamilton came to a complete halt and did a full restart before the FIA abandoned the lap and reloaded new software. The ruling body apologised for the chaos.
The energy management cutouts, in systems created as part of car controls for the new 'hybrid era', may have delivered frustration, but they also enticed teams to take risks.
Ferrari chose dry slick tyres, sending both Hamilton and Charles Leclerc down the order after starting in the wet.
Red Bull and Mercedes stayed on intermediates.
"When I saw they were on "inters", my heart sank," said Hamilton.
He produced a vintage recovery from 19th to third ahead of Leclerc and thrilled an enthusiastic crowd as Verstappen reprised his 2017 win.
"The software was tested," said the FIA's Nikolas Tombazis. "It just wasn't tested in those specific conditions."
Antonelli benefits from Russell's bad luck
George Russell's continued ill fortune enabled Antonelli to pull 84 points clear with seven races remaining, this time due to a power failure while running third in the closing laps.
It was a reminder of F1's adage that "to finish first, first you must finish" and painful for both Russell and Mercedes boss Toto Wolff.
Mercedes introduced an extensive upgrade package but ended the weekend well beaten by Verstappen and wondered whether the changes had worked.
Antonelli suggested the problem may be that their cars are sensitive to open, low-grip asphalt.
"I'm sure the team - with a lot of data, especially after this weekend - will come with a better view of the package for Singapore. Hopefully, we can extract full potential."
For the precocious 20-year-old, it could prove a key race in his charge for Italy's first drivers' title since 1953.
Russell admitted it was "exceptionally unlikely" that he could become champion.
But the Englishman won last year in Singapore, where Mercedes have taken five of the last 10 races, including three with Hamilton, and where Verstappen has never won.

00:36:37 KST

The Jerusalem Municipality on Sunday approved a protest tent at Shimon Agranat Square for the family of Haymanot Kasau, who was nine when she disappeared from Safed more than two and a half years ago and has not been seen since.
The agreement allows the tent to remain near the Supreme Court through October 22. It also rendered moot an administrative petition filed by the family and the Association for Civil Rights in Israel. The Jerusalem District Court, sitting as a court for administrative affairs, struck the petition from its docket at the petitioners’ request and canceled a hearing scheduled for Monday.
Haymanot’s father, Tesfaye Kasau, thanked those who helped the family obtain approval after what he said was a five-month effort.
“We would like to invite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief David Zini to the protest tent, in the hope that we will be able to dismantle it quickly because the Shin Bet will take responsibility for the case,” he said.
“Haymanot was kidnapped 953 days ago [on Monday], and it is clear to everyone that the investigation is not being handled properly,” he added. “All Benchi and I are asking is that everything be done to bring her home.”
Police continue to classify Haymanot as missing, while her family maintains that she was abducted.
The family’s original application sought permission to establish the camp from September 23 through October 22 at the intersection of Zusman and Kaplan streets, near the Prime Minister’s Office in Jerusalem’s government complex.
Family of Haymanot argues police investigation failed to produce answers
The purpose was to press the government to place the investigation under full Shin Bet responsibility and maintain public awareness of Haymanot’s disappearance. The family argues that the police-led investigation has failed to produce answers and that the security agency should use its broader intelligence capabilities to try to locate her.
The investigation was transferred to the police’s Lahav 433 National Crime Unit in December 2025. Despite extensive searches involving police, rescue units, canine teams, and volunteers, no confirmed trace of Haymanot has been found.
In its response to the family’s application, the Jerusalem Municipality said that tents erected for extended periods generally create sanitation, safety, and accessibility problems and interfere with public use of shared spaces.
The petitioners argued, however, that the municipality had not identified any specific hazard posed by their proposed camp and had instead relied on general concerns and municipal policy.
The formal application followed several attempts, beginning in July, to obtain permission for a camp near the Supreme Court, the Knesset, and the prime minister’s official residence. The petition said the family was turned away even when it proposed using existing protest sites or infrastructure.
Haymanot went missing on February 25, 2024, after she was last seen near the Jewish Agency absorption center in Safed where her family lived.
The family agreed to remove the protest tent after October 22 unless another decision is issued.
If responsibility for the investigation has not been transferred to the Shin Bet by then, the family plans to file a new petition with the assistance of the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, a protest organizer told The Jerusalem Post. A new filing would be required because the existing petition had been withdrawn.
In the meantime, the family is urging the public to visit the tent and attend a demonstration planned for October 12 in Jerusalem. It will also continue meeting with party leaders and hopes that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will agree to meet with the family, the organizer said.
“Thank you to everyone who supports and strengthens us,” Tesfaye said. “Please come to the protest tent.”

Who gets to choose Brazil's future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:36:35 UTC
00:36:35 KST

- Marcus Vinicius De Freitas is visiting professor at the China Foreign Affairs University and a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, based in Morocco.
Brazil's voters have issued warnings that neither Brasília nor foreign capitals can afford to ignore. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's first round lead over President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva reflects frustration with the cost of living, insecurity, debt, and institutions, particularly the Supreme Court. Foreign endorsements featured in the campaign, but the discontent was Brazilian. Defending sovereignty cannot excuse failing to govern.
Lula's most formidable opponent is his own record. His political camp has held the presidency for roughly 16 years since 2003, with a brief interruption. It cannot indefinitely present itself as the answer to problems that persisted under its watch. Earlier achievements remain relevant, but political memory does not pay today's supermarket bill. The difficulty is convincing voters that familiar leadership can produce a different future. Political exhaustion cannot be overcome by invoking past accomplishments alone.
 
Diplomacy or sponsorship?
Yet domestic disappointment does not entitle foreign governments to realign Brazil's loyalties. Benjamin Netanyahu's video endorsement, Javier Milei's appearance at Bolsonaro's campaign launch, and Donald Trump's reception of the candidate revealed explicit preferences. A presidential audience alone proves little; Trump also met Lula. Together, however, these gestures raise a question about where diplomacy ends and political sponsorship begins.
Economic pressure makes that boundary harder to defend. Washington offered trade and diplomatic justifications for tariffs and visa restrictions. Yet official terminology does not erase political consequences. Trump publicly linked earlier tariffs to the treatment of former President Jair Bolsonaro, while members of the Bolsonaro family claimed credit for mobilizing American pressure. A country subjected to economic punishment cannot expect those imposing it to be disinterested observers.
On Oct. 2, two days before the first round vote, the United States suspended in-person consular services, and Australia closed its embassy, citing security concerns. Brazilian police reported finding no concrete evidence of an attack plan. The episode fueled online speculation about a coup, although claims of an official coup warning were false. Whatever the intentions, such measures risk reinforcing a narrative of instability at a politically sensitive moment.
The larger issue is Washington's understanding of the hemisphere. Trump's revival of the Monroe Doctrine recalls a persistent historical confusion: the belief that excluding outside powers gives the United States authority over its neighbors. Latin American independence was not achieved to exchange European tutelage for an American entitlement to obedience. Geography creates shared interests and responsibilities; it does not establish a hierarchy of sovereignty.
Viewed through this lens, pressure on Brazil also advances Washington's ambition to reduce Chinese influence. Brazil's markets, infrastructure, and critical minerals, including rare earths, make its partnerships strategically significant. Lula has defended the country's right to maintain those partnerships without seeking permission. Whatever his administration's shortcomings, that principle serves the enduring national interest. Brazilian diplomacy must turn international competition into development opportunities while resisting demands for exclusive loyalty. Brazil needs access to competing sources of investment, technology, and markets, and the freedom to negotiate.
A change of government may legitimately alter diplomatic priorities. It should not mortgage the country's future to foreign leaders' preferences. Mineral wealth must underpin Brazil's development. Alignment that narrows commercial and diplomatic possibilities carries costs long after the applause at campaign rallies has faded.
 
Israel, the Arab world, and partisan diplomacy
Israel's involvement has a distinct political logic. Netanyahu's endorsement resonates with evangelical and conservative voters for whom Israel holds religious and civilizational significance. In February 2024, Israel's foreign minister declared Lula persona non grata after Lula compared Israel's actions in Gaza to the Holocaust. Bolsonaro's promised embassy relocation to Jerusalem would mark a diplomatic reversal.
Brazil's relationships across the Arab world matter both commercially and diplomatically. A country aspiring to speak across regional divisions weakens its credibility when partisan affinity becomes the organizing principle of its foreign policy. Friendship with Israel need not require abandoning independent judgement about its government's misconduct.
The BRICS group of countries, a quintessential platform for Brazil's global ambitions, poses another test. Bolsonaro's willingness to consider withdrawal warrants scrutiny, but Brazil's economic structure constrains ideological freedom. Fellow member China is deeply embedded in trade and production, and influential domestic constituencies favor preserving those ties. A political downgrading of involvement appears more plausible than withdrawal: less commitment to the grouping and less ambition to organize the Global South.
None of this relieves Lula of responsibility for the frustrations driving the vote. Nor does Bolsonaro's domestic support render foreign pressure politically innocent. A serious account must acknowledge both.
The coming Oct. 25 runoff will demand answers that neither foreign endorsements nor sovereignty speeches can provide. Lula must explain what another mandate would change. Bolsonaro, whose undistinguished political career has also been marred by controversy, must explain what closer alignment would cost. Brazil's partners must recognize that cooperation confers no right to dictate Brazil's political direction. The choice belongs to Brazilians, including their right to disappoint Washington, Tel Aviv, or any other capital. Whoever wins will receive a temporary mandate to govern a sovereign country, not a license to place its future in someone else's hands.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

"To be frank, I do not believe in any initiatives involving some kind of extension of Russian gas supplies to Europe or the restoration of any Nord Stream 2 pipeline routes," he said at a press conference. Gromov noted that despite the rationale behind the idea, Europe was unlikely to change its chosen political course.
"So, I don’t think we should harbor any illusions. Russian gas has left Europe, and I see no grounds for its return. Yes, Europe will pay for this, and it is already paying an increasingly high price," the expert added.

On September 26, 2022, a terrorist attack was carried out on the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, leaving only one of the system’s four pipelines intact - a string of Nord Stream 2. The 1,224-km Nord Stream gas pipeline runs along the bottom of the Baltic Sea from Vyborg in Russia to Greifswald in Germany and has a capacity of 55 bln cubic meters per year. Construction of Nord Stream 2, which has the same capacity, was completed on September 10, 2021, but the pipeline was never commissioned. The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office initiated a criminal case over an act of international terrorism.

First ton-scale drone lifeline: Ukraine flies 4 more tons of aid into a starving Russian-occupied town of Oleshky

Nearly 400 parcels containing food, medicine, and children's kits were delivered to occupied Oleshky on the night of 4 October, weighing almost 4 tons in total, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. All the parcels reached their destinations, he added.
The operation was the second ton-scale drone delivery into the blockaded occupied town in a week. Ukrainian drone deliveries to Oleshky have run regularly since March, and on 27 September Ukrainian forces flew about 4,000 kg of food to 100 locations across the town.
What happens to the parcels after they land
Delivery does not mean the aid stays with the people it was meant for. Kherson Oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin said Russian forces shoot down drones carrying food and take supplies from residents. He also said Russian forces detain and use violence against people who receive the aid.
Russia holds 2,000 people hostage in Oleshky without food or water—Ukraine flew 4,000 kg of food to locals across the Dnipro
Prokudin also said Russian forces take food intended for children and sell it, according to Radio Svoboda. Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said Russian troops question residents about where the food came from and treat receiving Ukrainian aid as cooperation with Ukraine.
Monitors describe a blockade, and the Kremlin blames Ukraine
About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, including nearly 50 children, Prokudin said. In June, Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said that food could not get into Oleshky and that sick and injured people were not receiving the medical assistance they needed. Residents had reported that no shipments had reached the town for nearly a month.
The Institute for the Study of War has described Russia's restrictions on the town as an effective blockade. The Kremlin acknowledged a "genuine humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky but blamed Ukraine for it: spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed to The New York Times that Ukraine was preventing residents from leaving and disrupting supplies of food and water with drones.
The drone crews behind the deliveries
Several Ukrainian units carried out the 4 October delivery. Vyhivskyi named the National Guard's 11th Mykhailo Hrushevskyi Brigade and 34th Kherson Regiment, the 30th Marine Corps, the 34th Separate Marine Brigade Borysfen, and the 79th Border Guard Detachment. The Perun drone crew also rescued six animals from the occupied territory, he said.
What has changed since 2023
Drone aid to Oleshky is not new. In 2023, Ukrainian drone operators dropped water and other supplies to civilians in Oleshky and nearby settlements. What distinguishes the current effort is its repeated, ton-scale deliveries into the occupied town.

Why are banana prices soaring in Algeria?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:33:59 UTC
00:33:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria's banana prices triple as government targets market manipulation
Banana prices in Algeria have soared to record levels, reaching as much as 1,500 dinars (around $11.20) per kilogramme in some shops, as authorities step up inspections amid wider concerns over rising food prices and market manipulation.
The price of the imported fruit has nearly tripled from around 500 dinars (around $4) per kilogramme, although significant disparities remain between retailers.
Some large supermarkets are selling bananas for around 420 dinars (around $3) per kilogramme, albeit reportedly of lower quality, raising questions over how prices are being set and the margins being taken across the distribution chain.
The surge comes amid growing pressure on fruit and vegetable prices in Algeria, prompting the Ministry of Internal Trade and Market Regulation to intensify inspections of wholesale and retail markets.
Officials are examining stocks, product availability and storage conditions, as well as whether retailers are properly displaying prices and complying with commercial regulations.
Banana prices are closely watched in Algeria because they are often considered an indicator of wider agricultural produce prices.
The gap between prices has also drawn scrutiny of the various stages products pass through before reaching consumers, including imports, transport, storage, wholesale and retail.
Transport and storage costs, spoilage and profit margins can all influence the final price, but the scale of the current disparity has fuelled questions over how prices are being determined.
Tebboune vows action against market manipulation
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has reiterated the government's commitment to protecting consumers' purchasing power, while largely absolving farmers of responsibility for recent price increases.
Speaking during his regular meeting with representatives of the national press, broadcast on Saturday evening, Tebboune said the government would investigate the factors behind market disruption.
"Most farmers are not responsible for the level prices have reached," Tebboune said. "But everyone who has caused this must bear their responsibility, and we must preserve citizens' purchasing power."
The president said protecting purchasing power remained central to maintaining Algeria's social model and stressed the need to tackle practices that place additional financial pressure on households.
Imports make banana prices difficult to predict
El Hadj Tahar Boulenouar, head of the Algerian Association of Traders and Craftsmen, told The New Arab that banana prices were particularly difficult to predict because the fruit is imported.
Unlike domestically produced fruit and vegetables, banana prices are directly linked to import volumes as well as storage and distribution conditions, making a steady supply to the market crucial to determining the final price paid by consumers.
Boulenouar said recent increases in fruit and vegetable prices more broadly were driven by several factors, including speculation, problems in storage and distribution networks and weather conditions that affected agricultural production.
An intense summer heatwave and fires in several provinces, particularly vegetable-producing areas, damaged crops, reducing supply and putting further pressure on prices, he said.
The government has also moved to cap potato prices after they exceeded 120 dinars ($0.90) per kilogramme in some areas.
Under the measure, prices were set at between 60 and 70 dinars ($0.45-$0.52) at the farm level and between 80 and 90 dinars ($0.60-$0.67) for retailers.
Boulenouar said the measure was intended to curb the recent surge and return potato prices to more stable levels, helping protect consumers' purchasing power.
He said the intervention was likely to be temporary, with new supplies of potatoes and other vegetables from winter harvests expected to enter the market in the coming weeks, particularly from Mostaganem, Ain Defla and El Oued.
The additional supplies expected from late October into early November could lead to a noticeable fall in fruit and vegetable prices, particularly potatoes, he added.

National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, whose visit has not been disclosed by Britain’s government, held talks with Israeli officials but failed to reach an agreement to keep the consulate open, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Israel on Sept 8 ordered Britain to close the East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city, after Britain said it would ban goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
France and Canada joined in the sanctions. Israel has not taken action against them.
Israel-UK relations increasingly strained
The incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. Israel disputes this.
The 30-day deadline for Britain to close the consulate runs out on Oct 8. Two of the sources said talks were still ongoing, and while an agreement to keep it open was possible, it is unlikely one would be struck by the Oct 8 deadline.
Asked about Powell’s visit and talks with London over the consulate, a spokesperson for Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar told Reuters that it would close on Thursday, as announced.
A UK government spokesperson had no immediate comment.
In announcing the sanctions, Britain said that Israel’s actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution — the idea of a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government openly rejects the idea of Palestinian statehood.
Britain cited Israeli government-backed plans to expand settlements and rising settler attacks targeting Palestinians in the West Bank. The British sanctions are to take effect in 2027.
The British consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem, handles the country’s relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
Israel’s foreign minister has said that Britain’s decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted”, accusing Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country, and of interfering in Israel’s upcoming general election on Oct 27.
The British sanctions announcement, and Israel’s response, marked a new low in the relationship between the once steadfast allies. Britain has repeatedly criticised Israel over its actions in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians. REUTERS

US meeting in Poland excluding France, UK Baltic risks dividing NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:33:45 UTC
00:33:45 KST

US Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby is hosting representatives from five key NATO members in Poland to discuss defence capabilities and the future of the alliance. Critics warn the exclusion of some Allies risks creating a “toxic” divide.
Talks between US Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby and five European countries have raised concerns among NATO experts who warn the format risks dividing the alliance as Washington presses Europe to take greater responsibility for its own defence.
Known as the Bergen Group after its inaugural meeting in Norway last year, the format brings together Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands.
The UK, France and the Baltic states were not invited.
"The bottom line is this is very toxic for an alliance that relies of collective play," said Fabrice Pothier, CEO of geopolitical consultancy, Rasmussen Global.
"Clearly this is about the US having favourites," he told Euronews.
The group was established to discuss NATO’s future as the alliance shifts towards so-called NATO 3.0: a US invented model in which Europe takes the lead the conventional defence of the continent.
It also involves the US scaling back its traditional role, and withdrawing key capabilities including bombers, submarines and personnel it makes available to the alliance.
Meanwhile, NATO is playing down the significance of the separate, US-led subgroup.
“It’s not unusual for groups of Allies to meet in smaller formats,” a NATO official told Euronews.
NATO 3.0 involves the US withdrawing from its traditional role as the leading defence provider in Europe, pulling capabilities such as bombers, submarines and personnel available to the alliance.
While officials dismiss the talks as routine, others argue the arrangement will split members into "good European versus bad European" categories while reinforcing Washington's influence across the alliance.
Pothier acknowledged that smaller groups can advance new ideas within organisations, such as the publication of 'non-papers', but he argued that Washington had selected the Bergen countries as they fulfil important defence criteria.
"Initiatives, often come from smaller groups," he said.
"These countries bring a certain desired mass – ground, air and maritime," said Pothier.
"But why is the US picking some rather than others when this is not a policy exercise?" he said.
Pothier, who is former director of policy planning said the separation of the parts of alliance into subgroups creates concern that the US might be more inclined to defend one ally over another.
"You introduce the notion that the US favours some allies and would be likely to defend those allies ahead of the rest," said Pothier.
He suggested US President Donald Trump’s “grudge” over the UK and France’s initial refusal to join the war in Iran, along with France’s push to buy European military equipment, could explain their exclusion.
UK diplomats, however, rejected the suggestion that Britain was being sidelined, saying they remained in regular contact with their US counterparts.
Baltic exclusion
The Baltic states’ absence is particularly striking. They are among NATO’s biggest defence spenders as a share of GDP and sit on the alliance’s frontline with Russia. The region has faced repeated hybrid attacks, including drone incursions, arson and sabotage.
Their exclusion follows Colby’s visit to NATO headquarters in Brussels in August, when, according to NATO sources, he urged Baltic officials to adopt a less confrontational tone towards Russian aggression.
One source said Colby cited renewed US efforts to end the war in Ukraine as a reason to tone down talk of being at “war” with Russia.
Washington has also invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami in December, at a golf resort owned by Trump.
"It's probably the first time since NATO enlargement that there’s a split between the US and Baltics," said Pothier.
"We know that this US administration is far less fazed by Russian aggression," he said.
The situation for the Baltics remains tense due to the ongoing drone and other shadow war hostilities. Government, military and civilian populations are on constant alert.
On Saturday, Vilnius airport was forced to shut down for around an hour, prompting the deployment of two NATO jets in response to a suspected drone intrusion from Belarus.
Lithuania invites Colby
A source confirmed to Euronews that the Lithuanian government has invited Colby to visit the region to witness the ongoing airspace violations first-hand.
"We say what we see," a Baltic diplomat told Euronews defending their forward military posture. The diplomat added that Moscow must understand the cost of its shadow war to be "harsh."
EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, a former Lithuanian prime minister, also called for a stronger response at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit last week.
"If we are hit by Russian hybrid attacks, our answers should be as painful as that attack," Kubilius said.
Meanwhile, a Washington-based source told Euronews that the exclusive meeting appears to be "mischief-making" on the part of the US, warning that it actively divides the alliance.
French officials had no response time of publication.

Starbucks sued over ‘sugar-free’ claims for protein beverages

Starbucks sued over ‘sugar-free’ claims for protein beverages
- Consumers sued Starbucks for falsely advertising eight protein drinks as "sugar-free" despite containing 13 to 21g of lactose sugar per venti serving.
- The lawsuit claims Starbucks violated federal law by using "sugar-free" on products with more than 0.5g sugar per 12-ounce serving and lacked required disclaimers.
- The beverages launched in September 2025 as part of Starbucks' menu update, marketed as "protein-packed" with "no added sugar" and 270-340 calories per venti.
AI generated
Starbucks has been sued by consumers who said the coffee chain falsely advertised eight protein beverages as “sugar-free” because they contain lactose, a naturally occurring sugar in milk.
According to a proposed class action filed on Oct 2, reasonable consumers would not expect the beverages to contain 13g to 21g of sugar per 20 ounce or 24 ounce “venti” serving.
Federal law prohibits Starbucks from using “sugar-free” to describe beverages containing more than 0.5g of sugar per 12 ounce serving, the complaint said.
Consumers accused Starbucks of trying to capitalise on the desire of 75% of Americans to reduce or eliminate sugar consumption. They also said Starbucks failed to provide federally required disclaimers that the protein beverages are not low-calorie food or meant for weight control.
Starbucks, based in Seattle, had no immediate comment on Oct 5. A lawyer for the consumers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The complaint in Seattle federal court seeks unspecified damages for false advertising and violations of various state consumer protection laws.
Food producers are regularly sued for alleged false advertising, including in dozens of recent cases challenging “sugar-free” or “zero sugar” claims for products containing a sugar substitute known as allulose.
The eight Starbucks beverages are Sugar-Free Vanilla Protein Latte, Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte, Sugar-Free Vanilla Protein Matcha, Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha, and equivalent versions containing ice.
The Starbucks website says the beverages are “protein-packed” with “no added sugar”, and venti servings contain between 270 and 340 calories. The company launched the beverages in Sept 2025 as part of its “Back to Starbucks” updated menu. REUTERS

Yemeni gov’t forces aim for Sanaa, but Houthi defeat will be a challenge
Yemeni government forces claim strategic advances near Bab al-Mandeb strait amid a major anti-Houthi offensive.
Yemeni government forces have claimed advances along the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait after the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced the start of a major offensive to capture all territories lost to the Houthis.
On Monday, forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government claimed the advance and headed north along the Red Sea coast, and said they had retaken Dhubab Airport and the port city of Mocha – claims the Houthis disputed. They also earlier said that they had launched a “strategic offensive” on the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Government forces are also attempting to reverse gains made by the Houthis in recent days around the key city of Taiz, in southwestern Yemen.
The Houthis, an Iranian-allied movement, have held the capital Sanaa since September 2014, before making other territorial gains in northern and western Yemen.
After four years of relative calm, fighting flared once again in July, before a Houthi offensive in early September saw the group make sweeping gains along the Red Sea coast, including the port city of Mocha and Bab al-Mandeb.
The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, is now attempting to regain that lost territory, but still faces divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.
“The [internationally recognised government’s] ground forces are big on paper and quite sizeable, but scattered across a bunch of fronts and running on old pre-war gear, so they can hold their lines but [currently] can’t push the Houthis out of their mountain strongholds,” Raiman al-Hamdani, a London-based Yemen analyst, told Al Jazeera.
The most recent fighting hints at a new escalation in the conflict, al-Hamdani said.
“This all seems to be moving into a more dangerous phase, and while the appetite for a full-scale war may exist among elements of the leadership on both sides, the reality is more complicated,” al-Hamdani said.
“In the longer term, the more plausible outcome is not the military destruction of one side by the other, but a negotiated and imperfect political settlement in which the Houthis retain substantial influence in northern Yemen, Saudi Arabia obtains greater security guarantees, and Yemen’s competing political and military factions are forced into some form of power-sharing arrangement,” al-Hamdani added.
“The problem is that reaching that point may require another period of serious escalation before any settlement.”
Government setting the agenda
Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera’s Yemen correspondent and a specialist in Yemeni affairs, reported that the recent moves by the Yemeni government show “complete operational and political integration”.
“These moves lend a serious and decisive dimension to the announced battle to liberate Sanaa and restore the state,” he said.
Al-Shalafi said the government’s offensive is intended to start the confrontation on their own terms, rather than allowing the Houthis to dictate the stages of the war.
And even if the United States and Iran agree a deal to end their ongoing conflict, which began in late February, it might not seriously impact the fighting in Yemen.
Nicholas Brumfield, an independent Yemen analyst, told Al Jazeera that he believes the balance of power has not yet shifted in favour of either side.
“The Houthis are going to keep pushing in Taiz and Marib,” he said. “[Government] forces have been better on the defensive in Taiz … But the Houthis have been able to push in all directions at once in a way [government] forces just aren’t.”
However, Saeed Thabet, the head of Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau, said the government’s advances, coming soon after al-Alimi’s announcement of the beginning of a new large-scale offensive against the Houthis, were a way of demonstrating that the government was serious about reversing Houthi gains.
“The military expansion is a message that the government is determined to implement what it says in its statements,” Thabet said. “In the past, a lot of Yemenis would not take these statements seriously.”
“The government forces will now attempt to … control Taiz’s Red Sea coast,” he added. “It will also attempt to contain the Houthi infiltration into some villages and areas in Taiz governorate, especially in al-Shamayatayn and al-Waziya districts. Sources there have told us that government security forces are sweeping those areas and capturing some [Houthi] armed men.”

When Is the Best Time to See Peak Fall Foliage?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:28:24 UTC
00:28:24 KST

Autumn is officially here—and with it comes leaf-peeping season. Millions of people are expected to travel to view the changing autumn leaves across the United States, bringing billions of dollars in tourism for the towns that can capitalize on their regions’ vivid colors. A 2025 estimate from the U.S. National Park Service showed that fall tourists spend over $8 billion in the New England region annually.
If you’re looking to pin down the best time and place to catch a brief glimpse of reds and oranges before winter descends, you might find the task trickier than expected. Experts say that predicting peak fall foliage has never been an easy task, and climate change is only complicating the matter.
“There's a lot of things that create variation in the colors across the landscape, and all these things can interact somewhat unpredictably,” says William Keeton, a professor of forest ecology and forestry at the University of Vermont. “Climate change, as with everything, just scrambles the deck.”
Where are the best fall colors expected in 2026?
Across the vast United States, fall foliage takes many forms, with leaves of different shapes and sizes turning vibrant colors against backdrops ranging from mountain peaks to rolling farmland.
New England and upstate New York were among the most promising areas in AccuWeather’s August forecast, with wet weather in late spring and early summer and the prospect of drier conditions and cooler nights heading into autumn potentially setting the stage for memorable views.
However, AccuWeather forecast less vivid colors in parts of the lower Mississippi Valley and Southeast, citing cloud cover, rain, and a lack of clear, cool nights.
Colorado and the Carolinas could also see duller colors and brittle leaves due to drought conditions in the region.
How will climate change affect the pastime of leaf peeping?
It’s hard to know for certain just how much climate change is impacting the changing of the leaves each fall. That’s because a number of factors—including rain and temperature—can affect when we begin to see fall colors and how vibrant they become.
As days shorten, chlorophyll production in deciduous trees slows and eventually stops, while existing chlorophyll breaks down. Weather conditions also influence the timing and intensity of fall colors. The years 2015 through 2025 have been the warmest on record globally—and the heat impacts trees.
“There is some evidence that warming temperatures, especially warmer nighttime temperatures that extend later into the fall, can delay the onset of fall foliage,” says Keeton.
Extreme weather events—including droughts and heavy rainfall—can play a part in the vividness of the colors, while a cold snap can trigger leaves to fall early.
“Extreme climate events like severe drought, can reduce the production of the chemical compounds that produce fall color,” says Keeton. “Drought can also stress trees, leading to them dropping their leaves sooner than they otherwise might.”
Warmer fall temperatures typically lead to a shorter peak fall foliage season. However, some research is finding that climate change could lead to a longer season in some instances, as different species of trees respond at different times.
“We still have the early changers, but some of the other ones are a bit delayed. Instead of having lots of different species all flipping the switch around the same time, we're going to have this extended period,” says Chris Martine, a professor of biology at Bucknell University and president of the Botanical Society of America.
“What would have been a mosaic of lots of different colors, within the same period, is going to be now this extended thing where we see a few species change here and there, and then maybe a couple weeks later, another set of species,” he says.
Don’t be fooled by leaves that appear to “turn” ahead of peak season—it could be leaf scorch, which is common during periods of drought.
“Depending on how bad of a drought you're in and how stressed the trees are. You see the leaves crinkle and die before they can even change,” says Stephanie Spera, an associate professor of geography, environment, and sustainability at the University of Richmond.
All these factors mean it’s just going to become increasingly difficult to predict when peak foliage might be. “There are changes afoot, and I think knowing when [peak foliage] is going to be each year is actually a harder thing to predict,” says Martine.
When is the best weekend to view fall foliage? For the most part, that’s anyone’s guess, according to Spera.
“You're just gonna have to bet on a weekend and hope for the best,” she says.

Ukraine demines over 1,300 hectares in September. Now, it has new plan to tackle 132,000 km²
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:28:04 UTC
00:28:04 KST

Ukraine continues to demine its 132,000 square kilometers of potentially hazardous territory. During the last month, Defense Ministry demining units cleared 1,347 hectares of that liberated territory, the ministry said.
In September, Tymur Pistryuha, head of the Board of the Ukrainian Deminers Association, said that Ukraine is the most heavily mined country in the world — a fact recognized by the international community. The contaminated area continues to grow with every day of the war, Suspilne reports.
Ukraine clears 483,366 explosive devices overall
During the month, Ukraine surveyed and cleared 339.84 hectares of agricultural land, 21.31 kilometers of roads, 40.4 kilometers of railway tracks of mines and explosive remnants of war.
In total, in September, demining specialists detected and destroyed 364 explosive devices. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, 483,366 such devices have been detected and destroyed.
Such missions are conducted by several structures at once. Among them are the Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection and Environmental Safety, and the Defense Ministry, which engages demining units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the State Special Transport Service in clearing liberated territories of explosive remnants of war.
Explosive ordnance disposal units of the National Police of Ukraine and pyrotechnic units of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine are also involved in demining operations.
Those deminers now fly drones fitted with special magnetometers that register changes in the Earth's magnetic field, picking out hidden metal from the air and keeping sappers off ground that may be sown with mines.
New plan for mass demining
To make the process more effective, the government has approved a procedure under which the Ministry of Defense’s Mine Action Center will prepare a single national humanitarian demining plan every year, while the National Mine Action Authority will approve it.
The plan will be prepared according to a clear timetable for everyone involved in the process, including government authorities, demining operators, and local communities. The Mine Action Center will collect data on contaminated areas, local communities' needs, and demining operators' capacities, and use this information to develop humanitarian demining plans.

His comments come amid growing calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI systems following a series of security incidents involving advanced models.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last month called on AI companies to deliberately slow improvements in model capabilities to give developers and independent evaluators more time to address emerging risks.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in a Sept. 12 essay.
Altman backed parts of Amodei's proposal at the time, saying: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”
'Unacceptable tradeoff'
But he drew a line in the Politico interview over how far restrictions should go, arguing against concentrating control of increasingly powerful AI in the hands of a small number of developers.
“I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like: ‘This technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits’,” Altman said.
He called that approach “a completely unacceptable tradeoff,” favoring instead a lighter regulatory approach and broader access to AI.
The debate has intensified following incidents in which advanced AI systems have shown unexpected or potentially dangerous behavior, raising concerns over whether safety measures are keeping pace with rapidly improving capabilities.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying: ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen’,” said Altman. “Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff.”
The OpenAI CEO later added that he does not accept “the really catastrophic risks,” including the potential for “a serious loss of control to AI.”

‘I thought I was having a heart attack’: Nova rescuer reveals PTSD battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:26:45 UTC
00:26:45 KST

On the morning of Oct. 7, 2023, Oz Davidian woke at his home in Moshav Maslul in southern Israel to an unusually heavy barrage of rockets. He and his wife gathered their daughters and searched for shelter. During a lull, as they collected water and diapers, a message appeared in the family WhatsApp group.
His sister Dikla, who was near the Nova music festival site, said several terrified young people had reached her husband, who owns a farm in the area, and were asking for help. “I’ll be out in a few minutes,” Davidian replied. He told his wife and daughters to remain at home, threw a six-pack of water into his pickup truck and drove out. Instead of taking the roads, he drove through open terrain. In retrospect, he says, that decision may have saved his own life as well.
‘Not every location still had people alive’
At first, Davidian did not understand what he was driving into. Near his brother-in-law’s farm, he encountered terrified young people who had fled the festival and only then began to grasp what was happening.
“I told my brother-in-law and my nephews: Load everyone up. I know the terrain, I have a four-wheel-drive pickup, I’m going in to get the kids out.”
He entered through a wadi. Then he went back in. And again. With every trip, the scale of the disaster became clearer: terrorists, relentless gunfire, explosions and young people running for their lives. Whenever he saw them, he stopped and called out: “My name is Oz. Come, I’m here to get you out.”
They crowded into his truck, and he drove them to safety, sometimes under fire. Amid the chaos, Davidian began taking photographs. Selfies with survivors, and later a photograph with Democrats party leader Yair Golan, became part of the visual record of that day.
He says the pictures served two purposes. The first was chillingly simple: he thought they might be the last photographs ever taken of those in the vehicle, and if they were killed he wanted people to know who had been inside.
The second was a plea for help. “I sent them everywhere, to every WhatsApp group I had, so people would understand the scale of what was happening, so they would send reinforcements, send me help,” he says. The images did reach others, some of whom headed south after seeing them.
Davidian also handed his phone to the young people he rescued. “I told them: Everyone gets 10 seconds on the phone. ‘Dad, Mom, I’m alive. I’m on my way to Moshav Maslul or Moshav Patish.’”
Residents in the two communities gave the survivors food, water, clothing and assistance, and helped them contact their families. “There are many kids who may have come back alive from the festival, but they didn’t come back to their lives,” Davidian says. “I think none of them returned to who they were, and they won’t. It’s hard for all of them. Some are really suffering much more.”
Meanwhile, more locations began arriving on Davidian’s phone. Survivors passed his number to friends still hiding in the area, and soon parents, siblings and friends were contacting him as well.
One after another, locations appeared on his screen, people hiding and waiting for someone to come. Davidian says he went to every one of them. Not every location still held someone he could save.
“I didn’t give up on a single location,” he says. At some he found people alive. At others he found bodies. Some were already empty, apparently because those hiding there had been forced to flee.
Before each trip, he opened the locations, mentally arranged his route and drove from one point to the next. Davidian entered and left the danger zone 15 times and rescued 120 people alive. Three years later, that number has not erased the thoughts of those he could not save.
“It’s something that doesn’t leave me,” he says through tears. “There are locations I reached and there was no one alive. A lot of times I think, maybe if I had driven from this side, I could have reached more people in time.”
When told that he did everything one man with one pickup truck could possibly have done, Davidian agrees. But what his mind understands is harder for his heart to accept. “It’s true, I did everything I could. I didn’t give up,” he says, before returning once again to the “maybe” that continues to gnaw at him.
He also struggles to accept the label of “hero” for himself alone. To him, that day was filled with people who fit that description: civilians, police officers and soldiers. “I think we are a country of heroes,” he says. “I met many heroes who came into the area. Not all of them survived. Not all of them are alive.”
Post-trauma
After Oct. 7, Davidian had little time to return home and process what he had experienced. He was called up for reserve duty, in part because of what he had witnessed and footage captured by cameras in his vehicle. For nearly four months, he assisted security forces in the festival area, including with locating bodies and identifying evidence.
He later continued his reserve service with the IDF’s Gaza Division. It was then, after the first mission had ended, that something inside him broke.
While driving near Kfar Aza and Re’im to deliver food to soldiers, Davidian suddenly felt pressure throughout his body. His heart began racing and heat spread through him. Davidian, who was over 50 and a smoker, was convinced he was having a heart attack.
He told his wife he did not feel well, messaged his battalion commander that he was going home and left. Those around him understood what was happening before he did.
When he arrived home, his wife and daughters were waiting. His battalion commander also came, and Davidian was later referred for treatment. “That was the day I understood,” he says. “They explained to me that it was post-trauma and that we were going to start treating it.”
Since then, he has undergone psychological and psychotherapeutic treatment, remains under psychiatric supervision and takes medication. After about a year and a half, he stopped treatment for several months because the process itself became too difficult, then returned.
He remains in treatment today. “The medication helps, the treatment helps, the conversations help,” he says. “Those conversations are incredibly hard, but they really save lives. It’s very difficult to start treatment or to say that you’re being treated. If I hadn’t collapsed out there, I wouldn’t have thought I needed it.”
There are also different moments in his life now. The 120 young people he rescued did not disappear from it. They share a WhatsApp group, and Davidian calls them “my children.”
Tehila, one of the survivors, gave birth to a son about a year and a half after the massacre and named him Oz after Davidian. Shani Arditi, whose photograph in the back of his pickup became one of the images associated with the rescue efforts, has since married.
But for some survivors, time has not turned survival into a return to normal life. “There are many of my kids, and other kids too, who may have returned alive from the festival, but they didn’t return to their lives,” Davidian says. “I think none of them returned to themselves and they won’t return to themselves. It’s hard for everyone. Some are really suffering more.”
He tries to help them in their dealings with state authorities and remains in contact with bereaved families, including families who contacted him that day and asked him to reach their children, only for him to arrive too late.
Oct. 7 has not ended inside his own home either. His wife and daughters were in Maslul while he drove toward the festival. They heard the gunfire and explosions, knew terrorists were in the area and waited to find out whether he would return.
They too have been in treatment ever since, he says. “I’m not the only one who experienced it,” he says. “We’re not just a family with post-trauma. We’re a country with post-trauma.”
‘I don’t know if I’ll be myself again’
Three years later, Davidian says the intensity with which Oct. 7 occupies the public consciousness may be fading, but the event itself cannot be forgotten.
He says he deliberately avoided politics for three years and still wants the memory of the massacre kept separate from election battles. “I think this event is too big for us to use it for politics,” he says. “It hurts me that bereaved families and heroes are being used too, with people attacking one another for political purposes.”
He is particularly disturbed by conspiracy theories surrounding the events of that day. Among them are claims surrounding his photograph with Golan, which circulated online in versions in which Davidian had been cropped out. In Golan’s glasses, the reflection of Davidian’s pickup can be seen.
Some conspiracy theories claimed the pickup, the same vehicle Davidian used to rescue 120 people, belonged to terrorists.
Davidian says he took the photograph himself during the rescue operation after encountering Golan in the field. For him, the acts of courage on Oct. 7 did not belong to one political camp or another. “When we rescued people, we didn’t ask them about their political views,” he says. “We rescued them because they are our children.”
This Oct. 7, Davidian is not expected to spend the day, as he usually does, with his family and the survivors he rescued. He is due to be at the United Nations, where he was invited to address hundreds of diplomats and ambassadors and describe firsthand what he saw and experienced.
He says he initially did not want to travel, but was persuaded that there was value in telling the story there. Three years from now, he hopes to be in a different place. Not necessarily the person he was before that morning. He no longer takes that possibility for granted. But he hopes at least to be closer to the life he once had.
“I don’t know if I’ll manage to return to myself, but I really hope I’ll return to a life fairly similar to the one I had,” he says. “At the end of the day, I’m a moshavnik. A person who gets up in the morning, in the moshav, at home, a wife, children, like any ordinary person.”
And he has one more hope: that three years from now, the country will look different too. “More united, more cohesive,” he says. “Fewer divisions, less polarization, less tearing each other apart and turning one against another. Because in the end, we are all brothers.”
“I may be only one person,” he says, “but whatever I can do, I will do.”

Could Russian strikes on the bridges divide Kyiv into two banks? An expert outlined a scenario
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
18:26:29 EEST
00:26:29 KST

Could Russian strikes on the bridges divide Kyiv into two banks? An expert outlined a scenario
Kyiv • UNN
The complete destruction of Kyiv’s bridges is unlikely, expert Pavlo Narozhnyi believes. Repairing the damage could take anywhere from several days to months.
Recently, the risk of the capital effectively being divided into the left and right banks due to Russian strikes on Kyiv’s bridges across the Dnipro has been actively discussed online. Military expert Pavlo Narozhny told a UNN journalist more about how realistic such a scenario is and how much time might be needed to restore the damaged crossings.
Details
According to the expert, completely disabling all of Kyiv’s bridges is unlikely.
Pavlo Narozhny notes that it is technically possible to destroy an individual bridge span, but even serious damage would not necessarily mean a prolonged suspension of traffic. As an example, he cited the situation with the Crimean Bridge.
To completely destroy a bridge so that no equipment could pass over it—in theory, such a scenario is possible. One bridge span can be destroyed—from one support to another. However, we can recall, for example, the Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge, when two spans were destroyed—one in each direction. The Russians repaired it within several months, that is, they installed the span back in place. It would also be entirely realistic for us to repair it in the event of such a strike
At the same time, according to the expert, Russian drones do not have sufficient power to completely destroy a bridge span, so even in the event of a hit, they can only damage the “roadway.”
It is unrealistic to destroy a span with a jet-powered “Shahed,” “Geran-4,” “Geran-5,” or some other drones. The maximum damage a jet-powered “Shahed” can cause is a hole, speaking in layman’s terms. That is what happened on the Northern Bridge. However, such damage is relatively easy to repair
Can Russia destroy bridge supports?
Pavlo Narozhny also separately explained the situation regarding bridge supports, in particular, that their destruction would make the situation significantly more difficult.
Even if we take some missile containing, say, a tonne of explosives, this still does not guarantee that a support would be destroyed, even in a direct hit. For a support to collapse, an extremely precise hit is required, and achieving that is actually very difficult. In any case, a support is much more difficult to restore, but it is also possible. Such repairs could take several months, but that is an optimistic timeframe
Moreover, to completely block transport links between Kyiv’s banks, it would be necessary to disable not one, but several crossings at once. Pavlo Narozhny believes that such a scenario is unlikely to occur.
We have six bridges: the Southern, Northern, Darnytskyi, Metro Bridge, Paton Bridge, and Podilskyi bridges. So, the scenario in which all the bridges are destroyed, in which they are all put out of operation—I can hardly imagine such a scenario. Purely from a technical point of view, if the enemy is indeed prepared to spend dozens, if not hundreds, of missiles on such a scenario, one bridge can be destroyed. But I think this is unlikely
However, if we are talking specifically about damage to the bridges, it could indeed temporarily complicate movement around the city. In the expert’s opinion, this would affect crossings used by public transport and the metro most of all.
The enemy attacked Kyiv’s Northern Bridge; there is damage — the mayor04.10.26, 10:40 • 20871 view
We have two bridges used by metro trains. If a hit lands on the roadway, it can be restored relatively quickly. Across Ukraine, railway infrastructure is hit fairly often, but this has not led to a complete halt of the railway. I think that even if this happens, the metro would be stopped for a maximum of a few days. If a hit lands on the roadway of a road bridge, then it could be shut down for several weeks, perhaps even a month, while everything is repaired
The closure of the bridges could hit Kyiv’s economy
The prolonged shutdown of several bridges would be a problem not only for Kyiv residents' mobility. A significant number of people cross the Dnipro every day to get to work or use services and facilities on the opposite bank, which means that such a scenario could also affect the capital's economic activity.
If we imagine a situation in which vehicular traffic on two bridges is halted, we have various estimates—from half a million or more people who travel from the left bank to the right bank every day and then return in the evening. Therefore, if this happens, it will be a very serious blow to Ukraine's economy. Kyiv is Ukraine's largest city, and the greatest economic and business activity takes place here
At the same time, Pavlo Narozhnyi emphasizes that even if the bridges were damaged, the situation would not mean the complete division of the capital. Moreover, the strategic importance of Kyiv's crossings is taken into account when protecting them, so there is no need to panic about this.
This is a highly unlikely scenario. Even if a ballistic missile or a cruise missile hits there, I think it will be restored relatively quickly. Of course, this is not a very pleasant scenario, but I think we will get through it if it happens. In addition, the Air Force understands how strategically important this bridge is and will defend it by all possible means

Russian Paratroopers Airdrop Kurier UGV from an Il-76 for the First Time During Center-2026 Exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:25:56 UTC
00:25:56 KST

During the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercises, Russian paratroopers airdropped the Kurier ground-based robotic complex from an Ilyushin Il-76 military transport aircraft for the first time.
The Russian Ministry of Defense published a video of the airdrop.
The system was dropped from about 600 meters on a P-7 parachute platform.
The operators of these systems had previously landed in the mission area, after which they took control of the robotic vehicles.
According to the exercise scenario, the robots were to operate behind enemy lines.
They were intended to provide fire support for assault units, deliver ammunition and supplies, evacuate the wounded, and destroy road infrastructure.
During one exercise, the Kurier was deployed to provide fire support for an assault group. A 7.62-mm machine gun was mounted on the system. According to a Russian operator, after landing, the robot requires about three to five minutes to prepare for the mission.
Separately, during the exercises, reconnaissance teams parachuted from an An-26 aircraft at an altitude of 6,000 meters.
The troops used special Stayer parachute systems equipped with oxygen apparatus. After jumping, they glided more than 17 km and landed behind enemy lines.
In addition to Kurier, the Omich-2 and Bogomol-7V ground-based robotic systems also participated in the exercises.
Militarnyi previously reported that in the Chelyabinsk region, the Russians conducted exercises to repel external aggression and establish a security zone on the territory of a Central Asian country.
After repelling the main assault in the South Ural direction, the troops went on the offensive to liberate the occupied territory and establish a security zone in the adjacent territory.
UGV Kurier is a Russian multi-purpose ground robot on a tracked chassis with remote control. Its design allows for the installation of various equipment and weapons depending on the mission.
According to publicly available data, the base version measures about 1.4 × 1.2 × 0.58 m, weighs up to 250 kg, and can reach speeds up to 35 km/h. The control range is 3 to 10 km, and the operational endurance is up to 72 hours.
The Kurier delivers ammunition, food, and other cargo; evacuates the wounded; conducts reconnaissance; and lays mines. For combat missions, the robot is equipped with various weapons, including a 7.62-mm PKTM machine gun, 12.7-mm NSVT or Kord machine guns, and AGS-17 and AGS-30 automatic grenade launchers. In 2025, the Ignis laser system was also tested on the Kurier platform to destroy mines at distances up to 150 m.

Sainsbury’s and Morrisons ‘held talks this year’ on multibillion-pound merger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:24:29 UTC
00:24:29 KST

Sainsbury’s held merger talks with rival Morrisons this year to discuss a multibillion-pound deal that would have been the biggest shake-up for UK supermarkets in decades, according to reports.
The two companies held exploratory negotiations, according to the Financial Times and Sky. It is believed they are no longer in live discussions.
Morrisons, which was once one of the big four UK grocers alongside Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Asda, was bought by the US private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021.
The deal loaded it with more than £7bn in debt on its balance sheet, and it has since struggled to grow as fast as its rivals. The German discounter Lidl overtook it in market share this year.
A merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would have created a business with a 23.6% market share, putting it still some way behind Britain’s biggest retailer, Tesco, which has 27.8% of the market, according to analysts at Worldpanel by Numerator.
The last attempt to merge two of the big four supermarkets was in 2019, when Asda and Sainsbury’s almost joined forces. That £7bn deal was blocked by the Competition and Markets Authority on the basis that it would result in a loss of competition and higher prices for customers.
The CMA would have almost certainly reviewed any merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons, and could have required the former to sell some of its stores to gain approval for any deal.
Reducing competition in the grocery sector could also be politically sensitive, given that millions of households have grappled with persistent food inflation in recent years.
Clayton Dubilier & Rice, however, is open to a tie-up between Morrisons and another major supermarket, according to Sky. It reported that Asda, which is majority owned by the private equity firm TDR Capital, could also be drawn into deal talks.
Shares in Sainsbury’s, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, were flat on Monday afternoon. The stock has fallen by 3% so far this year, compared with a 6% rise for its FTSE 100 rival Tesco.
Sainsbury’s, which employs about 140,000 people, is the second biggest grocer in the UK by market share at 15.2%.
It agreed to sell Argos for £120m in the summer to allow it to concentrate on its core food business, a decade after buying the retail chain for more than £1bn.
News of supermarket takeover talks came as Lidl GB reported a 10% jump in its annual revenue to more than £13bn on Monday.
The company said pre-tax profits at its British arm rose by 30% to £245.5m in the year that ended in February as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables, as well as its Deluxe upmarket food range.
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons declined to comment.

Source: Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski speaking to journalists, as reported by European Pravda

Background:

- Poland is also preparing a law on a "pre-war state", which is intended to establish rules for action in a situation where the country is not formally at war but the level of threat is already significantly higher than in peacetime.
