Yemen air campaign against Houthis under way, says Saudi-led coalition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:21:54 UTC
00:21:54 KST

Leaders of a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen claimed a broad air campaign involving 100 jet aircraft was under way on Monday against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coastline and farther north in the capital, Sana’a.
The Saudi coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the 100 fighter jets participating in Operation Dawn of Yemen were providing support to forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. He claimed hundreds of Houthi fighters had been besieged in the Dhubab district, including the airport, close to the Bab al-Mandab strait, with some Houthi fighters fleeing across the Red Sea in boats.
Southern Yemeni forces known as the Giants Brigades, who are allied with the government, earlier on Monday launched a ground offensive against the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis seized in their latest advances. The government forces also claim to have cut the road between Mocha and Dhubab, and that Houthi forces were deserting the recently captured city of Mocha as residents stayed behind closed doors.
Previous Saudi-led statements about territorial gains in recent weeks have often proved partial, but footage appeared to back up the Saudi claims of Houthis retreating by the seashore.
The president of the Saudi-backed government, Rashad al-Alimi, had promised a new offensive on Sunday, saying patience with the Houthis had run out. “Today we are embarking on a decisive phase in the history of our nation,” he said.
Airstrikes were also reported on Monday in Sana’a and the Houthi stronghold of Saada in the north of Yemen. Command and control centres, camps and weapons depots were targeted.
The Houthis, who captured Sana’a in 2014, have in recent weeks made lightning advances down the west coast of Yemen, reaching the Bab al-Mandab and seizing strategic islands on the strait.
On Monday Houthi sources denied reports of a retreat, and pointed to the explosions at a Saudi Aramco plant in Riyadh as a sign of the damage the group could still inflict on exposed Saudi oil installations, and by extension the world economy.
It appears a political agreement reached between the two main external Arab actors in Yemen – Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – permitted the UAE-backed Southern Giants to coordinate with the Saudi air force in the attack towards the coast.
It is being stressed by the Giants Brigades that no other ground forces supporting the Saudi-backed government are involved in the offensive. The brigades, who are linked with the Southern Transitional Council, a political group outlawed in Yemen for trying to set up a secessionist state, are certain to have sought political commitments about the future status of Yemen in order to have thrown their military weight behind it.
It is not clear how the Saudis propose to address the age-old southern question. Concessions to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) about the future governance of the south are certain to have been demanded, even if the UAE itself does not return to Yemen.
But the cooperation between the Saudi air force and the Giants Brigades is a remarkable turnaround, since as recently as January the Saudi air force was bombing UAE shipments of arms arriving in southern Yemen for STC-backed forces.
The Saudi bombing triggered the UAE pullout from Yemen in January, the sudden dissolution of the STC, and the exile of its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi. At the weekend his supporters vowed to hold demonstrations later this month in support of the return to a separate southern state.
Houthi government officials claimed British fighter jets were supporting the Saudi air force with refuelling, something the UK Ministry of Defence has already announced.
The fighting was under way as senior ministers from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh to discuss the support Saudi Arabia might need to protect itself from the Houthis. They have formed a joint defence pact but it is not known how it will operate.

Spectator referred to IPSO over 'racist' Palestine article, ICJP tells TNA
A UK-based legal group has referred The Spectator to an independent press regulator over an article describing Palestinians as "probably the worst migrant population on Earth", the group told The New Arab.
The International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) confirmed to TNA that it had lodged a complaint with the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO) over a "racist and discriminatory" article about Palestinian refugees.
The group told TNA that it expects to receive a response from IPSO in the coming weeks.
The complaint concerns a 29 September article by David Shipley titled "Taking in more Palestinian refugees is a terrible idea", which the ICJP says used misleading crime statistics to "stigmatise an entire people".
Shipley's article referred to a cohort of 321 Palestinian refugees from Lebanon who moved to Denmark in 1992, claiming that 63% had been convicted of a crime and that 67 had been jailed — figures the ICJP said were inaccurate and misleading.
"Even then, in the 1990s, Palestinians were highly criminal and highly economically inactive," Shipley wrote. "Now, having been ruled by Hamas for over two decades, fed endless anti-Semitic and anti-Israel propaganda, they are even worse," the article continued.
Shipley is himself a convicted fraudster who was sentenced to 45 months in prison in 2020, but served just 19 months of the sentence, including time at HMP Wandsworth - one of the UK's most prominent and notoriously troubled prisons.
According to Shipley's own account, he pleaded guilty after lying to a private-equity firm about how much money his business had made and producing false documents to support the claims.
The ICJP challenged both the statistics in his Spectator article and the conclusions drawn from them, pointing out that the Palestinian refugees who arrived in Denmark in 1992 had never lived under Hamas rule.
Following an initial complaint, The Spectator amended the article to clarify that the figure of 67 people described as having been "jailed" included 30 conditional sentences.
The ICJP said the amendment failed to address broader problems with the way the data were presented.
"The article does not disclose that two thirds of those cases ended in a fine or other disposal, or what conduct they involved," the group said.
"The article is racist in both its premise and its method. It attributes criminality and undesirability to Palestinians as people, on the basis of their national origin, and it applies this method to no other nationality," the ICJP said in a statement on Friday.
"No nationality could fairly be judged by it. 321 people cannot speak for more than 9 million Palestinian refugees worldwide, the product of decades of displacement and the continued denial of the right of return," it added.
The ICJP's referral alleges that The Spectator breached two clauses of IPSO's Editors' Code, including requirements not to publish inaccurate, misleading or distorted information and to distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact.
The complaint comes after The Spectator, Britain's oldest continuously published magazine, was the subject of a report by the Centre for Media Monitoring (CfMM) earlier this year that found the publication was systematically biased against Muslims.
The analysis examined almost 4,000 articles published by the magazine and found that more than half were classified as "biased" or "very biased" against Muslims.
The New Arab contacted The Spectator for comment.

Energy Minister Iva Petrova
PHOTO Ministry of Energy
Font size
Natural gas transmission capacity from Greece to Bulgaria has increased by around 30% this year to 93 gigawatt-hours per day, Bulgarian Energy Minister Iva Petrova said in an interview with Greek business publication Powergame.gr, published on Monday.
Petrova said the Vertical Gas Corridor was being strengthened, opening up new energy routes for southeastern Europe, BTA reported. The next step was to ensure that the corridor operated as a single, fully interconnected regional system rather than a series of separate national projects, she said.
Petrova stressed the importance of the Greece-Bulgaria gas interconnector and Greece’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure in diversifying supplies. These gave Bulgaria access to Azerbaijani gas via the Trans Adriatic Pipeline and to LNG imports through Greece, she said.
Further development of the Vertical Gas Corridor would allow gas supplies to reach Serbia, Romania, Moldova, Ukraine and Hungary, Petrova added.

How Lula’s successes in Brazil may have paved the way for his presidential defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:21:10 UTC
00:21:10 KST

How Lula’s successes in Brazil may have paved the way for his presidential defeat
Brazil’s veteran leftist President Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva trailed Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of his far-right predecessor, in the first-round presidential vote on Sunday. Some analysts suggest that the sweeping anti-poverty measures Lula put in place over two decades may have helped give rise to a growing lower-middle class drawn to the far right’s promise to get the government out of people’s lives.
As right-wing governments backed by Washington rise to power across Latin America, Brazil now looks like it will be the next domino to fall.
Far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro led the first round of Brazil’s presidential election on Sunday, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a veteran left-wing leader and former trade unionist, trailing narrowly behind him. With neither candidate winning an outright majority, an October 25 run-off will determine who will lead the country of more than 214 million people over the next four years.
Bolsonaro’s father Jair is serving a 27-year sentence for having plotted a coup d’état after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula. His eldest son, whom the former president anointed as his ideological successor a few scant months ago, has promised a pardon if he emerges triumphant in the second round.
While less than two percentage points separated the leading candidates, the results were a shock to supporters of Lula’s centre-left Workers' Party (PT); opinion polls had put Lula ahead of his rival in the days leading up to the vote. And with a handful of other right-wing candidates knocked out in the first round, the second round seems as though it’s Bolsonaro’s to lose.
Even if Lula does manage to mobilise enough of the more than one in five voters who abstained in the first round, the presidential palace of Planalto was not the only prize being contested in Sunday’s elections.
Across the country, congressional and gubernatorial elections have also seen the country lurch sharply to the right, with Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party (PL) likely to emerge as the leading force in the lower-house Chamber of Deputies, as well as the Senate.
Despite his decades-long legacy of social-democratic policies that have lifted tens of millions of people out of poverty, Lula seems to have struggled to mobilise his base in the face of a far right that has succeeded in welding together a coalition of the country’s business elite and rising lower-middle classes.
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro: In the name of the father, sons, and holy ideology
Thomas Zicman de Barros, a fellow at the centre for political research at Sciences Po university in Paris, said the younger Bolsonaro has maintained his father’s appeal to voters frustrated by the status quo.
“Despite the fact that his father is now in prison, and the fact that Flavio Bolsonaro himself and the whole family are involved in many scandals in Brazil, they still succeed in embodying some kind of anti-establishment feeling,” he said.
“And Lula, despite the fact that he comes from a trade union background, and he was kind of a populist – and I don’t use the word in a pejorative sense – nowadays he embodies the establishment, and the very defence of a liberal democratic system that we have, that … has its flaws, its blind spots.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
For some Brazilians, the man who previously served two terms as president from 2003 to 2011 remains deeply entrenched in the system, despite his leftist credentials.
Felipe Krause, a former Brazilian diplomat and the head of Oxford University’s Brazilian Studies Programme, said in an interview with FRANCE 24 television that the global cost-of-living crisis and mounting levels of household debt had eaten into the economic gains made under Lula’s most recent term in office.
“Interestingly, if you actually look at the economy, there’s kind of a mixed situation,” he said. “You do have relatively low unemployment and income is even rising to some extent, but prices are really high – and I think most of all, there’s a lack of a sense of hope for prosperity in the future.”
Krause said that Lula, who first won office in 2002 on a platform of social welfare reforms that earned him a strong following among Brazil’s poorest communities and organised working class, had failed to keep up with the social and economic changes sweeping the country.
“In my view, the Lula camp hasn’t really appreciated how the country has changed relative to Lula’s first two terms – and how the country in fact has changed due to the success of Lula’s own policies,” he said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
“You now have this rising middle class, which is far more interested in entrepreneurialism, a pro-market individualistic approach – and far less interested in the social protections, the formal employment, the labour unions and all those things that the Lula camp is used to offering.”
Zicman said that, for many people in Brazil’s lower-middle classes juggling more than one job in an expanding gig economy, Bolsonaro’s campaign pledge to lower taxes and – borrowing a phrase from Argentina’s far-right libertarian President Javier Milei – “take a chainsaw to bureaucracy”, may well have resonated.
“We’ve had transformations in labour relations all over the world, but notably in what we might call the Global South,” he said. “So nowadays, many precarious workers don’t even dream of having more stable jobs … They might sell some services or products [on] the internet.”
Zicman said a new sense of distrust is also permeating Brazil's politics. “There is this ‘self-made person’ spirit, that is, on one hand, individualistic – some might call it neoliberal subjectivity. That might explain why some people are now thinking, ‘I don’t trust the government anymore, I don’t think that the left, if it gets to power, [will] be capable of transforming my situation.’”
Whether or not the far right would be any more capable of doing so, he said, is a matter of sharply divided opinion.
“The far right is not necessarily lying to those people, because it is delivering what it promises: That is, ‘I will do nothing, and then you, by your own merit, you will succeed,’” he said.
“The lie – and this is my personal opinion – is that most people won’t succeed.”

Drone Reportedly Sinks Grain Ship Near Romania, Kills 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:21:00 UTC
00:21:00 KST

Two crew members were killed and 11 rescued after a Turkey-owned grain ship reportedly came under a drone attack and sank in the Black Sea near Romania on Monday, Oct. 5.
The Royad Mammadov had departed the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail carrying grain and was sailing toward Ravenna, Italy, according to Romanian broadcaster Digi24.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Romanian media reported that one or more drones struck the ship near the Pescăruș offshore oil and gas platform operated by OMV Petrom. However, Romanian authorities have so far officially confirmed only a fire aboard the vessel and have not determined its cause or identified who may have been responsible.
The Romanian Interior Ministry said the burning ship sank while rescuers were searching for its crew.
“Eleven crew members were rescued. Two deceased persons were also identified,” the ministry said.
Three injured sailors were lifted from the area by helicopter for emergency medical treatment, while eight other crew members were taken aboard rescue vessels, Digi24 reported.
Ship sank outside Romanian territorial waters
The incident occurred in Romania’s exclusive economic zone but outside its territorial waters, according to the Romanian Naval Authority.
Romanian officials placed the ship approximately 30 nautical miles south of the coastal settlement of Sfântu Gheorghe. Media reports said it was about nine nautical miles southeast of the Pescăruș platform and roughly 20 nautical miles from Romania’s coast.
India Moves to Broker Black Sea Deal Between Russia and Ukraine
Romania’s Maritime Rescue Coordination Center received the emergency call at approximately 10:37 a.m. and dispatched the rescue vessels SAR Apollo, SAR Artemis, and SAR Ares. A Romanian Coast Guard vessel and an Interior Ministry helicopter also joined the operation.
The 140-meter (460-foot) Royad Mammadov sailed under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis, rather than Turkey. Shipping records identify Turkey-based MG Shipping 5 Co Ltd as its registered owner and list Turkish companies as its commercial and safety managers.
VesselFinder data showed that the general cargo ship had last called at Izmail and was scheduled to arrive in Ravenna on Oct. 12.
Drone strike not yet officially confirmed
Digi24 and other Romanian outlets described the incident as a drone attack, while witnesses reportedly said that two or three drones may have struck the vessel.
The Romanian Naval Authority, Interior Ministry, and Coast Guard have not publicly confirmed that a drone caused the explosion and fire. They have also not attributed the incident to Russia, and no publicly released evidence has yet established the drone’s origin.
Several hours before the maritime incident, Romania’s defense ministry said its radar systems detected an airborne target east of Vylkove, Ukraine, close to the Romanian border.
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed in Romania for NATO air-policing duties were scrambled, and residents of northern Tulcea County received an emergency alert. The ministry said the target did not enter Romanian airspace.
Authorities have not established any connection between that overnight incident and the fire aboard the Royad Mammadov.
Growing danger to Black Sea shipping
Commercial vessels serving Ukrainian ports have repeatedly been damaged during Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube infrastructure.
In April, a Russian drone struck a Liberia-flagged merchant ship traveling toward an Odesa region port to load corn. Its crew extinguished the fire and no casualties were reported.
The Ukrainian Ports Association has said that more than 300 commercial vessels have been damaged or destroyed since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, with attacks increasingly targeting ships traveling to and from Ukrainian ports.
The escalating danger has severely disrupted agricultural exports. Russia and Ukraine ordinarily account for more than a quarter of global wheat trade, while interruptions to Black Sea routes have pushed wheat prices to three-year highs and raised concerns about a new global food-security shock.
Romania has also experienced repeated incursions by Russian drones and the discovery of drifting naval mines since 2022. At the same time, Romanian authorities have investigated incidents involving Ukrainian naval drones, including one that exploded near Constanța in June after Kyiv said Russian electronic warfare had caused it to lose control.

Imran Khan’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed.
The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-west Pakistan on Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
Concerns have grown over the health of the 74-year-old former Pakistan cricket captain who has been in prison since 2023. Party colleagues and family claim he is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied visits by his doctor or relatives despite having a serious eye condition and high blood pressure.
The government had gone to extreme lengths to try to stop PTI holding the long march, including shutting down Islamabad and barricading the capital’s entrances with shipping containers and sandbags. Khan’s three sisters were among those detained last week on grounds of national security.
Two rounds of negotiations between the government and PTI leaders took place over the weekend but broke down when Khan’s allies insisted that he be part of political talks.
Attaullah Tarar, the information minister, accused the PTI of “double standards and hypocrisy”.
Thousands of supporters had joined the protest by Monday afternoon and the crowds are expected to grow on the way to Peshawar, the main city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which the marchers should reach by Wednesday.
The march is being led by the province’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, who described those taking part as “Imran Khan’s soldiers”.
“I call upon you all to come out, the youngsters to come out for the sake of your leader who is sitting in jail,” he said.
Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022, when he was toppled by a parliamentary vote of no confidence. Since then, he and the PTI have faced mounting government pressure, which culminated in his arrest in 2023. The harassment and detention of other PTI leaders continues.
Khan is widely considered the country’s most popular politician, while the ruling coalition government, which is backed by the military, is facing discontent over an economic crisis and a surge in terrorism.
Ministers say the march is illegal and all measures will be taken to ensure it does not break through the capital’s boundaries.
Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed to Islamabad and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa last week, raising fears that Khan’s supporters will be met with state violence. Government politicians falsely claimed that the PTI was allowing militants from the Pakistan Taliban to take part in the march.
Opposition leaders fear the prime minister will impose emergency rule on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to stop the march.

Teen loses hand to police grenade as French school protests enter second week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:18:08 UTC
00:18:08 KST

More than 400 schools across France remained closed Monday as student protests over classroom conditions entered a second week, with the unrest increasingly marred by violence. In the most serious incident yet, French media reported that a 15-year-old boy lost a hand after picking up a police stun grenade during a demonstration.
The protests have erupted about seven months before France’s presidential election, with the far-left France Unbowed party of Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused by opponents of encouraging the unrest in an effort to destabilize the country and demonstrate its political strength.
The teenager was injured Monday morning in the northern city of Lens after apparently picking up a stun grenade used by police for crowd control, apparently intending to throw it back toward officers. The grenade exploded in his hand.
François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of the Pas-de-Calais department, described the incident as ‘extremely serious’ but said the teenager’s life was not in danger. France’s police oversight authorities opened an investigation into the circumstances of his injury.
The demonstrations began last week, when students at hundreds of schools, particularly in poorer working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, began blocking school entrances and roads, setting garbage bins on fire and, in some cases, attacking police officers and passersby. Protesters say they are demonstrating against neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages.
The unrest comes as the French government seeks to pass its 2027 state budget, which aims to reduce the country’s deficit.
Since the demonstrations began last Monday, at least 24 schools have been set on fire or looted and 78 education workers have been injured. About 5,000 people have been arrested nationwide, most of them teenagers, while property damage is estimated at tens of millions of euros.
Critics of the protests have accused Mélenchon’s France Unbowed of inciting violence and inflaming the unrest. Mélenchon, a fierce critic of Israel, is one of the leading candidates in the presidential race. Opponents of the protests have also pointed to the involvement of immigrants and children of immigrants in some of the street violence.
Organizers have called for a nationwide day of demonstrations Tuesday, but between 400 and 500 of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools announced that they would close fully or partially on Monday.
Fears that violence would return even before Tuesday’s demonstrations were quickly confirmed. French media published footage of clashes between police and students in the northern city of Lille, police using tear gas in Toulouse in southwestern France and a fire being set during an attempt to break into a school in central Paris.
Carole Zerbib, principal of Vauquelin High School in Paris’ 13th arrondissement, said the school was attacked by a "very determined" group of hooded and masked individuals who tried to force open its entrance before setting a fire.
Police and firefighters quickly extinguished the blaze, the school was evacuated and classes were suspended.
"It was very violent and happened very quickly," Zerbib said, adding that those behind the attack were not students at the school. She said the assault lasted between 15 and 20 minutes. "It was terrible for the students who witnessed this outbreak of violence," she said.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure said in an open letter published Saturday on X that those who launched the protests were no longer in control of them. He urged students to end school blockades and demonstrate peacefully.
Student organizations nevertheless called for nationwide demonstrations Tuesday, and security officials are particularly concerned that a large rally planned in central Paris could descend into further violence if far-left activists and anarchists attempt to take control of the protest.
Sophie Binet, head of France’s powerful CGT trade union federation, told TF1 on Monday that union members would join Tuesday’s demonstrations "to defend high school students."
"We were horrified by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented repression the government has used against high school student protests," she said.
The unrest is unfolding against an already tense political and social backdrop, with fuel prices rising sharply and Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally leading presidential polls.
Current polling suggests Le Pen would advance to a second-round runoff against Mélenchon and defeat him. Such a matchup would mark a dramatic weakening of France’s political center, leaving voters to choose between two forces widely regarded as representing the country’s political extremes.

Global oil inventories ‘scarily thin,’ Saudi Aramco CEO warns — Bloomberg

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

00:18:03 KST

NEW YORK, October 5. /TASS/. Global oil stockpiles have become "scarily thin," creating a risk of worsening market conditions unless shipping through the Strait of Hormuz fully resumes, Saudi Aramco President and CEO Amin Nasser warned, Bloomberg reported.
"Until Hormuz fully re-opens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify," the chief executive said at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. "While the squeeze on crude is serious, refined fuel prices have risen even more sharply."
According to Nasser, global oil consumption continues to rise, meaning that countries will require additional supplies for at least the next two years to replenish their inventories. This could trigger an extra demand of at least 2 million barrels per day.
The Aramco chief noted that at the onset of the US-Iran military conflict, global oil inventories stood at approximately 10 billion barrels. They have since plummeted to less than 6 billion barrels, with only about 10% of that volume practically available due to technical constraints. Meanwhile, Persian Gulf producers have already managed to ramp up exports to near prewar levels, Nasser added.
Earlier, Reuters reported that Saudi Aramco had unexpectedly slashed its November official selling prices (OSPs) for Asia to six-year lows. According to company data, the price of its flagship Arab Light crude for Asian buyers was set at $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai benchmark. The agency noted that this adjusted discount marked the widest since June 2020.
On October 2, the Group of Seven (G7) nations agreed, in coordination with the International Energy Agency (IEA), to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products from strategic reserves over a four-month period. The G7 specifically indicated that, during the first 20 days, member countries and their partners intend to prioritize the drawdown of significant volumes of diesel fuel.

Kyiv • UNN
Rheinmetall and Argotec have launched the partnership's first satellite into orbit. It will collect data for early warning and air defense systems.
German defense contractor Rheinmetall, together with Italian space company Argotec, has launched the first satellite as part of a strategic partnership. It is intended to collect intelligence on aerial threats and transmit information to air defense systems. This was stated in a Rheinmetall press release, reports UNN.
Details
The satellite was launched into orbit on October 1 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the U.S. Space Force’s Vandenberg base in California. Rheinmetall is developing this capability through its Italian subsidiary, Rheinmetall Italia S.p.A., as part of a broader expansion of its activities in the space sector.
Unlike traditional Earth-observation satellites, which are primarily intended for mapping or imaging the planet’s surface, this Rheinmetall program focuses on collecting intelligence relevant to the operation of air defense systems.
The satellite’s sensors are intended to detect ground-based indicators associated with the emergence of aerial threats. The resulting imagery and situational data are intended to provide early-warning information that defense and air defense systems will be able to use.
Rheinmetall says it will process the data collected using artificial intelligence before integrating it into existing national defense and air defense systems. The company plans to combine space-based surveillance with ground stations and tactical networks, connecting the various components through a command-and-control center.
This approach is intended to provide access to information obtained from orbit within existing defense networks, rather than turning the satellite into a standalone surveillance system.

Astronomers catch dwarf stars gobbling up their orbiting companions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:16:21 UTC
00:16:21 KST

As far as fairytales go, dwarfs can be Bashful, Sleepy, Grumpy or Dopey. But in space, dwarfs might be better called Hungry, according to a pair of studies published Monday in Nature Astronomy.
These are dwarf stars, of course. Some dwarf stars are small, dim stars that can be orbited by other dwarf stars or planets. Our own sun is a yellow dwarf star; other types include orange and red dwarfs. White, brown and (if proven to exist) blue dwarfs are the dead remnants of stars or failed stars. Understanding these stars and their remains is key to unlocking the history of galaxies—and planets.
In the new research, scientists describe two dwarf stars—one red dwarf and one white dwarf—seemingly acting out: eating the objects that orbit them.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The observations “seek to understand the effect stars have on the planets that they host,” says Jamie Williams, lead author of one of the studies and a Ph.D. student at the University of Warwick in England.
“The key takeaway is that planets don’t exist in isolation, but their evolution is directly tied to the star they orbit,” he says. “In order to understand the life of planets, we must understand star-planet interactions.”
Williams and his colleagues observed a white dwarf that showed some unusual chemical signatures, including zinc, copper and niobium. At the same time, the star’s brightness seemed to dim periodically, suggesting an orbiting planet. Together, the results suggest the planet formed after the star had died and that its atmosphere is now feeding the white dwarf.
The finding suggests “planetary systems can experience a rebirth,” a phenomenon astronomers haven’t observed in our solar system before, Williams says.
The second study also reveals a never-before-seen interaction: a red dwarf slowly and steadily consuming its orbital object, a brown dwarf. Usually, either a star and its companion mind their own business or the star completely and rapidly devours its neighbor. In this system, material seems to be flowing from the brown dwarf to the red dwarf in a process that could continue for millions of years.
The discovery was “a happy accident,” says Aaron Householder, lead author of that study and a graduate student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Now that the team has observed this, Householder adds, he’s curious what else is out there.
“We’re excited to see if we can find a star eating a planet or maybe even two planets eating each other—different types of combinations of these objects,” he says.
Both studies have implications for our own planet. A second-generation planet could theoretically form after our own sun dies, Williams says. Meanwhile, Householder’s research suggests that rather than make a quick and fiery meal of Earth, the sun might one day nibble away at our atmosphere.

The New Nixon Shock? Why Japan Fears a Trump-Xi Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:16:00 UTC
00:16:00 KST

The latest China-U.S. summit, held from September 23 to 25, raised concerns in Japan, not so much because of its substance as because of how it appeared. Japanese media have paid particular attention to Donald Trump and Xi Jinping’s references to their respective countries as former “allies” that fought against imperial Japan, as well as to Trump’s apparent intentions. Within the Japanese government, “confusion” has reportedly been expressed internally.
Before the summit, the Japanese government had been preparing for the worst-case scenario, a concern presumably heightened by the U.S. president’s suggestion, immediately after his previous summit with Xi, that arms shipments to Taiwan could be used as a possible “negotiation tool.”
Japan’s Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae was able to secure a meeting with Trump before his meeting with Xi. Following her brief meeting with Trump, Takaichi indicated that their conversation had “the U.S.-China summit in mind” and that they had exchanged views in a timely manner on various issues concerning China. She also noted that “it is important that U.S.-China relations contribute to stability in international relations, including between Japan and the United States,” implying that Japan would prefer the U.S. not to pursue a unilateral deal with China that could come at Japan’s expense.
After the Trump-Xi summit, Japan has seemingly sought to manage expectations and reassure the public. Immediately after the meeting, Takaichi posted on X in Japanese that Trump had provided her with a “detailed explanation of the recent U.S.-China summit.” She also highlighted the significance of holding “two meetings between our leaders within the span of a single week,” describing this as a “demonstration of the strength of the Japan-U.S. alliance.”
Reports reinforcing the narrative that the China-U.S. détente does not overshadow Japan-U.S. relations have also emerged from unofficial government sources. According to the Yomiuri Shimbun, several Japanese government officials told the newspaper that Trump reportedly praised Takaichi in his talks with Xi, describing her as a “strong leader,” and urged the leaders of Japan and China to hold talks with each other, among other remarks.
Despite Trump’s propensity for unconventional remarks, which understandably raise concerns about the future direction of U.S. policy toward Japan and the rest of the world, bureaucratic cooperation between the two countries has continued to deepen. Meanwhile, Piero Tozzi, a policy expert affiliated with the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a conservative U.S. think tank close to Trump, has emphasized that the current administration continues to view China as a strategic competitor.
However, perceptions matter when it comes to maintaining a stable Japan-U.S. relationship, which helps explain the Japanese government’s considerable efforts to influence the outcome of the China-U.S. summit and shape the narrative surrounding it.
Following the Vietnam War, which a significant portion of the Japanese public regarded as an immoral and unnecessary war against the Vietnamese, and the two so-called “Nixon Shocks” – Washington’s abrupt shift toward China and its unilateral economic measures in 1971 – the Japanese public’s perception of the United States deteriorated sharply. Both developments were particularly jarring because they were undertaken with little or no prior consultation with Tokyo, reinforcing a sense in Japan that Washington could fundamentally alter the strategic and economic environment without taking Japanese interests into account.
Indeed, the U.S. government itself recognized that Nixon’s dual announcement, which came without prior consultation with Japan, had produced major shock waves in the country. Seeking to repair the damage to bilateral relations, Nixon subsequently made a point of meeting with the Japanese emperor and empress. While Nixon’s secrecy surrounding the opening to China, which rattled the Japanese public most deeply, was driven more by his desire to outmaneuver his “enemies” – ranging from State Department officials to the media – than by a commitment to unilateralism, what mattered to Japan was less the substance of the decision than the lack of diplomatic courtesy.
The deterioration in American popularity in Japan was striking. According to polling, the proportion of Japanese who said they liked the U.S. fell from 33 percent in 1970 to 18 percent in 1973 – a decline of nearly half. The dynamics seen in the 1970s attest to the importance of the “theater” of international relations and its impact on Japanese perceptions of the world. A similar concern – or perhaps the lessons learned from that period – seems to be shaping the present moment, as the notable shift in tone between the United States and China is generating speculation about how the structure of world affairs will continue to evolve.
However, there are important differences in the concerns of the Japanese public today. While U.S. distrust in the 1970s was partly driven by fears of being entrapped in the Vietnam War, as well as by a sense that the U.S. was attempting to contain Japan’s postwar economic miracle – a source of considerable national pride – these are not the same emotions that Japanese people are experiencing today. In one of the most tense security environments in recent decades, and amid the decline of U.S. relative strength, Japanese concerns are centered more on abandonment than entrapment. Moreover, Japan no longer sees the U.S. as an economic competitor, as it did during the 1970s, but rather as an opportunity for economic growth.
This is not to say that Japanese concerns are trivial. The highly personalized nature of U.S. foreign policy today will continue to fuel concerns that spheres of influence could emerge in the Indo-Pacific and that Taiwan could be “lost.” To avert such a situation, day-to-day diplomacy with the United States matters. In the immediate aftermath of the Trump-Xi summit, Japan’s approach appears to be working.

Dennis Hastert, former US House speaker and admitted child molester, dies at 84

Dennis Hastert, former US House speaker and admitted child molester, dies at 84
- Dennis Hastert, former US House speaker and admitted child molester, died at 84 from natural causes, having served as a powerful Republican leader from 1999 to 2007.
- Hastert pleaded guilty to bank fraud linked to hush-money payments for sexual abuse of boys he coached, but was not charged for abuse due to the statute of limitations.
- His legacy was marred by scandal, removal of his portrait, and the controversial "Hastert Rule" that deepened partisan divides in Congress.
AI generated
Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican US House of Representatives speaker who later admitted to sexually abusing boys as a high school wrestling coach and pleaded guilty to charges arising from the scandal, has died, CBS News reported on Oct 5, citing a coroner in Illinois. He was 84.
Hastert, sentenced in April 2016 to 15 months in prison for bank fraud for trying to cover up payments to keep his molestation secret, died at his home over the weekend due to natural causes, Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell told CBS News.
Known as “Denny” to his friends, Hastert was one of the United States’ most powerful politicians during his time leading the lower chamber of Congress from January 1999 to January 2007, during the presidencies of Democrat Bill Clinton and Republican George W. Bush.
The burly Midwestern conservative had been seen as an amiable lawmaker, although his leadership tactics perpetuated the partisan polarisation in Congress. His reputation was destroyed eight years after he quit the House when revelations emerged about his sexual abuse of boys as a civics teacher and coach at Yorkville High School in suburban Chicago from the 1960s to the early 1980s.
“The defendant is a serial child molester,” US District Judge Thomas Durkin said of Hastert when he sentenced him, at age 74, to prison. “Some actions can obliterate a lifetime of good works.”
‘Don’t be a coward, Mr Hastert’
Hastert pleaded guilty to violating federal banking laws by structuring financial transactions to evade bank reporting requirements to try to keep hush-money payments to a sexual abuse victim hidden. Hastert did not face criminal charges for sexually abusing the boys because the statute of limitations had long expired.
Prosecutors detailed Hastert’s actions towards five boys as young as 14. They said Hastert, exploiting his position of authority as the school’s wrestling coach, committed acts including “intentional touching of minors’ groin area and genitals or oral sex with a minor”.
In one instance, they said, Hastert asked a boy during a wrestling camp to stay in his hotel room, and then abused him. That boy, decades later, confronted Hastert about the abuse. Hastert made a secret deal to pay him US$3.5 million (S$4.5 million) to compensate him for his ordeal and buy his silence.
When law enforcement authorities investigated suspicious withdrawals from Hastert’s bank account stemming from payments to his victim, he initially said they were nothing unusual. Hastert, through his lawyer, then lied to investigators that he was the victim of an extortion attempt by someone falsely accusing him of sexual abuse.
After suffering a stroke, a frail Hastert entered his sentencing hearing in a wheelchair.
“I want to apologise to the boys I mistreated when I was their coach,” Hastert told the judge.
“Don’t be a coward, Mr Hastert,” the sister of one of the victims said in court. “Tell the truth. What you did wasn’t misconduct. It was sexual abuse of a minor.”
The judge also ordered Hastert to enter a sex offender treatment programme and pay US$250,000 to a victims’ fund.
Hastert’s portrait was removed from the US Capitol building. His alma mater Wheaton College stripped his name from a public policy centre.
‘The Hastert rule’
John Dennis Hastert was born on Jan 2, 1942, in Aurora, Illinois, and grew up on a farm. After six years in the Illinois legislature, he was elected to the US House in 1986. He represented his Illinois district outside Chicago for two decades.
Fortuitous circumstances led to his accession as speaker.
With House Republicans moving towards impeaching Clinton over his extramarital affair with White House intern Monica Lewinsky, the abrasive and strident Georgian Newt Gingrich stepped down as speaker three days after the 1998 elections.
Gingrich’s designated successor, Bob Livingston of Louisiana, then abruptly resigned after acknowledging his own extramarital affairs.
House Republicans turned to Hastert, a self-described born-again Christian seen at the time as untainted by scandal and who called Clinton’s affair immoral. Hastert served as speaker for eight years, placing him second in the line of succession to the presidency.
In 2006, he passed Joseph Cannon as the longest-serving Republican House speaker. Hastert resigned from the House in November 2007, having lost the speaker’s job when Democrats regained control of the House in the 2006 elections.
Hastert contributed to the increasing partisan divide in Washington. As speaker, Hastert marshalled his own often-fractious Republican legislators to pass conservative Bills with little or no outreach to the Democratic minority.
He was credited with instituting the “Hastert Rule” under which only Bills supported by “the majority of the majority” party would be brought to a vote on the House floor. As a result, he let major legislation die rather than allow it to pass with mostly Democratic support.
The House ethics committee in 2006 found Hastert, along with other Republican leaders, negligent in failing to protect teenage boys from sexual advances by a gay Florida Republican congressman named Mark Foley. The boys were congressional pages, doing chores and errands for members of Congress.
The panel said the inaction by Hastert and the other Republicans might have been intended to insulate fellow Republican Foley from political harm. The Foley scandal contributed to the Republicans losing control of the House.
After leaving Congress, Hastert became a highly paid lobbyist.
Hastert married his wife Jean in 1973. They had two sons. REUTERS

According to Monteput, Montenegro's state-owned highway company and the project investor, the bypass will connect the Budva-Cetinje road near Markovici with the Budva-Tivat road near Lastva Grbaljska.
The project is part of Montenegro's broader plan to develop an integrated network of highways and expressways. ■

British Army Brings Cavalry Back—This Time for Modern Battlefield Recon
The British Army is experimenting with horses for reconnaissance, patrol, and security missions in terrain where conventional military vehicles may struggle to operate, according to imagery released by the UK Ministry of Defence and reported by UK Defence Journal on October 5.
Soldiers and Military Working Horses from the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took part in a mounted combat capability experiment at the Barossa training area in Sandhurst on September 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The trial explored whether mounted troops could offer useful mobility in modern battlefield environments beyond the regiment’s better-known ceremonial role.
The exercise focused on difficult ground where narrow routes, broken terrain or limited vehicle access could complicate the movement of conventional military platforms.
Soldiers conducted patrols in pairs from horseback while using SA80 sighting systems to locate and track simulated enemy positions, testing how mounted personnel could maintain observation and identify potential threats while moving through challenging terrain.
The Ministry of Defence stressed that the experiment was intended to examine a niche capability rather than signal a return to large-scale cavalry formations across the British Army. Instead, planners are looking at whether horses could provide a practical option in specific environments where vehicles are less effective or unable to move freely.
Mounted troops offer a different mobility profile from mechanized units, particularly in areas with steep, wooded, narrow or heavily disrupted terrain. Horses can move across ground that may restrict larger vehicles while allowing soldiers to carry equipment and cover greater distances than they could comfortably manage on foot.
According to the MOD, the Sandhurst experiment also drew on lessons from international partners as the Army considered how mounted units might contribute to reconnaissance, patrol and security operations.
While the last cavalry charge in British military history took place in 1917, the idea of mounted units is being revisited—not for traditional combat, but for mobility in difficult terrain where vehicles struggle.
Previously, the British Army was exploring whether horses could once again play a practical role in modern warfare, drawing on lessons from allied forces and recent battlefield experience.

Held for the first time in Türkiye, the five-day event runs until Friday under the theme "The World Needs More Space."

World Insights: What could shape Brazil's tight presidential runoff
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
23:13:32 CST
00:13:32 KST

by Xinhua writers Lu Junyu, Chen Haoquan and Wu Hao
RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's presidential election is heading to a runoff on Oct. 25 after a tight first-round vote on Sunday, with Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party and incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party separated by only about 2 percentage points.
The first-round results underscored the continued polarization of Brazilian politics, with the two candidates together securing over 90 percent of valid votes. Over the next three weeks, attention will focus on why the race remains so close, how U.S.-Brazil ties could affect the campaign, and where the two candidates could find additional support.
WHY THE CLOSE RACE?
The first-round vote was highly concentrated around the two leading candidates. Flavio Bolsonaro led the first round with about 47 percent of valid votes, followed by Lula with about 45 percent, while all other candidates received less than 5 percent each.
Brazilian media said the gap of less than 2 percentage points between the two was the narrowest presidential first-round margin since Brazil's return to democracy.
Both candidates also have relatively firm political bases but face considerable public rejection; therefore, the runoff begins with two relatively consolidated political camps, leaving less room to win over committed supporters of the other side, local media reported, citing political analysts.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, voters can decline to support any candidate by casting blank or null ballots, a choice that can also serve as an expression of political discontent.
Low voter enthusiasm has added another layer of uncertainty to the election.
According to official results, with more than 99 percent of ballots counted, turnout in the first round was weighed down by an abstention rate of 21.08 percent, while blank and null ballots together accounted for about 5 percent of votes cast.
A pre-election survey by Brazilian pollster Datafolha found that 47 percent of respondents were less interested in this election than in the previous one. Another poll, by consultancy Quaest, showed that 23 percent were "completely uninterested" in the race, while a further 10 percent said they might abstain or cast a blank or null ballot.
With the two political camps already highly consolidated, supporters of the eliminated candidates and voters aligned with neither side could become more important in the runoff.
For Flavio Bolsonaro, consolidating support from voters who backed other right-wing and center-right candidates will be important. Lula, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to voters outside his traditional base with measures addressing livelihood concerns, including tighter regulation of online betting and help for indebted households.
Turnout will also matter for both sides. With less than 2 percentage points separating the two candidates, mobilizing potential supporters who stayed home could dominate the runoff campaign.
HOW COULD U.S. TIES AFFECT THE RACE?
Beyond the complex domestic political landscape, the United States has continued to affect this year's election. U.S.-Brazil relations have become increasingly strained over the past year, with disputes ranging from tariffs and judicial proceedings to visa restrictions.
The U.S. administration has imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods and criticized the conviction of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was found guilty of attempting a coup after losing his reelection bid, while Lula's government has accused Washington of exerting political pressure on Brazil.
Those tensions have increasingly intersected with the presidential race. U.S. President Donald Trump, who maintained close ties with Jair Bolsonaro, said shortly before the election that he was watching the Brazilian vote "very closely."
Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, has advocated closer ties with Washington, while Lula's campaign has accused the Trump administration of seeking to interfere in Brazil's presidential election.
But the U.S. factor may prove counterproductive in electoral terms. Pressure from Washington could give Lula more room to emphasize national sovereignty and resistance to foreign pressure.
Daily newspaper Folha de S.Paulo noted that when the United States imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian goods in 2025, Lula's approval ratings rose as his government adopted a stronger sovereignty-focused response. ■

Ireland coach wants UEFA to keep team apart from Israel

Breadcrumb
Ireland coach wants UEFA to keep team apart from Israel after contentious games
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrímsson wants UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future competitions after their contentious Nations League games.
The teams drew 1-1 in Ireland's "home" game in Backa Topola, Serbia, on Sunday, a week after Ireland's 3-0 win in Israel's "home" game in Debrecen, Hungary.
Irish players came under pressure not to play the games because of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza; however, players voted to play, sparking fierce backlash from pro-Palestine supporters.
Ireland's goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu boycotted the match against Israel last Sunday.
Irish players wore black armbands and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the first match. They repeated the gesture for the second match, when the Israeli players wore black armbands for the 7 October attacks.
Hallgrímsson told Ireland's national broadcaster RTÉ afterwards that he thinks UEFA should keep the sides apart in future.
"There is obviously a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There are not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does," Hallgrímsson said.
"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we have gone through these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."
Contentious pairing
Calls in Ireland to boycott the games against Israel started as soon as the Nations League draw pitted the countries against each other in February. Israel's visit to Dublin would likely have triggered large protests and posed a major security challenge for the local police.
The FAI, which filed a motion the previous November calling on UEFA to ban Israel from club and international competitions, resisted calls for a boycott, arguing the team could face punishing sanctions from UEFA. Ireland is co-hosting the 2028 European Championship with England, Wales and Scotland.
In June, the FAI said it was moving Ireland's home game to Serbia for "operational reasons" and that no fans would be present.
Israel was already playing its home games in Hungary because of the war.
Damaged relations
Relations between Ireland and Israel will not have improved following their meetings on the field. Tempers boiled over at times on Sunday, and a clash occurred before halftime when Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle said an Israeli player spat at him.
"There's been a lot of those incidents that could have escalated," Hallgrímsson said. "We were clever enough to stop it before it went too far. I felt it was kind of the intention to try to intimidate us and make us do something stupid."
An Israeli journalist said at the pre-match press conference the day before that the Irish players had called the Israeli players "monkeys" during the previous match, prompting an immediate rebuke from Irish communications officer Kieran Crowley, who said it was "a lie" and ended the press conference.
Ireland forward Adam Idah, who is Black, was reportedly racially abused by a small number of Israeli fans present during the first match.

Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:08:58 UTC
00:08:58 KST

Ukraine's Security and Defense Forces have "put out of action" more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity through recent long-range strikes, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said in a statement published by the Defense Ministry on 4 October. These "carefully thought-out" actions were aimed at "bleeding the Russian war machine" and "destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
Ukraine treats Russia's refineries as a priority target because their revenue helps fund the war. Even Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 1 October that the strikes had cost Russia 1% of its GDP and had "partially" achieved their goal, Interfax reported.
The ministry did not publish how it calculated the figure.
"The consequences of Ukrainian operations are not always visible immediately. But the effect accumulates and produces a tangible result," the ministry said.
Ukrainian deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory
The ministry named eight recently struck facilities, among others. One of them is the Moscow Oil Refinery, which Ukraine targeted in a massive drone attack on the night of 20 September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The refinery, operated by Gazprom Neft in Moscow's Kapotnya district, supplies about 40% of Moscow's fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region's demand for gasoline and aviation fuel, according to Russian news Telegram channel Astra.
Another was KINEF, which Ukraine has attacked repeatedly. It is Russia's second-largest oil refinery by capacity, and the Ukrainian military struck it on the night of 30 August, setting off a fire at the facility.
The ministry also named the Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries and the Ust-Luga port complex.
Ukraine triples production and procurement of long-range drones—and this is not the end
This year, Ukraine has tripled the production and procurement of long-range attack drones, the ministry said.
"This is not the limit. We will continue to scale up deep-strike capabilities," the statement said.
International cooperation is part of that push. Berlin will fund the production of additional DeepStrike-class long-range drones in Ukraine, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said after a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on 15 April. The sides also agreed to jointly develop and produce a medium- and long-range drone system.
Ukraine and Germany also signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on 8 July. The Bars' modular design allows it to be used for deep strikes, among other missions.
Oil refinery output has fallen
Russian refineries cut crude oil processing by 14% in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year amid Ukrainian drone attacks, according to calculations by two industry sources.
Experts' estimates of the decline differ widely. In August, Serhii Vakulenko of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center put it at 25–28%, while Russian economic commentator Vyacheslav Shiryaev put it at 65–70%, according to Defense-Aerospace.
Fuel production data give a more concrete picture: in July, Russia's gasoline and diesel output was about a quarter to a third lower than in March 2026, the outlet reported.

Russia's military spending masks a longer-term strategy for a prolonged war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:08:52 UTC
00:08:52 KST

What does Russia's rising military budget say about its plans for the war?
Russia's President Vladimir Putin (C) looks on as he visits an observation post during the "Center-2026" strategic command-and-staff exercise at the Chebarkulsky training ground in Chelyabinsk on Oct. 2, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
The Russian government began the month by submitting a three-year budget plan to parliament, proposing yet another increase in funding for its war against Ukraine.
On the surface, the planned increase looks substantial. Russia's overall military budget is set to rise to around 17 trillion rubles (approximately $200 billion) in 2027, up from 12 trillion rubles in 2026 — a 27% increase in nominal spending.
When combined with spending on law enforcement, another heavy budget line, expenditures on the military and security forces account for 43% of the total government spending.
The figures are striking, but experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent cautioned that they can be misleading.
Rather than pointing to a sudden surge in military spending, the latest budget figures suggest that Russia is continuing to gradually build up and sustain its military capacity, signaling a readiness for a prolonged war.
read also
Big numbers
Next year, Russia's military and security forces will get more money than any other sector — only 21% of the 2027 budget is allocated to healthcare, education, and social payments combined. That is generally similar to what is directly funneled to the military, but only half of the number when allocations to security forces are added.
Russia's high military budget would also be maintained in 2028 and 2029, according to the three-year budget plan.
"It's difficult to speculate, but the planned budget hike suggests that (the Kremlin) may intend to recruit more people (into the army) under contract in 2027," said Michael Kofman, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Guesses on the actual purpose of the increases can only be speculative, argued in turn Pavel Luzin, a researcher with the Center for European Policy Analysis.
On top of the already high military budget, the Russian government can additionally increase funding throughout the year without parliamentary approval, said Sergey Aleksashenko, an exiled Russian economist and former deputy finance minister.
"Basically, the numbers we are seeing, this is what the Kremlin wants us to see," he said. "Around May (this year), the Defense Ministry requested additional funding from Vladimir Putin, and this request was granted."
While Russia does not publish detailed data on military spending, Luzin agreed that the figures for 2026 were likely higher than what was settled in the Russian government's initial budget: "approximately 16-17 trillion rubles, in my assessment," the researcher told the Kyiv Independent.
As for funding on healthcare, education, and social payments, these are set to decrease next year, Russian economist Alexandra Prokopenko found in a recent study.
Nothing dramatically new on the military spending front
The 27% army budget increase may sound significant, but this number is a bit misleading, Aleksashenko said.
"Russian military expenditures are growing step by step, but not as dramatically as (this figure) would suggest, because that number was calculated on the wrong basis," the Russian economist added.
According to him, instead of basing the increase on Russia's initial plans for 2026, these should be compared to what Russia actually spent throughout the year: in that case, the increase would be much lower.
"It's not extraordinary that the government admitted that it will spend at least 17 trillion rubles on the military in 2027," Luzin agreed.
The bulk of the on-paper increase is linked to inflation, specifically cost-push inflation in the military industry, but also salaries and payments to wounded and families of killed Russian soldiers, the researcher added.
"At the same time, the Russian government is also beginning a new round of investments, trying to modernize the sector, because Russia's military industry cannot produce more than it did (at its peak) in 2024," he added.
In fact, Russia's upcoming budget says more about how the government wants to raise money for the war, Prokopenko explained — more than it does about how much money will be spent and on what.
"Officially, Russia's budget deficit is to be cut to 2.2% in 2027, but since the start of the full-scale invasion, the government never managed to stick to the original budget deficit plans," Prokopenko said. "For instance, for 2026, the plan was to keep the deficit to 1,6%, as opposed to 2,6% in 2025, but in the end the projection for this year is 3,2%."
Russia fills its deficit either through taking out money from its National Wealth Fund or by borrowing on the internal market, Prokopenko said.
However, the Russian government is having trouble attracting private businesses and citizens to invest in bonds — as a result, when Russia's Central Bank conducted its most recent bond auction, major state-owned banks bought around 84% of the total sum, Prokopenko said.
To raise money for the war in Ukraine, Russia also raised taxes, for instance by hiking VAT rates to 22% in 2026, by overall increasing income tax the previous year, and by introducing a planned tax on dividends and yields on bonds starting in 2027.
While Russia is clearly looking for money for the war, and the prime role of state-owned banks in financing debt can look awkward, this says little about the actual state of the Russian economy, Aleksashenko said.
"I don't see any problems on the financial or the economic side which would make Putin stop the war," the Russian economist argued.
"He is generally conservative with expenditures, so I don't think we'll be seeing a sudden boost in boots on the ground. As for the cost of this war (to the Russian economy), unfortunately, while it might not be sustainable in the long run, Putin sees the price to pay as acceptable."

The Czech Ministry of Defense has canceled a tender to purchase 185 armored vehicles worth 24.7 billion Czech korunas (approximately €1 billion).
This is evidenced by an official notice of the procurement cancellation, published in the Czech public procurement register, according to Ekonomický deník.
The bidding process was halted while awaiting preliminary proposals, which were due by September 30.
The decision was justified by circumstances requiring special attention and economic factors.
Officially, the project involved procuring equipment for the engineering corps, medical services, and military police.
The procurement process became complicated because of the large number of specifications and requirements, which caused potential bidders to lose interest.
According to a market analysis conducted back in 2018, the Australian Bushmaster armored vehicle was considered the most suitable platform for the army.
This vehicle met the criteria for combat experience and did not require time-consuming development of a new platform.
Joint production and maintenance of the vehicles were planned to be carried out at the Czech state-owned enterprise VOP CZ.
Currently, the issue of providing the Czech Army’s medical and engineering units with armored wheeled vehicles remains unresolved.
Previously, the American company Flyer Defense, in partnership with the Czech STV Group, delivered the first batch of F72-HD heavy tactical vehicles to the Czech Republic.
In total, the country is set to receive 46 such vehicles, which the U.S. government is providing free of charge under the Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program in gratitude for its support of Ukraine.

Why the U.S. Bomber Withdrawal From a U.K. Air Base Is Significant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:07:36 UTC
00:07:36 KST

President Donald Trump said Monday afternoon that "threats" had prompted the U.S. to remove all of its B-1 Air Force bombers from the RAF Fairford base in southern England over the weekend. The move came a week after several men were arrested nearby in relation to a suspected terror plot, which the U.K. government believes may be linked to Iran.
When asked if there was a specific threat that led to the bombers being moved, Trump told reporters: “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident. There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy… why should we leave them there? We moved them around a little bit, not very far.”
He added that Washington “actually knows the people that made the threat.” When asked if they are linked to Iran, Trump responded: “They would be linked to Iran.”
A U.S. Defense Department official had earlier told TIME that all the U.S. bombers had been ”re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” but did not offer a specific reason behind the move, instead saying that U.S. bombers “routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.” The official added that America’s bomber force remains “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities… anywhere, anytime.” Hours before Trump's remarks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed the idea that the removal of U.S. bombers was directly connected to the foiled Fairford plot, insisting he has “confidence” in the security of U.S. bases.
A spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the RAF Fairford base remains safe, but refused to offer any specific comment on the military operations of “foreign nations.” The British Ministry of Defense directed TIME to the U.S. Air Force when approached for comment.
The move comes after five men, all U.K. nationals, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses on Sept. 27, following a suspected terror plot nearby RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base. Amid ongoing investigations, British counterterrorism police arrested a dual British-Iranian national in central London on Oct. 1 on suspicion of terrorist acts in connection with the incident. All arrestees have been released on bail.
David Dunn, a professor of international politics at the University of Birmingham, says the U.S. withdrawal from Fairford is “historic, unprecedented, and an indication of the sense of vulnerability” surrounding U.S. military assets abroad.
“Fairford is normally the place during a crisis where America sends bombers to beef up America's military capability and its formal operating bases, whether that's for operations in Europe, like the Kosovo campaign, or for operations in the Gulf through 2003 onwards, or indeed for operations in Iran,” Dunn tells TIME. “This [removal] is an indication of concerns about the safety of those assets in their forward operating bases.”
Dunn adds “the haste” with which the operation took place over the weekend is also noteworthy, referencing reports that some of the aircraft had only been there for a relatively short period of time, having arrived recently as part of a rotation.
U.K. and U.S. officials suspect Iranian involvement in RAF Fairford plot
Both U.K. and U.S. officials have voiced suspicion of Iranian involvement in the suspected terror plot that has led to several arrests.
Burnham on Sept. 30 said the U.K. believes Iran was likely involved in the incident. “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” he said, adding that British forces were “working closely” with U.S. counterparts.
Iran has vehemently denied any involvement. In the immediate aftermath of the initial arrests, the Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. After Burnham’s comments, Iran doubled down on its denial, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing the U.K. of “barking up the wrong tree.”
Trump previously said the five men arrested at the scene had been under “investigation” prior to the arrests and were looking to cause “big damage.” Asked whether Iran was involved in the suspect terror plot, he said, “it might be,” but did not offer further details.
Dunn says that although Iran “hasn't got the range to [directly] attack bases in the U.K.,” it does not necessarily remove the potential threat to U.S. assets stationed there. “Iran—by doing things via proxies, organized criminal gangs, or hiring people gangs through payments through the dark web—can still have a military effect and a deterrent effect on the operation of a base like Fairford,” he says.
Counter Terrorism Policing has said it is looking at all angles, citing possible foreign-state involvement as one line of inquiry. It has urged against conclusions being drawn in what is a high-profile and active investigation.
How RAF Fairford has supported U.S. military operations for decades
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. The base, which opened in 1944, has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
The U.S. Air Force describes RAF Fairford as its “preferred” European “bomber forward operating location” and previously said it has used Fairford “nearly continuously” since the base was constructed.
Former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially refused to allow U.S. access to U.K. military bases in its offensive strikes against Iran—a move that earned him the wrath of Trump. Starmer changed his position in March, authorizing the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned the base could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military, insisting it makes the U.K. a “participant in aggression” in the war.
Starmer had previously warned the British public of the general threat posed by Iran. On Feb. 28, in an address to the nation hours after the U.S. and Israel launched its initial strikes against Iran, he said: “Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community. Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil.”

15:05:07 UTC
00:05:07 KST

A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.
"Ukraine has repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate and guarantee security in the Black Sea. There have also been corresponding proposals from third countries," Zelensky said.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian ships instead of normal navigation. Pressure is needed to restore global food security. And everyone who is truly interested in this should help."
Romania's Interior Ministry later said 11 crew members had been rescued. The vessel was sinking, while injured survivors were evacuated for emergency medical treatment. Romanian authorities had not provided details about the cause of the fire.
The incident is the latest in a string of Russian attacks that has crippled civilian and commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Ukraine's maritime corridor, opened in 2023 after Russia withdrew from the U.N.-backed grain deal, has been largely closed again after a spate of Russian attacks, both on port infrastructure and ships themselves, over summer 2026.
The International Maritime Organization has warned that the war poses a "serious and immediate threat" to crews and vessels operating in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
The latest incident comes two days after a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged cargo ship in Ukraine's Odesa region killed one person and injured three, according to Ukrainian port authorities cited by Reuters.
