Economic Watch: Holiday travel highlights China's transport strength, economic vitality
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
22:26:47 CST
23:26:47 KST

Passengers prepare to board a train at Nanjing South Railway Station in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, Sept. 30, 2026. China's railway network saw a peak in passenger flow on Wednesday, one day before the beginning of the seven-day National Day holiday. (Photo by Su Yang/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- For Zhang Yang and his family in Ankang, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, this year's National Day holiday was a memorable one. On Oct. 1, following the opening of the Xi'an-Ankang high-speed railway, they took a direct high-speed train from Ankang to Yan'an, a city known for its revolutionary history.
The journey, which used to take more than seven hours, now takes just over two hours.
The Zhang family was among millions on the move during the National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, one of China's peak periods for travel and spending.
Data from the Ministry of Transport showed cross-regional passenger trips exceeded 300 million on each of the first three days of the holiday. China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said the country's railways handled over 25.2 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record.
For a country as vast as China, moving hundreds of millions of people during a holiday rush is a feat of scale. Behind this feat lies a transport network built up over decades.
By the end of 2025, China's comprehensive transport network spanned more than 6 million km, including the world's largest high-speed rail network. High-speed railways, expressways, airports and ports connect cities, towns and rural areas across the country.
The network is continuing to expand. On Sept. 28, China opened four major high-speed railway sections across northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, with a combined length of more than 1,100 km. The new lines further shorten travel times and put more destinations within easy reach of families like Zhang's.
China's transport development goes beyond faster journeys. Better supporting services are also making travel more convenient.
New energy vehicles (NEVs) have become increasingly common among Chinese households and are now a popular choice for long-distance travel. The Ministry of Transport expects NEV trips on expressways during the holiday to reach 1.8 times the usual level, pushing up demand for charging services.
China's extensive charging infrastructure is helping to meet growing demand. The country now has more than 24 million EV charging facilities, forming the world's largest EV charging network. Highway service areas have about 89,000 charging facilities in total, covering virtually all service areas.
To handle the holiday peak, mobile emergency chargers have been added at key service areas, while drivers are encouraged to leave after charging their batteries to 80 percent to improve charging turnover.
Faster connections and more convenient services are making it easier for travelers to visit more destinations in a single trip. Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that nearly 30 percent of travelers had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year.
The trend extends beyond China's borders. China's expanding transport links are supporting a rise in cross-border travel, with Chinese airlines operating regular international passenger routes connecting 177 cities in 80 countries.
For outbound travel, Qunar data showed that hotel bookings for multi-country trips more than doubled year on year during the holiday. Inbound tourism also recorded double-digit growth, according to Trip.com Group, with day-tour bookings up more than fourfold and train ticket bookings up more than 170 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks.
The transport network that carries millions of travelers is also keeping goods moving, linking businesses and markets and sustaining economic activity across the country.
Even during the holiday, the Liujing operating area of Nanning Port in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region bustles with activity, as ship horns sound and workers load and unload goods.
The increase in cargo traffic is closely linked to the opening of the Pinglu Canal. Stretching 134.2 km from Hengzhou in Guangxi to the Beibu Gulf, the canal opened to navigation on Sept. 16, providing a shorter river-sea route for cargo from southwest China to international markets.
Bulk cargo, including construction materials, auto parts and grain, is being shipped from Nanning Port via the Pinglu Canal to the Beibu Gulf for export. On average, the route now handles an additional 20,000 tonnes of cargo per day.
"We expect to transport 200,000 tonnes of cargo during the National Day holiday," said You Tong, deputy manager of the production operations center at Nanning Port Development and Investment Co., Ltd.
You said the port has optimized operations and maintained round-the-clock staffing to keep cargo moving smoothly during the holiday surge. ■

'We will get every last one': IDF says two-thirds of Oct. 7 terrorists eliminated, 2,000 remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:26:09 UTC
23:26:09 KST

Three years after the October 7 Hamas-led terrorist attack on southern Israel, with the manhunt and targeted killings of its perpetrators still ongoing, Military Intelligence Directorate chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder revealed Sunday night at a meeting of the Security Cabinet that most of the Gazans who crossed into Israel had been killed.
“Of the 6,000 who crossed the fence, 4,000 have been killed,” Binder said. “Two thousand remain — we will get every last one of them.”
His remarks came in response to Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu, who asked how many terrorists remained from among those who had infiltrated Israel during the attack.
Ministers were told in a briefing Sunday night that intelligence officials have recently identified increased Hamas preparations for renewed fighting in Gaza. Shin Bet chief David Zini also told ministers that Hamas was planning an attack or a localized kidnapping attempt close to the elections or shortly afterward.
According to the assessment, Hamas was biding its time to recruit manpower and stockpile weapons, including moving arms into civilian areas, on the assumption that until the elections in Israel and the United States, Israel’s hands are tied and it will not receive a green light for a large-scale operation in the Gaza Strip. Ministers were also presented with a warning about a possible multi-front incident.
Senior officials assess that Hamas’ military wing still has tens of thousands of operatives, a figure they say is not dramatically lower than before the Oct. 7 attack.
Officials say that is largely to be expected as long as Hamas remains Gaza’s governing authority, allowing it to continue indoctrinating young people and drawing from a steady pool of recruits. Hamas also offers salaries far higher than many young Gazans could earn elsewhere.
As long as Hamas retains its governing structure, the officials say, it can sustain forces on that scale. But they assess that those forces are now far less skilled and poorly trained, with significantly diminished weapons and military capabilities compared with before the Oct. 7 massacre.
The decline in proficiency is also tied to Hamas’ inability to conduct practical field training without risking Israeli detection and strikes, officials say.
The group also faces serious command-and-control problems after extensive losses among its leadership ranks. Hamas has struggled to find experienced commanders, with operatives promoted to key positions often killed and replaced in rapid succession.
While the positions themselves do not remain vacant for long, each successive replacement generally brings less experience, authority and training, steadily eroding the organization’s command structure.
Hamas seeks a 'Lebanon model' in Gaza
The senior officials analyzed Hamas’ current situation compared with the period before the massacre according to three strategic dimensions: the extent of its isolation from Egypt, the loss of territory and its rocket capabilities.
First, the terrorist organization is physically cut off from Egypt, its smuggling capabilities have diminished and the Rafah crossing is under full Israeli control. The officials described this as a dramatic development that harms Hamas’ ability to rebuild its military strength.
Smuggling now consists mainly of dual-use materials brought in through humanitarian aid entering Gaza, but not on the same scale as before the war. According to officials, this strategic shift has cut Hamas off from its main pipeline for rearmament.
Second is the loss of territory, as more than 60% of Gaza is controlled by Israel. According to the officials, Hamas has lost the ability to invade southern Israel. Nearly all of Gaza’s agricultural land has been lost, while entire cities and villages have been leveled.
They say that, even if Israel withdraws, rebuilding would take decades, both in the cities and villages that were destroyed and in terrorist infrastructure such as tunnels and other facilities.
Taken together, the officials said, these factors present Hamas with a strategic challenge. Ultimately, the organization has only limited ability to provide for the population’s needs, rearm itself and exercise effective control.
Third is its rocket capability. According to the officials, that capability still exists, though in a limited form, and Hamas is preserving various stockpiles for future use.
As for surrendering its weapons, officials assess that Hamas will deceive inspectors, perhaps hand over some of its weapons, which are limited in any case, and claim that it has given up everything it possesses.
Israel believes Hamas is seeking to shift toward a model resembling Hezbollah’s in Lebanon: transferring formal responsibility for managing civilian life to a national committee for the administration of Gaza, while preserving influence over that body through its own operatives and officials who remain within governing institutions.
Under that model, officials assess, Hamas could retain a significant degree of civilian influence without formally bearing responsibility for running the enclave, while at the same time diverting resources toward rebuilding its military strength.
Senior officials also point to Hamas' efforts to form a political front against Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas, together with additional Palestinian factions and the camp of former Gaza strongman and Abbas rival Mohammed Dahlan. They say this development could prove significant not only for the future of the Gaza Strip, but for the Palestinian political system as a whole.
In this context, Israeli officials believe Dahlan identified an opportunity after October 7 to return to the center of Palestinian politics amid the expected upheaval. According to them, he essentially had three options: move closer to Hamas and make use of his ties with the organization in Gaza, conclude that Hamas would not survive the war and move closer to Israel, or seek reconciliation with Abbas and return to Fatah ahead of the succession struggle that will follow.
Israeli officials believe Dahlan ultimately chose cooperation with Hamas, based on the assumption that the organization would remain a significant force in Palestinian politics.
As for the continued implementation of U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan for Gaza's reconstruction and the effort to disarm Hamas, senior officials assess that the identity of Israel’s next government will also be a decisive factor. They say that if a right-wing government takes office, Israel could sooner or later find itself in another round of fighting with Hamas.
A different government, they assess, might choose an arrangement instead, but even in that scenario Hamas would seek to preserve influence over civilian government and give up only part of its weapons. They say Hamas and the Arab world are also taking into account the possibility of a change in Israeli policy following a change of government.
The blow to Hezbollah — through Syria
As for Hezbollah, senior officials assess that its strength today is nothing like what it was on the eve of the October 7 attack. According to them, the organization has lost about 80% of its rocket potential, and its command structure has been severely degraded.
According to the assessment presented by the officials, of the roughly 20 senior figures who made up what they describe as “Hezbollah’s general staff,” only the current military commander remains, after the others were killed. Hezbollah’s elite forces have also been hit, especially the Radwan Force, which played a significant role in the fighting against the IDF. According to the officials, the rate of attrition among these forces is even higher than in the organization as a whole.
Israeli officials also point to the change in Hezbollah’s political standing within Lebanon. According to the officials, in the past it would have been difficult to imagine a Lebanese government and state officials adopting decisions that outlaw Hezbollah’s military and security activity and demand that it hand over its weapons to the state.
They say that even if there remains a significant gap between those decisions and the ability to enforce them on the ground, the willingness to adopt them at all reflects a shift in the balance of power and Hezbollah’s weakening.
That has been compounded by the blow to the organization’s strategic rear following the fall of Bashar Assad's regime in Syria. Israeli officials say Hezbollah thereby lost the territorial continuity that for years served as a route for transferring weapons from Iran, alongside damage to its weapons supply lines.
The NAZA film controversy
Ministers also discussed the public opinion damage caused by the film “NAZA,” which presents disturbing testimony purportedly from soldiers in the IDF's elite SIGINT Unit 8200 who claim they were involved in “war crimes and genocide,” and describe policies regarding collateral damage, shelling and targeted killings.
At the meeting, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir said the military had not yet obtained the film’s materials, after Justice Minister Yariv Levin asked whether an investigation had begun into the identities of the soldiers who participated.
“We have not seen it yet. We are still examining the legal tools available to us, within the existing constraints,” Zamir replied.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu then added: “There must be an investigation. If you do not know whom to investigate, investigate in order to find out.”
Levin argued that “it has nothing to do with whether you have seen the film or not. This is terrible damage,” while Transportation Minister Miri Regev said: “The military must check whether there really are soldiers who spoke this way against the IDF, and if it is true, I do not accept that we are doing nothing.”

Russia Ordered MZKT Chassis, Presumably for Pechora-2M Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:26:09 UTC
23:26:09 KST

The Minsk Wheeled Tractor Plant (MZKT) has signed a contract with the Moscow-based JSC Defense Systems to supply 30 specialized wheeled chassis.
This is evidenced by documents obtained by the Belarusian association BELPOL.
Under the terms of the agreement, the Russian customer is to receive 20 MZKT-8021-021 chassis, as well as five units each of the MZKT-8022-021 and MZKT-80211-021 models.
The contract is long-term and provides for equipment delivery through 2029.
The MZKT-8021/8022 series of specialized chassis was developed specifically to house components of the Pechora-2M air defense missile system.
In addition, these wheeled platforms also mount other air defense systems and radar stations.
The Russian joint-stock company Defense Systems specializes in developing, modernizing, and serially producing air defense and electronic warfare systems.
The company’s main and best-known project is the extensive modernization of Soviet short- and medium-range air defense systems of the Pechora series to the Pechora-2M and Pechora-2K standards, supplied to both the Russian Armed Forces and for export.
The size of the order indicates Russia’s intention to use Pechora-2M systems or air defense systems compatible with them.
Against the backdrop of a shortage of air defense capabilities, a return to Soviet-era systems is a practical step due to the availability of significant stockpiles of corresponding ammunition.
The system is a major upgrade of the S-125M air defense system and is designed to engage air targets at ranges from 3.5 to 32 km and at altitudes from 20 meters to 20 km.
In 2024, Belarus was to supply Russia with 18 MZKT-7930-312 chassis for producing Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun-missile systems.

'All weapons on the table to protect Kaliningrad': Why the Baltic exclave matters so much to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:25:37 UTC
23:25:37 KST

With the Ukraine war, Russia-West tensions have escalated across the Baltic region, where Moscow has a strategic territory: Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave with no land connection to the mainland Russia.
In recent weeks, the Kremlin has become increasingly alarmed by the Western alliance’s naval manoeuvres in the Baltic, repeatedly warning that Moscow would respond with full force to any potential attack on Kaliningrad, including, potentially, the use of nuclear weapons.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," Russian President Vladimir Putin said during a speech last week.
In a recent diplomatic note to the Western alliance, Moscow also described any blockade of the exclave as a "dangerous and reckless course" carrying "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict", which would trigger "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset”.
But why is Kaliningrad so important to Russia?
“Kaliningrad is part of Russian territory and as such is important by default,” Nikolai Sokov, a senior fellow at the Vienna Centre for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation, tells TRT World.
Sometimes described as the Kremlin’s “unsinkable aircraft carrier” in the Baltic Sea, Kaliningrad holds significant strategic and military importance for Russia.
Baltiysk hosts the Russian Baltic Fleet’s main base, and Moscow has also deployed tactical Iskander missiles in the exclave.
In May 2022, Russian forces in Kaliningrad simulated strikes with nuclear-capable Iskander missiles against mock military targets, including airfields and command posts.
But for Moscow, its significance begins with something even more fundamental: sovereignty.
Russian sovereignty matters to the Kremlin more than anything else, according to Sergei Markov, a former Putin advisor.
“Kaliningrad is important only for one reason because it’s part of Russia,” Markov tells TRT World.
On Sunday, Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, underlined that any territory, including parts of Ukraine it claims to have annexed, will be protected with the country’s “entire available arsenal of weapons”.
“Even if it were half a percent, or one-hundredth of a percent - this is the Russian Federation. There is nothing to discuss here.”
Strategic region
Beyond the question of Russian sovereignty, Kaliningrad also serves important economic and transportation interests for Moscow.
Its ice-free port gives Russia year-round access to the Baltic Sea, unlike ports such as St Petersburg, where winter conditions can restrict navigation.
But Kaliningrad’s strategic value comes with a geographical disadvantage.
The territory became part of the Soviet Union following the defeat of Nazi Germany in 1945.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, it lost its land connection with the rest of Russia as Lithuania and Latvia became independent states, leaving the Russian exclave sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania.
“It is an exclave between Lithuania and Poland and as such is more vulnerable than any other part of Russian territory. In particular, access over land through Lithuania is already effectively blocked; the sea route over the Baltic Sea can be blocked quite easily, too,” Sokov tells TRT World.
Yet the same geography also gives Moscow a strategically important military position inside the Baltic region.
The exclave hosts a major Russian naval base and weapons systems, including missiles with a range of around 500 kilometres, placing almost all of Poland and much of the Baltic Sea within reach, according to Sokov.
For Russia, Kaliningrad is “strategically vital” as “a forward platform for air defence, electronic warfare, and power projection into northern and central Europe,” Denys Kolesnyk, a Paris-based strategic intelligence consultant, tells TRT World.
But its position deep inside NATO territory also leaves it exposed.
Kolesnyk says Kaliningrad’s “isolated geographical position” between Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members, makes it “highly vulnerable and in the event of an armed conflict it would likely be one of the first Russian territories to be overwhelmed by superior allied forces”.
That vulnerability makes access to Kaliningrad particularly important.
The exclave is separated from Russia’s ally Belarus by the Suwalki Gap, a narrow stretch of territory along the Polish-Lithuanian border that has long been regarded as a strategic pressure point between Russia and NATO.
Special “transit arrangements” allow Russian citizens and cargo to cross Lithuanian territory to Kaliningrad and are anchored in Lithuania’s 2004 EU accession framework, policy analyst Juraj Majcin tells TRT World.
These arrangements give Moscow “grounds to challenge restrictions imposed by Vilnius on national security grounds,” he adds.
Overall, Kaliningrad provides Russia with “leverage over NATO and the EU”, according to Majcin. But its strategic value is inseparable from its vulnerability.
“Nuclear threats concerning Kaliningrad can therefore be understood as an attempt to compensate for that vulnerability,” he says.
Kaliningrad’s strategic importance, however, predates its role in Russia’s confrontation with NATO.
Long before Putin and Russia’s nuclear threats against the West, Kaliningrad carried significant weight in European history.
Moscow named the region after Mikhail Kalinin, a communist Bolshevik revolutionary leader, but it had previously been the capital of the old Prussian kingdom.
Before Soviet rule, the region’s capital, founded by the Teutonic Knights, a German-origin Catholic crusading order, was known as Konigsberg.
For centuries, Konigsberg was the capital of the Prussian monarchy, the predecessor state of present-day Germany. In 1701, the German royal family moved its capital from this Baltic city to Berlin.
Russia-West equation
Moscow has signalled that any Western blockade of Kaliningrad would be unacceptable and could trigger a military response, including the potential use of nuclear weapons.
While much of the focus has been on whether the Ukraine war could lead to a nuclear confrontation, Russia-West tensions in the Baltic have largely been underestimated, according to Markov.
He argues that the West, seeing sanctions against Russia as ineffective, might turn to other forms of pressure, including a blockade of Kaliningrad.
This possibility, he says, explains the Kremlin’s strong reaction.
“European countries opened the door for a nuclear war,” Markov says, describing the current tensions in the Baltic as an “extremely dangerous situation”.
Western analysts, however, assess the risk differently.
While a blockade of Kaliningrad is theoretically possible, nothing indicates that such a move is likely under current circumstances, according to Kolesnyk.
He sees such a step as viable only in response to a Russian attack on Poland or the Baltic states. Russia, however, says it has no intention of attacking NATO territory.
From a logistical standpoint, the Western alliance could “find it easier to disrupt Kaliningrad's sea and air links than its land connections through the Suwalki Gap”, Kolesnyk says.
But “the absence of political will, the demands of alliance cohesion and the certainty of a severe Russian response, albeit non-nuclear, make any deliberate peacetime blockade improbable,” he adds.
Referring to a 2025 NATO statement, Majcin says that the calculation could change in the event of a Russian attack on allied territory.
NATO could then act against Kaliningrad to degrade Russia’s ability to threaten the Suwałki Gap and reduce the risk of the Baltic states being cut off by land from the rest of the alliance.

Ukraine and Germany Sign 15 Deals Worth €8.5B for Air Defense, Radars, and Interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:24:36 UTC
23:24:36 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine and Germany Sign 15 Deals Worth €8.5B for Air Defense, Radars, and Interceptors
Ukraine and Germany have reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion covering air defense, drone interceptors, missiles, radars, artillery, unmanned ground systems, and energy support, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said following talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy in a Telegram post on October 4, the 15 agreements cover drone interceptors, small missiles, radars, unmanned ground systems, artillery, air defense, Patriot missile production in Germany, and support for Ukraine’s energy sector.
“As of today, we have 15 agreements and documents with the German side, and most of them concern security cooperation, production, relevant procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine. The total value of our agreements today is more than €8.5 billion,” Zelenskyy said.
The agreements include cooperation on drone interceptors, small anti-drone missiles, radars, artillery, unmanned ground vehicles, and additional air defense capabilities. Kyiv and Berlin will also work to increase production in Germany of missiles used by Patriot air defense systems, according to the Presidential Office.
Ukraine has also placed a major order with German defense manufacturer Diehl Defence for IRIS-T air defense systems. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry signed three memoranda with Diehl covering IRIS-T systems and missiles as well as ammunition. Separate agreements were reached with Hensoldt on radar procurement and Quantum Systems on testing and supplying interceptor drones.
Zelenskyy also reported positive testing of the German-Ukrainian Spear interceptor. Work is continuing on another weapon, the Nika small missile, designed specifically to counter Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type drones and which has yet to undergo testing.
Germany separately announced a new support package for Ukraine worth more than €1.3 billion, which includes defense assistance and funding for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of winter. Part of the funding will go toward producing new interceptors designed to engage jet-powered Russian attack drones.
“It includes weapons that will help us now, as well as support for our energy sector, which is very important, ahead of winter—an important energy package. This comprehensive package from Germany also includes funding for the production of new interceptors specifically against jet-powered ‘shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said.
Germany is also involved in FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile defense project led by Ukrainian company Fire Point, with Germany’s Hensoldt supplying radar technology. The system is expected to integrate FP-7.x interceptors, launchers, and TRML-4D radars.
The agreements also cover energy cooperation, including equipment for Ukraine’s power grid and projects with Siemens Energy involving gas turbines, infrastructure protection, and power generation.
The focus on faster interceptors comes as Russia increasingly uses jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which fly significantly faster than conventional propeller-driven variants and reduce the time available for interception. Zelenskyy said Russia launched around 900 jet-powered Shaheds in the week before Merz’s visit.

Germany Could Be Pulled Into an Armed Clash With Russia as Moscow’s “Shadow War” Escalates, Spy Chief Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:24:14 UTC
23:24:14 KST

- Category
- World
Germany Could Be Pulled Into an Armed Clash With Russia as Moscow’s “Shadow War” Escalates, Spy Chief Warns
Germany faces an increasingly serious risk that its confrontation with Russia could escalate into the use of military force, according to Martin Jäger, head of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, who warned that Moscow is already conducting what he described as a “shadow war” against the country, according to Ukrinform on October 5.
Speaking during a public hearing of the Bundestag committee responsible for overseeing Germany’s intelligence services, Jäger said the nature of the Russian threat had changed significantly and now represented the most direct and comprehensive security challenge facing Germany.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The confrontation in which we find ourselves with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous quality. Germany risks finding itself in a conflict with Russia involving the use of force. The attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example. At present, no other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and specific threat to Germany,” Jäger said.
He argued that Moscow increasingly views Germany as one of its principal adversaries because of Berlin’s support for Ukraine and its role in resisting Russian pressure against European states, particularly those on NATO’s eastern flank.
“We did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on us and sees us as one of its main adversaries. Because we do not accept Russia’s revisionist, expansionist policy and its war of aggression against Ukraine. Because we oppose Russian intimidation of our allies in the Baltics and other parts of Europe,” the BND chief said.
Jäger described Germany as “one of the main obstacles to Russia’s hegemonic projection of power in Europe,” arguing that this position has made Berlin an increasingly important target for Russian intelligence operations, sabotage, intimidation and political interference.
“Anyone who does not submit becomes an adversary. That is Moscow’s logic,” he said.
According to Jäger, Russian authorities closely monitor how Germany responds to provocations and interpret hesitation or political uncertainty as an opportunity to increase pressure. One of Moscow’s central objectives, he said, is to weaken European political support for Ukraine and create conditions in which governments become reluctant to make decisions that run counter to Russian interests.
“We must be prepared for attempts at intimidation and further interference. There will probably be nuclear threats again. We have to withstand that,” Jäger said.
The intelligence chief described Russia’s broader campaign as an undeclared “shadow war” that operates below the traditional threshold of an openly declared military confrontation, combining covert operations and political pressure with other forms of hostile activity.
“The Russian leadership wants to ensure for the future that political decisions against Moscow are not made in Berlin and other European capitals. Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war cannot be described using conventional military or legal categories. We are not in a state of defense, and yet we are being attacked. That is precisely what a shadow war is,” Jäger said.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia is preparing a new wave of drone operations in Europe that could target Mediterranean countries, with Spain, France, and Italy among the states potentially at risk.

European Commission monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
The European Commission is monitoring a suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia "very closely" and is prepared to coordinate a response among member states if necessary.
Source: a European Commission spokesperson on Monday 5 October, quoted by Euronews, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The European Commission stressed that it is "aware of the reports concerning the laboratory incident in Russia, seemingly involving a pathogen causing plague".
Quote from the spokesperson: "Public health is always a priority for us, so we are in touch with our experts from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. We monitor very closely what is going on."
More details: The European Commission also stressed that the international community is "much better prepared for any pandemics" following COVID-19. The spokesperson said countries have stocks of antibiotics available.
The European Commission is using the World Health Organisation's channels to get updates from the Russian authorities.
According to local Russian media outlets, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, an employee of the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Irkutsk Oblast, eastern Siberia, broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen on 25 September.
She was admitted to hospital with symptoms of severe pneumonia on 29 September and died overnight on 1-2 October. Following her death, the authorities introduced a quarantine in several of the region's medical facilities and placed nearly 200 people who had been in touch with Shipilova under medical observation.
Russian media outlets speculated that Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not confirmed this diagnosis.
Media reports indicate that the White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case and related quarantine measures in Russia.
Background: An outbreak of hantavirus occurred on a cruise ship in May. The first batches of an experimental antiviral drug to treat hantavirus were sent to France, Spain and the Netherlands.

India’s supreme court demands answers over changes to voter roll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:22:16 UTC
23:22:16 KST

India’s supreme court has demanded accountability from the government and the election body over a controversial exercise that has led to the deletion of tens of millions of voters from the electoral roll and prompted mass protests.
Demonstrations have erupted across the country in recent days as opposition parties, student groups and the youth-led Cockroach movement have demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
They have accused Kumar of overseeing a direct attack on India’s democracy through an exercise to verify and “purify” the electoral roll in states across the country, which so far has led to 130 million names being removed. In Delhi, hundreds of people were detained as they tried to protest over the weekend.
On Monday, the supreme court issued notices to Narendra Modi’s government, the ECI and Kumar to demand answers over concerns raised about the voter list revision, saying it expected all “to respond in a clear, transparent manner”.
The ECI has claimed the exercise is simply cleaning electoral rolls of duplicate, dead and ineligible names, as well as removing “illegal infiltrators”. However, large numbers of people in Delhi and states such as Bihar and West Bengal say they have been wrongly stripped of their vote and have struggled to get it back.
There are accusations that revision of the electoral rolls particularly targets minorities such as Muslims, who are traditionally not voters of Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The opposition alliance, led by the Congress party, have accused the ECI of being hand in glove with the government over alleged vote “chori” or cheating. Kumar was chosen to head the ECI by a panel headed by Modi.
While the exercise, known as the special intensive revision (SIR), began last year, widespread outrage only recently erupted after a report in the Indian Express newspaper revealed multiple irregularities in the process, which were flagged in more than a dozen internal objections.
The two petitions taken up by the supreme court on Monday alleged that the credibility of the ECI was now in question and called for an independent inquiry into the decisions taken by Kumar in how the SIR process was conducted.
“Deletions of voters have been made in the largest democracy,” said Menaka Guruswamy, a lawyer acting for one of the petitioners. “We have grown up with free and fair elections, that is not the case now.”
Another advocate told the supreme court judges that if action was not taken to ensure that India’s electoral rolls remained fair, “this country will burn”. Another hearing in the cases will be held next week.
The controversies over the ECI have once again driven India’s young people on to the streets in protest, amid rising frustration at the Modi government.
The Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which led massive unrest over the summer that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, have once again mobilised and called for the resignation of Kumar. Thousands of CJP supporters took to the streets of Mumbai last Friday in protest and another demonstration was held on Saturday in Delhi.
In Delhi, police have been criticised for their heavy-handed approach to stopping any student groups protesting in the heart of the capital. Officers have been accused of sexually assaulting three journalists at the protests over the weekend and hundreds of young people were forced on to police buses. Delhi police said it was investigating the assault claims.

Riigikogu election campaigning gets going 5 months before polling day

Riigikogu election campaigning gets going 5 months before polling day
Many political parties have already activated their Riigikogu election campaigns with five months still to go.
This relatively early start is deliberate, with factors such as campaign costs, voter fatigue and what the other parties are doing all being weighed up.
Another new development is that social media campaigning is now banned, "Aktuaalne kaamera" reported.
The Riigikogu elections take place in early March, but campaigning season is already underway just as the days get shorter and the weather grayer. To counter this, parties were seen to set up colorful tents, with flags and other decorations.
If anything, campaign season has started a little early, something which the opposition Social Democrats (SDE) party's campaign manager, Karmo Kuri, put down to election-fatigue setting in with the public when polling day gets nearer.
"What we have noticed is that at the height of the campaign, when people are already starting to get fed up with it, they say, 'Why do you only come out here just before the elections?' That has also been our starting point," Kuri told "Aktuaalne kaamera."
Parties can end up spending millions of euros on their campaigning, and members, leading and grass roots alike, are often expected to chip in too.
Isamaa MP Riina Solman said she was stumping up thousands of euros of her own money.
"My budget right now is €10,000, which I can set aside from my salary. But on top of that there is also the party's campaign. Senior politicians are also included in the party's campaign and on its posters," Solman, whose party is also in opposition nationwide, though in office with Center in Tallinn, noted.
As for the Center Party, its members will have to dig deepest into their own pockets, as the party's financial situation has not been good for a long time, and as a result it is focusing mainly on direct contact with voters.
"If you also want posters, they actually cost quite a lot. Take the last local elections, for example. Right here on Pirita Road, a large poster for two weeks cost three and a half thousand euros," explained Pirita district elder and Center Party member Kaido Saarniit.
So what are the parties talking to the voters about? The economy and cost of living featured highly.
"The closer we get to winter, the more home heating, as well as our party's general approach to family policy and such issues, have come into focus," Kuri said.
"What we are asking people about today is how they feel about the excise duty increases that have now been imposed on fuel. And that grates on people. We are also collecting signatures against the fuel excise duty increase," Solman added.
Things will really get going in the new year, when strests, roadsides, advertising hoardings, shopping malls and other locations will start to fill with ' posters of politicians and their parties; TV and radio spots will accompany this.
"The tent campaign taking place across Estonia right now is still modest. These elections are going to be very active," Saarniit said.
One party which has not kicked off its campaign just yet is the coalition Reform Party. This is set to start in the second half of this month, by which time it should be clear what their current coalition partner Eesti 200's plans are – possibly including a merger with the Greens.
Similarly, the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) has still to unveil its campaign.
Campaigning will continue right up to polling day, March 7, 2027.

Already 77% of hospitals in the capable network are fully autonomous
Kyiv • UNN
According to the Ministry of Health, all hospitals in Ukraine have generators, 96% have autonomous heating, and 78% have their own water sources.
The Ministry of Health reported that in Ukraine, 77% of hospitals in the capable network are fully autonomous, UNN writes.
The ministry emphasizes that strengthening the autonomy of medical institutions remains a priority. According to the Ministry of Health, 100% of hospitals are equipped with generators, 96% have autonomous heating, and 78% have local water supply sources. In addition, 468 institutions are equipped with Starlink satellite communication systems.
As UNN wrote, full autonomy includes not only the provision of backup power sources, but also autonomous heating (their own boiler houses or the ability to quickly connect to mobile boiler houses in the event of interruptions to centralized heating), as well as their own water supply source.
The ministry also reported on the development of alternative energy. Solar power systems have already been installed at 303 hospitals in the capable network. More than 200 additional such systems are planned to be installed by the end of the year.
The state is paying particular attention to the safety of patients and medical workers: 750 healthcare institutions have 1,362 civil defense protective structures on their premises. Work is currently under way to modernize the existing shelters, bring them into compliance with the established requirements, and further expand the network of protective structures at medical institutions.
At the same time, protected medical spaces are being developed, allowing treatment to continue even during shelling. In particular, construction of the "Ark" underground medical complex is under way in Kharkiv, while protected medical premises with wards and an operating room have already been equipped in Zaporizhzhia.
The situation regarding the autonomy of hospitals in Kyiv
On September 11, the Kyiv City State Administration Department of Health reported that more than 65% of the institutions in the capable network were already fully autonomous. Readiness is planned to reach 100% by the end of October.
Particular attention is being paid to institutions receiving patients with polytrauma and injuries; according to the Department of Health, they have already been equipped not only with primary but also additional generators in case the main equipment fails. Overall, the issue of backup power supply in the capital's hospitals is practically resolved, but full autonomy, as we have written, means alternative sources of water and heat, and some of the capital's medical institutions are still working on these aspects. At the same time, there are institutions such as the capital's Perinatal Center, which built a pellet boiler house and have a private well even before the start of the full-scale war.

US pulls bombers from UK base: Is Iran manoeuvring Trump’s war plans?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:19:44 UTC
23:19:44 KST

US pulls bombers from UK base: Is Iran manoeuvring Trump’s war plans?
The withdrawal will not prevent the US from continuing to strike Iran, but it does reduce its ability to rapidly generate and sustain heavy bombing missions, said experts.
Last week, a British bomb disposal robot roamed the area near the Royal Air Force (RAF) base at Fairford and 85 homes were evacuated as the threat of an attack appeared imminent.
Days later, the United States speedily sent B-1 bombers stationed there, which were used to strike Iran in its ongoing war, back home. About a dozen had been stationed at the air base.
The foiled incident resulted in no charges and the release of five suspects, and subsequently a separate British-Iranian suspect. But the US cited concerns about more potential attacks for its decision to withdraw its fleet. Tehran has denied any link to the alleged plot to target the base.
RAF Fairford was a pit stop for US bombers during the war – but more importantly, it allowed Washington to rapidly unleash intensive strikes on Iran, say analysts.
They added that their withdrawal reduces Washington’s ability to rapidly generate and sustain bombing missions, but it will not prevent the US from continuing to strike Iran.
“The United States has lost a convenient launchpad, not its underlying strike capability,” Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum and a lecturer at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera.
Long bombing campaigns made more demanding
The analysts were in agreement that the British base gave the US a faster and more efficient way to sustain strikes on Iran.
The bombers at the Fairford base were officially stationed there for defensive strikes – at the behest of the UK government – and likely had a modest targeting list, said Christoph Bergs, an analyst at the world’s oldest defence and security thinktank, the Royal United Services Institute.
“Their withdrawal reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat,” Bergs told Al Jazeera.
Thafer explained that while the loss of the bombers does not remove the US’s ability to strike or escalate, “depending on where other assets are positioned, it could make a prolonged bombing campaign more demanding”.
The removal of B-1 bombers imposes a number of tactical costs, says Arun Dawson. He is a PhD candidate at King’s College London’s Freeman Air and Space Institute and a researcher with the UK Nuclear Deterrence Network.
Unlike the more modern B-2 stealth bomber designed to make enemy tracking difficult – which has also previously been stationed at RAF Fairford – “the B-1’s principal advantage is its conventional weapons payload – the largest of any aircraft in the US military”, Dawson told Al Jazeera. The B-1 carries at least 34 tonnes of ordnance, he said.
“This makes the B-1 particularly effective at delivering large volumes of precision-guided weapons against multiple targets during a prolonged air campaign,” said Dawson.
“In the Iran war, those targets may include air-defence infrastructure, ballistic missile sites and IRGC facilities,” he added, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.
With the B-1s withdrawing, the US may now have to rely more heavily on longer-range missions from the US or other distant bases, increasing flight times, crew fatigue and the need for aerial refuelling, he explained.
Still, the US may have made the withdrawal decision based on an examination of risks, said Dawson.
“Their abrupt departure suggests that specific threats may have been directed at the aircraft, their crews or the base itself,” he said.
Washington may have also calculated that temporarily withdrawing the bombers could protect it for future operations, especially if the US does not expect the Iran war to intensify any time soon, said Dawson.
For David Des Roches, a professor at the Thayer Marshall Institute and a former Pentagon official, the B-1 withdrawal suggests that the risks outweighed the benefits of keeping the jets at the UK airbase.
The security incident last week “exposed a vulnerability” as the aircraft were “out in the open” and only about 300 yards (275 metres) from where the public could see them.
“So they were very vulnerable to, say, drone attacks or other kind[s] of mortar attacks,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Just a small drone or any kind of a drone with explosives on board could conceivably cause significant damage,” said Des Roches.
The former Pentagon official acknowledged that the deployment of the US bombers means “you lose a little bit of operational ability,” but said that given the threat seen at Fairford, “we should have had overhead cover for all of our aircraft, globally, years ago”.
Can the bombers go elsewhere?
The US has two potential options if the bombers are to be redeployed: to Diego Garcia, the remote coral atoll in the central Indian Ocean hosting both a US and UK military base; or to its many US bases in the Gulf.
Thafer pointed out that Diego Garcia offers greater protection from potential Iranian attacks, but requires longer flight distances.
Rerouting the bombers to Diego Garcia will also depend on how quickly additional aircraft can be folded into the local basing infrastructure, pointed out Bergs.
Stationing them in the Gulf closer to Iran would give them the advantage of shortened transit times, reduced tanker requirements and the ability to generate sorties more rapidly, said Dawson.
But basing in the Gulf region, the analysts agreed, will require more deliberate negotiations around risk mitigation, given that these countries have taken the brunt of Iranian counterstrikes throughout the war. They also want to avoid being seen as direct participants in a US campaign against Iran.
Fairford had therefore offered a “useful” middle ground between the two options, said Thafer.
But with Fairford no longer an option, Diego Garcia would be the more obvious choice, Dawson said, offering not only greater distance from Iran but also a more secure operating environment. It has infrastructure designed to support large-scale US air operations, he said.
US capabilities in the war ahead
For now, the withdrawal appears to blunt rather than eliminate US bombing capacity against Iran.
However, the practical impact on US military options will depend largely on whether the administration sees a need for such strikes now, or whether the threat posed by similar aircraft stationed at Diego Garcia is sufficient for the time being, said Bergs.
The expected arrival of the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force to the Middle East by November, meanwhile, will add significant US carrier-based air power in the region, said Dawson.
“Aircraft for aircraft, carrier fighters cannot substitute for the B-1’s enormous payload, but there are many more of them, giving commanders additional options for shorter-range strikes,” he said.
What this episode highlights, said the researcher, is the importance – and the vulnerability – of the US’ alliances and overseas basing.
Washington has long enjoyed access to a global network of military facilities – which has been key for its ability to project power rapidly and at scale, he said.
But if those bases face attacks or political restrictions – the implications would extend beyond the Iran war, warned Dawson.
They would affect “how the US military structures its forces, distributes its assets, generates combat power and sustains operations overseas”.

LONDON, October 5. /TASS/. Europe’s gas storage facilities are currently 72% full, a record low for this time of year, The Economist reported.
According to the magazine, the average storage level in 2022-2025 was 90%. Weather forecasters expect the heating season to begin earlier this year. Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:18:18 UTC
23:18:18 KST

Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work
The winners of the Nobel Prizes in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics will be announced in the week.
American scientist Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their pioneering discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand how the brain works.
The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university said on Monday that Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, were honoured “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells”.
Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviours like learning, fear, addiction and movement.
“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary-general of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute, added that optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain”.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” Perlmann added.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.
Researchers also hope optogenetics could improve cochlear implants, allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin. Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg. The three of them will share a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m).
“All three said the same thing: that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two who they call their friends – that it’s such an honour to receive the prize together,” Perlmann said.
Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with the Nobel Prize for physics announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.
But perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize – the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo. Experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate this year who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s controversial winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado.
Laureates receive their awards on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death, in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s royal families, with banquets held in their honour.

====================================================================================================

China’s LinkedIn Espionage Is Only Getting More Advanced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

On June 3, in a rare – and telling – indication of collective alarm, the member states of the “Five Eyes” intelligence-sharing alliance published an unprecedented joint bulletin highlighting China’s use of professional networking sites like LinkedIn to carry out an aggressive, industrial-scale online espionage campaign. Armed with the personal data of millions of U.S. security clearance holders and applicants, acquired during China’s 2014-15 hack of the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), spies from the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) have approached tens of thousands of U.S. and NATO government staffers, military personnel, academics, and others with access to sensitive information through LinkedIn and other professional networking sites over recent years.
The massive scale of China’s spy campaign does not preclude precision: MSS agents use generative AI to craft messages tailored to each individual target’s resume and expertise. Posing as corporate recruiters or business consultants, agents promise their targets easy money in exchange for writing freelance “consulting” reports on seemingly innocuous topics related to their targets’ work. These fictitious identities are often bolstered with AI-generated profile pictures and fake corporate websites. Once the agent has established a relationship with their target, they’ll push the target to divulge more sensitive information or even pass classified documents directly to the agent.
The environment is target-rich. LinkedIn is widely used by current and former U.S. government employees. Spies on the prowl can easily browse lists of users with specific career experience to quickly build a list of viable targets. This makes online espionage recruitment especially appealing to China’s intelligence apparatus, and the extensive use of fake company webpages and AI-generated messages means that targets often don’t initially realize they’re being deftly cultivated by a foreign spy agency.
Although less bombastic than China’s efforts to hack American critical infrastructure or cultivate U.S. politicians as agents of influence, China’s networking site espionage has proven particularly long-running and pernicious. Reports of Chinese intelligence operations using LinkedIn to recruit informants go back to at least 2011. In 2018, then-head of the U.S. National Counterintelligence and Security Center William Evanina publicly called on LinkedIn to address the issue. LinkedIn responded by “restricting” a few dozen fake accounts, but the problem continued. Evanina told the New York Times a year later that China’s espionage activity on the platform had not decreased. Despite periodic media attention and U.S. counterintelligence efforts over the past 15 years, China’s intelligence apparatus has continued to run aggressive online spying campaigns on an industrial scale, obtaining technological, military, and economic secrets through these efforts.
China’s online espionage recruitment poses an urgent threat to the U.S. and allied governments, but solutions for detecting and preventing it have remained frustratingly elusive. Fortunately, there exists a wealth of research and real-world models for cooperation between governments and industry to address a similar threat: transnational online fraud and scam rings. Government and industry stakeholders should draw on this existing body of expertise and best practices and adopt a novel approach to combating China’s network espionage.
China’s online espionage shares some key characteristics with transnational online fraud. Both Chinese espionage recruitment and online romance scams, such as the “pig butchering” operations that earn billions of dollars each year for cybercriminals operating internet scam compounds in Southeast Asia, use deceptive, flattering initial approaches to their target. These initial messages are often written and translated with the aid of generative AI and tailored to fit the target’s profile. MSS spy handlers and online scammers also seek to cultivate a relationship and build trust with their targets before eventually pressuring them to disclose sensitive information, such as military secrets or personal financial details.
Finally, both transnational fraud schemes and China’s online espionage recruitment originate from overseas but use U.S. and partner nation platforms and internet infrastructure to contact their targets. This leaves scammers and spies similarly vulnerable to disruption efforts by law enforcement and counterintelligence authorities in the US and partner nations.
One recent example is “Disruption Week,” organized by the U.S. Department of Justice’s “Scam Center Strike Force.” From May 18 to 21, U.S. law enforcement bodies met and shared information with major private sector firms like Apple, Meta, and Microsoft to identify and shut down fraud activity on over 1.4 million scam-linked social media and email accounts, as well as decommissioning servers, hosting infrastructure, and platforms linked to scam networks operating from Southeast Asia. Law enforcement agencies also identified and opened new investigations into overseas scammers and arrested several suspected cybercriminals with the cooperation of partner nations.
On June 10, the FBI seized 13 web domains used by Chinese intelligence agents to lure targets on LinkedIn and other networking sites. The domains hosted webpages for fake consultancies – fronts for MSS spies posing as recruiters online. The deception paid off. FBI documents show that China’s spies used the fake consulting firms to recruit at least eight current and former U.S. government and military personnel with security clearances.
While U.S. counterintelligence officials’ work in disrupting part of China’s illicit digital intelligence infrastructure is praiseworthy, 13 domains represents a mere drop in the bucket of China’s extensive online espionage. Researchers at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD) have already identified over 100 web domains and fake firms likely serving as fronts for Chinese espionage recruitment – none of which were seized during the FBI’s June operation.
One of these fake firms, “Nimbus Hub Consulting,” was also independently identified as a front for Chinese espionage by publicly-available industry and media reports. The U.S. government, think tanks, and industry should establish information-sharing channels to allow law enforcement agencies and professional networking sites like LinkedIn to cross-reference suspicious firms with a list of known front companies and flag or delete profiles linked to these fronts. Authorities should be catching these fraudulent sites as they are identified, not playing catch-up with siloed and incomplete data.
On the industry side, professional networking and job site operators can draw on recent advances in scam detection and prevention to combat Chinese espionage on their platforms. Online scammers often create and follow AI-generated scripts that function as templates for enticing and exploiting victims, even across language barriers. These scripts allow the scammers to automate and expand the scope of their operations, targeting victims en masse. China’s cyber spies use similar techniques to quickly generate personalized messages, allowing them to approach thousands of targets with minimal time and effort.
But AI cuts both ways for scammers: recent anti-scam research has demonstrated that AI models can effectively identify scam messages. Google has already developed tools to detect and flag likely scams in real time on its Android devices, and this technology could be easily adapted to detect likely Chinese espionage recruitment approaches, which make similar use of AI models to generate and customize approach messages for each target. LinkedIn and other professional networking platforms should implement a similar feature in their chat functions to detect likely espionage attempts and warn users in real time.
The U.S. government shouldn’t be shy about pressing LinkedIn to take this much-needed step to address rampant espionage recruiting on the platform. The Department of Defense’s Transition Assistance Program (TAP) explicitly encourages servicemembers to use LinkedIn to search for their next role, and the platform’s well-established ecosystem of professionals and employers has attracted a significant community of current and former U.S. government employees and clearance holders. All fo this makes it a particularly appealing target for Chinese intelligence. If the platform’s operators drag their feet on improving security and addressing rampant abuse by China’s spy agencies, authorities could strip it from federal programs like DOD’s TAP. Legislators could even move to treat the platform similarly to pre-divestiture TikTok or WhatsApp, banning its use on government-issued devices. It would also behoove the House Select Committee on the CCP to use its subpoena power to call recalcitrant platform operators to account. After all, MSS spies targeted the Committee itself in December 2025, using a fake consulting firm (complete with a falsified LinkedIn presence) in an attempt to solicit sensitive information from a Committee staffer.
A hardball approach would create predictable headaches for both parties, though, and a more cooperative arrangement based on establishing information-sharing channels, clear efforts towards identifying and banning spies from the platform, and improved safeguards against espionage recruitment in LinkedIn’s chat client would be preferable.
While detection and disruption are the most immediate concerns for authorities and platform operators, the ease with which Chinese intelligence agents can create new front companies and fake identities means that preparing platform users to protect themselves is also crucial. Preventative measures warning potential targets and equipping them to recognize the signs of espionage recruitment attempts are urgently needed.
Much like China’s AI-enabled online espionage recruitment, phishing and other traditional cybersecurity threats use social engineering techniques to manipulate targets into engaging with malicious messages. An extensive body of scholarship, including anti-fraud research sponsored by the Federal Trade Commission, has explored the effectiveness of anti-phishing cybersecurity education and has identified some best practices for helping internet users protect themselves from malicious actors.
One surprising and relevant finding from this research concerns the effectiveness of regular cybersecurity trainings. Multiple large-scale studies concluded that formal cybersecurity trainings are largely ineffective in preventing users from engaging with phishing messages, indicating that oft-repeated calls for more or intensified counterespionage training sessions for U.S. government and military personnel, while well-intentioned, are unlikely to be effective.
Researchers studying anti-phishing training found that simple reminders about cyber threats are likely to provide an equivalent benefit to detailed cybersecurity trainings, while being much less costly and time-consuming. With this in mind, LinkedIn and other professional networking sites should implement occasional short, attention-grabbing, and user-friendly reminders about espionage recruitment threats to warn users while avoiding desensitizing them through the overuse of warning messages.
Fortunately, more robust preventative measures are available to platform operators: anti-phishing research has identified prominent warnings that flag probable scam messages within email clients as an effective tool for alerting users to malicious activity. LinkedIn and other professional networking sites should implement highly-visible warnings embedded within their chat functions to warn users about likely espionage recruitment attempts. LinkedIn has already introduced an optional feature designed to detect and flag malware and harassment in chat messages; adding espionage recruitment to the list of threats is an obvious next step. TAP and programs like it should also highlight and explain this feature to DOD and other federal personnel when discussing LinkedIn use.
Research on phishing prevention also found that simple, user-friendly reporting functions to flag phishing attempts can help organizations rapidly identify and disrupt likely phishing campaigns without putting significant strain on the organization’s operational load. LinkedIn should implement a user-friendly reporting feature directly into the chat function to enable users to quickly and easily report likely espionage recruitment attempts. This feature could also support information-sharing and collaboration between LinkedIn and law enforcement agencies, allowing for faster and easier cross-referencing and identification of likely Chinese intelligence agents and front companies.
Chinese espionage recruitment may be occurring on an unprecedented scale, but the U.S. is far from powerless to stop it. Easy wins are readily available in the form of research-backed measures for dramatically reducing the effectiveness of Chinese intelligence activities online. LinkedIn announced in March that it had joined (alongside Meta, OpenAI, and other major tech firms) an industry accord dedicated to combating online scams and fraud. Signatories promised to increase their cooperation with law enforcement and government bodies, develop scam detection tools that utilize advanced AI, and create user-friendly reporting channels to flag likely scams. Meta has also publicly discussed its cooperation with OpenAI to crack down on online transnational scam and fraud activity operating across their respective platforms. Taking advantage of these tools, techniques, and channels to address China’s online espionage operations is a clear next step for policymakers, law enforcement authorities, and professional networking platforms.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday that Türkiye will continue pursuing its space ambitions until it becomes a strong and respected player in the global space ecosystem, highlighting advances in lunar exploration, satellite technology and space infrastructure.
“We will not deviate from our goal until we make Türkiye one of the strong and respected actors in the global space ecosystem,” Erdogan said at the opening of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
He said Türkiye had made significant progress in a relatively short period despite technological and other challenges, adding that Ankara would continue investing in its capabilities to ensure the country does not fall behind in the global space race.
Türkiye completes lunar spacecraft integration
Erdogan announced that production, assembly and integration work on the lunar spacecraft developed under Türkiye’s Lunar Research Program has been completed.
The spacecraft weighs around 3.5 tons and has a domestic production rate of more than 80 percent, which Erdogan described as a source of “great pride.”
He also pointed to Türksat 6A, Türkiye’s domestically developed communications satellite, as evidence of the country’s growing engineering capabilities, industrial infrastructure and human resources in space technologies.
Türkiye has also expanded its international space ambitions, including plans for a spaceport project in Somalia.
Erdogan said the initiative would improve Türkiye’s access to space while helping strengthen Africa’s broader space ecosystem.
The country’s space push comes as Antalya hosts the 77th International Astronautical Congress from October 5 to 9, marking the first time Türkiye has hosted the event.
More than 10,000 participants are expected to attend, with representatives from more than 100 countries taking part.
Erdogan calls for wider access to space
Erdogan said space exploration should not be dominated by a small group of countries and warned against turning outer space into another arena for military competition.
“Space is not made up of spoils to be seized by whoever gets there first,” he said, arguing that weaponising space and using it as an instrument in an arms race would be fundamentally wrong.
He also highlighted TEKNOFEST, Türkiye’s flagship aerospace and technology festival, saying its latest edition attracted applications from more than 730,000 teams from all 81 Turkish provinces and 97 countries.
The congress in Antalya is being held under the theme “The World Needs More Space” and is bringing together space agencies, scientists, engineers, companies and policymakers to discuss exploration, technology and international cooperation.

Iran’s oil minister resigns as country’s economic crisis worsens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:16:14 UTC
23:16:14 KST

Iran’s oil minister has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars’ worth of export receipts to the state.
Mohsen Paknejad’s departure comes as Iran grapples with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. An overall drop in oil receipts has led to a massive shortfall in foreign exchange earnings and one of the biggest drops in the value of the rial since the Iranian revolution in 1979.
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he had accepted the resignation of Paknejad, who had given personal reasons for going.
The rial is trading more than 10% lower than a month ago, largely due to the US naval blockade preventing Iran from selling oil, the mainstay of government receipts.
Emergency government meetings over the weekend to combat the crisis have yielded little tangible progress, and there are growing reports that the professional middle class, notably teachers and nurses, are resigning in large numbers because their salaries are not keeping up with price rises. The central bank says its role is not to defend a specific rate, but manage fluctuations.
Iran’s economy contracted by 10% in the first three months of the year. Despite concerns that continued sanctions may lead to protests, Iranian diplomats are not planning any new concessions after a proposal to speed the process of nuclear negotiations was rejected by Donald Trump a week ago.
Iran has been using informal networks known as “trustees” to bypass US sanctions and repatriate oil revenues. A report last week by the Farhikhtegan newspaper alleged that a trust set up on Paknejad’s watch to recoup income from Iran’s overseas oil sales owed the state-owned National Iranian Oil Company nearly $2bn (£1.5bn) in revenues. Three individual trustees awarded oil contracts allegedly owe hundreds of millions of dollars each to the NIOC.
Some of the leaks behind the reporting may reflect a power struggle inside the oil industry. Reza Sepahvand, a spokesperson for the parliament’s energy commission, has announced the launch of an inquiry.
Although Iran’s oil export problem, and its impact on foreign exchange reserves, is primarily caused by the US naval blockade on Iran’s oil exports, reports of lax management or possibly corruption will do little to bolster confidence in government at a time when most Iranians are going through an unprecedented squeeze on their standards of living.
It is claimed the difficulties were regarded as so serious that they were conveyed by one security official to the president and then before the US attack on Iran in February to the supreme Leader himself. The president apparently took up the complaint with the oil minister but no satisfactory response was received.
In an attempt to shore up public confidence in the government’s strategy, ministers have been seeking to rebut Donald Trump’s claim that oil is now flowing through the strait of Hormuz at near pre-blockade rates.
The number of attacks on ships trying to use the strait’s southern route close to the Oman shoreline has risen in recent days, including four attacks in the past 48 hours. It was also reported that Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline had been forced to close again after a further attack.
Reuters reported last week that the seven-day moving average of the region’s crude oil exports reached 18.5m barrels a day on 1 October. About the same amount was exported before the US-Israeli war with Iran began.
The dollar traded at 269,000 tomans (a toman is 10,000 rials) this week, a record high, and has risen 12% since 9 September. The minimum monthly wage of 166m rials is worth about $66. Food inflation is 130%.
Alireza Zakani, the mayor of Tehran, has announced he is freezing the price of 12 basic items including sugar, rice, oil and detergent for six months. There has been scepticism about how these price controls will be enforced, but he claimed the national government was going to study his plan. Ministers also said a second rise in public sector wages was likely.
Mohammad Sharifi Moghaddam, the secretary general of the Nurses’ House organisation, stressed the scale of the squeeze on living standards: “Nurses have explored all possible avenues – logical, legal, professional, and every type of protest or critical path – to achieve their demands.
“The current healthcare system has shown no regard for the issues and demands of the nursing community.️ Nurses have come to the conclusion that it is more cost-effective and less damaging to their wellbeing to stay home and receive a salary of 25m tomans.”
At the same time, repression of mainstream dissidents has continued, with the summoning of the leadership of the Reform Front by the ministry of intelligence to explain criticisms it had issued during the crackdown on protests.
The front has already written to the government calling for transparency about corruption at a time when people are facing pressure from inflation, high prices and falling living standards.
