What China's new military foothold in Laos means for Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

What China's Laos foothold means for the region
October 5, 2026
China has opened a new military training and logistics facility in Laos, extending Beijing's security presence deeper into mainland Southeast Asia and potentially giving the Chinese air force its first dedicated foothold overseas.
The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport, north of the capital Vientiane, formally began operations late last month alongside the new China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
Beijing says the center will primarily help train Lao air force pilots and will be jointly maintained and operated by the two countries.
The opening adds to China's still relatively small network of overseas military facilities.
Beijing established its first foreign military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in 2017. A Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia's Ream Naval Base was formally inaugurated last year, giving Chinese forces access to a facility strategically positioned near the South China Sea.
Laos and Cambodia are widely regarded as China's closest political partners in Southeast Asia, and military cooperation with both has expanded substantially in recent years.
"The two institutions … are not directed against any third party and aim to help further deepen practical cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to maintaining peace and stability in the region," said the Chinese Defense Ministry in a public statement.
Could Ban Keun become a permanent Chinese base?
The facility's infrastructure gives Beijing the option of expanding its military use in the future, Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at Australia's Lowy Institute, told DW.
"The focus may well be on joint training, but it has the potential to become a more permanent base. Should Beijing choose to use it as such, it has ample political leverage over Vientiane to demand exclusive access in the future," he added.
Laos has become heavily dependent on Chinese investment and financing during the past two decades. Critics have frequently accused Beijing of engaging in "debt-trap diplomacy."
The International Monetary Fund estimates Laos' public debt at around 81% of GDP last year, with China by far the largest bilateral creditor.
In 2020, China's state-owned China Southern Power Grid acquired a reported 90% stake in Electricite du Laos Transmission Company, which operates much of Laos' electricity transmission network.
A more durable Chinese military presence in Laos would also add another dimension to the strategic competition between Beijing and Washington in Southeast Asia.
The United States still enjoys far more extensive military access across the wider Indo-Pacific, particularly through alliances with the Philippines, Japan and Australia.
Beijing has historically lacked comparable overseas facilities. But Ban Keun, alongside Ream, could gradually reduce that disadvantage by giving the Chinese military additional locations from which to train, maintain equipment and potentially preposition supplies.
It is a particularly ominous development for Vietnam, Euan Graham, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Hanoi and Beijing retain close party-to-party and economic relations, but they remain rivals in the South China Sea, where their competing territorial claims have repeatedly generated tensions.
Vietnam has also traditionally viewed Laos and Cambodia as strategically important buffers along its western flank and has worked for decades to maintain considerable political and military influence in both countries.
"Hanoi has always perceived the Indochinese peninsula as within its sphere of influence, offering a buffer against external aggressors, especially given Vietnam's narrow midriff," said Graham. "Now, it faces an alarming possibility of strategic encirclement by China. The new air base in Laos will certainly complicate Vietnam's defense planning."
Strategic importance should not be overstated
Other analysts caution, however, that geography places clear limits on Ban Keun's military value.
Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told DW that China could gradually expand its presence at the facility.
Beijing could deploy more personnel, particularly advisers and instructors, as well as trainer aircraft and eventually more advanced aircraft, while also using the site to preposition equipment and supplies, he said.
But the "operational usefulness for the PLA's projection of military power in Southeast Asia is constrained by the landlocked nature of Laos."
Unlike Ream, Ban Keun provides no sea access, while Chinese military aircraft already operate from substantially larger and better-equipped bases in southern China.
While Vietnam will closely monitor Ban Keun for its potential role in any future South China Sea conflict, the site's geography doesn't give the Chinese military a significant operational advantage, said Koh.
Simon Creak, an associate professor at Singapore's National Institute of Education and a historian of Laos, noted that Vientiane has maintained a policy of non-alignment since adopting its current foreign policy in 1986.
"It has not had similar joint facilities in the past despite boasting close political and military relations with Vietnam, as well as China and Russia … and any mention of foreign bases in Laos typically recalls the CIA's bases during the Indochina Wars," Creak said.
Still, he believes it's "highly unlikely" that Laos will adjust its formal foreign policy settings or its longstanding effort to balance relations with Vietnam, Thailand and China.

Gallery: Pre-war statesman reburied in Kuressaare over a century after death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

Gallery: Pre-war statesman reburied in Kuressaare over a century after death
Estonian statesman Otto Pukk has been laid to rest on his home island of Saaremaa, 126 years after his birth there and 75 years after his death.
Pukk (1900–1951) was the last chair of Estonia's Riigivolikogu, the lower chamber of the legislature between the two world wars.
His remains, together with those of his wife, Agnes, were reburied at Kudjape cemetery in Kuressaare, the capital of Saaremaa, where he was born.
Pukk took part in the Estonian War of Independence (1918–1920) before fleeing to Sweden ahead of the Soviet occupation in 1944. He worked as a journalist, lawyer and politician. He served in two Riigikogu compositions and was the last chairman of the Estonian Riigivolikogu before the Soviet occupation. He was also a member of the Otto Tief government, briefly in office in September 1944 in the vacuum left by the Nazi occupiers' withdrawal and before the return of the Soviet occupiers later that same month.
The Kuressaare reburial was organized by family members including his grandchildren.
"It is a joyous event that my grandfather and grandmother are home again. That wish has always been there. In the early 1990s, when many statesmen were reburied, he had the opportunity too, but then my grandmother was still alive — over 100 years old — and he didn't quite want to. We finally took it on. This is a family initiative, and in that sense a circle is complete and their wish has been fulfilled," said Pukk's grandson, also named Otto.
Riigikogu Speaker Lauri Hussar was among those who addressed the ceremony.

ARX and Roboneers deepen Ukraine drone partnership
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
15:00:46 BST
23:00:46 KST

German defence technology company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian firm Roboneers have agreed a wider partnership covering unmanned ground systems, including technical integration and joint development work for Ukrainian and other European forces, according to ARX Robotics.
The agreement was signed in Kyiv during a German state visit to Ukraine, in the presence of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Under the partnership, the two companies plan to deepen the integration of their respective unmanned systems and continue joint development work around ground robotics for military use. Both companies are already supplying uncrewed ground vehicles to the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The latest agreement follows an earlier deal reached in June 2026 to establish ARX Industries, a production joint venture intended to manufacture the Rys Pro unmanned ground vehicle in Ukraine and Germany.
The Rys Pro is developed by Roboneers, which produces a range of Ukrainian unmanned ground and aerial systems alongside software and remote weapon technologies. The company says its platforms are used for roles including frontline logistics, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance and combat support.
ARX Robotics, meanwhile, develops its Gereon family of unmanned ground vehicles and the Mithra OS software platform, which is designed to provide autonomous and digital functions across military land systems.
According to a news update from ARX Robotics, company chief executive Marc Wietfeld said: “Software-defined unmanned defense solutions are key for landforces on a modern battlefield where every action can be seen by the enemy. Together with Roboneers we provide the Ukrainian forces with a robust but smart UGV fleet at scale and at the same time ensure that the lessons learnt from the battlefield are incorporated into the landsystems development of other western armies.”
The companies are positioning the partnership around both immediate Ukrainian requirements and the wider development of autonomous land systems for European armed forces. ARX said feedback from systems operating in Ukraine would be incorporated into future land-platform development, allowing lessons from frontline use to influence software, vehicle design and operating concepts elsewhere.
The Ukrainian government estimates that national demand for unmanned ground systems could reach 50,000 units during 2026, according to the company.
ARX also states that its Gereon vehicles currently represent the largest fleet of Western-built unmanned ground systems operating in Ukraine. The use of UGVs has expanded during the war as Ukrainian forces have increasingly used unmanned platforms to move supplies, evacuate casualties, conduct reconnaissance and support combat activity while reducing the need to expose personnel to direct fire.
For manufacturers, the scale and pace of operations in Ukraine has also created demand for systems that can be produced in quantity, repaired quickly and adapted through software or modular payloads as battlefield requirements change. ARX has been expanding its industrial capacity alongside the operational partnership. The company has recently worked with German industrial firms including Deutz as it seeks to increase production of unmanned ground vehicles. The Roboneers partnership adds a Ukrainian manufacturing and development component to that effort through the previously announced ARX Industries joint venture.
Roboneers says its Rys Pro UGV and Saber remote weapon station have been deployed across units of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, with its systems collectively used during more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014. ARX Robotics was founded in 2022 and currently employs around 300 people across Munich, Berlin, London and Kyiv. Its work is centred on autonomous ground platforms and software intended to add digital and autonomous functions to both new and existing military vehicles.
Roboneers describes its own approach as a multi-domain robotic ecosystem spanning unmanned ground vehicles, unmanned aerial systems and associated software, with development and manufacturing conducted in Ukraine. The latest agreement expands an existing relationship between the two companies from production of individual systems towards closer technical integration, joint development and a broader approach to unmanned land warfare.

Male managers start hiring more women after their first daughter is born, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

Male managers who become fathers to their first daughter tend to start hiring more women, raising women’s share of jobs and earnings at the businesses they run, according to research accepted for publication in The Review of Economic Studies. The shift appeared almost immediately after the birth and had no detectable effect on the firm’s overall performance.
The research revolves around the daughter effect, a sociological concept describing how fathering a daughter makes men more sensitive to issues of gender equality. The research, led by Maddalena Ronchi, an assistant professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management, and Nina Smith of Aarhus University, sought to understand if this shift in personal attitudes translates into concrete professional actions.
“Economists increasingly see gender attitudes as one reason why gender gaps persist in the labor market,” Ronchi told PsyPost. “Most of that research, however, has focused on how attitudes shape women’s own choices—whether and how much to work, for example, or whom to marry.”
“But managers’ attitudes could matter just as much, because managers decide whom to hire, retain, and promote,” she continued.
The authors note that managers hold a lot of power over hiring, firing, and promotions. Because of this, their personal biases or beliefs could be a driving force behind why women continue to face unequal pay and fewer opportunities in the corporate world. It is difficult to study how a manager’s personal views affect their employees because attitudes are hard to measure.
“The challenge is that it is very hard to isolate the effect of a manager’s attitudes,” Ronchi explained. “We rarely observe what managers actually think about women’s role at work.”
“And even if we did, managers with different attitudes are likely to differ in many other ways,” she noted. “A manager with more progressive views may be younger or more educated, for example. He may also choose, or be chosen by, a firm that already treats women differently. So simply comparing managers or firms cannot tell us whether managers’ attitudes themselves affect women’s careers.”
In addition, managers are not randomly assigned to companies, making it tough to separate a single person’s influence from the company’s existing culture. By looking at what happens to female employees when a male manager becomes a father to a daughter rather than a son, the researchers hoped to capture a natural experiment, a situation where chance, rather than researchers, sorts people into comparison groups.
“Ideally, we would change a manager’s attitudes at random, keep him in the same firm, and see whether his treatment of female employees changes,” Ronchi said. “Of course, we cannot run that experiment. Instead, we use the birth of a manager’s first daughter. Whether a newborn is a boy or a girl is essentially random, and previous research suggests that having a daughter can make fathers more attentive to gender inequality.”
This approach allowed them to see how an external shock to a manager’s worldview might shift their workplace behavior. To investigate this, the researchers used Danish administrative registry data spanning from 1992 to 2017. These records linked employer and employee information with longitudinal data on family composition. The authors focused on single-manager establishments, which are workplaces with only one person in a management role. These businesses averaged 12 to 13 workers, but made up more than 90 percent of Danish establishments and accounted for about a third of total employment.
This setup increased the likelihood that the manager being studied was directly responsible for personnel decisions like hiring and supervising employees on a daily basis. Because previous research indicates that the daughter effect is mostly observed in fathers, the study restricted its focus to male managers. The final sample included 6,701 periods of employment where a male manager experienced the birth of a child while working at the same company.
The researchers tracked two outcomes within the same company before and after the birth: the share of employees who were women, and a measure comparing women’s average earnings with men’s, scored so that 0.5 means women and men earned the same on average. At the companies studied, women made up 34 percent of employees on average, and the earnings measure averaged 0.39. They controlled for the total number of children a manager had, comparing fathers who had a daughter with those who had a son while also adjusting for workforce characteristics like average education and company size.
After the birth of a manager’s first daughter, the earnings measure rose by about 0.017, a 4.4 percent increase over its average of 0.39, and women’s share of employees rose by about 1 percentage point, a 2.9 percent increase. “To put those numbers in perspective, these effects amount to roughly 20 to 50% of the difference in women’s outcomes between firms run by male and female managers,” Ronchi pointed out.
This positive effect on female employment and earnings was concentrated among managers having their first daughter. Experiencing the birth of additional daughters produced a positive but smaller effect that was not statistically reliable. Furthermore, among managers having their first child, a son did not reduce women’s outcomes, suggesting the effect reflects daughters raising them rather than sons lowering them.
When breaking down how these changes happened, the data showed that managers shifted their hiring practices. Instead of completely restructuring the workforce to be more family-friendly by offering more part-time roles, managers simply substituted male hires with female hires who had similar qualifications. Following the birth of a first daughter, managers hired more women who were highly educated, worked full-time, and commanded higher salaries. The researchers also found that women already working at the firm who were good candidates for promotion were more likely to see earnings increases, while male employees did not experience a similar change.
“The main takeaway is that managers’ attitudes toward women can shape women’s opportunities at work—and that those attitudes may change quite quickly,” Ronchi observed.
These results fit with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that among managers, having a daughter weakened the link between a rivalrous form of narcissism and traditional gender role attitudes, though that study measured self-reported attitudes rather than hiring and pay. The findings also align with a study of Japanese fathers covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that men whose firstborn child was a daughter were more likely to reject traditional gender roles and support gender-equality policies, again based on self-reported attitudes rather than workplace decisions.
The study also assessed whether these shifts in hiring and promotion affected the financial health of the companies. Looking at sales, total employment, and value added per employee, which is the value a business creates per worker, the researchers found no detectable effect on firm performance.
“Importantly, we find no evidence that these gains for women came at a cost to the firm,” Ronchi noted. “So the results suggest that at least some of the men these managers would previously have hired could instead be replaced by similarly qualified women without a detectable cost to the firm.”
This indicates that managers were able to hire observably similar women without sacrificing productivity. It also suggests that any previous bias favoring men did not provide an economic benefit to the firm.
Additionally, the researchers looked at the timing of these changes. The shift in hiring and in women’s earnings happened almost immediately after the daughter’s birth, and the effect persisted for years afterward. This rapid change suggests that managers did not need years of seeing their daughters grow up to learn about gender barriers in the labor market.
“That timing is important,” Ronchi said. “A newborn daughter is decades away from entering the labor market herself, so the manager cannot be improving opportunities for women in order to directly benefit his own child.”
“Instead, the evidence is consistent with having a daughter changing how managers think about women more broadly—and those changes showing up almost immediately in their decisions at work,” she added.
A separate comparison of managers whose oldest daughters were different ages found that the effect grew stronger as daughters reached adolescence and adulthood, suggesting that continued exposure may reinforce the initial shift. The effect was also larger among managers born in 1965 or later and for births after 2001.
The authors interpret the lack of a performance effect as a sign that the bias they detected mostly affected close calls between a man and a woman with similar education, hours, and pay. Theoretical work they cite suggests that even subtle bias of this kind can carry long-run costs, for example by discouraging women from investing in skills if they expect to lose such close calls.
“The gender bias we uncover seems to operate ‘at the margin’—affecting whether a man or an equally qualified woman gets the job, rather than leading managers to choose substantially less qualified workers,” Ronchi explained. “That helps explain why changing these decisions can improve women’s opportunities without producing a detectable change in the firm’s output. The absence of a productivity effect does not mean the bias is harmless. A manager choosing a man over an equally qualified woman may make little difference to that firm’s output, while repeated decisions like this can make a large difference to women’s careers.”
As with all research, there are a few caveats to consider. “One important misinterpretation is that fathers of daughters are somehow better managers, or that firms should care about whether a manager has sons or daughters,” Ronchi emphasized. “That is not the point of the study. The birth of a daughter gives us a research tool: an essentially random event that previous research links to men’s attitudes toward gender, allowing us to study whether workplace decisions change after that event.”
The study focuses entirely on single-manager businesses in Denmark. It is unknown if managers in larger corporations would have the same level of freedom to change hiring practices based on their personal attitudes. Formal human resources policies in larger firms might constrain an individual manager’s ability to act on their updated worldview.
Another limitation is that the researchers cannot directly read the managers’ minds or measure their exact beliefs. Because the research relies on administrative data, it only tracks the outcomes of the managers’ decisions rather than their internal psychological states. Future research could explore whether diversity training or other interventions might produce a similar shift in perspective for managers who do not have daughters.
The study, “Daddy’s Girl: Daughters, Managerial Decisions, and Gender Inequality,” was authored by Maddalena Ronchi and Nina Smith.

studio KO turns historic 1960s bus palladium nightclub into five-star hotel in paris

studio KO turns historic 1960s bus palladium nightclub into five-star hotel in paris
the legendary nightlife address trades its old dance hall for six floors of rooms, keeping its red neon, club downstairs, and rock ‘n’ roll pulse alive.
STUDIO KO REIMAGINES BUS PALLADIUM IN PIGALLE
On rue Pierre Fontaine in Paris’ Pigalle district, Studio KO has brought Bus Palladium club back into the night — this time as a five-star hotel. Opened on April 10, 2026, the project brings together 35 rooms and suites, a restaurant and bar, a rooftop and an underground club within a building that rises six floors above the street and extends deep below it. Led by architects Karl Fournier and Olivier Marty, the intervention does not attempt to recreate the former venue room by room. Instead, it translates its history through materials, atmosphere and a few carefully preserved signals. The red neon is back; the program simply got taller.
The original Bus Palladium was founded by James Arch in 1965 as something close to an anti-private club: a place where suburban youth, beatniks, artists and Paris’ more polished crowds could somehow end up on the same dance floor. Salvador Dalí arrived shortly after its opening, while Serge Gainsbourg, Jane Birkin, Patti Smith and generations of musicians would later become part of its mythology. The venue closed in 2022, but its next chapter had already begun taking shape through building owner Christian Casmèze and Nicolas Saltiel of hotel group Chapitre Six, who imagined hospitality, music and nightlife occupying the same address rather than neatly separating from one another.
BUS PALLADIUM’S ARCHITECTURE LAYERS PAST AND PRESENT
For Studio KO, preserving the Bus Palladium did not mean preserving its old structure at all costs. The existing building, assembled from brick, stone, concrete and metal, could not structurally support the proposed addition, and was ultimately demolished. ‘Buildings do not have only a structural life: they also contain history and emotion,’ Fournier explains. The architects instead recovered traces of its architectural vocabulary, including the rhythm of its entrances and horizontal lines across the new façade that recall the former brickwork. ‘We made sure that the layers of past and present would add up and accumulate, rather than erase one another,’ he adds.
The result fills what had been a low gap in the surrounding Parisian streetscape, while a 14-meter excavation pushes the building down into four underground levels. Above ground, a restrained sandblasted concrete façade uses aggregates selected to echo the warm tones of Haussmannian stone. Inside, restraint begins to misbehave. Raw concrete meets thick patterned carpets, reflective surfaces, vivid color and references to the 1960s and 70s. Studio KO describes the approach as one of deliberate contrast, conceived to connect the building to a DNA ‘marked by a certain impertinence.’ Five-star polish is present, but it is not allowed to become too well behaved.
STUDIO KO SHAPES THE ROOMS, RESTAURANT AND CLUB
Across the hotel’s 35 rooms and suites, concrete ceilings are paired with enveloping cork walls — a distant nod to Marcel Proust’s cork-lined bedroom — while powder-pink carpets, blue mirrors and corduroy curtains soften the harder surfaces. Bathrooms sit behind translucent voile curtains, alternately revealed and concealed, and smaller details keep returning to music: switches resemble vintage amplifiers, door handles borrow from microphone grilles, and bespoke wooden speakers allow guests to play the hotel’s playlists. For Fournier, these oppositions are more than decoration: ‘contrast is not just a visual effect, but a way of making space feel more alive.’
Objects add another layer of controlled eccentricity. Transparent bedside cubes contain artworks, old cassettes, books and miniature buses, while the Dalí Suite leans furthest into the building’s 1970s afterimage with a modular DS-600 De Sede sofa, mirrored alcove and balcony overlooking the neon sign. Artistic director Caroline de Maigret extends the experience through music, scent and staff uniforms, while downstairs the building eventually returns to its original business: dancing. The underground club and live stage turn the hotel into a place where checking in and going out do not necessarily require two different addresses.
BUS PALLADIUM’S VINYL-LINED RESTAURANT
The restaurant makes that overlap particularly visible. Studio KO places a dense pocket of vegetation inside a glass cube at its center, with diner-style alcoves and high and low banquettes wrapping around the planted patio. Psychedelic crystal motifs spread across the carpet, while one wall becomes a vinyl archive built from more than a thousand records, including James Arch’s historic collection. A console can be pulled from the vinyl bar for DJ sets, allowing dinner to drift rather easily into whatever happens next. Fournier says the aim was to create a place where guests would want to remain ‘at home’ while still feeling in tune with the pulse of Paris.
In the kitchen, chef Valentin Raffali picks up on the same tension between refinement and informality. His concise menus prioritize ingredients sourced as locally and directly as possible, with dishes shaped around seasonal produce and straightforward combinations rather than elaborate construction. It is an appropriate ending to a project built around collisions: hotel and nightclub, concrete and carpet, sleep and sound, memory and an entirely new building. Bus Palladium may now have room keys and five stars, but the address still seems most comfortable when the boundaries between one thing and the next get a little blurry.

design: Studio KO | @studioko
location: Paris, France

Hundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal graves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in unmarked communal graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.
A Guardian Australia investigation has identified more than 100 unmarked graves across New South Wales, and some in Queensland, that are being used by state governments to bury those deemed too poor to afford their own funerals.
Using evidence from family, friends and the homelessness sector, together with analysis of cemetery registries and aerial imagery, the Guardian has established that the NSW government is using bare stretches of earth between dirt walkways and old headstones at Rookwood cemetery in Sydney to bury the remains of four to six strangers together in communal graves.
Among those being buried together are war veterans, cancer sufferers, people with gambling addictions and severe mental illness, and migrants from developing countries whose families cannot afford exorbitant repatriation costs.
In at least six cases, the Guardian has identified failures by authorities that meant friends, family or support workers were either not contacted or not told of the use of unmarked and common graves. The failures are likely breaches of a NSW policy designed to “avoid causing unnecessary distress to people who may have wished to make other funeral arrangements”.
Shocked family and friends say they have been left feeling robbed.
“It’s unspeakable,” said Chantel Dubsky, whose brother Roger Davies, a rough sleeper, was buried in an unmarked grave with four strangers at Rookwood without her knowledge. “He should have had the opportunity to be laid to rest with his mother, his grandparents and the people he loved, at his home in Adelaide.
“He wasn’t just someone off the street – he was someone’s son, he was someone’s brother. He was my brother.”
By crosschecking names with homelessness services in Sydney, Guardian Australia has also identified a further 18 individuals in the communal graves who had experienced homelessness.
The homelessness sector is outraged by the revelations.
Two leaders in Sydney’s homelessness sector say they were never made aware of the practice of using unmarked communal graves and are not being given the chance to intervene on behalf of their clients to fund a proper burial.
A third service, the Rev Bill Crews Foundation, an inner-city Sydney homelessness charity, says it has repeatedly raised concerns with the state government about the possible use of unmarked and communal graves but has been ignored.
The Rev Bill Crews, who runs the foundation, identified three of his clients as being among those in the communal graves but said he had not been told about their deaths and impending burials.
“It’s outrageous,” Crews said. “We did not know – they would all have had a dignified funeral and a proper cremation, and their ashes would have been scattered in the sea.
The foundation regularly uses its own funds to conduct funeral services for rough sleepers when it becomes aware they have died. It was given no notification in the three cases.
“For us, it’s frustrating. Incredibly frustrating.”
Guardian Australia has also established that two veterans of the Vietnam war, who both served in the Royal Australian Navy, were buried in unmarked communal graves in 2024 and 2025.
The pair were buried despite the availability of a federal funding program run by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to help pay for the funerals of impoverished veterans. NSW policy recommends state health authorities approach DVA in such cases.
DVA was never asked for funding for the 2024 and 2025 burials. A spokesperson said it has “not been approached to help fund the burials of destitute persons since 2020”.
The Guardian’s investigation has prompted an apology from NSW Health, which has flagged changes to improve the process, and criticism from the health minister, Ryan Park, who described the failings as “unacceptable”.
In the first half of this year alone, a 17-metre stretch of earth adjacent to a dirt pathway at Rookwood has been dug up and used to bury the remains of more than 40 people in unmarked communal graves, including a rough sleeper who was well-known to most major homelessness services.
Nothing has been left to mark the 17-metre stretch of graves. Inspections of the sites of hundreds of other burials at Rookwood since 2010 show only about a dozen are marked by crosses or plaques.
The vast majority have no crosses, plaques or headstones to name the groups of deceased in each plot. There are also no signs to indicate the presence of graves.
Older sites, where the earth has settled, appear simply as long stretches of grass.
Markings are generally not used in Queensland for the smaller number of people buried under its scheme. The use of communal graves is much rarer in that state.
The situation contrasts sharply with the process embraced by Victoria, where each individual is given their own grave and a simple marking, identifying who is interred below.
The NSW government has previously pledged to stop the use of unmarked graves for destitute burials.
That came after lobbying by Barbara Davis, who was never told that her foster daughter Christine Halpin had been buried in Rookwood in 1989.
Davis and Christine’s biological daughter Jayne say they were told by the NSW government in 2013 that the use of unmarked graves would cease. The cemetery erected a “path of remembrance” that allows people to pay more than $800 to put a plaque on a rock, about 1km from some of the gravesites, but this has been used in a few dozen cases since 2020.
Christine’s gravesite remains unmarked. Davis and Jayne are both furious.
“It is a disgrace,” Davis said. “Whether you’re a prince or a pauper, you deserve a decent burial site, even just with a wooden cross with your name on it.”
In another case, a young Fijian who came to Australia to play rugby in Leeton, in NSW’s Riverina region, was buried in a communal unmarked grave after dying of cancer in 2022.
A former Leeton mayor, Paul Maytom, now president of the Leeton Multicultural Support Group, said he had previously helped raise funds from local Solomon Islander and Vietnamese communities to provide repatriation or proper burials.
He was not informed about the Fijian’s death.
“There should be a point of contact when this type of thing happens,” Maytom said. “And you should never have a situation where someone ends up in an unmarked grave, particularly when there are community members who are willing to help pay.”
A NSW Health Pathology spokesperson apologised for the failings, acknowledging they meant the dead and families and friends were not always treated with dignity and respect.
“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a spokesperson said.
“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”
NSW Health said it had made changes to the process in 2025 and in recent months to improve the way the funerals were handled. That includes giving NSW Health greater control, in place of police, and creating a dedicated six-person team within NSW Health Pathology to provide “alternative funeral arrangements and alternate sources of support for families and friends that may be willing to assist”.
It also flagged improving its relationships with “religious, cultural, charitable, community, and government organisations” to find funding for funerals after deaths.
Two NSW ministers, Park and the homelessness minister, Rose Jackson, said the dead and their families should be treated with respect, regardless of their financial circumstances.
“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable,” Park said.
“Since early 2025, NSW Health has made significant changes to establish a more comprehensive and person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve.”
A spokesperson for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood general cemetery, said the NSW government did not fund it to provide grave markings for persons without means.
MMP said destitute burials were not the only burial type that used multiple interments in a single plot, and rejected any suggestion that those buried through the process were being placed between individual headstones, under walkways or in trenches.
It also said it had identified no legislation or regulation that had given effect to the government’s 2013 promise to mark graves.

Snakes, bobcats, mountain lions: the secret animal world beneath the Hollywood sign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

Atop Mount Lee, in the heart of Los Angeles, the wind is quiet. Two red-tailed hawks sail above, barely flapping as they coast the thermal air like surfers on a wave. Standing beside the giant letters of the Hollywood sign, the city seems peaceful. On a clear day, blocks and blocks of homes unfold beneath and the skies reveal sights all the way to Catalina Island – 10 miles out, across the Pacific.
That’s the beauty seen from the Hollywood sign.
The sign sits on a hillside in Griffith Park, which, at about five times the size of Central Park, is the largest municipal park in the city. The letters have long been an international symbol for human residents in the metropolis – of dreams, film-making ambition and success. But it’s also a hallmark of the region’s environmental richness.
Because the area is closed off from the public, it has become a favorite of animals seeking respite from the city. There are birds nesting in the sign, snakes curled up at its base, bobcat roaming around the letters. It was the backdrop that made the famous wild mountain lion P-22 into an LA icon when a 2013 National Geographic photograph captured him prowling at night with the illuminated Hollywood sign in the background.
Now, a team of scientists is preparing to outfit the letters with cameras, able to capture any fire outbreaks that the basin may experience. The sign’s caretakers are collaborating with Torch Systems, a technology company that uses solar-powered sensors, on an AI fire-detection service that can identify smoke from miles away. Fire is considered the area’s largest anticipated risk, particularly as visitors may bring lit cigarettes into the park.
On a recent Wednesday, the Guardian hiked up the mountain with the team to survey the environment of the sign. As we don gloves, skirt a steep trail and rappel down a private trail to the letters, mounds of coyote scat are a constant reminder of who has walked these paths before us.
“Los Angeles is butted up against nature,” says Diana Wright, official caretaker for the Hollywood Sign Trust. She gestures around the hillside, part of the 4,310 acres, or about 6.5 sq miles, that exist in the shadow of the sign. “We’re inside this huge natural park – way bigger than Central Park – and also much more native. And then you’ve got this man-made sign of it that’s meant to withstand rockslides and landslides and winds.”
The park is home to many creatures. The Educational Research Center at the University of California, Los Angeles, has designated Griffith Park a Significant Ecological Area, in part for its crucial role “as a corridor for any gene flow and species movement between the Santa Monica, San Gabriel and Verdugo Mountains”. Researchers have documented about 200 species of birds in the park, along with 50 species of butterflies and 40 species of mammals.
Like many parts of Los Angeles, the sign was originally a publicity stunt – and a temporary one. It was originally constructed of tin and telephone poles in 1923, to advertise a local housing development called “Hollywoodland”. Eventually, the “land” section was dropped. Over the years, the structures deteriorated. Hugh Hefner led a campaign in 1978 to replace the letters with massive steel beams set in concrete foundations.
Over the century, it became a real anchor point for life in the city. Wright points to streetlights in downtown Los Angeles that are designed to resemble New York, and other parts of the city where Parisian city scenes are filmed.
“Much of the city is designed to look like other places due to our filming background,” says Wright. “The sign offers that sense of place that so many parts of the city lack.” She thinks that is why it is often the sign that is blown up in movies – or photographed when something unusual, like a once-in-a-decade snowstorm happens.
The sign may have stronger footholds in the earth now, but it is also facing challenges. Mount Lee is steep, and the hillside, and the animal habitat it is home to faces risks from earthquakes, climate change, changing rainfall and events such as El Niño. The conservancy caregivers have ongoing projects to clear brush to keep fire dangers down, but they have to balance erosion control, fire concerns and unobstructed views of the sign.
Wright and the other caretakers are also developing a plan with the city to plant more native California flora and potentially create a native flower super bloom near the sign. “The Hollywood sign is such a celebration of California,” Wright says. “It should be beautiful and stunning in its natural glory.”
Will the letters still be here in 100 years? And what will the wildlife surrounding it look like then? Wright says it all depends on the land beneath. “The hillside is going to define what the sign is like in the future,” she says, pointing out that the whole city could look different after a big environmental shake-up like an earthquake. “I think that’s a real metaphor for Los Angeles in general.”
But on that day, it was only blue skies and lizards scuttling away from our footsteps, in the shadow of giant letters.

What happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital? | Ranjana Srivastava
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:26 UTC
23:00:26 KST

“Doctor, do you know I have a little dog?”
My team exchanges a glance. It’s my turn today.
“Tell me about your dog.”
Her face lights up. “Well, he is just a lovely little thing. When I am knitting, he curls up on my lap and keeps me company. We are very happy, the two of us.”
It is unlikely that our patient has knitted in the last year, during which a series of mishaps has brought her in and out of hospital. But the rest of her account rings true.
For as long as possible, she stayed at home, managing miraculously well despite her cognitive impairment, with little help beyond an occasional carer. But now, a fall has brought her undone. For weeks, she has been waiting for residential care, one more statistic in the familiar story of “bed block”.
From our medical perspective, she is waiting for a facility. But from hers, she is waiting to see her dog. She can recall very little about her life but, when it comes to her pet, her descriptions are unwavering. Her words paint a small brown dog, quietly following her around her apartment. Jumping into her lap when she settles into her armchair. Ready to do it all over again tomorrow.
The paramedic who rescued her from her garden noted that the neighbour had offered to take the dog until the patient’s return. But this time, the patient is not going home.
Seeing how much she enjoys the nurses fussing over her – and because she has never once asked to go home – we have not mentioned her living arrangement. But she longs for her dog – and our decision not to lie is far easier in principle than in practice.
There is no easy provision to reunite her with her dog. The neighbour can’t bring the dog in. The hospital won’t let the dog in. (“Imagine the other patients.”)
What if seeing her dog proved distressing afterwards? What if it created a safety risk? And if we made an exception for her, what would we do for the next patient who pined for her turn?
The more frequently I encounter the problem, the more I see it as an emblem of the things medicine considers peripheral to patient care, even when they may not be peripheral at all.
Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. They provide physical activity, psychological comfort and social connection. For some older people, an animal is their most constant companion.
But concern for a pet’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare. Patients may delay seeking care, worry about coming to hospital, or discharge themselves because there is a pet at home.
A recent essay in the New England Journal of Medicine on human-animal relationships points to a perhaps delayed recognition of something we have understood for years: the wellbeing of humans and their pets is intertwined.
When I was an intern, just two questions often formed the social history: Does the patient smoke? Does the patient drink?
Today we do better. We ask: Where does the patient live? What services exist? Is there a history of falls? Is the family involved?
Perhaps we should add another question: Are you concerned about a pet?
It is a deceptively easy question to ask. Because what happens when the answer is yes?
Who will feed the cat? Who will walk the dog? What if the patient cannot return home?
The solution can’t be another mental responsibility casually added to the medical worklist. Yet ignoring the issue doesn’t obscure the problem.
More of us are starting to notice what we have traditionally neglected – not only where a patient lives but also which animal lives with them and what will happen to that animal if the patient doesn’t go home.
For many people, pets are part of the social determinants of health. Hospitals cannot take on this responsibility alone. But it’s time to ask how hospitals can work effectively with community services and animal welfare agencies to care for the whole patient.
Know thy neighbour – and thy neighbour’s dog.
For as long as we cared for her, one doctor from our team sat down with our patient and heard her retell the story about her dog. We never let our interest drift, even when our hearts slightly broke each time. Every one of us would have brought in her dog – if only we could.
One day, all of us rotated out. We left her in the hands of another team, hoping they would continue the ritual.

Mohammed Dahlan: The man who could help reshape Gaza after Hamas – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

On July 9, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas announced that parliamentary elections would be held on November 28 in the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and Gaza.
If they indeed take place, they will be the first in 20 years.
The last, in 2006, was won by Hamas. They were followed by a violent power struggle with Fatah, culminating in Hamas gaining control of Gaza in 2007.
Ever since, the continuing popularity of Hamas with the Palestinian people has inhibited Abbas, fearful of losing power, from holding elections.
Perhaps it is the Trump peace plan for Gaza, currently being implemented by the Board of Peace and committed to disempowering Hamas, that has encouraged Abbas to try to regain some democratic credibility by approving new elections.
In any event, the announcement has brought Mohammad Dahlan once again to the forefront of the Palestinian political arena.
Hamas wins Palestinians’ popular vote
Dahlan was born in the Khan Yunis refugee camp in the Gaza Strip in 1961. He joined Fatah’s youth movement as a teenager and was repeatedly imprisoned by Israel.
Following the Oslo Accords in the 1990s, Abbas appointed him head of the Palestinian Preventive Security Service force in Gaza. He became so powerful that the Gaza Strip was nicknamed “Dahlanistan.”
Their relationship subsequently collapsed amid growing fears within Abbas’s camp that Dahlan was being primed by the US to succeed him.
Dahlan was expelled from Fatah in 2011 amid allegations of corruption and involvement in a plot to assassinate Yasser Arafat, allegations he denied.
He went into exile in the United Arab Emirates, where he became an adviser to Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, now UAE president.
By removing Dahlan from Palestinian politics, Abbas unintentionally converted him into a regional political operator who was no longer dependent on the PA.
Over the subsequent decade, Dahlan accumulated regional connections and became an important political operator for Abu Dhabi. He also developed relationships in Egypt and elsewhere and maintained connections with Israeli security figures.
While living in exile in the UAE, Dahlan founded a party called Democratic Reformist Current inside Gaza.
The DRC worked hard to secure a joint alliance with both Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and on October 1 an electoral coalition was announced. Palestinian sources say the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine could also join.
Dahlan is attempting a political reentry via Gaza. He is not seeking to govern it personally. He seems to be trying to turn his UAE-backed Fatah dissident network into a bridge between Hamas, other Fatah breakaways, Egypt, the UAE, and the US-led Gaza peace process.
He has proposed what amounts to a political formula for overcoming the Palestinian split. Rather than a contest for control of the PA, he advocates a “national partnership.”
Fatah’s Mohammad Dahlan eyes taking control of the West Bank via Gaza
This would incorporate elections to determine political representation and office, alongside a new constitution or “national social contract” emphasizing popular legitimacy and the peaceful transfer of power.
His proposals are deliberately broad in scope. They give Hamas some say in Palestinian national decision-making; they offer a future Palestinian leadership a language of unity; and they give the UAE, Egypt, and the US a Palestinian figure with Gaza roots who can speak to all the parties involved, including Israel and external sponsors.
His electoral allies have not yet endorsed Dahlan’s plan, but they have not disavowed it either. His involvement places him at the center of the Palestinian political game. He has brought himself closer than ever to a return to Palestinian political leadership.
Moreover, Dahlan seems to have taken on a mediating role – a position he could not have aspired to 10 years ago. He now appears to have channels of communication with Hamas and other Palestinian factions, as well as with the UAE, Egypt, Washington, and parts of the Israeli security establishment.
He will be aware that the Palestinian parliamentary elections could possibly bring to an end the transitional administrative arrangements in Gaza being overseen by the Board of Peace.
The Gaza peace plan, endorsed by the UN Security Council, envisages Gaza moving through a temporary, internationally backed arrangement.
The Board of Peace was established to oversee that transition, while the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was created as a Palestinian, technocratic, and explicitly apolitical body to administer Gaza’s civil affairs. It is intended to operate until the PA has completed its reform program.
The ultimate objective is therefore not an international administration of Gaza, but the reconstitution of Palestinian government, with Gaza eventually reunited politically with the West Bank.
Nobody has yet formally declared that the November elections are the mechanism by which the Board of Peace will hand Gaza to its eventual government.
But Dahlan’s recent contacts with Hamas and his involvement in discussions over Gaza’s reconstruction appear to fit remarkably well into this political problem.
One possible scenario could see Palestinians participate in national elections and a substantially reformed Palestinian government emerge. Gaza and the West Bank could be brought back under one Palestinian political authority.
In short, the election could become the mechanism through which the old Palestinian political order is replaced, without the Board of Peace itself choosing its successor.
An American- or Arab-appointed Palestinian government taking power in Gaza would be vulnerable to the accusation that it was simply an externally imposed administration. An elected Palestinian legislature producing a new government would have a much stronger claim to legitimacy.
If Dahlan succeeds in bringing Hamas, his DRC, Fatah dissidents, and other Palestinian currents into a workable political arrangement, he would inevitably become central to Gaza’s political future.
The wider issue is whether Dahlan can help construct a bridge between Hamas’s exit from government, international reconstruction, Palestinian elections, and a reformed Palestinian Authority.
If that bridge can be built, the Board of Peace would cease to be merely an international administration imposed upon a devastated territory. It could become temporary scaffolding for building a new Palestinian political system.
Far from simply rebuilding Gaza, Dahlan could therefore play a central role in providing the Gaza Strip with a truly viable and hopeful future.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com

Ammodo Architecture Announces First Edition of Architecture Days in Amsterdam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Ammodo Architecture will launch the first edition of Ammodo Architecture Days in Amsterdam on November 9 and 10, 2026. Organized by Ammodo Architecture, a programme of the Ammodo Foundation, the event will bring together architects, landscape architects, urban planners, artists, communities, collectives and multidisciplinary design teams, alongside recipients of the 2024 and 2025 Ammodo Architecture Award. Taking place at Westergas, a former industrial complex now used as a cultural and public venue, the two-day programme will combine a symposium, exhibition, publication launch and award ceremony, creating a setting for exchange between practices working across different geographic, cultural and disciplinary contexts.
The programme draws on 49 projects recognized through the first two editions of the Ammodo Architecture Award and is structured around six themes: Reclaim, Heritage, Urban Acupuncture, Rebalance, Mastering Material and Reuse. These themes bring together projects that work with existing buildings and materials, local knowledge, community participation, and changing urban conditions, with an emphasis on the processes behind the work as much as the completed projects. Among those featured are Machan_Korail Community Platform by Paraa in Bangladesh, which transformed a former dumping ground into a community and cultural space; VinziRast am Land by gaupenraub+/− in Austria, which adapted a former luxury hotel into a residential and working community; and Sustainable Alleys by RAMA estudio in Ecuador, which explores the potential of Quito's alleys as greener and more socially connected public spaces.
The programme will begin with the symposium on November 10, bringing together award recipients, members of the Ammodo Architecture Advisory Committee and invited practitioners for a series of lectures, conversations and workshops. Speakers include Andrés Jaque, architect and Dean and Professor at Columbia University GSAPP; Anupama Kundoo, architect and Professor at TU Berlin; Floris Alkemade, architect and former Chief Government Architect of the Netherlands; Loreta Castro Reguera, architect and Professor at UNAM in Mexico City; and Aric Chen, Director of the Zaha Hadid Foundation in London.
Related Article
Ammodo Architecture Awards 2025 Announces 26 Recipients for Socially and Ecologically Responsible Design
Alongside the discussions, an exhibition designed by Thonik, Studio LMNOP and Fiction Factory will present projects by recipients of the 2024 and 2025 Ammodo Architecture Award. Rather than presenting the work solely as a collection of completed projects, the exhibition will examine the ideas, processes and contexts that shaped them, offering a closer look at the different approaches represented across the two award editions. Following its presentation in Amsterdam, the exhibition is planned to travel internationally, with further locations to be announced.
The event will also mark the launch of a new publication by Hatje Cantz, bringing together essays by invited contributors and in-depth examinations of projects from the two award editions. The programme will conclude with a ceremony celebrating the 2024 and 2025 Ammodo Architecture Award recipients, whose work is recognized across three categories: Social Architecture, Social Engagement and Local Scale. From 2026 onward, the Ammodo Architecture Award and Ammodo Architecture Days will alternate biennially, extending the award programme with a recurring platform for bringing its projects and practitioners into dialogue.
In other recent news, the Copenhagen Architecture Biennial has announced its second edition, taking place from September 9 to October 15, 2027, under the theme "Elements," which examines architecture's relationship with planetary forces and environmental control. The Sharjah Architecture Triennial has also released three documentaries exploring architectural archives in Baghdad, Damascus, and Tunis, while the Danish Architecture Center is celebrating architect and urban planner Jan Gehl's 90th birthday with an exhibition and programme on his influence on people-centered urban development.

Turkey has completed construction of the 153-kilometer high-speed railway section from Çerkezköy to Kapıkule on the Bulgarian border, with the line set to be officially inaugurated on October 9 in a ceremony attended by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
"We are extending our high-speed train network from Çerkezköy to Kapıkule, all the way to the European border," Turkish Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said.
Uraloğlu said the new section would bring the cities of Tekirdağ, Kırklareli and Edirne into Turkey's high-speed rail network.
The railway is intended for both passenger and freight services and was built at a maximum design speed of 200 km/h. Construction started in 2019 with funding from Turkey and the European Union.
The project forms part of the larger Halkalı-Kapıkule railway, which is planned to link Istanbul with the Bulgarian border at Kapitan Andreevo.
Once the full route is completed, travel between Halkalı in Istanbul and Kapıkule is expected to take one hour and 30 minutes, down from about four hours. Freight journeys will be shortened from 8 hours and 30 minutes to approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes.
Uraloğlu said construction was continuing on the remaining sections of the Halkalı-Kapıkule line.
The railway link is expected to serve passenger travel between Turkey and Bulgaria as well as freight traffic between Turkey and European countries, connecting to one of the key road and rail routes between Turkey and the European Union.

Children among dozens injured as Russian glide bombs hit Kharkiv, 3 dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:59:59 UTC
22:59:59 KST

At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, including children, injured after Russian forces struck Kharkiv with glide bombs on Oct. 5.
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram.
"As a result of the strikes… warehouse buildings are on fire, and residential buildings have been damaged. There may be people under the rubble of a residential building that was hit in the attack. A search and rescue operation is underway," he added.
Russian glide bombs, often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.
Unlike traditional free-fall bombs, KABs can glide tens of kilometers before impact, allowing Russian aircraft — typically the Su-34 — to release them from a distance, safe from the operating range of Ukrainian air defense missiles or fighters.
Warhead sizes vary by model, ranging from about 300 kilograms to 3 metric tons, enough to destroy multistory buildings with a direct hit.
Russian forces use glide bombs against important, hardened, or entrenched targets, such as bridges, command posts, or drone teams spotted by reconnaissance assets.
Russia regularly launches fatal strikes on civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war. Kharkiv is a frequent target given its proximity to the front line.

HANOI, October 5. /TASS/. Around 1.1 mln Russians visited Vietnam in the first nine months of 2026, making Russia the country’s largest European tourism market, according to data from the Vietnam National Authority of Tourism.
China accounted for the largest number of visitors to Vietnam from January through October, at 3.9 mln, or 22.4% of the country’s foreign tourist arrivals in 2026. China was followed by South Korea with 3 mln tourists, or 17.3% of the total. Russia ranked third.
The Vietnam National Authority of Tourism previously noted that the number of visitors from Russia had risen by more than 165% this year, giving the country the highest growth rate among Vietnam’s major international tourism markets.
Overall, Vietnam welcomed more than 17.7 mln international tourists in the first nine months of the year, up 14.5% from the same period last year.
In late September, Russia and Vietnam signed a memorandum expanding opportunities for their air carriers to increase the number of flights. Under the agreements, Russian and Vietnamese airlines will each be able to operate 105 flights per week. Currently, four Russian airlines operate flights to Vietnam on 11 routes at a frequency of 39 flights per week, while two Vietnamese airlines operate 13 routes at a frequency of 31 flights per week.

What did the IRGC say in its letter to Americans — and Why now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:58:50 UTC
22:58:50 KST

What did the IRGC say in its letter to Americans — and Why now?
TEHRAN - On Sept. 29, 2026, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published a 25-26 page open letter addressed to “the honorable people of the United States of America — the scholars, the students, and the members of the media.”
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi presented it at a press conference in Tehran.
The letter comes seven months into the direct U.S.-Israel war against Iran that began Feb. 28, 2026, and five weeks before the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Mohebbi was explicit about the timing and audience: he did not expect it to change the Trump administration’s behavior, but hoped American voters would hear it. Reuters, TIME and Al-Jazeera all summarized the pitch as: oppose Trump’s policies, “wrest control back from corrupt politicians,” and vote for change.
The U.S. State Department on Sept. 30 dismissed it as a “smokescreen” and “latest act of desperation.”
What does the letter say?
Opening with Qur’an 13:11 — “God does not alter the affairs of a people until they alter their own affairs” — and salutations to Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad, the letter poses seven questions it says are hidden from Americans, then answers them:
The war and who won: Iran says the U.S. started the war by striking an elementary school in Minab, killing 168 schoolchildren and teachers, and simultaneously striking the offices of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killing him, several family members including his 14-month-old granddaughter, and starting a war that has since killed more than 3,600 Iranians, mostly civilians including 400 children, and hit 8 universities, 3 hospitals and 8 schools.
Tehran declares a “decisive victory” and “crushing defeat” for the U.S. and Israel. Its logic: the U.S. listed shifting goals — regime change, partition, unconditional surrender, seizing Kharg Island, ground invasion, destroying industry, energy, civilization, nuclear, missiles, controlling Hormuz and annexing it with a 20% toll, controlling airspace, cutting support for resistance groups — and achieved none, except damaging some nuclear-related buildings and limited air-defense sites.
Iran in turn says it neutralized 200+ strategic drones, 12 tanker/transport aircraft, 30 fighter jets, at least one AWACS, dozens of helicopters and radars, destroyed 350+ primary facilities and reduced 18 U.S. bases in the region to near-zero operational capability.
“Death to America”: The letter says it is not hatred of the American people but “a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House” — “Death to the crimes perpetrated by the American elite.”
Is the IRGC terrorist? No, it argues. It presents itself as a people’s force that thwarted regime change and partition, reinvigorated national and religious unity — especially among youth after Minab — and defended the concept of “Velayat-e Faqih”, now continued under new Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, introduced as a jurist, war veteran and longtime adviser to his father.
73 years of hostility: The war, it says, is only the latest chapter since the 1953 CIA-backed coup against Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh, SAVAK repression, support for Saddam in the 1980s, sanctions, and now direct war.
U.S. decline and economy: The U.S., with a military budget 100 times Iran’s, still failed, proving hegemonic decline. It warns of an imminent “massive economic earthquake” and collapse, accusing President Donald Trump of lying that “the economy is booming.”
It closes with an offer: “We can live together in peaceful coexistence” if Americans “remove from power the evil, deceitful, and violent politicians,” stop wars, end aid to Israel and “entrust your affairs to the wise, not the wily.” It urges Americans to visit Iran, even Hormuz, to see for themselves.
 
Why write to the people, not the government?
The letter argues the first casualty of U.S. wars is truth, and taxpayers bear the cost. Therefore Americans “deserve to know the truth” to protect themselves from “unjust aggression” and coming collapse. It says: “You are the ones who empower, with your votes, the government.”
In short: bypass Washington, speak over its head to voters before the midterms.
Does this have precedent?
Yes from Iran, no from the IRGC.
Iranian leaders have written directly to Americans three times before:
President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s 2006 letter “To the American People” criticizing the Bush administration, Iraq war and Israel, and calling for dialogue.
Late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei’s two letters “To the Youth in Europe and North America” in Jan. 2015 after the Charlie Hebdo attack and Nov. 2015 after Paris attacks, urging youth to study Islam from its sources rather than media, and not to judge Islam by terrorism.
Martyr Ayatollah Khamenei’s May 2024 letter to U.S. university protesters against the Gaza war, praising their “awakened conscience” as standing “on the right side of history” and part of the Resistance Front.
What is new is the author: this is the first lengthy public letter from the IRGC as a military institution to the American public, and the first to explicitly link battlefield facts, nuclear and Hormuz issues, and a direct electoral appeal to change the administration.

Inside Al-Aqsa as Israeli restrictions tighten on Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:57:58 UTC
22:57:58 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside Al-Aqsa as Palestinians fear growing Israeli control over holy site
Fear and anxiety have become increasingly palpable in occupied East Jerusalem and around Al-Aqsa Mosque, where growing Israeli restrictions, surveillance and settler incursions are changing daily life at one of Islam's holiest sites.
During a two-day tour of the Old City and Al-Aqsa Mosque, The New Arab witnessed Israeli police questioning worshippers, arrests inside the compound and settlers openly referring to the site as the "Temple Mount".
The atmosphere was particularly tense during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, when residents and business owners described how unprecedented numbers of settlers and religious Jews passed through the Old City.
More than 9,000 Israeli settlers entered the Al-Aqsa compound during Sukkot alone, according to Palestinian estimates.
Palestinian residents, shopkeepers and worshippers told TNA they increasingly speak cautiously and in low voices, fearing that comments to the media about Al-Aqsa could result in their shops being closed or them being barred from the mosque.
Despite the restrictions, Palestinians who spoke to TNA described an enduring spiritual and national connection to Al-Aqsa, with some travelling considerable distances and navigating checkpoints to reach the mosque.
'This is the Temple Mount'
Israeli security forces moving around inside the Al-Aqsa compound have become an increasingly common sight, alongside continued incursions by Israeli settlers.
On Thursday, 1 October, TNA's correspondent was stopped by three Israeli police officers while walking through the Old City to attend dawn prayers at Al-Aqsa.
"Where are you going?" one officer asked.
The officers then claimed that "the prayer is over", although it was still taking place.
They demanded his identity card and ordered him to stand against a wall. After noticing his press card, they questioned him further, while one officer made mocking remarks and began singing off-key as the dawn prayer reached its final moments.
References to the "Temple Mount", the Jewish name for the site on which the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound stands, were also repeatedly heard around the Old City.
In two incidents witnessed by TNA, ultra-Orthodox Jewish men approached a police checkpoint at Bab al-Nazir, opposite the Dome of the Rock, and asked officers: "Is this the entrance to the Temple Mount?"
"Yes, this is the Temple Mount," an officer responded.
At the entrance to the Qattanin Market, an Israeli settler woman standing with her children at another police checkpoint pointed towards Al-Aqsa and told them: "Can you see the end of the road? There is the Temple Mount."
Arrests and restrictions
During Friday prayers, TNA witnessed Israeli forces arrest two young men inside the compound.
A worshipper said a third man was arrested in roughly the same area, between the Dome of the Rock and the Qibli Mosque, after Israeli forces allegedly suspected him of filming officers.
TNA could not establish whether the three were subsequently released or whether further measures were taken against them.
A Jerusalem journalist familiar with Al-Aqsa affairs said Palestinians risk arrest or being barred from the mosque for filming settler incursions or visits by Israeli ministers and Knesset members.
One Al-Aqsa worker, who spoke to TNA about the restrictions, said the balance inside the compound had changed dramatically in recent years.
"A few years ago, the men and women who maintained a presence at Al-Aqsa were always there. At the same time, the number of settlers entering it through the Moroccan Gate was relatively small. Today, the number of people entering is many times greater than before, while those maintaining a presence have been barred," the worker described.
"There is significant facilitation of incursions so that the settlers can move freely and do whatever they want."
The worker said restrictions had also increasingly affected guards employed by the Islamic Waqf.
"A guard can no longer approach a settler to see what he is doing, and even simply looking at him could result in the guard being barred for six months, with the possibility of an extension," he said.
"Filming is, of course, prohibited. They no longer limit themselves to asking guards to stay 50 metres away from the settlers but sometimes require them to stay 200 or 300 metres away. The authority of Al-Aqsa guards has become very limited. In fact, the settlers have more authority inside Al-Aqsa than the guards do. The guards have become as if they are merely guarding the doors and nothing more."
'Every movement is monitored'
The worker also pointed to extensive camera surveillance throughout the compound.
"The movement of employees and people is all monitored by cameras," he said.
"Therefore, there is no reaction to incursions, and anyone can later be arrested from their bed at home and barred from the mosque. This applies to guards, employees, young people and everyone who enters the mosque. Of course, this is in addition to the checkpoints before reaching Al-Aqsa in the first place."
The fear of being barred from Al-Aqsa was echoed by a Palestinian from the Galilee who asked not to be named because he had previously been prohibited from entering the mosque.
He said he regularly attempts to visit but believes Israeli police have placed "a black mark" against his name because of a social media post he made during the war.
"Although there is no legal obstacle preventing me from visiting Al-Aqsa, if they check my identity at the mosque entrances, they prevent me from entering," he added.
'Al-Aqsa is my soul'
Despite the restrictions, worshippers described a connection to Al-Aqsa that they said Israeli measures could not sever.
After Friday prayers, TNA met Alia Abu Ghannam Abu Subaitan sitting near the Dome of the Rock.
"Al-Aqsa is my soul," she said. "It is difficult for me to describe how I feel and how much I miss it because I only come on Fridays."
Abu Subaitan said declining health had made it increasingly difficult for her to visit. "I wish I could come every day, but my health has declined. Previously, we would come and pray the noon and afternoon prayers. During Ramadan, we would come every day."
She recalled that her brother, despite struggling to walk, continues to visit Al-Aqsa daily.
Abu Subaitan said she was heartened to see Palestinians from inside Israel visiting the mosque, but saddened that Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank generally cannot reach it except in limited circumstances.
She urged anyone able to reach Al-Aqsa "not to abandon it".
Ali Hassan had travelled from the occupied West Bank city of Qalqilya despite the difficulties Palestinians there face reaching Jerusalem.
"This is the most important mosque for us in Palestine, the third holiest mosque and the first qibla," he told TNA. "It is one of the most important Islamic holy sites, and we always call on people to make the journey to it and maintain a presence there. This is the least we can offer under these circumstances."
For Palestinians living in the cramped neighbourhoods surrounding the compound, Al-Aqsa is also an important communal space.
Children could be seen running and playing football in its courtyards as families gathered after prayers.
"Al-Aqsa Mosque is not just for prayer and worship for us. Our homes are cramped, and it provides us with an outlet. We and Al-Aqsa are neighbours," one nearby resident told TNA.
But the resident said even those everyday visits had become increasingly fraught.
"Sometimes we come for the dawn prayer, but we have begun to fear harassment by settlers and the possibility that they may attack us. We feel suffocated. The situation is very sad," they said.
Another neighbour described visiting the compound with her sisters and children, particularly during summer afternoons.
"We pray, and the children play," she said. "But sometimes the police prevent them from bringing a football, claiming that this is a place of worship. If they catch a ball at the entrances, they may confiscate it."
The mosque continues to draw Muslim visitors from much further afield. Among those TNA encountered was a group of 46 Moroccans who had travelled from Tangier.
"This is the best place on Earth. Thanks be to God Almighty for enabling us to pray at the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque," Ahmed Mishisho, one of the visitors, said.
"We are visiting Al-Aqsa Mosque, then the city and Mecca to perform Umrah. Visiting Al-Aqsa Mosque is our contribution and our acknowledgement that this is the most beautiful place on Earth."
