More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.

Christmas seals are special decorative stamps sold before Christmas to raise money for the five Christmas seal homes in Denmark.

Denmark’s Christmas seals were first issued in 1904. This year’s design is the 123rd edition. Copenhagen postmaster Einar Holbøll originally proposed the idea.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

Electric bicycle injuries reach six-year high as imports approach 100,000 in Denmark
Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Cars powered only by petrol now account for less than half of Denmark’s passenger vehicle fleet, according to figures from bilstatistik.dk.
Petrol-only cars make up 49.98 percent of registered passenger cars, down from 65 percent at the end of 2020.
The category does not include hybrid or plug-in hybrid vehicles because they use more than one source of power.
Over the same period, electric cars have increased their share of the Danish fleet. They now account for 24.3 percent of passenger cars.
Mobility Denmark, the main association representing Denmark’s automotive industry, said the figures showed how quickly the country’s vehicle fleet was changing.
“Pure petrol cars have for decades been completely dominant on Danish roads. Now they make up less than half of the passenger car fleet,” CEO Mads Rørvig said.
“That says something about how strongly electric cars have moved in a few years,” he added.

The Lego Foundation is a Danish commercial foundation that owns 25 percent of the Lego Group.

Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Türkiye will resolutely stick to its space ambitions until it becomes a strong, respected player in the global space ecosystem, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday.
Speaking at the opening of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, on the Turkish Riviera, Erdogan highlighted Türkiye’s progress in satellite technologies and lunar exploration while calling for broader international participation in space activities.
“We will not deviate from our goal until we make Türkiye one of the strong and respected actors in the global space ecosystem,” he said.
Never allowing itself to lag in the space race, Türkiye has made significant progress in a short time despite hurdles and difficulties, Erdogan said.
He announced that production, assembly, and integration activities for the lunar spacecraft developed under Türkiye’s Lunar Research Program have been completed.
The spacecraft weighs about 3.5 tons and has a domestic production rate exceeding 80%, which Erdogan called “a source of great pride.”
The president also highlighted Turksat 6A, Türkiye’s domestically developed communications satellite.
“Turksat 6A has also affirmed Türkiye’s engineering capabilities, industrial infrastructure, human resources, and confidence in space technologies,” he said.
Erdogan said TEKNOFEST, Türkiye’s major aerospace and technology festival, which just wrapped up last week in the southeastern city of Sanliurfa, had drawn applications from more than 730,000 teams from across the country’s 81 provinces and 97 countries worldwide.
Turning to Türkiye’s spaceport project in the African nation of Somalia, one of Ankara’s allies, Erdogan said it aims to strengthen the country’s access to space while contributing to the development of Africa’s space ecosystem.
 
Space race cannot be confined to few countries
Erdogan stressed that the space race cannot be a competition of only a few countries and criticized efforts to weaponize space.
“Space is not made up of spoils to be seized by whoever gets there first,” he said. “Weaponizing space and turning it into an instrument of an arms race, in particular, is profoundly wrong.”
Erdogan voiced hope that the congress, which Türkiye is hosting for the first time, would benefit participating countries and humanity’s shared future.
The gathering brings together the international space community in Antalya through Friday. Anadolu serves as global communication partner for the event.

Ebola disease outbreak spreads like a megafire in North Kivu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:54:27 UTC
22:54:27 KST

The Ebola disease outbreak in North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo, has intensified dramatically since early September, with the province now accounting for nearly 40 per cent of all newly confirmed cases nationwide. This is up from 24 per cent at the end of August.
With new hotspots emerging every week, treatment capacities remain largely insufficient and inadequate. This situation places current patients and entire communities at even greater risk.
“It is like fighting a megafire,” says Stéphanie Hoffmann, coordinator of the Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) Ebola treatment centre in Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations. As long as new hotspots continue to emerge while the virus spreads across northern North Kivu, containing the epidemic will remain extremely difficult.”
As long as new hotspots continue to emerge while the virus spreads across northern North Kivu, containing the epidemic will remain extremely difficult.
Stéphanie Hoffmann, coordinator of the MSF Ebola treatment centre in Butembo
“Although Butembo has reported a slight decline in confirmed cases in recent days, neighbouring Beni has seen infections rise,” she says. “This does not mean that case numbers will not rise again in Butembo, or other locations later. The outbreak remains highly unpredictable, with transmission patterns changing from week to week.”
North Kivu is bearing an increasing share of the country's Ebola burden at a time when access to specialised care remains insufficient. As of 28 September, 34 per cent of confirmed Ebola patients were still being treated in non-specialised health facilities because of limited bed capacity in dedicated treatment centres and delays in diagnosis.
Many of these facilities lack the resources and expertise required for Ebola case management, raising the risk of further transmission among patients and healthcare workers.
“For weeks, treatment capacity has stretched to its limit,” says Hoffmann. “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment. This is extremely concerning.”
Until recently, Butembo health zone, home to an estimated two million people, had only two Ebola treatment centres. Two additional treatment centres have recently opened, but substantial investments are still needed to ensure adequate quality of care.
As part of our support to health authorities in the Ebola response, MSF works with three healthcare facilities in the area: the Kitatumba Ebola treatment centre, with a capacity of 29 beds for suspected and confirmed cases; the Catholic University of Graben transit centre, with 16 beds for suspected cases awaiting diagnosis; and the Musienene health zone transit centre, which has five beds, also intended for suspected cases.
Community trust remains essential
“Having transit and treatment centres is essential, but it is only part of the response and is not enough to contain the outbreak,” says Hoffmann. “More than 60 per cent of Ebola-related deaths continue to occur in the community.”
“Building trust between local communities and response teams is just as important as expanding treatment capacity,” she says. “Patients must be willing to seek care early and accept isolation measures. Without that trust, we risk seeing more deaths and further spread of the disease into neighbouring areas.”
To strengthen community engagement, MSF works with community leaders, healthcare providers, and youth organisations to encourage awareness and acceptance of Ebola response measures.
Given the scale of the needs, MSF cannot respond to the crisis alone. We are calling for an urgent mobilisation of all stakeholders to immediately increase treatment capacity and guarantee access to quality healthcare in Butembo and throughout North Kivu province.

Man caught with 300 tortoises and 77 parrots bound for Malta at Sicilian port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:52:30 UTC
22:52:30 KST

A Maltese man is facing animal cruelty charges after allegedly attempting to transport 300 tortoises and 77 parrots from Sicily to Malta.
The animals were found packed into a car near the boarding area for a Malta-bound catamaran during an inspection at the Sicilian port of Pozzallo, the local unit of Italy’s financial police squad said on Monday.
Police said they spotted the man “while he was transporting numerous animals” inside a car that lacked adequate space and temperature control.
Subsequent checks by veterinarians found that 76 of the parrots belonged to species protected by the Washington convention, a global agreement signed in 1973 to protect endangered plants and animals from the risk of international trade. Police said the seizure was one of the most significant under the convention.
The animals have been entrusted to a breeding facility, police added.
The Maltese man faces charges of keeping animals in conditions that were incompatible with their nature and causing them severe suffering, along with breaching laws governing international trade in protected species.
The discovery comes a month after police found the dried head of a critically endangered crocodile in the luggage of an Italian man at Turin’s Caselle airport after he landed there from Miami via Istanbul. The man was placed under investigation on allegations of smuggling a specimen belonging to a protected species.
Italy is a major transit hub for the illegal trade of exotic animals, much of it rooted in organised crime. In a report published earlier this year, the Italian branch of the WWF said animals including “tortoises, ornamental birds, tropical reptiles and even small primates are illegally traded via online channels and cross-border exchanges”. In 2025, a chimpanzee held illegally in Sicily was seized, the report said.

Ethiopia rejects pressure over Nile and Red Sea access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:52:04 UTC
22:52:04 KST

Ethiopia rejects pressure over Nile and Red Sea access
Ethiopia has warned that coercion and aggression will not undermine its interests in the Red Sea and Nile, a day after Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia declared maritime governance the exclusive responsibility of coastal states and rejected unilateral measures harming downstream water supplies.
In a statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry cited the East African country’s historical and geographical connections to the Red Sea and its position as the source of the Blue Nile, saying these realities cannot be altered by coercion or destabilization measures.
“Actions taken through proxies or acts of aggression will not change the facts on the ground,” the ministry said, declaring Ethiopia ready to defend its sovereignty and “core national interests.”
The statement did not name the four countries, whose leaders met in New Alamein, Egypt on Sunday for talks on regional security and cooperation. In a joint declaration following the summit, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia reaffirmed “the principle of freedom of navigation” and called for cooperation on transboundary rivers, including the Nile, through “prior notification, consultation and consensus.”
Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan have long clashed over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Africa’s largest hydroelectric dam with a generating capacity of 5,150 megawatts, which Ethiopia built on the Blue Nile and inaugurated in September 2025. Egypt and Sudan fear its operation could threaten their water supplies and demand a binding agreement on filling and operation. Ethiopia considers the dam essential for electricity generation and development and maintains that it will not harm its downstream neighbors.
According to the Foreign Ministry’s statement, the Blue Nile originates almost entirely in the Ethiopian highlands and supplies around 85% of the Nile’s total flow.
Ethiopia became landlocked when its former province, Eritrea, gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long liberation war. Its pursuit of sea access, which Ethiopia considers vital to its economy and security, has fueled tensions with neighboring countries. In January 2024, it signed a deal with Somaliland to obtain coastline access for a naval base in exchange for recognition. Somalia condemned the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty.
A Turkish-mediated agreement in December 2024 eased tensions and provided for negotiations on commercial sea access under Somali sovereignty. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud told Al Jazeera over the weekend that his government has “no objection to Ethiopia gaining access to the sea through Somalia.” He said the country could offer Ethiopia access to up to three ports for trade.
Ethiopia’s push for sovereign access to Eritrea’s Assab Port has also strained relations with Eritrea, which accuses the country of plotting to take its ports by force. The two countries broke diplomatic ties last week after Ethiopia accused the Eritrean authorities of financing armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

QR codes for online drug sales popping up near Estonian schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:52:00 UTC
22:52:00 KST

QR codes for online drug sales popping up near Estonian schools
QR code stickers appearing near schools in Estonia are directing users to a website selling drugs online, police say, raising concerns about access by minors.
The stickers have appeared in larger cities and lead to a site designed like an online store, with drugs, prices, payment options and even customer reviews included.
Police have received numerous reports about the stickers, many of which have been placed along children's routes to school.
At the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), Rain Vosman, head of the South Prefecture's Criminal Bureau, said the website was created in late 2025, but identifying those behind it is difficult.
He said police have a dedicated team working to take down drug-selling sites, but the process can take time. Vosman urged people to report such websites and remove QR stickers when they encounter them.
"We can see that the QR codes are changing, so there are probably several people printing or distributing them," he explained.
A single person could also be behind the operation, he continued, with those involved in printing and distributing the stickers recruited and paid to do so but unaware of where the codes actually lead.
Police believe the stickers are being deliberately placed near schools because minors are among the intended audience. Vosman said youths' curiosity and growing familiarity with cannabis may make some more willing to experiment without fully understanding what they are consuming.
Drug trade slides into DMs
Much of the drug trade has moved to messaging apps, Vosman said, with Telegram groups among the most common channels.
QR codes can be used to direct people to such groups, where drugs are offered and payments can be made by bank transfer or in cryptocurrency.
Police also say QR codes are used to recruit people as runners who hide drug packages and send their GPS coordinates to sellers in exchange for money.
While minors who take on such jobs may not realize they are participating in drug trafficking, those caught can face criminal liability for illegally handling narcotics.
"These are very serious offenses that can even land you behind bars," Vosman emphasized, adding that police will also confiscate any money earned from the activity.

Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining her former boss’s favorite network, Fox News, as an on-air contributor, the channel announced on Monday.
Considering that two of her predecessors from Donald Trump’s first administration, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Kayleigh McEnany, had also joined Fox after leaving office, Leavitt was seen as a logical fit for Fox, on which she will begin providing commentary on 1 November.
In the announcement, the Fox News chief executive, Suzanne Scott, praised Leavitt’s “authentic and sharp insight” and said her “first-hand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape”.
In her own statement, Leavitt said she was “grateful for the opportunity”, adding, “I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.”
Leavitt, 29, who was the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year. She said at the time that she planned to spend more time with her family and take a role with the Trump-aligned Super Pac Maga Inc.
When she announced her pregnancy in December, she became the first sitting White House press secretary to do so.
During her tenure, Leavitt sought to reshape the White House media landscape. She moved to exert greater control over the press pool, the small group of journalists who closely track the president’s daily activities; created a “new media” briefing room seat, often filled by conservative commentators and pro-Trump personalities; and frequently clashed with reporters.
One of Trump’s most steadfast defenders, Leavitt emerged as a key ally for the president and regularly drew praise from him during her time in the West Wing.
Despite his long-term relationship with the network, which helped launch his political career, Trump still regularly criticizes Fox News for being insufficiently loyal, including a lengthy Truth Social post on Sunday criticizing the network’s morning show Fox & Friends for not airing his recent rallies. “Our people want to see our Rallies, and reports on our Rallies, on FoxNews, or they will very quickly stop watching (like I am doing right now!). Fox spends more time talking to Communists, Socialists, and Dumocrats, often without rebuttal, and MAGA is not, to put it mildly, happy.”
He also repeated his familiar attacks on the left-leaning Fox News commentator Jessica Tarlov and criticized the network for cutting ties with longtime host Maria Bartiromo.
But many of Trump’s former associates – and even his daughter-in-law Lara – remain Fox News regulars. Larry Kudlow, who served as his director of the national economic council during his first administration, was recently tapped by Fox to replace Bartiromo on Fox News’ Sunday morning lineup through the midterm elections next month.

More than 100 Estonian reservists have participated in the U.S.-Estonia Military Reserve Exchange Program  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:49:10 UTC
22:49:10 KST

This year marks the tenth anniversary of the Military Reserve Exchange Program (MREP) between the United States and the Estonian Defence Forces and Estonian Defence League. More than 100 Estonian reservists have participated in the exchange program over the course of its operation.
“Ten years is a very important milestone and demonstrates how valuable the exchange of experience with our allies has been. It is encouraging that, in addition to the Estonian reservists who have participated in the exchange, nearly 140 U.S. reserve officers have also come to Estonia for training, including participation in our major exercises Spring Storm and Hedgehog,” said Tõnis Sõnum, Head of the Analysis and Planning Department at the Defence Resources Agency (DRA).
The U.S.-Estonia Military Reserve Exchange Program is organised in cooperation between the U.S. Department of Defense, the Estonian Defence Forces and the Estonian Defence League.
As part of the program, an Estonian reserve officer or non-commissioned officer travels to the United States for two to three weeks, while their U.S. reserve officer or non-commissioned officer counterpart comes to Estonia. Exchange partners are matched to have as similar a rank, qualification and level of training as possible. The U.S. Department of Defense also has similar bilateral exchange programs with the armed forces of Denmark, Germany and the United Kingdom.
According to Sõnum, all Estonian units have the opportunity to participate in this voluntary training exchange. “We receive suitable candidates from different Estonian military units and from the Estonian Defence League, while on the U.S. side, all branches of the armed forces and state National Guard units are involved,” Sõnum added.
According to Second Lieutenant Indrek Hein, Commander of the Defence League´s Tallinn Academic Company and Wartime Air Force Personnel Officer at the Defence Resources Agency, what surprised him most during the training of U.S. reservists at Fort McCoy was the sheer size of the base and the diversity of the equipment and infrastructure available there. “What I remember most was how all these resources were used during the training and how we practised working together — from evacuating casualties by helicopter to responding to an ambush and a chemical attack.”
The exchange program demonstrated that strong personal contacts and trust have developed between Estonian and U.S. reservists, supporting broader defence cooperation. “Estonia is known remarkably well in the United States. Many of the reservists had participated in Spring Storm or served in the Baltic region and spoke very warmly about their experiences. This is actually a clear sign that the work done over the past ten years has borne fruit.”
The Defence Resources Agency is the Estonian-side coordinator, liaising with both the Estonian reservist and the U.S. unit. “We also arrange travel documents, reimburse travel expenses and, when necessary, provide reservists with the equipment required for training, such as desert uniforms,” Sõnum explained.
In Estonia, host units primarily accommodate U.S. forces during the major exercises Spring Storm and Hedgehog. They are also responsible for arranging accommodation for U.S. reservists and organising a cultural programme for them.
Applications for the program are submitted through Defence Forces and Defence League units. The Defence Resources Agency determines the number of available places, while the units select their own candidates. “The application period for 2027 is coming to an end, but next July we will launch the 2028 program, for which we welcome applicants,” said Sõnum.

Baltic Region’s Largest Short Film Industry Event Kicks Off in Vilnius  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Baltic Pitching Forum, running from 6-9 October in Vilnius, becomes a meeting point for the international short film industry
Between 6–9 October the 14th Baltic Pitching Forum (BPF) welcomes a record number of international industry guests. Festival programmers, producers, distributors, broadcasters and representatives of industry platforms will meet filmmakers from Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Italy, which will be the guest country of this year’s BPF.
At the heart of the Forum are 12 short film projects currently in development, ready to be pitched to the international industry with an aim to connect to potential partners and explore where their films might go next.
This year’s guests include programmers from leading international film festivals such as Locarno, PÖFF Shorts, Concorto and Filmfest Dresden; sales and distribution professionals from companies including Lights On, Kurzfilm Agentur Hamburg and oriGine Films; as well as representatives of Finland’s Yle TV and Switzerland’s SRF TV. Producers and representatives of film markets, co-production platforms and other international film organisations will also travel to Vilnius.
Since 2019, Baltic Pitching Forum has invited a different European country to join filmmakers from the three Baltic states. This year’s Guest Country is Italy. This builds on a partnership developed over several years between the Baltic Pitching Forum, the Italian Short Film Center and Turin-based short film industry market ShorTO Film Market. Last year, ShorTO Film Market selected Lithuania as its focus country; this year, the exchange continues, with Italian projects and film professionals travelling to Vilnius.
“Over the past fourteen years, we have seen that the Forum’s value lies not only in the projects presented here, but also in the long-term professional relationships that begin in Vilnius. Some filmmakers return with new projects, while industry professionals come back in search of new talent and potential partners. This year, we are welcoming a record number of international guests, but what matters most to us is not the number itself, but the diversity of their professional backgrounds and perspectives. For smaller film industries such as those in the Baltic states, being part of an ongoing international professional network is particularly important,” says Baltic Pitching Forum Head Rimantė Daugėlaitė.
The return of Forum alumni with new projects is also reflected in this year’s line-up. Producer Giedrė Burokaitė has had projects presented at Baltic Pitching Forum on five occasions. In recent years, she produced Saulė Bliuvaitė’s debut feature Toxic, which won the Golden Leopard at the Locarno Film Festival. This year, Burokaitė returns to the Forum with Nina Chubinishvili’s animated film project The Phonebook.
While Baltic Pitching Forum is primarily aimed at film industry professionals, part of its programme will be open to anyone interested in the film sector and the issues currently shaping it. On Wednesday, 7 October, Italian marketing strategist and audience designer Nicolò Gallio will present Short Films, Big Stakes: What AI Can and Cannot Do for Filmmakers, exploring the ethical, environmental and creative implications of generative AI, as well as the point at which its capabilities reach their limits and human judgement remains essential. Later that day, Belgian film producer Anne-Laure Guégan will lead the seminar Building a Sustainable Relationship Between Director and Producer, focusing on how lasting and sustainable professional relationships can be built between producers and filmmakers. On Friday, 9 October, Baltic Talent Agency co-founders Simona Inta and Viktorija Cook will address the international visibility of Baltic film talent in Let’s Stop Whispering, The Baltic Moment (Your Moment) Is Now, discussing how creatives from the region can position themselves more confidently within the global film industry. The Forum will also feature further talks and discussions on current challenges and opportunities in the film sector, international collaboration and creative partnerships. All talks are free and open to the public, with advance registration required.
Alongside the selected film projects and talks by international experts, a new generation of Baltic producers will also take part in the Forum. From 5–9 October, Vilnius will host the second edition of UP!, a training programme for emerging film producers. Launched last year for Lithuanian participants, the initiative has expanded in 2026 to encompass all three Baltic states. Fifteen producers from Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have been selected for the programme and will spend the week exploring the international short film ecosystem and project pitching before introducing themselves to the Baltic Pitching Forum audience on 8 October. The programme is led by producer Marija Razgutė together with Amos Geva, producer, T-Port TalentBridge mentor and co-founder of the T-Port platform.
On Friday, 9 October, the Forum will conclude with a short film screening open to both industry professionals and the general public. The final evening will take place at Muzeoteka, part of the Lithuanian Theatre, Music and Cinema Museum, with a programme of contemporary Italian animation, Contemporary Italian Animated Short Cinema, curated by the Italian Short Film Center. The screening will offer audiences a chance to discover this year’s Guest Country not through projects still in development, but through a selection of recent completed films. Entrance is free.

A separate discussion on cross-border payments will bring together representatives from Bolt, Paybis, Nexpay, SEB and Latvijas Banka to examine why international payments can still be slow and costly.
The programme will also feature discussions on the development of the Baltic fintech ecosystem, partnerships between banks and businesses, financial literacy and the future of payments. Practical workshops will cover MiCA, licensing for payment and electronic money institutions, crowdfunding and AML requirements. Participants will also have the opportunity to meet with experts from Latvijas Banka and other industry organisations.
Latvia is emerging as a launchpad for fintech and crypto companies looking to build and scale across Europe. A growing ecosystem, forward-looking regulation and a crypto-friendly business environment make the country an increasingly attractive base for EU-wide businesses. Latvia is also among the pioneers in creating practical ways for companies to work with digital assets, including allowing company share capital to be paid in crypto, with further digital-asset initiatives on the way.
“Northern Europe’s fintech scene continues to grow, attracting increasing interest from businesses and retail investors alike. We believe the UN:BLOCK Fintech Forum will create valuable opportunities for business development, while giving private investors the chance to explore emerging sectors, innovative financial products, and compelling new investment opportunities,” says Reinis Znotiņš, Executive Director of The Latvian Blockchain Association.
UN:BLOCK Fintech will bring together more than 600 founders, regulators, investors and experts shaping the future of financial technology. Participants will include representatives from companies such as Bolt, SEB, Citadele, Twino, Paybis, Backpack EU, NBX and other leading industry players. Conference partners include the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), Magnetiq Bank, Digilo, Nexpay, Mastercard, Bolt, Mintos and Tribe Payments.
The UN:BLOCK Fintech programme will feature panel discussions, expert presentations and thematic workshops. This format will give participants the opportunity to stay up to date with the latest industry developments, explore topics in greater depth and build new professional connections. The conference is designed to offer practical value to every participant – from early-stage startup founders to leaders of established companies.
UN:BLOCK Fintech is a new one-day conference from the team behind Northern Europe's leading annual blockchain and fintech conference UN:BLOCK Europe, taking place in Riga on March 10-11, 2027. The conference is organized in cooperation with the Latvian Blockchain Association.
Support is provided within the framework of the project “Support for the Improvement of the Technology Transfer System”, co-financed by the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget.

Erdoğan urges peaceful use of space at Antalya summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:48:39 UTC
22:48:39 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Oct. 5 warned against turning space into a theater for an arms race, saying its future should be shaped through international cooperation as Türkiye hosted an international declaration supporting the peaceful and sustainable use of space.
“Space is not spoils to be seized by whoever gets there first. Weaponizing space, and especially turning it into an instrument of an arms race, is dangerous,” Erdoğan said at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in the resort city of Antalya.
Erdoğan said the future of space should be shaped by a common will among states and international organizations, thanking the countries that endorsed the Antalya Declaration.
Representatives from 21 countries adopted the accord in support of the peaceful and sustainable use of space. The text was endorsed by 32 ministers, lawmakers and heads of space agencies at a meeting held ahead of the congress.
Türkiye initiated the declaration and prepared it in consultation with the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) and international partners, according to officials.
Erdoğan said Türkiye’s efforts to expand its presence in space were aimed at making life on Earth safer and more sustainable.
“We set our goals, strengthened our institutions and invested in our human resources. We did not allow Türkiye to fall behind in the space race,” he said.
“Despite obstacles and difficulties, we have made significant progress in a short time. Today, Türkiye is one of the few countries that can design, develop, produce, test and operate its own satellites in space.”
Erdoğan said one of the most ambitious goals of Türkiye’s National Space Program involved the Moon.
“We have completed the production, assembly and integration of our lunar spacecraft. We are now conducting environmental tests,” he said, describing the spacecraft’s more than 80 percent domestic content as a source of pride.
The congress is being held under the theme “The World Needs More Space,” with an emphasis on the peaceful use of outer space.
More than 6,800 delegates and participants from 108 countries have registered for the event, where critical issues in the space sector will be discussed.
The program includes roundtable meetings, panels, presentations and workshops. A new “Future Space” area will showcase next-generation space technologies, simulations and interactive experiences for the first time at IAC 2026.
A leaders summit scheduled for Oct. 6 will bring together senior officials from more than 40 countries. The congress will conclude Oct. 9 with public events.

Millmax as a Promising Contract Manufacturer in Latvia  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:48:21 UTC
22:48:21 KST

Brands looking for a production partner in Europe often find that Latvia offers a practical balance of EU regulation, manageable costs and convenient access to Baltic and Nordic markets. Millmax, a full cycle factory based in Riga, has built its offer around exactly this combination and works with both small startups and larger companies that need dependable volumes.
Who Millmax Is and Where It Operates
Millmax contract manufacturer runs its production site and private laboratory on Kengaraga street in Riga. The company focuses on three directions: cosmetics, nutritional supplements and dietary supplements. Because the research and development team works under the same roof as the factory, an idea can move from a laboratory sample to a finished product without being passed between several contractors. Alongside made to order projects, the company also keeps a ready made product catalog, which gives new clients a faster starting point.
Comprehensive Services Under One Roof
For wholesale clients, the main advantage is access to comprehensive services for the production of cosmetics from a single partner. Instead of coordinating a formulator, a filling site and a packaging supplier separately, a brand can hand the whole project to one team.
• Custom formulation, including entirely new recipes or changes to existing ones
• Adaptation of popular product types to a client's own requirements
• Private label and white label production
• Filling and packaging in a wide choice of containers
• Laboratory testing and R&D support
• Documentation and registration support for EU markets
Cosmetic Formats and Product Types
The cosmetics line covers skincare, haircare, body care and herbal products. Skincare can be produced as gels, creams, balms, lotions, serums, sprays, emulsions, oils or powders, while herbal ranges include tonics and oils alongside creams and serums. This breadth allows a brand to build a complete collection with one manufacturer rather than splitting it between several.
Packaging That Matches the Product
Packaging is selected together with the client, depending on the product type and the image the brand wants to project.
• Glass bottles and vials for serums, tonics and oils
• Tubes and jars for creams, balms and gels
• Cartons for retail presentation
• Plastic jars, doypacks and capsule containers for supplement lines
Quality Control and Compliance
Cosmetics made at the Millmax factory follow EU Regulation 1223/2009 and ISO 22716:2007, and the site operates under GMP principles, while supplement lines are covered by GMP and HACCP certification. Every batch of raw materials is tested in the laboratory before production starts, equipment is maintained regularly and staff receive continuous training. For supplement lines, independent testing, sensory evaluation and nutritional analysis add a further layer of control. Brands that want a sharper market position can also request Vegan, Cruelty free or Organic certification.
Flexible Volumes for Brands of Every Size
Millmax accepts orders of all sizes and highlights low minimum quantities for companies testing a new idea. For larger programmes, the factory can produce up to 10,000 product units per shift. This flexibility lets a new brand launch a pilot batch and later scale up without changing supplier. It suits several types of client.
• Startups validating a first collection
• Established brands extending an existing range
• Retailers developing a private label line
• Companies that outsource production to focus on sales and strategy
How Cooperation Usually Works
A typical project follows a simple path from first contact to dispatch.
1. Share the concept, target audience and any existing formula
2. Agree on the formulation route, whether new, modified or adapted
3. Approve samples and choose the packaging
4. Confirm the order volume and production schedule
5. Complete filling, packaging and quality checks before shipment
Why Latvia Works for European Buyers
Production inside the EU means ingredients, labelling and documentation follow one regulatory framework, which simplifies sales across member states. Riga's position on the Baltic Sea also supports delivery to Northern and Central Europe, and Millmax offers consulting on product distribution for European markets. Clients also benefit from a single point of contact, since formulation, production and compliance questions are handled by one team in one country.
Final Thoughts
Millmax combines a certified factory, an in house laboratory and flexible order sizes in one Latvian location. For brands that want a manufacturing partner able to guide a product from formula to finished pack, it is an option worth a closer look. Whether the goal is a first skincare serum, a herbal body line or a full private label collection, clear communication and transparent standards make the difference between a smooth launch and a costly delay.

US monitoring suspected plague case in Russia, Rubio says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:48:02 UTC
22:48:02 KST

The United States is monitoring reports of a suspected plague infection at a Russian research facility but sees no immediate cause for alarm, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday.
“We’re watching and monitoring it closely,” Rubio told reporters before departing for Iceland. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we’re doing that.”
The comments came after a female employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in southeastern Siberia died last week after developing pneumonia of unknown origin.
Russian authorities have not confirmed that she had plague, and tests have so far found no microorganisms associated with her professional work.
Russian authorities reject plague reports
Russia’s consumer and public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said extensive testing found no pathogens linked to the woman’s work at the institute and no evidence of an incident involving dangerous microorganisms there.
Two people who had contact with her tested positive for a virus associated with the common cold, while two others tested positive for COVID-19, the agency said.
The case nevertheless prompted precautionary measures after unconfirmed reports suggested the woman may have died from pneumonic plague, a rare and severe form of the disease that can spread between people through respiratory particles.
A hospital in Shelekhov, near Irkutsk, was placed under quarantine, while people who had contact with the woman were put under medical observation. Russian officials have urged the public to rely on official information rather than unverified reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also urged the public and media to follow statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than “rumors or speculation.”
Why pneumonic plague is drawing attention
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is usually associated with small mammals and their fleas.
The World Health Organization says pneumonic plague is the least common but most virulent form and can spread from person to person through respiratory particles.
The disease can be severe if untreated, but WHO says early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment can save lives.
The uncertainty surrounding the Siberian case has prompted heightened monitoring rather than confirmation of an outbreak.
Rubio said the relatively limited travel between the US and Russia was another factor, while stressing that Washington was continuing to watch developments closely.
For now, Russian health authorities say the epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region remains stable.

The ruling Tisza party’s parliamentary group said that "this move raises serious concerns from the standpoint of national security, conflict of interest and ethical norms." Pal Czako-Czirbus, a Tisza member of parliament and committee member, said, citing the Foreign Ministry’s documents, that "as minister, Szijjarto transferred state infrastructure facilities to BYD - roads, railways and water supply networks - worth billions of forints."

"The government support provided for its construction fell entirely within the standard framework established for investments of such scale," the former minister stressed.
Szijjarto maintained that no rules had been broken and that "BYD’s investment in Szeged is a huge success for all of Hungary." "There was fierce competition across Europe to host this plant and many European countries sought to secure the project. Szijjarto noted that he had come to the parliamentary hearings voluntarily, although the law did not require him to respond to the national security committee’s request. "I was a member of parliament for 24 years and I respect this institution. It is natural for me to be here, even if it is not legally mandatory," he added.
Szijjarto was Hungary’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade from September 23, 2014, to May 12, 2026. After the Fidesz - Hungarian Civic Alliance party lost the parliamentary elections and the government changed, he remained a member of parliament, but on July 15, he resigned as an MP, saying he had accepted a senior role at BYD. The hearings in the national security committee with his participation were held behind closed doors and the parliament will not publish a transcript of their results.

Poland Unveils New Ryś Camouflage Uniform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:47:06 UTC
22:47:06 KST

The Polish Ministry of National Defense has unveiled a new tactical uniform featuring the Ryś camouflage pattern.
The presentation took place in Ciechanów and was attended by Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and military commanders.
The new uniform features not only a different camouflage pattern—Ryś (“Lynx”)—but also a revised cut. As a result, the Polish Army will gradually phase out the wz.93 Pantera, which has been in use for over three decades.
Service members from the Polish Special Operations Forces helped develop the new camouflage. According to General Dariusz Mendrala, head of the Polish Armed Forces Support Inspectorate, the Military Research and Development Center developed the camouflage pattern variants in collaboration with special operations personnel.
The prototypes were tested under various natural, weather, and seasonal conditions. Their visibility through optical devices and night-vision equipment was evaluated separately, after which the military formulated recommendations for the final design.
The general emphasized that during development, attention was also paid to the uniform’s comfort and ergonomics, so the new set will differ from the previous one in terms of design as well.
Darius Mendrala noted that the transition to the Ryś will take place gradually, as the camouflage change affects about 24 pieces of equipment. The old Pantera uniforms will remain in use for some time, particularly to supply reservists.
The Polish military is considering a phased re-equipment of individual units. The pace of the transition will also be influenced by cost: as the general noted, a two-piece winter uniform alone costs about PLN 2,000 (approximately UAH 23,000) and is designed to last several years.
The uniform upgrade is part of a broader Polish program to modernize individual military equipment. As part of the Szpej program, the Polish Ministry of Defense purchased over 200,000 Kevlar helmets, 100,000 body armor vests, and tactical vests.
At the same time, the Polish ministry is introducing the so-called “Green List” mechanism, which allows service members to independently purchase ministry-approved personal equipment. The list includes only products that meet established military requirements.
Other European armies are also updating their combat uniforms—in August, Denmark and Sweden unveiled the new M/26 and MSU26 combat uniforms, based on solutions from Crye Precision, while the Norwegian Armed Forces are continuing their phased transition to the new M23 NCU multi-layered combat clothing system, developed jointly with Sweden, Denmark, and Finland.
In Germany, the Bundeswehr’s transition to the KBS SK modular combat clothing system is also underway, with Ukrainian troops already receiving certain components of this system.
In September, Militarnyi reported on preparations to introduce the VARAN ZSU and VARAN ZSU Winter camouflage patterns for the Airborne Assault Forces.

Top global government ministers discuss goals, strategies at astronautical/space congress in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:46:34 UTC
22:46:34 KST

Top international government ministers and senior officials gathered Monday in the southern Turkish city of Antalya for the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) to discuss national space strategies and address the commercialization of the Earth’s orbit.
Mehmet Fatih Kacir, Türkiye’s industry and technology minister, said at the gathering that space science investments are key to producing high-value-added technologies and maintaining a competitive edge.
“Space is the backbone of value-added goods and services production, and Türkiye has made investments in recent years, including launching our homegrown satellites,” he said, telling how Ankara initially launched high-resolution imaging satellite Imece in 2023, and since the launch of the Turksat 6A communications satellite, Türkiye joined the ranks of just a dozen countries worldwide that can design and make their own communications satellites.
Kacir said one of Türkiye’s top priorities is to land on the lunar surface, while efforts are underway to construct a technopark in the capital Ankara and a spaceport in the African nation of Somalia, one of Türkiye’s allies, to secure independent access to space. 
United Arab Emirates
Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi, the Emirati sports minister and chair of the United Arab Emirates Space Agency, said the UAE’s national space strategy for 2031 is focused on doubling the revenue growth of their space sector and ranking among the top 10 space economies worldwide.
“We’ve come to realize that it’s not necessarily funding — they (startups) need access to markets with our bilateral trade agreements, and they need access to space infrastructure, such as fire testing, launch sites, clean rooms,” he said.
“Thirdly, access to talent — we’ve been lucky in the UAE we’ve been able to attract the smartest talent within the region and locally.”
“In summary, the first decade was building the basics, but now in the second decade, we want to get the private sector involved to develop a vibrant and interconnected ecosystem that strikes a balance between the public and private,” he added. 
Poland and Uzbekistan
Michal Jaros, Poland’s economic development and technology secretary, said next year’s International Astronautical Congress will be hosted by Poland, in the western city of Poznan.
Space has great importance for both security and the economy, he said, adding that satellite technologies grew to support many areas, such as navigation, transportation, communications, agriculture, and crisis management.
Since Poland hosted the congress 60 years ago, in 1964, the country has undergone a complete transformation, he said.
“We moved from isolation and cooperation, and this is the direction we all need to take when we think about space — if we want space to remain safe, sustainable, and available for peaceful activities, and for the future generations, we need more cooperation,” he said. “See you in Poznan next year.”
Sherzad Shermatov, Uzbekistan’s digital technologies minister, said space has been one of his nation’s priorities for six centuries, back from “when the ruler of Samarkand built the (word’s) biggest observatory.”
“Our aim is to bring this national priority back under the leadership of our president,” he said, adding that one of the nation’s goals is to reignite the youth’s interest in science and technologies, and that the country is preparing to host the International Astronautical Congress in 2028 alongside other efforts to launch their satellite and send young Uzbek space travelers into orbit. 
Spain
Juan Cruz Cigudosa, Spain’s science, innovation, and universities secretary, said the Spanish space sector grew exponentially in 2022-2025, as Spanish space firms boosted their revenues by 40% to €1.5 billion ($1.68 billion) per year, while employment in the sector surged 52%.
“At the latest ministerial meeting of the ESA (European Space Agency) in November 2025, Spain became for the first time the fourth-largest contributor to ESA — we will contribute €1.55 billion between 2026 and 2030,” he said. “This represents a threefold increase in our annual contributions from 10 years ago.”
Cigudosa added that Spain is a candidate to host the 80th International Astronautical Congress in Barcelona in 2029 to discuss sustainability, climate resilience, and water issues.

Russia Sentences ‘Masyanya’ Creator to 4 Years in Absentia Over Anti-War Cartoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:46:00 UTC
22:46:00 KST

A St. Petersburg court has sentenced Oleg Kuvaev, creator of the animated series “Masyanya,” to four years and one month in prison in absentia over an episode that investigators said urged Russian soldiers to surrender or desert.
The city’s Nevsky District Court found Kuvaev guilty of publicly calling for actions against state security and failing to comply with obligations imposed on people designated as “foreign agents,” the city courts’ press service said.
The court also barred him from publishing online or administering websites for four years. Kuvaev has lived in Israel since 2006.
Investigators said Kuvaev’s 2023 episode “Idoliada,” the 169th installment of “Masyanya,” contained calls for Russian servicemen to surrender, desert and disobey their commanders.
The episode also promoted “I Want to Live,” a Ukrainian project that helps Russian soldiers surrender, according to investigators.
Case materials cited by the courts’ press service described the cartoon as expressing “ideological hatred and hostility” toward Russia’s government and officials, as well as opposition to the invasion, which Moscow calls a “special military operation.” Investigators argued that its verbal appeals were directed against Russian state security.
Those allegations placed the cartoon’s political message at the center of the criminal case. According to the exiled news outlet Mediazona, the court questioned Justice Ministry expert Vladislav Ivanov and two viewers, Nikita Sotnikov and Nikita Grishchenko.
The viewers objected to the episode’s portrayal of the Russian military, saying it mocked the Armed Forces and could lead audiences to side with Ukraine, Mediazona reported.
The criminal case was opened three years ago. Russian authorities designated Kuvaev a “foreign agent” in December 2023.
Kuvaev has continued to produce anti-war work from abroad, including an AI-generated animated video parodying the Soviet song “May There Always Be Sunshine” released in November 2025.
The video depicted rag dolls dressed as Soviet schoolchildren, wearing red Young Pioneer neckerchiefs, flying on missiles above ruined cities and sheltering from bombardment. Its lyrics replaced the original song’s wish for peace with wishes for perpetual war and slaughter.
Kuvaev presented the video as “new Russian children’s songs.”
He has also said he hopes Russia will break up and its ethnic republics will become independent, contrasting that position with what he described as the views of the Russian opposition.
Responding to the verdict, Kuvaev dismissed the proceedings.
“There is really nothing to say,” he said in comments reported by the Astra Telegram channel. “Except perhaps: ‘I regret and express concern about the state of sanity in the rotten empire’.”
