Can Japan Optimize Its Record Defense Budget?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:46:00 UTC
22:46:00 KST

Japan’s Ministry of Defense (MOD) released its fiscal year 2027 budget request in early August. At approximately 9.3 trillion yen – a 3.8 percent increase from FY2026 – it is the largest defense budget request in the country’s postwar history.
Predictably, all the attention has been paid to the size of the request, particularly the fact that the it is the highest in Japan’s postwar history. The topline number definitely matters, especially because it allowed Japan to hit the 2 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) target it set for its defense spending ahead schedule.
It is also noteworthy that the request has been followed by a couple of decisions that attracted little attention but are potentially consequential in Japan’s attempt to revitalize its defense industrial base. At the end of August, MOD announced a plan to acquire former Nippon Steel industrial sites in Kure, Hiroshima and turn them into mixed-use facilities that the government can lease to defense companies. In mid-September, Mitsubishi UFJ Bank, one of Japan’s megabanks, also announced new, more lender-friendly guidelines for financing defense firms.
This series of steps come as Japan finalizes the revision of its National Security Strategy (NSS), National Defense Strategy (NDS), and Defense Buildup Plan (DBP), which are slated to be released in December. Together, those documents will set the course for Japan’s national security policy over the next five years. As such, the FY2027 budget request offers a preliminary look at how these documents likely to take shape.
The request’s most notable feature is its emphasis on a “new way of fighting” (atarashii tatakai-kata), followed by operational sustainability and the industrial and personnel base. Across these categories, the MOD identifies nine priority areas for investment, including artificial intelligence, uncrewed systems, stand-off – or counterstrike – capabilities, space, cyber, sea-lane defense, the defense industrial base, and personnel. Investment in all of these areas is much overdue.
The request also appears to seek a better balance between what Japan calls shomen sobi (frontline equipment) and koho (the logistics and support systems that keep a force operating) in the budget allocation. Finally, it makes an explicit effort to harness emerging technologies such as AI and uncrewed systems.
In many ways, the FY2027 request could be a precursor to a genuinely transformational effort to strengthen Japan’s defense capabilities, if fully implemented.
At the same time, however, the request also reminds us of the challenges in executing such transformation. Nine priority areas is a lot. In other words, with this many so-called “priorities” running concurrently, Japan risks spreading its investment too broadly and too thinly. All nine areas require substantial spending, and not only in the initial stage – the investment needs to be sustained over many years to come. At a time when the government faces intense pressure to lower taxes, a basic question remains: does Japan have the fiscal capacity to fund all of them at the necessary scale?
A persistently weak yen makes the problem worse. Japan’s defense budget has risen steadily since FY2013 when Prime Minister Abe Shinzo returned to office. The increases accelerated after FY2023. But the impact of the increase is far less impressive when measured in dollars. The yen’s declining value, particularly since 2022, has eroded Japan’s purchasing power, especially for equipment and components that are imported. In other words, the label “largest defense budget in postwar history” obscures the extent to which currency depreciation can and has offset that budget increase’s real impact.
To be fair, the current government did not create this predicament. The reality is that Japan has been struggling to address the consequences of decades of underinvestment, including years when the yen was much stronger. For example, from FY2000 through FY2012, Japan’s defense spending remained largely flat even as China began to accelerate its military modernization. Put simply, Japan failed to invest when it could more easily afford to do so.
This forces Tokyo to try to recover those lost years while confronting mounting pressure from China, the impact of closer alignment among China, Russia and North Korea, and uncertainty about the long-term reliability of the United States’ defense commitments to its allies, including Washington’s capacity to uphold such commitments. As such, Japan must pursue two difficult goals at once: reverse the hollowing out of its defense force while racing to catch up with its China, its principal strategic threat.
In fact, Japan is not the only country which finds itself in this predicament. Other U.S. allies also spent years deepening economic ties with China in the hope that interdependence would discourage Beijing from using force to change the status quo, while making modest investment in their own national defense. They now face their own versions of the same reckoning underway in Japan.
Japan’s FY2027 request is therefore both encouraging and sobering. It shows that Tokyo finally seems to be grappling with the scale of the transformation required – from emerging technology and munitions to logistics, industry, and personnel – and has begun genuine efforts in tackling them. That said, in order for Japan to leverage this request to begin this strategic turn, it will also need to identify a roadmap to protect funding and ensure that every additional yen is set to be used most efficiently to contribute to these priorities.
The FY2027 budget can jump-start Japan’s real defense transformation. Whether it actually does, however, will depend on the choices that follow.

Russia is paying oil companies record subsidies amid refinery strikes, eating into its state coffers - Bloomberg

Unknown Publisher

16:45:38 EEST

Russia is paying oil companies record subsidies amid refinery strikes, eating into its state coffers - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
In September, Russia paid oil companies 305.5 billion rubles in fuel subsidies. Payments increased due to strikes on oil refineries and a gasoline shortage.
Last month, Russia's government paid oil companies its largest subsidy in more than four years for supplying motor fuel to the domestic market, amid drone strikes on oil refineries. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to data from Russia's Finance Ministry published on October 5, subsidies amounted to 305.5 billion rubles ($3.6 billion) in September. This was the highest monthly payment since April 2022, when a record figure was recorded.
Strikes on Russian oil assets reportedly reduced petroleum product production in Russia, leading to gasoline shortages across the country, fuel rationing, and long lines at gas stations.
These payments "provide vital support to Russian producers that have been forced to carry out extensive unscheduled repairs at refineries that reduced or completely halted operations after the strikes," the publication writes.
However, the payments, as noted, "are eating into Russia's state coffers." According to Bloomberg calculations based on ministry data, September's subsidies fell only slightly short of the total net revenue of 323.3 billion rubles paid by the oil industry into the state budget last month. Since the beginning of the year, the subsidies have exceeded $14 billion, according to the calculations.
Subsidies to refineries are calculated based on the volume of motor fuel supplied to the domestic market and the difference between domestic and export wholesale prices. To ensure incentives for the oil-refining industry, payments continue even amid the current bans on fuel exports. The government in Moscow has imposed a ban on most exports of gasoline, diesel fuel, and aviation fuel. The ban on diesel fuel exports is in effect until the end of October.
Most of the payments go to the country's largest oil companies, including PJSC "Rosneft" and PJSC "Tatneft," as they operate the country's key refineries. To ensure sufficient supplies to the domestic market, the Russian government has also reportedly authorized payments to fuel importers.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Reuters interview over the weekend that his country would double its efforts to strike Russian energy facilities in response to devastating round-the-clock attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure.
Russia expects subsidies for the whole of 2026 to reach 1.93 trillion rubles and fall to 1.18 trillion rubles the following year, Russian media reported on Friday, citing documents submitted to the State Duma along with the 2027–2029 budget draft.
Russia's total net revenue from oil and gas reached 452.4 billion rubles in September, more than 22% lower than a year earlier, according to Bloomberg calculations based on data from Russia's Finance Ministry. The decline occurred despite an increase in the price of Russian Urals crude compared with last year and the ruble's weakening against the U.S. dollar. The decline in net revenue from the oil and gas industry was driven by large fuel subsidies, the publication writes.

This new Japanese walking trail connects six cities across 320 kilometres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:44:41 UTC
22:44:41 KST

Japan’s longest loop trail is now fully open. Spread across 320 kilometres, the Hitachinokuni Long Trail takes hikers through mountains, rural villages, waterfalls, beaches and historic ruins.
If you’re heading to Japan for an active holiday you should lace up your walking boots and tackle a 320km-long hiking trail that is now fully open.
The Hitachinokuni Long Trail, Japan’s longest loop trail, has been in the works for seven years since first announced in 2019 by the Ibaraki Prefecture and the Hitachi Province Trail Club.
Now having opened in September, the hiking destination links six cities and towns across the northern Ibaraki Prefecture, less than a two-hour train ride away from Tokyo.
Connecting Kitaibaraki, Takahagi, Hitachi, Hitachi Ota, Hitachi Omiya and Daigo, the route takes hikers through landscapes known as “satoyama”, which are rural spaces where communities have lived alongside mountains, meadows, ponds and rice fields.
The trail is not high in elevation, nor easily impacted by heavy snowfall due to its geography, making it an experience that can be enjoyed year-round. However, there aren’t many refuelling points, while some areas are rocky and others include steep slopes.
Where to start?
Due to its design, hikers can choose where to tackle the circular trail, which is roughly divided into five areas.
The Central Area is one of the more challenging sections of the trail, featuring continuous steep ascents and descents for especially skilled hikers. Located in the Yazimo mountain range, on the northern edge of the Japanese town of Daigo, the Central Area rewards hikers with views including the Fukuroda Falls, the rocky peaks of Okukuji Nantaiyama as well as the Ryujinkyo Gorge valley.
The Northeastern portion of the trail covers mountains, like the high peaks of Eizomuro and Hanazono Yama, as well as coastal destinations, including the Kohama and Sasaki beaches. The area also takes hikers through history, including the Salt Road, which is an ancient trade route, and the Jikkoku Canal, which has been in use dating back to the Edo period from 1603 to 1868.
Within the Southeastern area, which first opened in 2024, the hike begins at Hananuki Valley with a climb up Mount Tsuchidake, which offers sweeping views of the surrounding scenery. The area is also marked by waterfalls, historic sites like the Kitadaimon Castle ruins before ending at the Kuji River.
The Southwest area is in Hitachiomiya City and takes hikers through mountains that are home to diverse flora and fauna, including Iwauchiwa flowering plants. This area also features a once thriving gold mining region.
Mt. Yamizo is just one of the stops along the Northwest area. Here, visitors can explore sacred sites steeped in history, such as the Yamizomine Shrine, which is thought to date as far back as the 1st century. At the summit of the mountain, there is also a castle-shaped observation deck that offers panoramic views of Fukushima and Tochigi's mountains.

Three years of genocide: Israel’s traditional Asian allies shift stance on Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:44:28 UTC
22:44:28 KST

After three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands, Tel Aviv's relations with its traditional Asian allies have increasingly fractured, deepening its diplomatic isolation.
A recent illustration of that isolation came at the UN General Assembly late last month, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cut a lonely figure as scores of delegates walked out of his speech.
The departing delegates included representatives from Asian nations such as Pakistan, Malaysia, Indonesia and Bangladesh.
Here is a look at how Asian countries have responded to Israel and the Gaza war.
Israel has faced strong state-level criticism from its longtime East Asian allies, such as Japan and South Korea.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi opposed US sanctions against International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane, who sought an arrest warrant for Netanyahu over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
Takaichi reaffirmed Tokyo’s consistent support for the ICC during the UN General Assembly, pushing back against pressure from the US, and saying that the country takes the US sanctions against Akane “very seriously.”
Washington sanctioned Akane, the first Japanese national to head the ICC, in August, accusing the court of encroaching on state sovereignty.
With Seoul, tensions began in April after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung shared a video on social media alleging that Israeli soldiers abused a Palestinian child and then threw him off a rooftop.
Lee said it was necessary to determine the authenticity of the video and assess what actions were taken, stressing the seriousness of the allegations.
“Wartime homicide is no different from matters that we take issue with, such as the forced (enslavement of) comfort women, and the massacre of Jewish people,” he said.
The issue of “comfort women” refers to the sexual enslavement of thousands of women and girls, many of them Korean, by the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.
Israel strongly criticized Lee for posting the video, calling it “unacceptable.”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry claimed that Lee relied on a “fake account” and had revived an incident from 2024 that had already been investigated.
The ministry accused Lee of trivializing the massacre of Jews on the eve of Holocaust Remembrance Day in Israel.
China, which has long supported a two-state solution, continued to reiterate its call.
President Xi Jinping said the two-state solution is the “right direction” for resolving the longstanding Palestine issue.
Sri Lanka, one of the first countries to recognize the State of Palestine, called at the UN General Assembly for the “early” recovery and reconstruction of Gaza, reiterating its support for Palestinians’ “inalienable” rights and a two-state solution.
“Recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be an early priority,” Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath said in his address.
He added that Colombo supports resolving the Palestine issue in line with the 1967 borders.
Pakistan, a member of the Gaza Peace Board, also reiterated its “unwavering” support for the Palestinian people and the establishment of an independent State of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said that Palestine must also be granted full membership in the UN.
India, for its part, continued to pursue its strategy of maintaining diplomatic and strategic ties with Israel while continuing to express traditional support for a two-state solution and Palestinian statehood.
India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi has significantly deepened its strategic relationship with Israel, including through Modi’s February meeting with Netanyahu, when the two countries elevated their ties to a “Special Strategic Partnership.”
According to Jatin Desai, a Mumbai-based political analyst, India has historically stood with the Palestinian people. He said India’s position was clear even before the establishment of Israel.
Thailand, which has maintained long-standing ties with Israel, continues to cooperate closely with Israel, particularly in agriculture and education.
Every year, around 100,000 Israeli tourists travel to Thailand, and thousands of Thai workers, both skilled and unskilled, are employed in Israel. The country is also a popular destination for Thai students pursuing academic studies.
Bangkok established diplomatic relations with Israel in 1954, while it officially recognized Palestine in 2012.
In January, US President Donald Trump, as chair of the Board of Peace for Gaza, invited Australia, Vietnam and Thailand to join the international body.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Canberra would consider the offer, though no decision had so far been taken.
“We’ve received correspondence from the president that arrived, I think, last night. That’s something we haven’t had time to consider. We’ll consider all of these approaches respectfully and through our proper processes,” Albanese said after receiving the invitation.
Thailand said it was reviewing the details of the offer.
Vietnam’s Communist Party General Secretary To Lam accepted Trump’s invitation to join the Gaza Peace Council and “affirmed Vietnam’s readiness to participate as a founding member state of the council.”
New Zealand, which did not join neighboring Australia and other European nations to recognize the State of Palestine last year, said recognition of Palestinian statehood is “inevitable.”
In his final speech as foreign minister in the incumbent government earlier this month, Winston Peters said his decision in 2025 not to join most other UN member states in recognizing Palestine was an example of truly independent foreign policy.
But he said that recognition was a question of when, not if.
The Pacific, a cluster of small island nations, has provided Israel with a bloc of supportive voices in international forums, even as global criticism intensifies and more countries move to recognize Palestine.
Fiji further strengthened ties with Israel in September 2025 by opening a new embassy in Jerusalem. Days earlier, it abstained in a UN vote on a two-state solution. Like many of its neighbors, Fiji does not recognize Palestine.
Papua New Guinea followed a similar path. In September 2023, it also opened an embassy in Jerusalem and has since repeatedly opposed calls for a ceasefire at the UN. The country continues to reject recognition of Palestinian statehood.
Nauru has long been a loyal supporter of Israel. It recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital in 2019 and, in September last year, voted against a resolution backing a two-state solution.
Palau and Micronesia have consistently voted in line with Israel at the UN.
Samoa signed a visa-waiver deal in 2019 but took a slightly different line in September last year, when it abstained in the two-state resolution. Still, like most of its neighbors, it has not recognized Palestine.
Other Pacific nations such as Vanuatu, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati, the Solomon Islands, Tuvalu and Tonga maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, regularly support it at UN forums and do not recognize Palestine.
Tonga and Israel signed a visa-waiver agreement in 2010, while Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands have consistently backed Israel in UN votes.

How Netanyahu is using the near-tragic flydubai incident as an election issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:43:24 UTC
22:43:24 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has already turned an under-investigation cockpit fight into his election campaign material that paints the country as a victim of terrorist threat – a challenge that only an experienced ‘security premier’ can meet.
On September 30, a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Saudi Arabia after a reported cockpit altercation.
Investigations are still underway, but initial reporting quoted officials as saying that the co-pilot – who they identified as an Omani national – allegedly stabbed the captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar.
The alleged altercation sent the aircraft carrying 174 passengers, mostly Israelis, plunging 17,000 feet within minutes before some passengers overpowered the co-pilot and a second pair of flydubai pilots landed the plane.
Netanyahu did not wait for the investigation to establish conclusively whether it was indeed a terrorist attack.
Tugce Ersoy-Ceylan, a professor of international relations at Izmir Katip Celebi University, tells TRT World that there are “clear signs” Netanyahu is trying to turn the flydubai incident into an election campaign issue.
“The investigation is still ongoing. Yet, Netanyahu has already described the incident as an attempted ‘9/11 disaster’ and linked it to (so-called) Islamist radicalisation,” she says.
Netanyahu immediately called the episode a “serious security incident”, claiming that the attacker had tried to crash the plane with the passengers on board.
He claimed that the wounded captain and the Israelis who stormed the cockpit had “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster”.
He also met returning passenger Yaniv Hayun, still in blood-stained clothes, at Ben Gurion airport and called him a hero.
Netanyahu has clearly overplayed the alleged hijacking plot, raising the spectre of a 9/11-like terrorist attack on Israel only four weeks before the general election.
That’s because Netanyahu, already Israel’s longest-serving premier, has built his political identity as a security hawk.
But analysts say Netanyahu’s security credentials have taken a hit after Hamas’ cross-border blitz on October 7, 2023, helping internationalise the issue of Palestinian suffering at the hands of Israel.
For the last three years, Israel has become an international pariah under Netanyahu’s premiership as it waged a genocidal war in Gaza, besides the on-again, off-again military offensives in Lebanon and Iran.
Interestingly, the day before the alleged hijacking, Netanyahu had warned of plots against Israel in the run-up to the October 27 general election.
Experts say Netanyahu's conversion of a near-tragedy into campaign material is meant to shore up dwindling electoral support for his Likud party.
Netanyahu’s team connected the incident “very quickly” to the warnings he had issued a day ago, while he personally associated himself with the passengers who stopped the alleged attack.
“That means that a genuine security event is already being incorporated into an electoral narrative,” she says.
Netanyahu on the backfoot
Pre-election public polls show Netanyahu’s ultra-right bloc is unlikely to win a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset to form a government.
His opponents within Israel seem to have seen through Netanyahu’s political gimmickry. Israeli media reported that Netanyahu turned the episode into an election flashpoint within hours.
Naftali Bennett, former Israeli premier, said he doesn't need the government to warn him.
“You’re not a warning app, you’re the prime minister of Israel. If you suspected there was a danger that a plane would blow up, what did you do about it? Start taking responsibility for security. It’s exactly like October 7,” he said.
Yair Lapid, another former premier, accused Netanyahu of doing “cheap politics at the expense of Israel’s security”.
According to Ersoy-Ceylan, the alleged hijacking supports two completely different political narratives: Netanyahu presents it as evidence of continuing threats to Israelis and of the need for higher vigilance.
But the opposition has equated it with the October 7 blitz, when the state failed to prevent the danger, and people ultimately had to save themselves.
But which narrative will ultimately prevail during the election depends largely on voters’ prior views of Netanyahu, she says.
Israeli politics is highly polarised, she says, adding that October 7 “fundamentally complicates” Netanyahu’s traditional claim to be ‘Mr Security’.
“Unlike previous elections, emphasising threat does not automatically translate into emphasising his competence. It can simultaneously remind voters of security failure,” she says.
According to Ozden Zeynep Oktav, head of the international relations department at Istanbul Medeniyet University, the alleged hijacking has become a “remedy for Netanyahu”, who was treated at the recent UN General Assembly session as an “outlaw” and a “criminal” by nearly 70 countries.
“On the eve of the elections, he badly needed such a thwarted terror plot. Therefore, this can be a planned one beforehand,” she notes.
She says Netanyahu could not give “satisfactory answers” to accusations from opposition parties that he knew about the October 7 blitz before it happened.
These allegations have “weakened Netanyahu’s hand”, leaving him with “very little chance” of winning the elections.
Doubts galore
Sceptics have started casting doubt on the sequence of events on the day of the alleged hijacking.
The footage from the flight raised many questions, such as the absence of oxygen masks, which drop automatically in a rapid descent, and few injuries among ordinary passengers.
The Iranian state broadcaster Press TV claimed that Netanyahu had planned a false-flag hijacking to draw the US into a new war with Tehran.
Netanyahu told the media that he knew the pilot “underwent Islamist radical indoctrination”.
Even US President Donald Trump spoke cautiously about the incident.
“This is the story that I heard. I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story that I got from Bibi,” he said.
Asked how often an Israeli prime minister has turned a late-campaign security scare into measurable votes, Ersoy-Ceylan points to 1996.
A series of suicide bombings damaged Shimon Peres’s security and peace message and strengthened Netanyahu, contributing to his very narrow victory, she says.
The historical pattern, however, shows security crises benefit security-oriented and far-right narratives “rather than consistently rewarding the incumbent prime minister”.
But Oktav notes that security in Israel remains the “most crucial issue”.
“Therefore, the flydubai plot makes the Israelis believe that Netanyahu’s criminal policies are just for their security purposes,” she says.

Has Iran's Hormuz card really been burned?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:42:30 UTC
22:42:30 KST

Has Iran's Hormuz card really been burned?
TEHRAN - Senior U.S. officials have spent months declaring the Strait of Hormuz "open" and Iran's leverage over the waterway "burned." A first-hand Bloomberg report from the strait itself tells a different story — and the facts it contains point to a single conclusion: Iran's Hormuz card remains very much in play.
What the Bloomberg report actually documents
In a report published on October 1, 2026, under the headline "No Lights, No Radio: Getting Oil Through Hormuz Is a Risky Job," Bloomberg interviewed a tanker captain who transits the strait by evading rather than passing. His account is factual, not rhetorical:
Vessels move through the southernmost edge of the strait, hugging Oman's coastline, within sight of land — far from the main shipping lanes.
The crossings are made in total darkness, with navigation lights off and no radio communication.
Transits are conducted under the shadow of U.S. aircraft and helicopter patrols, effectively under escort.
Crews are paid several multiples of their normal wages; one ship owner has offered six months of bonus pay simply to sail the crossing.
Contracts have been shortened because crews consider the voyage dangerous.
The captain confirms that vessels transiting near his own have, on occasions, come under Iranian fire.
Reading the facts against the "open strait" claim
Before the war, the strait carried a steady 110–130 vessel transits per day. What the Bloomberg report documents is something categorically different: a trickle of covert, high-cost, high-risk crossings that structurally cannot approach pre-war levels. Three measurable gaps separate the two:
Volume. Night-time, radio-silent, coastline-hugging transits — however many — are by definition a fraction of routine traffic. No logistical arrangement of this kind can scale to 110+ daily passages.
Risk. Pre-war transits were safe and insured under standard conditions. Current crossings involve war-risk exposure, documented incidents of vessels coming under fire, and dependency on continuous military coordination. Energy trade does not operate sustainably under these conditions.
Cost. Shipping lines face sharply inflated expenses — insurance premiums, hazard pay, shortened crew contracts. These are the cost structures of a closed or constrained waterway, not an open one.
Each of these indicators is drawn directly from the American outlet's own reporting. Far from corroborating the White House line, it undermines it.
Why the card still works
The strategic logic is straightforward. Iran's leverage over Hormuz has never depended on fully closing the strait; it depends on the cost and risk of every single transit. By that measure, the current situation represents the card functioning, not burning:
Every crossing now carries elevated insurance, labor and operational costs — a permanent tax on traffic through the strait.
Traffic flows only in a degraded, escorted, covert mode that cannot sustain normal energy commerce.
Iran retains the demonstrated capability to put vessels under fire — an active deterrent that keeps war-risk premiums high and shipping lines cautious.
The "open strait" narrative exists precisely because the strait is not open: Washington, having failed to seize the lever by force, is running a sustained messaging campaign to convince Tehran that its leverage has evaporated and to alter its calculations, particularly its demand for a security order over the Hormuz orbit.
An open strait requires neither darkness, nor silence, nor danger pay, nor naval escort. The Bloomberg report documents all four. The current state of the Strait of Hormuz is neither safe, nor normal, nor sustainable for ordinary commerce — which is exactly what gives Iran leverage. The claim that Iran's Hormuz card has been burned is not supported by the facts on the water; it is a psychological operation, and its very intensity is the clearest evidence that the card is still being played.

Cat and five kittens rescued from occupied Oleshky in drone evacuation across Dnipro River
Ukrainian troops have used a drone to evacuate six cats from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast. The pets travelled over 10 km in the air.
Source: Oleksandr Pivnenko, Commander of the National Guard of Ukraine; Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs
Details: The rescue operation was carried out by service members from the Bolharychi special-purpose attack UAV company.
Left without owners for various reasons, the cats risked being left to fend for themselves on the streets and starve in temporarily occupied Oleshky.
Quote from Pivnenko: "Thanks to the help of local residents, we managed to evacuate six cats, all born during the occupation, in an unusual operation. They were placed in a cage specially designed for the operation, and our soldiers carried them across the Dnipro beneath a heavy bomber drone."
More details: The cat and her five kittens were transported slowly so they would not feel unwell, the commander of the Bolharychi company told Suspilne, a Ukrainian public broadcaster. During the evacuation, the military monitored the sky to ensure the drone was not shot down.
The cats travelled over 10 km by air to the location where they were met by National Guard soldiers.
Representatives of Kherson Oblast Military Administration will help rehome the cats, the commander of the Bolharychi company said.
Quote from Pivnenko: "They landed safe and sound, though perhaps a little scared, so the operation codenamed Tiger was a success. All the kitties will soon find new homes."
Background: The Ukrainian military previously used a drone to evacuate a cat with five kittens from their positions. The special operation was codenamed Meow-Meow.
Ukrainian soldiers also evacuated a cat and a dog from frontline positions using an unmanned aerial vehicle which flew the animals 12 km to safety.

AI is reshaping tourism beyond digital services, Iranian researcher says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:40:43 UTC
22:40:43 KST

AI is reshaping tourism beyond digital services, Iranian researcher says
TEHRAN – Artificial intelligence is moving beyond digital tools and online services to reshape the structure of the tourism industry, influencing how travelers choose destinations, how experiences are designed and how destinations are managed, an Iranian researcher has said.
The theme of World Tourism Day 2026, “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Redesign Tourism,” reflects a broader shift in the industry's approach to technology, Habib Mahmoudi-Chenari told in an interview with Miras Aria news agency published on Wednesday.
Mahmoudi-Chenari said the emphasis on digital transformation, innovation, artificial intelligence, smart tourism, data governance, skills development and ethical technology use points to the need to rethink how tourism systems operate.
He distinguished tourism digitalization, which largely involves transferring traditional processes to online platforms, from tourism redesign, which questions whether existing structures should be rebuilt around new technological capabilities.
Online reservations, electronic payments, websites, mobile applications and digital marketing have helped digitize tourism services. However, artificial intelligence could influence the entire travel process, from inspiring a trip and selecting a destination to planning an itinerary, booking services and analyzing post-trip feedback, he said.
AI could influence destination choices
Artificial intelligence could become a major gateway through which travelers discover tourism products and destinations, Mahmoudi-Chenari said.
Rather than simply answering where to travel, intelligent systems can help travelers identify the experiences they want and match destinations with their interests, budgets, schedules and personal circumstances.
Such systems could recommend accommodation, transport routes, attractions, restaurants and activities based on individual preferences. Travelers interested in cultural heritage, nature, food, agricultural experiences or low-carbon travel could receive tailored itineraries, while families could account for children, older adults or dietary restrictions when planning their trips.
This shift could also affect destination visibility. While tourism promotion has traditionally relied on advertising, branding, location, travel agencies and search engines, a destination's representation in digital data and AI-driven recommendation systems could increasingly influence whether potential visitors discover it.
Connected data essential for smart tourism
Mahmoudi-Chenari cautioned that smart tourism cannot be achieved simply by introducing mobile applications or chatbots.
Information on flights, accommodation, transportation, attractions, events, payments, destination capacity and tourist behavior must be connected and capable of being exchanged across systems, he said. Without such integration, even advanced AI systems may struggle to provide a comprehensive and reliable picture of the travel experience.
He also called for destinations to be redesigned around data-driven management rather than the mere presence of digital infrastructure.
By continuously collecting and analyzing information on visitor flows, attraction capacity, accommodation availability, traffic, water and energy consumption, weather conditions and demand patterns, destination managers could anticipate congestion and resource pressures before they escalate.
Such systems could also help distribute visitors across lesser-known areas, manage pressure on popular attractions and reduce tourism's impact on natural resources and infrastructure.
Data governance and digital inclusion
The researcher said artificial intelligence offers opportunities to improve productivity, personalize services, expand market access for small businesses and support more effective destination management. However, its benefits will depend on how the technology is governed and deployed.
If data and digital infrastructure are controlled primarily by a small number of major platforms, he warned, market power could become more concentrated. Algorithms that repeatedly recommend established destinations could also make it harder for emerging or lesser-known places to gain visibility.
Small rural destinations, family farms, guesthouses and local producers may offer distinctive tourism experiences but remain largely invisible online if they lack digital content, usable data and marketing skills, he said.
Addressing this imbalance requires investment in digital infrastructure, training, data security, common standards and fair access to technology. Tourism workers, local communities, small businesses and emerging destinations should also have a role in shaping the industry's digital future.
Keeping technology human-centered
Mahmoudi-Chenari stressed that tourism redesign should not aim to replace people with machines. Instead, technology should strengthen human capabilities, improve service quality and support the resilience and sustainability of destinations.
He described a smart destination as one that continuously collects data, converts it into information, analyzes the findings, uses them to inform decisions and evaluates the results.
Artificial intelligence can serve as a powerful analytical and decision-support tool in this process, he said, but sustainable transformation requires high-quality data, appropriate infrastructure, shared standards, data security and skilled personnel.
Ultimately, he added, tourism redesign extends beyond technology to encompass economic, social, human, environmental and governance considerations.

Iran, Belarus stress expanding monetary, banking cooperation
TEHRAN- The 19th meeting of the Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Belarus, held in Minsk with high-level delegations from both countries, focused on facilitating banking transactions and expanding financial cooperation.
According to IRNA, citing the Central Bank, the bank’s delegation, headed by Hossein Kashiri, Director General of International Relations and Cooperation, discussed and exchanged views with Belarusian counterparts during the four-day meeting (September 29-October 2) on practical solutions to remove obstacles to foreign exchange and banking transactions. Establishing a regular mechanism for holding bilateral meetings at the level of central banks, commercial banks, and financial institutions of the two countries was one of the key decisions of the meeting—a move aimed at effectively supporting trade and economic flows and expanding mutual investments.
In part of his negotiations, Kashiri, referring to Iran’s abundant economic capacities, expressed the full readiness of the country’s banking network and financial institutions to attract direct investments and for Belarusian banks to participate in Iran’s major economic and commercial projects.
This meeting, held with the aim of deepening bilateral relations in specialized financial areas, is considered an important step toward monetary independence and diversifying financial pathways between the two countries under the current conditions of the international economy.
On the eve of the Iran-Belarus Joint Economic Committee, the Director General of the Central Asia, Caucasus and Russia Office of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization announced: The value of trade exchanges between Iran and Belarus in 2025 amounted to $76 million.
According to IRNA, citing the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, Mehdi Babaei stated that agricultural and petrochemical products had the largest share in Iran’s exports to Belarus, and added: The 19th meeting of the Iran-Belarus Joint Economic Cooperation Committee will be held with the participation of Seyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, and the Minister of Industry of the Republic of Belarus.
Babaei considered the holding of joint committees as a foundation for strengthening and expanding mutual cooperation between the two countries and added: At this meeting, emphasis will be placed on developing cooperation in the fields of trade and industry, agriculture, investment, health and pharmaceuticals, as well as strengthening interaction between the private sectors of the two countries, with the aim of expanding Iran-Belarus economic and trade relations as much as possible.
According to him, at the end of this meeting, a memorandum of understanding on cooperation between the industry ministers of the two countries will be signed. Also, meeting with the Prime Minister and officials of the Republic of Belarus and the opening of Iran’s dedicated trade pavilion with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union at the “InnoProm Belarus” exhibition are among the other programs planned within the framework of this meeting.
Back in mid-August, Iran’s Deputy Agriculture Minister for planning and Economy Affairs met with the Minister of Agriculture and Food of Belarus, emphasizing the development of bilateral cooperation in the fields of agricultural fertilizers, machinery, and joint investment.
According to Mehr News Agency, Akbar Fathi, Iran’s Deputy Agriculture Minister for planning and Economy Affairs, met and held talks with Yuri Gorlov, Minister of Agriculture and Food of the Republic of Belarus, on the sidelines of the 7th meeting of the Policy Council of Agriculture and Industry of the Eurasian Economic Union, held in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
During the meeting, the capacities and areas for developing agricultural and economic cooperation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Belarus were reviewed, and both sides emphasized the need to strengthen bilateral interactions and utilize existing capacities to develop trade and investment in the agricultural sector.
One of the main axes of the negotiations was the continuation and development of cooperation between the two countries in the supply and trade of potash and phosphate fertilizers. In this regard, existing capacities for expanding trade cooperation, as well as examining areas for joint investment in the production and supply of agricultural inputs, were taken into consideration.
The Iranian side, referring to the importance of sustainable supply of inputs needed by the agricultural sector, emphasized the use of capacities of EAEU member states to diversify input supply sources and develop long-term cooperation.
Also during this meeting, capacities for joint cooperation in the field of agricultural machinery and equipment were discussed and exchanged.
Both sides emphasized identifying the capacities of manufacturing companies and private sector activists of the two countries and paving the way for the development of exchanges, technology transfer, and joint investments in the field of agricultural machinery and equipment.
The development of trade in agricultural and food products between Iran and Belarus was another focus of this meeting. Within this framework, existing capacities for increasing trade exchanges in the fields of poultry meat, dairy products, and various fruits were reviewed, and the need to facilitate trade and create suitable grounds for greater presence of producers and exporters of the two countries in each other's markets was emphasized.
Also, the issue of developing trade relations and utilizing the capacities of existing agreements and mechanisms to increase the volume of agricultural and food product exchanges between the two countries was taken into consideration.

“Chapa Meets Fellini” to feature at international film festival in Rome
Monday 5 October 2026 15:38
Monday, 5 October 2026, 15:38
PHOTO Courtesy of the production team
Font size
 Bulgaria has a special place in the programme of the sixth Coliseum International Film Festival (COLIFFE) in Rome. On October 6, 2026, at 9 pm, Bulgarian culture will be showcased through cinema, folklore and discussion at Rome’s Teatro Marconi.
The highlight of the evening will be a screening of “Chapa Meets Fellini”, a documentary by journalist and director Georgi Toshev exploring the friendship and creative relationship between renowned Bulgarian sculptor Georgi Chapkanov, known as Chapa, and legendary Italian filmmaker Federico Fellini. Their story is an unusual encounter between Bulgaria and Italy, between sculpture and cinema, and between two different creative worlds that crossed paths in Rome.
“Chapa Meets Fellini” tells the story of the friendship between Chapkanov and Fellini, who met in the early 1990s on Via Margutta, a street known for its artistic community. It was there that Chapkanov persuaded Fellini to make a bas-relief for him.
Immediately after the screening at Teatro Marconi, Georgi Toshev will take part in a public discussion with well-known Italian journalist Massimiliano Spinella. The conversation will give the audience an opportunity to learn more about the making of the film, the relationship between Chapkanov and Fellini, and the place of their story in the broader European cultural context.
A special guest of the evening will be actress Yana Yakovleva, deputy director and artistic director of the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Italy.
The programme will also feature a performance by a Bulgarian folk ensemble, adding one of the most recognisable elements of the country’s living cultural tradition to the evening’s presentation.

Dozens quarantined in Siberia after plague institute lab worker dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:38:53 UTC
22:38:53 KST

Dozens quarantined in Siberia after plague institute lab worker dies
MOSCOW - A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting the authorities to quarantine dozens of people and the head of Russia’s health watchdog to fly to the Irkutsk region.
The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said on Oct 5 the situation was under control.
The World Health Organization said that based on available information, “the public health risk to the general population appears to be low”. New risk assessments would be conducted once further information became known, it said.
US President Donald Trump said the death was a “big problem for Russia” and offered to help Moscow deal with it.
“We’ll help,” Trump said. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was closely monitoring the situation.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas. It is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, though cases occur every year in other parts of the world — notably Africa.
Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, prompts the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
If identified quickly, it can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days.
Local media have named the laboratory worker who died as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
There were conflicting reports about how and where she fell ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia of as-yet unestablished origin.
The authorities say no new cases reported, all contacts traced
Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, told state media the institute had not found evidence of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens after rumours spread on social media that the woman had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria.
Nevertheless, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Siberia for an emergency meeting over the weekend.
According to Russian media reports, about 200 people who had been in contact with the dead woman were quarantined, parts of the hospital in the town of Shelekhov where she died were cordoned off and an aluminium plant told its workers to wear masks.
Rospotrebnadzor, in a later statement quoted by the TASS news agency, said officials in Irkutsk Region had found two cases of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with her. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted.
Authorities urged people to remain calm and said there was no evidence that the woman’s death was linked to her work.
Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement that she had died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, adding: “Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified.”
He said the situation was under control and that all known contacts of the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision. REUTERS

South Africa sees sharp rise in multiracial households
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:38:06 UTC
22:38:06 KST

South Africa sees sharp rise in multiracial households
Multiracial households have become increasingly common in South Africa over the past two decades, with more than one in ten now comprising people from different racial groups, Statistics South Africa reported.
The proportion has risen from just 1.3% in 2001 and 1.7% in 2011 to 11.4% in 2022, with most of the change taking place in the decade between the last two censuses. Statistics South Africa defines a multi-racial household as one in which two or more people from different population groups live together as one household. These include black African, white, coloured, Indian or Asian, and other population groups.
The report says the shift reflects changes in how South Africans live and form families, with intermarriage, migration, urbanisation and greater social mobility contributing to increasingly integrated households. However, the picture differs considerably across the country.
The Western Cape has the highest proportion of multi-racial households, where they account for almost one in five households. Gauteng follows, while Limpopo has the lowest proportion. This partly reflects the racial make-up of individual provinces, with multi-racial households more common in areas with more diverse populations, according to the report.
Johannesburg and Cape Town stand out among South Africa’s metros, although multi-racial households are increasingly found outside the country’s major cities. More than four in five multi-racial households were located in urban areas in each of the three censuses studied.
However, the proportion living outside urban areas has also grown, from about 15% in 2001 to more than 18% in 2022. Indeed, about two in five multi-racial households are now found in non-metropolitan municipalities.
The make-up of these households has changed substantially too. In 2001, large households were common, with almost three in 10 multi-racial households containing six or more people. By 2022, they accounted for fewer than one in 25. At the same time, three-person households have become dominant. Fewer than one in five fell into this category in 2001, compared with almost half by 2022, according to the Census figures.
”In terms of living arrangements and culture in general, South African society continues to adopt new ways of living, including mixed-race household formation, and these emerging social interaction patterns have an impact on household size,” says the agency. Two-person households have also become considerably more common, while the proportion containing five people has fallen sharply.
”The rise of multi-racial households in South Africa is a direct reflection of democratic freedom in several aspects of life,” says Statistics South Africa. According to the report, the increase reflects greater cultural integration through urbanisation, migration and education, as well as the freedom to marry, cohabit and form families across racial lines.

Russia names eight fatalities in Tu-95MS crash in the Far East, The Insider confirms three officers linked to combat missions in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:37:30 UTC
22:37:30 KST

Eight Russian service members — rather than the six initially reported by the Ministry of Defense — were killed on Sept. 29 when a Tu-95MS long-range bomber crashed in the Amur Region. The Insider has established that at least three long-range aviation officers were among the dead: Andrei Lobanov, Fedor Pavlyukov, and Andrei Gerasimov. Ukraine links all three to Tu-95MS combat missions.
On Oct. 4, the local outlet Port Amur was the first to report that the death toll had risen to eight, adding that nine service members had been on board and that two of the dead had not been found right away. Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District in the Amur Region, soon published a photograph featuring portraits of those killed. The Ministry of Defense had initially reported six dead and one hospitalized.
According to the captions under the portraits, the dead include Andrei Lobanov, Vladislav Moskovskikh, Artur Enokyan, Mikhail Kotyshev, Sergei Moisevich, Vladimir Kelip, Fedor Pavlyukov, and Andrei Gerasimov. Piven said local authorities intend to ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state honors.
Three of the dead appeared in a Ukrainian database
The Insider cross-checked the data on those killed against the Ukrainian database Russian Torturers, a project launched in 2022 on the initiative of President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its creators say the entries are verified by Ukrainian law enforcement or intelligence agencies.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in Russia’s 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at Ukrainka airfield. The database claims that he directly commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as deputy commander for flight training for the same 182nd Regiment. From August 2021 to April 2024, he commanded a Tu-95MS squadron. The database’s creators say Pavlyukov was responsible for preparing flight crews for combat missions and directly commanded the unit. As early as March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence had placed Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots suspected of direct participation in the war against Ukraine.
Major Andrei Gerasimov is listed as commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. The database claims he directly commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatoliy Shtefan (“Stirlitz”) also claimed that at least three of those killed were involved in organizing and carrying out missile strikes on Ukraine, though he did not specify which of those killed he had in mind.
The Sept. 29 plane crash
The Tu-95MS crashed on Sept. 29 during a training flight near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky District. The Ministry of Defense said the plane had been flying without weapons and went down “in an uninhabited area.” The local government in the Amur Region said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential areas in order to avoid causing further casualties, and no one on the ground was hurt. The ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to investigate the crash. No publicly confirmed findings have established its cause.
Ukrainka airfield, where the 182nd Regiment is based, has taken on particular importance for Russia’s long-range aviation over the past year. The Insider previously reported that most of Russia’s long-range bombers (that are still able to fly) were redeployed from the western part of the country to the Far East following Ukraine’s behind-the-lines Operation Spiderweb.
As a result, Ukrainka became the main base for operational Tu-95MS aircraft, significantly complicating combat missions. In order to launch missiles at targets in Ukraine, the aircraft must fly upwards of 12,000 kilometers round-trip, refueling at the Engels or Olenya air bases in western Russia. A typical mission thus lasts around 23 hours, putting significant strain on the aging aircraft.

Foreign issuers take majority share of panda bond proceeds in H1
China

2026-10-05
21:37:13 CST
22:37:13 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Foreign issuers accounted for 54 percent of funds raised through panda bonds in China in the first half (H1) of 2026, exceeding the share raised by Chinese issuers for the first time, according to the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE).
Foreign issuers raised 58.7 billion yuan (about 8.7 billion U.S. dollars) for intended overseas use, accounting for 68 percent of their total proceeds, the SAFE said in its report on China's international balance of payments for H1.
Panda bonds refer to renminbi-denominated bonds issued in China's onshore market by overseas entities such as sovereign governments, international financial institutions and multinational companies.
In recent years, the panda bond market has seen steady growth, becoming increasingly attractive to global issuers. To date, cumulative panda bond issuance has exceeded 1.3 trillion yuan, with issuers from 26 countries and regions.
As of Sept. 17 this year, the issuance of the renminbi-denominated debt securities has surpassed 240 billion yuan, up 81 percent from a year earlier, according to Shanghai-based data provider Wind Information.
Analysts say that lower renminbi financing costs have been a major reason for the record-high panda bond issuance this year, while the booming panda bond market is also creating a positive interplay with the yuan's internationalization.
The People's Bank of China, the country's central bank, said it will support more eligible overseas entities in issuing such bonds. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: From a candlelit room, African student chases her Chinese championship dream
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:36:52 CST
22:36:52 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Power cuts are nothing unusual in Kibera, Nairobi's largest informal settlement. On many nights, a small solar lamp and a few candles are all that light Miriam Achieng Kenyatta's books.
The 23-year-old university student, with a Chinese name "Mi Yao," could not afford tuition for Chinese classes. So she turned her cramped home into an immersive Chinese environment.
She renamed every contact in her phone in Chinese, repeated lines from Chinese TV dramas, found language partners on learning apps, and joined Chinese-language voice chat rooms where she forced herself to keep talking.
"I used the phone and internet I could afford to fill my life with Chinese as much as possible," she said.
Within six months, she found she could follow a full 40-minute episode of a Chinese drama without subtitles.
In April, Kenyatta reached the Kenya division finals of the 25th "Chinese Bridge" Chinese Proficiency Competition for Foreign College Students.
Wearing a red cape, she struck a large drum painted with dragons and recited "Song of the Great Wind," a poem over 2,000 years old by Liu Bang, the founding emperor of China's Han Dynasty.
"At first I was so nervous that I was shaking," she said. "But once the music started, I became absorbed in the story and everything fell into place."
The performance helped her win the Kenya division of the 25th edition of the competition and a place among the top 15 contestants in the global finals in China.
She had very little formal training in Chinese. She studied for three months at the Confucius Institute at the University of Nairobi, then dropped out when she could not raise the 2,000-shilling (about 15.5 U.S. dollars) examination fee required to advance to the next level.
Self-learning and practice with the institute's drumming club changed things. Her spoken Chinese was "very good," said the club's coach, who then recommended her to the Confucius Institute.
The institute made her a key contestant for the competition, gave her special training, and waived her fees, bringing her back into the classroom.
"She is smart and very resilient," said Meng Lingyao, a teacher at the institute. "No matter how late it was, she would record voice messages and send them to us so we could correct her pronunciation and tones word by word."
During the intensive training, Kenyatta turned down the dormitory room the institute offered. She went home every day, rain or shine, to look after her younger brother, Meng said.
That home is in Kibera.
Twenty-five years ago, Kenyatta's parents moved from Kisumu in western Kenya to Nairobi in the hope of giving their children a better education. They settled in Kibera.
The settlement has too little piped water and too few waste and sewage facilities. Homes are built from mud, sticks and corrugated iron, hot during the day and cold at night.
The family of six shared an iron-sheet and mud hut of about 15 square meters. The monthly rent of 700 shillings (about 5.4 dollars) was among the cheapest in Kibera.
Hellen Juma Bonyo, Kenyatta's mother, has not bought herself a new piece of clothing since her children were born. For most of those 25 years, she left home at around 5:00 a.m. local time to sell peanuts and soap on the streets and rarely got back before 9:00 p.m. local time.
Even so, money was always short. The family needed about 600 shillings a day for food, and often did not have it. When Kenyatta got into university, tuition, housing and living costs came to 130,000 shillings (about 1,000 dollars) for the year.
They borrowed from every relative and friend they had. Kenyatta's 92-year-old grandfather organized a harambee, a traditional Kenyan community fundraiser, in his village and raised 40,000 shillings.
"For all these years I have been struggling to climb a mountain," Bonyo said. "At the top is a life where I don't have to worry about paying for my children. I'm only halfway there."
Bonyo never finished high school. "If you don't study now, you will end up like me," she often told them.
Despite the hardship, she has never regretted staying in Nairobi. "Because we stayed in Nairobi, my daughter got into university, learned Chinese, and became the first person in our family to board a plane to go to places we had only seen on television," she said.
When Kenyatta called with the news that she had won and would travel to China for the finals, Bonyo was selling peanuts.
At first, she was anxious about the cost. After learning that the Chinese side would pay all expenses, she worried about her daughter's safety, since no one in the family had ever flown.
Before Kenyatta left, Bonyo fasted for three days to pray for her, as she has done whenever any of her four children faced a major exam.
In China, Kenyatta climbed the Great Wall and toured the Palace Museum. She also heard about China's campaign to lift people out of poverty.
What she saw changed how she thought about home. Before university, she had wanted nothing more than to get away from Kibera.
"In high school I studied as hard as I could and won a scholarship every year," she said. "Apart from easing the burden on my family, my biggest wish was to get into university, find a job that paid well, and leave Kibera forever."
But sitting on a bus in China, she found herself thinking of home.
"I felt very homesick. An ordinary road in China looks like a highway in Nairobi," she said. "I thought, why can't my home have wide roads everywhere? I hope Kibera can become like this one day."
"Many people move to Kibera to escape poverty, but end up trapped here for the rest of their lives," she said. "Poverty is exactly what has pushed me to work so hard."
Had she been born into a different family, she might not have studied as hard, said Kenyatta. Now she hopes to use what she learns to give dreamers in Kibera better opportunities.
Her mother is confident about her future.
"Chinese people have built very good infrastructure in Kenya," Bonyo said. "If my daughter speaks Chinese and works with Chinese people, she will learn many more skills. Her life will not be as hard as mine."
The road ahead is taking shape. Kenyatta, an engineering student, has already secured a scholarship to study Chinese for a year and a half at Tianjin Normal University after she graduates. She then plans to apply for a master's program in China.
Her two middle siblings now board at school, and her parents have moved back to Kisumu. Kenyatta stays in Kibera with her youngest brother. She commutes to class, cooks for him, and teaches English online to help cover expenses.
Asked to describe her ideal day, she thought for a moment.
"A very ordinary day," she said. "I wake up and don't have to worry about where breakfast will come from, or whether eating breakfast means I can't have lunch."
"I won't have to ask, 'What can we do?' anymore." ■

Somalia issues emergency alert over El Nino flood risk
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
21:36:46 CST
22:36:46 KST

MOGADISHU, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Somalia has issued an emergency alert to communities living in flood-prone areas as it strengthens early warning and evacuation measures ahead of potential heavy rains and flooding linked to El Nino.
The Somali Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) announced on Sunday that the country has entered the Deyr rainy season, with heavy rainfall expected across several regions.
"SoDMA urges communities to remain alert and take necessary precautions to prepare for the expected rains and potential flooding," the disaster agency said in a statement issued in Mogadishu on Sunday evening.
The country's meteorologists have confirmed that 2026 is a Super El Nino year, with forecasts pointing to exceptionally heavy rainfall during the October-December Deyr rainy season.
According to SoDMA, the greatest risk lies along the Jubba and Shabelle river basins.
The disaster agency also warned that ongoing El Nino conditions could trigger heavy rains, flash floods, and river overflowing, posing severe risks to low-lying areas, riverine communities, and flood-prone locations.
The El Nino threat comes as many Somali communities struggle to recover from compounding climate shocks, including severe drought, localized flooding, ongoing conflict, and displacement.
According to the United Nations, heavy flooding risks triggering further population displacement, destroying infrastructure, disrupting livelihoods, and elevating the threat of waterborne diseases, particularly for vulnerable populations in riverine and low-lying areas.
SoDMA advised residents to monitor official alerts, identify evacuation routes, and assemble emergency kits containing food, water, medical supplies, and essential documents. Communities situated along the Jubba and Shabelle rivers are urged to track water levels continuously.
In September, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that projected El Nino rains and severe flooding could affect up to 3.4 million people in Somalia across 16 regions between October and December.
OCHA warned that the combination of flooding, displacement, and poor sanitation threatens to trigger widespread waterborne disease outbreaks, compounding a crisis where at least 380 health facilities have already closed or scaled back operations due to severe funding shortages.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification warned in September that flooding linked to El Nino could push internally displaced people in Baidoa, in the southwestern Bay region, into a risk of famine between October and December, with a follow-up review due this month to confirm the assessment. ■

Israeli math professor charged with plotting to kill hundreds of Arabs, force mass expulsions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Lina Altawell
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Israeli prosecutors charged a Bar-Ilan University mathematics professor Monday with preparing a terrorist attack, blackmail and obstruction of justice for plotting to kill hundreds of Arab citizens and force thousands more to flee to Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, according to Israeli media.
The State Prosecutor’s Office said the suspect, whose identity remains under a gag order, developed a “thorough and detailed” plan over nearly three years and sought assistance from “subversive elements” in the Israeli Air Force, artillery and armored corps, The Times of Israel reported.
The suspect, around 60 years old, was arrested Sept. 17 and has admitted to the charges against him, according to prosecutors.
The indictment says he spent the past 18 months trying to recruit people for the plan and sought a “significant political figure” who could help enlist armed participants.
He eventually approached former Likud lawmaker Moshe Feiglin, whose Zehut faction has teamed up with extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party ahead of the Oct. 27 election, the newspaper said.
After Feiglin did not respond, the professor tried about a month ago to blackmail him into joining while using methods to conceal the plan and obstruct its discovery, prosecutors said.
Feiglin, his deputy Yitzhak Hai Zaga and Zehut executive director Shai Malka later handed police threatening letters they received from the suspect, according to a court filing.
The professor called the plan “Ayit,” Hebrew for “eagle,” also used as an acronym for a phrase meaning “the nation will carry out transfer,” referring to the expulsion of Palestinians.
He began working on the plan in February 2023 following the 2021 protests in mixed Arab-Jewish cities, the newspaper said.
 
Mass killings plot
As part of the preparations, the Israeli professor obtained numerous aerial photographs of the northern Bedouin town of Tuba-Zangariyye in northern Israel in March 2023 and visited the area several times to identify what he considered suitable access and attack routes.
He also prepared a 20-page document for recruits, which he kept at both his home and his Bar-Ilan University office.
The plan called for 72 armed Jewish attackers, divided into 12 groups of six, to simultaneously attack Arab population centers with firearms and axes, with support from sympathetic elements in the military.
It estimated that 600 to 700 people would be killed and stipulated that at least half of the attackers, including the professor, should hold gun licenses.
The document also called for women and children to be targeted and for the attacks to be broadcast on social media in real time to drive Arabs to flee Israel and the occupied West Bank.
It envisioned appeals for soldiers, police officers, Israeli occupiers, and criminals to join the attacks after they began.
The professor planned to gather 71 other participants at an event organized by a candidate in the 2026 election under the guise of a campaign gathering, with the attacks scheduled for the following day, the indictment said.
Around June, he asked his daughter to recruit acquaintances among the so-called “hilltop youth,” a term referring to extremist Israeli occupiers in the West Bank, but she refused.
The Central District Attorney’s Office filed the indictment at Lod District Court and asked that he remain in custody until the end of the proceedings.
Bar-Ilan University said it was “shocked” by the charges and suspended the professor pending the conclusion of the legal process.
Arab Israelis make up about 21% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.

Russia ratifies employment pact with India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:35:23 UTC
22:35:23 KST

Russia ratifies employment pact with India
Russia’s parliament has ratified a temporary employment pact with India as Moscow prepares to take in thousands of Indian skilled workers this year, particularly in construction and logistics.
The State Duma approved the agreement on October 1, followed by the Federation Council a day later. The pact was signed in New Delhi on December 4 last year and governs temporary employment of Indian citizens in Russia and Russian citizens in India. 
Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 skilled Indian workers during 2026, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar told a parliamentary consultative committee last week, the Press Trust of India news agency reported. 
The agreement covers employment and service contracts, as well as full-time students who take temporary jobs outside their studies. Moscow says the framework will help regulate labor flows from India in line with the needs of the Russian economy. 
Workers covered by the pact cannot receive worse pay or working conditions than local citizens in comparable jobs. Employment generally requires a work permit, while compensation in cases of layoffs, as well as pension, social security, and medical insurance, will be governed by host-country laws and applicable bilateral agreements. 
Russia has increasingly turned to India to meet workforce shortages. Authorities estimate an immediate shortfall of at least 2.3 million workers, including around 800,000 in manufacturing and 1.5 million in services and construction.
The number of work permits approved for Indian nationals has risen sharply, from around 5,000 in 2021 to almost 72,000 last year, accounting for nearly a third of Russia’s annual quota for migrant workers requiring visas.
The labor pact was among several agreements announced during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s state visit to India last December, including a separate accord on combating irregular migration.
The agreement will formally enter into force once both governments complete the required domestic procedures and the final written notification is issued.

Why the creative brain feeds on movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:34:36 UTC
22:34:36 KST

Luke Borsten, age 38, has been backpacking and making music since childhood. Today the Portland, Ore.–based filmmaker and musician often combines the two by writing music on the trail. Likewise, Amanda McCracken, a 48-year-old, Boulder, Colo.–based runner and author, finds movement essential to her writing practice.
“There’s something in movement that allows me to better see the things I want to describe,” Borsten says. “There’s an underlying feeling of honesty that creates a through line for writing.”
Borsten and McCracken are not unique in their habit of combining creativity with movement: from Ludwig van Beethoven to Henry David Thoreau, from Maya Angelou to Joyce Carol Oates, creative people are often in motion. And there’s solid science to back up that approach: consistent movement—especially in nature—helps unlock the words, notes or brushstrokes that make artists’ work.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Christian Rominger, a researcher in the department of psychology at the University of Graz in Austria, has spent years studying the link between creativity and movement. In 2022 he led a meta-analysis of 115 effect studies that found a link between motion and creativity. Another 2024 study found that the more movement—in terms of step count—participants engaged in, the greater the creative output they had.
“The empirical data is growing in this field,” he says. “We’re trying to capture this effect in detail.”
David Strayer, a professor of cognition and neural science at the University of Utah, co-authored a 2025 study that investigated how movement in nature influences brain activity. “We took measurements at the trail head, before and after hiking and backpacking trips,” he says. “We found a big boost in creativity after.”
Still, scientists have yet to identify exactly why movement seems to spur greater creative thinking. But there are several hypotheses. “We believe that all our multitasking on a daily basis overloads our mental workspace,” Strayer says. “Time moving outside frees up space to create.”
Another working theory is that movement often boosts mood, Rominger says, and that, in turn, allows you to create. “We know that creativity is related to mood,” he says, “but we can’t definitively tie the two together. It may also be that physical activity enhances brain health and therefore creativity. But these are all theories right now.”
When McCracken encounters writer’s block, she often takes a run or a swim to get the juices flowing again. She makes notes on her phone or on scraps of paper as ideas start popping up. “There’s something about it that shakes things loose,” McCracken says.
There is no clear optimal dose of movement that is guaranteed to boost creativity, but Strayer says that cognitive benefits appear to begin after about three sessions per week of 30 to 60 minutes of activity. “You start to develop new neurons at that dosage,” he says. “You think more clearly and have the mental space to support creative thinking.”
While the research is still nascent, McCracken is unequivocal. “Some of my best ideas have come during movement,” she says.

Kanyshai Butun

Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak’s The First Honest Day won the Grand Prix and a $450,000 prize at the Astana AI Film Festival, “world’s largest international competition for AI-generated film,” Qazinform reported Sunday.
Kazakhstan hosted the festival for the first time, attracting 8,067 entries from 125 countries, according to the report.
India’s SITARA took second place and $200,000, while Spain’s Looking For Perseida placed third and won $100,000.
