What do we know about the suspected Iranian plot to attack UK's Fairford airbase? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:16:43 UTC
22:16:43 KST

The United States has removed its fleet of bombers from a British airbase a week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts as part of a suspected Iranian plot, the details of which remain largely unexplained.
Below is what we know so far:
What happened?
Police were called to RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) west of London, early on Sunday, September 27, and arrested five suspects who were released on bail a day later.
A local farmer had called police, saying she saw three large white vans parked near the base and a group of "hooded and masked men" running into a field nearby. The Times reported that another person who contacted the police was one of the five arrested.
Armed officers responded to the calls and made the arrests in the Whelford area, about a mile from the base, before evacuating nearby properties and searching three vehicles.
The five were initially arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.
What happened next?
US President Donald Trump said those involved in the plot had planned "big damage," while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the "hands of a foreign actor."
In July, Iran's Revolutionary Guards had said the base was a legitimate target.
British counter-terrorism police later confirmed they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved, before Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Wednesday there might have been an Iranian link.
A 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was then arrested in London on Thursday, in what police called a "hugely complex" investigation.
A week after the initial arrests, a Pentagon official said all US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford had returned to their home stations in the US, without giving a reason.
A NATO military source said on Monday: "It is still believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK."
What has Iran said?
Iran has dismissed accusations that it was involved and on Thursday summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the issue.
What about those arrested?
Counter-terror police have said the investigation is complex. They have said no explosive devices had been found as part of the investigation, but that a quantity of petrol had been recovered during searches of the vehicles.
The five men detained were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 who lived in London, police said, before they announced they had released them all on bail.
The dual UK-Iranian national arrested on Thursday was also later released on bail.
They remain under investigation and are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.
Trump said he would not have released the suspects on bail.
Why would Fairford be a target?
Fairford, which opened in 1944 and was used by Allied troops for the D-Day invasion of Normandy, has this year been used by US forces targeting Iran after Britain approved a US request for the base to be used for defensive strikes.
It is one of the US Air Force's only European airfields suitable for heavy bombers and is the preferred base for such operations. It played a key role in both the first Gulf War in 1991 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect Fairford after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. The Guards said any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
The bombers deployed there were big enough to carry the large precision-guided "bunker-busting" weapons which are designed to penetrate fortified weapons stores.

Germany to build new naval base in Emden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:16:03 UTC
22:16:03 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Germany is planning to build a new naval base in the northwestern city of Emden amid a worsening international security environment, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Monday.
"This is significant for us, because it will be a major naval base," Pistorius said during a ceremony in Emden, where top officials signed a letter of intent for the base.
"From here we can quickly reach the North Atlantic and the North Sea," he said.
“The strategic location is also crucial - particularly with regard to our NATO allies, our shared training and operational areas, as well as joint training activities,” he added.
The new base will be Germany's fifth major naval base and is expected to ease the load on Wilhelmshaven, now the navy's most important site on the North Sea.
Defense Ministry sources said Wilhelmshaven will remain central, and the Emden base will complement it.
Pistorius said Germany has decided to expand its navy in response to rising international threats and a worsening security environment and to meet its commitments to NATO deterrence.
"We currently have the smallest navy in the history of the Bundeswehr, and at the same time the largest and most extensive set of tasks. So the navy must grow, and it will," he said.
"Given the current international security situation, especially with a view to the Baltic Sea, but above all the North Sea and the North Atlantic, this is of decisive importance, because with it we increase the deterrence of Germany and NATO," he said.
The planned naval base is expected to be a multibillion-euro investment, according to media reports. It is supposed to reach full operational readiness in 2030, and the site could eventually be home to up to 2,000 military and civilian personnel.

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.
The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before.
Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”.
Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening.
US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.
A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year.
But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away. The Ukrainian operation took about 18 months to plan.
Donald Trump said on Monday that the US had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were.
“There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said.
UK sources indicated they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran could orchestrate a fresh attack, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.
Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence nor Gloucestershire police commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.
RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target.
The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran destroyed a US Awacs radar plane on the tarmac during fighting in March. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.
Experts cautioned there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute.
Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged.
No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later.
Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited.
A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.

Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:11:42 UTC
22:11:42 KST

Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz?
Crude exports bypassing Hormuz surged in September, yet oil prices remain high. Could a secret fee be the reason?
Middle East oil exports have climbed back above levels seen before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, despite Tehran’s attempts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz and attack vessels.
Crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September, reaching between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day (bpd), according to provisional data from maritime tracking firm Kpler. Before the war, exports averaged about 18 million bpd.
This surge in oil exports from the region has so far largely been attributed to US ships shepherding tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with increasing ship-to-ship transfers that reduce the risks of being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones. Meanwhile, the fact that oil prices have remained high has been explained by analysts as the result of still-elevated insurance rates — driven by fears of Iranian attacks — and a market factoring in the possibility of a return to a hot war.
But a senior Kpler analyst last week offered a different explanation for the rise in oil exports at high prices. Gulf countries, she suggested, may be paying Iran to allow their oil through – potentially handing Tehran a significant portion of the value of the cargo.
Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas exports passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Does this explanation hold up, and what does it mean for the war and oil prices?
What did the Kpler analyst say?
Michelle Brohard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, recently said some countries could be paying Iran for passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
“I suspect there is a toll that’s being paid, which is giving these ships safe passage,” she said in an interview last week with energy analyst Rory Johnston.
“I also suspect that these countries know that this is unsustainable from a perspective of [the] US escorting [ships], and also unsustainable from them paying Iran 10 percent of their cargo, or 20 percent of their cargo,” she added.
“So you’re starting to see like what I would call like a race to get out as much as possible, as quickly as possible before the war restarts.”
The claim has not been independently verified, and Brohard presented it as speculation rather than a finding backed by evidence.
But as early as March, the shipping journal Lloyd’s List reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had already imposed a “toll booth” system to control vessel traffic through the strait.
The Trump administration, during the course of the war, has repeatedly said Iran will not be permitted to charge a toll under any potential agreement with Washington.
Closure of the strait has caused global fuel costs to soar and has tested agricultural sectors across the world.
What does traffic in the Hormuz look like?
Oil is increasingly getting out of the Middle East, marine trackers report.
In the last week of September, the seven-day average climbed above the roughly 18 million bpd recorded before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February – the first time since the conflict started.
Kpler said crude exports excluding Iran had also recovered to at least 16.5 million bpd as an average over September.
The pattern of increasing oil exports has continued into October. Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company on Saturday announced that it had transported two million barrels of crude on a very large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general said was the company’s first such operation in decades.
According to Kpler, “40 percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore”, with much of it flowing through Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates pipelines.
The export figures also include supplies moved through the Red Sea, which has become an increasingly important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Moreover, the Kpler figures exclude any vessels that may have crossed the key transit route with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
Iran, however, disputes suggestions that it has lost control of the waterway.
Senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi said on Sunday only three to four million bpd were travelling along a US-supervised route and described that amount as “negligible” compared with pre-war traffic.
Before the war erupted seven months ago, the strait routinely saw about 125 large commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships.
Where are oil prices right now?
Oil prices have eased marginally as exports from the Middle East recover. Last week, the Group of Seven countries also announced a decision to release 100 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves.
But crude prices remain significantly higher than pre-war levels. Brent crude was trading at about $101.59 a barrel on Monday, down 0.71 percent, while US West Texas Intermediate fell 1.2 percent to about $90.05.
“Despite exports from the region resurging, much will depend, longer-term, on the security of energy supplies,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, noting that the “situation is still tense”.
“The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, with the attack on another tanker on Sunday keeping worries bubbling about the potential for further disruption to supplies, particularly if shipping companies become increasingly reluctant to risk sending vessels through the crucial chokepoint.”
On Monday, an oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was instructed by the IRGC to turn back or risk being targeted, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) group that monitors shipping traffic.
Does the Kpler analyst’s claim hold weight?
Academic Abdul Khalique says while Kpler analyst Brohard’s speculation that a transit-fee arrangement has been put in place may be “plausible”, it is best described as an “informal security mechanism rather than a formal maritime levy”.
“No public proof confirms a systematic, state-run Iranian toll system,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.
He said the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) safeguards transit passage through international straits, “rendering formal tolls legally dubious”.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that Brohard’s suspected scenario was “in part” possible.
“Everything appears to be happening under the radar in the Middle East, from the US convoying ships to Iran quietly charging tolls,” he told Al Jazeera.
In September, the US government also imposed sanctions on a digital assets firm, BitBank, that it said had been used by Iran’s Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority — a body set up by the country’s government to collect fees for allowing the safe transit of vessels through the strait — to transfer money to Tehran.
However, Beauchamp said the biggest challenge for oil exports was now what he called the “problem of shipping”.
“The shuttle system in the Gulf is doing wonders in getting oil out, but it requires plenty of ships, and that has pushed freight rates higher while also reducing supply beyond the region itself,” he added.
According to Beauchamp, Asian buyers are having to find crude from further away too, “lengthening transit times”.
“Previously a supply story, this is now one about the underlying mechanics of shipping. While less exciting, it is arguably much more important and trickier to solve,” he said.
“Ships don’t get built overnight.”

Respondents were asked what feelings they had toward the authorities and were given a list of 12 feelings or emotions, from which they could choose up to three options (or name their own). The same poll was conducted in December 2025, allowing KIIS to show how opinions had changed over a 10-month period.
According to the poll results, the largest share of respondents reported disappointment with the authorities (44%, up from 36% in December 2025), followed by feelings of shame (33%, up from 20%). After that were anger (20%, up from 14%), hatred (14%, up from 11%) and indifference (12%, up from 7%).
At the same time, positive feelings or emotions among respondents remained stagnant. Hope was reported by 23% (unchanged), sympathy by 16% (unchanged), liking by 4% (unchanged) and pride by 7% (unchanged).
The nationwide poll was conducted on September 12-21, 2026, using telephone interviews based on a random sample of mobile numbers. It surveyed 1,002 adult citizens residing in territory controlled by Kiev.

HAIKOU /China/, October 5. /TASS/. The Hainan Island International Film Festival (HIIFF) has received a record number of applications from filmmakers from Russia and 132 other countries and regions, with more than 4,600 entries registered in 2026, the organizers said.
The HIIFF said on its WeChat page that China, Russia, Brazil, India, Iran and Spain were the most active in submitting applications. According to calculations, 824 applications were for feature films, 374 others for documentary films and another 3,434 for short films.
The organizers noted that the films submitted to the festival "span all five continents." They were shot in 135 languages and dialects.
Thus, the film screenings on China’s southern Hainan Island that traditionally take place in December will bring together the most diverse parts of the world "from the Caribbean coast to the inland areas of Central Asia, from the highlands of South America to the islands of the Atlantic Ocean." Roughly half of the submitted films come from Asia, with about a third from Europe. Around 9% of them were co-produced by two or more countries.
Diversity of genres
As for themes, the 2026 HIIFF will feature a wide variety of genres, including animation, documentary, historical, social, family, drama, detective, comedy, teen, fantasy, melodrama, sports and science fiction films.
About a quarter of the films are student works and a third are directorial debuts. More than 57% of the directors are from the 1990s generation or younger. People involved in the creation of the submitted films are representatives of many professions, including doctors, lawyers, engineers, teachers, journalists, dancers, athletes, scientists and video game developers.
The organizers noted that the festival’s films "maintain a high level in both quantity and overall quality." They will select "new works demonstrating an exploratory spirit and creative potential," and thanks to international exchange of experience, "the film festival’s global horizon will expand even further."
Sanya has hosted the annual film festival since December 2018 when the inaugural event took place. Co-organized by China Media Group and the People’s Government of Hainan Province, the major film screenings are considered one of China’s main film festivals, drawing industry stars from across the globe, including Russia. Notable participants have included world-famous actors and film directors such as Jackie Chan, Nicolas Cage, Johnny Depp, Nuri Bilge Ceylan and Sophie Marceau.

A Woman Exposed China’s Cat-Abuse Networks – and Paid a Terrible Price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:04:00 UTC
22:04:00 KST

In April, a 29-year-old woman traveling in Hainan swallowed a bottle of pills in a hotel room. Two days earlier, a fellow volunteer had told her that her national ID number, her parents’ home address, and her grandparents’ phone numbers were circulating online. Her offense, in the eyes of the people who posted her and her family’s private information, was reporting cat abusers to the police.
The woman goes by the alias Zhima. She had spent early 2026 investigating networks devoted to torturing and killing cats on camera, working with other volunteers to gather evidence, identify participants, and repeatedly bring their findings to police. What happened to her afterward illustrates a recurring problem in Chinese online governance: when the law lags behind a form of harm, citizens end up doing the investigative work themselves, and pay for it when the people they expose strike back.
Zhima’s involvement began almost by accident. According to Southern Metropolis Daily (Nandu), on January 4, she was in a pet-owners’ chat group when strangers flooded in, posted graphic videos of cats being mutilated, and renamed the group to advertise cat abuse. She reported it to Shanghai police on January 8, and the case was opened as an administrative matter.
That report drew her deeper into the world she had stumbled onto. Volunteers who track these networks describe a tiered structure: joining the most restricted core groups reportedly requires a “pledge of allegiance” (投名状) in the form of an unedited video of the applicant abusing a cat, a practice Chinese media have documented for years.
Zhima and fellow volunteers spent the following months identifying suspects and pushing police in multiple cities to act. One man she reported, a Jiangxi university student surnamed Qiu, kept posting abuse videos even after police opened a case against him.
Instead, it was Zhima who faced consequences. On April 8, a volunteer told Zhima her ID information had been leaked. Within days, her employer, education history, and her family’s identity numbers and addresses were circulating online, according to Nandu. Strangers were seen photographing her family’s home. The next day, in that Hainan hotel room, Zhima attempted suicide; she was found and rescued, Taiwan’s World Journal reported.
The harassment continued. Chat screenshots her father shared with Cover News showed vulgar doctored images, made using her profile photo, circulating in group chats. Rumors falsely claimed she had shared explicit photos of herself. Her father said the leaks did not come only from the cat-abuse networks: some appeared to originate from within the volunteer community itself, from people who had gained trust as fellow investigators before leaking information.
On July 17, overwhelmed by the renewed harassment, Zhima attempted suicide again and was hospitalized.
Accountability came slowly and unevenly. Qiu was placed under 10 days of administrative detention and expelled from his university on May 14, Tencent News reported. Shanghai police separately opened a criminal case against him on April 17 over the leak of Zhima’s personal information. But as of her father’s interview in July, whoever first obtained and circulated her family’s identity documents remained unidentified and unpunished.
Despite public demand for such a law following high-profile cases of animal abuse, China has no standalone national law against animal cruelty. Qian Yefang, a law professor at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, has told reporters that while existing statutes cover wildlife, livestock, and laboratory animals, companion animals like cats and dogs fall into a regulatory gap with no dedicated law of their own. Police are left relying on public order and cybersecurity statutes, an approach that works case by case but offers no consistent standard.
One local government tried to close that gap this year, then quickly backed away. In March, Sanming, in Fujian province, published a draft regulation that would have been China’s first local rule explicitly banning abuse and abandonment of “companion animals.” Less than a month later, before the public comment period ended, the draft was quietly taken down with no official explanation, Hong Kong’s The Standard reported.
Legal experts cited in that report noted a related weakness: even where rules exist, the absence of specific penalties in China’s Public Security Administration Punishments Law makes them hard to enforce.
The gap in animal-protection law that pushes accountability onto volunteer investigators, and another gap in the legal system offers little protection to those investigators once exposed. Some of the doxxing reportedly took place on Telegram, outside the platforms Chinese authorities can police directly, helping explain why the trail went cold.
China can punish individual animal abusers, case by case. Its personal-information protections offer little accountability for those who release others’ personal information out of spite. Until that changes, citizens like Zhima will keep shouldering investigative work the state has left undone, with far less protection than the people they investigate.

Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:03:09 UTC
22:03:09 KST

Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism?
Israel condemns the move as the party’s vote causes an uproar, including among party members.
The United Kingdom’s Green Party has voted to define Zionism as a form of racism, drawing condemnation from the Israeli government.
In a binding vote held at the party’s conference over the weekend, members voted to usher in the new definition as well as a series of other strongly pro-Palestine policies.
However, just as the resolution has drawn international criticism, it has also proved internally controversial with four of the party’s five members in parliament opposing it.
Israel on Monday banned party leader Zack Polanski from the country just a day before the politician faces a by-election as he runs in the London constituency that former Prime Minister Keir Starmer represented.
Zionism emerged as a political ideology in the late 19th century. It called for the creation of a Jewish homeland at a time of rising anti-Semitism and persecution of Jews in Europe. Theodore Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist considered the father of political Zionism, originally proposed an independent and colonial Jewish state in either Palestine or Argentina.
Here’s what we know about what the Greens have said:
What is the resolution?
The Greens endorsed the motion to equate Zionism with racism by a vote of 1,022 to 813.
In addition, the party restated its “commitment to Palestinian liberation” and called for the “establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”.
The party also recommitted to its support of Palestinians’ right of return as well as to the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement against Israel.
“The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians,” a Green Party statement said.
A significant number of party members, including four of its five MPs, were against parts of the resolution, exposing divisions within the party.
Codeputy leader Rachel Millward said in a post on X that while the party is committed to “stop the genocide”, the term Zionism means “different things to different people, … so I personally do not think the policy helps us do the work we all want to”.
Meanwhile, Polanski, who is Jewish and was away campaigning during the vote, told journalists afterwards that if Zionism equates to the displacement of Palestinians, “that is clearly racist.”
Polanski said he, however, did not support the reference to a single Palestinian state and external entities should not decide what a future state would look like.
How has Israel responded?
Israel has accused the party of legitimising “terrorism”, and senior officials equated it to anti-Semitism.
“The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on social media.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it would “deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the party was “racist”.
The Green Party has rejected equating criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism and reiterated its stance against “any form of discrimination or harassment”.
“We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people,” Polanski and other senior party members said in a statement on Sunday.
Has Zionism been equated to racism before?
Yes. In 1975, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution that “determines that Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”.
The vote was sponsored by the Soviet bloc and the Arab League. It passed after 72 countries, largely from the Middle East and Africa, voted for it. Israel and 34 other countries – chiefly from the West – were against it. Thirty-two other countries abstained.
Just a year before, at the 1974 General Assembly, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat had given his “olive branch” speech at the General Assembly.
About the same time, African countries opposing the apartheid regime in South Africa, which was increasingly allying with Israel, had resolved separately that the Israeli government was “racist” and both had an “imperialist origin.”
Also, in 1975, at the first international women’s conference, held in Mexico City, attendees decided there would be no international peace outside the “elimination of foreign occupation, Zionism, apartheid” and all other forms of “racial discrimination”.
However, the General Assembly vote proved controversial. Chaim Herzog, then-Israeli ambassador to the UN and later president, told the assembly in a speech that it was “based on hatred, falsehood and arrogance” and proceeded to rip up copies of the resolution in front of the audience.
The US too accused the UN of making “anti-Semitism international law”.
In December 1991, the US, under President George HW Bush, stepped up a campaign to revoke the resolution with Bush declaring at the UN that equating Zionism with racism “is to reject Israel itself” and to “challenge its right to exist”.
Israel also insisted it would not participate in the Madrid Peace Process to continue negotiations between Israel and Palestinian leaders if the resolution was not cancelled.
After much pressure from the US, an overwhelming majority of countries voted for its revocation – 111 to 25, including European and African countries.
Who else equates Zionism with racism?
Jewish Voice for Peace, the American anti-Zionist and pro-Palestinian advocacy group, has also named Zionism as a movement that creates a “racist hierarchy with European Jews at the top”.
In a February statement, the group reiterated its stance against what it called the “colonial ideology” of Zionism’s founders.
Similarly, in the United Kingdom, an employment tribunal in 2024 backed anti-Zionist activist and professor David Miller, who was earlier sacked from his post at the University of Bristol in 2021 for his views that the movement was “inherently racist”.

Rospotrebnadzor said tests found no pathogen linked to the deceased lab worker's work at the Irkutsk anti-plague institute, but more than 60 colleagues remained isolated inside the building and several hospitals stayed closed without explanation.
Russian health authorities said on Monday that a laboratory assistant at an anti-plague institute in Siberia who died last week did not have plague, even as quarantine restrictions remained in place across multiple hospitals in the region.
Daria Shipilova, 28, a staff member at the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, may have contracted pneumonic plague after a test tube broke in the laboratory, regional outlets reported, citing unnamed sources close to regional security services.
Authorities placed more than 60 institute employees under isolation inside the building from Friday.
A relative of one employee told Siberia.Realii they slept on the floor and chairs without beds, with food parcels passed through a checkpoint. No positive test results had emerged among staff by Saturday, the relative said.
Several Irkutsk hospitals were also placed under quarantine, including three city clinical hospitals, the Ivano-Matreninsky children's hospital and the city maternity hospital.
The Central District Hospital in Shelekhov, a satellite town where Shipilova lived, was also closed. Sources for People of Baikal said ambulances transporting contacts of Shipilova for examination had been escorted by FSB officers since Thursday.
A mask mandate was introduced at the Irkutsk Aluminium Plant in Shelekhov.
Russia's national health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said tests of biological material from Shipilova found no microorganisms linked to her professional activity and no accidents involving pathogenic micro-organisms had been detected at the institute.
Among those who had contact with her, two cases of COVID-19 and two rhinovirus infections were found; no other infectious agents were identified, it said.
Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said a special expert commission had concluded the cause of death was "pneumonia of unknown aetiology" and described the public health situation as stable.
"The situation remains under our control and under the control of experts," he said.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday told journalists to focus on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor and not on "various rumours, various speculations."
Rospotrebnadzor has not explained why dozens of staff were isolated and restrictions imposed on several hospitals simultaneously if test results were negative, according to Current Time.
Plague is a bacterial disease with several forms. Pneumonic plague, the most contagious, is transmitted between people and is fatal without early antibiotic treatment, according to the World Health Organization.
Russia has recorded isolated plague cases since 2014, most involving transmission from rodents during skinning, and has contained them successfully.

British Army tests troops in Drone Wars contest
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:00:47 BST
22:00:47 KST

The British Army has held its first Drone Wars competition, putting 23 teams through a series of tactical scenarios designed to test how soldiers use unmanned systems during combat rather than simply how well they can fly them, according to the British Army.
The competition was held at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst and brought together teams from units across the Army, including armoured, engineering and logistics formations. Each four-person team followed a patrol route containing six separate tasks, with soldiers assessed on both speed and accuracy while using several types of drone.
The scenarios included using a First Person View, or FPV, drone to strike a moving vehicle, flying another into a bunker, and interpreting video supplied by a separate drone operator before directing an FPV aircraft onto a target. Other tasks required teams to locate friendly troops and deliver medical supplies by drone, conduct aerial reconnaissance ahead of a simulated infantry assault, and identify an enemy position before calling in an artillery strike.
The competition was organised by 16 Air Assault Brigade, which leads the Army’s work on developing tactics for operating both with and against unmanned aircraft.
According to a British Army news update, Major Callum Jones of 1st Battalion The Royal Gurkha Rifles said: “The British Army is embracing drone technology as a key element of modern soldiering. Drones are no longer a specialist field, and every soldier needs to be aware of how to use drones and how to defend against drones used by the enemy.”
Teams were deliberately drawn from a broad range of formations rather than units specialising in unmanned aviation, reflecting the Army’s effort to distribute drone skills more widely across the force.
Jones added: “The teams taking part in this event are not just from combat units, with engineers and logistics troops competing as well, and that demonstrates how broad the adoption of drones is.”
The event placed particular emphasis on integrating drones with existing battlefield tasks. Rather than testing flying ability in isolation, soldiers had to use information gathered from unmanned aircraft to support reconnaissance, artillery and infantry activity.
“What we are testing is how soldiers use drones tactically, not how well they can fly them,” Jones said. “As well as striking targets, soldiers are using drones to gather information to inform other actions, such as calling in artillery or launching an infantry attack. As well as a competition, this is a chance to learn from each other and share skills.”
A combined team from the 2nd and 4th Battalions of The Ranger Regiment won the inaugural competition.
Among the soldiers taking part were Troopers Darel Anderson and Harvey Chilman, who operated as a hunter-killer pair. Anderson used a Skydio drone to locate targets before passing information to Chilman, who operated an FPV drone to conduct simulated strikes.
Anderson, who drives an Ares armoured personnel carrier with the Household Cavalry Regiment, said his role depended as much on observation and communication as piloting.
“I’ve been flying drones for two years, and we’re working hard as a unit to understand how best to use them. Drones help us see more of the battlefield, so we can strike the enemy before they get close enough to target us.”
He added: “My role is to find targets and guide an FPV pilot for their drone to make the strike. You need good observation skills to interpret what the drone is seeing, and then to clearly communicate that information to other soldiers. These are basic soldiering skills that we’re using in a different way with new technology.”
Chilman serves on Challenger 2 main battle tanks with the Queen’s Royal Hussars and was the first soldier in his regiment to qualify as an FPV pilot. He said he had accumulated more than 170 flying hours before the event.
“We’re integrating drones into how we operate under armour, and it’s been interesting to operate as dismounted troops on this event,” he said.
Chilman also compared FPV operations with tank gunnery, saying: “For me, there’s a similarity between flying drone missions and tank gunnery – both are about getting into the right position to line up on the target and hit it.”

Brain receptors for dopamine and insulin coordinate to control compulsive eating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:00:39 UTC
22:00:39 KST

A new study in mice reveals how receptors for dopamine and insulin act together in a specific brain region to regulate compulsive eating habits. The research, published in Molecular Psychiatry, highlights a cellular mechanism that stops animals from overconsuming sugary and fatty foods. These findings offer a biological explanation for why certain eating disorders and metabolic conditions frequently occur together.
Compulsive eating involves an intense drive to consume highly palatable foods regardless of negative health consequences. This behavior shares behavioral traits with substance addiction. Repeated overconsumption of foods high in fat and sugar can lead to obesity and metabolic diseases like diabetes.
Previous research linked both food cravings and metabolic disturbances to the reward pathways in the brain. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that helps the brain evaluate rewards and motivation. One specific docking station for this chemical, the dopamine D2 receptor, influences impulsivity and food addiction.
Another key component of metabolic health is insulin, a hormone that regulates blood sugar. The brain also contains insulin receptors, which help manage feeding behaviors. The precise relationship between these two receptor types during food consumption has remained largely unexplored.
The current research was led by Bokyeong Kim and Ja-Hyun Baik at Korea University, alongside a team of scientists from several South Korean institutions. The researchers focused on the central amygdala, a deep brain structure that processes emotions, motivation, and environmental cues. They noticed that dopamine D2 receptors and insulin receptors were often located on the exact same cells within this region.
The researchers first observed how a total lack of D2 receptors affects eating behavior. They used a small study of mice genetically engineered to lack these receptors entirely, comparing them to unaltered mice. Both groups were trained to press a lever to receive a sugary food pellet.
Once the animals learned this task, the researchers introduced a mild electric foot shock alongside the food reward. The unaltered mice stopped pressing the lever to avoid the punishment. The mice lacking D2 receptors kept pressing the active lever despite the shocks, exhibiting a compulsive drive for the sweet food.
To see if this effect was specific to the central amygdala, the team conducted a second experiment. They used targeted viral injections to remove D2 receptors only in the central amygdala of normal mice. When these mice faced the foot shock test, they also demonstrated heightened lever pressing for the sugary pellets.
Next, the team examined the relationship between dopamine and insulin receptors on these specific cells. They found that roughly 60 percent of the central amygdala neurons containing D2 receptors also carried insulin receptors. When the researchers removed the D2 receptors, the expression of insulin receptors in that brain region dropped by more than half.
The scientists then infused insulin or a dopamine-mimicking drug into the central amygdala of the mice. In unaltered mice, both chemicals triggered a process called phosphorylation, a chemical modification that activates the insulin receptors. In mice lacking D2 receptors, neither chemical activated the insulin receptors.
This demonstrated that dopamine receptors actively control insulin receptor function. The researchers traced this connection to a specific protein that normally inhibits insulin signaling. Activating the D2 receptors suppressed this inhibitory protein, which allowed the insulin receptors to function more freely.
To test if the insulin receptors themselves influence feeding, the researchers engineered a group of mice to lack insulin receptors exclusively on the neurons containing D2 receptors in the central amygdala. These mice were subjected to the lever-pressing task with foot shocks. Similar to the dopamine receptor mutants, these mice ignored the punishment and continued seeking the sweet food.
The researchers also examined the electrical properties of these brain cells using isolated brain tissue. They recorded the electrical activity of the central amygdala neurons in a controlled laboratory setting. Applying the dopamine-mimicking drug alone did not change the baseline electrical excitability of the cells.
However, when the researchers bathed the cells in a mixture of both insulin and the dopamine-mimicking drug, the neurons became highly electrically active. This indicated that the two types of receptors work together synergistically. The combined chemical signals drastically increased the electrical firing capacity of the specific brain cells.
The team then monitored the real-time activity of these specific brain cells in live animals. They used fiber photometry, a technique that employs tiny optic fibers to measure the calcium signals of active neurons. The researchers recorded the brain activity of mice while they consumed standard chow and while they ate a high-fat, high-sugar diet.
The activity of the central amygdala neurons containing D2 receptors decreased substantially when the mice ate the highly palatable food, while normal chow produced no change. Mice with lower neuron activity ate higher quantities of the rich food. When the researchers injected drugs to activate these receptors, the neuron activity stabilized, and the mice reduced their consumption of the sweet and fatty food.
To manipulate this circuit directly, the researchers utilized optogenetics. This method allows scientists to turn specific brain cells on or off using targeted flashes of light. In a small study of mice, they used light to silence the neurons containing D2 receptors in the central amygdala.
Silencing these cells caused the mice to eat vastly larger amounts of the sugary and fatty food. Conversely, using light to artificially activate these cells reduced the animals’ food intake.
However, there was a biological catch to this suppression. When the researchers blocked the insulin receptors with a chemical inhibitor, the light-induced activation of the D2 receptor-expressing neurons no longer stopped the mice from overeating. These neurons required functional insulin receptors to put the brakes on compulsive food consumption.
Finally, the scientists measured dopamine release in the central amygdala during extended access to the rich diet. Mice with reduced dopamine receptors in this region exhibited blunted dopamine release when they had constant access to the food. In a separate group given access to the rich food for only one hour a day, mice with reduced D2 receptors consumed roughly 64 percent of their daily calories during that hour, a binge-like eating pattern.
These experiments were conducted in mice, and animal models of feeding do not perfectly replicate human eating disorders or food addiction. The researchers used a lever-pressing task with foot shocks to model compulsivity, which measures the persistence of a habit despite physical punishment. This represents only one facet of human compulsive behavior, which involves complex emotional and psychological triggers.
Future studies will need to investigate exactly how this cellular machinery adapts over a longer lifespan. Researchers also hope to explore how these cells change after prolonged exposure to obesity-inducing diets. Understanding this receptor partnership might eventually guide new medical treatments that target both dopamine and insulin pathways to treat metabolic diseases and eating disorders simultaneously.
The study, “Dopamine D2 receptor modulation of insulin receptor signaling in the central amygdala: implications for compulsive-like eating behavior,” was authored by Bokyeong Kim, Minji Kim, Hyun-Yong Lee, Jung Hyun Pyo, Jihee Seo, Yoon Jeon, Ho Lee, Joung-Hun Kim, Seung Hyun Ahn, Sung Wook Chi, Je Kyung Seong, and Ja-Hyun Baik.

EXPLAINER – Closed or open? Tanker data tells a different story in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:00:08 UTC
22:00:08 KST

Iran’s insistence that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed contrasts with evidence of continuing oil shipments, highlighting the distinction between unrestricted navigation and cargoes moving through a disrupted export system.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Sunday that the waterway would not reopen until seven conditions under the Islamabad memorandum were fulfilled, according to state news agency IRNA.
He said US proposals had been conveyed through intermediaries and that Tehran would pursue diplomacy alongside military preparedness. IRNA’s account did not enumerate the seven conditions.
 
Regional exports recover through different exits
Kpler, an intelligence firm providing maritime data, using data available on Sept. 29, put non-Iranian crude and condensate exports from the Middle East Gulf region at a minimum of 16.5 million barrels per day over Sept. 1–28, matching their pre-war average.
Of that volume, 60%, or 9.9 million barrels per day, crossed Hormuz, while 23% loaded on the Gulf of Oman coast and 17% departed through the Red Sea.
Although some vessels continue passing the strait, confirmed flows remained more than a quarter below pre-war levels.
Country-specific figures show confirmed Saudi crude crossing the strait rose from 0.7 million barrels per day in August to 2.8 million in September.
Kpler also identified September regional crude exports of 3.2 million barrels per day from the UAE and 2.6 million from Iraq. These measure country-origin exports rather than ship passages, and the UAE total includes bypass routes.
Iranian crude crossings have remained near zero since July following the reimposition of the US blockade, according to Kpler.
Hormuz carried 20.9 million barrels per day of oil in the first half of 2025, according to the US Energy Information Administration. That historical figure covers crude and petroleum liquids, a broader category than Kpler’s September measure.
 
Windward finds a gap between visible ships and moving oil
Visible ship passages remain sharply below pre-war levels.
Maritime intelligence firm Windward’s Sept. 29 assessment recorded 55 AIS-visible transits during Sept. 16–23, about 94% below its pre-war benchmark of roughly 910 a week. However, ships operating with their Automatic Identification System transmitters switched off are missing from the visible count, so that percentage does not establish the decline in all actual passages.
Using satellite detections alongside Vortexa cargo data, Windward estimated that 26.72 million barrels of crude exited through Hormuz during Sept. 20–22.
That equates to approximately 8.9 million barrels per day across the three days, but Windward stressed that convoy movements represented peaks rather than a sustained export rate. Roughly two-thirds subsequently moved through ship-to-ship transfers.
Windward also reported 55 crude tanker loading events at Saudi Gulf ports in September, including 50 involving very large crude carriers, citing Vortexa data. Almost all loaded with AIS switched off. Those are loading events, rather than counts of distinct ships crossing Hormuz.
The figures illustrate why ship counts, cargo volumes and terminal activity need to be distinguished when assessing the strait’s status.
 
Tanker shuttles keep cargoes moving
A separate Kpler analysis published Sept. 21 described an expanding shuttle trade through Hormuz, with cargoes transferred between tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
Ships carry oil out of the Gulf before handing it to other vessels for onward transport. Fujairah and Sohar have become important transfer points, although their supporting services face capacity constraints.
Kpler warned that transfer activity is not equivalent to the volume crossing Hormuz: a cargo can undergo several transfers, causing the same barrels to appear repeatedly in transfer statistics.
 
Tracking can miss crossings or create false ones
Switching off transmitters can conceal real movements, while distorted positioning signals can generate apparent crossings that never occurred.
In a separate August study, Windward classified 393 of 642 logged Hormuz transits, or 61.2%, as false movements associated with GPS jamming.
Its verification method compared transit logs with a daily baseline of vessels actively transmitting AIS and excluded vessels operating without signals. The result therefore concerns errors in that tracking dataset rather than a complete count of all ships crossing Hormuz.
Kpler likewise uses satellite imagery, vessel draught changes, port information and destination checks to verify movements. Its recent export totals represent minimum confirmed volumes and can be revised as evidence arrives.
 
Bypass routes have physical limits
Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline carries crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea, while the UAE’s Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline connects to Fujairah outside Hormuz.
These routes reduce dependence on the strait, but pipeline capacity alone does not determine how much oil reaches buyers.
In a July assessment, Kpler identified Yanbu’s loading infrastructure as a constraint on further Saudi bypass exports, estimating sustainable terminal capacity at around 4.5 million to 5 million barrels per day. Further expansion would require improvements at the ports as well as along the pipelines.
 
Continuing flows come with logistical constraints
Maintaining shipments through shuttles and offshore transfers requires more vessels and handling.
Kpler estimated that shifting transfer operations from the Gulf of Oman to western India would extend round voyages from roughly 17 to 21 days. Using offshore Malaysia would increase them to about 38.5 days, reducing the transport capacity each tanker provides.

Astronomers say they’ve spotted the first miniature quasar pointed at Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Astronomers may have spotted a fun-sized version of one of the brightest and most mysterious cosmic objects. An elusive microblazar, a scaled-down form of the giant, ravenous black holes that haunt the distant universe, seems to have cropped up in our own Milky Way galaxy.
Even more intriguingly, the exotic object may explain the longstanding mystery of how some of the highest-energy particles in the universe came to be, researchers report in a forthcoming paper in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
Blazars are a particular form of quasars, supermassive black holes whose gravity pulls surrounding material into a whirling disk. In this extreme environment, the quasar flings superheated material out in a pair of jets like the axle of a wheel. A blazar is any quasar that points one of its jets approximately toward Earth.
Astronomers haven’t found quasars or blazars anywhere near Earth, but for nearly 35 years they have hunted for miniature ones in the Milky Way. Such a microquasar consists of a small black hole devouring a large star and sending jets of material spewing out into space. Because they are so much smaller than quasars, material falls into them faster than their massive counterparts.
“What takes days or weeks to change in a microblazar would take thousands of years in a supermassive blazar,” says astrophysicist Pedro Luque-Escamilla of the University of Jaén in Spain. “It’s a perfect scale model where we can watch a ‘cosmic movie’ in fast-forward.”
Luque-Escamilla and his colleague Josep Martí have spent two decades hunting for these hyperactive objects in archival telescope data, with little success. “We found many candidates in the past,” Martí says. “They turned out to be extragalactic objects,” full-sized and slower-changing.
The pair’s luck changed as they pored over a 1983 catalog produced by a Dutch-American spacecraft and spotted an object referred to as IRAS 18293−0941. When Martí and his colleague cross-referenced this catalog with modern observations by radio telescopes, they saw a small but very bright emission with additional light coming from only one side. That’s “the fingerprint of blazars,” Martí says.
The researchers assumed that, like their previous candidates, IRAS 18293−0941 was a full-sized blazar from beyond the Milky Way. But they were intrigued enough to keep investigating. The team ultimately used data from three different observatories on Earth and in space to pinpoint the location as inside our galaxy after all.
“The authors took a truly multi-wavelength approach, making use of all different types of astrophysical data from many telescopes,” says astrophysicist Alexandra Tetarenko of the University of Lethbridge in Canada, who was not involved in the new research. “This is not only what distinguishes this work from past claims on other microblazar candidates but also makes it far more convincing.”
The scientists also noticed that IRAS 18293−0941 was quite near a known patch of ultrahigh energy particles — particles with energy 100 times higher than the Large Hadron Collider can create, that scientists have struggled to explain what could juice them up to such extremes.
Martí and his colleagues argue this isn’t a coincidence: the “hotspot” marks where the microblazar’s invisible jet pointing away from Earth slams into a cloud of matter, acting as a massive particle accelerator. The team is already working to gather additional observations of the proposed hotspot.
The hotspot observations, as well as observations of the visible jet, should both give scientists a better understanding of the microblazar’s dramatic capacities, Luque-Escamilla says, as if the universe made a special particle accelerator just for scientists. “It’s like comparing a high-tech human laboratory to a supreme cosmic engine,” he says.

Is Kazakhstan the birthplace of apples? Here’s how the fruit spread across the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:59:22 UTC
21:59:22 KST

The part of the Tian Shan mountains that stretches from south-eastern Kazakhstan to Kyrgyzstan is home to the wild Sievers apple (Malus sieversii), the ancestor of every apple we know today. But how did it travel from Central Asia to orchards around the world?
The humble apple is one of the most affordable, widely grown and popular fruits in our diet. But have you ever wondered how this fruit travelled across continents and eventually landed on your table?
For years, the apples' story was shrouded in mystery. Thanks to genetic research, we now know that two wild apple species, Malus sieversii from Central Asia and Malus sylvestris from Europe, played key roles in the transformation of the apples.
Nestled in the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia, forests of Malus sieversii, or the wild Sievers apple, still thrive.
This species was named after the German botanist Johann August Carl Sievers, who wrote about the wild apple forests he encountered in the region in the 18th century.
"In the 1930s, scientist Nikolai Vavilov studied the forests of Central Asia and established that Kazakhstan is the home of the Sievers apple,” said Gulnara Sitbayeva, Doctor of Biological Sciences.
"In one study, scientists analysed more than 10,000 cultivated apple varieties. The fact that 46% of the samples contained genetic material from the Sievers apple provided evidence that it is a progenitor of modern cultivated apples," she added.
But how did the Sievers apple spread from Central Asia to the rest of the world?
Birds and animals first spread apple seeds across the Tian Shan mountain slopes. Later, people carried wild apples along the Silk Road.
Sievers apple blossom festival
Today, the blossoming of the Sievers apple is celebrated as one of Kazakhstan’s most breathtaking natural spectacles, often compared to Japan’s famous sakura blossom season.
Each spring, the Zhetisu region hosts a festival celebrating the Sievers apple's bloom.
A traditional yurt camp is set up for the festival, alongside exhibitions of national crafts and workshops. Visitors can watch traditional sports and take part in other national games.
What links Almaty and New York?
Unlike New York, known as 'The Big Apple', Almaty is a city whose very name is linked to the apple.
In Kazakh, "alma" means apple, and the name Almaty is traditionally associated with a place rich in apples. Here, the fruit is not just part of the city’s name, but a symbol of its spirit.
Almaty lies at the foot of the mountains, where wild apple trees have grown for centuries. Apple shapes and motifs appear in urban design, decorative details, sculptures, murals and public spaces throughout the city.
Over time, orchards appeared, along with varieties that became known far beyond the region. One of the most famous is Aport. The variety was developed through selective breeding and became known for its large fruit and distinctive aroma.
Ivan Sergeev and his family have been growing the legendary Aport for almost 20 years.
"The aroma of Aport apples is like French perfume. These apples also have very delicate skin, so we harvest the entire crop by hand," he said.
"My orchard also has Sievers apple trees. The main difference between Sievers and Aport is that Sievers is a wild apple, and the tree can live for 250 to 300 years. Aport trees live for around 40 to 70 years."
Today, apple orchards have also become places to visit. Around Almaty, people can find farms where they can come during the harvest season, walk through the orchards and pick apples straight from the trees.
Beyond that, Almaty hosts the annual Alma Fest, a major harvest festival where farmers bring apples from their orchards.
Here, apples can be seen and tasted in many different forms: fresh juice, dried apple slices, jams and other products. This year, more than 200 tonnes of apples were brought to the festival.

Germany risks being drawn into an armed conflict with Russia, the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service warned on Oct. 5, describing Moscow’s activities against Berlin and other NATO members as a growing “shadow war.”
“Germany is in danger of getting into an armed conflict with Russia,” Martin Jäger, president of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), said during a public hearing of the Bundestag’s Parliamentary Oversight Committee.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us,” Jäger said, pointing to intimidation attempts and other low-level hostile operations against NATO members. Such actions are “no longer an exception,” he warned.
Jäger said Russia is imposing the confrontation on Germany because Berlin supports Ukraine and the Baltic states, with the latter all being members of the EU and NATO.
“No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany” as Russia, Jäger said.
He described Germany as the “main obstacle to Russia’s hegemonic power projection in Europe” and therefore a target for Russian actions.
Russia is prepared to use force to achieve its goals, Jäger said, adding that this was behind the “increasingly aggressive activities” of Russian intelligence services in and against Germany.
Russian Authorities Won’t Confirm Pneumonic Plague Outbreak in Central Siberia
Russia’s ‘Shadow War’
The activities described by Jäger include sabotage, cyberattacks, airspace violations and disinformation campaigns.
Sinan Selen, head of Germany’s domestic intelligence service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, said Russia was also demonstrating a willingness to carry out sabotage and assassinations.
The threat spectrum includes disinformation and attempted attacks such as the recent incident at Halle/Leipzig Airport, where a drone equipped with explosives was found near Ukrainian cargo aircraft, Selen said.
German intelligence services have already succeeded in preventing some attacks, Selen said, but warned that the situation continues to deteriorate.
The officials’ warnings come as Germany and other NATO members have raised concerns about Russia’s ability to escalate its covert activities against European countries while continuing its war against Ukraine.
‘Supporting Ukraine is a core German interest’
Jäger said continued support for Ukraine remains a “core German interest” and warned against assuming that an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine would end the broader confrontation with Moscow.
“It is a great illusion to think that the conflict with Russia will be over when the war in Ukraine ends,” he said.
Jäger also warned that Russia’s war against Ukraine had entered a “new, very dangerous phase,” marked by increasingly brutal attacks since the summer.
German intelligence and military officials have previously warned that Russia could eventually pose a direct military threat to NATO.
Russia has repeatedly denied plans to attack NATO countries and has accused the alliance of escalating tensions with Moscow.
The Bundestag is also considering legislation that would expand the powers of Germany’s domestic and foreign intelligence services, allowing them in certain cases to take operational action, including efforts to stop cyberattacks or disrupt weapons projects.

International train connection from Groningen to Leer returns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:57:48 UTC
21:57:48 KST

International train connection from Groningen to Leer returns
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
After almost 11 years, people can again travel by train from Groningen to the German city of Leer.
Services were suspended in 2015 after a cargo ship crashed into the Friesenbrücke, the rail bridge over the Ems on the German side of the border.
At Groningen central station, travelers lined up at 5:30am to catch the first train in over a decade.
The rebuilt Friesenbrücke is 335 metres long and is Europe’s largest lift-swing rail bridge. Its 145-metre central section lifts and turns to let ships pass.
The new bridge was opened in 2024, but needed additional testing before rail service could resume.
Regional Director Gerrit de Groot of Arriva, which maintains the rail service, told RTV Noord he was “delighted” with the reopening. “It is fantastic that, as a regional carrier, we are making international transport possible in this way. It is a wonderful moment,” he said.
The journey takes around 90 minutes. Arriva expects that they will see peaks of travel during the holiday season when people want to visit the Christmas markets across the border.

Former Hungarian Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto on Monday denied allegations related to an investment by Chinese automaker BYD.
Szijjarto’s remarks come in the wake of an investigation by a national security committee, which decided in September of this year to clarify the circumstances surrounding Szijjarto’s working relationship with BYD as well as potential risks to national security.

After coordinating government support, public infrastructure and diplomatic assistance for BYD as the minister responsible for foreign direct investment in the previous government, Szijjarto was hired by BYD as head of external relations and new business development.
Vehicle assembly at the plant in Szeged is scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. Initial test production had already begun in early 2026.
Completion was originally scheduled for late 2025. However, establishing local supply chains and adapting to European regulations took longer than expected.
The project involves an investment of approximately $3 billion and is expected to create up to 10,000 jobs.
The factory is a strategic milestone for the company in avoiding additional EU tariffs on electric vehicles produced in China.
In addition to the new factory, BYD has already relocated its European headquarters to Budapest.

Pyongyang’s Ukraine Gamble: What Kim Jong Un Bought With North Korean Blood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

Four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and one of the war’s stranger subplots may be its most consequential: soldiers from an Asian country with no direct stake in the conflict, and no public declaration of belligerency, are dying by the thousands on European soil, thousands of kilometers from home.
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 troops to Russia’s Kursk region, and absorbed roughly 6,000 casualties based on the intelligence estimates of South Korea and the United Kingdom. According to Ukrainian officials, North Korea may be asked to contribute tens of thousands more troops. What has Kim Jong Un bought with that blood?
North Korea’s calculus was never primarily about Ukraine, a country with which it has no border, no quarrel, and little history. It was about what Pyongyang could extract from a desperate Russia. By mid-2024, Moscow badly needed manpower and ammunition and had few partners left willing to supply either.
In June 2024, Kim and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Pyongyang that included a mutual defense clause, the first of its kind for North Korea since the Cold War. Troop deployments followed within months. In return, analysts at institutions from the Council on Foreign Relations to Chatham House point to a fairly consistent list of North Korean gains: cash payments estimated in the billions of dollars, food and energy supplies for an economy that chronically struggles to feed and fuel itself, and, most significantly for Pyongyang’s long-term ambitions, technology transfers that would otherwise have been unthinkable. Russia has reportedly supplied North Korea with air defense systems, older but still capable Su-27 and MiG-29 fighters, and, more sensitively, technical assistance connected to satellite launches and naval reactor technology for submarines.
Money and hardware, however, may be less important than what North Korean soldiers are learning. South Korea’s National Intelligence Service has assessed that despite considerable losses, North Korea’s military has gained something it could not otherwise buy: live experience of drone warfare, electronic warfare, and modern combined-arms combat, together with direct exposure to Russian battlefield tactics and equipment. North Korean soldiers rotated home from the front have reportedly gone on to serve as instructors, seeding lessons from Kursk through the wider Korean People’s Army, a pattern documented in detail by 38 North. For a military that has not fought a large-scale war since 1953, that is an intelligence windfall no amount of cash could easily replicate.
There is also a domestic and dynastic logic. Framing the deployment as solidarity with Russia – Kim has publicly praised soldiers for fighting “for the fraternal Russian people” – lets Pyongyang dress a mercenary arrangement in the language of ideological alliance, useful for internal propaganda about North Korea’s rising international stature.
Before 2022, Russia and North Korea were not especially close. Moscow had, at various points, supported U.N. sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs. The war has inverted that relationship entirely. North Korea has gone from a marginal, sanctioned pariah state to a battlefield-tested security partner that Russia now treats as an equal in a way China never has. The mutual defense treaty, the flow of advanced military technology, and Putin’s own visit to Pyongyang in 2024 all mark a qualitative shift from transactional arms sales to what Foreign Affairs described as a long-term strategic and ideological partnership.
That shift has complicated, rather than strengthened, the informal China-Russia-North Korea alignment that Western officials sometimes describe (misleadingly, most regional specialists argue) as a unified axis.
Beijing has watched Pyongyang’s deepening entanglement with Moscow with open unease, as detailed in a Foundation for Strategic Research assessment of the evolving triangle. China has no formal say over what Russia transfers to North Korea, and reports of sensitive technology moving from Moscow to Pyongyang without Beijing’s knowledge have reportedly fed distrust between the two communist neighbors.
Kim, for his part, has gained new leverage over Beijing: with Moscow now willing to treat him as a peer and to backfill North Korea’s economic and military needs, Kim is less dependent on Chinese patronage than at any point in decades, and better positioned to resist Chinese pressure to rein in his nuclear program, a dynamic the Council on Foreign Relations has flagged as a growing headache for Beijing.
China is wary of jeopardizing its own relationship with Europe, and visibly uncomfortable with a North Korea-Russia partnership it can neither control nor fully endorse. Still, Beijing has responded with something closer to silence than alarm, avoiding direct criticism of either Moscow or Pyongyang. The result, as Modern Diplomacy put it, is less a trilateral alliance than a triangle of powers with overlapping but not identical interests, in which Pyongyang has quietly gained room to maneuver at Beijing’s expense.
Militarily, the record of North Korean troops in Kursk is mixed. In their first months of deployment, North Korean units suffered catastrophic losses. By some estimates, 40 percent of the initial 11,000-strong contingent was killed or too badly wounded to fight within three months. U.S. officials described North Korean assaults on entrenched Ukrainian positions as “human wave tactics” that were, in Washington’s assessment, largely ineffective. Soldiers were used as bait to draw out Ukrainian drone operators, and troops sometimes took their own lives rather than risk capture, a reflection of the harsh consequences reportedly awaiting the families of anyone who surrenders.
Yet the “cannon fodder” framing, embraced early on by Ukrainian and American officials, has been challenged by military analysts who argue it understates what is actually happening. Researchers at RAND have cautioned that dismissing North Korean troops as unsophisticated fanatics risks recycling old stereotypes about Asian communist militaries. Many of the deployed units come from North Korea’s elite special operations Storm Corps – troops that, by multiple Ukrainian frontline accounts, proved highly motivated, resilient under fire, and increasingly adept at countering the first-person-view drones that have come to define this war. Ukrainian intelligence has also reported the arrival of dedicated North Korean drone units and reconnaissance specialists, a more technical role than the infantry-assault image that dominated early coverage.
Materially, the more significant North Korean contribution to Russia’s war effort may not be soldiers at all but ammunition: Ukraine’s military intelligence chief estimated that North Korean-supplied artillery shells and missiles have accounted for roughly half of what Russian forces fire at the front. Troop deployments helped Russia recover Kursk territory that Ukraine had seized in its August 2024 incursion, but North Korean units have so far been confined largely to Russian soil, with reports suggesting Moscow has been reluctant, at least officially, to send them into Ukraine proper. That distinction lets both governments continue denying direct North Korean involvement in the invasion itself, even as evidence of attacks on Ukrainian border communities accumulates.
Whether North Korean troops have changed the trajectory of the war is, in the end, a narrower question than whether the deployment has changed North Korea. On the battlefield, the contribution has been real but bounded: enough manpower and ammunition to matter at the margins in one contested region, not enough to shift the war’s fundamental stalemate. Off the battlefield, the returns for Pyongyang look considerably larger: modernized air defenses, combat-tested doctrine, hard currency, food, and fuel, and a Kremlin now invested in North Korea’s survival and expansion for reasons of its own.
Four years ago, North Korea was a country largely locked out of great power politics, dependent on China and periodically threatened with further isolation over its nuclear program. Today it has a mutual defense treaty with Russia and North Korean soldiers are gaining experience in modern warfare on European battlefields. For a regime that has always measured success in decades rather than news cycles, that may be the trade Kim intended to make all along.
