Pedro Sánchez has lost control of the narrative. So he's calling an election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:55:47 UTC
21:55:47 KST

On the back foot since the Ceuta crisis, Sánchez is taking his biggest gamble yet with a snap election. He thrives on main-character energy, but the momentum has shifted and reality is catching up with his carefully crafted image.
Pedro Sánchez has lost control of the narrative – and that’s why he’s calling a snap election.
In eight years in office, the Spanish prime minister has survived every obstacle thrown his way, proving himself as cunning as he is ruthless. He has reshaped Spanish politics, transformed his party and remade the left.
He is the ultimate political operator. But that only works if you control the conversation.
Since the Ceuta crisis broke – a stampede that saw more than 70,000 migrants cross into the enclave in what became the worst national security breach in modern Spanish history – Sánchez has lost his grip on what the Spanish political world calls el relato.
Literally, el relato means “the story”.
But it often has little to do with reality. It is about perception: a carefully constructed narrative that the Spanish premier has shifted, reshaped and flipped whenever necessary to stay ahead.
Time after time, he has outmanoeuvred his rivals, proving himself the better politician.
Along the way, he has cast himself as the last progressive standing in a reactionary Europe increasingly willing to bend to Trump and close its borders. The one man standing against the internationale réactionnaire – led by the US president, the Muskian tech lords and the new digital oligarchy.
And as he announced a snap election for November 29, Sánchez made sure Spain heard his message: throughout his time in office, he had fought “very powerful elites”.
The problem is that the story is wearing thin. Reality has come crashing in.
Ceuta remains unresolved. Migrants are stranded. Minors remain unaccompanied. And Sánchez’s humane migration policy is no longer resonating with a public increasingly viewing the crisis as a matter of national security.
His government is paralysed – incapable of passing a budget, presiding over a fractious coalition and increasingly at the mercy of Catalan separatists. The Spanish Socialists have also lost large swathes of regional government, testament to the difficulties Sánchez faces at home even as his standing abroad has soared.
In politics, the details matter – and they can be hard to see from Brussels, where national agendas are often swept up in the larger currents of European politics.
Sánchez is the last progressive leader around the European Council table, while the Spanish delegation leads the progressive faction in the European Parliament. That has given him an outsized role in Europe compared with his weaker position at home.
And he has played that role very well.
But in Spain, the picture is far more complicated.
His left-wing partners, Sumar and Podemos, have all but disappeared – which, for Sánchez, is not necessarily bad news. The weaker the space to his left, the greater the dominance of his Socialist Party. But it also complicates any future coalition: fewer partners mean fewer seats.
Meanwhile, his conservative rivals are tapping into a broader European zeitgeist: a hardening stance on migration and growing resistance to progressive social attitudes.
A tie-up between the mainstream conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox would no longer come as a shock. Similar alliances are already taking shape across Europe. And if the PP was once hesitant, few doubt it would enter government with Vox if that were the price of power come November.
Sánchez has shown he can take punches, but only if he can dictate the terms.
With a snap vote, he hopes to push Ceuta aside, mobilise his base around social justice and return to his winning formula: either he wins, or Spain ends up on the wrong side of history.
A touch populist? Certainly. But Sánchez has always been one. To win, he has to.
The timing is no coincidence. He wants to harness growing public anger over the housing crisis, turning public squares into spaces of mass protest over an issue affecting millions of Spaniards.
Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman evicted from her apartment last month, became a symbol of that movement – a spark for a wider mobilisation that Sánchez now sees as his last chance to change el relato.
It’s smart. It’s bold. It’s Sánchez being Sánchez.
Back in 2016, as a much younger reporter, I covered one of the most hallucinatory episodes I had encountered in politics.
A far less well-known and successful Sánchez had been forced out as leader of the Socialist Party after a series of poor election results. What followed was an extraordinary psychodrama, broadcast live on television, complete with accusations of mutiny, fake ballots and fraud.
In the end, Sánchez announced he would step aside.
I remember telling one of my colleagues: este tío va a volver.
This guy will be back.
And he was.
What followed was one of the most spectacular comebacks in modern Spanish political history. He became prime minister after a successful vote of no confidence, survived crisis after crisis and, with Trump’s return, found another opportunity to position himself on the European stage.
Sánchez has always defied political gravity – as long as he is running the show.
And that is why this crisis feels different.
For the first time, the story is being written for him, not by him. The momentum is with the right.
For a man who has spent his political career making himself the main protagonist, that is uncharted territory.

Citing unnamed security sources, Walla said around 3,000 US military personnel are currently deployed across Israel, including troops operating air defense systems as well as pilots, support crews and logistics personnel.
It said additional US forces and aircraft are expected to arrive in the coming weeks as Washington strengthens its military presence in the region.
The outlet said the Israeli military is continuing preparations for a possible new confrontation with Iran or a rapid deterioration in regional tensions, while maintaining close coordination with the US Central Command (CENTCOM).
The reports come as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready to continue pursuing diplomacy to reach what he called a “fair solution.”
Iran presented seven conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators during meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in late September concerning the opening of the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump later said Washington had not accepted the Iranian conditions.

Meloni wants to register her voice as a trademark to protect against deepfakes
Kyiv • UNN
The Prime Minister of Italy has filed an application with EUIPO to register her voice as a trademark. The document contains a four-second recording of her saying, "I - Giorgia Meloni."
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has filed an application with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) to register her voice as a trademark, in order to protect herself from artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The application, dated October 5 and confirmed by her office, contains a four-second audio recording in which Meloni repeats the phrase "I am Giorgia Meloni" twice in Italian.
"Io sono Giorgia" ("I am Giorgia") is the title of the prime minister’s 2021 autobiography, reflecting a famous statement Meloni made at a political rally in 2019, which was even turned into a disco track.
As the publication notes, altered images of Meloni have repeatedly been circulated online in recent years, sometimes being presented as genuine. One of them, in particular, depicted her on a bed wearing underwear.
Meloni condemned such material as part of campaigns to spread disinformation and attacks on people, urging users to verify content before sharing it. She stated that she could protect herself, but that many other people do not have that opportunity.
The EUIPO application is currently under review.
However, as Italian media point out, even if approved, the registration itself will not prohibit the use of her voice in AI-generated deepfakes, but it could create additional legal obstacles for those attempting to reproduce it.
In 2024, Meloni filed a civil lawsuit against a man from Sardinia who is accused of creating and publishing pornographic deepfakes featuring her face online. The case is still pending before an Italian court.

Zelensky could celebrate fresh EU accession breakthrough in Brussels next week, source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:54:34 UTC
21:54:34 KST

Zelensky could celebrate fresh EU accession breakthrough in Brussels next week, source says
President Volodymyr Zelensky will attend a summit of the EU's 27 national leaders on Oct. 15 if Kyiv is able to unlock the next step in its EU accession process before then, a Ukrainian official confirmed to the Kyiv Independent.
The Ukrainian parliament is expected to pass a law on Oct. 12 that will bolster the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority, which Hungary has required of Kyiv in order for it to drop its veto on advancing Ukraine's EU accession process.
If that happens, and the EU therefore unlocks the next two so-called enlargement clusters, then Zelensky will attend the European Council summit, a Ukrainian official familiar with the president's agenda told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine has opened two of six enlargement clusters so far, listing the reforms that Kyiv must implement to be fully aligned with EU rules and thus able to join the bloc.
The first two clusters opened in June and July, respectively, but further progress has been held back after months of Ukraine failing to pass the ethnic minorities reform, despite agreeing with Budapest in July to do so.
"It is possible that we would open the next two clusters ... next week," the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said at an Oct. 5 press conference in Brussels.
"Of course, the member states will have to speed up the procedure," Kos said.
The steps taken between the passage of the law and the holding of an intergovernmental conference (IGC), which marks the opening of an enlargement cluster, are essentially just formalities, but they take some time.
Normally, IGCs are held on the margins of a meeting of European ministers called the General Affairs Council. The next one of those is scheduled to take place in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
However, that would mean the bloc has to carry out the formalities overnight, so it could be that the IGCs instead take place on Oct. 14, one day before EU leaders are set to meet.
If all goes smoothly, Ukraine is expected to open clusters two and three, broad areas of economic reform.
That would leave still to open clusters four and five, which cover more sectoral areas of the economy where some countries still have reservations, for example, due to the size and competitiveness of Ukraine's agricultural and transport sectors.
But Kos remained hopeful that all six clusters would be unlocked by the end of the year.
If Zelensky attends the Oct. 15 European Council, he will have several topics to weigh in on.
The Summit is expected to discuss the future of EU enlargement, with a key set of proposals to be published on Oct. 6, as well as Ukraine's war effort, and wider European defense and security.
It will also touch on negotiations over the EU's 2028-2034 budget, which includes a separate line for Ukraine support, currently set at 89 billion euros ($100 billion).

Russian Authorities Won’t Confirm Pneumonic Plague Outbreak in Central Siberia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:54:25 UTC
21:54:25 KST

On Monday, authorities in central Russia expanded quarantine measures and restrictions to public movement following a probable outbreak of the highly-lethal disease pneumonic plague and the death of a health worker from exposure, according to local news reports.
In the town of Shelekhov, in Russia’s Irkutsk region near Lake Baikal, both patients and medical personnel in the district hospital’s inpatient department were placed under complete lockdown. The hospital suspended admissions and discharges, according to a video report by the regional news outlet Liudi Baikal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Reports by local media that Russian authorities had mobilized police, security services, and even military units to contain the outbreak were contradicted over the weekend by officials, who insisted the situation was under control and that there was no conclusive evidence that the disease, known in medieval times as the Black Death, had appeared in the Irkutsk region.
According to Liudi Baikal and other regional news platforms, medical researcher Darya Shipilova, a laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, died in late September after breaking a test tube containing the most dangerous strain of the plague disease, called the pneumonic plague, while at work. She became ill and was hospitalized at Shelekhov Hospital, near the city of Irkutsk, and died during the night on Friday, Oct. 2, according to the news report.
‘We’re Staying’: European Embassies Defy Russia’s Warning to Leave Kyiv
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and depending on means of infection, can develop different strains in victims. Bubonic plague is moderately contagious and usually transferred by flea and rodent bites. The disease affects a victim’s lymph nodes with usually high mortality if untreated. The normal treatment of all plague forms is common antibiotics.
Pneumonic plague – the strain that killed Shipilova according to reports - is highly contagious and usually transferred by respiratory droplets from an animal or person infected with Yersinia pestis. The disease attacks a victim’s lungs with usually extremely high mortality. The less common and less contagious clinical plague form Septicemic plague infects a person via blood contamination and is also highly lethal if untreated.
As Shipilova’s health deteriorated, authorities reportedly tracked down at least 90 people believed to have come into contact with her and transported them by ambulance to an Irkutsk quarantine facility. By Thursday, all were being held at a treatment center formerly used for COVID-19 patients. Local media reports claimed that Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) played a leading role in locating and detaining potential contacts.
By Monday, around 200 people believed to have had potential contact with Shipilova were being held at the quarantine center, according to local media reports. Quarantine measures were also imposed on several Irkutsk medical facilities, including hospitals No. 1, No. 3, and No. 10, the Ivano-Matryoninskaya Children’s Hospital, a maternity hospital, and the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, where Shipilova reportedly contracted the infection, Liudi Baikal reported.
However, Russia’s national health authority, Rospotrebnadzor, pushed back against the reports on Sunday. In its first public statement, issued about 60 hours after Shipilova’s death, the agency said she had died from pneumonia “of an undetermined origin” and denied that any pathogenic microorganisms had been accidentally released at the anti-plague institute. A follow-up statement carried by the state news agency TASS further stated that plague was not responsible for her death.
Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev, in comments published by the local news platform Ir.City.Ru, said that the “epidemiological situation in Irkutsk and Shelekhov is stable” and that there was no evidence of even a single plague infection.
Yet, in comments to RFE/RL, a state department spokesman said the disease outbreak was possibly plague: “We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia. We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” adding that they “urge Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
Governor Igor Kobzev’s messaging was undermined by comments from local officials. On Friday, Maxim Modin, head of the town of Shelekhov, told local media that the hospital’s former COVID-19 ward had been repurposed as a quarantine center to isolate people who may have been exposed to the “especially dangerous infection” that had reportedly caused Shipilova’s death.
On Saturday, Alexey Tsydenov, governor of the neighboring Republic of Buryatia, told reporters that a confirmed case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region had resulted in the death of a female researcher. He said the infection stemmed from a laboratory accident rather than exposure in Buryatia. A sparsely populated region adjacent to Mongolia, with large swaths of wild territory, Buryatia is a known source of the plague bacterium that is present in some rodent populations, especially marmonts.
On Monday, according to the independent Russian news agency Astra, residents of Shelekhov reported that masks and gloves had been distributed in kindergartens, while in neighboring Irkutsk, a citywide community cleanup was canceled.
Motorists traveling along the R-258 highway between Shelekhov and Irkutsk reported that staff at fuel stations were wearing protective masks under orders from health authorities. However, according to Exilenova+ on Monday, mask-wearing was not mandatory.

Who holds the keys to Europe’s emergency oil reserves?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:51:48 UTC
21:51:48 KST

National leaders command the valves, the International Energy Agency coordinates global oil volumes, while the European Commission is a vital central switchboard.
Behind Europe’s bureaucratic machinery sits a vast insurance policy for a rainy day: millions of tonnes of crude oil, diesel and other fuels held in reserve for a major supply crisis.
But as governments prepare to tap those emergency stocks again, who actually holds the keys? Can Brussels order oil onto the market, or does the decision lie with national capitals?
The answer involves a complicated mix of EU rules, national sovereignty and international coordination.
The European Commission sets the rules and monitors whether countries are keeping enough oil in reserve. But the stocks themselves remain under national control, while major international releases are coordinated through the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA).
"The decision to release and the organisation to release is with the IEA. We stand ready to convene an oil coordination group or, as needed, an EU energy security task force meeting to further coordinate amongst us and assess the situation further," a Commission spokesperson told reporters on Monday.
The comments followed the G7’s announcement that recent G7 announcement that 100 million barrels of oil are expected to be released over the next four months, with diesel stocks frontloaded to help curb soaring prices and fears of supply disruptions.
Exactly how much diesel and crude oil will be released remains unclear. Ahead of the official announcement, EU diplomats told Euronews the release would be evenly split between the two.
The IEA did not reply to a Euronews request for comment before publication.
In March, European countries contributed 107.5 million barrels to a 400-million-barrel IEA emergency release after the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted global markets – around a quarter of the total, according to IEA data.
Of those 107.5 million barrels, 32.7 million came from state-owned emergency stocks, with the remainder drawn from mandatory industry stocks.
The Americas contributed 195.8 million barrels and the Asia-Pacific region 108.6 million barrels.
Europe’s reserves are also far from evenly distributed, particularly when it comes to refined products such as diesel and gasoil.
The 90-day shield
So how much oil does Europe actually keep for an emergency?
Under EU rules, every member state must maintain emergency stocks equivalent to at least 90 days of net imports or 61 days of domestic consumption.
But there is no giant European oil reserve sitting somewhere under the control of Brussels.
Instead, the stocks are held nationally, either directly by governments, through specialised national stockholding agencies or as mandatory reserves held by industry.
And their distribution creates some important centres of gravity.
Of the EU’s roughly 39 million metric tonnes of emergency gasoil and diesel – equivalent to around 290 million barrels – France and Germany account for about 35%. Smaller countries, including Belgium and Malta, also keep some of their emergency stocks in France and Germany.
That raises another question: if the oil is stored in one country but belongs to another, who gets to turn on the taps?
Ultimately, the crucial decisions remain in national capitals. Brussels can set the rules, monitor stocks and coordinate governments, but the Commission cannot simply order millions of barrels onto the market.
The reserves remain under national control, meaning governments decide when their stocks are released and how their contribution is made.
For a major international intervention, however, another player enters the picture.
IEA to the rescue
A single country releasing oil may do little to calm a global supply crisis. That is where the IEA comes in.
The Paris-based agency coordinates emergency releases among its member countries, allowing governments to put large volumes of oil onto the market at roughly the same time.
“It’s for the IEA to manage the prices and then for the member states participating in a possible release to determine a level of transparency when it comes to concrete products subject to the release,” the Commission spokesperson said.
If a supply shock is severe enough, the IEA’s governing board can agree a coordinated collective action, with its 32 member countries contributing to the emergency response.
The mechanism has already been triggered twice since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, putting emergency reserves – normally an obscure corner of energy policy – at the centre of governments’ efforts to contain the fallout from the conflict.
The next question is how Europe will deliver its share.
A meeting bringing together the Commission, EU governments and oil industry representatives, originally due on October 15, will “likely be early next week”, an EU official said on condition of anonymity.
The aim is to assess how EU countries plan to meet their IEA commitments to release diesel within the next 20 days, as well as their plans for the remaining four months, the official said.

Germany facing potential ‘violent conflict’ with Russia – spy chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Germany facing potential ‘violent conflict’ with Russia – spy chief
Germany could become “embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia,” the country’s foreign intelligence chief has warned, claiming that a mysterious drone incident at Leipzig airport is an example of the “real and imminent” threat posed by Moscow.
Speaking to lawmakers at a parliamentary hearing on Monday, Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) head Martin Jaeger declared that “the confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension.”
“Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia – the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example,” he continued, referring to the discovery of an explosive-laden drone next to a Ukrainian transport plane at the city’s airport in August.
German authorities have not released any evidence linking the incident to Russia, and Moscow has described the episode as a “hastily cobbled-together provocation” serving “exclusively the aims of Kiev and the militaristic wing of the European political class.” It is “obvious that Germany is pursuing a further course of escalation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last month.
Nevertheless, Jaeger claimed that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that there is a “real and imminent” threat of attacks against targets in Germany. “No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany,” he added.
Jaeger is one of dozens of Western political, military, and media figures to accuse Russia of waging a “hybrid war” or “shadow war” against Europe in recent weeks. The accusations are, by their nature, impossible to verify, and Moscow has written them off as pretexts to deepen Western involvement in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, justify military spending hikes, and expand surveillance and persecution of domestic opponents.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has explicitly and without evidence described the country’s most popular political party, the right-wing AfD, as “Russia-backed.” Martina Rosenberg, the head of Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD), alluded to this claim during Monday’s briefing, telling lawmakers that the country is “threatened by diverse dangers from both outside and within.”
Jaeger, Rosenberg, and domestic intelligence (BfV) chief Sinan Selen all praised Merz’s recent efforts to grant the BND greater offensive powers, and called for further strengthening of the MAD and BfV’s capabilities.
Despite their allegations of “hybrid war,” European leaders have repeatedly stressed that they do not believe Russia to be planning any actual attacks on NATO territory. The BND has seen “no indication of an imminent large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory,” Jaeger added on Monday.
Amid an unprecedented escalation in the West’s rhetoric toward Russia, RT is tracking the statements, accusations, and threats in our ongoing ‘Escalation Watch’ special. Keep an eye on it here as we sort the facts from the propaganda and debunk the psyops in real time.

Minister seeks inquiry into benefit fines for non-Dutch surnames
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:50:29 UTC
21:50:29 KST

Minister seeks inquiry into benefit fines for non-Dutch surnames
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
People with non-Dutch surnames get fined more often and more harshly by the benefits agency UWV’s fraud unit, according to an internal analysis the agency’s board has had since December, AD and current affairs programme EenVandaag reported on Monday.
Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief said he wants the claims thoroughly investigated and the UWV to take appropriate measures. “Your surname or background must play no role at all in whether you get a fine or how high that fine is,” he told AD.
The two outlets based their joint investigation on confidential documents and interviews with more than 10 current and former staff, including managers, at the fraud unit, which employs around 600 people.
The analysis divided 1,682 case files into Dutch and non-Dutch surnames. In the region covering Alkmaar, Amsterdam and Utrecht, 44% of the people in the files had a non-Dutch surname, but they received 74% of the fines.
In the southern district, which includes Heerlen and Eindhoven, the figures were 36% and 71%. Because their fines were also higher, that group paid 98% of the total there, although fewer files were examined in that district.
The authors recommended further research, but this was never carried out, according to EenVandaag.
Country of origin
A 2015 work instruction for detecting fake employment contracts also listed the applicant’s “country of origin” as a possible risk characteristic. When a court asked about the document, the UWV denied in an official letter that it used risk characteristics at all, AD said.
After 2020, a thin line was drawn through the criterion, but it remained legible until at least mid-2026. “I have never seen such clear evidence that it happens as in this document,” lawyer Ayhan Kara, who obtained the uncensored version, told AD. He is considering filing a criminal complaint with the public prosecution service.
The UWV says the criterion was never used, was officially removed in 2020 and has now been taken out of all documents.
Current and former staff also described racist remarks in the fraud unit. Managers born outside the Netherlands were referred to as the “Arab League”, and during a case meeting someone said the solution was “to kick all Moroccans out of the country”.
Political reaction
MPs from both coalition and opposition parties reacted angrily. Stephan Neijenhuis of the centrist D66 told AD there was possibly “institutional racism” at the agency.
Mariëtte Patijn of the opposition party Pro said the revelations reminded her of the childcare benefits scandal, in which thousands of parents were wrongly labelled fraudsters by the tax office. “It is not systems selecting wrongly by accident, it is the UWV’s own people,” she told AD.
Dogukan Ergin of the left-wing, multicultural party Denk said it fitted a pattern. “First it was the tax office, then [student finance agency] DUO, now the UWV again: if you have a migration background, you are distrusted and dealt with more harshly,” he said.
According to AD, the minister was only informed of the analysis after the paper put questions to the ministry. The UWV told broadcaster NOS it had informed the ministry in January.
Apologies issued 
Abdeluheb Choho, who became the UWV’s chairman on September 1, said in a statement that it was reprehensible that some staff still made discriminatory remarks to one another. “We apologise to everyone who feels discriminated against or has been treated in a racist way,” he said.
However, the agency said in a statement that the analysis was not scientific research, and that its data and method were not suitable for drawing conclusions about structural unequal treatment. A separate external study into equal treatment is due later this year.
The UWV has asked anyone who has experienced discrimination by or within the agency to report it to integriteit@uwv.nl.
In 2024, a reader who took part in a DutchNews survey on discrimination said UWV staff had told them to go back to their own country when they applied for unemployment benefits.

The force arrested Andrew on his 66th birthday on Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office, related to his links to the late U.S. sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Andrew was released the same day after hours of police questioning, but remained under investigation. He has denied all wrongdoing in his associations with the disgraced American financier.
His shock arrest prompted Charles to issue a statement insisting "the law must take its course."
The Daily Telegraph reported the legal challenge late on Sunday. The newspaper noted it was the first time a member of Britain's royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
It said Andrew's legal team wanted to examine whether the search warrants granted by a judge at London's Old Bailey court — formally known as the Central Criminal Court — were lawful.
Andrew's legal team did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
Andrew's effort to have court "quash search warrants"
The judiciary's press office said "the case concerns an application by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor for a judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February 2026."
If the review were to throw out the warrants, it would potentially deprive prosecutors handling the case of any evidence discovered during the searches of the former prince's homes.
Andrew's arrest and the police searches marked a new low for the royal, who was stripped of his royal titles last year and ousted from his Windsor home over his Epstein connections. The government has even mulled passing a law to remove him from the royal line of succession.
Scandal has engulfed the king's younger brother since one of Epstein's accusers, Virginia Giuffre, claimed in her posthumous memoirs that she had been trafficked three times to have sex with Andrew when she was a teenager. Giuffre died last year by suicide at the age of 41.
The former prince has repeatedly denied the claims. He settled a U.S. civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability.
The Thames Valley Police probe follows new revelations from documents relating to the American financier released by the United States earlier this year, including emails in which Andrew appeared to share potentially confidential information with him.
"Investigation into misconduct in public office continues"
In one November 2010 email released by the U.S. government, Andrew appeared to share with the U.S. financier reports on his visit to several Asian countries. Two years earlier, Epstein had been convicted in the United States of procuring a child for prostitution.
At least nine British police forces confirmed they were looking into claims — some related to Andrew — stemming from the batch of some 3 million Epstein files released by the U.S. authorities in January.
However, the Thames Valley investigation appears to be the most advanced. Its officers, who swooped on the remote Sandringham royal estate in eastern England to detain Andrew, searched his home there and his former Royal Lodge residence in Windsor, west of London.
The raid in Windsor lasted six days.
In response to Andrew's legal challenge, Thames Valley Police said in a statement that its "investigation into misconduct in public office continues."
"We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained," it added. "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."

US warships have ‘fled’ Strait of Hormuz – IRGC
Iran has forced the US fleet to retreat more than 1,000 km from its borders, leaving no American warships in the Strait of Hormuz or surrounding waters, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander claims.
Rear Admiral Ali Fadavi made the remarks in a televised interview, Iran’s Press TV reported on Monday, amid competing claims by Washington and Tehran over control of the critical shipping route, through which around one-fifth of global oil and natural gas supplies passed before the conflict.
“The Americans fled and moved more than 1,000 km away from our borders. This was not their choice; it was due to the authority of the Islamic Republic and the authority of the IRGC Ground Force,” he said.
Fadavi claimed that no US vessels remain in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, Sea of Oman, or northern Indian Ocean, and described US warships as “100 percent vulnerable” to Iranian attacks.
He insisted that the strait remains under Iranian control and warned that ships using the US-supervised southern route could be targeted.
On Monday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a tanker near Oman complied with an IRGC instruction to turn back or risk attack.
The US, meanwhile, continues to enforce its naval blockade of Iranian ports. US Central Command said last week that it redirected 125 commercial vessels since July to ensure compliance.
The standoff has persisted despite indirect negotiations. Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday that Hormuz would not reopen until Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions.
Iran’s seven-day proposal offers to restore passage and resume nuclear negotiations in exchange for lifting the blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, and releasing frozen assets.
US President Donald Trump rejected the terms and threatened to “annihilate” Iran if talks fail. Axios and the Wall Street Journal report that major US combat operations could resume after the midterm election in November.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Iran is committed to diplomacy but is ready to defend against another attack.

====================================================================================================

What does the Brussels 2027 budget mean for me?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:47:11 UTC
21:47:11 KST

The Brussels government has reached an agreement on the Brussels Region’s 2027 budget. Under the agreement, PM Boris Dilliès (Francophone liberal MR) has pledged to reduce the deficit to 719 million euros.
The agreement follows two days of difficult budget among members of the Brussels coalition. “We started with a deficit of more than 1.3 billion euros. Today, we have halved that to 719 million euros,” Dilliès explained in the Brussels Parliament on Monday. “Everyone has had to make an effort.” According to Dilliès, a significant step towards a balanced budget by 2029 has now been taken.
“The ambition to return to a balanced budget must also be reflected in the way we govern,” Dilliès said with Gallic flourish. “Because returning to a state of reasonableness does not just mean restoring our finances. It also means changing what needs to be changed. It means removing obstacles and putting public administration back at the service of results.”
Government administration to play its part
The Brussels Government aims to reduce the number of civil servants and deploy them more efficiently. It hopes this will save 74 million euros annually on staff costs and a further 39 million euros on operating costs.
Vacancies will no longer be filled automatically. Staff will be deployed in a more targeted manner through internal mobility.
The reform of government departments will continue. As a result, even more departments will be merged.
The Brussels PM’s official residence on Brussels Park – a classical-style townhouse – is to be sold (although the sale is not scheduled until the next term of office). In due course, the PM will move to the building that houses the Brussels government.
Mobility and transport
The price of tickets on Brussels local transport MIVB will not be increased, even though revenue is lower than forecast. The government is offsetting this by cutting the transport company’s operating expenditure.
Brussels road tax is being reformed: from the second half of 2027, there will be an exemption for motorists driving a small city car or a zero-emission vehicle (ZEV).
The Baljuw and Vleurgat tunnels are due to be renovated from 2029. There are also plans to redesign the Louisalaan.
The Brussels government hopes to make significant progress on tram line 15, between the Belgicalaan and Brussels North Station, from next year.
Taxes
Supplementary personal income tax is being reduced by 1 percentage point.
The BeHome allowance, which is intended to offset part of the higher property tax for homeowners living in Brussels, is being doubled.
Health, welfare and poverty
Over 1 million euros extra will be allocated to prevention, including cancer screening and a heatwave plan.
The Region is allocating 1.8 million euros for the accommodation of homeless families and is providing 6.3 million euros for the prevention of addiction. “Our ambition is clear,” says Dilliès. “No child in Brussels should have to sleep on the streets. We are reserving 185 shelter places for families and, through the collective autonomous shelter system, have nearly 900 places spread across 13 locations.”
Brussels municipalities and Brussels local social services centres will receive an additional 15 million euros in 2027.
Unlike in Flanders, there is no change to the cost of service vouchers, often used to play cleaners and odd jobs workers, or child benefit (contrary to what the Flemish Government decided earlier).
Safety and cleanliness
Next year, the Region will allocate 5 million euros to improve safety and cleanliness in public spaces around stations.
Brussels is appointing its own drugs commissioner, who will work in collaboration with the national drugs commissioner.
10 million euros have been earmarked to strengthen the Brussels fire services. A total of 92 new recruits will be taken on by 2027.
A new headquarters will also be built for the fire service. The Region will allocate 20 million euros for this in 2027.
120 underground refuse containers will be installed by the end of the legislative term.
Regional cleanliness brigades will also be set up in collaboration with the municipalities and police districts. “Anti-social behaviour will be monitored more strictly and fined,” warns Dilliès.
Housing
Interest-free energy and renovation loans are to be introduced for Brussels families. These are intended to replace the Renolution grants and be better targeted at people who genuinely need this support.
Employment
Next year, the government will save 55 million euros on employment policy; by 2029, this figure will rise to 75 million euros. Brussels employment agency Actiris must “focus on its core tasks”, says Dilliès. Above all, this means having more staff on the ground and helping citizens more quickly.
At the same time, the Activa scheme in Brussels (worth 27 million euros) is being scrapped. This was a subsidy for employers who took on long-term jobseekers.
Companies creating jobs at the Audi, Solvay, Schaarbeek-Vorming and TIR warehouse and customs clearance sites can, however, count on lower social security contributions. Schaarbeek Vorming is the massive former railway marshalling yard that stretches from Schaarbeek to Haren (City of Brussels).
From 2027, Brussels will invest 2 million euros a year in the Bilingualism Master Plan. The aim is to improve knowledge of Dutch and French within the administration and in hospitals.

Israel 'progressively asphyxiating' Gaza, continues genocide: Doctors Without Borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:46:53 UTC
21:46:53 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Monday that Israel was continuing its genocide in Gaza and was "progressively asphyxiating" the region, urging governments to take immediate action.
In a statement, MSF said the conditions for the people's survival were being "systematically destroyed" through sustained violence, "deliberate" blockade of essential supplies and the destruction of healtcare as well as infrastructure.
"In the past year, the physical trapping of people in Gaza has been made increasingly definitive by the establishment of Israel’s Yellow Line," the French medical charity said. 
Recalling that it was originally presented as temporary, MSF noted that the line is now reinforced by military positions, berms and ongoing demolitions while it has continued to move west, "squeezing people into a smaller and smaller area." 
MSF said people risk being shot by Israeli forces when approaching the area, while its teams continue to treat those wounded by gunfire nearby.
"The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map," said Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza. "It has become a mechanism of encirclement and ethnic cleansing, while cutting communities off from the infrastructure, healthcare, water and other essentials they need to survive."
MSF said violence was not only confined to the areas around the "Yellow Line," reporting having treated over 1,200 cases of violent trauma across Gaza in June and July alone.
It recalled that MSF teams treated more than 200,000 trauma cases over the past three years while Israel's military offensive killed over 74,000 people.
The organization said overcrowding and limited access to clean water, sanitation, shelter and healthcare are contributing to the spread of disease. Its teams also treated over 11,000 skin disease cases and 1,500 chickenpox cases in June and July.
It also pointed to the dramatic deterioration of access to healthcare over the past three years as hospitals run out of basic supplies and patients unable to access essential medicines and treatment.
"Restrictions on essential supplies, such as engine oil and spare parts, are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances and water systems running, with generators already breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced," the statement said.
It added that the crisis is not limited to Gaza as violent occupier attacks, military operation and raids on homes, displacements as well as home demolitions escalated rapidly across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
“It will take generations to recover from the harm that has already been done over the past three years, and in the preceding decades, while the excruciating consequences of Israel's ongoing genocide are still being felt every day,” Bazerolle said.
She warned that Israel carried out destruction, displacement and deprivation "with impunity" while such practices became "normalised."
"Governments must act now to ensure Israel stops the destruction and killing, prevents ethnic cleansing, and stops denying Palestinians the means of survival," Bazerolle added.

Soviet TV Hypnotist Anatoly Kashpirovsky Dies at 87
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:46:45 UTC
21:46:45 KST

Anatoly Kashpirovsky, the Soviet-era hypnotist whose televised “healing sessions” drew enormous audiences in the late 1980s, died on Saturday in Moscow at the age of 87.
“Anatoly Mikhailovich passed away from advanced cancer that had spread to his lungs and brain,” Kashpirovsky’s nephew Yury Mamayev told state media.
“There was multiple organ failure, meaning that the affected organs simply stopped functioning as a result of the cancer,” the TASS news agency quoted Mamayev as saying.
A representative said earlier that Kashpirovsky suffered “sudden” cardiac arrest following a sharp drop in blood pressure.
Born in Soviet Ukraine in 1939, Kashpirovsky graduated from the Vinnitsa Medical Institute in 1962 and spent 25 years working as a psychiatrist in a regional psychiatric hospital.
He became a household name in the 1980s as public interest in the occult grew across the country during Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s perestroika reforms.
Soviet Central Television started airing his six-part program, “Health Sessions of Psychotherapist Anatoly Kashpirovsky,” in October 1989. Its audience was estimated at more than 200 million people.
Following the Soviet collapse, Kashpirovsky entered politics, winning a seat in Russia’s first State Duma in 1993 on the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR)’s ticket.
In June 1995, he took part in negotiations during the Budyonnovsk hospital hostage crisis, convincing Chechen rebel warlord Shamil Basayev to release some of the 1,500 hostages but failing to persuade him to surrender.
Later in life, Kashpirovsky clashed with health regulators over allegations that he was practicing folk medicine illegally. While the Russian Academy of Sciences dismissed his methods as “absolute pseudoscience,” Kashpirovsky defended his medical credentials and won multiple defamation lawsuits.
He maintained a loyal following, touring and hosting “healing sessions” on YouTube until March this year.
His funeral will be held on Thursday, Oct. 8, at Moscow’s Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, on the anniversary of his six-part television program’s premiere.

EU suspends Namibian meat imports over FMD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:46:17 CST
21:46:17 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) has temporarily suspended the entry of fresh meat and certain processed meat products from Namibia's previously foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)-free zone following an outbreak of the highly contagious livestock disease.
In a statement issued on Monday, EU Ambassador to Namibia Ana Beatriz Martins said the measure covers fresh meat from cattle, sheep and goats, as well as relevant farmed and wild ungulates and certain processed meat products such as biltong and jerky.
The restrictions follow Namibia's confirmation of an FMD outbreak on Sept. 23 on a commercial farm in the Karasburg State Veterinary District in the Kharas Region, which resulted in the World Organization for Animal Health suspending Namibia's FMD-free status, effective Sept. 22.
Martins said consignments of fresh ungulate meat certified by Namibian authorities before Sept. 23 should be permitted to enter the EU during a 90-day period from that date, subject to decisions by EU member states' border control posts.
Processed meat that has undergone the most stringent risk-mitigating treatment prescribed under EU legislation remains eligible for entry, she said.
The restrictions are precautionary animal-health measures consistent with international standards and do not affect Namibia's preferential trade access under the EU-Southern African Development Community Economic Partnership Agreement, according to Martins.
"The EU will continue to assess the epidemiological situation in close cooperation with Namibia and stands ready to review the measures as animal-health conditions allow," Martins said.
Namibian authorities have introduced measures to control the movement of cloven-hoofed animals and suspended exports of affected animals and products following confirmation of the outbreak. ■

Having attended two China-focused forums in Cairo this September, Saad said China's development model and cooperation frameworks offer Global South nations a real pathway to build their own capabilities.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:45:44 CST
21:45:44 KST

NADI, Fiji, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Fijian government on Monday launched a five-year plan to participate in international carbon markets under the Paris Agreement.
The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan (2026-2030), launched on the opening day of the preparatory meeting for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (Pre-COP31) in Nadi, is estimated to cost 5.2 million Fijian dollars (about 2.3 million U.S. dollars). It aims to enable Fiji to complete its first international carbon trade by 2030.
The plan outlines five-year measures covering regulation, technical capacity, institutional arrangements and market infrastructure. It also provides a framework for the government to seek financial and technical support from development partners, donors and potential carbon buyers.
International carbon markets allow countries to generate and trade verified emissions reductions. Fiji said participation in such markets could help mobilize additional climate finance for renewable energy, sustainable forestry, waste management, resilient livelihoods and the protection of natural ecosystems.
Fijian Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu said carbon markets should deliver benefits beyond carbon trading and ensure that local communities and resource owners benefit from related investments.
Bulitavu added that the country needs to put in place the necessary systems, safeguards and partnerships to participate in international carbon markets while protecting its national interests. ■

Nepal halts search-and-rescue phase after Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
20:45:43 CST
21:45:43 KST

KATHMANDU, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Nepal has decided to halt the search-and-rescue phase launched following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Aug. 26, as hopes of finding survivors among those missing have faded 40 days after the disaster, the Prime Minister's Secretariat said on Monday.
A meeting of the National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, chaired by Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Monday, directed the concerned agencies to accelerate reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts while continuing only essential search operations.
The Prime Minister's Secretariat said the decision was taken based on recommendations from district security committees, district disaster management committees, the Executive Committee of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), and findings from field inspections.
As many as 1,455 people have been confirmed dead and 5,285 remain missing as of Oct. 3 following the deadly floods, according to the NDRRMA.
The meeting also decided to propose a budget of 559.18 billion Nepalese rupees (3.62 billion U.S. dollars) to the Ministry of Finance for plans and programs aimed at reconstructing and rehabilitating areas affected by the floods and other monsoon-related disasters.
During the meeting, Shah said disaster management efforts had been carried out through coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments, adding that reconstruction and rehabilitation would also proceed through the same mechanism. ■

20:45:40 CST
21:45:40 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Hambantota International Port (HIP) in Sri Lanka has surpassed 1 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in cumulative container throughput since new quay cranes were commissioned in 2025, said the port's operator, Hambantota International Port Group, in a Monday press release.
HIP handled 428,036 TEUs in 2025, while throughput reached 574,196 TEUs so far in 2026, taking the combined total to 1,002,232 TEUs.
The port is expanding its container-handling infrastructure to sustain growth, adding new equipment, boosting berth capacity, enlarging container-yard space and expanding reefer facilities, alongside upgrades to accommodate larger container vessels.
HIP is targeting an annual container-handling capacity of 2 million TEUs following the planned expansion. ■

Japan, Australia boost economic security ties with finance dialogue
The two countries’ finance ministers will meet regularly to promote cooperation across a broad range of economic themes
Japan and Australia have agreed to establish an annual finance ministers’ dialogue aimed at deepening cooperation in financial and economic policy, as well as strengthening bilateral collaboration on economic security.
Under a memorandum of understanding signed on Monday that is effective for five years, the two countries’ finance ministers will meet regularly to promote cooperation across a broad range of economic themes.
“Recognising that Japan and Australia’s economic and security futures are deeply connected, the Finance Ministerial Dialogue will enhance bilateral cooperation on economic security matters,” the memorandum said.
“We will work together to promote stable economic growth in the Indo-Pacific region and around the world,” Japan’s finance chief Satsuki Katayama said during the signing ceremony.

Russia ready to supply everything needed for Africa’s food security — energy minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:45:31 UTC
21:45:31 KST

MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. Russia is ready to supply everything needed to ensure food security in Africa, including animal vaccines and fertilizers, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev told RT following his visit to several African countries.
"Ensuring food security is, of course, very important for all African countries. And we are ready to supply everything they need from Russia. But in addition to food, we also supply animal vaccines and mineral fertilizers. Most importantly, we are promoting new agricultural technologies. Our task is to ensure that each country can eventually reach a level of agricultural development that will allow it to meet most of its needs through domestic production," he said.
According to Tsivilev, Russia takes a similar approach to mineral extraction, as mining in these countries was often carried out in a "predatory" manner, with almost everything being exported and little left for the state. "Our task is to transfer technologies and teach people how to work in a way that, first, takes into account natural conditions and meets all environmental requirements and, of course, ultimately ensures that products with the highest possible added value are exported. We are ready to provide our technologies for this purpose and train specialists who will work with them," he said.
Tsivilev also expressed confidence that Africa could become an exporter of agricultural products in many areas if the work is properly organized. "But that is still ahead. For now, the main task is to ensure food security in each country," the minister stressed.

Şahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
 The Sudanese army said Monday that it shot down an FH-95 strategic drone in West Kordofan state, the sixth of the same type it has downed in the Kordofan region in less than a month.
In a brief statement, the army said its air defenses downed the “hostile drone” northwest of Al-Khuway in West Kordofan on Monday morning.
According to an Anadolu tally based on military statements, the army previously announced that it had shot down five FH-95 drones in North Kordofan, the latest on Sept. 27.

Sudanese authorities have accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of carrying out drone attacks on civilian facilities. The RSF generally does not comment on such accusations and says it works to protect civilians.
The army and RSF have been fighting since April 2023 over disagreements about integrating the paramilitary group into the military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Chirag Paswan's UP gamble: Why PM Modi's 'Hanuman' is flexing his muscle against allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:44:46 UTC
21:44:46 KST

LJP (Ram Vilas) chief Chirag Paswan is set to contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, with the party preparing for all 403 seats.
NEW DELHI: Chirag Paswan once described himself as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's "Hanuman". Six years later, the LJP (Ram Vilas) chief offered another approach of his politics: "I can stand up to my government ... I am in the alliance but I am not the BJP."This distinction becomes relevant as he prepares to take his party into the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly election. LJP(RV) has announced that it will contest the polls and is preparing for all 403 constituencies, while leaving open whether it will eventually contest alone or as part of an alliance.
We want this to take the form of a legal right for the youth. Wherever exams are cancelled, students should receive reimbursement for their travel expenses, arrangements for their accommodation, and provisions for their food. We have firmly presented this stance of the party on the floor of the House as well.
Chirag Paswan
The UP move comes after a significant change in Chirag Paswan's political position. In 2020, the undivided LJP broke with the NDA in Bihar, contested 135 seats and targeted Nitish Kumar's JD(U), while maintaining its support for PM Modi. Its slogan captured the strategy: "Modi se bair nahi, Nitish teri khair nahi." The party won only one seat, but its 5.66% vote share had a measurable impact on the results.Since then, LJP(RV) has moved from being a marginal alliance partner to a more consequential NDA component.
It won all five Lok Sabha seats it contested in Bihar in 2024, giving Chirag Paswan a 100% strike rate, and in the 2025 assembly election it contested 29 seats under the NDA arrangement and won 19. The BJP and JD(U) contested 101 seats each, while LJP(RV) secured 29.That progression provides the context for the 403-seat announcement. Chirag Paswan now has five Lok Sabha MPs, 19 MLAs in Bihar and a Union cabinet position. The question is whether that political weight can be extended beyond Bihar.
The 403-seat gamble
The latest phase of the UP push took shape in September, when Paswan launched his party's youth outreach in Prayagraj. At the "Youth Bole Toh" programme, he spoke about education, employment, skills and greater youth participation in politics, and announced plans for a National Youth Commission.On September 28, he made the electoral plan explicit: "There is no doubt that LJP (Ram Vilas) will contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections."The following day, he said the response in Prayagraj had strengthened his confidence in the UP plan. LJP(RV) MP Rajesh Verma subsequently said the party was preparing for all 403 seats, while making clear that the eventual alliance arrangement would be decided later.
Chirag Paswan on law and order in Bihar.
The 2020 flashback
The 2020 Bihar assembly election was the debut test of Chirag Paswan's leadership. His father, Ram Vilas Paswan, had just died a few days ago.The LJP won only one seat but emerged as a significant factor in 54 constituencies where its vote total was greater than the victory margin. In 25 seats where JD(U) finished second, LJP's vote exceeded the winning margin. Chirag was explicit about the objective, saying after the election: "My main idea in the election was to make the BJP stronger. I am happy with the impact I have had in this election."The BJP finished with 74 seats in that election, ahead of JD(U)'s 43 for the first time. The episode demonstrated that LJP did not need to win seats itself to affect the relative strength of its larger alliance partner.The 2025 Bihar election showed the other side of the equation. LJP(RV) was no longer operating as a spoiler outside the alliance. It contested 29 seats as an NDA partner and won 19, converting its electoral relevance into representation inside the alliance.UP could now test both models: LJP(RV) as an alliance partner with an electoral base of its own, and LJP(RV) as a potential vote-splitter in constituencies where even a few thousand votes can decide the outcome.
The Dalit arithmetic
The potential constituency is significant, but far from straightforward.The BSP won no seats in the 2024 Lok Sabha election in UP and polled around 9.4%. At the same time, the SP expanded its support among Dalit voters as part of its broader PDA coalition. A Lokniti-CSDS post-poll analysis showed a sharp difference between Jatav and non-Jatav Dalit voting patterns, with the BSP retaining much stronger support among Jatavs than among non-Jatav Dalits.For Chirag Paswan, the challenge is therefore larger than taking the Paswan identity from Bihar to UP. Pasis, Valmikis, Khatiks and other non-Jatav communities have distinct political histories and local calculations. Whether LJP(RV) can persuade sections of these voters that it is a credible political vehicle will determine whether its UP expansion produces votes or merely an organisational footprint.The impact could also vary by constituency. A modest LJP(RV) vote could matter in a close BJP-SP contest if it draws disproportionately from one side's potential support base. But unlike Bihar in 2020, there is no single obvious target. The BJP, SP, BSP and Congress have overlapping social coalitions, making the direction of any vote transfer harder to predict.
Why UP and why now?
The UP expansion also fits Paswan's attempt to establish LJP(RV) beyond its Bihar base. The party has already demonstrated that it can operate outside the state: in the 2023 Nagaland assembly election, it contested 16 seats, won two and finished runner-up in eight, securing more than 8.6% of the vote.But UP is on a different scale. A credible organisation here would give Chiag Paswan a political presence in the country's largest state and potentially strengthen his position in future NDA negotiations.
Chirag Paswan asked CEC to address recent SIR controversy.
His recent conduct suggests that maintaining an independent identity is part of that calculation. He has criticised the Bihar government's handling of law and order while remaining part of the NDA, and questioned the Election Commission over concerns surrounding SIR before welcoming its subsequent clarification.
The UP experiment, therefore, would not simply be about how many seats LJP(RV) could win. It would be abot whether Chirag Paswan can build an influence outside Bihar to make his party a more consequential NDA partner, while retaining the political independence he summed up in his own words: "I am in the alliance but I am not the BJP."

Rosatom says 2 Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant facilities damaged in overnight attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:44:25 UTC
21:44:25 KST

Kanyshai Butun
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom said Monday that two facilities at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) were damaged in an overnight attack.
Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said a laboratory building located about 200 meters (656 feet) from the plant’s fourth and fifth reactors and a radioactive waste processing facility were damaged.
“The roofs were damaged in both cases, but there is no threat to nuclear safety,” Likhachev said, according to Russian state media Tass.
He said plant workers continued to maintain the facility’s main equipment in safe condition despite ongoing attacks.
Rosatom informed the International Atomic Energy Agency of the need for repairs and called for a temporary ceasefire to allow the work, Likhachev said.
“In normal circumstances, transformer repair is a routine task; today, however, it is an operation that entails a direct risk to the lives of our repair crews. We have no right to put our people at risk,” he said, adding that the parameters of a temporary localized truce at the plant were being coordinated.
The situation around the ZNPP, Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and one of the world’s 10 largest, remains tense amid persistent concerns over a potential nuclear disaster, as Moscow and Kyiv frequently accuse each other of carrying out attacks around the facility.
Since Sept. 1, 2022, IAEA personnel have been stationed at the plant, which has been under Russian control since March 2022.

Ivan Kunev, executive director of Avtomagistrali EAD, has resigned for personal reasons and was not pressured to step down, Regional Development Minister Ivan Shishkov told reporters in Vratsa.
The resignation was confirmed by Shishkov after the Institute for Road Safety announced earlier that Kunev had submitted it on Friday. Shishkov said Kunev had not personally informed him about the decision.
"I learned that the director had resigned for personal reasons; he did not inform me personally. There was no problem," Shishkov said, adding that he did not want to interfere in Kunev's private life.
The minister said there had been no dispute between them over the replacement of guardrails and rejected the claim that the issue had prompted Kunev's departure.
"He did not inform me; he resigned for personal reasons. I do not wish to intrude on anyone's private life. He certainly did not leave because of the 'guardrail' issue. There was no conflict between us on that subject; I had simply asked 'Avtomagistrali' to begin replacing guardrails in a transparent manner," Shishkov said.
He added that the company could achieve transparency by selecting a lower-cost product, which he said was not owned by the people currently being discussed in connection with purchases of private jets, flights and other matters.
Shishkov also said there had been no conflict or other problem between him and Kunev and called for the former director's personal reasons to be respected.
"The work is indeed very active and intense; everyone makes their own assessment. I hope the issue isn't something more serious - something personal. I wish him a speedy resolution to his problems," Shishkov added.
The Institute for Road Safety had said Kunev resigned because he disagreed with the approach to replacing guardrails and with Shishkov's actions, a claim the regional minister rejected.
Kunev was appointed in mid-July by an order from Regional Development and Public Works Minister architect Ivan Shishkov. The newly reconstituted Board of Directors of Avtomagistrali EAD was assigned to run the state-owned company until a competitive procedure could select a permanent board.
Engineer Ivan Kunev holds a Master's degree in Automotive Technical Expertise from South-West University Neofit Rilski in Blagoevgrad. He worked in the road sector for many years, serving as director of the Regional Road Administration in Blagoevgrad from 2009 to 2024, and also has professional experience in construction.

Lights not out on Tallinn's War of Independence Victory Column, but being replaced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

Lights not out on Tallinn's War of Independence Victory Column, but being replaced
The lights recently being off on Estonia's War of Independence Victory Column in Freedom Square in Tallinn has a simple explanation.
While rumors have swirled that the column, unveiled in June 2009 and commemorating the 1918-1920 Estonian War of Independence, is due a major overhaul, this is not the case.
Ando Voogma, portfolio manager at the Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) told ERR the reason the column is not currently fully lit is because lighting replacement work is underway.
"Every technical system has its own lifespan, and this is the the case with the current elements too — their lifespan is practically over, some of the light sources have burned out, some have dimmed, and we are now replacing them with new ones," he said.
No further work is required, he said. "The previous owner replaced some glass elements. But I don't know of any major renovation having been done, and at the moment we have no need for major repairs. The current issue is replacing the light sources."
While in its early years the column had some teething problems and frequently needed minor works, things have settled down since then, Voogma went on.
"There are isolated issues from time to time, for example with the cladding on the outside of the column. As with any structure, we have to keep the whole in order, and that's part of routine maintenance and upkeep," Voogma said.
The column is nearly 24 meters high and is made up of 143 glass plates, topped off with the Cross of Liberty. It is the focal point of commemorative events such as the Independence Day military parade every February 24.

Ukraine’s Robotic Turrets Record First Shootdowns of Russia’s Jet-Powered Geran-5 Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:41:37 UTC
21:41:37 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Robotic Turrets Record First Shootdowns of Russia’s Jet-Powered Geran-5 Drones
Ukraine has recorded its first confirmed interceptions of Russian jet-powered drones using automated gun turrets equipped with artificial intelligence and machine-vision systems, according to Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on October 5 that Ukraine’s robotic turret systems have already downed jet-powered UAVs, including Russia’s Geran-5. “There have already been shootdowns of even jet-powered UAVs, even the Geran-5, using those same turrets,” Ihnat said during Ukraine’s national telethon.
He said the systems rely on machine vision and artificial intelligence to automate targeting and reduce the role of human error during interception.
“The use of innovative technologies—artificial intelligence—eliminated human error. Machine vision is used specifically in the interception. Artificial intelligence makes it possible to engage even jet-powered UAVs,” Ihnat said.
The turrets have a relatively limited engagement range because their primary weapon remains a machine gun, according to Ihnat.
Russia has increasingly combined conventional Shahed-type attack drones with faster jet-powered UAVs during strikes against Ukraine. Ihnat said Russian forces launched around 50 jet-powered drones per night during each of the previous two nights.
According to figures cited by Ihnat, Ukrainian forces currently intercept approximately 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed-type drones. The estimated interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is lower, at around 50% to 70%.
The automated turrets are being deployed at selected locations, including around bridges, as Ukraine expands a layered defense network intended to protect infrastructure from low-flying attack drones.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 4 that more than 12 such turrets had already been deployed in Kyiv, with another eight planned for the surrounding Kyiv region.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs a combination of different air-defense systems as Russia adjusts its strike tactics and increasingly introduces faster drones and ballistic missiles alongside conventional Shahed-type UAVs.

NATO Drafts "Theory of Victory" Plan Using Drones and AI to Repel Russian Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:41:16 UTC
21:41:16 KST

- Category
- World
NATO Drafts "Theory of Victory" Plan Using Drones and AI to Repel Russian Attack
NATO’s top military commander is preparing a strategy to quickly defeat any Russian attack on the alliance’s eastern flank, using drones and artificial intelligence alongside conventional forces.
Bloomberg reported the plan on October 5 after reviewing an unclassified version of the document and speaking with senior officials and diplomats familiar with the initiative.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The document, titled "Theory of Victory," is being developed under Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich. He is expected to present the strategy in Poland on October 12.
The plan is intended to clarify how NATO would respond to a potential Russian incursion into allied territory. It places particular emphasis on integrating emerging technologies, including drones and AI, with NATO’s existing conventional military capabilities.
Rather than replacing traditional forces, the strategy seeks to integrate technological systems with established military power to accelerate decision-making on the battlefield and strengthen NATO’s ability to stop an attack before Russia can achieve its initial objectives.
The document comes amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia and growing concern among allied governments about Moscow’s intentions toward the alliance’s eastern members.
The outlet noted that officials have been assessing repeated reports suggesting Russia could consider military action against NATO territory.
The strategy also reflects NATO’s broader effort to absorb lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine, where drones, automated targeting, electronic warfare, and rapidly changing battlefield technologies have become central to combat operations.
The alliance has increasingly focused on integrating such capabilities into its eastern defenses while retaining conventional forces as the foundation of deterrence.
NATO's shift toward automated warfare has already begun taking shape along the alliance's eastern flank.
Earlier reports indicated that the alliance plans a unified surveillance and defense system stretching from Finland to the Black Sea, built on drones, satellites, sensors, and AI to detect and help repel incoming attacks.
The approach draws on Ukraine, where AI-guided drone swarms can identify targets and strike autonomously even when Russian electronic warfare severs human control.
During the Freedom Shield 2026 exercises near the Belarusian border, Germany's 45th Armored Brigade fitted its Leopard 2 tanks and Fuchs carriers with anti-drone screens modeled on Ukrainian combat experience.

Russia Drops Armed Ground Robot From Il-76 for First Time in Military Exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:41:11 UTC
21:41:11 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Drops Armed Ground Robot From Il-76 for First Time in Military Exercise
Russian airborne forces deployed the Kurier unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) from an Il-76 military transport aircraft for the first time during the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercises, Militarnyi reported on October 5, citing the Russian Defense Ministry.
According to Militarnyi, the robotic system was dropped from an altitude of approximately 600 meters using a P-7 parachute platform. Operators had deployed to the exercise area in advance and assumed control of the vehicles after they landed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the exercise scenario, the UGVs were tasked with operating behind the lines of a simulated enemy. Their missions included providing fire support to assault units, transporting ammunition and other supplies, evacuating wounded personnel, and damaging road infrastructure.
The Kurier UGV is a Russian multipurpose remotely operated ground robot built on a tracked chassis. Its design allows it to be fitted with various equipment and weapons depending on the mission, Militarnyi reported.
According to open-source data, the basic version measures approximately 1.4 × 1.2 × 0.58 meters, weighs up to 250 kilograms, and can reach speeds of up to 35 km/h. Its control range is between 3 and 10 kilometers, while its operational endurance is up to 72 hours.
The Kurier is used to transport ammunition, food, and other supplies, evacuate wounded personnel, conduct reconnaissance, and lay mines. For combat missions, it can be equipped with various weapons, including a 7.62 mm PKTM machine gun, 12.7 mm NSVT or Kord machine guns, and AGS-17 and AGS-30 automatic grenade launchers, according top the outlet.
The deployment of the Kurier formed part of the broader Center-2026 exercises, during which Russian forces also rehearsed offensive operations involving the territory of a neighboring Central Asian state. The drills involved more than 47,000 personnel across several training grounds and the Caspian Sea.
Interfax reported on October 2 that the exercise scenario initially involved Russian forces repelling an attack in the South Ural direction before transitioning to an offensive aimed at retaking captured territory and establishing a “security zone” inside a neighboring state.

Ukraine Develops New Nika Missile to Shoot Down Jet-Powered Shahed Drones

Ukraine Develops New Nika Missile to Shoot Down Jet-Powered Shahed Drones
Ukraine has developed a new small missile called Nika to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones, while additional anti-drone turrets are being deployed in Kyiv and the surrounding region, Suspilne reported on October 4.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the new interceptor while speaking with journalists ahead of talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new systems come as Ukraine works to improve interception rates against faster jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy previously reported that Ukraine was intercepting around 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed drones, while the interception rate for jet-powered UAVs stood at approximately 50% to 60%.
“We now have a new small missile, Nika, against jet-powered Shaheds,” Zelenskyy stated. “The Germans and we are responding positively. There will be testing. For now, we are looking at what could prove successful.”
Zelenskyy also reported a successful test of Spear, a new Ukrainian-German drone interceptor.
“It is important that today we heard about the test of our new interceptor, the German-Ukrainian Spear interceptor,” Zelenskyy added. “The test was successful.”
Ukraine is also expanding the use of specialized turrets against jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy reported that more than 12 had already been installed in Kyiv, with another eight due to be deployed across the Kyiv region.
“There will be dozens of these turrets at different facilities, and we will defend ourselves as best we can,” Zelenskyy stated.
The expansion of Ukraine’s air defenses comes as Russian drone and missile strikes continue hitting Ukraine’s critical civilian infrastructure. On October 2, a Russian strike set fire to a warehouse belonging to one of Ukraine’s largest pharmaceutical distributors near Kyiv, the fifth reported attack on pharmaceutical storage infrastructure in a month.
