Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China without registering as a foreign agent as legally required, first assistant US state attorney Bill Essayli of California’s central federal district announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.
Citing real-estate licensing and listing records, the Los Angeles news outlet KTLA reported that Zhang was a licensed real-estate salesperson based in the southern California city of Irvine.
She was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and it was also not immediately clear if she had an attorney representing her.
She was due to appear on Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.
Taiwan’s presidential office confirmed relatives of the Taiwanese president, Lai Ching-te were the targets. The office did not specify if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression”.
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts – which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families – as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
The Chinese embassy in the US did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. And the foreign ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949. But China claims the island as part of its own territory.
Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and China do not belong to each other. He also has said the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan”.
China considers Lai a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace”.
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan – notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

Gallery: Decades of wild mushroom photography on display in Saaremaa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Gallery: Decades of wild mushroom photography on display in Saaremaa
On the Western Estonian island of Saaremaa, nearly 300 photographs are now on display at a local nature center, spotlighting decades of work by mycologist Vello Liiv.
The exhibition at Viidumäe Nature Center opened Sunday, and unlike most mushroom displays, may remain open to visitors for a year or more.
"Look, there they are," Liiv remarked in passing when he spotted mushrooms growing beside a tree stump outside the center.
"When you've spent nearly half your life walking with your head down, you can't really start looking up anymore," he quipped. "You keep seeing the grass and that part of the forest floor."
Still, the nearly 300 photographs on display represent only a small fraction of the mushrooms he has photographed over more than half a century. The University of Tartu's collections, he noted, contain around 3,000 species.
The Viidumäe exhibition is both artistic and scientific in nature, said artist Anna Talvi, who worked on the display.
"The way Vello photographs these mushrooms is beautiful in its own right," Talvi said. "But he also photographs and arranges them in ways that most clearly highlight each species' unique characteristics."
Liiv said he has never deliberately tried to make mushrooms look beautiful. Many of the species he has photographed, however, are ones he has only ever encountered once.
"Oh, there are so many of them," he said. Of the roughly 3,000 species, he estimates he has seen, photographed and identified about 2,500 only once before adding them to a herbarium.
The mushrooms people typically recognize as mushrooms, he added, actually only make up a much smaller bunch of around 300 species.

"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and definitive, and until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened," Ghalibaf said.

====================================================================================================

​​​​​​​What is Iran's 7-Day plan to reopen the Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:34:55 UTC
21:34:55 KST

What is Iran's 7-Day plan to reopen the Hormuz?
TEHRAN - It is not a final peace treaty. It is a one-week, step-by-step starter deal.
Iran says: if the United States accepts our conditions — all of which, Tehran insists, were already promised in the interim agreement of June 17, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) — then:
Days 1 to 5: the U.S. lifts military and economic pressure, fighting stops, and Iranian and Omani technical teams prepare the Strait,
Day 6: the Strait of Hormuz reopens and normal commercial shipping resumes,
Day 7: Iran and the U.S. start talks on a final deal on “mutually agreed subjects,” including the nuclear program.
“The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters outside the UN Security Council in New York on September 25. “And on day seven, the talks with the U.S. will be started for the final deal.”
The formal paper was handed to the U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner through Qatari mediators during the UN General Assembly, September 22-25. The U.S. sent back its views last week, also via Qatar. Tehran says those views are now under review in Tehran.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Bagher Qalibaf — who is also Iran’s chief negotiator — says reopening depends on seven conditions based on the Islamabad MoU:
“The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met.” — Qalibaf, October 4, in parliament.
No official English text of the plan has been published. What follows is reconstructed from the consistent statements of Araghchi, Qalibaf, Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei, and Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi.
Why do we need to know about the Islamabad MoU of June 17?
You cannot understand the 7-Day Plan without it.
After months of war that began in late February with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Iranian retaliation against shipping and regional bases, Pakistan and Qatar mediated a short interim understanding signed by Iran and the U.S. in Islamabad on June 17.
 
It was a 14-point MoU that did three things:
Established a brief ceasefire;
Created a 60-day window to negotiate a final peace;
Linked two files: (a) security in the Strait of Hormuz and (b) Iran’s nuclear program.
Under that MoU, Iran agreed to facilitate safe passage of commercial vessels from the Persian Gulf to the Sea of Oman and back, without tolls, while talks continued. Iran immediately opened technical talks with Oman — the other coastal state of the Strait — to implement it.
The MoU collapsed within weeks. Each side blames the other: Iran says the U.S. never lifted its naval blockade, never eased oil sanctions, and continued strikes; the U.S. says Iran kept attacking ships that did not follow its authorization rules, so President Donald Trump declared the deal “over” in July.
Iran’s argument today is simple, repeated by President Masoud Pezeshkian to Al-Jazeera: “We want nothing new. Just go back to that MoU and stick to it.”
Araghchi in New York put it the same way: “The actions the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU.”
The difference is speed: 60 days in June is now compressed into 7 days.
What does Iran want the U.S. to do?
Tehran has not released a numbered list, but four core demands were detailed by Araghchi in New York plus three clarifications added by Baqaei and the Supreme National Security Council. Together they make the “seven conditions” Qalibaf refers to:
A full ceasefire on all fronts, including Lebanon
Not only in the Persian Gulf. Fighting must stop everywhere from day one. Araghchi explicitly named Lebanon. It remains unclear whether this also covers the renewed fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
End of the U.S. naval blockade
Lift the blockade of Iranian ports and islands in and around Hormuz and stop intercepting Iranian tankers. Baqaei’s wording on October 4: “a complete end to disruption of Iran’s commercial navigation.”
Oil sanctions waiver
Issue a license allowing Iran to legally sell and ship oil again.
Release of frozen assets — at least $12 billion
Make accessible Iranian funds frozen abroad. Iranian officials present this as a trust-building and humanitarian step, not payment for talks.
Cancel post-June unilateral sanctions
Lift the extra sanctions imposed after the June MoU on shipping, petrochemicals, airlines, rail and banking. Baqaei: “lifting all recent unilateral sanctions.”
Stop strikes and military intervention
End air and naval strikes and guarantee no new attacks during implementation. Qalibaf stressed Iran judges “actual behavior, not daily statements or tweets.”
Accept the Iran-Oman safe navigation route
Accept the safe lane mechanism agreed between the two coastal states, Iran and Oman, as the basis for traffic management — rather than a U.S.-led escort operation. Baqaei, citing Tasnim on Sept 23: “acceptance of the safe shipping route based on understanding between the two coastal governments [Iran and Oman].”
Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei summarized the first cluster as the three main ones: end war on all fronts, free the assets, end the maritime blockade.
How would the seven days actually work?
Araghchi gave the clearest timetable:
Day 0 – Acceptance: Washington says “yes” through Qatar. The clock starts the next morning.
Days 1-5 – Parallel steps: Fighting stops. The U.S. announces the ceasefire, stands down blockade forces, issues the oil waiver, and orders the release of funds. At the same time, Iranian-Omani teams do 4-5 days of technical work: clearing hazards, restoring vessel-traffic systems, notifying shippers and insurers.
Day 6 – Reopening: “The strait would be open,” Araghchi said. Normal maritime passage is restored.
Day 7 – New talks begin: With Hormuz open, nuclear and other issues go on the table for a final deal.
In short: Hormuz first, nuclear second. Tehran says nuclear talks cannot happen under blockade and bombing.
What does the U.S. say? Where is the deadlock?
President Trump said on September 26-27 he rejected the Iranian proposal as “unacceptable” / “insufficient” and, according to the Wall Street Journal, told aides that bombing could resume after the congressional midterms.
But diplomacy did not stop. Reuters reported on September 30, quoting an official briefed on the talks, that Washington’s reply had reached Araghchi via Qatar.
The U.S. public position, from UN Ambassador Mike Waltz and a White House official to CNN, is:
Iran wants “sanctions relief and billions in frozen assets before negotiations over its nuclear programme.” Washington is willing to give relief, but only with “concrete progress” on nuclear first.
In other words, both sides largely agree on what a final package contains — Hormuz + sanctions relief + nuclear steps. They disagree on *in what order*.
Baqaei confirmed this on October 4: “The Americans’ propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus at this stage is the Strait of Hormuz.” He denied reports, notably in Bloomberg, that Tehran had offered IAEA access to bombed nuclear sites in exchange for sanctions relief: “Iran has not entered into nuclear discussions.”
Gharibabadi added the same day: U.S. views “are currently being examined inside the country... At the same time, Iran is preparing itself for any other possible scenario.”
Bottom line: Tehran’s message to an American reader is — Do in 7 days what you signed in June, then we talk about everything, including nuclear. Washington’s reply is — Show nuclear movement first, then you get relief. Qatar is now shuttling that sequencing dispute between the two capitals, while a second U.S. carrier stays in the region and Iran keeps Hormuz closed as its main leverage.

Bolsonaro favourite to win: What Brazil’s first round of elections tells us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Bolsonaro favourite to win: What Brazil’s first round of elections tells us
Analysts say Flavio Bolsonaro is projected to win a run-off vote on October 25 and become Brazil’s next president.
Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has exceeded expectations in the first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, triggering a run-off later this month.
“Brazil wants change, and I am very happy with the results,” Bolsonaro told reporters in Brasilia on Sunday as he saluted “the end of the era of [Lula’s] Workers’ Party”.
The 45-year-old son of right-wing former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, now faces an October 25 showdown with the 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.
In the run-up to Sunday’s first-round vote, a series of polls showed a close race between Lula and Bolsonaro, with the incumbent president poised to win by about 3 percentage points against his right-wing challenger.
In a surprise result that defied opinion poll projections, Bolsonaro beat Lula with 47 percent of the vote, while Lula got 45.1 percent.
Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round. That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro.
Why is Bolsonaro favoured to win Brazil’s election?
Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected performance is likely to buoy his campaign and may bolster Brazil’s currency and stock market, which have risen on the prospects of the business-friendly challenger.
Oliver Stuenkel, professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) in San Paulo, Brazil, said Lula was in a difficult position as he could not count on voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates to vote for him in the second round.
“Not only is he behind now after this first round, but the other candidates who received a total of nearly 8 percent are largely centre-right, which means that the people who voted for these other candidates are very unlikely to shift for Lula,” Stuenkel told Al Jazeera.
“So he must change his campaign tactics and above all mobilise a significant part of people who stayed at home,” he added. About 30 million Brazilians – 21 percent of the electorate – did not vote in the first round.
Al Jazeera’s Monica Yanakiew, reporting from Rio de Janeiro, said Lula supporters felt their candidate had not used social media as effectively as the right-wing camp. “This is something they have to work on in the second round,” Yanakiew said.
From a historical perspective, however, such efforts are unlikely to change the outcome. “Unless something very unusual happens in the next three weeks, Flavio Bolsonaro is set to win,” Stuenkel said. “In Brazilian presidential politics, no candidate who came second in the first round ended up winning the presidency since 1989.”
Has the Bolsonaro family taken hold of Brazil?
Several politicians from the Bolsonaro family have won congressional races taking place as part of the broader nationwide general elections.
Michelle Bolsonaro, wife of former President Jair Bolsonaro and stepmother of Flavio, won a Senate seat in the Federal District, home to the capital, Brasilia.
In June, the 44-year-old, who has never held government office, had a public falling out with her stepson, whom she accused of disrespecting her in lengthy videos posted on her social media. The pair later made up.
Ex-leader Bolsonaro’s second son Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, was the second most-voted senatorial candidate in the southern Santa Catarina state and won a seat in the Senate.
The fourth and younger son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of Congress.
Some experts credit “antipetismo” — a trend of hostility against Lula’s PT movement — with fuelling the Bolsonaro family’s rise to political power.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 of the 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies while Lula’s PT got 70.
What are the implications of a Bolsonaro win?
Brazil’s presidential election carries significant regional and geopolitical implications.
Reporting from Sao Paulo, Al Jazeera’s Lucia Newman said Lula has been “on a collision course” with United States President Donald Trump, who is a vocal and ardent supporter of the Bolsonaro camp.
“That puts Brazil in the middle of a fierce competition between Washington and China for political, diplomatic and economic dominance, especially since Brazil is a powerhouse on all these fronts,” Newman said.
While Bolsonarism is strongly aligned with the US and Israel, Brazil also has a tight economic relationship with China, its largest trade partner. Bolsonaro has portrayed Trump as an ally and is expected to strengthen ties with Washington if elected.
In case of a win, the younger Bolsonaro has pledged to seek a congressional amnesty for his father, who is in prison over his role in a coup plot following his election loss to Lula by 1.8 percentage points in 2022. That would need approval from both houses of Congress, which are currently dominated by conservatives.
Similar to Trump, the Bolsonaros have made rigged election claims. The insurrection that shook Brasilia in January 2023 shared similarities with the storming of the US Capitol two years prior. Like Trump, Bolsonaro has also pledged to release his father’s supporters responsible for the coup.
Concerns about US intervention in Brazil’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign. Lula has accused the Trump administration of using tariffs and other means to interfere with Brazilian affairs.
Vinicius de Carvalho, a lecturer in Brazilian studies at King’s College London, UK, stressed that Latin America has been experiencing a right-wing wave, with the election of US-aligned governments. This includes Ecuador, El Salvador, Panama and Paraguay.
By contrast, Lula was part of the so-called “pink tide” in Latin America, a wave of left-leaning governments that came to power in the late 1990s and early 2000s. With Congress stacked against him, if Lula is re-elected, he will still need to “respond to some demands of the right”, de Carvalho said.

Air traffic in Stuttgart suspended due to hoax bomb threat
Germany's Stuttgart Airport saw the temporary suspension of all departures and arrivals due to a bomb threat that turned out to be a hoax.
Police looked into a claim a man had made to an employee that he had been carrying a bomb in his luggage, which resulted in the terminal being evacuated and all air traffic being stopped.
Germany's Federal Police said no threat was detected, and the airport's operations resumed shortly after the threat was found to be not true.
The 24-year-old man who claimed to be carrying a bomb is under investigation for allegedly disturbing the peace by making threats of criminal offenses.
German Book Prize best novel award goes to Shida Bazyar for 'The Gaps'
The 2026 German Book Prize has been awarded to Shida Bazyar for her novel "Die Lücken" (which could perhaps be translated as "The Gaps"), with the jury describing her book as "a novel against ambivalence."
The book is set in fictional community, Heimesbach in Hunsrück, "in which 90 years of German history have nested themselves in the walls and the biographies," as the prizegivers put it.
"The novel leads us through the years and the heads of those who shaped the village: from Jewish families who lost everything, via Nazi profiteers, who later reinvented themselves as innocent hangers-on, through the Sharifi and Karimpour families, who fled from Iran decades later," the book prize writes. "Shida Bazyar succeeds in providing a virtuoso storytelling mosaic about the burden of history, the lie of the new start, and the desire to finally find a home."
The jury praised Bazyar's storytelling format in particular, saying it was an ideal vehicle to convey disparate and yet interconnected ideas.
"The author chooses compelling literary strategies: The view of an omniscient narrator, and the caleidoscopic structure of the text make it possible to jump between times and to create both closeness and distance at the same time," they wrote in their explanation for the award.
The 38-year-old Bazyar was born in Germany to Iranian parents who fled in the 1980s.
"It's not so easy for me to truly experience joy, I have to say," Bazyar said in her acceptance speech. "Because it is quite a strange feeling when you write a novel about people who were persecuted, terrorized and murdered. To then be truly happy about its success, that doesn't seem quite right to me." Therefore, Bazyar said, she'd like to dedicate the accolades to the people the book is about.
Bazyar also made this year's shortlist for the International Booker Prize for her debut novel from 2016, "The Nights are Quiet in Tehran," which became a hit when translated into English in 2025.
READ — Merz, Macron call for tougher EU tools against unfair trade
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have written to the EU's Ursula von der Leyen, saying the bloc needs tougher — and faster — means to respond to unfair trade practices by third countries.
Their appeal names no names but it seems most likely to have China in its crosshairs, or just maybe the US under Donald Trump's erratic trade policies.
This comes days before the EU trade commissioner heads to Beijing for talks, and just over a week before this month's EU leaders' summit, where the issue might well come up again.
Merz tells pupils: Do better in school than I did
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has returned to his former high school on a visit marking the school's 100th anniversary, telling pupils they should aim for better grades than he managed.
Merz graduated from the Friedrich-Spee-Gymnasium in Rüthen, western Germany, 51 years ago.
"Do a slightly better Abitur than I did," the chancellor told pupils, referring to Germany's school-leaving qualification that allows students to attend university.
Merz has kept his exact final grade a closely guarded secret. Last year, he joked that his school certificate was locked in a safe at home.
He did, however, suggest that his overall grade was somewhere around 3.8 — a relatively poor result in Germany's grading system.
Merz has previously said he lacked discipline and motivation at school and at one point had to repeat a year.
"I didn't have difficulties with school; the school had difficulties with me," he joked on Monday.
He said things improved after he changed schools and moved to Rüthen, where mathematics and physics eventually became two of his favorite subjects.
Hundreds of pupils greeted Merz on his return, with some calling out "Hello, Chancellor" as he arrived.
The visit came less than a week after Merz presented the German School Award in Berlin, where he said he wanted to focus more personally on education policy and visit schools more frequently.
Germany plans new naval base in Emden
Germany plans to build a new naval base in the northern city of Emden as it expands its armed forces.
The federal government and the state of Lower Saxony signed a declaration of intent for the project on Monday, the Defense Ministry said.
Germany currently has only one North Sea naval base, in Wilhelmshaven. The ministry said it would not have enough capacity to accommodate the navy's planned expansion.
"New ships and boats need berths. Our soldiers need accommodation and training facilities," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said.
Pistorius said the new base could create up to 2,000 military posts and that Emden's access to the Atlantic made it an ideal location.
Lower Saxony Premier Olaf Lies said the aim was for the base to be operational by the early 2030s.
Chinese high-tech could be security risk — domestic intelligence agency
High-tech goods from China, such as electric vehicles or even robot vacuum cleaners, could represent a security risk, the BfV domestic intelligence agency has warned.
BfV head Sinan Selen told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin that the issue was of "great concern" to him.
"I already see substantial shortcomings that create potential for abuse," he said.
Data collected via the products could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products."
"In terms of resilience and availability (this) could confront us with problems," he said.
The warning comes as sales of high-tech products to Germany are growing and Chinese manufacturers compete ever more strongly with their German counterparts.
Deutsche Telekom targets billions in AI savings
Deutsche Telekom plans to use artificial intelligence and automation to cut annual costs by around €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) by 2030.
The target covers the German telecommunications giant's operations outside the United States.
Deutsche Telekom is already using AI for repetitive tasks in network operations, customer service, software development and administration.
Its "Frag Magenta" chatbot handled around 2.6 million customer service calls in the first half of 2026, the company said.
At T-Mobile US, in which Deutsche Telekom holds a majority stake, AI agents now handle 40% of customer contacts.
Outside the US, Deutsche Telekom expects savings from AI and automation to reach €1.1 billion by 2027 and €2.5 billion by 2030.
"AI is fundamentally changing Deutsche Telekom," CEO Tim Höttges said. He said the technology was improving networks and customer service while opening up new business models."
IN DEPTH: Germany trainer Klopp's first internationals

Social Democrat groups oppose coalition's working week reform
Grassroots groups within the Social Democrats (SPD) — the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government — have spoken out against plans to "flexibilize" the working week in a position paper.
In question is a paragraph in the coalition agreement that speaks of "the possibility of a weekly rather than a daily maximum working time."
The conservative Christian Democrat (CDU)-Christian Social Union (CSU) bloc has pushed to have a maximum number of hours that can be worked per week rather than the current daily standard limit of eight hours.
Although the four SPD groups fundamentally accept the idea, they are calling for strict controls, among other things wanting collective labor agreements under which both parties work out details as "a necessary prerequisite."
They also say exceptions should made in certain sectors where illegal employment is prevalent.
Employers' associations in June objected to the idea of collective labor agreements as a coercive measure when it was put forward by the Labor Ministry, leading to its retraction, with the CDU saying that it went against the coalition agreement.
The position paper submitted by the SPD groups could thus lead to a new split in the coalition, stating as it does: "It is not in keeping with a modern reform of working hours regulation or a better compatibility of work and family when bosses can decide alone when employees can knock off work."
German court sets limits on deportation detention
Germany's Federal Court of Justice (BGH) has ruled that a person facing deportation cannot be detained as a flight risk simply because their past behavior suggests they might try to avoid being deported.
The case concerned a stateless Palestinian man who sought asylum at a police station in Germany in April 2023. Austrian authorities had already issued a decision requiring him to return.
A court in the German city of Duisburg ordered the man detained while his transfer was being arranged.
The courts argued that his previous actions indicated a risk that he would try to evade deportation. He had lived in Austria since 2020, where two asylum applications had been rejected, and had also applied for asylum in Belgium and Germany.
But the man had never explicitly said that he intended to avoid deportation.
The BGH ruled that his behavior alone was not enough to establish this particular ground for detention.
A person's words do not necessarily have to state the intention literally, the judges said. But it must be "clear and unambiguous" from what the person says and the circumstances that they intend to evade deportation.
The court found that the man's detention from May 7 to June 6, 2023 had therefore violated his rights.
German immigration law provides several other grounds on which people can be detained pending deportation.
IN DEPTH: Two German scientists in Nobel-winning trio
Peter Hegemann from Germany's Humbolt University and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg have won this year's Nobel Prize in medicine alongside their US colleague, Karl Deisseroth.
You can read more about their achievements in this article: German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine
Germany at risk of 'violent conflict' with Russia — intelligence chief
Germany is facing a growing risk of a violent confrontation with Russia as Moscow continues a campaign of hybrid warfare with other countries in Europe, the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence service warned on Monday.
Speaking before the Bundestag at the annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs, Martin Jäger said: "The confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension."
"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia — the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example," he said.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," he added.
Jäger was referring to a drone attack at Leipzig airport in August that the German government has blamed on Russia.
Russia has repeatedly denied any intention of attacking NATO
countries, with President Vladimir Putin, however, saying on Thursday: "But if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond."
Draft bill aims to help domestic abuse victims move house
The Justice Ministry has put forward a draft bill making it easier for domestic abuse victims to leave joint tenancy contracts and obliging perpetrators to pay for any ensuing costs.
"The path to a self-determined and safe life after domestic abuse is often still a long one," Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig told newspapers from the Funke media group.
"We want to make it a bit easier," she added.
She said the draft bill aimed to give domestic abuse victims clear legal rights against their abusers, including being able to demand that the latter pay any costs arising from the premature termination of the joint lease.
More protection for others in the household
The bill also envisages increased protection for children and relatives of victims.
Under current German law, family courts can impose bans on domestic abusers taking up contact with or approaching their victims but not other members of the same household.
Hubig said the draft law foresaw such protections being extended to other people dependent on the abuser without any separate application being made.
According to police statistics, nearly 266,000 people in Germany were affected by domestic abuse in 2024, 70% of them women and girls.
The Justice Ministry has said the real figure is likely to be much higher, estimating that 95% of cases go unreported.
E-vehicle subsidy program has 'exceeded our expectations' — environment minister
Since May, the German government has paid out subsidies to 100,000 households wanting to procure an electric vehicle, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper on Monday.
Schneider, from junior coalition partner the Social Democrats (SPD), said the program, worth €3 billion ($3.36 billion), had "far exceeded our expectations."
He said that every additional electric vehicle protected households from high fuel prices and made the county less dependent on expensive oil imports and international conflicts.
According to the Bild article, half of households applying for the subsidy had a maximum annual income of €45,000 and three-quarters of them €60,000.
Schneider said he found it particularly important that this graduation of payments according to income functioned properly.
Preliminary assessments have shown that less than 15% of households that applied for the subsidy were looking to buy vehicles from China, contradicting expert views that Chinese automakers would profit the most.
Left Party takes Economy Minister Reiche to top court
The Left Party is taking a row about a remark made by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche to the Constitutional Court after Reiche failed to give a declaration to cease and desist on time.
Reiche had posted a remark on the official Instagram site of her ministry saying: "Antisemitism and expropriation endanger Germany and the economy."
The comment refers first to the unproven accusation that the Left Party is antisemitic in its ideology and then to the Left Party's plan to socialize apartments from corporate landlords in a bid to reduce skyrocketing rents in the capital.
Reiche doubled down on her criticism of the socialist party in comments she made during a visit to Ukraine over the weekend, telling the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild she feared a national loss of growth if a leftist coalition took power in Berlin.
"What the Left Party represents here in Berlin and the people that it represents is dangerous not only for Berlin but for our country," she said.
The Berlin branch of the Left Party has accused the Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Reiche and Chancellor Friedrich Merz belong, of carrying out a "large-scale campaign" against its top candidate, Elif Eralp, who won recent state elections in Berlin.
It has taken legal action over similar statements on CDU interior ministry websites in various states, criticizing the use of official government channels to denigrate another party.
The ministries in Saxony and Schleswig Holstein withdrew the statements, but those in Baden-Württemberg, Brandenburg and Hesse have so far not done so.

More than half of Ukrainians say Zelensky should not run for president again, poll says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

More than half of Ukrainians say Zelensky should not run for president again, poll says
Some 53% of Ukrainians think President Volodymyr Zelensky should not run for a second term, according to a poll published by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on Oct. 5.
In turn, 42% think Zelensky should participate in Ukraine's next presidential election, while 5% were undecided, according to the latest poll.
Ukraine's constitution does not allow elections under martial law, which was declared when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The survey shows a steady decline in support for Zelensky's second term. In December 2023, 59% of respondents said the incumbent president should run again, and only 45% shared this view in December 2025.
The study comes as the president faces growing scrutiny over corruption scandals implicating figures from his inner circle and unexpected personnel decisions, including the firing of popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Nevertheless, recent polls continue to show Zelensky among the leading candidates in future elections, alongside Fedorov and Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former military chief and current ambassador to the U.K.
A little over a year ago, Zelensky told Axios that he would not seek re-election once the war with the Kremlin ends.
"If we finish (the) war with (the) Russians, I'm ready not to go for the second term because it's not my goal — elections," Zelensky said in September 2025.
The same survey found that a vast majority of Ukrainians — 71% — oppose holding presidential elections during wartime.
The possibility of holding elections during wartime was briefly raised in August by Fedorov, whose sudden dismissal sparked nationwide protests.
However, the Ukrainian public did not respond favorably to Fedorov's call for elections due to the many logistical constraints faced by military personnel, millions of Ukrainians abroad, and those living near the front line.
The KIIS survey also revealed that 45% of Ukrainians believe their country's affairs are moving in the wrong direction, while 40% think the opposite.
Furthermore, 44% said they "mostly feel disappointment" about Zelensky's current government, and 33% said they feel shame. Both markers have increased since the KIIS's last survey in December 2025.
"There is a significant demand in Ukrainian society for the renewal of political elites, and it has only intensified in recent years," commented Anton Hrushetskyi, executive director of KIIS, in a press release.
The poll was conducted between Sept. 12 and 21, with the participation of 1,002 respondents living in government-controlled territories.

Tajikistan Taps Iran as Russian Fuel Runs Dry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:32:00 UTC
21:32:00 KST

Tajikistan has started importing oil and petroleum products from Iran. Deliveries began in late August, the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources told Asia-Plus on September 24, without disclosing the volumes, prices, suppliers, or transit route.
The shipments followed August 15 talks in Tehran, where Energy Minister Daler Juma and Transport Minister Azim Ibrohim met Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad and agreed to set up a working group to prepare a long-term supply agreement. Dushanbe asked for up to 2.55 million tons a year (2 million tons of crude, 300,000 tons of diesel, 150,000 tons of gasoline, and 100,000 tons of jet fuel) along with discounted prices, dedicated tank-car trains, and a “green corridor” across Iran’s rail network.
The scramble is a product of Russia’s fuel crisis. Russia supplied 91.1 percent of the 599,500 tons of petroleum products Tajikistan imported in the first half of 2026, free of export duty. Tajikistan is not a member of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), and Carnegie Politika’s Galiya Ibragimova described the cheap Russian fuel as “payment” for Dushanbe’s “political loyalty” to Moscow. But loyalty bought less fuel once Ukrainian drones began disabling Russian refineries, including the Omsk plant, which was knocked offline in early July.
Moscow has extended its diesel export ban month by month, most recently through October 31. Deliveries under intergovernmental agreements are exempt, but the carve-out has not kept Tajikistan supplied: diesel shortages began in June. By July, some stations were capping sales at 20 liters per vehicle and diesel had climbed to $1.40-$1.66 per liter.
In Tajikistan, domestic refining covers about 0.5 percent of gasoline consumption. Alternatives are scarce and expensive. U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, and Iran’s subsequent restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz kept oil prices above $100 a barrel in September. Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan are competing with Tajikistan for the same limited supplies from Belarus, China, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan.
Iran is an unlikely lifeline. Relations collapsed after Tehran hosted exiled Islamic Renaissance Party leader Muhiddin Kabiri in December 2015, months after Dushanbe banned his party as an extremist organization. In 2017, Dushanbe accused Iran of involvement in political killings during the 1990s civil war. The thaw came with the 2022 opening of an Iranian drone factory in Dushanbe and accelerated with President Masoud Pezeshkian’s January 2025 state visit, when the two sides signed 23 agreements. Bilateral trade reached $438 million in 2025, up 28 percent from the year prior.
However, Tajikistan and Iran don’t share a border. Moving 2.55 million tons of petroleum products by rail through third countries would take about 51,000 tank cars a year, according to Tajikistan’s Transport Ministry – roughly 140 a day. Iran may have little to offer beyond crude oil and jet fuel: Hamid Hosseini of Iran’s Union of Oil, Gas and Petrochemical Products Exporters said gasoline and diesel exports were not under discussion because of shortages in Iran itself, and put likely shipments at around 5,000 tons a month. The requested crude also exceeds Tajikistan’s refining capacity. The TK-Oil plant in Danghara has a design capacity of 1.2 million tons a year but has long run below it for lack of feedstock; another Asia-Plus report put the country’s two refineries at about 500,000 tons combined.
Then there is Washington. On August 24, the U.S. Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast, widening the range of Iran-related conduct exposed to secondary sanctions and promising every country a “defined timeline” to shut down Iran-related activity. A Treasury official told RFE/RL that anyone in Iran’s petroleum sector “incurs that risk themselves.” Edward Lemon of the Oxus Society noted that the modest scale of Tajik-Iranian trade may keep Dushanbe below Washington’s threshold of attention. The practical exposure likely lies with whichever Tajik banks settle payments for Iranian cargoes, particularly if they clear dollars or deal with designated Iranian entities.
Russia still supplies nine of every ten tons of Tajikistan’s fuel, and on available evidence the Iranian route is unlikely to change that this winter. But it gives Dushanbe a second supplier at a moment when Moscow cannot guarantee much, albeit at the cost of sanctions exposure that grows with every ton delivered.

Extreme heat is raising risks for mothers and babies - but experts say cooling solutions already exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:31:34 UTC
21:31:34 KST

73 per cent of maternal healthcare workers surveyed say they have seen heat-linked cases rise in the last five years.
Extreme heat is making pregnancy and childbirth more dangerous, health experts warn. Nearly three in four doctors, midwives and other maternal health workers say that heat-related cases or complications have increased over the past five years, according to a survey commissioned by global health foundation Wellcome.
Simon Stiell, the head of the UN’s climate body, cited the findings today, 5 October, at the pre-COP summit in Nadi, Fiji, as he warned about the less obvious dangers of extreme heat.
Higher temperatures have been linked to premature birth, stillbirth and low birth weight, as well as complications for mothers. According to Wellcome, every 1°C rise in temperature correlates with a five per cent increase in premature births and a seven per cent increase in gestational diabetes.
But many of these risks can be reduced through better planning, Stiell says, whether it’s improved heat alerts or simply reliable water and electricity in clinics.
Health workers want help tackling extreme heat
The Wellcome survey included 1,000 maternal health professionals in Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe. 98 per cent had cared for a pregnant woman whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat, and 99 per cent said the same of a baby.
The vast majority surveyed also said they need more support. 92 per cent called for more training, guidance and resources to protect pregnant women from heat.
Stiell delivered his speech at a Wellcome-organised event on the opening day of pre-COP, which runs from 5 to 8 October. The meeting is the final major gathering before COP31, held from 9 to 20 November in Antalya, Türkiye.
This year’s co-hosts – Türkiye and Australia – have billed this as an “Implementation COP” focused on turning pledges into progress. Their priorities include climate finance, building resilient cities and infrastructure, and protecting vulnerable regions. However, both countries have come under scrutiny for embracing coal, which is often referred to as the ‘dirtiest’ form of energy.
Stiell argued that governments should make maternal and newborn health part of the climate action, too.
Pregnant women who work outdoors, live without adequate cooling at home or have to travel long distances for medical care may have little protection during extreme heat, he said. Clinics can also struggle when water, electricity or cooling are unreliable.
“‘Staying cool’ is simply not an option when there is no cool place to go,” Stiell says.
From heat alerts to cooling roofs, solutions already exist
In his call to action, Stiell said governments should invest in practical solutions such as heat alerts, better trained healthcare workers, water and electricity infrastructure, and clinics better prepared for extreme temperatures.
Around the world, some of these ideas are already being tested.
In Zimbabwe and South Africa, a Wellcome-funded project involving 1,600 women is testing low-cost protections for extreme heat, including sunhats, water bottles, umbrellas and fans. Some communities are also painting roofs white, broadcasting heat advice on the radio and training health workers to deliver daily warnings through an app.
Cities can also reduce the heat pregnant women and children face in their daily lives. Some of the most promising fixes are relatively cheap and can make use of infrastructure that already exists. For example, University of Manchester researchers found that rooftop rainwater systems could help keep cities cool by spraying stored rainwater onto hot roofs.
As the water evaporates, it cools the roof, reducing the amount of heat entering the building as well as the need for air conditioning. Using less air conditioning also means less heat is expelled outdoors.
In Spain, meanwhile, hundreds of existing public buildings have been designated as climate shelters, giving people somewhere cool to go during dangerous heatwaves. Barcelona alone has around 400 of them, including libraries, museums and municipal markets.
The COP31 host city is already searching for solutions to extreme heat. Antalya has mapped neighbourhoods where high temperatures and vulnerable populations overlap, then used the data to direct shade, green space, early-warning systems and health support towards those areas.
Paying for measures like these that safeguard society’s most vulnerable will be another test for governments. At COP30, the participating nations agreed to triple climate adaptation financing by 2035. COP31 could test whether their promises translate into real action.
“A changing climate must never be accepted as a reason pregnancy and birth become less safe,” Stiell says. “A newborn’s healthy start must never depend on a family’s ability to escape the heat.”

AI microdramas are a test case for China’s next big export wave
A quiet shift is happening in China’s services exports as its competitive manufacturing capabilities start moving into entertainment content
3-MIN READ3-MIN
5
 Listen
Kok How Lee is a seasoned economist, consultant and strategist. 
China’s US$1.2 trillion goods trade surplus last year has focused attention on electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels and industrial overcapacity. Tariffs, anti-subsidy investigations and localisation requirements have followed as trading partners respond to China’s manufacturing scale.
Yet the less visible shift is happening in services. Services exports rose by 17.1 per cent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, while exports of personal cultural and entertainment services surged by 57.8 per cent. China still runs a trade deficit in services, which are nowhere close to replacing manufacturing. But digital services can scale up globally without factories, containers or ports.
Microdramas generated by artificial intelligence (AI) offer an early example. China industrialised the format domestically: one-to-three-minute episodes, rapid plot twists and cliffhangers designed around smartphone viewing and payment. The sector’s revenue rose from less than 1 billion yuan in 2020 to an estimated 100 billion yuan (US$14.91 billion) last year. Chinese-backed platforms such as ReelShort already have sizeable overseas audiences.

Can Japan Counter China’s Dominance in AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Japan, a nation historically known for innovations and new technologies, has not held that advantage in artificial intelligence (AI). The United States and China dominate AI’s development. According to one Japanese expert, Dr. Takahiro Tsuchiya of Kyoto University, Chinese companies in Japan even dominate Japan’s domestic market. A major factor is cost. Prices for Chinese-developed AI products are well below those charged by Japan’s home-grown AI enterprises.
This is a sea change in the global technology pecking order, but not one that the Japanese are willing to passively accept. While Japan has ceded market territory to Chinese firms in AI, Japan is nonetheless quickly establishing a leading position in “physical AI” – integrating AI into robotics and machinery – and sovereign AI deployment.
Critically, the Japanese government has woken up to the problem. Since 2025, Tokyo has acted boldly and decisively to ward off foreign AI-related threats by developing AI for Japan, in Japan.
The fact remains that Japan has not kept up with global leaders – the United States and China – in core AI, Tsuchiya confirmed. AI is globally considered to be both a revolutionary technology as well as a potential threat mechanism for those who dominate its use and development.
Speaking to reporters at the Japanese Embassy in Washington, D.C., and to his lecture attendees at the Japanese Consulate in Boston, Tsuchiya “strongly advocates for a robust U.S.-Japan alliance to counter regional threats” (read: China and North Korea). However, the readout highlighted “a growing school of thought in Tokyo regarding strategic autonomy.”
Tsuchiya emphasized that “while Japan must tighten technology export controls alongside the U.S. to counter China’s military-civil fusion, Tokyo’s defensive and economic calculations must remain grounded in its own reality.” Part of that reality, suggested Tsuchiya, is that Japan is not only geographically close to China, but is also deeply tied in trade with China, as well.
The Diplomat asked Tsuchiya to describe Japan’s priorities in handling the delicate balancing act of maintaining its strong and strategic relationship with the United States while maintaining at least a stable relationship with China.
Tsuchiya said that “Japan cannot copy the U.S. Japan makes its own assessments” of the threats it may face, and how to handle them. Those assessments include risks related to AI development and rollout.
The Japanese government launched a $6.34 billion initiative beginning in fiscal year 2026 with the goal of wedding Japan’s unmatched industrial robotics industry with next-generation AI. Heavy industry, transport, and infrastructure are all planned to be AI-automated. As an example, autonomous AI pipelines are due to manage the heating and cooling infrastructure of Tokyo.
Japan’s population is aging. One of the most immediate impacts of that demographic dilemma is a labor shortage. As a result, some Japanese companies are heeding the call to modernize and develop new AI capabilities.
Nikkei reported on September 9 that trading house Sumitomo Corp. “has partnered with Sakana AI to bring the startup’s artificial-intelligence models to its 100,000 or so client companies, helping the Tokyo-based company sell its solutions even to small businesses and giving a huge push to Japan’s homegrown technology.” Nikkei added, “Sakana AI’s models are said to be comparable to cutting-edge overseas models.”
The new partnership reflects the AI-related security concerns facing Japan, particularly those related to and coming from China. “Japanese companies have fallen behind U.S. and Chinese rivals in leveraging AI for structural and operational reforms. Japan Inc. has been cautious, partially due to security concerns, as full-fledged adoption would mean exposing confidential data to a generative AI model,” Nikkei explained.
Critically, there are “high expectations for Sakana AI as a provider of AI models that do not rely on overseas companies’ services.” In other words, neither the U.S. nor China are involved, keeping the new Sumitomo-Sakana AI enterprise a Japanese homegrown venture, one intended to be safe from prying eyes.
Japan is now committing vast resources to its own AI development, Hello World Japan reported in May 2026. It started by putting an AI Act into force in June 2025. The government then “adopted a formal AI Basic Plan in December 2025, created a Prime Minister-led AI Strategic Headquarters, and committed more than 10 trillion yen in public support for AI and semiconductor infrastructure – all in under a year.”
The Japanese Cabinet then passed its Second Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan on July 14. The plan explicitly targets agentic AI and tech sovereignty. This is backed by a massive road map aiming to mobilize 370 trillion yen ($2.3 trillion) in public and private funding by 2040 for AI and semiconductors.
Hello World Japan noted that the official language in the initial plan is “unusually direct.” The plan explicitly noted “gaps between Japan and other growing countries in utilization rates and private investment” – gaps that “widened” up through 2025. As a result, Hello World Japan noted, “the strategy is framed as recovery, not regulation.”
Such stark and transparent language is indeed a rare phenomenon for the Japanese government.
“That is a different story from the ‘Japan is cautious on AI’ read that still circulates outside the country,” concluded Hello World Japan.
This proactive approach from the Japanese government is an antidote against Chinese dominance in Japan’s AI environment, and the risks that come with that presence.

Russia quarantines dozens after Siberia plague researcher death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

Russian authorities have quarantined dozens of people after a laboratory worker at a Siberian plague research institute died under undisclosed circumstances, prompting the head of the national health watchdog to travel to the Irkutsk region.
The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said Monday the situation was under control.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas.
It is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, though cases in other parts of the world – notably Africa – occur every year.
Local media named the woman as Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
There were conflicting reports about how and where the laboratory worker, whose age was given as 28, had fallen ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia of as-yet unestablished origin.
Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, told state media the institute had not found evidence of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens after rumors spread on social media that the woman had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria.
Nevertheless, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Siberia for an emergency meeting over the weekend.
An unspecified number of people who had been in contact with the dead woman were quarantined, parts of the hospital in the town of Shelekhov where she died were cordoned off, and an aluminum plant told its workers to wear masks.
Authorities urged people to remain calm and said there was no evidence that the woman's death was linked to her work.
Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement that she had died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology," adding: "Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified."
He said the situation was under control and that all known contacts of the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.
Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, prompts the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
If identified quickly, it can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard. We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,” Jaishankar said.
He added that the ongoing discussions also cover grain and energy exports and what he described as “non-attack possibilities.”
Jaishankar made the remarks during the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi on Sunday.
“We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy,” he said.
The minister did not disclose the specific proposals under consideration, a potential timetable or whether Moscow and Kyiv were close to reaching any agreement.
India seeks larger diplomatic role
Jaishankar’s remarks represent one of New Delhi’s clearest public acknowledgments that it is directly engaging both sides in efforts to negotiate limited arrangements related to the war.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha recently said Kyiv had received proposals from India, the US, Turkey and Egypt concerning a possible ceasefire.
Merz in Kyiv: Support Under Fire
Sybiha described India’s proposal as the most comprehensive and said it addressed attacks on energy and port infrastructure, Black Sea security and a potential ceasefire along the front line.
India has maintained close economic and defense ties with Russia throughout the full-scale invasion. It has increased purchases of Russian oil, abstained from several United Nations votes condemning Moscow and avoided directly criticizing the Kremlin.
At the same time, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has repeatedly called for dialogue. During a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin at a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan in late August, Modi urged countries to resolve disputes through peaceful means.
India and Russia nevertheless pledged to deepen their economic relationship when Modi and Putin met again during the BRICS summit in September.
Attacks threaten Black Sea food exports
India’s initiative comes as attacks on ports, grain terminals and commercial vessels have severely disrupted Black Sea shipping.
Russia and Ukraine together account for more than a quarter of global wheat exports and roughly two-thirds of international sunflower oil trade. The disruption has pushed wheat prices to three-year highs and forced importers to seek more expensive suppliers.
Ukraine’s Odesa-area ports normally handle approximately 90 percent of the country’s grain exports, but repeated Russian missile and drone attacks have damaged port infrastructure and discouraged ships from entering the region.
A Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged civilian cargo vessel in an Odesa region port on Saturday killed one crew member and injured three others.
Ukraine’s ports association has said hundreds of vessels have been damaged during Russia’s campaign against Ukrainian maritime infrastructure, warning that the disruption threatens both Ukraine’s economy and global food supplies.
Jaishankar did not say whether India was seeking to revive an arrangement similar to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which allowed Ukrainian food exports to pass through a monitored maritime corridor until Russia withdrew from the agreement in July 2023.

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launch ops to retake Bab el-Mandeb

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:27:00 UTC
21:27:00 KST

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces on Monday seized key positions on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, military sources said, in an effort to reverse Houthi advances and clear the vital waterway.
The government forces have taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks the strait and are asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition, three military sources and one government source told Reuters.
Houthi-aligned media earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area, describing such claims as "completely untrue."
Meanwhile, the Houthis late Sunday advanced onto sections of the mountain road to the major city of Taiz, besieging government forces there, according to five government sources. One other government source denied the road had been cut.
Fighting has raged along several front lines in Yemen for weeks after a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the U.S.-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.
With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Hormuz Strait, the fighting in Yemen has threatened another major oil export route, pushing up global prices and raising new risks in a region already aflame.
The internationally recognized Yemeni government announced Sunday the launch of its offensive to recapture territory, with President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia."
Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory.
Riyadh said Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets in Yemen to provide air cover for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces.
The Yemeni government said it had launched attacks on several fronts including in the province of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.
While the war has raged on several front lines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz, where the Houthis have been battling to surround government forces.
Last week, Houthi attacks damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable.
On Sunday night the group's fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, sitting atop a high promontory on the road, five government military sources said, though another government source denied this.
A Houthi-run news agency Monday meanwhile cited a military source as saying that the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council.
Those fresh advances leave Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city with a population of over half a million and a garrison of thousands of government fighters, surrounded by Houthi forces, the government military sources said.
The city, nestled among Yemen's southern highlands, has been on the front lines since early in the civil war, often under Houthi shell and sniper fire.
Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the Iran-backed group.
The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate, with most front lines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022 that held until this summer.

In Russia-occupied Oleshky, Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:26:40 UTC
21:26:40 KST

In Russia-occupied Oleshky, Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines
Ukrainians suffering from food shortages are turning to weeds for sustenance in a town where bodies are reportedly eaten by dogs.
Kyiv, Ukraine – On the day of her 41st wedding anniversary, Vera Gulyaeva recalled her husband’s life and death.
In March, a Russian drone plunged into a bread line in the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky, killing several people and wounding Serhiy Gulyaev, a retired 63-year-old driver.
The town in the Kherson region had already been occupied for more than four years, and its 2,000 remaining residents spent the last two and a half years without electricity, running water, natural gas or healthcare.
The Gulyaevs, who had met at a friends’ wedding in 1985, lived in a small house they had built. They were reluctant to leave even after their children fled to Kyiv-controlled areas.
They had an orchid, a vegetable patch, five hens, a water well and a power generator that ran on the overpriced gas they occasionally bought from middlemen.
“I almost never left the house,” Gulyaeva, a stately 64-year-old retired schoolteacher told Al Jazeera. “The husband occasionally went out to buy bread.”
The bread-line attack left him with deep cranial wounds. She tried to get him to a hospital 80km (50 miles) away in the city of Skadovsk but failed as the ambulance ran over a landmine on the road.
Days later, a second attempt worked – but Gulyaev died in the hospital.
She recovered his remains, had them cremated and returned home with his ashes.
Now, she lives in western Ukraine with her daughter-in-law and two grandchildren while her son fights Russian forces.
Gulyaeva left behind all her family photos, friends and neighbours – several of whom have since died.
“People ate all of the food they’d stashed. People are starving,” Gulyaeva said of the food shortage stalking the town.
After four decades of teaching in the elementary school she had attended as a child, she still cannot fathom “how people can kill other people”.
Some residents survive on what they have farmed, stashed or found in abandoned apartments or houses. Others try to reach the nearest functioning grocery shop in the neighbouring village of Radensk, 20km (12.4 miles) away, to buy food.
But some never return.
A resident who fled the town but remains in contact with some residents told Al Jazeera that people have been killed by Russian drones or landmines. The bodies left out in the open are eaten by feral dogs.
On Thursday alone, there were four casualties. As they tried to get to Radensk, two people were killed and two were injured and brought back on a wheelbarrow and a bike.
“The choice that Russia leaves every day to civilian residents – stay and starve to death, leave and risk getting blown on a landmine,” Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram on Saturday.
European officials said the situation in Oleshky proves that Kyiv should not give in to Moscow’s demands to cede its land.
“When someone says: ‘Why don’t they just give up these territories?’ it sounds so simple. Right? But in reality, this is about the people who will suffer on those territories,” European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said on September 28.
Moscow, which has denied targeting civilians throughout the war, has acknowledged the humanitarian disaster but blamed Kyiv.
“There are, indeed, problems with delivering food and medical drugs [because] the Kyiv regime literally does everything to thwart these deliveries,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed on September 20. “Drones always hover in the air, killing people.”
Pro-Russian figures in occupied areas support his claims.
“Those who wanted to leave have left. No one is being held here,” an anonymous pro-Russian woman who runs a Telegram channel on life in Oleshky wrote on September 28. “Unfortunately, locals are afraid to speak on camera” because they have relatives on the Ukrainian side, she claimed. “The elderly live under Ukrainian shelling but are afraid to talk.”
Her claims are a far cry from what Ukrainian officials say.
‘There’s nothing’
Most Oleshky residents eat once a day, according to Tetiana Khasanenko, Oleshky’s mayor, who fled to the Kyiv-controlled side but maintains constant contact with the remaining residents.
Some have found old, dried macaroni to sustain themselves. Some eat whatever they manage to grow next to their houses. And some resort to common purslane – a watery weed that contains next to no protein and can be eaten raw.
“There’s no flour, no meat, no oil, no sugar, no salt,” Hasanenko told Al Jazeera. “There’s nothing.”
She accused Russia of using the residents as human shields.
Russian soldiers are a constant threat in the town with no functioning civilian administration, she said.
They move into the remaining houses without permission and force the residents to feed them and find alcohol.
“They’re often on drugs,” Hasanenko claimed. “But they’re armed. They threaten.”
Oleshky is about 10km (6 miles) west of the regional capital, Kherson, but Russians blew up the 1,400-metre (1,530-yard) bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Europe’s largest, in November 2022 while retreating from the city.
The delivery of food and drugs is perilous and complicated.
The last attempts to get lifesaving cargo to Oleshky in cars were cut short by landmines and drone attacks.
Ukraine has managed to fly several tonnes of food on drones, but retrieving it is complicated.
Most survivors have left their war-damaged houses and apartment buildings to move to the buildings that are more or less intact.
And even if some people manage to charge their mobile phones and contact the Ukrainian side, they “don’t give exact geolocations because they’re afraid”, Hasanenko said.
“Because if there’s a food drop, Russian soldiers will punish them for it,” she said.
Knowing about the remaining residents’ daily ordeal, those who escaped are tormented with guilt.
“You don’t get any joy from life knowing that something like that is happening in our country,” Gulyeva said. “This is a huge tragedy.”

New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:26:15 UTC
21:26:15 KST

New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
Automated machine gun turrets using artificial intelligence to aim have downed their first Russian jet-powered drones over Ukraine, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Oct. 5.
A day prior, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
"There are already cases of shooting down even jet UAVs, even 'Geran-5' from the those very turrets," Ihnat said on national television.
"The use of innovative technologies — artificial intelligence — has eliminated human error. Machine vision is used in the shooting down. Artificial intelligence allows you to target even jet-powered drones."
Since Russia started using jet-powered drones en masse against Kyiv toward the end of summer this year, they, especially the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, have presented an air defense problem for which Ukraine has not yet found a single solution.
Most existing interceptor drones, which were responsible for downing the majority of Russia’s Shahed-type attack drones until recently, are not fast enough to intercept jet-powered drones.
Jet-powered interceptors are actively in development, but producing them at the scale required to contain the jet-powered drone threat is likely impossible due to the lack of supply chains for cheap jet engines in the West.
In the meantime, advances in artificial intelligence technology have led to better automatic aiming systems, allowing small arms like U.S.-made Browning heavy machine guns to add to Ukraine's anti-drone air defense network.

Details: The figure stood at 14.1% in 2025 and rose to 22% in August 2026. All three of the indicators monitored – the number of air-raid warnings, number of warnings issued during shopping centre opening hours, and total duration – increased over the past month.
Yellow-level alerts accounted for 60.9% of the total duration of warnings in September, compared with 39.1% for red-level alerts. [In Ukraine's air-raid warning system, yellow alerts indicate a drone threat and red alerts a missile threat – ed.]

On average, air-raid alerts have forced shopping centres across Ukraine to close for 176.5 working days since the full-scale invasion began, including 9.6 working days in September.

Lauch declined to comment on the exact circumstances, but said between 150 and 200 protesters had been hurling a series of objects at police when riot officers intervened. It was uncertain if the incident had involved a police stun grenade or how the injury happened. Lauch said an investigation had been opened.
The family of a 16-year-old school pupil in Tours also filed a complaint about police violence after he lost sight in his right eye last week. The state prosecutor said the boy’s injuries were in line with the impact from a police rubber bullet. A police investigation is under way.
The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, had earlier attempted to calm the protests by accepting schoolchildren’s grievances as “legitimate” and saying the government must listen.
Lecornu ordered ministers to tackle the students’ five major demands. These include organising the replacement of absent teachers, in recognition that pupils in some areas miss months of teaching because of staff absences – even in key exam years. Lecornu also called for a review of France’s lengthy school days, which are among the longest in Europe.
The government will also look at repairs to dilapidated school buildings. Children on blockades across France have described water leaking into classrooms during class, cockroaches, collapsing ceilings and unbearable heat in summer. Lecornu said ministers must come up with proposals by the end of the month.

“Amid such anger, a few measures just for show aren’t going to satisfy demands,” Binet said. She called for the government to instead stop all budget cuts as well as cuts to teachers’ positions.
Student unions have called for a national day of protest on Tuesday with more schools expected to be barricaded. Thousands of trade unionists, teachers, public sector workers and parents’ groups are expected to join marches of support in cities and towns across France.
Binet said trade unionists would march to ensure there was no violence on the edge of any protests on Tuesday, as she criticised heavy policing. “We’ve been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students,” she said.
University students continued to support the school protests on Monday, with up to 40 university buildings blockaded across France. Philippe Baptiste, the minister for higher education, told French radio he felt student and high school protests could intensify with the national protests due to take place on Tuesday.
Between 400 and 500 high schools are expected to remain completely or partly closed on Monday out of a total of 3,700, the minister said.
A government spokesperson, Maud Bregeon, told CNews television on Monday: “Our priority is to restore order.”
The protests began in late September at a high school in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages. The government was taken by surprise as protests then spread nationwide, amid anger at social inequality and a lack of investment in the education system.
Since last Monday, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across France and dozens injured.
Teachers have also been injured. Damage to property is estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

They have referred the case to police internal affairs, which is now engaged in six investigations into serious injuries that have occurred during the student protests.

Scrutiny
The Lens incident has added to scrutiny of police tactics during the demonstrations. Amnesty International France has criticised what it described as disproportionate police force against minors, saying it was alarmed by reports of students being hit with batons and subjected to tear gas and rubber-bullet fire known as LBDs.
The rights group said many of those taking part were minors under 18 and called on authorities to ensure policing methods were proportionate and compatible with France’s human rights obligations.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”.
The Education Ministry said 589 schools had been disrupted on Monday, down from 735 on Friday, according to figures reported by Le Monde. Earlier estimates had suggested between 400 and 500 of France’s 3,700 high schools could be fully or partially closed.
Equal right
Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide.
Geffray said on Sunday that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked during the protests, with 78 teaching staff injured.

“They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added.
