Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:55:00 EEST
20:55:00 KST

Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
Eight military personnel were killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast on 29 September. At least three of them were officers involved in combat missions or their preparation, according to the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and people who betrayed Ukraine.
Source: Russian media outlets Mediazona and The Insider
Details: Russian media outlets reported that the names of those killed had been posted in the Selskiye Novosti (Rural News) social media group for Seryshevo, a settlement near the Ukrainka strategic air base. OSINT analyst duke garland was the first to flag the post.
A photo featuring the portraits of the eight men killed was also released by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast. He said the local authorities would ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state awards.
Mediazona verified the list and confirmed that all eight served in Russia's strategic aviation.
According to the media outlets, those killed are:
- Andrei Lobanov, 40
- Vladislav Moskovskikh, 31
- Artur Yenokian, 30
- Mikhail Kotyshev, 23
- Sergei, 47, whose surname is reported as Monsevich by Mediazona and Moisevich by The Insider
- Vladimir Kelip, 55
- Fedor Pavlyukov, 43
- Andrei Gerasimov, 36.
The OSINT analyst believes the portraits in the announcement follow the standard order in which Tu-95MS crew members are listed. On that basis, Lobanov was the crew commander, Moskovskikh the co-pilot, Yenokian the navigator, Kotyshev the navigator-operator (responsible for operating the bomber's mission systems), Monsevich the flight engineer, and Kelip the radio operator. Pavlyukov and Gerasimov were likely passengers or inspectors.
Mediazona says the quality of the photograph makes it difficult to establish the military ranks of all those killed with certainty.
The Insider checked the names against the Ukrainian Book of Executioners database and found Lobanov, Pavlyukov and Gerasimov in its records. Details about them had been added before the plane crashed.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as the deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at the Ukrainka airfield. According to the project, he directly commanded the unit and personally participated in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as the regiment's deputy commander for flight training. He commanded a Tu-95MS squadron from August 2021 to April 2024. According to the project, he was responsible for preparing flight personnel for combat missions and directly led the unit.
Furthermore, in March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence included Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots who, according to its data, were being prepared to participate in the war against Ukraine.
Andrei Gerasimov is listed in the Book of Executioners as a major and commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. According to the database, he commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions. However, Mediazona's casualty list gives his rank as lieutenant colonel.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatolii Shtefan also reported that at least three of those killed were involved in organising and executing missile strikes on Ukraine. Shtefan did not specify whom exactly he was referring to.
According to Port Amur, cited by The Insider, there were nine military personnel on board. The bodies of two of the crew members were not found immediately. The Russian Ministry of Defence initially reported six dead and one taken to hospital.
Background:
- On 29 September, the Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast.
- The Russian Defence Ministry claimed that the bomber was conducting a training flight without ammunition when it crashed in an unpopulated area. Regional authorities said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential buildings, and no one on the ground was injured.
- The Russian Defence Ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to the site to establish what caused the crash. Kommersant reported that investigators had tentatively attributed it to a technical malfunction. The Insider notes, however, that no conclusions about the cause of the crash have been publicly confirmed.
- According to Mediazona, most of those killed had served at the Engels strategic bomber airbase in Saratov Oblast before moving to the Ukrainka airbase. According to the outlet, Russia began pulling its strategic bombers out of Engels after Ukraine launched its first drone attacks on the airfield.
- After the Security Service of Ukraine carried out Operation Spider's Web, the Ukrainka airbase in Russia's Far East became one of the main bases for its strategic aviation. According to The Insider, a Tu-95MS combat mission from the base, involving stopovers at Engels or Olenya airfield, missile launches and the return flight, can cover more than 12,000 km and last around 23 hours. The outlet notes that flights of this length accelerate wear on the aircraft and their engines, shortening their service life.

Monogatari Corp., operator of the Yakiniku King barbecue restaurant chain, said information belonging to more than 10 million customers was leaked after unauthorized access to its reservation and rewards app, according to Kyodo News.
The compromised information included customers’ names, email addresses, phone numbers and membership numbers.

Separately, Daiwa Securities Group said data belonging to around 110,000 customers of its brokerage unit may have been compromised following unauthorized access to a contractor-operated server, Kyodo reported.

Potentially exposed information includes names, email addresses and account numbers.
Including inquiries that contained no personal information, around 220,000 pieces of data may have been affected.
Daiwa said the compromised information could not be used to conduct transactions, including online trades.
The brokerage has also found no evidence so far that the potentially compromised information has been published or circulated online.

Russia’s New Molniya-13 Recon Drone Reaches Ukraine Months After Its Debut—and Gets Downed
Ukrainian forces have intercepted a new Russian Molniya-13 reconnaissance drone, a system first unveiled in Russia in June 2026, Ukraine’s 8th Air Assault Corps reported on October 5.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The unit said it had successfully intercepted the UAV and released footage showing the wreckage of the downed aircraft.
“This is a new Molniya that flew our way. It is one and a half times larger than the standard one. It has four engines,” a Ukrainian service member said while examining the remains of the drone.
According to the 8th Air Assault Corps, the Molniya-13 is designed for reconnaissance, monitoring, and search-and-rescue operations. The drone is a relatively recent Russian development, having been publicly presented for the first time in June 2026.
In general, the Molniya is a relatively simple Russian fixed-wing attack drone designed mainly to carry explosive payloads. It has an estimated operational range of 30 to 40 kilometers and can transport a warhead of up to seven kilograms. Adapted variants have also been used for reconnaissance missions and to adjust artillery fire.
Beyond strike and reconnaissance missions, Russian forces have also been experimenting with Molniya drones for logistics. Footage previously released by the Sunstrike unmanned systems unit of Ukraine’s 82nd Separate Air Assault Brigade showed the drones being tested to deliver weapons and other supplies to frontline positions.
The footage showed several configurations adapted to transport different types of cargo, including one drone carrying a rifle and another fitted with a package of supplies.

Ai Weiwei: "We are losing privacy and without it we stop being individuals"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:49:44 UTC
20:49:44 KST

The artist warns of the dangers of using AI as a tool of censorship during his visit to Belgium, where he will open a major retrospective this autumn.
If there is anyone in the art world with the legitimacy to question narratives of power, it is Ai Weiwei. The Chinese artist spent his childhood in exile with his family in a remote region of China because of Mao's repression and decided to leave his country in 2015 after suffering intense state persecution for drawing attention to the more than 5,000 schoolchildren who died in the 2008 Sichuan earthquake. Now, at 69 and living a quiet life in his country house in Portugal's Alentejo, he remains on his guard and directs his distrust towards Western democracies and their use of artificial intelligence as a subtle form of censorship.
"It may be too late to avoid its dangers. We no longer have privacy and when individuals have no privacy they are no longer individuals, but become the perfect product," declared Ai Weiwei at Brussels' Bozar Centre for Fine Arts, in front of the more than 2,000 people who had packed the main auditorium to attend the conversation between the artist and Belgian cultural manager Chris Dercon, of the Fondation Cartier, about his latest book 'Ai Weiwei on Censorship' (Thames & Hudson, 2026), held at the beginning of October.
For a creator who cannot conceive a separation between art and political dissent, the main obstacle citizens face in Western society is the tendency towards self-censorship for fear of reprisals. "But in fact, here everyone is free to express and think whatever they like," remarked Chris Dercon. "In reality it is not like that, because there is always a shared agreement guided by authority, by the state, which sets what is correct and acceptable and what is not," replied Ai Weiwei, and he insisted on "the power of the individual" to change unjust realities, since "each of us is different", he added.
This respect for difference, made invisible by those in power, is a common thread in Ai Weiwei's work. One example is the piece 'Sunflower Seeds' (2010), in which he filled London's Tate Modern with millions of seeds crafted by thousands of artisans as unique ceramic pieces which, once brought together, created a perceptual play between homogeneity and difference and invited the viewer to reflect on the tensions between the individual and the mass.
The message was even clearer in his work 'Remembering' (2009), when he intervened on the façade of Munich's Haus der Kunst, a building that the Nazi regime used to spread its idea of culture through works of art, with 9,000 school backpacks belonging to children who died during the Sichuan earthquake, arranged so that they formed the phrase in Chinese "She lived happily for seven years in this world". The words came from a conversation the artist had with one of the mothers of the girls who died. "She only wanted people to know that her seven-year-old daughter had been happy while she was alive and I promised I would help her fulfil her wish," explained Ai Weiwei.
Art as activism
He recalled the consequences of his activism in denouncing the poor state of school infrastructure in China, as well as the secrecy of the state in failing to reveal the names of the victims or the real number of dead.
"The police came for me at three in the morning and I realised how weak I was because a single blow knocked me to the ground," he recalled. He then showed selfies of his condition afterwards in hospital, in which he stuck his middle finger up at the camera, at the Chinese government. Later came the nightmare of arrest, with more violence, followed by a period of confinement in his own home and years of being unable to leave his country after his passport was confiscated.
As interviewer that evening, Chris Dercon raised a question: why are your artworks always either very small or very large? "Small or large is only an illusion," replied Ai Weiwei. "Planet Earth may seem big, but the Earth is so small within the universe that you could not even find it," he continued. "Thousands of people have been killed in Uganda; and in Ukraine thousands of soldiers have lost limbs in the war and they may even consider themselves lucky because they are not dead. Compared with all that, what I do with my art is nothing," the activist stressed.
This gave rise to a dialogue laced with irony, as befits artists who are aware of their own contradictions. "I have never considered myself a Chinese artist, although my stomach is certainly made for Chinese restaurants," Ai joked. There were also revealing anecdotes, such as the time when Lego refused to sell him bricks to use in a work because it did not want its products to be used for a political purpose; "as if that statement were not political in itself," the artist confessed.
After a brief tour through a life story entwined with protest and art, shaped by the legacy of his father Ai Qing's poetry, there was a desire to round off the portrait with a question about how he would describe himself. "I would give a completely different answer depending on the era of my life," he replied. "But I would define myself as someone with a great curiosity about the human condition, freedom of expression, human rights and artistic creation."
For the culture lovers who had gathered to welcome Ai Weiwei in Brussels, it became clear that no action is fortuitous for a contemporary artist who is always conscious of the context in which he places his works. "Some people are not more civilised because they make others suffer more," he said, referring to the suffering of Congo at the hands of Belgium during the colonial era.
Two exhibitions
Thus the autumn cultural season in Brussels was inaugurated, and this year a large part of the spotlight falls on this artist with the show 'Ai Weiwei: The Art of Defiance' at the Patrick Derom gallery until 14 November, and 'Ai Weiwei: Life, Revolt, Poetry. An homage to Ai Qing & Emile Verhaeren', on display at the Émile Verhaeren museum until 13 December.
The former is presented as the first major Ai Weiwei retrospective in Belgium, with works that span the different formats he has used throughout his career to defend freedom of expression in the face of state repression. The latter, more personal in tone, brings the great Belgian poet Émile Verhaeren into dialogue with the poet Ai Qing, Ai Weiwei's father, who helped spread Verhaeren's legacy in Asia by being the first to translate his poems into Chinese.
A fitting moment in the European capital to welcome an artist who invites us to awaken our critical awareness and not to go through life without at least attempting some act of dissent, however small, against widespread injustice.

China-Linked Hackers Pose as US Officials in Bid to Breach America’s AI Experts

China-Linked Hackers Pose as US Officials in Bid to Breach America’s AI Experts
China-linked hackers attempted to breach the cloud accounts of US artificial intelligence policy experts by posing as former senior American officials and an employee of AI company Anthropic, using fake policy outreach to lure targets into handing over their Microsoft credentials.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense One on October 1, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint linked the campaign to TA419, a China-aligned hacking group that researchers say operates in support of Beijing’s intelligence interests. The hackers targeted AI specialists at US think tanks, universities, and law firms.
The attackers approached researchers with invitations to advise on AI policy and export controls, presenting the messages as legitimate professional outreach. Once a recipient engaged, the hackers followed up with links directing them to a fake OneDrive page designed to steal Microsoft login credentials.
Among those impersonated were Lynne Parker, a former principal deputy director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, and Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who previously served as the State Department’s first chief economist.
Beginning July 8, the hackers posed as Parker and Crebo-Rediker while inviting AI experts to join a fictitious “AI Policy Advisory Committee” or contribute to a purported Senate Foreign Relations Committee report on AI export controls and supply chains, according to Defense One.
Proofpoint also identified a similar operation in February, when the group impersonated a senior Anthropic employee while contacting an AI policy analyst at a US think tank. The message carried the subject line “Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude,” referring to discussions over the military use of Anthropic’s AI models.
Proofpoint said the hackers have “consistently shown an interest in defense, national security, energy, international relations, and foreign policy targets, predominantly with a nexus to the US and Japan.” The company assessed that targeting AI policy experts represented an expansion of the group’s existing intelligence interests.
Parker learned about the impersonation on July 9 after two recipients contacted her separately to verify whether she had sent the emails. She confirmed the messages were fraudulent and subsequently warned other colleagues, Defense One reported.
The hackers also registered web addresses impersonating the Heritage Foundation, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, and the Japan–Taiwan Exchange Association, according to Proofpoint. Such domains could be used to make fraudulent approaches appear more credible to potential targets.
The report did not establish how many people were targeted, whether any accounts were successfully breached, or whether the hackers ultimately obtained sensitive information.
Earlier, Russian state-backed hackers were reported to have targeted the email systems of US nuclear scientists, defense contractors, and government employees, with researchers linking the campaign to intelligence gathering on nuclear research, military logistics, procurement, and policy.

Geran-5 Gets Kh-101-Like Guidance as Russia Pushes Its Jet Drones Toward Full Autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:49:25 UTC
20:49:25 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Geran-5 Gets Kh-101-Like Guidance as Russia Pushes Its Jet Drones Toward Full Autonomy
Russia has equipped its newer jet-powered Geran drones with an electro-optical navigation system that lets them autonomously fly toward targets by comparing camera imagery with a stored visual map of the route, bringing their guidance concept closer to that used on some Kh-101 cruise missiles, Defense Express reported on October 5.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence recently released new details on the Geran-5 K5 and a newer Geran-4 variant that Russian forces began using this fall. Both reportedly carry a system known as Susannin, designed to reduce the drone’s dependence on an external control signal during the flight.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rather than relying on an operator continuously steering the aircraft through a communications network, Susannin uses onboard imagery. The drone compares what its camera sees below with reference images loaded into the system and uses those visual matches to determine where it is and continue along its programmed route.
In practical terms, the aircraft can navigate by “looking” at the terrain. Defense Express notes that this means mesh modems and airborne mesh repeaters are not necessarily required for the drone to reach its intended target, since the navigation process can continue autonomously without a constant outside command link.
A similar principle has already appeared in more sophisticated Russian long-range weapons. One version of the air-launched Kh-101 cruise missile, known as Izdeliye 504AP, used an optical navigation system called Otblesk-U during Russian missile strikes against Ukraine between 2022 and 2025.
That comparison is important because it shows Russia gradually transferring technologies associated with expensive cruise missiles into cheaper unmanned strike systems. The goal appears to be making jet-powered Geran drones increasingly independent, accurate, and less reliant on vulnerable communications links during their approach to a target.
The change also comes as Ukraine becomes more effective at intercepting Russia’s newer jet-powered UAVs. Defense Express estimates that Ukrainian forces are already destroying roughly 50% to 60% of them, meaning that only around four or five out of every 10 launched may currently reach their targets.
Improving autonomous navigation could therefore be part of Russia’s effort to increase the number of drones that survive long enough to complete their missions, particularly as Ukraine expands dedicated interceptor-drone units and other counter-UAV defenses.
The Geran-5 and newer Geran-4 are part of a broader Russian effort to move beyond the original propeller-driven Shahed concept. Their jet propulsion already gives them significantly greater speed, while systems such as Susannin add another layer of sophistication by allowing the aircraft to navigate visually without depending on continuous external guidance.
The result is a weapon that increasingly sits somewhere between a conventional one-way strike drone and a small cruise missile: cheaper and simpler than weapons such as the Kh-101, but borrowing some of the same ideas in navigation and terminal autonomy.
Earlier, a Geran-type drone equipped with a turbojet engine entered Moldovan airspace and later crashed and exploded near a road in the Orhei district on the evening of September 30.

Estonia Moves Troops Toward Russian Border, Prepares 300-Km Deep Strikes Under New Defense Strategy
Estonia is moving key combat units closer to its border with Russia and expanding its long-range strike capabilities under a new “active defense” strategy aimed at confronting a potential attack from forward positions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 5, the headquarters of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade—the country’s main combat formation—is being permanently relocated from Tapa to Jõhvi, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Russian border, where new military facilities are under construction.
“We have to start at the border and win the first battles,” Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the brigade, told the Financial Times.
The move represents a shift from Estonia’s previous strategy, which envisioned slowing an invading force while waiting for NATO reinforcements. Under the new approach, Estonian forces intend to defend territory from forward positions and strike military targets deep behind enemy lines from the beginning of an attack.
Estonia is also building a military base in Narva, directly on the Russian border. The facility is expected to permanently host about 200 troops and accommodate up to 1,000 personnel during a crisis.
At the same time, Tallinn is expanding its long-range firepower. Estonia is set to field nine US-made HIMARS and nine South Korean K239 Chunmoo launchers, with available munitions capable of reaching approximately 300 kilometers. The Financial Times noted that St. Petersburg is about 260 kilometers from Estonia’s eastern military positions.
“To make deterrence credible, we have to make aggression against us unthinkable. Our goal is clear: keep the enemy and the destructive consequences of war away from Estonian territory,” Estonia’s Defense Ministry said, according to the Financial Times.
The shift comes as Estonia increases defense spending to approximately €2.4 billion in 2026, or about 5.4% of GDP, with €1.27 billion allocated to weapons and other defense procurement.
Estonian intelligence does not currently assess a Russian attack on NATO as imminent. Officials cited by the Financial Times said they do not expect Moscow to seek a full-scale war with NATO within at least the next two years, but warned that Russia’s military restructuring could increase the threat in the longer term.
Earlier, Estonian security officials warned of a pro-Russian influence campaign promoting the creation of a so-called “Narva People’s Republic.” The campaign, reported by BILD in March, included calls for sabotage and armed resistance, with Estonian intelligence warning that it could be intended to prepare the ground for a scenario similar to Russia’s actions in eastern Ukraine in 2014.

Instagram turns 16 with 3 billion users under shadow of data privacy, mental health concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:49:11 UTC
20:49:11 KST

Dilara Zengin and Emir Yildirim 
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Instagram is celebrating its 16th anniversary since the social media giant was launched and emerged as a dominant force in the global digital economy, boasting over 3 billion monthly active users, but escalating scrutiny over data privacy and youth mental health casts dark shadows over the platform’s success.
Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger launched Instagram as a photo-sharing app on Oct. 6, 2010.
The platform was acquired by Meta two years later for around $1 billion, and the social media titan grew even further with the introduction of video sharing and direct messages in 2013 and short-form Reels in 2020.
India has the platform’s largest user base, accounting for 480 million active users, followed by the US, Brazil, Indonesia, Japan, Türkiye, Mexico, the UK, Germany, and Argentina, according to Statista’s October 2025 data.
The platform is overwhelmingly youth-led, with around 34% of its global users aged 25-34, while those aged 18-24 make up 27.6% of the user base.
Instagram gave rise to the modern influencer economy as profiles with large followings are able to leverage their demographic reach on the app.
In-app shopping features released in 2020 established an e-commerce showcase for major brands and independent entrepreneurs.
At the same time, the platform is facing regulatory and legal pushback around the world amid its commercial and social expansion.
The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Instagram €405 million ($453.6 million) in 2022 for violating EU regulations protecting the personal data of minors.
Some 41 US states sued Meta the following year over allegedly addictive features of the app that harm children’s mental health. The dispute led to a settlement in August this year.
Yasmin Ibrahim, deputy dean of the business school and digital economy professor at Queen Mary University of London, told Anadolu that Instagram reshaped the relationship between visibility, social interaction, and commerce, allowing users to turn their routines into marketable assets without a high entry cost.
Ibrahim stated that Instagram users often struggle to tell commercial endorsements apart from real social interactions due to the seamless integration of sponsored products, which places social media influencers in an ambiguous position, blurring the line between friend, celebrity, and sales representative.
The platform has also fostered a culture of comparison among its young user base.
Ibrahim said the platform’s visually driven architecture makes users evaluate and compare their bodies, achievements, and unedited realities with the heavily edited and curated lives of internet strangers.
She warned that this environment fuels and exacerbates social anxieties about not being enough, not consuming enough, or not living life to the fullest.
She mentioned that content saturation leads to a situation where users feel attention fatigue but still feel compelled to return due to the fear of missing out, while the platform allows users to consume other people’s experiences and imagine possibilities by seeing the lives of others enhanced by filters and edits.
She added that Instagram integrates ads into social spaces and transforms the social sphere into a source of commercial value.

Ukraine turns to AI against Russia’s new jet drones

Their introduction caught Ukrainian defenses off guard. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has acknowledged that Kyiv is currently intercepting only about 60% of the new drones, relying heavily on F-16 and MiG fighter jets.
Ukraine is now racing to develop another answer.
Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said 12 automated firing positions have been deployed around Kyiv to intercept the new jet-powered Shahed drones.

The new drones pose a particular problem because their speed makes them harder for existing Ukrainian interception systems to catch.

Moscow warned Monday that Kyiv would face consequences if the campaign intensified.

Will Yemen's massive new anti-Houthi offensive succeed in bid to reclaim lost territory? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:45:15 UTC
20:45:15 KST

Yemeni government forces launched a new offensive against the Iranian-backed Houthis on Monday. They claimed to be advancing near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and carrying out strikes on Houthi positions across several provinces.
The offensive marks a new phase in the conflict. In September, the Houthis seized a strip of land on the Red Sea coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This shocked Saudi Arabia, which has backed the Yemen government. It also led to alarm bells in Washington.
Now, with the apparent prodding of Riyadh, Yemen’s government is trying to rally its numerous disconnected front lines to fight the Houthis.
The problem is that the government forces are not well united. They have fronts in southern Yemen, around Taiz, and others in northern Yemen.
Southern Yemen was, until last December, controlled by the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council. The front lines had remained relatively stable following the 2022 truce.
Yemen aims to retake territory, banish Houthis, and restore state institutions
Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council President Rashad al-Alimi has called the new campaign “Dawn of Yemen.” The operation is intended to restore state institutions, eventually retake Sanaa, and end Houthi control over large parts of the country, Saudi Arabia-based newspaper Arab News reported.
The problem is that the government also hinted at an offensive in September, but it was dealt a blow by the Houthis.
The Houthis are continuing to advance, according to a recent report by the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank. What that means is that even as the government tries to advance, the Houthis appear to still be winning on some fronts.
“With the will of our people, the bravery of our forces, and the support of our brothers, Yemen will move toward a new dawn,” Arab News quoted Alimi as saying on Monday.
The operation follows several days of escalation. On Sunday, Alimi said government forces would begin operations to recapture territory still controlled by the Houthis.
“Today, we are embarking on a decisive phase in the history of our nation,” he said, according to Arab News. The operation was aimed at the Houthis rather than civilians living in Houthi-controlled areas, he added.
The fighting is particularly important along Yemen’s western coast. Government forces had taken control of Thubab, near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, after advancing from the Kahbub Mountains, Arab News reported on Monday. Government forces are also seeking to secure the area around the strait and push north along the coast, the report said.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is strategically important because it connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Control of territory overlooking the strait gives the Houthis potential leverage over a major international shipping route, particularly at a time of wider regional tensions involving Iran.
Yemeni government forces also say they have intensified operations on other fronts. Maj.-Gen. Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the Yemeni Armed Forces, said Yemeni forces had carried out 1,122 strikes or targeting operations against Houthi military infrastructure in Saada, Al-Jawf, and Taiz.
The operations had killed or otherwise “neutralized” 1,747 Houthi personnel and destroyed or disabled 364 vehicles and other pieces of equipment, he said. These figures are government claims and have not been independently verified. Arab News reported the figures based on Nuzaili’s statement.
The Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen has pledged continued support for the offensive. On Monday, the coalition said 100 aircraft had participated in the opening phase of Operation Dawn of Yemen, and that it was providing air cover around Bab el-Mandeb Strait as well as continuous support for Yemeni forces on the ground, Arab News reported.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, emerged from the Zaydi Shi’ite community in northern Yemen and have fought a series of wars against the Yemeni government since 2004. The group expanded during the instability that followed the 2011 Arab Spring and seized Sanaa in 2014.
Saudi Arabia led a military intervention in March 2015, supporting the internationally recognized government, while Iran increasingly provided support to the Houthis. The Houthis developed ballistic missiles and long-range attack drones with Iranian advice and support.
Years of fighting left Yemen divided and created a humanitarian crisis. A UN-mediated truce in 2022 significantly reduced large-scale combat even after it formally expired, leaving the front lines largely stagnant.
The Houthis, nevertheless, continued developing increasingly capable ballistic missiles and drones. Beginning in late 2023, they launched attacks against shipping in the Red Sea and toward Israel.
Government forces determined to reverse territorial losses
The US under the Biden administration encouraged some countries to help keep the Red Sea shipping route open. The Trump administration carried out strikes against the Houthis in March 2025.
The latest fighting could change things, but previous reports of offensives tended to not pan out.
Government forces are now attempting to reverse their territorial losses and reassert government control over strategically important areas of Yemen. They face the Houthis, who have strong interior lines and have tended to win in the past.
On Monday, the Houthis said they had seized Alimi's home in Taiz, UAE-based news site Al-Ain News reported.
“Earlier on Monday, Houthi militias seized control of the Aloum area, where Alimi’s house is located, in Taiz province (256 km southwest of Sanaa),” the report said. “Hundreds of Houthi fighters attacked the Aloum area in Al-Mawasit district in the countryside of Taiz governorate early this morning.”
“Sources told Al-Ain News that the Houthi militias seized Al-Alimi’s house following violent clashes with Yemeni forces and residents in Al-Mawasit district, located in the heart of the historic Al-Hajariya region,” it added. “The Houthi militias seized Al-Alimi’s house in Al-Uloom after they took control yesterday of the house of the speaker of the Yemeni Parliament, Sheikh Sultan Al-Barakani, and captured the city of Al-Turbah, the capital of Al-Hujariya and the second-largest city in Taiz.”
The Houthis had imposed a siege on the city of Taiz, the report said, adding that they were trying to preempt the government offensive.
They attacked “in anticipation of the military operation being carried out by the Southern Giants forces on the coasts of the governorate, specifically in Bab el-Mandeb and the Dhubab district,” Al-Ain News reported.

Israel is the second-most targeted country in the world, and first in the Middle East, by cyberattacks, according to Microsoft’s 2026 “Digital Defense Report ” published on Thursday.
The United States ranked first with 531 observed events, while Israel had 210. Taiwan and Japan follow with 193 and 172, respectively, before a significant drop-off with the United Kingdom in fifth place.
The report also mentioned that Israel experienced a 21% surge in ransomware attacks since 2025.
Iran is considered to be a major source of Israel’s cyber incidents, the report mentioned, noting that the government of the Islamic Republic is known to be conducting broad, multi-layered campaigns against Israel and other adversaries throughout the Middle East, especially since the start of its war with the US and Israel this year.
The report also said that Iranian forces have recently expanded cyber and influence operations designed to target and disrupt military and information activities, while attempting to expand “strategic messaging and operational impact.”
Israel's head of National Cyber Directorate says Israel in a constant battle
Israel National Cyber Directorate Chief Yossi Karadi addressed the report, saying, “The State of Israel is in an intense campaign in cyberspace and stands at the forefront of global threats. As the national cyber defense organization, our mission is to minimize as much as possible the impact of attacks, prevent harm to citizens and essential services, and enable the country to continue functioning even under a continuous threat.”
He went on to say, “The fact that Israel maintains functional continuity under such a volume of threats is not to be taken for granted. It is the result of an integrated national defense system in which the INCD operates alongside defense bodies, government ministries, the economy, the cyber industry, and global companies.”
Karadi emphasized that in cyberspace, there is no ceasefire, and although “you may not see missiles in the air, the fight in cyberspace is waged on a 24/7 basis.”
He also discussed AI’s accelerating role in the field, and the challenges that come with its ability to intensify attacks and transform the cyber landscape.
“Faced with this reality, we will continue to develop advanced capabilities, deepen collaborations, and strengthen national resilience. In cyberspace, victories are often quiet victories expressed in blocked attacks, prevented damage, and the continuation of routines,” he said.

After meeting in Turkey, can Syria's new government manage tensions with Hezbollah? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:44:41 UTC
20:44:41 KST

A disputed report of secret talks between Syrian officials and Hezbollah representatives in Turkey has raised a broad question: Could border security, weapons smuggling, and armed networks lead Syria’s new government and Hezbollah to establish a limited channel for managing tensions?
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Such contact would not necessarily signal reconciliation or restore the previous alliance Hezbollah maintained with Bashar Assad’s government.
Reuters reported on Oct. 1 that Syrian government officials and Hezbollah representatives held direct talks in Turkey in September aimed at reducing friction between the two sides. The report cited six sources, including two Syrian officials, a US official, and a senior Lebanese security source close to Hezbollah.
According to Reuters, Turkish security and intelligence officials helped facilitate the contact, which addressed issues including weapons smuggling and Hezbollah-linked cells inside Syria.
Damascus and Ankara, however, categorically denied the account.
Syrian authorities deny meeting with Hezbollah
Syrian authorities said the claims were false and that “no such meeting took place.” The denial was accompanied by a more detailed statement from Syrian presidential media adviser Ahmad Muwaffaq Zaidan, who rejected reports of contacts with Hezbollah and said Damascus’ approach toward Lebanon is based on dealing with the Lebanese state and its official institutions.
Zaidan said negotiations with Lebanon should be conducted “with the state, not a militia,” while stressing Damascus’ support for Lebanese sovereignty, border control, and the concentration of political and military decision-making in the hands of state institutions.
Turkey also denied hosting any such meeting. The Turkish presidency’s Center for Combating Disinformation said claims that Syrian officials and Hezbollah representatives met in Turkey under the auspices of Turkish intelligence were “completely baseless.” It said the reported date, location, content, and participants did not reflect reality and described the allegations as fabricated.
The result is a direct contradiction between the Reuters account and the official Syrian and Turkish denials, meaning the alleged meeting cannot be treated as an established fact.
But the issues said to have driven the contact do not disappear with the denials: a long and difficult border, weapons smuggling, wanted individuals, Syrian allegations of Hezbollah-linked networks operating inside the country, and tensions between Hezbollah and the government that replaced its longtime ally, Assad.
According to Reuters, the Syrian side sought Hezbollah’s help in stopping weapons smuggling and addressing sleeper cells, while Syrian officials reportedly told the group that Damascus did not plan to send forces into Lebanon to disarm it. The report also said indirect contacts preceded the alleged meeting, without producing a final agreement.
Syrian politician Fawaz Tello, however, doubts that Damascus has any real interest in establishing such a channel.
Tello told The Media Line that, in his view, Hezbollah does not have sufficient independence when it comes to strategic decisions involving Syria or its wider regional role.
“Hezbollah is not the decision maker,” Tello said. “In the end, it implements Iranian policy, and therefore there is no interest in opening any dialogue with it.”
Any serious dialogue, he said, would require Hezbollah to stop protecting wanted individuals who may be sheltering in Lebanon, reveal networks affiliated with it inside Syria, and cooperate with the Lebanese government in allowing state institutions to exercise full security authority across the country.
Those conditions, Tello said, make the prospect of dialogue more of a “hypothetical question” than a realistic political track, because he does not believe Hezbollah can provide what Damascus would require.
He also rejected the idea that Turkey has played a mediating role, saying he does not believe Ankara has opened such a channel and arguing that Syria’s relationship with Lebanon should be conducted through state institutions rather than an armed party.
From Lebanon, however, the calculation looks different.
Lebanese journalist Mariam Majdoline Lahham told The Media Line that Hezbollah may now have a greater interest than Damascus in opening a limited channel of communication.
She said the fall of Assad deprived the group of a strategic environment that had been deeply important politically, militarily, and logistically. Syria, once an ally, a supply corridor, and a strategic rear base for Hezbollah, is now governed by a new authority that views the group through the role it played alongside Assad’s forces during the war.
Hezbollah wants clarity on Syria's intentions with the terror organization
“If the information about a communication channel is accurate, I do not read it as reconciliation or the beginning of a return to the old relationship,” Lahham said. “At a minimum, Hezbollah wants to manage the level of hostility with Damascus.”
She said Hezbollah now wants clarity on Syria’s intentions toward the group, how Damascus will handle the border, and whether it will view Hezbollah solely as a Lebanese domestic issue or also as a security adversary.
“The party that once entered Syria from a position of strength is now interested in obtaining assurances from Syria that the confrontation will not move against it inside Lebanon,” Lahham said.
Lahham said Hezbollah could, in theory, make certain security commitments if the networks Damascus is concerned about are directly controlled by the group.
“If these networks actually belong to Hezbollah or operate under its direction, then it can stop them,” she said. “If it says it does not have the ability to do so, then that raises another question: Who is running these networks?”
She distinguished those networks from weapons smuggling across the border more broadly, noting that numerous groups and networks operate along the Lebanese-Syrian frontier and cannot all be attributed to Hezbollah.
At the same time, she said Hezbollah’s significant influence in some border regions makes it difficult to treat the group as a passive observer with no connection to what happens there.
On the question of Syrians wanted by Damascus who may be in Lebanon, Lahham said the issue should be handled through the Lebanese state and judiciary, not through Hezbollah.
If the group is protecting particular individuals, she said, it can withdraw that protection, “but it has no right to manage the issue of wanted individuals between two states.”
Her position intersects with the Syrian government’s public message: Any lasting arrangement concerning the border, wanted individuals, or security should remain a matter between Damascus and Beirut.
“The border is not Hezbollah’s border with Syria,” Lahham said. “It is the border of the Lebanese Republic with the Syrian Arab Republic.”
She said limited communication aimed at preventing a confrontation or containing an immediate security incident could be understandable under exceptional circumstances. Turning such contacts into a permanent mechanism, however, would once again give Hezbollah a sovereign security role parallel to Lebanese state institutions.
Iran is another factor that cannot be separated from any possible track.
Tello believes the form of Iranian influence that existed in Syria ended with Assad’s fall and that the new government will not allow the previous structure, which gave Tehran and its allies extensive military and political influence, to return.
Lahham sees the relationship in more nuanced terms.
She said it is an exaggeration to assume Hezbollah needs Iranian approval for every minor decision, but it is equally misleading to portray the group as independent from Tehran on strategic matters.
“It may negotiate on its own, yes. It may send a security official and reach limited arrangements on the ground, yes,” she said. “But the more we move from the tactical to the strategic level, the more Iran becomes present, even if it is not sitting at the table.”
As for a possible Turkish role, Lahham said it would not be surprising if the reported channel were eventually confirmed, given Ankara’s influence in Syria under its new government. But she cautioned against interpreting that as Turkey replacing Iran in Hezbollah’s regional relationships.
Turkey could provide a communications channel between two parties that do not trust each other, she said, but the question that should be asked in Lebanon is: “Where is the Lebanese state?”
“When we have an issue involving the Lebanese-Syrian border, weapons, smuggling, wanted individuals, and security, and then discover that the discussion is taking place between the Syrian government and an armed Lebanese party, that in itself is a problem,” she said.
For Lahham, the most important meaning of any meeting, if one is eventually confirmed, would not be the restoration of Hezbollah’s influence but the scale of the change in its position.
“Years ago, Hezbollah entered Syria militarily to support the regime and participated in shaping realities on the ground,” she said. “Today, if the report is accurate, it goes to a security meeting in search of rules that prevent a confrontation with the new Syrian authorities.”
“I do not see us rebuilding an old axis,” she added. “We are looking at a party trying to adapt to a balance of power that changed fundamentally after Assad’s fall.”

Confronting Islamism: What America must do at home and abroad - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:44:26 UTC
20:44:26 KST

America has an Islamism problem. The danger is that we fail to recognize how deeply Islamist ideas are already embedded in parts of our society, reinforced by a red-green alliance between Islamists and progressive socialists seeking to fundamentally transform America.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The public often prefers simple stories and easily identifiable adversaries. Political Islamism is neither, making the challenge even more difficult to confront.
In a May 2025 Free Press investigation titled “How Qatar Bought America,” Frannie Block and Jay Solomon reported that Qatar had spent almost $100 billion over two decades on US investments, weapons purchases, universities, lobbying, and other activities. The authors portrayed that spending as part of a far-reaching effort to build access and influence in Congress, universities, newsrooms, think tanks, and corporations.
Through the Qatar Foundation, Qatar has poured money into partnerships with American universities, particularly their branch campuses in Doha, while Al Jazeera has given a major platform to figures associated with the Muslim Brotherhood and political Islamism. Qatar has also hosted senior Muslim Brotherhood and Hamas figures. In America, this combination of money, access, and media influence can give Islamist ideas a wider platform while Qatar benefits from its status as a US security partner.
Political Islamism is an ideology that seeks to make Islamic religious doctrine a governing principle of the state. The Muslim Brotherhood helped shape modern political Islamism. Hamas emerged from the Palestinian Muslim Brotherhood, while the writings of Brotherhood ideologue Sayyid Qutb deeply influenced al-Qaeda and, through the broader Salafi-jihadist movement, the Islamic State group. Qutb’s writings also influenced some Iranian revolutionaries despite the Sunni-Shi'ite divide. Yet largely unnoticed by most Americans, Islamist influence has been slowly seeping into the fabric of American society.
America has been largely oblivious to the threat. Confronting it requires a four-step process:
- Define Islamism clearly, without fear of being labeled anti-Islamic.
- Understand why Islamism’s ideology, strategy, and long-term objectives threaten America and the West.
- Learn to identify Islamism in its different forms, both domestically and internationally.
- Develop a comprehensive strategy to counter it while educating the American public about the threat.
It will not be easy.
Political Islamism is remarkably adaptable. Like a chameleon, it changes its appearance to fit its environment. In democratic societies, it can patiently build influence through politics, education, philanthropy, media, and social networks, waiting years or decades for opportunities. This, I believe, is part of the Qatari strategy in America.
The progression can become a slippery slope. After October 7, some anti-Israel protests and campaigns on American campuses involved intimidation, harassment, threats, attempts to silence opposing views, and, at times, physical violence against Jews and others with whom activists disagreed, while participants also invoked constitutional protections for even their most provocative actions. I see the overlap between far-left anti-Zionism and Islamist politics in parts of this movement as one manifestation of the red-green alliance.
Jewish Americans became particular targets in some cases because their actual or perceived support for Israel and Zionism was equated with complicity in genocide. That rationale was sometimes used to target Jewish students, organizations, and even events associated with synagogues and Jewish institutions.
Elsewhere, including France, Britain, Sweden, and Germany, societies have faced repeated jihadist violence and threats targeting non-Muslims as well as Muslim critics of radical Islam. Ayaan Hirsi Ali was forced into hiding under police protection after her colleague Theo van Gogh was murdered in the Netherlands and a death threat addressed to her was pinned to his body. She later moved to the United States.
What can America do?
Qatar can remain an important American security partner, but Washington should demand greater transparency about support for Muslim Brotherhood-linked organizations and an end to the hosting of Hamas leaders. If Qatar wants the privileges of a major US security relationship, there must be consequences for conduct that undermines America domestically. Unfortunately, this administration emphasizes Qatar’s financial value while underestimating the ideological danger.
America needs a comprehensive strategy, a policy checklist followed by action, not rhetoric:
- Define the threat: Distinguish Islam from Islamism, while defining radical jihadism, lawful political advocacy, and terrorism. Terrorism should be named plainly rather than softened with euphemisms. The target is a political ideology, not a religion or its adherents.
- Protect American institutions: Require full public disclosure of foreign funding and influence in universities, schools, nonprofits, think tanks, and advocacy organizations. No authoritarian money influencing American education, whether from Qatar or China.
- Protect education: Islamist influence can operate through foreign funding, curricula, campus organizations, and advocacy networks that normalize Islamist political narratives while marginalizing opposing views. Schools should teach religions and civilizations fairly, including Jewish peoplehood, civilization, tradition, and religion, not merely the Holocaust. Confront antisemitism using the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance framework.
- Demand accountability: Condition US cooperation with governments that support anti-American Islamist organizations.
Michigan illustrates why this debate can no longer be avoided. Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has refused to affirm Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state. Opposition to Israel’s existence as a Jewish state has long been a priority of Islamist movements. He invokes the antisemitic trope that Jewish money (AIPAC) buys influence, while linking good standing in progressive politics with anti-Zionism. This reflects a growing willingness within the progressive-Islamist alliance to normalize the rejection of Jewish national self-determination.
America can protect Muslim Americans from discrimination while confronting Islamism, foreign influence, and terrorism. It can defend free speech while strictly enforcing laws against violence, true threats, and constitutionally unprotected incitement. These principles are not contradictory.
The objective is to prevent any radical ideology, Islamist or otherwise, from capturing American institutions, purchasing influence with foreign money, intimidating citizens, or displacing the primacy of the Constitution as the framework of American public life.
A free society survives by identifying threats accurately and confronting them lawfully without surrendering its constitutional principles. The time to confront political Islamism is before it becomes too entrenched and powerful to confront. We are getting dangerously close to that tipping point.
Dr. Eric R. Mandel is the director of MEPIN, the Middle East Political Information Network, and the senior security editor of the Jerusalem Post magazine, The Jerusalem Report.

Average five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:39:37 UTC
20:39:37 KST

The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.
Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.
In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise.
Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level.
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.
Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”.
She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.”
The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property.
Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February.
There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September.
Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability.
He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

Eurozone producer inflation hits highest since February 2023 at 8.2%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:38:15 UTC
20:38:15 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Annual industrial producer inflation in the euro area accelerated to 8.2% in August, its highest level since February 2023 and above market expectations of 8.1%, according to Eurostat figures released Monday.
The annual increase quickened from 5.8% in July, while producer prices rose 1.9% month-on-month, following a 1.6% increase in the previous month.
Energy led the increase, with producer prices in the sector climbing 21% from a year earlier and 5.6% from July.
Excluding energy, euro area industrial producer prices increased 3.4% annually and 0.2% monthly.
Prices for intermediate goods rose 6.8% year-on-year, while capital goods and durable consumer goods recorded increases of 2.6% and 3.4%, respectively. Non-durable consumer goods prices fell 0.8%.
Across the wider EU, industrial producer prices increased 8% annually in August, accelerating from 5.6% in July. The monthly increase stood at 1.9%.
Ireland recorded the largest annual rise among EU member states at 17.1%, followed by Bulgaria at 16.8% and Lithuania at 14.6%. Luxembourg was the only country to register an annual decline, with prices falling 7.9%.
Bulgaria and Estonia posted the strongest monthly increases, both at 3.3%, followed by Italy at 3.1% and Denmark at 3%.

Russian large-scale attack on NATO not likely – German intelligence chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:38:00 UTC
20:38:00 KST

Germany risks becoming directly involved in a violent conflict with Russia as Moscow’s confrontation with the West takes on a more dangerous form, the head of Germany’s federal intelligence service warned Monday.
Martin Jäger, head of the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, told a public hearing of the Bundestag’s parliamentary oversight committee that Russia currently poses the most direct and comprehensive threat to Germany of any country, German daily Die Welt reported.
“The confrontation we are in with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous form: Germany is at risk of becoming involved in a violent conflict with Russia,” Jäger said.
He cited an incident involving a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport as one example of the threats facing Germany. Russian intelligence services are operating “very professionally and ruthlessly”, he said.
“The threat of attacks against targets in Germany remains real and acute. We must counter it,” Jäger said.
He described Moscow’s activities as a “shadow war” aimed at ensuring that Berlin and other European capitals do not make political decisions directed against Russia in the future.
Jäger said Russia’s main objective is to undermine European political support for Ukraine and warned that Moscow could again resort to nuclear threats as part of its efforts.
At the same time, the BND currently sees no indications that Russia is preparing a large-scale attack on NATO territory. However, Jäger warned that “low-intensity Russian military actions” could occur, particularly in the Baltic states.
“We did not seek this confrontation; Russia is imposing it on us, seeing us as its main adversary,” Jäger said. “Because we are resisting Russia’s attempts to intimidate our allies in the Baltic states and elsewhere in Europe.”
Germany has become a key obstacle to Russia’s efforts to project hegemonic power in Europe and has consequently become a target of Russian actions, he said.
“Those who do not submit become an adversary: That is Moscow’s interpretation,” Jäger said.
He also warned that Russia’s war in Ukraine, where Moscow is carrying out increasingly brutal attacks, is entering a highly dangerous new phase.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has already crossed a threshold beyond which he could no longer simply halt pressure on Ukraine without risking the foundations of his domestic power, Jäger said.
“He has to achieve a success in Ukraine that, from Russia’s perspective, would justify the enormous sacrifices made so far. This forces him to take action,” he said.
Despite the pressure, Jäger said there were no signs of panic within the Russian leadership. Moscow is aware of the limits of its military and economic resources, he said.

FP-7 expands Ukraine’s strike capabilities against Russia: expert names potential targets
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:35:36 EEST
20:35:36 KST

FP-7 expands Ukraine’s strike capabilities against Russia: expert names potential targets
Kyiv • UNN
Tactical ballistic systems could give Ukraine an additional tool for striking Russian command posts, warehouses, logistics hubs and air defense systems.
The first combat use of the FP-7 opens up new opportunities for Ukraine to strike military targets at a considerable distance from the front line. The emergence of tactical ballistic capabilities makes it possible to plan strikes on command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, air defense systems, and other important facilities supporting Russian forces. Military expert Ivan Stupak expressed this opinion in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Ukraine used the FP-7
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy published a video of the launch and reported the first combat use of the Ukrainian FP-7 ballistic missile. At the same time, Ukraine has not disclosed exactly where or against what target the missile was used.
The FP-7 was developed by Fire Point, a leading Ukrainian defense company. It is a ballistic missile designed to strike targets at a distance of up to 250 km and deliver a payload weighing up to 200 kg. Such a system is a cheaper response to the U.S. ATACMS.
The emergence of such weapons expands Ukraine’s ability to operate against the Russian rear, since tactical ballistic capabilities make it possible to reach facilities that the enemy is trying to move farther away from the combat zone.
The very emergence of such a weapon is a very important development. Ukraine becomes stronger when it has not merely an individual missile, but the ability to plan its use
What targets could the FP-7 potentially strike
Potential key targets for such weapons could include command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, air defense systems, and other military facilities.
According to Ivan Stupak, the creation of the FP-7 is a "strong card" that Ukraine either did not previously have or had in a much more limited form.
In his view, the mass or at least regular use of such missiles could potentially affect the situation on particular sections of the front, as well as how Russian troops deploy their forces and infrastructure.
The Russians are already being forced to withdraw some of their forces, equipment, repair bases, depots, and other facilities farther from the front line. условно, if they place them more than 100 kilometers away, while the Ukrainian missile has a range of about 200 kilometers, then a significant portion of such facilities potentially falls within the strike zone. And here intelligence is extremely important. If we see a facility, understand its coordinates, know its importance to the Russian army, and have a missile with which we can engage it, then we gain the ability to strike the enemy’s rear much more effectively
Logistics infrastructure could become a separate area of focus. The aggressor country’s forces require a constant supply of ammunition, fuel, equipment, and spare parts.
It is possible to strike depots, command posts, repair bases, and other facilities that support the Russian grouping at the front. The more such facilities fall within range, the more difficult it will be for the Russians to organize their logistics
Potential targets could also include facilities in the fuel and energy sector if they have military significance and are within the missile’s range.
At the same time, Ivan Stupak emphasized that the effectiveness of strikes against protected facilities would depend on the missile’s accuracy and the power of its warhead.
What serial production will provide
The military expert emphasized that a stable supply of missiles would allow the military command to plan their use over a longer period and distribute the missiles according to priority targets.
Let us imagine a situation—the command knows for certain that from the 1st to the 30th of the month, it has ten missiles at its disposal. Then it is a completely different story. The military can plan which targets are of the greatest value, which facilities need to be destroyed first, and which can be left for later. For example, Alabuga, where Russian attack drones are produced, could be designated as one of the priority targets. If we accumulate ten missiles over the course of a month, we can plan to use them against such facilities. And if the warhead and accuracy make it possible to strike fortified structures, that is an entirely different level of capability
Therefore, important factors include not only the missile’s range, but also its production rate, accuracy, and the effect of its warhead.
After the first large-scale deployments, we will see much more. We will see how accurate the missile is, how powerful its warhead is, how effectively it overcomes air defenses and, most importantly, how quickly Ukraine will be able to ramp up production
In his opinion, the FP-7 is a "very promising prospect" for Ukraine, but its real impact will become clear after combat experience has been accumulated.

Israel bans Greens' Zack Polanski after 'Zionism is racism' vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:35:05 UTC
20:35:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel bans UK Greens' Zack Polanski after 'Zionism is racism' vote
Israel has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country after party members passed a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
In a statement on Sunday, the foreign ministry described the proposal as a "clear antisemitic text" that denies Jews the right to self-determination.
The motion, adopted at the party's conference over the weekend, defines Israel as an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" and supports a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
The issue has divided the party's membership and its leaders, with Polanski and deputy leader Rachel Millward declining to back the motion. It was passed on Sunday with the support of 55% of members.
"The Green Party in Britain adopted a resolution equating Zionism with racism, legitimising armed struggle against Israel, and calling for the establishment of a Palestinian state 'from the river to the sea' - meaning the destruction of the State of Israel," Israel's foreign ministry said.
"As a first step, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar has decided this evening to declare Green Party leader Zack Polanski barred from Israel."
Polanski, himself Jewish, did not vote and left the conference to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in Thursday's by-election.
He called for two amendments to safeguard Jewish members of Zionist synagogues and soften the motion's position on the creation of a single Palestinian state. Both were rejected by members.
The adoption of the motion makes the Greens the first mainstream political party in the UK to define itself as anti-Zionist.
Proposed by Palestinian activist Lubna Speitan, it states that Zionism is responsible for "the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians".
"Zionism has created and seeks to maintain – and where possible – expand, an apartheid regime between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, designed to cement the supremacy of on group, Jews, over another, Palestinians. As such, Zionism is racist," it reads.
Deputy leader Mothin Ali endorsed the proposal ahead of the vote, saying it called for a democratic state that protects the rights of both Israelis and Palestinians.
But most senior party figures voiced opposition, including four of its five MPs. Bristol Central MP Carla Denyer warned that it risked alienating Britain's Jewish community, while Ellie Chowns and Adrian Ramsay said they were "deeply saddened".
Former leader Caroline Lucas had appealed to members to vote against the proposal, saying during the debate that it had left many Jewish members feeling "scared and unwelcome" in the party.
Following the vote, the party's leadership and MPs issued a joint statement pledging to ensure the Greens remain an "anti-racist party in every way".
"We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people," it said.
Supporters of the motion celebrated its adoption, with its author, Speitan, describing the vote as a message against "occupation, oppression, genocide, apartheid, and racism".
"This is hope for the future of our people, for the future of all oppressed, and sets an example and a precedent that we, as a people, are unified," Speitan told The New Arab following the vote.
She also dismissed opposition from senior party figures, saying they were "entitled to their opinion" but "need to start listening to the members of the party if they want to keep the support and the vote and the trust of the people".
