"A student was killed and two others were wounded in a Saudi attack" on the Bani Hashish area, the Houthi-affiliated TV channel Al-Masirah reported, adding that strikes also targeted Saada, a region known as a stronghold.
The Houthis seized Sanaa more than a decade ago, at the outset of Yemen's grinding civil war, which has now become intertwined with the wider war in the region sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran at the end of February.
CBS/AFP
Tanker turns back in Strait of Hormuz after Iranian threats, U.K. navy maritime agency says
A tanker turned back after being threatened by Iranian forces in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, according to the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO).
"A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz inbound was hailed by the [Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps] and instructed to turn back or the vessel would be targeted," UKMTO said, adding that the "master of the tanker has confirmed that they have complied with the instruction."
The ship was entering the strait near Oman's coastline, the agency added, using a route touted repeatedly by the U.S. government as safe and open.
On Sunday, UKMTO said it received a report of a possible attack on another tanker in the region's other vital shipping chokepoint, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
Multiple explosions detonated close to a tanker south of Al-Mukha, Yemen, in the Bab el-Mandeb, the monitor said, adding that the crew were reported safe.
Hormuz, through which about one fifth of the world's oil and gas transited before the war, remains a key sticking point in negotiations between Iran and the U.S. to end their conflict.
While attacks on ships blamed on Iran have continued, the U.S. has not announced strikes against the Islamic Republic since Sept. 1.
CBS/AFP
Head of state energy giant Saudi Aramco warns global oil stockpiles "scarily thin"
Global oil stockpiles are "scarily thin" owing to the U.S.-Iran war, Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said Monday, days after G7 nations agreed to release more of their inventories to ease supply concerns.
"The system is already straining," Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. "And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin."
His remarks came hours after the news that oil flows from the Middle East surpassed pre-war levels last week. That welcome news for markets has been tempered, however, by furious fighting between Saudi-backed forces and Iran's Houthi rebel allies in Yemen over control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another key energy chokepoint and the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
CBS/AFP
Conflicting reports about flow of oil through Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline after new strike
Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline was struck again Sunday, a source working in the kingdom's energy sector told French news agency AFP on Monday, adding that the flow of oil through the pipeline had stopped.
"The East-West pipeline was attacked again yesterday," the source told AFP. "A pumping station east of Riyadh in Khurais. It wasn't targeted before. There was big damage and the pipeline stopped again."
The Reuters news agency reported Monday, however, that oil was still flowing through the pipeline, also citing an unnamed source. Bloomberg also reported that oil was still flowing, citing people familiar with the matter.
News of the strike came a day after the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen said they had targeted sites in Saudi Arabia belonging to state oil giant Aramco, including infrastructure in Khurais.
The East-West pipeline has been targeted multiple times since war erupted across the Middle East, following the U.S. and Israel launching joint strikes on Iran at the end of February.
Last month, Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, shut the East-West pipeline, which runs about 700 miles between its main oil fields in the east and the Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea.
The pipeline was shut down from Sept. 11 to 22, according to commodity-tracking platform Kpler.
CBS/AFP
Yemen's military announces broad strikes against Houthis, claims control of Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The Yemeni military announced a broad set of strikes against Houthi targets on Monday after the government declared a new campaign to retake all territory from the rebels, even as the Iran-backed group made fresh gains on the ground.
The declared offensive sets a lofty goal for the beleaguered Saudi-backed government a month after it lost swathes of the country's Red Sea coastline, including key territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a key choke point for international shipping.
Hours after the Yemeni government's announcement, Yemen's military spokesman said its forces launched over 1,000 "strikes against artillery and rocket launcher positions, defensive fortifications, approach and reinforcement routes, supply lines and logistics assets, combat reinforcements" belonging to the Houthis.
He later said the military had taken back control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Houthi-aligned media earlier denied government forces had retaken territory in the area, the Reuters news agency reported.
The government strikes appear to have had little immediate impact on the Houthis' ongoing advances on the ground. On Sunday, the group effectively encircled the key city of Taiz after cutting the main supply route linking it to the interim government capital of Aden.
Fighting between the two sides in and around Taiz province killed more than 70 people in a single day, sources from both sides of the conflict told the French news agency AFP on Sunday. The agency previously reported that 80 combatants had been killed on Friday.
CBS/AFP
Iran's top diplomat says only talks can end the war, not military moves
Iran's foreign minister insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States' war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.
A campaign of heavy U.S. bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war as it began, and Washington has dialed back military operations in recent weeks in favor of economic pressure.
The main point of contention remains Iran's continuing attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a U.K. maritime agency reported on Sunday that another tanker had been struck by an unknown projectile.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of his counterparts.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
The two sides signed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the strait prompted the U.S. to resume military operations.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that try to transit without its authorization.
The U.S. has imposed a counterblockade of Iranian ports and has struck vessels it accuses of violating the countermeasure.
Mideast oil exports exceeded pre-Iran war levels last week, tracking firm says
Middle East oil exports, excluding those from Iran, surpassed their pre-war levels last week, despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.
For the first time since the U.S. and Israel launched their offensive against Iran at the end of February, the weekly average of shipments rose for several days above the pre-conflict average of 18 million barrels per day.
Crude oil exports reached pre-war levels in September, with at least 16.5 million barrels leaving the region excluding Iran, Kpler said.
"Forty percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore," Kpler said, adding that most of the oil flowed through Saudi and United Arab Emirates pipelines.
Those figures include flows via the Red Sea, a route increasingly used to bypass the blockade Iran is attempting to impose on the strait, through which around a fifth of the world's petroleum supplies crossed before the conflict.
Iran still claims control over the strait, and ships without its authorization risk coming under attack, but more and more are making it out, and alternative routes meant to bypass the waterway are operating at full capacity.
Despite the rebound, experts stressed that the situation is far from normal, and Iran is still being deprived of a large share of its own exports by a U.S. counterblockade of Iranian ports.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright says Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching Iran war
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that President Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching the war in Iran earlier this year, but argued "the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran."
"He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run, he said, 'I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing,'" Wright said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Americans have been feeling the financial squeeze of soaring gas and diesel prices in recent months. But the Trump administration has pointed to the potential threat a nuclear-armed Iran could pose, and how it could represent a long-term threat to energy prices. Wright defended the president on Sunday, arguing that Mr. Trump has taken a "strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons."
Wright expressed confidence that prices will fall, pointing to increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. gasoline production, the summer driving season slowing, among other factors. Asked whether he expects prices to go down over the next four weeks — as Republicans eye a tough environment in the lead-up to the midterm elections — Wright said, "absolutely."
Iran preparing response after U.S. rejects conditions to reopen Hormuz, Iranian officials say
After President Trump rejected Tehran's proposed conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz — while leaving the door open to further talks or renewed military operations — Iranian officials said the U.S. response was being reviewed, and it was preparing one of its own.
"The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures," Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told reporters on Sunday, according to the Iranian state news agency IRNA.
"Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly," he said. "At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario."
Meanwhile, Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei characterized the latest U.S. counterproposal as being "in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues."
"We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz," he said Sunday, adding that reopening the waterway required "an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions."
The U.S. and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Strait of Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.

Snap elections to be held in Spain in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:34:14 UTC
20:34:14 KST

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced on the 5th of October that snap elections would be held in the country on the 29th of November; this could signal the departure of the European Union's last major socialist government and, consequently, the exit of a fierce critic of US President Donald Trump's policies from the political forefront, reports Politico.
Sánchez, whose party was already weakened by corruption scandals, suffered another blow this summer when, in late July, more than 75,000 migrants entered the Spanish territory of Ceuta in North Africa in a single day. The migration crisis has not yet been fully resolved.
Meanwhile, the housing issue intensified in September. It is a primary concern for Spanish voters and has sparked nationwide protests, ultimately serving as the final straw that prompted Sánchez to call for snap elections.
On the 2nd of October, lawmakers rejected two bills aimed at alleviating the housing crisis. Widespread protests erupted in late September when 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from the apartment where she had lived since 1956.
Although Sánchez has earned a reputation as a master of political comebacks, he faces an uphill battle this time to turn the crisis to his advantage. 
Polls consistently indicate that the country will vote for an administration led by the center-right People's Party (PP), which currently enjoys 34% voter support. Sánchez's Socialists are the first choice for 26% of voters. It is likely that the PP will partner with the far-right Vox party, which is projected to garner 18% of the vote.
Upon announcing the snap election, Sánchez urged the public to prevent the far-right from coming to power. Addressing the nation, he stated that the Spanish people must decide what role they wish to play and what role Spain should assume. They must choose whether to align with the far-right wave—which brings regression wherever it gains power—or whether they want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice, and responsible environmental policy. Sánchez also used his televised address to highlight the achievements of his minority government since 2023. He emphasized economic successes—noting that the country has become the fastest-growing economy in the European Union—and highlighted investments in green energy production. Sánchez also spoke about his role in international politics, where he has gained prominence as a Western leader who has strongly condemned both Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over military actions in Gaza and Iran, and has stood up to tech giants such as Elon Musk.
The Spanish Prime Minister stated that Spaniards can be proud of a government that condemns the perpetrators of genocide while others remain silent. 
He described his government as fighting against tyrants, oligarchs, and speculators who seek to destroy children's futures in order to line their own pockets. While insisting that his government has transformed Spain into an international model for peace, feminism, and prosperity—achieving the best economic, social, and environmental indicators in the history of the country's democratic governments—he also acknowledged that many Spaniards feel dissatisfied. Ordinary citizens are not feeling the impact of Spain's strong growth and record-high employment. Inflation is outpacing wage growth, leaving most households without additional purchasing power as both housing costs and the prices of goods rise.
Incidents such as last year's nationwide power outage have tarnished the reputation of the country's green energy grid, while the international response to the migration crisis in Ceuta has cast doubt on Spain's standing on the global political stage. Sánchez acknowledged that his government had made mistakes and failed to achieve everything it had set out to do. He stated that many injustices remain to be rectified and many problems addressed, particularly regarding the accessibility of services and housing.
A tough battle lies ahead for Sánchez. The PP—which has been calling for snap elections ever since Sánchez secured a new term as national leader in 2023—responded to the announcement with a brief post on X: "At last."
Now, Spain's fragmented left-wing camp will attempt to regroup. This is a problem for Sánchez’s Socialists, as they need left-wing forces to unite in a viable alliance capable of forming a new coalition government.

Tourists increasingly choosing Tallinn over rest of Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:34:00 UTC
20:34:00 KST

Tourists increasingly choosing Tallinn over rest of Estonia
Foreign tourists are increasingly focusing trips to Estonia on Tallinn, with the capital setting a July tourism record as other destinations lag behind pre-pandemic levels.
Some 964,000 tourists stayed in accommodation establishments across Estonia in July, compared with more than 1 million in July 2019. Tallinn, however, set a record with 455,000 overnight stays, up from 399,000 before the COVID-19 pandemic hit.
Outside the capital, the recovery has been weaker. The number of tourists staying around Tallinn is still about 20 percent below 2019 levels.
"Tallinn stands out the most," said SEB economic analyst Mihkel Nestor. He said tourism depends heavily on how aware foreign visitors are of destinations beyond the capital.
Many may even simply see it as one of several capital cities in the region, he added, "So they'll say, 'Okay, let's visit Tallinn then too.' Getting tourists to venture beyond Tallinn has always been a challenge."
One in three tourists are Finns
Finns accounted for about a third of all tourists in Tallinn this July, with Finnish tourist numbers up by more than 20,000 on year to total 145,000.
"Finns have started traveling to Tallinn more than ever before," said Harles Tammeleht, general manager of Mercure Tallinn and the Oru Hub Handwritten Collection.
He noted, however, that their numbers have fallen elsewhere, both in the rest of Harju County "and in places like Pärnu and Kuressaare, which once relied heavily on the Finnish market."
Nestor said the shift is partly linked to Finland's economic situation.
"Tourism has started to pick up a bit again there too, and Finns are traveling abroad more," he explained, but high unemployment continues to limit spending. "When one in ten people there are unemployed, travel isn't exactly very reasonable."
'It's close and it's nice'
Tammeleht also pointed to demographic changes. While traditionally popular spa tourism to places like Pärnu and Saaremaa continues to decline, he said, younger generations have different travel preferences.
Finnish visitors typically say for one or two nights, with entertainment, leisure and cheaper alcohol among the main draws.
"We sing in a chorus, and we had a full day here — actually two days," said Minna and Erika, two ferry passengers at the Port of Tallinn who had been in town for choir practice.
"Drinks," said Tumppi, who made the trip across the Gulf of Finland to stock up on alcohol.
Kira, meanwhile, was in Tallinn with friends to celebrate their birthdays. "We stayed for one night, because we all turned 40," she said. "It's close and it's nice."

West-defying Serb leader celebrates victory in Bosnia and Herzegovina election
Milorad Dodik, the former president of Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, has celebrated his party’s performance in Sunday’s general election.
The Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) is set to retain its lead in the Republika Srpska parliament, keep the entity’s presidency and hold on to the Serb seat in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s three-member collective presidency, according to preliminary results released by the Election Commission after more than 90% of ballots had been counted. The party is projected to get roughly 40% of the seats in the regional legislature.
Dodik himself was not on the ballot after being barred from holding public office over his 2025 conviction for defying Christian Schmidt, the German politician who at the time served as the international high representative overseeing implementation of the 1995 Dayton Agreement. Dodik argued that Schmidt lacked UN Security Council backing for the post and had abused the office to curb Republika Srpska’s autonomy, leading to a bitter political standoff.
Speaking to supporters late Sunday, Dodik thanked voters for backing SNSD and its allies, declaring that “no one should ask us to change our politics.” He also praised US President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory and thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for supporting the Serb entity.
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, whose sovereignist politics have often aligned with Dodik’s, hailed the result as a “grand slam” for SNSD.
Grand slam! Congratulations to President @MiloradDodik and all our friends at SNSD - especially President Cvijanović and President Minić - on sweeping today’s elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. A strong mandate to continue standing up for the interests and rights of Republika Srpska.
— Orbán Viktor (@PM_ViktorOrban) October 5, 2026
More than 3 million people were eligible to vote in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They chose representatives on multiple levels from the ten cantons of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to the national presidency. The country used biometric voter identification and ballot scanners for the first time in an effort to streamline voting and counting.
Dodik ally Zeljka Cvijanovic and Croat nationalist politician Darijana Filipovic are on course to join incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic in leading the Balkan country, whose political system is divided along ethnic and religious lines.
Savo Minic is set to become the next president of Republika Srpska, succeeding Sinisa Karan, another SNSD member.
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s complex system of government was established under the Dayton Agreement in a bid to balance the interests of its constituent peoples and prevent a return to the violence that engulfed the Balkans during the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

New financing formula for vocational colleges to take effect in 2027 – Koretsky
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
14:33:26 EEST
20:33:26 KST

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky has announced that a new financing formula for professional colleges will be launched starting in 2027, ensuring that each institution receives baseline funding while a portion of its budget will depend on performance results.
"The government has adopted a package of decisions to implement changes in vocational education. The key task is to train qualified specialists who are genuinely needed by the labor market and the country's economy. We approved a new standard of vocational education: at least 40% of the educational program is allocated to practical training. Students will be able to acquire up to three professional qualifications, and professional colleges will have greater autonomy in shaping educational programs. Training will be integrated with the European credit system," Koretsky wrote on his Telegram channel.
According to him, starting in 2027, the new financing formula for professional colleges will take into account regional demand for specific professions, student enrollment, graduate employment rates, and the attraction of additional funds, meaning that the better the performance indicators, the more funding an institution will receive.
Furthermore, the government is expanding academic mobility, enabling students to study and undertake internships directly with employers.
"Instructors will be able to teach and intern at educational institutions and enterprises. This will provide more practical experience and direct cooperation between professional colleges with employers," he added.
In turn, Minister of Education and Science of Ukraine Andriy Butenko detailed that the new standard provides for: at least 40% of the educational program allocated to practical training; students being able to acquire up to three professional qualifications—under one or different types of occupations, expanding their employment opportunities; the volume of the educational program ranging from 40 to 180 credits, depending on the person's prior education, level, and number of qualifications acquired; institutions receiving greater autonomy in forming educational programs; integration into the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System and key competencies recommended by the European Union.
According to him, based on this standard, colleges will update their educational programs and begin teaching according to them as early as 2027.
He also stated that starting in 2027, funds among colleges will be distributed according to a new formula: each institution will receive baseline funding for stable operation, while a portion of the funds—up to a third of the total volume—will depend on its performance indicators.
In particular, the factors considered will include: the number of students; the demand for professional qualifications in the regional labor market; the fulfillment of planned admission targets; the employment of graduates; the implementation of short-term programs; and the attraction of additional funds by the institutions.
"Thus, institutions that train in in-demand professions and whose graduates find employment will receive more resources. I emphasize separately: the formula does not increase the total volume of vocational education funding, and the amount for each institution will be determined by its founder within the local budget. The approval of the formula is also one of the indicators of Ukraine's cooperation with the World Bank," the minister added.

Canada head coach Jesse Marsch has called for Manchester City to be relegated after the Premier League club was found guilty of serious breaches of financial regulations.
“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down,” Marsch told The Guardian in an interview published Sunday.
Marsch, who managed Leeds United between 2022 and 2023, said the financial disparity between City and clubs without similarly wealthy ownership had been apparent during his time in the Premier League.
The American coach pointed to the summer 2022 transfer window, when Leeds raised substantial funds by selling Raphinha to Barcelona and Kalvin Phillips to City.
Marsch said Leeds reported making money during that window because its outgoing transfers exceeded its expenditure on new signings. He questioned how City had also recorded a profit despite its different financial position and transfer activity.
He also expressed skepticism about the reported £52 million ($69 million) fee City paid Borussia Dortmund to sign Erling Haaland that summer, saying he believed there were inconsistencies in the club’s financial operations.
Leeds were relegated from the Premier League at the end of the 2022-23 season, although Marsch was dismissed in February 2023. The campaign was outside the nine-season period examined in the financial case against City.
Marsch also noted that Everton and Nottingham Forest subsequently received points deductions for financial breaches connected to the season in which Leeds were relegated.
An independent commission found City guilty of all charges involving serious breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
According to the Premier League, the commission found that City used sham commercial contracts and agreements to artificially increase revenue and reduce costs. It also concluded that the club submitted misstated accounts, concealed the true condition of its finances, and exceeded Premier League and UEFA spending limits.
Three of four charges concerning City’s alleged failure to cooperate fully with the league’s investigation were also upheld.
City has consistently denied wrongdoing and lodged an appeal Thursday evening. The club said the commission’s decision contained “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact” and maintained that evidence supported its position.
The Premier League said the appeal was submitted to the chair of its Judicial Panel and would be considered privately by an independent Appeal Board. The proceedings will remain confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted.
No sanction has yet been announced. Potential consequences under Premier League rules include financial penalties, points deductions and other sporting measures, while relegation or expulsion has been discussed among the possible outcomes.
The English Football Association said Friday that the commission’s findings had significant implications for the integrity of football and that it was considering whether further action would be appropriate.

American warship opens fire with main gun
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:30:51 BST
20:30:51 KST

US Navy destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. has fired its Mark 45 5-inch main gun during a live-fire exercise while operating in the US 7th Fleet area, according to the US Navy.
The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer carried out the firing on 23 September while underway on what the service described as routine operations. Imagery released by the Navy shows the ship’s forward gun being fired over open water.
USS Frank E. Petersen Jr., designated DDG 121, is one of the newer Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class destroyers in US service. The ship’s Mark 45 naval gun is mounted forward of the bridge and provides the destroyer with a conventional surface-fire capability alongside its missile armament.
The 5-inch weapon can be used against surface targets and for naval gunfire support, while also providing a means of engaging some airborne threats depending on the ammunition and fire-control arrangement being used.
The live-fire event formed part of training intended to maintain proficiency with one of the destroyer’s principal gun systems. US Navy surface combatants routinely conduct live-fire exercises during deployments to test weapons, crews and fire-control procedures under operational conditions. USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. is currently operating within the US 7th Fleet area of operations, which covers much of the western Pacific and Indian Ocean. The fleet is the US Navy’s largest forward-deployed numbered fleet and regularly operates alongside allied and partner navies across the Indo-Pacific.
According to information released with imagery, units assigned to 7th Fleet conduct continuous patrols intended to deter aggression, strengthen alliances and partnerships, and maintain a sustained American naval presence across the region.
The Arleigh Burke class is built around the Aegis combat system and carries a large vertical launch system for surface-to-air, anti-submarine and land-attack missiles. The ships also carry torpedoes, close-in defensive weapons and embarked helicopters, giving them the ability to conduct several missions during a single deployment.
Despite the emphasis placed on missiles aboard modern destroyers, the main gun remains an important part of the ship’s weapons fit. It provides commanders with an alternative to guided weapons for certain surface engagements and can support forces operating ashore where naval gunfire is required.
USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. was named for Lieutenant General Frank E. Petersen Jr., the first African-American Marine Corps aviator and the first African-American Marine Corps general officer. The destroyer entered US Navy service in 2022.
The vessel is homeported at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam in Hawaii and has since operated across the Indo-Pacific as part of the US Navy’s forward presence in the region.

Norway plans to ban AI glasses in some public places
Kyiv • UNN
The Norwegian government is preparing a temporary ban on AI glasses in crowded places due to the risk of covert recording. A complete ban is not planned.
The Norwegian government said on Monday, October 5, that it plans to propose a temporary ban on the use of artificial intelligence glasses in certain places, expressing concern that people could be photographed, filmed, or recorded on audio without their knowledge. UNN reports this with reference to Reuters.
Details
The proposal reflects a broader global backlash against camera-equipped smart glasses due to privacy concerns, the publication notes.
The ban could apply to places where the public regularly gathers, such as parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, and public events, the government said in a statement.
"I am concerned that new, powerful technologies are being introduced in which people risk being photographed, filmed, or recorded on audio without knowing about it," said the country's Minister of Digitalisation and Public Administration, Torgeir Mikalssen.
It could also apply to schools, playgrounds, and youth clubs, as well as places where privacy is important, such as doctors' offices, swimming pools, and gyms with changing rooms.
The government said it was not considering a total ban, and that private use and use in places where others are not at risk of being filmed without their consent would still be permitted.
The government said it would examine which technologies the ban would cover, including whether it would apply to glasses with a camera and audio recording, glasses with a camera and artificial intelligence functions, as well as other wearable technologies with a camera, audio recording, and/or artificial intelligence.
The minority government said it would present a bill to parliament as soon as possible and would also establish an expert group to advise on permanent national regulation of wearable technologies.

Taiwan expands startup investment program to offshore-registered firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:28:20 UTC
20:28:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will soon be able to invest in offshore-registered companies whose operations are primarily based in Taiwan, the Ministry of Digital Affairs said Sunday.
The ministry amended the rules to allow more companies to qualify for a program that aims to invest NT$10 billion ($310 million) from the National Development Fund over 10 years in startups focused on artificial intelligence and digital economy innovation, per CNA.
MODA official Lin Jiunn-shiow (林俊秀) said the program initially targeted Taiwan-registered companies, but the ministry decided to expand its scope after finding that many Taiwanese companies registered overseas to access international markets or attract foreign investment.
“Taiwan has to internationalize, so we decided to leave the door wide open,” Lin said. “We will consider companies that have proper connections with Taiwan.”
Many of these companies, he said, continued to keep their research and development and operational bases in Taiwan.
Under the new rules, companies will be eligible for the program if they meet at least one of three criteria: having an R&D center in Taiwan and spending more than half of their R&D budget locally, generating more than half of their revenue in Taiwan, or employing more than half of their workforce in Taiwan.
As of August, the program has invested around NT$225 million in a total of 10 companies and driven an additional NT$570 million in private investment.
The program works with venture capital firms, accelerators, and corporate venture capital investors to identify startups and jointly fund their development. The investment period is seven years, followed by three years of divestments.

Swiss scammed out of millions by Ukraine-linked call centers – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:28:06 UTC
20:28:06 KST

Ukraine’s scam-call networks targeting Swiss – anti-fraud squad
Swiss police are investigating a sprawling fraud operation with suspected links to Ukrainian scam call centers, an industry said to be worth billions to corrupt officials in Kiev, Neue Zurcher Zeitung (NZZ) has reported, citing law enforcement officials.
According to a report on Sunday, NEDIK, the police network coordinating Switzerland’s fight against digital crime, recently recorded an increase in fraud offenses suspected of having links to Ukraine. The network declined to provide nationwide figures “for tactical reasons,” but noted that at least four fraudulent call centers in Ukraine have been identified in international investigations involving Swiss authorities, with Swiss and German citizens among their main victims.
One investigation by Bern authorities, reportedly underway for years, concerns a man suspected of operating several call centers in Kiev. On just one platform allegedly linked to the operation, reported losses in Switzerland amounted to nearly 4 million Swiss francs ($4.8 million).
Several Ukrainian nationals have also recently been arrested in Swiss cantons for allegedly acting as cash collectors in telephone scams. In St. Gallen in early September, a person posing as a bank employee called a 93-year-old man and instructed him to withdraw and hand over a large sum of money. Police later arrested a 38-year-old Ukrainian who allegedly collected the cash.
Police in Aargau have similarly reported a growing number of suspected cash collectors holding Ukrainian citizenship. Authorities, however, have not established whether they are being directed by call centers in Ukraine or acting independently. NZZ noted that it remains unclear to what extent Ukraine-based operations are connected to fraud networks and cash collectors operating in Switzerland.
While Russians have long been portrayed as the main targets of Ukrainian scammers, sources cited by NZZ challenged that narrative. Brian Lee, head of the Eurasia Observatory at the Geneva-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), said Russians accounted for just 10%-15% of targets even at the height of the so-called “patriotic fraud” narrative, under which young Ukrainians were recruited into scam networks on the pretext of taking revenge for Moscow’s military operation against the Kiev regime. Victims have been identified in at least 29 countries, with scam centers increasingly targeting Europe and the US, according to a GI-TOC report published earlier this year.
Lee also reported that bribing Ukrainian officials for protection is central to the business model, saying GI-TOC investigations found that criminal elements “operate seamlessly and efficiently alongside law enforcement agencies, public officials and the private sector.” Such protection reportedly costs scam operators $10,000-$15,000 per month.
Scam networks and state structures
Corruption has long plagued Ukraine, with high-level scandals including last year’s $100 million Energoatom kickback scheme, reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. Western-backed investigators have since uncovered further graft involving Ukrainian officials.
The scam call center network reentered the spotlight last month after Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – a key pillar of Zelensky’s increasingly fragile governing structure – resigned amid the exposure of an industrial-scale network across the country with alleged links to senior figures in Kiev. Ukraine’s Western-backed National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) accused Sergey Kropiva, head of the cybercrime unit at the Prosecutor General’s Office, of leading a ring that collected protection payments from notorious Ukrainian scam call centers. NABU said it identified assets worth almost $1 million allegedly purchased with proceeds from the scheme.
The sums involved in Ukraine’s wider scam industry are reportedly far larger. Ukrainian media earlier estimated that roughly 2,000 scam offices were operating nationwide as of early August, about half paying protection money to corrupt officials. Such payments were estimated at $240 million annually, while the industry itself has been valued at up to $1 billion a month.
The scam industry has also been linked to powerful security structures under Zelensky’s government. In September, personnel from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and military intelligence (HUR) exchanged fire in Kiev in a confrontation that left three servicemen injured. The clash centered on Stepan Kaplunov, a member of an HUR-linked armed unit detained by the SBU. A law enforcement source cited by Ukrainian outlet Strana said Kaplunov may have been involved in operating scam call centers, pointing to a broader struggle between rival security agencies over the lucrative industry. Ukrainian journalists have also reported that proceeds from criminal operations help finance parts of the HUR’s activities.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has described phone scams as a key tactic employed by Kiev to extract money from Russian citizens, suggesting the practice has effectively become state policy. Moscow considers the industry a national security threat and claims Ukrainian scam networks operate in coordination with the country’s intelligence services.
Russian forces have recently intensified strikes on Ukrainian telecommunications infrastructure, mobile operators, and data centers in response to Kiev’s botched “pressure campaign” of drone attacks on civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia. The strikes have disrupted internet access, digital television, and other services, including by hitting data centers in Kiev that Moscow says were used by Ukrainian military and intelligence services. Media reports late last month also claimed a Russian strike hit one of the scam call centers in Dnepropetrovsk.

Growing outrage in Japan after US Marine arrested in woman’s killing

About 54,000 US military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, are stationed in Japan. The majority of these forces are based in Okinawa, a Japanese island that came under US administrative control at the end of World War II and was returned to Japan in 1972.

“The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that Tokyo will “continue to urge the US side to thoroughly enforce discipline” among its soldiers in Japan.
Kihara, who is in charge of mitigating the impact of US forces in Okinawa, said Tokyo has protested to the US at “various levels”.
The incident has caused outrage across Japan, and the Japanese Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Defence have summoned the US ambassador and the commander of US forces in Japan.

WATCH: Israel honors October 7 victims, heroes at second Mount Herzl ceremony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:25:21 UTC
20:25:21 KST

The official state ceremony to remember the victims and heroes of the October 7 massacre was held at the monument for fallen terror victims on Mount Herzl on Monday, following the national memorial ceremony for the massacre.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog were among the key political figures present at the event.
Noam Bettan, Israel's 2026 Eurovision representative, and Yuval Raphael, Nova music festival survivor and Israel's 2025 Eurovision representative, performed at the event.
Opposition leader and former prime minister Yair Lapid did not attend the ceremony. In a statement regarding his absence, Lapid stated that he would not attend ceremonies alongside individuals who refused to take responsibility for the massacre, blamed IDF commanders, and refused to establish a commission of inquiry.
Lapid noted that he would instead be attending ceremonies held by the families of October 7 victims.
Speaking at the ceremony, Herzog called on Israelis to preserve the solidarity and mutual responsibility displayed during the October 7 massacre, telling bereaved families that the country’s shared covenant must endure even amid political division.
Herzog focused on Route 232, the road running through the Gaza border communities that became both an escape route and a killing ground as Hamas-led terrorists attacked southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
October 7 on Route 232
The road, Herzog said, became a symbol not only of the failures and horrors of that morning, but also of the civilians, soldiers, police officers, and rescue personnel who drove toward the danger to save others.
“On the map of grief of October 7 there are communities and towns, kibbutzim and moshavim, fields and bomb shelters. And there is also one road. Route 232,” Herzog said.
The highway, which connects communities along the Gaza border, became one of the central sites of the massacre.
Survivors of the Nova music festival described fleeing along Route 232, while terrorists moved through the area and attacked vehicles, shelters, and communities.
Herzog contrasted those fleeing for their lives with Israelis who drove in the opposite direction, toward the attack, to rescue strangers.
“Private citizens whom no one had called raced into the inferno, some of them for people they had never met,” Herzog said. “They dropped the survivors off in a safe place, then turned around. And went back in. Into the danger.”
He also said that rescuers did not ask whom they were saving, which community they belonged to, how they prayed, or whom they voted for.
“In those hours, Route 232 was a picture of Israel as a whole,” Herzog said. “There was the terrible failure and its horrifying consequences, but there was also the strength and responsibility that arose in the face of those failures.”
Route 232 became closely associated with the devastation of the massacre, with burned vehicles, bullet-riddled cars, and roadside memorials marking the route in the years since the attack. A Jerusalem Post visit to the Gaza border area two years after the massacre described how the road and surrounding communities had been transformed by both destruction and commemoration.
Herzog said that while Israelis remembered Route 232 as “the road of blood,” it should also be remembered by another name: “the road of heroism.”
That heroism, he said, belonged to civilians, IDF soldiers, police officers, and rescue teams who “looked danger in the eye” and entered the fighting because other Israelis were still there.
“From their heroism, we discovered one of the great truths about Israel: When someone is left by the side of the road, there are Israelis who are incapable of simply driving on as though they had not seen them,” Herzog said.
October 7: Deeper 'covenant' binding Israeli society.
He then broadened the theme from the events of October 7 to what he described as the deeper “covenant” binding Israeli society.
“A state is built from laws, institutions, and borders. But the society that lives in a state thrives together because of a covenant,” Herzog said.
That covenant, he argued, did not require Israelis to agree politically or live in the same way. Rather, it required them to recognize a continuing obligation toward one another despite their differences.
The appeal came just over three weeks before Israelis were scheduled to vote in the October 27 general election, a date formally set earlier this year.
“In a few weeks, we will go to elections,” Herzog said. “Many issues are at stake, and I call on and urge all the citizens of Israel to exercise their democratic right and duty on Election Day.”
He acknowledged that the campaign would bring disputes and arguments, while urging Israelis to remember what he called the “simple covenant between us” that emerged during the massacre.
“This covenant is greater than all the disagreements between us. It is greater than all the arguments and differences. It belongs to all of us, all Israelis,” Herzog said.
“Israelis leave no one behind. Not on the battlefield and not in bereavement. Not in rehabilitation and not in the hospital.”
Israel marked the third anniversary of the massacre with state ceremonies at Mount Herzl and remembrance events across the country. Some 1,200 people were killed in the Hamas-led attack, and more than 250 people were kidnapped into Gaza.
Herzog closed by telling the bereaved families that Israel would continue to remember those murdered and the communities devastated on October 7.
“We will forever remember what happened that day,” Herzog said. “We will forever remember the homes that became graves, the terrible atrocities we might wish to forget, but will remember forever. All of them.”
“And in the words of the lament, we will know that our tearful eyes are the ones watering the fields of Be’eri. We will remember, and we will continue for their sake.”
Netanyahu echoes sentiments of mourning, remembrance, resilience
Netanyahu echoed Herzog's sentiments of mourning, remembrance, and resilience in the face of Israel’s enemies in his speech.
He shared his condolences with the bereaved families of the victims of the October 7 massacre, bowing his head in memory of the fallen.
“We mourn not only what was - but also what will no longer be,” Netanyahu said, quoting Chaim Habshoosh, the father of IDF Staff-Sergeant Nave Habshoosh, who was killed while fighting Hezbollah in Lebanon in June.
“Wherever we go - the fallen will always be part of our journey. We will continue to love the land, we will continue to travel throughout the land, we will continue to protect the land.”
Netanyahu asserted that despite the scars left by the massacre, the State of Israel is stronger than ever.
“The October 7 massacre in the Gaza Border Communities exposed for all to see the monstrous evil of our enemies,” he continued. “The fate of every human being touches the deepest fibers of our souls, and therefore we made an unrelenting effort until we brought back all of our hostages, down to the very last one.”
Netanyahu claimed that the massacre was the opening shot in Iran’s multi-step plan to destroy Israel in conjunction with proxy terrorist groups in the region.
“But through our combined strength, we shattered it step by step. Through our combined strength, with our fallen heroes, we acted with initiative, momentum, and on the offensive,” the prime minister asserted.
Yaakov Godo, the father of October 7 victim Tom Godo, interrupted Netanyahu during his speech.
"It’s a disgrace that you didn’t protect those murdered on October 7," exclaimed Yaakov Godo. "The blood of my son and of another 1,200 people murdered in a single day is on his (Netanyahu's) hands and on his head."
Netanyahu vows to defeat Israel's enemies, expand peace efforts
Netanyahu recalled that during the final steps of approving Operation Roaring Lion, he told officials that the responsibility for combating existential threats to Israel can not be passed on to future generations because if the state’s enemies are not defeated, there may be no future generation.
“Thanks to the heroism of our fighters, we turned the tables,” he continued. “But there are still tasks ahead of us, and we intend to complete them.”
Netanyahu vowed that there will be no Hamas rule in Gaza and that all terrorists involved in the massacre and holding of Israeli hostages “are living on borrowed time.”
In Lebanon, he added, the IDF will continue fighting Hezbollah and push efforts to make peace with the people of Lebanon.
“And as for Iran, we will not allow the regime of terror to threaten our existence,” Netanyahu asserted. “The tyrannical regime is weaker than it has ever been since its establishment. It is fighting for its life, and ultimately it will pass from the world.”
Netanyahu also emphasized that he would expand efforts to create reconciliation and peace in the region.
“Let us always remember: Our resilience rests upon the finest of our sons and daughters, who gave their lives for us,” Netanyahu said. “Our resilience rests upon the finest of our people, who act with courage and determination to secure the eternity of Israel.”
Netanyahu concluded his remarks by wishing a full physical and spiritual recovery to all wounded over the course of the war, pledging to all citizens of Israel that he would not relent in achieving the nation’s goal of remaining strong, united, and victorious.

Ebola outbreak has passed its peak – DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:25:11 UTC
20:25:11 KST

Ebola outbreak has passed its peak – DR Congo
The current Ebola outbreak has passed its peak, the DR Congo Health Ministry said on Friday, citing a decline in new cases in the country and a shrinking number of areas reporting active transmission.
According to the statement, transmission is now concentrated in individual health zones rather than across entire provinces. Of the 63 health zones under surveillance, 12 have recorded no new cases for at least 42 days, while another eight have gone between 22 and 42 days without reporting an infection. The share of identified contacts being monitored has nearly tripled, climbing from around 28% in May to 82% by September 28.
“The peak is really behind us,” Congolese Health Minister Roger Samuel Kamba said at a press briefing in Kinshasa, according to the Congolese Press Agency (ACP). The trend allows health teams to concentrate their response on areas where infections are still being detected, Kamba added.
Despite the improving trend cited by the minister, the virus continues to spread in several parts of the country. The latest Health Ministry data recorded 66 new confirmed cases and 38 deaths, bringing the toll as of October 2 to 8,442 infections and 4,080 deaths. The case fatality rate stood at 48.3%.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned on Thursday against interpreting a recent decline in reported cases as evidence that the outbreak is easing, stressing that insecurity has disrupted surveillance in some affected areas. At the time of its briefing, 45 of the 63 affected health zones were still reporting active transmission.
“Falling in this curve doesn’t mean that the outbreak is totally under control,” Africa CDC’s Wessam Mankoula said. “We cannot say at this stage the outbreak is under control.”
DR Congo continues to grapple with instability as the M23 rebel group maintains control over parts of the country, fueling clashes and humanitarian emergencies.
The DR Congo’s mineral-rich east has been plagued by decades of violence, with dozens of armed groups, including M23, fighting Congolese forces for power and control of resources such as gold and coltan. Clashes escalated in early 2025, killing thousands and forcing large-scale displacement, according to UN agencies. The rebels seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu, in late January and later captured Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu.
Ceasefire efforts have repeatedly faltered, including Qatar-facilitated talks in Doha. Congolese authorities have long accused Rwanda of supporting the militants, allegations backed by a UN panel of experts. Kigali has denied the claims. The accusations have strained Rwanda’s relations with Western partners, including Belgium. In March, Kigali severed diplomatic ties with Brussels, accusing it of harboring “neo-colonial delusions” and interfering in the conflict.
In December, Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi and his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame, ratified a US-brokered agreement committing Kigali to withdraw its forces from the border and end alleged support for M23, while Kinshasa pledged to curb militias hostile to Rwanda. US President Donald Trump has said the pact, which includes calls for a joint security mechanism, gives Washington rights to local mineral wealth. The fighting has continued despite Trump’s claims that he ended the decades-long conflict.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has raised similar concerns, warning that insecurity in eastern Congo has hampered surveillance, case detection and contact tracing.

EXPLAINER - Why has Russia’s Kaliningrad become a point of tension with the West?
Exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania, and borders the Baltic Sea
Burc Eruygur
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
ISTANBUL
Russia said could use 'all weapons' in arsenal in case of direct attack on region; NATO dismissed warnings, urging to 'stop the nuclear threats'
Russia’s westernmost Kaliningrad region has recently become a focal point of tensions with the West, as Russia threatened to use "all weapons" in its arsenal to defend the territory.
At a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow last week, President Vladimir Putin said any direct attack on Russia or attempt to annex the exclave would inevitably raise the issue of using "all weapons and means at Moscow’s disposal."
Noting that a Foreign Ministry letter on the protection of the Kaliningrad region does not mention nuclear weapons, Putin said the memo was issued in response to statements about a possible blockade of the exclave, and that Russia would have to respond if the region faced a direct attack.
A number of Russian embassies in Europe, including Ireland and the UK, also commented on “provocative” statements concerning Kaliningrad's blockade.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte did not disclose what was in the letter, but said the organization responded that "we are a defensive alliance," calling on Russia to "stop the nuclear threats" and "stop the war in Ukraine."

Russia’s sole exclave
With a population of about 1 million, the Kaliningrad region is a semi-exclave bordering Lithuania to the north and east, Poland to the south, and the Baltic Sea to the west.
It is separated from Belarus, a close ally of Russia with which it is formally part of a union state since 1999, by a roughly 65-kilometer (40.3-mile) corridor at its shortest point, known as the Suwalki Gap.
Named after the nearby Polish town of Suwalki, the gap serves as NATO’s only land route to the Baltic states and has gained particular geopolitical importance following Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania’s accession to the alliance in March 2004. All three Baltic states also joined the EU later that year.
The regional capital of Kaliningrad, a major port city on the Baltic coast that served as a former capital of the Kingdom of Prussia under the name of Konigsberg, became part of the Soviet Union after the end of World War II.
It was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946 in honor of Mikhail Kalinin, a Soviet politician who served as a chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet between 1938 and 1946.
The city is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet.
From here, Russia oversees large swaths of the Baltic’s airspace and maritime territory, but in the event of a war, it could struggle to sustain its forces if communications were disrupted.
Why the latest tensions?
Tensions have continued since the start of the Ukraine war in February 2022, leading to NATO strengthening its eastern flank. Finland and Sweden, which have a coast to the Baltic Sea, also joined the alliance in 2023 and 2024, respectively.
The latest spike came after NATO conducted a planned yet unannounced air exercise above northeastern Poland near the Kaliningrad region in August. The operation is said to have demonstrated the capability to cut off the exclave's radio and radar links as well as its air defenses in the event of a conflict with Russia.
The flights came after German newspaper Bild reported that the alliance developed the Land Warfighting Concept for responding to a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states, including strikes on missile and air defense systems in the region.
In May, Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said NATO has the means to destroy air defense capabilities in Kaliningrad.
"We must show the Russians that we are capable of breaking through their little fortress in Kaliningrad. If necessary, NATO has all the means to level the Russian air defense and missile bases there," Budrys said in an interview with the Swiss Neue Zurcher Zeitung newspaper. Russia had slammed the remarks as "verging on insanity."

Moldova aims to complete EU technical talks by 2028, join bloc by 2030

Unknown Publisher

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Moldova hopes to have completed all the technical work required to join the EU by the start of 2028, with full membership by 2030, the country's Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said at a press conference on Oct. 5.
Moldova has "taken major strides towards membership," the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said at the end of the 10th EU-Moldova Association Council meeting in Brussels. The country's "reform pace is very strong," Kallas said.
Tofan said he hopes Moldova can open the remaining four of six enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms the country needs to complete to be fully aligned with the EU — by the end of 2026.
The opening of clusters for Moldova and Ukraine has been politically coupled together by EU countries, and in June and July, Chisinau and Kyiv opened the first two of those six clusters.
However, political concerns over Ukraine have hindered progress for both countries.
A dispute with Budapest over Ukraine's Hungarian minority has prevented the opening of two clusters on macroeconomic topics.
Kyiv hopes to resolve this matter once its parliament adopts a relevant law addressing Hungary's concerns. The bill is expected to be put to a vote on Oct. 12.
Likewise, fears about Ukraine's large agricultural and transport sectors are sparking sectoral concerns, holding up the remaining two clusters.
Tofan said his country is "not afraid of ambitious timelines" and "not asking for shortcuts," but rather believes that Chisinau will have enacted all the reforms by early 2028. He voiced hope that Moldova will be part of the bloc by 2030.
"European integration is truly our national project," Tofan said.
The EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos signaled that this timetable could be possible and emphasized the "impressive pace" of Moldova's reform agenda.
EU accession "could happen during your mandate," Kos told Tofan during the press conference.
Moldova's parliamentary term is four years long, and the last election was held in September 2025.
Kos also signaled that she believes Ukraine will be able to pass its minorities bill on time, so that "it is possible we will open the next two clusters next week."
"This really is the autumn of enlargement," Kos said.

Ukraine touts gains from Operation Vivaldi as Russia claims major encirclements. What’s really happening on the battlefield?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:19:57 UTC
20:19:57 KST

Ukraine touts gains from Operation Vivaldi as Russia claims major encirclements. What’s really happening on the battlefield?
The Russian and Ukrainian armies continue their offensives in different sectors of the front. Because these operations have coincided with a new burst of activity in the negotiations mediated by Donald Trump, they have been accompanied by loud public relations campaigns. The Russian command describes its offensive as “destroying encircled groupings,” though in reality it has failed to encircle any major Ukrainian forces. Ukrainian military officials claim they have already moved on to the third phase of “Operation Vivaldi” near the city of Lyman in Donetsk region. Judging by open-source videos, however, they are still working — successfully — to push Russian forces off their first line of defense. In reality, the nature of the fighting has not changed. The Russian army is trying to break through to the Kramatorsk-Sloviansk urban area from different directions, while Ukrainian forces are trying to stop this advance with counterattacks. This battle is of decisive importance for the course of the war even without the additional public relations campaigns, which are more likely to mislead.
Vladimir Putin, speaking last week at a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, said “the authorities in Ukraine and Europe themselves believe they’ll be able to hold Donbas for only a year and a half to two years.” Russian forces, he said, will capture it “much sooner.” Putin assured the experts gathered at the event that the pace of the offensive is “accelerating.”
In reality, the Russian army captured Pokrovsk and Siversk by early 2026 and Kostiantynivka that summer, but over the following nine months failed to break through into the cities defending the Kramatorsk urban area from the south, northeast, and southwest. In the northeast, around Lyman, Russian forces lost much of the territory they had captured the previous year.
‘Operation Vivaldi’ and fighting on the Siverskyi Donets
- Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, who recently took charge of all forces defending Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from the north, east, and south (the newly formed “Center” grouping), said troops have begun the next phase of “Operation Vivaldi.” The goal of the operation — which, like the Italian composer’s famous work, is supposed to have four parts — remains unclear. Ukrainian forces are likely planning to push Russia’s 20th and 25th armies back across the Chornyi Zherebets, a tributary of the Siverskyi Donets. As a result, Russian forces risk losing all the gains they have made in this sector since the summer of 2025, when they crossed the Chornyi Zherebets along a broad front.
- Biletskyi has described the operation’s progress only in general terms, but many in Ukraine, unofficially, see it as something close to a harbinger of a new tactic that could help Ukrainian forces defeat the Russian army. The pace of “Vivaldi” so far shows no sign of such a shift: Ukrainian troops, who began the offensive in mid-summer, have advanced no more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) in different sectors.
- Videos that surfaced in recent weeks were meant to confirm Ukrainian successes. They show Ukrainian forces liberating several villages on the perimeter of the Russian salient around Lyman — Novoselivka, Shandryholove, and Nove — and attempting to gain a foothold in Serednie, Karpivka, and Katerynivka, villages that had been on the line of contact for months.
- Russia’s 20th Combined Arms Army, which faces Ukrainian forces in this sector, was previously thought to have largely withdrawn across the Chornyi Zherebets. Now, if the published videos mark the farthest extent of the Ukrainian advance, the 20th Army appears to still hold positions on the western bank of the Chornyi Zherebets near Zarichne and in the surrounding forests and ravines. The Russian position is worsening, however: Ukrainian assault troops have pushed deep into the flanks at Nove and Kolodiazi.
- To the south, meanwhile, Russia’s 25th Army continues to hold positions on the outskirts of Lyman. One video shows Russian assault troops back in the city center, which had largely been cleared of them earlier in the summer after a failed assault. Problems facing the neighboring 20th Army are worsening conditions on the 25th Army’s northern flank, and if Ukrainian forces capture the Chornyi Zherebets crossings at Torske and Zarichne, the 25th Army will have to withdraw from Lyman.
- The Russian offensive on Lyman was meant to support the 3rd Combined Arms Army’s advance along the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets toward Sloviansk. That plan worked until Russian forces were stopped near Lyman and on the approaches to Sviatohirsk, farther west. Problems facing its neighbors on the northern bank have recently forced the 3rd Army to fight its way toward Sloviansk alone. By late summer, its troops had reached the city of Mykolaivka, 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Sloviansk, but failed to take it in a quick assault, though Russian assault troops did reach its eastern outskirts.
- In recent weeks, Ukrainian forces have tried to eliminate the threat to Mykolaivka through counterattacks near Rai-Oleksandrivka, reaching the village center, where heavy fighting has broken out. Russian forces still control the southeastern approaches to Mykolaivka, though, and are trying to outflank the Ukrainian units advancing on Rai-Oleksandrivka near the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas canal in the Yurkivka and Orikhuvatka area.
- These battles will determine whether Russian forces get closer to Sloviansk’s outskirts in 2026. Biletskyi’s troops are likely to try a larger counterattack on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets.
Dobropillia and Druzhkivka
- Russian forces are trying to go around the Kramatorsk urban area from the west. In their path is one of Ukraine’s “fortresses”: the city of Dobropillia. Russian troops spent the first half of the year covering the 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Pokrovsk, which they had already captured, to Dobropillia’s southern outskirts. Forces in this sector needed significant reinforcement: the 76th Airborne Assault Division was redeployed to the area from other sectors first, followed by the 90th Tank Division.
- In September, the Russian Defense Ministry unexpectedly announced that Dobropillia had been encircled. A month earlier, Putin had expressed displeasure with the slow pace of the advance to the commander of the 76th Division. Judging by that conversation and the place names mentioned in it, Russian forces were only about five kilometers (3 miles) from the city at the time and were not even contemplating an encirclement.
- In the two weeks since the encirclement announcement, no evidence has emerged that Dobropillia has been outflanked from the west or east. Ukrainian forces, judging by published videos, managed to regain control of Hannivka, the city’s northeastern outskirts. Russian assault troops did enter Dobropillia itself from the south, however, beginning an assault on the city.
- At the same time, Russian forces are widening the front of their offensive around Dobropillia. The 90th Tank Division and its neighbors advanced several kilometers north in the sector between Dobropillia and Druzhkivka, while units of the 2nd Combined Arms Army pushed southwest of the city in the Hrushynka River valley.
- Although Dobropillia isn’t encircled, the situation around it is growing increasingly difficult for Ukrainian forces. Russian forces, after redeploying large reserves, now hold a significant advantage in the area.
- In September, Biletskyi described Russia’s plan for the Donbas offensive this way: the Russian “northern pincer” was meant to cut supply routes to Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by crossing the Siverskyi Donets near Sviatohirsk and Lyman and blocking the roads to Izyum and Kharkiv, while the “southern pincer,” advancing through Dobropillia, was meant to cut the road out of Kramatorsk near Barvinkove and complete the encirclement of the Kramatorsk urban area. The “defeat of the northern pincer” near Lyman, Biletskyi said, eliminated that threat. Russia’s plan now appears far more modest, however: after capturing Dobropillia, Russian forces want to push directly along the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road toward the center of the urban area, as well as from Chasiv Yar toward the heights south of Kramatorsk. Defending Dobropillia and the territory east of the city will require Ukraine’s military command to urgently redeploy additional forces.
The ‘Vovchansk encirclement’
- The Russian command has announced another “encirclement” far beyond the Donbas front. In May 2024, when Russia launched a new invasion of the Kharkiv region using forces of the Leningrad Military District (the “Sever” grouping), the Russian General Staff likely planned to combine this offensive with the assault on Donbas: after capturing Vovchansk, troops were supposed to push through Velykyi Burluk into the rear of Ukrainian forces defending Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. This mirrored the Russian operation in 2022, when Russian forces reached Izyum within the first days of the full-scale invasion, crossed the Siverskyi Donets after heavy fighting, and advanced almost to the northern outskirts of Sloviansk. Russian forces lost all of this territory in the Kharkiv region in the fall of 2022.
- The 2024 offensive was stopped in the center of Vovchansk itself, after which it lost any connection to plans for capturing Donbas. The “Sever” grouping’s forces, however, maintained contact with the “Zapad” grouping, which had spent years unsuccessfully attacking nearby Kupyansk. The top priority became reaching Velykyi Burluk, in the rear of the Ukrainian grouping defending Kupyansk.
- In the fall of 2025, Ukraine’s command decided to push Russian forces back from Kupyansk, using units that had been defending Vovchansk. Ukrainian forces managed to temporarily liberate central Kupyansk, but at the cost of a sharp escalation around Vovchansk: Russian forces crossed the Vovcha River in the city center and, by year’s end, had begun a slow advance toward Velykyi Burluk.
- In the summer of 2026, Russian forces unexpectedly launched an offensive across the state border east of Vovchansk. At the same time, groups of Russian assault troops began infiltrating south from Vovchansk toward the village of Bilyi Kolodiaz. In September, the Russian Defense Ministry announced that its troops had “closed the encirclement of a major Ukrainian grouping near the border” east of Bilyi Kolodiaz.
- Since then, no evidence has emerged that this encirclement actually exists. Russian assault troops have been spotted in Bilyi Kolodiaz (more precisely, a single assault trooper with a Russian flag). Russian units advancing from east of the border have reached Blahodatne, but a 17-kilometer (11-mile) “gap” remains between Bilyi Kolodiaz and Blahodatne, where no Russian troop presence has been recorded so far.
- Ukrainian forces haven’t experienced any supply shortages so far at the positions supposedly encircled. Judging by published videos, Ukrainian armored vehicles are still operating inside the hypothetical “pocket” even a month after Russia announced that supply lines had been cut.
- Despite all the Russian command’s exaggerations, the situation for Ukrainian forces in this sector continues to deteriorate: they clearly lack the strength to eliminate the Russian assault troops that have broken through into their rear. Ukrainian troops periodically counterattack with small groups of two or three tanks — a pattern that, given how this war is being fought, may point to a serious shortage of infantry and even drones.
- About 15 kilometers (9 miles) separate Velykyi Burluk from the positions where Russian assault troops have been recorded. Because fighting here is taking place without a stable front line, Russian forces could break through to this city, which is critical for supplying Ukrainian forces on the Vovchansk and Kupyansk fronts.
