Breadcrumb
Protesters disrupt New Zealand aviation and space summit over Israel, US military ties
New Zealand police arrested at least two protesters on Friday, 2 October, after vehicles blocked emergency entrances at the Te Pae Convention Centre in Christchurch, where protesters gathered outside the New Zealand Aviation and Space Summit.
Protesters gathered outside the venue to oppose links between the space and defence industries.
About 20 police officers were deployed around the city centre venue on Friday morning, where dozens of protesters opposed to links between the aviation and space sector and the defence industries gathered and chanted across the road in Victoria Square.
One protester also chained himself to a vehicle near one of the centre entrances. Slogans including "New Zealand is complicit in genocide" and "This vehicle is obstructing war crimes" were written on the car.
Christchurch Metro police area commander Lynn Todd told reporters that two men, aged 56 and 23, had been charged with obstructing a road.
The arrests came after vehicles blocked the building's emergency entrances.
Police had earlier announced that they would monitor the protest throughout the day.
Summit organisers warned participants to allow extra time for security checks and urged them not to confront protesters outside the centre.
"We respect the right to peaceful protest, but police will not tolerate any actions that threaten public safety or intimidate people exercising their legal rights," Todd added.
The protest was organised by Peace Action Ōtautahi, which had called for a "storm the summit" action.
The group urged protesters to march from Victoria Park to the Te Pae Convention Centre.
Joseph Bray, a spokesperson for Peace Action Ōtautahi, said in a video posted by the organisation on its Facebook account that he had lain on the ground in front of the entrance to the Te Pae Convention Centre for an extended period to prevent "these people from going about their day as usual".
Bray added that he would move the large concrete block to close the centre's vehicle gate entrance and prevent "war criminals and those profiting from them from going ahead with their deals".
"The need for these actions to highlight the degree of complicity in genocide and war crimes by New Zealand's aviation and space industries," he said. "These are the things that have been covered up, while our industries contribute to this global imperial satellite and missile network, and we are a key part of this."
Activist Jay Dogheed said the organisation opposed the participation of companies with military and defence contracts in the aviation and space sector.
Dogheed told The New Zealand Herald, "We are here today because there are a lot of companies involved in this aviation and space conference at Te Pae, and they do not want to use space for peaceful purposes. They want to use it for profit and for war."
He said companies operating in the sector had links to the US and Israeli militaries, and further explained that protesters wanted summit participants to know that they were "not welcome in this city".
"We are here to make them feel uncomfortable and to show that we are serious about our position," he added.
Activist Aurora Garner-Randolph told the same newspaper that protesters wanted stricter restrictions on the military use of New Zealand aviation and space technology.
"The aviation and space sector has huge potential to do good in climate change mitigation technologies, but clear legal and ethical standards must be put in place," she added.
She said the group wanted to halt the export of aviation, space and military components, as well as intelligence-related launches for foreign militaries, until stronger legal safeguards were put in place.
"Christchurch has a long history of peace; it is a city of peace. The time for discussion is over, and now is the time for clear legal change," she stressed.
By about 10:30 am, most protesters had left the area.
The New Zealand Aviation and Space Summit brings together companies operating in the aviation and space sector, researchers, investors, regulators and international representatives with more than 50 speakers from New Zealand and abroad taking part in this year's summit programme.
The programme covers autonomous aircraft, aviation and space equipment manufacturing, Earth observation, and climate monitoring, as well as defence applications.
Mark Rocket, chief executive of Kea Aerospace and organiser of the summit, said protesters had the right to demonstrate.
He told The New Zealand Herald, "We live in a free and democratic country, so we support the right of protesters to protest," while pointing out that defence represented only one part of the wider aviation and space sector.
"The reality is that we have an aviation and space sector working in environmental monitoring, communications and a wide range of areas, and defence represents one part of that for some aviation and space companies in New Zealand," he added.
Responding to protesters' concerns about companies working in defence technology, Rocket stressed that many aviation and space technologies have both civilian and military uses.
"But from what we see, New Zealand largely follows an approach focused on environmental monitoring and communications, which is broadly aligned with New Zealand's values and its approach to how it deals with the defence sector," he said.
The protest follows a similar action at last year's summit, when pro-Palestinian activists blocked entrances to the Te Pae Convention Centre, and the police intervened to remove several protesters.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has said the US is closely monitoring the case of a Russian laboratory worker who died last week after a reported accident at a plague research institute in Siberia.
“We’re watching and monitoring it closely,” Rubio said on Monday before leaving for a trip to Europe. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it.”
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, became ill at work. She died two days later on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov.
It remains unclear how she became unwell. Unconfirmed reports in Russian media have suggested Shipilova may have been infected after a mishap at the laboratory. Officials have not publicly confirmed that account.
Local media have reported that the institute has subsequently been locked down, with staff forced to sleep on the floor and on chairs. “They’ve been isolating everybody since Friday – more than 60 people,” one relative, Roman, told the news portal Siberia.Realities.
He said family members were allowed to drop off food at a checkpoint while tests were carried out inside the building. Similar quarantine restrictions have been placed on several other hospitals in and around the city.
Rubio, citing what Russians have released about the death, said it seemed a worker in the lab became infected and there was concern the disease may have spread internally.
“There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously,” he said. “But like anything else, something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads.”
Senior Russian officials have added to public disquiet by sending conflicting messages. Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the Buryatia region, which neighbours Irkutsk, initially wrote that Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”. It insisted that tests found no micro-organisms linked to her professional work and described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the area as stable.
Authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk briefly urged residents to avoid travelling to Shelekhov and surrounding settlements after what they said was unofficial information about a possible plague infection. They later deleted the post from social media.
“There are no obvious changes to daily life on the streets, but people are worried and anxious. Locals are angry that they are not being told anything,” said Elena Trifonova, a journalist with People of Baikal, an exiled Russian media outlet specialising in Siberia.
Despite the lack of a confirmed diagnosis, precautionary measures appear to have been introduced across the region. The US-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on Monday that several hospitals in Irkutsk had been placed under quarantine.
The outlet confirmed that staff from Shipilova’s workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had been kept inside the institute since 2 October.
Patients at Irkutsk city clinical hospital No 1 and the Ivano-Matreninskaya children’s hospital said relatives were not being allowed to visit and people inside were not permitted to leave.
On social media, local residents described some of the precautions being introduced.
Ulyana Gavryunina, who went on Monday to one of Irkutsk’s main maternity hospitals for a routine check-up on Monday, said doctors refused to allow her mother in, citing a quarantine imposed over the suspected plague case. Gavryunina said staff member checked her for flu-like symptoms and asked her to fill out a screening form for infections, on which “plague” was listed. She posted a photograph of the form on Instagram.
Elsewhere, a mask requirement was introduced at the Irkutsk aluminium smelter in Shelekhov. The plant’s director, Artyom Fominykh, called it a preventive measure, saying: “Better safe than sorry.” Over the weekend several public events in Irkutsk were cancelled.
Shipolova’s death has prompted intervention from senior federal health officials. Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and the country’s chief sanitary doctor, travelled to Irkutsk on Friday.
She attended an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission over what officials called a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection”.
Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, urged residents to remain calm after meeting Popova to coordinate the response. “All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none is showing signs of illness and laboratory tests have returned negative results,” he wrote on Telegram.
Kobzev made no reference to reports that a laboratory worker had died.
US politicians have raised concerns about the incident, which follows longstanding and unfounded allegations by the Kremlin that Ukraine has secretly carried out biological weapons research with the support of Washington.
A Republican representative, Don Bacon, a senior member of the House armed services committee, wrote on social media: “I remember hearing from anti-Ukraine voices about their so-called bio labs. It was Russian disinformation ops at their best. But in reality it is Russia with the bio labs.”
Plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian far east, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents and their fleas.
But human cases in Russia are rare. Before the suspected Irkutsk case, the country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in Siberia’s Altai Republic contracted plague after helping butcher a marmot.
“This case here seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further,” Prof Ian Jones, a professor of virology at the University of Reading, in the UK, said. “Although it is true that pneumonic plague is directly transmissible, the contacts of the primary case are known and can be treated if they show any sign of infection.”
He added: “Plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia, but the living conditions associated with previously spread plague are no longer generally true, antibiotics are available and its potential is therefore limited.”

Ukraine prepares to restore air connections: will domestic carriers be able to return
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:44:54 EEST
19:44:54 KST

Ukraine prepares to restore air connections: will domestic carriers be able to return
Kyiv • UNN
The authorities are preparing to reopen the skies, but without resolving aviation leasing issues, Ukrainian carriers may disappear. Their return should support the economy.
The authorities are considering the possibility of opening the skies to civil aviation before the war ends. After civil flights resume, it is important that domestic airlines be the first to return to the Ukrainian market. This will not only help restore the industry but also bring economic activity, jobs, and tax revenues related to air transportation back to Ukraine. Economist Viktor Halchynskyi told UNN in an exclusive comment.
The authorities are preparing to open the airports
After the full-scale war began, Ukrainian air carriers were forced to relocate a significant part of their operations abroad in order to preserve their aircraft, crews, and technical staff. Although the airlines’ operations are currently concentrated outside Ukraine, they continue to pay taxes in Ukraine. According to data from Daniil Menshykov, head of the State Aviation Service of Ukraine, aviation-industry enterprises paid nearly UAH 27 billion in taxes and fees to the budget in 2022–2025.
From time to time, proposals to resume airport operations in Ukraine in various forms are voiced in the public sphere. For example, ideas have also been voiced about restoring air connections in western Ukraine.
According to Mykola Kalashnyk, Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport, there is currently both a political decision and an economic understanding of the need to open Ukraine’s airspace, and the relevant preparations are already under way. In particular, work is ongoing to organize safe areas and shelters and provide alternative sources of electricity, among other things. Ukraine is also studying the experience of other countries whose airports operate amid wartime risks.
Ukrainian airlines may not live to see the skies reopen
Ensuring an appropriate level of security amid constant Russian shelling will obviously take time, but Ukrainian air carriers are already being forced to operate under extremely difficult conditions. The closed airspace deprived them of the domestic market, forced them to refocus on the international market, and imposed additional costs for maintaining their fleets, crews, and technical staff. Against the backdrop of these problems, criminal pressure has become an additional risk for the industry, affecting a number of domestic airlines because of the new approach taken by Ukrainian state bodies to taxing aircraft leasing. Under these conditions, there is a risk that some carriers simply will not live to see the moment when Ukrainian airspace is open to civil flights again.
As UNN previously reported, aviation-industry representatives have long been drawing attention to the problem of state bodies’ new interpretation of leasing payments made to nonresidents, which emerged without any amendments to the Tax Code or international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation. Since 2024, the Economic Security Bureau has begun interpreting transactions involving the leasing of aircraft from nonresidents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for leasing airplanes and helicopters. Based on this approach, the ESB opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Rosa Vetrov," H3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline—"Urga"—may also figure in a similar case.
The investigations were launched despite the fact that almost all air carriers successfully passed tax audits, and the tax authorities’ remarks concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Aviation-industry representatives insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the law and requires the establishment of a unified state approach. Moreover, interpreting aircraft leasing as royalties—a practice found in no other country in the world—makes Ukrainian carriers uncompetitive in the international market.
Analysis of data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft shows that as of July 29, 2026, 27 private airlines operated 152 aircraft. Of these, 131, or 86%, were leased, while only 21 airplanes and helicopters (14%) were owned by the airlines themselves. It is worth noting that all leased commercial aircraft are owned by foreign owners. Therefore, the majority of Ukrainian airlines could come under criminal pressure, which could prompt them to leave the Ukrainian market.
It is important that Ukrainian air carriers return to Ukraine
The return of Ukrainian airlines is significant not only fiscally but also symbolically. Unfortunately, not many of our airlines that survived this period remain. Therefore, their return will be an important signal of the restoration of Ukrainian aviation
According to him, the resumption of airport operations will also affect related sectors.
If we set aside the wartime situation and allow ourselves to dream, the restoration of civil aviation will have an effect not only directly on the aviation industry but also on a whole range of related sectors. First and foremost, these include tourism, passenger services, catering and other industries that serve aviation—from food services to airport shops. This will also provide additional revenue to the state, since there are specialized payments and fees for aerodrome services
Halchynskyi added that the resumption of civil aviation flights would mean that the country is returning to normal functioning.
The restoration of civil aviation will also have a noticeable indirect effect on tourism, the hotel business, catering, logistics and other sectors. Moreover, the restoration of civil aviation at least at one Ukrainian airport—most likely in western Ukraine—will in itself become a signal of a certain stabilization and that the country is gradually returning to normal functioning
Demand could be very high after the reopening of the skies
Halchynskyi predicts that after flights resume, the aviation market could come back to life fairly quickly, as significant pent-up demand for international and domestic transportation will emerge.
After the reopening of the skies, I think the aviation industry will be able to recover quickly enough, since demand for international and domestic air travel will initially be very high. It will be limited primarily by the capacity of airports—for example, Lviv or Uzhhorod
According to him, Lviv Airport has already demonstrated its ability to handle significant passenger flows, particularly during Euro 2012. Therefore, under favorable conditions, the restoration of substantial transport volumes is entirely realistic.
At the same time, safety remains the determining factor. If airport operations have to be constantly suspended because of air-raid alerts, this will result in aircraft downtime, flight delays and cancellations and, consequently, additional costs for carriers. This will particularly affect the decisions of foreign airlines, which will take into account security risks and the cost of insuring aircraft.
That is why, in Halchynskyi's opinion, Ukraine must use the time to prepare so that, once the security situation improves, flights can be restored as quickly as possible.
Today, we can only prepare so that we can launch aviation as quickly as possible when the time comes. Under favorable conditions, this could take literally 10–15 days, several weeks or a maximum of one month
When will the airports become operational?
The expert doubts that it will be possible to open Ukraine's airspace as early as next year.
I am not sure that this will happen in the coming months or even next year. The main prerequisite for restoring civil aviation should be a significant decrease in the intensity of the war specifically in the air. Today, we are seeing the opposite situation. It is unlikely that we will simply be able to build aviation according to the Israeli model, when attacks also occur frequently but are less intense and have a less negative impact than in Ukraine
Under these conditions, the state's task is not limited to technically preparing airports for the future reopening of the airspace. It is equally important to ensure that, by that time, Ukraine retains its own airlines capable of being the first to return to the domestic market.
The authorities are clearly aware of this. To resolve the situation involving pressure on domestic carriers, the issue of aviation leasing was submitted for consideration by the Committee on Tax Policy, Accounting and Auditing of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the creation of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft general tax consultation on the taxation of lease payments in favor of non-residents. This mechanism will make it possible to end pressure on Ukraine's aviation industry from the Bureau of Economic Security and establish uniform rules for the taxation of aircraft and helicopter rentals that comply with the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international law.
Representatives of the aviation industry warn that if the situation with aviation leasing cannot be resolved, Ukraine risks losing its civil aviation sector. This would mean that, after the reopening of the airspace, the existing demand for air travel would be met primarily by foreign carriers, and a significant share of the economic benefits from the restoration of air links would not accrue to Ukraine.

Musk to follow Trump and rebrand SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:42:21 UTC
19:42:21 KST

The company will be known as SpaceXSI, its third name this year alone, as Elon Musk follows Donald Trump’s push to rebrand AI into "super intelligence".
Elon Musk is changing the name of his combined AI and space company SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, embracing US President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming artificial intelligence as super intelligence in all government communication.
Musk only recently renamed xAI as SpaceXAI, about 90 days ago, after SpaceX's June stock market debut and February takeover of the company. The agreement valued SpaceX at $1 trillion (€892bn) and xAI at $250 billion (€223bn).
The South African tech tycoon revealed that the company is making the change yesterday in a reply to a user on his social media platform X, who asked if there was “any possibility of renaming to SpaceXSI?”
“Yes, we will make that change,” said Musk.
The user asked the tech tycoon following an earlier post where he stated: “No more AI. SI. It’s better.” He later tweeted, “SpaceX is a super intelligence company.”
No changes to the company’s websites or social media have been made as of publication, with no indication of when the changes will take effect.
SpaceXAI currently operates the AI chatbot Grok, which is built into Musk’s social media platform X, with roughly 117 million active monthly users.
Grok is also widely integrated into US government and military operations, as part of a $200 million (€178mn) agreement reached in July 2025.
The decision follows US President Donald Trump’s latest executive order to rename something globally recognised to a name more in keeping with his world view, such as changing the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The fact that Musk willingly agreed to Trump’s latest rebranding is nothing out of the ordinary, with Google and Apple both following Trump’s demand by renaming the bodies of water on their map platforms for US users.
Trump first mentioned his preference for super intelligence over artificial intelligence during a speech at the UN general assembly, where he argued that “artificial” makes it sound fake when it is actually “amazing,” claiming that “super intelligence" is a more accurate description.
On the same day Trump issued the executive order he hosted an AI summit with Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brokman (OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Musk.
The six tech leaders signed a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,” establishing a loose framework for companies to implement and self-regulate their own security controls. It is also legally unenforceable and carries no penalties.
It sets a worrying precedent given the escalating number of incidents involving AI agents carrying out “rogue” behaviour that has seen US and Australian government websites attacked, prompting calls for tighter regulation by world leaders and “pacing the frontier” by America’s leading AI companies.
Instead, Trump’s agreement allows these companies to regulate themselves without scrutiny or consequences.
On Sunday 4 October, Trump announced the creation of a “Super Intelligence Force” to coordinate American efforts and ensure the US stays ahead in the AI race.

Anatomy of a flop: ‘Digger’ a disaster at box office and a major misfire for Tom Cruise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:41:58 UTC
19:41:58 KST

The Tom Cruise starring black comedy 'Digger' has tanked at the box office and threatens to become one of the biggest box office disasters of recent times.
It was a big swing, and it has turned out to be a huge miss.
What was supposed to be the awards season heavyweight to finally get Tom Cruise to the Oscar podium has ended up as one of the biggest box office flops of the actor’s career. Worse, early indicators strongly suggest that Digger is on track to lose between $150-200 million. Those are John Carter numbers.
The movie, starring Tom Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon who has triggered an environmental disaster, made just $8 million in the US and $20 million globally in its opening weekend.
By comparison, Digger had a production budget of up to $180m.
On top of Digger ’s huge budget, the trades report that Warner Bros. spent another $100m on marketing, which means that the movie needs to make $300m just to break even.
Granted, intake never equates to quality, but when an Oscar-winning director of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s calibre teams up with Tom Cruise, one of the world’s biggest stars and box office magnets, this disastrous performance is notable.
Digger was always a gamble as a rare big-budget, star-driven original comedy. The metatextual eco-satire has proven to be audience antagonizing, with its bold twist being both admirable in its ambition and a baffling gambit.
In Euronews Culture’s review of Digger, we wrote: “Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant, Bardo), a polarising filmmaker to begin with, has made both the boldest film of 2026 and this year’s wildest misfire. Digger is certainly his most pretentious film to date. (...) It’s hard to write more about Digger without spoiling Iñárritu’s brave but misguided gambit, but safe to say that once he does pull the rug from under the audience, he leaves viewers with a boated folly that’s both hollow and heavy-handed.”
Read the full, spoiler-free review here.
Digger’s dismal box office numbers contribute to an annus horribilis for Warner Bros., as the studio has struggled throughout 2026 to gross more than $100 million domestically for each of its releases so far. Both The Bride and Supergirl produced big losses for the studio.
Additionally, the timing of Digger ’s commercial failure couldn’t be worse. Paramount Skydance’s controversial acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery is set to close next week after approval from the US district court for the $110bn deal was received last Wednesday.
Warner Bros.'s only hope at salvaging its disastrous year will come in December, with the release of Dune: Part Three, which is projected to open globally to around $200-230 million.

Luke Harding's 'Betrayal' charts the collapse of the rules-based order — and who is to blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:41:22 UTC
19:41:22 KST

Luke Harding's 'Betrayal' charts the collapse of the rules-based order — and who is to blame
Luke Harding's “Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest" begins with a turning point in the full-scale war most people probably haven't spent enough time coming to terms with: North Korean soldiers getting ready to join the biggest land war in Europe since 1945.
"Soon they would be stumbling through alien woods and fields, sent by one dictator to help out another. It was a sign of a world turned upside down. The rules-based international order — the post-1945 understanding that states didn't invade each other or change borders by force — seemed broken," Harding writes.
At the start of the full-scale war, the idea of North Korean soldiers fighting in Europe would have seemed implausible to most. Today, it is just one more sign of a world reverting to Great Power politics, the betrayal at the heart of Harding's book. The U.S., Russia, and China pursue their "strategic interests," and as a result, millions of people are left hostage to a system that should have died with the last century.
Who is to blame for the collapse of the post-1945 order? As the title suggests, Harding doesn't pin it on a singular country or individual. But Harding reserves some of his most acerbic digs for U.S. President Donald Trump, whom he calls, among other things, "the prostrator-in-chief when it comes to Russia." In his second term, Harding argues, Trump has emboldened authoritarian leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping to act with unprecedented impunity.
One of the most telling examples is the so-called Alaska summit in August 2025, when Trump invited Putin for his first visit to the U.S. in nearly a decade. Before the summit, as Harding reminds the reader, Trump warned that Russia would face "severe consequences" if it didn't agree to a ceasefire with Ukraine.
Although the Alaska summit was presented as a chance for the U.S. to press Russia for peace, it opened with pomp and ceremony: Trump applauded as Putin walked toward him along a red carpet, and the two stood side by side as a B-2 stealth bomber and F-35 fighter jets flew overhead. The talks ended without any hope of ending the war, and the visuals were disturbing — including Putin casually brushing off a journalist's question about civilian deaths.
As Harding writes, "Putin could be seen grinning (during the summit), smirking even, an international outlaw no longer. The invitation was a rare honor, granted to few statesmen. It was a sign of Trump's esteem for his visitor, and a scene that might have been scripted by the Kremlin's own talented dramaturgs."
Trump's praise of Putin over the years has fueled endless speculation about his motives, most famously including the theory that he is some "compromised asset." Harding acknowledges that the Czechoslovak security services kept files on Trump and his first wife, Ivana, in cooperation with the Soviet counterparts, and that the couple visited the USSR in July 1987. Two months later, Trump ran full-page newspaper ads criticizing U.S. foreign policy, which Harding describes as "an unusual move for a non-politician."
However, the record is suggestive rather than conclusive, and it raises as many questions as it answers. Harding wonders whether it is indifference, fear, the prospect of lucrative business deals, or a genuine wish not to imperil peace talks that drives Trump's actions – or lack thereof – toward Russia. Whatever the answer, he argues, Trump's inaction has been seen as "a moral choice of sorts" that "ignored the Kremlin had a long and outrageous history of lying," and the Kremlin, in turn, has interpreted his behavior as a sign of approval.
Perhaps most importantly, "Betrayal" ties this high-level state intrigue to Harding's on-the-ground reporting from Ukraine, introducing readers to Ukrainians still living in front-line cities who no longer fear the sounds of explosions, as well as the soldiers defending against Russian advances. These Ukrainians are reminders that there is no sense to Russia's talk of "defending" its so-called "sphere of influence," and that Ukrainians alone have the right to decide what's best for their country.
However, the book also looks beyond Ukraine to the aftershocks of the collapsing post-1945 order, like Trump repeatedly entertaining the idea of the U.S. taking Greenland — by force, if necessary. Putin, when asked about it, called it "an issue that concerns two specific nations and has nothing to do with (Russia)." According to Harding, the reasoning behind Putin's words was obvious: "if the Americans took Greenland, Putin's war in Ukraine looked like less of an aberration."
The U.S., long the world's leading power, still stands for a sense of order, even if that feeling is increasingly nostalgic. Leaders like President Volodymyr Zelensky, Harding notes, have no choice but to push on through Trump's erraticism — "self-appointed world peacemaker one day, warmonger the next" — for a greater cause.
If the book has any setback, it is one of scale: the events Harding describes are so vast, from the front line in Ukraine to covert Russian agents trying to influence U.K. politicians, that it is sometimes easy to get lost in the urgency of the book's underlying message. Yet the book earns its place in an argument that is only beginning, and it leaves the reader with a question that no one in power seems eager to answer: what sort of world do we want to inhabit, and whom do we want to lead it?

Hi, this is Kate Tsurkan, thanks for reading this article. There is an ever-increasing amount of books about or related to Ukraine, Russia, and Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine available to English-language readers, and I hope my recommendations prove useful when it comes to your next trip to the bookstore.

Russia's oil and gas revenues dropped by 22% in September despite rising oil prices

Russia's oil and gas revenues dropped by 22% in September despite rising oil prices
Russia's oil and gas revenues amounted to approximately RUB 452.4 billion (approx. US$5.43 billion) in September, down 22% from September 2025.
Source: Russian media outlet The Bell, citing data from the Russian Finance Ministry
Details: September revenues were 7% higher than the RUB 424 billion (US$5.1 billion) recorded in August. Oil and gas revenues in August fell by 16% year-on-year.
Much of the revenue is being swallowed up by budget spending to compensate oil refiners for the gap between domestic and global fuel prices. In September, these payments increased from RUB 197.3 billion (US$2.4 billion) to RUB 305.5 billion (US$3.7 billion).
These payments consumed the entire additional revenue from the mineral extraction tax, which brought in RUB 807 billion (US$9.7 billion) in September, compared with RUB 702.7 billion (US$8.4 billion) in August.
Since the beginning of the year, the Russian treasury has received RUB 5.47 trillion (US$65.6 billion) in oil and gas revenues, 17.2% less than in January-September 2025.
The September figure was close to the Russian Finance Ministry's expectations, falling RUB 10 billion (US$120 million) short after additional oil and gas revenues were taken into account.
In October, the Russian Finance Ministry expects to receive RUB 289.5 billion (US$3.5 billion) in additional oil and gas revenues.
Background: Russia's wealthiest people have contributed more than 1% of the country's state spending in 2026 through "voluntary" payments. In August, it emerged that these contributions to the Russian budget had reached RUB 383.69 billion (US$4.6 billion) by mid-month, compared with RUB 15.6 billion (US$187 million) before Vladimir Putin met business leaders in March.

NEW DELHI: The ruling BJP on Monday said the Supreme Court's decision to issue notices to the Election Commission (EC) and the Centre on pleas seeking the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar showed that all institutions in the country were "functioning independently" and there was no atmosphere of "fear and dictatorship"."The country is moving in a very democratic way. Drapatyi’s “War Plan”: Commander-in-Chief Submits First-of-Its-Kind Document to National Security and Defense Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:40:02 UTC
19:40:02 KST

The team of Mykhailo Drapatyi, Ukraine’s Commander-in-Chief, has reportedly prepared a “war plan” for the Ukrainian army – believed to be the first document of its kind.
Ukrainska Pravda reported on this.
Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council has reviewed the document for several weeks.
According to the media, the plan is intended to set out exactly what the Ukrainian army needs to do to ensure Ukraine’s survival and within what timeframe.
It outlines a strategic vision for how the war should be conducted going forward.
Beyond the broader strategic issues, the document also examines specific questions about how Ukraine should approach defense. One issue is whether troops serving on the front line as the army’s “eyes and ears” should remain there if they have little or no opportunity to engage the enemy.
The document is part of a broader effort by Drapatyi’s team to introduce changes across Ukraine’s Armed Forces since he became Commander-in-Chief.
These changes include decentralizing military command, reorganizing the military group structure, and giving commanders on the ground greater freedom to make decisions.
According to Ukrainska Pravda, Drapatyi is also seeking to move all commanders onto the Delta situational awareness system and is pushing for the practical use of digital solutions.
Meanwhile, according to one of the corps’ chiefs of staff, the General Staff should be responsible for building up reserves, strategic planning, and international cooperation, while the Joint Forces Command should oversee combat operations.
Militarnyi previously reported that Mykhailo Drapatyi, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, had outlined the principles that would guide his leadership of the Ukrainian military.
Drapatyi identified stabilizing the front line and regaining the initiative as his top priorities, aiming to prevent the enemy from achieving its operational objectives. Other priorities include strengthening the protection of Ukraine’s population, cities, villages, and critical infrastructure from enemy strikes.

Swiss tenants’ association sounds alarm over rent prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:39:20 UTC
19:39:20 KST

Swiss tenants’ association sounds alarm over rent prices
Rents in Switzerland have risen by around 32% over the last 20 years, according to the Swiss Tenants’ Association (ASI).
Today, to mark International Tenants’ Day, the organisation is drawing attention to the growing financial burden on tenants in Switzerland and is calling for measures to be taken.
In no other European country is the proportion of people living in rented accommodation as high as in Switzerland. According to the ASI, two-thirds of households are tenants.
+ Apartment for rent in Zurich? Why the search is so difficult
The rent index rose by 32.1% between 2005 and 2025 according to the ASI. During the same period, mortgage rates reached an all-time low. The reference rate currently stands at 1.25%. As rents are legally indexed to this rate, many of them should have fallen. In reality, however, they have continued to rise, the association laments.
It is primarily low- and middle-income households that are bearing the brunt of this heavy burden, the ASI continues. People whose gross income does not exceed CHF4,000 ($4,822) spend 37.8% of their income on rent. According to data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) covering eight countries, including Switzerland, one in two low-income households in rented accommodation spends more than 40% of its disposable income on rent. At the same time, affordable housing is becoming increasingly scarce.
The ownership structure of rental accommodation has also changed. While in 2000, 57.3% of rental accommodation was still owned by private individuals, by 2024 this figure had fallen to 43.2%. Over the same period, the share owned by investment companies rose from 28.7% to 44.4%. According to the ASI’s analysis, these companies have achieved high returns thanks to the property sector.
The Swiss Tenants’ Association is therefore calling for a change of course from policymakers. According to the association, the principle of “cost-based rent” must also be applied.
It also says there is a need to strengthen the Lex Koller to curb the inflow of financial capital into the residential property market. The Lex Koller is a Swiss federal law that restricts the purchase of residential real estate in Switzerland by foreign non-residents and individuals without residency permits.
The association also calls for a greater number of “public-interest housing” units and criticises the indirect counter-proposal put forward by the federal government in response to the Rent Initiative it tabled. The counter-proposal would lead to an “even sharper rise in rents”, claims the tenants’ rights organisation.

Border Police: Illegal Migration to Bulgaria Has Dropped Sharply
Illegal migration through Bulgaria has dropped by 40% compared with last year, Border Police Director Anton Zlatanov said
A projectile fired during a Russian attack on Ukrainian infrastructure struck a passenger bus and a border control booth at the Palanca-Maiaky-Udobne crossing between Moldova and Ukraine on Oct. 5, lightly injuring a Moldovan border guard, Moldova’s Border Police said.
The incident occurred at about 9:38 a.m. local time, according to the Border Police and Moldovan media reports by NewsMaker and Ziarul de Garda. The projectile ricocheted after hitting the ground before damaging the bus and control booth.
Operations at the border crossing were suspended while authorities investigated the incident. Moldova’s General Police Inspectorate said traffic from the junction of the R-30 and R-31 roads in the Stefan Voda district toward Palanca was temporarily halted.
Patrol officers were redirecting traffic to the Tudora border crossing, while drivers were urged to stay away from the area.
“The Border Police, together with the Customs Service, is continuously monitoring the situation in order to keep it under control and remains in contact with the competent Ukrainian authorities,” the Border Police said.
Authorities advised people to avoid traveling to the area. Anyone who hears drones or explosions near the border was told to remain calm, seek shelter indoors and rely only on official sources for information.
People were also warned against approaching aircraft debris, ammunition or other suspicious objects and were instructed to immediately call the 112 emergency service.
The incident occurred as Russia carried out attacks against Ukrainian infrastructure. Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 205 attack drones of various types overnight, including 49 jet-powered drones.
Ukrainian air defenses destroyed 172 drones, including Shahed-type and Gerbera drones and other unmanned aircraft, as well as two Banderol loitering munitions, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at three additional sites.
Palanca is located on the border with Ukraine’s Odesa Oblast, which is regularly targeted by Russian drone and missile attacks. Russian strikes on Ukraine have repeatedly resulted in violations of Moldovan airspace and explosions on Moldovan territory.
On Oct. 3, five Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, entered Moldova’s airspace and exploded on its territory during another overnight Russian attack on Ukraine, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
“(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova,” Sandu wrote in an Oct. 3 post on X, adding, “Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped.”
Moldova’s national airspace monitoring system detected several unmanned aerial vehicles on Oct. 3. The National Army’s Air Operations Service initially reported that five UAVs had entered Moldovan airspace between 7:45 and 8 a.m.
Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi later said the incident involved three missiles and two drones, with debris falling in four districts of Moldova. Moldova’s Defence Ministry subsequently reported a sixth unauthorized incursion into the country’s airspace during Russia’s large-scale morning attack on Ukraine.
Moldovan airspace was violated by drones on three separate occasions on Sept. 30 as Russia conducted a day-long attack on Ukraine that began overnight and continued into the following afternoon.
On Sept. 24, suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight during a sustained Russian drone and missile assault on Ukraine.
On Aug. 16, NATO fighter jets shot down a suspected Russian drone that had violated Romanian airspace near the Moldovan border, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta confirmed.
The following day, Aug. 17, a Russian S-8000 Banderol cruise missile entered Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Odesa before crashing in a cornfield about 3 kilometers, or 1.8 miles, from the village of Talmaz in Moldova’s Stefan Voda district.

Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:38:00 UTC
19:38:00 KST

Ukraine has developed a new missile to knock down Russia's fast, jet-powered Shahed drones, the ones its air defenses catch far less often than older models, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Suspilne reported. The weapon, called Nika, has not yet been tested. He announced it during a visit to Kyiv by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia's plants turn out an estimated 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence estimates, and the jets fly fast enough to outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower, propeller-driven Shaheds. Ukraine plans about 400 units of just one of five interceptor models it is testing by the end of October, as it scrambles to close the gap before winter.
A new missile heads into testing
Both the Ukrainian and German sides have reacted positively to the missile, Zelenskyy said, though he stayed cautious on the result: for now, he said, it only "could be positive." In the same remarks, he announced a successful test of a separate system, the German-Ukrainian interceptor Spys.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
Ukraine shoots down 85-92% of propeller-driven Shaheds, Zelenskyy said. Against the jet-powered variants, interception falls to roughly 50-60%, he noted at the press conference with Merz. F-16 fighter jets help close the gap, he said.
From interceptor drones to a new missile
Over the past month, Ukraine tested a new generation of drone interceptors built for the jet-Shahed threat. On 15 September, one struck a Shahed in trials, though Zelenskyy said developers still needed to refine its control system. On 19 September, he said the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) had created its own interceptor drone and used it to down a jet Shahed in combat. Nika adds a purpose-built missile to that mix.

Withings BodyScan 2 Review: Worth Its Weight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

I’m going to be honest from the start: No, you probably don’t need a $600 scale in your bathroom if you are just doing occasional weigh-ins. Hell, I don’t even know that elite athletes need to make this kind of extreme outlay even if they need to periodically check on how their training is going.
But I’m going to make the case for the Withings BodyScan 2 anyway. After spending several months with the device, the scale and its ecosystem have forced me to dig deeper into my health than ever before. At this point, I’m not sure I could go back to an older-model scale—even a very smart one like the original Withings Body Smart, which I used for years.
Getting a Handle on Health
There’s not much to distinguish the BodyScan 2 hardware from other smart scales aside from its handlebars, an indication that this device belongs to the now-burgeoning full-body scanner or body composition scale category. The device is, however, sleeker than most of its competition, featuring a svelte handle that somehow finds room for a small color LCD screen without the need for any extra bulk. All of your body metrics are showcased on this screen in real time, as they’re being measured, alongside any quick tips from Withings about how to get the best reading each time you hop on.
The unit offers two types of weigh-ins. Daily scans take about 30 seconds and include weight, an estimate of muscle and fat percentage (whole body and segmented across torso, arms, legs, and viscera), an estimate of basal metabolic rate, vascular age, and pulse wave velocity—though only a portion of these measurements are displayed live on the display.

The Financial Times (FT) reported on Monday, Oct. 5, that Estonia is permanently redeploying combat troops closer to the Russian border in line with its new “active defense” strategy to counter any future incursion by Moscow’s forces.
It cited government officials and military personnel who underlined the reasoning behind and nature of the new concept. Col. Tarmo Kundla, the commander of the Estonian army’s First Brigade said, “We must start from the border and win from the very first battles.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In preparation, the brigade is moving from its current Tapa, base about 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the Russian border, to Jõhvi, approximately 50 kilometers (30 miles) from Russia.
Another base is being built in Narva, the predominately Russian-speaking city that abuts the border, at a cost of around €20 million ($22 million). The barracks will permanently accommodate 200 troops plus an additional 800 during a crisis.
While the Estonian and NATO assessment does not believe that the Kremlin intends to initiate a full-scale war with NATO in the near future, they are concerned that Russia could take limited military action against a Baltic country, testing NATO’s preparedness to implement Article 5 in defense of an ally.
Estonia fears a repeat of the pretext that President Vladimir Putin used in 2014 to “protect” Russian-speaking minorities in Ukraine’s Donbas and make a move against Narva. A particular concern is that while many Russian forces are tied down by the war in Ukraine, battle-hardened troops could be rapidly deployed against the Baltic nations when peace or a ceasefire comes.
‘We’re Staying’: European Embassies Defy Russia’s Warning to Leave Kyiv
The FT quoted an unnamed Estonian intelligence official who said, “We were afraid of war. Now we fear the end of war.” Estonian military spending in 2026 has reached around €2.4 billion ($2.7 billion), or 5.4% of GDP.
Estonia relies on its 230,000 strong reserve combat force, – around one-fifth of the population – 40,000 of which are said to be “high-readiness reservists,” to augment its regular military force of only 4,200 personnel. The focus of training is being adapted to meet the new fighting concept.
As well as the forward deployment of combat troops, Tallinn is also expanding its ability to strike enemy forces deep inside Russian territory. Over the past year, it has signed contracts to acquire nine M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) and nine of South Korea’s K239 Chunmoo self-propelled, wheeled, multi-barrelled rocket launching systems, each with a range of up to 300 kilometers (190 miles) along with advanced drone networks.
All of these preparations include the construction of fortified border bunkers, tank obstacles, and pre-positioned engineer stores including land mines.
In September, Putin and his spokespersons constantly restated that Moscow had no intention to initiate military action against Europe, saying such allegations of a threat from Russia as “provocation” and “deliberate exaggeration of the situation.”
This sort of language was parroted by Russian officials immediately prior to its 2022 full-scale invasion, a reason fro Tallinn’s skepticism.

The previous monthly record was NT$946.5 billion in July, while September's figure also surpassed the previous September record of NT$837.1 billion set in 2025.
Third-quarter revenue reached NT$3.02 trillion, up 20.44% from the previous quarter and 47.12% from a year earlier, marking the highest revenue ever recorded for the third quarter. Revenue for the first nine months totaled NT$7.67 trillion, a 39.53% increase from the same period last year and the highest nine-month figure in the company's history.
All four major product categories posted significant month-on-month growth in September, with smart consumer electronics benefiting from new product launches and components and other products gaining from increased shipments. Cloud and networking and computing products also recorded significant growth.
Year on year, cloud and networking, components and other products, and computing products all posted strong growth, while smart consumer electronics was roughly flat due to higher shipment prices. Foxconn attributed the strong performance in cloud and networking products to continued demand for AI products.
In the third quarter, cloud and networking, components and other products, and computing products all recorded strong year-on-year growth, while smart consumer electronics posted significant growth. For the first nine months, all four product categories also posted strong or significant year-on-year growth.
Foxconn expects its AI business to continue growing in the fourth quarter alongside the traditional ICT product peak season, supporting overall performance in line with market expectations. The company said it will continue to monitor the impact of a volatile global political and economic environment.

Libyan teachers’ strike escalates as union demands major education reforms

Libyan teachers’ strike escalates as union demands major education reforms
School year is on hold with teachers on strike and other unions threatening to take action.
Teachers in Libya have escalated their protests over salaries into an open-ended strike at public schools.
Protests began on September 13, the day the school year was due to start. Sit-ins were held outside schools and government buildings in the capital, Tripoli.
Two weeks later, Libya’s teachers union stepped up the campaign with a nationwide strike. It has kept students out of classrooms across the country.
On Sunday, several Libyan unions representing other sectors threatened to join the strike unless the government entered talks to address a cost of living crisis.
Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah of the internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli met with cabinet members to discuss a response to this crisis.
Libya has struggled with economic and political instability since a 2011 uprising ended the rule of late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.
The strikes are occurring on both sides of Libya’s political divide: its western region, governed by the GNU, and its eastern region, which is under the control of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar’s self-described Libyan National Army.
In April, the rival legislative bodies of both sides agreed a unified budget for the first time.
Here’s what we know about the dispute:
What are teachers demanding?
Teachers said they are facing declining salaries, unpaid arrears, insufficient benefits and deteriorating school conditions.
They demanded an immediate halt to what they called the “erosion of workers’ incomes”, citing deteriorating economic and living conditions.
Principal Muftah Khalifa told Al Jazeera Arabic that teachers were protesting against the government’s failure to respond to their repeated demands for higher and unified wages, health insurance and protection on and off school premises.
Teachers told the Reuters news agency they face problems ranging from a lack of computer labs to desks being too dilapidated to use. Staff and parents often have to pay for equipment themselves.
A key demand is the adoption of a unified pay system that would balance a large disparity in pay between workers in different sectors. It is a call that other unions have now rallied behind.
Libya’s unions said on Sunday that the system should take into account changes in the cost of living and the fluctuating dinar-US dollar exchange rate. Retirees have also called for the implementation of previous agreements on pensioners.
The unions said no “arbitrary or punitive” measures should be taken against workers, retirees or union leaders over their activities. They also called on Libya’s attorney general to act quickly against any corruption concerning public spending.
What does the current law say?
According to an education budget brief prepared by Libya’s National Council for Economic and Social Development with UNICEF, 91 percent of the education budget goes to salaries and the rest to school costs, such as equipment.
The education sector had 560,000 employees in 2024, including about 270,000 teachers in basic and secondary education, a huge number for a country with a population of about 7.5 million people.
In 2018, the GNU passed Law No 4 to regulate the salaries, allowances and benefits of these workers.
It also provides for health and social care, insurance against illness and occupational hazards, and protection for teachers and their families.
In September 2021, the GNU ordered pay rises in line with this law, but it did not resolve the issue of salary arrears.
How did the dispute escalate?
Thursday’s strike announcement came after union chiefs and teachers’ representatives from western Libya withdrew from a meeting called by the Ministry of Education.
Ashraf Abu Rawi, head of the Tripoli teachers union, told Al Jazeera that the unions felt authorities had not taken the teachers’ demands seriously.
The teachers union has warned the Ministry of Education against reopening schools, saying such a move would only lead to further escalation.
The government has said the teachers’ demands are legitimate but the rights of students should also be considered.
Osama Abboud, a parent of two pupils, said the teachers’ demands were legitimate and parents backed them. But he also urged teachers to think of their students’ future and continue working without abandoning their demands.
Dbeibah’s meeting on Sunday with Finance Minister Rashid Boughofa and other senior officials focused on a proposal of a unified pay system to cover all sectors and state institutions.
But raising teachers’ pay would require a government decision, parliamentary approval and banking procedures. All of this would take time, given the legislative schism that has plagued Libya for years, according to Al Jazeera’s Ahmed Khalifa, reporting from Tripoli.

Ukraine’s EU neighbors reject new plea from Kiev – Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:33:21 UTC
19:33:21 KST

Ukraine’s EU neighbors reject new plea from Kiev – Politico
Poland and Romania have refused to help Kiev move millions of tons of grain – which got stuck in Ukraine following Vladimir Zelensky’s war on exports – into the EU, Politico reports, citing officials in Warsaw and Bucharest. Zelensky’s 40-day campaign resulted in Russia implementing a de facto blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, with the wider consequences of the strikes estimated at 1.5% of the country’s collapsing GDP.
Last week, Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky appealed to the EU for a €1.1 billion ($1.23 billion) allocation to improve transit capacity, which would help free large quantities of grain – Ukraine’s key source of income – trapped in the country.
The request came after Zelensky’s 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’ on Russia, which involved long-range strikes on oil refineries and civilian infrastructure. The effort backfired, as Russia ramped up strikes on Ukraine’s military-related logistics, including the key hub of Odessa, accounting for an overwhelming majority of Kiev’s agricultural exports.
Speaking to Politico, Vysotsky described the situation as “very, very critical,” after his ministry reported the export of 2.4 million tons of agricultural products in September, just 46% of what Kiev considers the required volume.
He added that export restrictions leave Ukrainian farmers without cash needed to plant seeds now for next year’s harvest. “If the situation stays like this till spring, it could mean the decrease of even 35-40% of the planted area,” he warned.
Last month, Ukrainian officials estimated damage to infrastructure from Russian strikes at nearly $10 billion, with wider consequences amounting to around 1.5% of GDP.
While the EU as a whole is yet to give a definitive answer to the €1.1 billion request, Poland and Romania – which are crucial to facilitating Ukraine’s exports – ruled out any significant assistance.
Romanian Agriculture Minister Barna Tanczos rejected the prospect of substantially expanding capacity, telling Politico that “the interest for our own farmers remains a priority.”
Ukrainian cargo and low Danube water levels are already straining Romanian ports, he said, adding: “Everybody knows we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the roads, railways and port capacity. It is what it is.”
The Polish Infrastructure Ministry spokesperson said, as cited by Politico, that Poland “has no plans to introduce any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products.”
Before the €1.1 billion plea, Ukraine requested €220 million from the EU in grants to support farmers affected by disrupted exports, but the bloc effectively turned it down, pointing instead to existing EU mechanisms.
Agricultural trade has long been a source of friction between Ukraine and its EU neighbors. After the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, Brussels suspended duties and quotas on Ukrainian exports, which triggered massive protests from European farmers over what they saw as unfair competition. As a result, the EU introduced an ‘emergency brake’ system in 2024, allowing tariff quotas to return for sensitive products if imports exceed set thresholds.
In addition, many of Ukraine’s neighbors, including Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia, maintain significant restrictions on Ukrainian imports at the national level.

Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”.
Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming.
It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets.

Trade talks with US are at an impasse – India
India-US trade negotiations have hit a “plateau,” making further concessions “very difficult,” Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday, days after Washington said a deal is not imminent. 
India and the US have been negotiating a Bilateral Trade Agreement since February last year, covering market access, tariff and non-tariff barriers, digital trade, and supply-chain resilience. The finance minister’s comments, despite repeated assertions by both sides in the last few months that a deal is near completion, is the first clear indication that the talks have hit an impasse. 
“Both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which, giving, or taking, might be very, very difficult,” Sitharaman said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. 
She said the talks are continuing, and left open the possibility of movement if either side finds additional negotiating space, describing the proposed agreement as “hard and very rigorously negotiated.”
India & US Trade Talks Hit 'Plateau’ – 🇮🇳 FM Sitharaman The negotiations are ‘still ongoing,’ Sitharaman said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi Monday. ‘Giving or taking beyond that plateau might be very difficult,’ Sitharaman noted. US Trade Rep Jamieson Greer said last week that a deal ‘was not imminent,’ after a meeting with Indian Trade Minister Piyush Goyal. 📹: ANI
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 5, 2026
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week, following talks with Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, that the two countries have identified the remaining sticking points, but that an agreement is not imminent. Among them are US demands for wider access for its farm and dairy products, a politically sensitive subject for New Delhi.
Goyal struck a more optimistic note last month, saying the deal was almost “done and dusted.” He added, however, that implementation depends on India securing a competitive tariff advantage over rival exporters in the US market.
US goods imports from India reached $103.8 billion last year, compared with $45.4 billion in exports, leaving the US with a $58.4 billion goods trade deficit. Total goods and services trade between the two countries stood at an estimated $239.6 billion.
The balance is in India’s favor and Washington wants to reduce the gap, Sitharaman said.
The failure to reach a deal “would not stop trade or raise tariffs” automatically, the founder of New Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Research Initiative, Ajay Srivastava, told RT. However, he said the tariff uncertainty would make pricing, contracts, and investment decisions harder.
“The bigger risk is fresh US tariffs over Russian oil purchases or alleged excess manufacturing capacity. Signing a trade deal may not remove that risk.”
A new law signed by President Donald Trump last month gives him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue significant purchases of Russian energy. India, the second largest importer of Russian oil, has warned that the tariffs could hurt bilateral ties.
Greer, however, has not publicly identified Russian oil as one of the unresolved issues in the trade negotiations.

Swiss senators flex muscles over EU treaty package
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:30:44 UTC
19:30:44 KST

Swiss senators flex muscles over EU treaty package
Switzerland’s Senate last week wrapped up its examination of the new EU treaty package, laying bare political divisions and signalling that parliament intends to shape, not simply endorse the government’s deal with Brussels. An analysis of the autumn session.
It is well past 8pm in the Senate chamber in Bern, day one of the European Union (EU) debate in the Swiss parliament. The 46 senators have already spent more than five hours deliberating. Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, too, has been speaking for quite some time about the results of the negotiations with Brussels. He lists all the key points once again. Each one is a negotiating success, he says, but also a milestone on Switzerland’s unique path, which has grown ever longer over the years. The Swiss-EU package of agreements, known as Bilaterals III,External link runs to 2,228 pages.
The foreign minister takes off his reading glasses. He looks up from his paper and scans the chamber. He leaves his prepared speech on the table in front of him and sketches a picture of Switzerland in 2026 in short sentences: “Brussels is not waiting for Switzerland, nor will they wait for Switzerland at the UN in New York or in Mercosur. But we are being heard. Little Switzerland ranks among the world’s 20 largest economies. That gives us a certain strength. But to retain that strength, we need markets,” he declares.
Moments of passion
This is no spectacle. But however measured the statement may seem, it is a moment of unfiltered passion for Swiss politics. When it comes to the EU treaty package that is something that has been distinctly lacking so far, particularly from the Federal Council, Switzerland’s executive body.
Several similar moments follow in the Senate in what was a thoroughly fascinating debate on the new EU treaties. Senators offered a degree of nuance to the debate that had previously been conducted in a lacklustre or simplistic manner. New aspects came to light, while familiar ones were examined anew.
During the debate on the Swiss-EU treaty package, Justice Minister Beat Jans also mentioned the Swiss Abroad. An extract from his speech: “It is important to look at the issue from the other side as well. What applies to EU citizens in Switzerland also applies to Swiss nationals in the EU, and there are quite a few of them: 460,000 Swiss nationals live in the EU; that is more than half of all Swiss Abroad.
Among them are many young people who are on exchange programmes or studying in the EU. The aim is to safeguard these people’s rights so they can live in EU member states with virtually the same rights as locals, so they can take up employment without additional administrative hurdles, and so they can study for the same tuition fees as Europeans. You must not forget this when discussing this package.”
EU treaties as a matter of faith
How would Brussels react if parliament or Swiss voters were to oppose the treaty package one day? Nobody knows that either. Much of the debate has become a question of faith. Some believe the EU has Switzerland’s best interests at heart and will remain fair, while others fear Switzerland is surrendering too much to Brussels.
“Which sovereign country delegates important parts of its legislation to a foreign country and then pays for it as well?” declares Hannes Germann, a senator from the right-wing Swiss People’s Party.
Franziska Roth, a senator from the left-wing Social Democratic Party, asks: “Just because the treaties are many pages long, does that mean they’re a sham?” She adds where she believes the 2,228 pages come from: “It’s called the rule of law”.
Clash with federal structures
Beat Rieder, a Centre Party senator from canton Valais, then explains why, in his view, a dynamic adoption of legislation [Switzerland taking over future EU rules in certain areas] poses a threat to Swiss democracy, drawing historical parallels that extend as far back as colonial treaties. “This treaty is on a collision course with federal structures; it undermines them in every single area in which we dynamically adopt legislation, and it destroys the Federal Court’s authority to administer justice independently in Switzerland,” he says.
It is striking to see who is now showing their hand. Opposition to the package comes from the political centre. It is becoming clear that the Centre Party and the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party are divided on this crucial issue for Switzerland and for the upcoming elections. And they can no longer hide the fact.
The following three days of debate focus on the details: security deposits for European companies wishing to operate in Switzerland, European trains on Swiss tracks, and a levy that European immigrants in Switzerland are to pay – “like a visitor’s tax”.
A show of strength by parliament
The Senate has taken a hard line on immigration. The right wing has introduced stricter measures – amendments to a treaty that has already been finalised. Is that permitted? Is the proposal to deny permanent residence to anyone who has previously received social assistance compatible with the free movement of persons? What about the suggestion that immigrants must provide a criminal record check? No, warns Justice Minister Beat Jans. The Senate passes the measure anyway.
This is not the government’s hour, but the Senate’s. At times the exercise feels almost demonstrative, a reminder that in Switzerland it is parliament, not the executive, that makes the laws. And that prerogative is what is being defended.
“A solution that divides the country creates no legal certainty, only conflict,” warns Petra Gössi, a senator from canton Schwyz, calling for compromise. And compromise does exist. Senators leave in place all the agreements that employers and trade unions had painstakingly negotiated with one another to protect Switzerland’s high wages.
Senators split over cantonal majority
The representatives of the cantons remain divided on the question of the voting procedure. Does voting on the EU treaty package also require a cantonal majority – approval by most cantons as well as most voters – or is a simple popular majority sufficient?
Since the smaller, more conservative cantons carry greater weight with a cantonal majority, this reduces the chances of the EU-Swiss package at the ballot box. This makes the issue highly political.
“You can sense that this issue gets under people’s skin; it strikes at the very heart of who we are,” said Cassis ahead of the decisive vote. It is unclear whether he was referring to the essence of Switzerland or to the people in the chamber who were wrestling with the issue for three days.
It is also a delicate matter. Senators represent their canton – and a political party. To whom do they feel more beholden? One senator from Zug is so torn that he abstains. In the end, the Senate votes in favour of the cantonal majority by 23 votes to 17. Support also come from the left and the centre.
This sends a clear message to the House of Representatives, which will discuss the EU treaty package in the winter session. Lawmakers in the lower chamber are expected to reject the Senate’s decision. This will lead to a dispute over the role of federalism in Switzerland, a potentially decisive test of unity.
A clear rebuff to the authorities
Earlier, the Senate had already given the government a clear demonstration of who held power. The Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property, under pressure from the Swiss footwear brand On, had relaxed the “Swissness” rules – which set out when a product can be labelled Swiss – without consulting the legislature. The Senate rectified this with a decisive vote bordering on protest: 32 votes to 5.
The Senate has also set down a first marker on the issue of banking regulation, resisting pressure from the once-powerful banking lobby. It is a simple question, said Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter: “Who should bear the risks that a major bank takes abroad? Is it the shareholders or also the taxpayers in Switzerland?” The Senate agreed. UBS, Switzerland’s biggest bank, will now have to underpin its foreign subsidiaries with 90% equity capital. Here, too, the House of Representatives must still give its position.
Defence spending was also a major topic in the recent session of parliament. “Switzerland has taken a long time to consider the question of how to strengthen its security. A question for which we have no time,” warned Defence Minister Martin Pfister. However, the idea of a debt-financed defence fund was met with scepticism, not least because a commission had recently revealed that the contracts for the purchase of the F-35 fighter jets had scarcely been read on the Swiss side. Yet urgency sometimes trumps public sentiment. The funding has been approved for the time being. But there is a growing impression that the battle over the F-35s has only just begun.
Join the debate:
Parliament approved the free trade agreement with Mercosur. Farmers were won over with CHF500 million ($600 million), while the left-wing and Green parties were persuaded with CHF25 million ($30 million) to protect the Amazon rainforest.
Parliament has rejected the “Democracy Initiative” that aims to simplify naturalisation. Only the Social Democratic Party and the Greens support the proposal.
Both chambers of parliament want to ban the import of fur produced using cruel methods. They have also put forward an indirect counter-proposal to the popular initiative calling for a ban on the import of foie gras, recommending that the initiative be rejected.

The Border Police and Moldova’s Customs Service said they were monitoring the situation and maintaining contact with Ukrainian authorities.
Residents and travelers were advised to avoid the area, seek shelter if they heard drones or explosions and not approach aircraft debris, ammunition or other unidentified objects.
The incident occurred two days after Russian strike drones entered Moldovan airspace and scattered debris across four districts during another attack on Ukraine.
Kyiv Could Face 16-Hour Power Cuts, Expert Warns
Moldova has repeatedly reported drones and debris crossing its frontier during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Moldovan President Maia Sandu has accused Moscow of deliberately directing some drones into the country’s airspace.
Russia has also repeatedly attacked border crossings between Ukraine and Moldova.
On Sept. 9, a Russian attack on the Starokozache international border crossing with Moldova killed two people and injured three others. Chisinau accused Moscow of deliberately striking the crossing and attempting to justify the attack with false claims that weapons were being transported through Moldovan territory to Ukraine.
