Nature is "inseparable from daily life" at House K in Vietnam
Blocky volumes in exposed concrete contrast with the lush greenery and rooftop vegetable garden at House K, a home in Vietnam designed by local architecture studio HGAA.
Located in Nghệ An, the 885-square-metre family home has a central courtyard and a series of stepped terraces, designed to provide residents with as much access to greenery as possible.
"The guiding idea was simplicity, sustainability, and harmony with nature and local lifestyle," HGAA told Dezeen.
"The integration of gardens at multiple scales – a central bamboo courtyard, rooftop vegetable garden, and private gardens for each bedroom – is the defining gesture," it continued. "It transforms circulation into a sensory experience, making nature inseparable from daily life."
A paved path set within House K's front garden leads from a street entrance and parking space into a central patio and barbecue area, which is hugged by the home's U-shaped concrete form.
Exposed concrete defines both the exterior and interior of the home's cubic volumes, a choice the studio attributed to its durability, fast construction speed and the contrast it creates with the green of the home's tropical plants.
Tall bamboo shoots help shelter the glazed walls of the home's ground floor, where a central hall and staircase are flanked by a large dining and kitchen space to the north and a double-height living area to the south.
While responding to the client's feng shui requirements, HGAA designed the layout to give the majority of House K's spaces access to a garden, including the bedrooms and bathrooms tucked on the ground floor's more enclosed eastern side.
The home's first-floor bedrooms overlook the central courtyard and have access to a garden terrace raised above the home's parking area, while on the second floor another bedroom sits alongside its own private roof terrace.
Atop the building, a rooftop vegetable garden and further planting conceal the home's technical and storage spaces, offering views across the site and over the street beyond.
"The house was set back from the street to reduce heat exposure, with a large front garden and rooftop vegetable garden acting as natural buffers," the studio said.
"Traditional elements like wide eaves and surrounding gardens were reinterpreted to provide shade and cooling."
Previous projects by HGAA include a preschool in Ha Long City, incorporating walkways surrounded by screens of metal mesh that were designed to be overgrown by climbing plants.
Elsewhere in Vietnam, Inrestudio recently completed 100 Windows, a multi-generational home surrounded by irregularly placed and mismatched openings.
The photography is courtesy of HGAA.

Saudi Arabia explored new routes oil export amid Hormuz crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:28:38 UTC
19:28:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi Aramco eyes new oil routes to bypass Strait of Hormuz
Saudi Arabia's Aramco is examining proposals for two new land-based oil export routes that would bypass the Strait of Hormuz, as continued military tensions disrupt shipping, tankers come under attack and freight rates soar.
According to a report published on 27 September by BN Report, a platform specialising in energy intelligence and business economics, the Saudi oil giant is conducting engineering and technical feasibility studies to expand its export routes.
The proposals include connecting pipelines to Oman's coast and the Duqm storage complex, giving Saudi Arabia direct access to Asian markets while reducing its exposure to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and rising insurance premiums.
US-based Business Insurance magazine, which specialises in risk and insurance intelligence, reported on 1 October that war-risk insurance premiums for Saudi-linked tankers had tripled to 3% of a vessel's value at Yanbu port. At southern ports, premiums had risen to 7%, adding millions of dollars to the cost of individual shipments.
The plans come as the Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi oil facilities, with the group announcing that it had carried out a "qualitative military operation" using several ballistic missiles and drones targeting Saudi Aramco in the capital Riyadh.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Saturday, 3 October, that the operation "comes as part of the response to Saudi Arabia's targeting" of the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other areas under the group's control.
The Houthis also said they would continue to impose the equation of "siege for siege and escalation for escalation".
Investment costs decline
Strategic, economic and infrastructure considerations are increasingly shaping the region's energy transport calculations, according to economic expert Hossam Ayesh.
Ayesh told The New Arab that the huge investment costs and lengthy construction periods involved in building new pipelines must be weighed against rising insurance premiums and the risks facing maritime shipping.
Although shipping oil by sea may theoretically remain cheaper than constructing thousands of kilometres of pipelines, geopolitical tensions and the risk of the Strait of Hormuz being closed are pushing policymakers to look beyond traditional export routes, he said.
These calculations also come amid shifts in international competition.
Bloomberg reported on 29 September that the vulnerability of logistical hubs in the Middle East coincides with rising production in the Americas, which is expected to exceed 32 million barrels per day by 2030. This puts further pressure on Gulf producers to secure reliable export routes and protect their market share in Asia as alternative supplies grow.
Gulf states are also drawing lessons from recent disruptions to international energy infrastructure, particularly the fallout from the Nord Stream pipelines linking Russia and Germany.
The pipelines were sabotaged and subsequently halted amid the war in Ukraine, causing major financial losses.
The precedent shows that new pipelines would not be immune to targeting or sabotage, particularly amid heightened global uncertainty and sharp fluctuations in oil demand, Ayesh said.
Through the proposed routes, policymakers at Aramco and in Saudi Arabia are seeking to diversify oil export options through the Red Sea, domestic pipelines and potential land routes towards Oman, Jordan and Syria.
The aim is to safeguard vital market share and ensure reliable supplies despite mounting security threats, according to Ayesh.
This makes the financial cost a secondary consideration compared with the strategic need to ensure the sustainability and reliability of Saudi oil exports, he added.
The project could also go beyond transporting Saudi oil and play a role in strengthening logistical and economic integration with neighbouring countries, particularly Oman.
Its scope could eventually expand to include the transport of Qatari liquefied natural gas towards the Arabian Sea, according to Ayesh, who said shared infrastructure could generate additional economic benefits across the region.
Riyadh-Muscat partnership
Aramco's study of new export routes represents a major strategic investment aimed primarily at strengthening the security and resilience of Saudi oil exports and protecting them from future shocks, according to economic expert Ali Metwally, who works at a London-based consultancy.
Metwally told The New Arab that the project could be implemented in stages over several years, particularly if one of the routes includes a direct connection to Oman's Arabian Sea coast.
The estimated cost of building a major regional pipeline with a capacity of between 1.5 million and 2.5 million barrels per day ranges from $8 billion to $15 billion for a single route.
Costs could rise further with the addition of major pumping stations, storage facilities, maritime export terminals and advanced protection and operating systems.
Metwally stressed that the figures remain preliminary until Aramco announces official details on the project's approved capacity and final budget.
The case for alternative routes is being strengthened by continued disruption to seaborne oil flows.
Lloyd's List, a London-based maritime data and intelligence provider, reported on 2 October that congestion affecting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the Gulf of Oman was prompting tanker owners to bypass bottlenecks around the strait in favour of alternative ports.
The shift reflects growing expectations that the shipping crisis could persist for years.
The project's economic value lies partly in avoiding soaring insurance premiums and maritime shipping costs, which could rise to tens of dollars per barrel during periods of heightened tensions and clashes around the Strait of Hormuz.
Rather than comparing pipeline construction costs with ordinary shipping costs during periods of stability, Metwally argues that the pipeline's fixed capital costs would be spread across long-term contracts and millions of barrels transported each day, potentially making the project financially viable as maritime risks increase.
A route linking Saudi Arabia and Oman would also provide additional strategic value by giving Saudi oil direct access to major Asian markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, using Duqm port and other terminals on the Arabian Sea, according to Metwally.
It would draw on Oman's developed logistics infrastructure and large storage facilities, potentially creating deeper regional integration in oil handling, tanker shipping and strategic stock management.
Aramco's commercial gain
For Aramco, the main commercial benefit would be greater supply reliability for major importers and a reduced risk of losing its established market share in Asia to competing energy suppliers.
The proposed routes would create a more flexible export network, allowing the Saudi oil giant to redirect shipments between the Gulf, Red Sea and Arabian Sea depending on security risks, insurance costs and global demand, according to Metwally.
However, one of the biggest obstacles would be constructing a route stretching more than 1,000 kilometres across harsh desert environments, including the Empty Quarter.
This would pose significant technical challenges, including extreme temperatures and shifting dunes, as well as the need to establish electricity networks, maintenance infrastructure and secure access routes.
The project would also require Riyadh and Muscat to reach comprehensive bilateral agreements governing ownership and operating rights, tariffs and security arrangements.

Former hostage Romi Gonen shared excerpts from footage of her abduction to Gaza on Monday during her podcast, "Romi Gonen's New Life," produced in collaboration with V1, describing the fear, pain, and helplessness she remembers from the moments she was taken captive.
Gonen was released from Hamas captivity in a hostage deal in January 2025 after 471 days in captivity.
Reflecting on the footage, Gonen said: "I'm lying there, the sun is shining right on me, my hair is blowing in the wind, and that's what's happening inside the car. Seeing myself lying there like that, alive, it's no longer an image that I had. It's something that's actually alive, breathing. It's crazy."
She continued: "All I felt during those moments in the car was that I was really scared by that point, really scared. My hand hurt, they were shouting a lot of nonsense, they hit me, but all that was going through my head was the pain. It wouldn't let go of me."
Gonen also said: "Toward the end of the video, you can see me opening my eyes. There's something about seeing myself open my eyes at that moment that gives me confirmation that I was conscious there. I wake up with it in the morning; I go to sleep with it at night; it's in my dreams."
Gonen held in Hamas captivity for over a year
Gonen was abducted from the Nova music festival near Kibbutz Re’im on October 7, 2023, after Hamas terrorists attacked the festival and communities across southern Israel. She was shot in the hand while attempting to flee the festival in a vehicle with friends before being taken into Gaza.
The Hamas-led October 7 attack killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw more than 250 people abducted to Gaza. The Nova festival was one of the main sites of the massacre, where hundreds of festivalgoers were killed, and dozens were abducted.
Gonen remained in Hamas captivity until January 19, 2025, when she was released alongside Emily Damari and Doron Steinbrecher on the first day of a hostage-ceasefire agreement. The three women were transferred by Hamas to the Red Cross in Gaza before being handed over to IDF troops.
Following her return to Israel, Gonen underwent prolonged medical treatment for injuries sustained on October 7 and complications stemming from the lack of adequate medical care while she was held in Gaza. She was discharged from Sheba Medical Center in July 2025 after undergoing two complex surgeries.

UAE-Israel ties may improve after flydubai event, akin to US-Saudi relations post-9/11 - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:27:40 UTC
19:27:40 KST

On Sunday, Transportation Minister Miri Regev met with United Arab Emirates Ambassador to Israel Mohamed Al-Khaja. Both Regev and Khaja posted about the meeting on their X/Twitter social media accounts.
The symbolism is important here. It shows Israel and the UAE working together toward the future in the wake of the attack aboard the flydubai flight. It shows how Israel and the UAE will be able to learn lessons and may increase their ties and coordination in the wake of the incident in which heroes stepped forward to save the plane.
The investigation into what happened on flydubai flight FZ1073 is still ongoing. The copilot attacked the pilot with an axe in an attempt to take over the plane and crash it.
The perpetrator, Hamam al-Hammami, had planned the attack for some time, Reuters reported. Hammami is from Oman, but he has lived in other places, including in Australia, and also studied in the UK.
It will take time to piece together all the details of the attack. What is clear is that the heroism of Indian pilot Capt. Smit Machchhar and the passengers saved the plane as the attack unfolded. Two reserve crew pilots then helped save the plane and landed it in Saudi Arabia.
In the wake of the attack, there is a lot of spotlight on the flights to Israel from the UAE. The Abraham Accords paved the way for a major air corridor between Israel and the UAE. Around 1.35 million passengers flew between the UAE and Israel in 2025.
Etihad and flydubai were praised by Israel for continuing to fly during the recent conflict. They continued flying even as US and other airlines often canceled.
This is a testament to the strength of the UAE-Israel relationship. It is part of the larger Abraham Accords relationships, which include Bahrain, Morocco, and other countries. The Tel Aviv-Dubai flight corridor is important, and it had several flights per day.
Symbol of Abraham Accords
The flights are a symbol of the Abraham Accords. When the Abraham Accords were signed, many people hoped there would be a warm peace with the UAE and Bahrain – different from the colder peace with Jordan and Egypt.
There are very few people flying to Amman or Cairo, compared with Dubai. This matters. The UAE worked hard to be a welcoming destination in the fall of 2020 and in 2021.
There were many hurdles. The COVID pandemic, for instance, was going on in 2020-2022. When it ended, there was a brief period when everything seemed normal – until the October 7 massacre in 2023.
Israel and the UAE have both suffered from Iran’s attacks. Beginning this past February, the UAE found itself on the front line of the conflict in the Gulf.
As such, Israel and the UAE are now both hardened by conflict. They have learned many lessons. The lessons are not just about air defenses; they are also other issues relating to the economy, trade, and security.
The attack aboard the flydubai flight could derail some of the progress. Nevertheless, it is clear that the UAE and Israel have weathered many challenges already.
The UAE did not like the terminology used in Israel to describe “rescue” flights going to the UAE after the flydubai incident, Israeli media outlets reported. Israeli airlines returned thousands of Israelis stranded in Dubai as the investigation unfolded.
This is why the meeting between Regev and the Khaja is so important.
“During the meeting, we discussed cooperation in investigating the incident that could have ended in a major disaster,” Regev wrote on X. “From the moment of the aircraft crashing attempt, the ambassador stands by our side and assists as much as possible. I greatly appreciate the clear stance and responsibility that the Emiratis are demonstrating in these complex moments.”
“We cannot allow extremist elements to undermine the strategic relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates,” she added. “We agreed to continue the cooperation and strengthen ties in the fields of aviation and transportation, and to work together to ensure the safety of passengers and flights.”
Khaja wrote: “We discussed the bilateral relations between the two countries and the ways to deepen cooperation in the fields of aviation and transport... [As] part of the ongoing consultation and coordination between us, we also discussed increasing flight frequency in the coming period. Additionally, we addressed strengthening preparedness and advance planning to address various developments, with the aim of ensuring smooth and orderly movement of passengers and goods.”
He said he greatly appreciated “the cooperation and ongoing support of Her Honor Minister Regev on this matter.”
These are important words and symbols of the relationship between Israel and the UAE. In addition, it is a practical development.
What comes next will be more investigations into what happened and also the lessons that can be learned. In addition, it is likely that security processes may be changed.
There will be lessons to learn not just in Jerusalem and Abu Dhabi, but also around the world. With each of these types of incidents there are lessons to be learned.
Challenges of flydubai incident are also an opportunity
The challenges that this incident presents also likely provide opportunities. Countries can take away from these types of hurdles a new commitment to their relationship.
Consider how US-Saudi relations have improved over the years, even though there was some anti-American extremism that emanated from Saudi Arabia in the 1990s. Osama Bin Laden was from Saudi Arabia, for instance.
The US and Saudi Arabia were able to work together after 9/11; however, al-Qaeda was eventually mostly defeated in the Arabian Peninsula.
This illustrates how security challenges can lead to taking threats seriously and working more closely.
Evidence shows that Israel, the UAE, and other countries have already been working together under the umbrella of US Central Command. This is a phenomenon relating to regional threats, such as Iran.
The Abraham Accords were signed during the COVID crisis. In fact, cooperation during the pandemic helped pave the way for the Abraham Accords.
In May 2020, an Etihad Airways plane flew from the UAE to Israel to deliver COVID support for the Palestinian community. More flights came in June.
Even before the Abraham Accords were signed, there was a deal in July 2020 between Israel Aerospace Industries and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems to develop breakthrough technology with Group42 in the UAE. The Abraham Accords were signed that September, and the first flydubai flight arrived in November.

Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline operating normally: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:27:29 UTC
19:27:29 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline is operating normally, Bloomberg reported Monday, following an earlier report that a fresh attack had halted flows through the key export route.
Oil continues to flow through the pipeline, Bloomberg said, citing people familiar with the matter.
Other media outlets earlier reported that a new attack on a pumping station in Khurais, east of Riyadh, had caused extensive damage and halted operations, citing an unnamed source working in Saudi Arabia’s energy sector.
Saudi Aramco and the Saudi Energy Ministry did not immediately respond to Bloomberg’s requests for comment, according to the report.
Oil prices pared gains after Bloomberg’s report. Prices had risen as much as 1.2% following the earlier report.
Aramco had increased flows through the pipeline to more than 80% of its 7 million-barrel-per-day capacity by late last week, according to Bloomberg. After supplying refineries on Saudi Arabia’s west coast, about 4.5 million barrels per day remained available for export, it added.
The pipeline connects Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil production facilities with the Red Sea coast, allowing crude exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry previously confirmed that attacks on Sept. 10 targeted the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions, prompting a precautionary shutdown.

Czechia Drops Charges Against Volunteer Who Fought for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:25:07 UTC
19:25:07 KST

The Czech Public Prosecutor’s Office has discontinued criminal proceedings against a Czech citizen who joined the Ukrainian military in 2022 without the president’s authorization.
Novinky reported this.
According to the case files, the man traveled to Ukraine in March 2022, shortly after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Before doing so, he asked then-Czech President Miloš Zeman for permission to serve in the Ukrainian military.
However, in July 2022, Zeman denied his request because the man had a previous criminal conviction. The conviction was later expunged. Despite the refusal, the Czech continued serving in the Ukrainian military.
Under Czech law, citizens require the president’s permission to serve in the armed forces of a foreign country.
After more than a year of investigation, police charged the man with unlawfully serving in a foreign country’s armed forces.
However, prosecutor Ondřej Bednář decided to drop the charges. He noted that the man had fought against Russian forces in Ukraine, which is located close to the Czech Republic.
According to the prosecutor, Ukraine’s defense can be seen as a way to protect the Czech Republic from Russian aggression approaching its borders. He also considered the man’s previous criminal conviction, which had since been expunged, as well as his expectation that he might be able to legalize his service.
The decision may still be reviewed. The Czech Prosecutor General has the authority to overturn it and order the case to continue.
The volunteer’s lawyer and Senator Václav Láska said this was already the eighth case in which he had successfully defended a Czech citizen against criminal prosecution for serving in Ukraine.
Militarnyi previously reported that in November 2024, Czech President Petr Pavel approved 60 requests from Czech citizens to join the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

The messages expressed concern about Russian threats against diplomats and foreign citizens and called on Moscow to comply with the Vienna Convention and international humanitarian law.
The assurances extend beyond the embassies that have issued individual statements. EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova said all 25 EU member states with embassies in Kyiv were maintaining their presence, along with the EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission.

Kyiv Could Face 16-Hour Power Cuts, Expert Warns

France endorsed Mathernova’s statement reaffirming the diplomatic presence in the capital.

European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand also dismissed threats issued on Saturday, Oct. 3, by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
In an official dispatch, Moscow had warned foreign citizens and accredited diplomats in Kyiv of “mortal danger,” pledging to sustain mass aerial strikes across the capital. However, Wigand reaffirmed that the EU would not be intimidated into reducing its diplomatic footprint or scaling back defense assistance.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Russian forces would continue carrying out large-scale strikes. It also sought to place responsibility for possible consequences on those who disregarded its warning, saying that foreigners who remained were exposing themselves to mortal danger.

Germany's AfD weighs shift from anti-EU roots, strategy paper shows

Germany's AfD weighs shift from anti-EU roots, strategy paper shows
BERLIN, Oct 5 - Members of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) are advocating a shift in the party's long-standing opposition to Germany's membership in the European Union and the euro, according to a strategy paper seen by Reuters on Monday.
The move would mark a change in one of the founding principles of the AfD, which was created in 2013 largely in opposition to euro zone bailout policies and has long advocated the dissolution of the currency union or Germany's exit from it.
The paper, first reported by Bild newspaper, calls for a wholesale renegotiation of EU treaties to turn the bloc into a looser alliance of sovereign nations. If those efforts fail, a referendum on Germany's membership should be held, it said.
The paper also advocates national opt-outs from areas such as migration, fiscal policy and jointly issued EU debt, but it does not fundamentally oppose the euro currency.
The paper was produced by AfD lawmakers from the European Parliament, Germany's lower house of parliament and its state parliaments, and discussed at a meeting last month.
A party convention next year would sign off on any change to its decade-old policy platform.
Peter Boehringer, the AfD's parliamentary spokesman on European affairs and a long-time critic of the euro, rejected suggestions that the paper marked a policy reversal.
He said the proposal to renegotiate EU treaties and pursue reform before considering an eventual withdrawal was consistent with longstanding AfD policy and described the document as an implementation plan for existing positions rather than a change of course.
The party's current programme calls for Germany to leave the euro and ultimately replace the EU with a new European framework.
The AfD has steadily expanded its support by campaigning against migration following an influx of people fleeing war in the Middle East in 2015, a strategy that has helped it achieve a series of election successes, most recently in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD, which came second in last year's national election after Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives, aims to enter the federal government by 2029. Germany's mainstream political parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD, which the domestic intelligence agency has branded as "right-wing extremist," a characterisation the party rejects.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel described the euro as a "soft currency" in an interview with broadcaster ZDF in August but stopped short of explicitly calling for Germany to quit the currency. REUTERS

Bosnia election: New technology might have stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead voters, but the result remains unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

Bosnia: Tougher on fraud, nationalist parties still win
October 5, 2026
Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the polls on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging.
Chief among the abuses was the casting of ballots in the name of deceased voters who had lingered for years on outdated voter rolls.
At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked.
In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher.
The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this.
New technology, same old politics
This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks.
This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate.
Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community: the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats.
The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted.
For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps: The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority.
A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member.
That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat.
Republika Srpska and the return of a fallen leader
For Milorad Dodik, the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection.
In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative, the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska.
Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD.
The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side."
Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next.
He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step.
"That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik.
A deal between Serbs and Croats?
The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message.
Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine.
That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out.
If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before.
Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Troika defeated
The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same.
The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law.
Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well.
The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat.
So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created.
"The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory.
A Croat surprise
The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader.
"HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote.
Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country.
What this means for the state
The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point.
Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton.
The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller.
So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it.
All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia, the EU and the US. Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory.
Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked.
In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher.
The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this.
New technology, same old politics
This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks.
This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate.
Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community: the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats.
The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted.
For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps: The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority.
A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member.
That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat.
Republika Srpska and the return of a fallen leader
For Milorad Dodik, the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection.
In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative, the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska.
Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD.
The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side."
Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next.
He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step.
"That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik.
A deal between Serbs and Croats?
The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message.
Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine.
That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out.
If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before.
Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Troika defeated
The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same.
The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law.
Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well.
The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat.
So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created.
"The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory.
A Croat surprise
The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader.
"HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote.
Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country.
What this means for the state
The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point.
Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton.
The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller.
So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it.
All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia, the EU and the US. Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory.
Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different.

As part of the celebrations marking the eighth centenary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, the National Museum in Warsaw hosted “No Sky Is Without Light,” an audiovisual performance by composer Luca Maria Baldini and artist, director, and photographer Salvatore Insana, organized by the Italian Cultural Institute in Warsaw. Through the interplay of sound, images, texts, and archival materials, the performance reinterprets certain themes of the Franciscan tradition in light of contemporary issues: the relationship with nature, the ecological crisis, care, and interdependence, extending to the relationship between spirituality, technology, and artificial intelligence. A dialogue between past and present that, as emphasized by Italian Ambassador Luca Franchetti Pardo, allows us to rediscover the enduring relevance of the Franciscan message.
                                    
“'‘No Sky Is Without Light’ offers us the opportunity to reaffirm, through contemporary art as well, the vitality of a philosophy that—eight hundred years after the death of St. Francis—‘the holiest among Italians and the most Italian among the saints’—remains highly relevant,” declared the ambassador. According to him, the Franciscan spiritual message has “transcended the borders of our country over time,” continuing to engage with diverse cultural contexts.
                                    
The presentation at the National Museum in Warsaw, which houses the painting “St. Francis in Ecstasy” by Giovanni Francesco Barbieri, known as Guercino, underscores the value of cultural collaboration between Italy and Poland, fostering a dialogue between Italy’s artistic heritage and the most innovative expressions of contemporary culture.

Two men die in Channel crossing attempt off northern France
- Published
Two men have died after trying to cross the English Channel off the coast of Berck in northern France.
According to local media, police saw migrants leaving the beach on a boat at about 22:00 local time on Sunday, and when rescuers arrived, they were bailing water out of the overloaded vessel with their shoes.
"When we arrived, there were at least 80 people on board and a terrible smell of gasoline,"Jean-Marc Lamblin, director of the French national sea rescue service (SNSM) told La Voix du Nord newspaper.
Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns that were caused by the mixture of gasoline in the seawater. Their condition has been described as not life-threatening.
Lamblin told the newspaper that there were so many people on the boat, including children, that about 20 people were left stranded in the water because they could not get on board.
He explained that when SNSM arrived, the two men, aged in their 30s and 40s, were in cardiac arrest.
The men and injured women were brought back to shore where firefighters and paramedics helped them, but the men died at about midnight.
Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor's office has opened an investigation to determine the circumstances of their death.
The two women were from Somalia and aged 20 and 26, La Voix du Nord reported, adding that they are now recovering in Rang-du-Fliers hospital.
Separately, the UK Home Office said 149 migrants were picked up on Sunday in a mid-Channel rescue operation and were brought to Gosport, in Hampshire.
About 150 anti-migrant demonstrators had gathered at the south coast town to stop the group being brought ashore, with flares being set off and some scuffles with police.
Figures from the UK Home Office have recorded 19,451 people crossing the Channel in small boats this year.
The number is 43% lower than at the same time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to US' Karl Deisseroth, Germany's Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:20:19 UTC
19:20:19 KST

Melike Pala
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was jointly awarded Monday to US scientist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for "their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics."
The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet said the three scientists were honored for discoveries that laid the foundation for optogenetics, a method that allows nerve activity to be controlled using light, according to a statement.
Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a protein with unique properties that makes cells sensitive to light.
They found that when the protein was introduced into different types of cells, the cells became light-sensitive, opening new possibilities for controlling cellular activity with light.
Deisseroth later introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats. 
By exposing the cells to blue light, he was able to trigger nerve signals.
He subsequently developed the technique to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice using light.
"This method for controlling nerve signals with light is now called optogenetics, and it has rapidly gained global impact," the statement said.

Saudi East-West oil pipeline is said to be flowing as normal
Saudi Arabia’s key cross-country oil pipeline is operating normally, people familiar with the matter said, after a report that it had shut following a new attack.
Oil continues to flow through the East-West link, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Saudi Aramco and the Energy Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The link has served as a vital conduit for keeping oil flowing during the Iran war with shipments through the Red Sea without relying on risky journeys via the Strait of Hormuz.
After accounting for supplies to refineries on Saudi Arabia’s west coast, Aramco had about 4.5 million barrels a day of flows available for exports as at last week, according to a person familiar with the matter.
However, the Red Sea route has come under pressure in recent months, with Yemen’s Houthi militants attacking tankers and Saudi infrastructure along the kingdom’s west coast.

'It was humiliating' — Ex-US Army Secretary says Washington lags behind Ukraine in war innovations
Former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll sees significant shortcomings in the U.S. military's ability to adapt to modern warfare compared with Ukraine's rapid innovations, he said in an interview with Rolling Stone magazine published on Oct. 4.
"When you would see what Ukraine's budget was and how small it was relative to ours and how, despite that, they had better weapons of war, it was a wake-up call," said Driscoll in his first-ever interview following his resignation on Aug. 31, after alleged friction with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
"In some ways, it was humiliating seeing how quickly a nation could change when it needed to," added Driscoll, who has long praised Ukraine's advances in drone technology and visited the country in 2025 as part of Washington-led peace talks.
During his time at the White House, Driscoll was a strong advocate for modernizing the U.S. Army through investments in counter-drone systems and the creation of the Unmanned Assault Battalion, a "drones-first" 600-soldier unit that cooperated with Ukrainian advisers.
However, Driscoll's ambitious modernization plans allegedly faced opposition from Hegseth.
"Once he (Hegseth) makes a decision, there's nothing I can do about it," said Driscoll.
"I don't have to like it," he added.
The two officials promoted different visions for strengthening the U.S. Army. While Driscoll focused on adjusting to the new realities of modern warfare, Hegseth has promoted a "warrior culture" centered on more traditional methods, such as soldiers' physical fitness.
After Driscoll's departure from the White House, the U.S. Army ordered the Unmanned Assault Battalion to return to being a standard airborne infantry unit.
"President Trump came into his second term with a military that had been very poorly prepared for modern war," said Driscoll.
"I viewed my role as to advocate as hard as I could for leaders who I thought were good," he added.

Education disrupted as French high school protests enter 2nd week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:19:00 UTC
19:19:00 KST

Hundreds of high schools across France were fully or partially disrupted Monday as student protests over deteriorating education conditions continued, one day before a new nationwide mobilization called by student organizations and supported by several trade unions.
The Education Ministry said 413 establishments were affected by actions or disruptions Monday, including schools that had been closed.
The ministry said 40% of the establishments disrupted Monday had not been affected previously. Education Minister Edouard Geffray had said Sunday that classes would be totally or partially suspended in between 400 and 500 of France's roughly 3,700 high schools where security conditions could not be guaranteed.
The protests, which began at a school in the Paris region late September, have spread nationwide. Students have been protesting against teacher shortages and high rates of teacher absenteeism, overcrowded classrooms, poor school facilities and long school days. They have also raised concerns about inequalities associated with the Parcoursup university admissions platform.
Students in working-class suburbs have described the movement as a demand for equality, dignity and decent conditions for studying.
Sociologist Eric Fassin, a professor at Paris VIII University, told France 24 that he saw the student protests primarily as a demand for equality, dignity and recognition, with students seeking the basic conditions needed to study and have the same opportunities as students elsewhere.
The protests have also been marked by violent incidents and clashes with security forces. According to the Education Ministry, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since the beginning of the movement.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested since the beginning of the movement; about 85% of them are minors.
In Belfort, eastern France, footage showing young people beating and kicking a police officer on the ground caused an outcry among officials.
Two Bulgarian nationals, aged 15 and 17, were arrested and investigated for suspected aggravated violence. One of them, whom the officer had attempted to arrest before the assault, subsequently filed a complaint alleging attempted murder through his lawyer.
The government's response has come under criticism from rights groups. Amnesty International's French branch accused police of using disproportionate violence and said students should be able to express their grievances without fear of being subjected to tear gas, batons or arbitrary detention.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez rejected that criticism, saying security forces were not cracking down on young people but were protecting students who wished to express their demands peacefully.
Minister Geffray has said that activists, particularly from the far left, had infiltrated the student movement, "hijacked" it and engaged in extreme violence.
The government has announced measures aimed at addressing some of the students' demands. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed local authorities to prioritize filling vacancies caused by long-term absences and unfilled posts. He has also scheduled a meeting with regional presidents to discuss the renovation of school buildings.
The organizers, however, have called for the protests to continue Tuesday, saying that the government has yet to propose concrete measures.
The CGT trade union has announced its participation in Tuesday's mobilization and said it would stand alongside the students. Several education unions have also called for participation. The Socialist Party has likewise called on its supporters to join the demonstrations.
The movement has also reached higher education. Higher Education and Research Minister Philippe Baptiste said he feared a national escalation involving universities and students.
He said between 30 and 40 higher education sites would be disrupted on Monday, either through blockades or administrative closures. Several university sites in Aix-en-Provence and Marseille were closed, and classes moved online.
Meanwhile, France's Senate is due to vote on Oct. 27 on a proposed law that would require protesters to pay for damage caused during demonstrations.
Under the proposal, an individual could be required to pay for damage without proof that they personally caused it, with the fine capped at 10,000 euros ($11,199).

Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:18:47 BST
19:18:47 KST

Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
- Published
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, Sánchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".
Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for Sánchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.
"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," Sánchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
Sánchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
Sánchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
Sánchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".
The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It was later lowered to €1,650 - still €300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home, but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".
Sánchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife Begoña Gómez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by Sánchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.
In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.
And in June, Sánchez's former transport minister, José Luis Ábalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

Court upholds ruling to bar early release of former EDF officer convicted of treason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Court upholds ruling to bar early release of former EDF officer convicted of treason
A court on Monday upheld a ruling denying convicted traitor Deniss Metsavas conditional early release from prison.
His 15-year sentence, imposed in 2019, is around half-way completed and he is being held at Tallinn Prison.
The second-tier Tallinn Circuit Court affirmed a ruling made in August by the Harju County Court which barred Metsavas, 46, from early release.
In its ruling the circuit court said it had not been convinced that serving only half of his sentence had done enough to prevent Metsavas from committing further crimes, despite expressions of remorse and efforts to rehabilitate himself while incarcerated.
The court said releasing a prisoner at the earliest opportunity allowed by law, after only half of a sentence has been served, requires compelling reasons to conclude that the aims of the punishment have already been achieved.
"In D. Metsavas' case, the court currently finds that no such circumstances exist," Tallinn Circuit Court spokesperson Anneli Vilu told ERR.
The ruling has not yet entered into force and can be appealed within 15 days.
In late August the first-tier Harju County Court rejected Metsavas' application for conditional early release. Tallinn Prison had submitted documents to the court in June seeking his release under electronic monitoring.
The lower court acknowledged several factors in Metsavas' favor, including that he had a stable home and supportive family, completed vocational training while in prison and worked as a librarian and instructor. He also had no unpaid claims, and had accumulated savings awaiting his release.
However, the court concluded that those circumstances on their own were not sufficient to reliably forecast that Metsavas would remain law-abiding post-release.
It noted that Metsavas had a job, home, family and supportive relatives prior to his imprisonment too, yet nevertheless chose to commit serious crimes against the integrity of the Estonian state.
The court considered his risk of reoffending to be high, taking into account the seriousness of the offense and the long period over which it was committed.
Metsavas, a former EDF major, was convicted of treason and sentenced to 15 years and six months in prison in 2019. His espionage activities on behalf of Russia's GRU military intelligence service covered a period of more than a decade, during which he passed classified and other internal information to Russian intelligence. His father, Pjotr Volin, was also found guilty of treason.
Metsavas had previously been something of a poster boy for integration, as an ethnic Russian citizen of Estonia fluent in the Estonian language and serving as an EDF officer. He had appeared on ETV panel shows on that basis.

Donor countries may demand back €14.5 million over failed ammo deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Donor countries may demand back €14.5 million over failed ammo deals
Estonia may have to repay €14.5 million to Denmark and the Netherlands from its own budget, after donor money was used in failed advance payments for ammunition for Ukraine, Postimees reported.
The money came from classified donor countries, not only the European Peace Facility (EPF), though the authorities have declined to disclose which ones.
From August 2024, the state Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed four contracts with Datasel, an Italian firm acquired by Indian-owned Neco Defense Munitions, paying roughly €70 million up front for artillery shells for Ukraine. None of the ammunition arrived, the agency terminated the contracts, and the state is now pursuing the money through Estonian courts and Swiss arbitration.
Parties familiar with the contracts told Postimees the donor nations are Denmark and the Netherlands — €9.5 million of the Datasel advance payments came from Denmark, and €5 million of the payment to an unknown company came from the Netherlands.
The Netherlands and Denmark very likely gave Estonia much more than €14.5 million in total, according to Postimees, most of which was spent or remains in an Estonian account and poses no risk.
That €14.5 million is a component of the advance payments to companies from which Ukraine received no suitable ammunition, and under the bilateral agreements Estonia is obliged to return all unused funds.
RKIK deputy director Asko Kivinuk confirmed Estonia must do so immediately if the donors request it, and said negotiations are underway on whether they will wait for the court proceedings to finish.
The interstate agreements expire within this year, meaning the repayment could hit Estonia's current state budget rather than a future one.
The Ministry of Defense denies Dutch involvement in the Datasel case, while the Dutch Ministry of Defense confirmed it allocated funds to Estonia and said the agreements provide for their return, Postimees reported.
The National Audit Office (Riigikontroll) warned the risks could create significant obligations on Estonia's state budget; the Ministry of Defense's earlier statement to the Riigikogu that there was no budget risk had been in error.
Intermediary donor activity has not ended — the 2027 budget plans up to €62.97 million in mediated grants, including €25 million in Norwegian support for ammunition for Ukraine.
The original Postimees piece is here.
Background
Fallout from the Datasel scandal contributed to Hanno Pevkur's resignation as defense minister on September 2, 2026.
Auditor General Janar Holm said last month the scandals pose no security threat and that open discussion makes Estonia stronger, but warned several problems are systemic.
The scandal has raised broader questions about the state's oversight of defense procurement and about wider accounting and oversight problems at the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF). Pevkur's replacement as defense minister, Martin Herem, a former EDF commander, has pledged to analyze these issues further.
The Riigikogu's Anti-Corruption Select Committee last week said it was demanding all correspondence documenting from the outset the Estonian authorities' contact with Datasel and also with Turkish ammunition manufacturer ARCA Defence, the committee's chair Anastassia Kovalenko-Kõlvart (Center) told ERR (link in Estonian).

Neom Stadium reportedly "shelved indefinitely"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:15:26 UTC
19:15:26 KST

Neom Stadium reportedly "shelved indefinitely"
Plans for Neom Stadium in Saudi Arabia, which was being built to host World Cup games in 2034, have been abandoned, according to reporting by news agency Reuters.
Reuters revealed yesterday that Saudi Arabia was "quietly shelving" the stadium.
"According to two sources, plans to build the Neom Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely," reported the agency.
One of 15 stadiums announced as the venues for the 2034 World Cup, the 46,000-seat Neom Stadium was billed as the "most unique stadium in the world" in the World Cup bid.
Set to be raised 350 metres above the ground, it was planned as part of The Line mega city, which was the centrepiece of the wider Neom development.
The news is the latest setback for the Neom project, with the planned 170-kilometre-long The Line city, itself, seemingly abandoned.
Saudi Arabia was planning to build and renovate 15 stadiums in four cities – Riyadh, Jeddah, Al Khobar and Abha – along with Neom, ahead of the tournament in eight years' time.
Neom Stadium was one of 11 new stadiums, with four existing stadiums set to be renovated or expanded.
It is unclear whether another stadium will be built to replace Neom Stadium, or if the tournament will be held in 14 stadiums. At the recently completed World Cup in the USA, Mexico and Canada, games were hosted in 16 stadiums.
The World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority said that "substantial delivery" of the World Cup venues was underway when questioned by Reuters.
Several other planned World Cup stadiums in the country are progressing, including the Aramco Stadium by Populous, which is planned to open early next year.
Progress on Neom, which is located in the northwest of Saudi Arabia, has slowed in recent years, with its CEO Nadhmi al-Nasr departing in 2024 after a series of delays and controversies.
Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund asked consultants to conduct a feasibility review on The Line in 2025, which seemingly spelt the end to the vast spending on the project. It was later revealed that Neom was planning widespread redundancies.
Plans to host another major sports event at Neom were also cancelled, with the Trojena ski resort no longer hosting the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Ethiopia reasserts Red Sea, Nile interests, rejects ‘coercive measures’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:15:09 UTC
19:15:09 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Ethiopia on Monday reaffirmed its “legitimate interests” in the Red Sea and its central role in the Nile basin, rejecting political pressure and “coercive measures” over its regional interests.
In a statement, Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said virtually all of the Blue Nile, or Abay River, originates in the Ethiopian highlands and contributes about 85% of the Nile’s total flow.
“Any discussion concerning the utilization and management of the Abay River should be informed by these fundamental realities,” the ministry said.
It also stressed Ethiopia’s geographic and historical ties to the Red Sea, noting that its nearest border is “barely 30 miles (48 kilometers) from the coast.”
The ministry said regional maritime and security arrangements must take Ethiopia’s interests into account.
“These geographic and historical realities cannot be altered by political rhetoric, coercive measures, or acts of destabilization,” the statement added.
“Actions taken through proxies or acts of aggression will not change the facts on the ground, nor will they diminish Ethiopia’s legitimate interests, role, and responsibilities in the region.”
The statement followed a quadrilateral summit in Egypt on Sunday involving Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.
The leaders reaffirmed respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity and rejected unilateral measures affecting Egypt and Sudan’s existing Nile water uses.
Ethiopia did not specifically mention the summit or the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam in its statement.
“Ethiopia continues to pursue peaceful engagement, mutual respect, and regional cooperation,” the ministry said, adding that Addis Ababa would defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity and core national interests while urging regional actors to pursue “constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighborliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”

Pedro Sánchez announces the calling of general elections for November 29th
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:15:00 CEST

Pedro Sánchez announces the calling of general elections for November 29th
President's News - 2026.10.5
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, during the institutional statement (Pool Moncloa/Fernando Calvo y Sandra Armada)
SPEECH BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE GOVERNMENT OF SPAIN, PEDRO SÁNCHEZ
Dear citizens,
As you know, more than three years ago, the electorate and the Lower House of Parliament decided once again to back a progressive coalition government.
They did so to ensure that Spain continued along the path of transformation, ambition and social justice it has been following since 2018.
Achieving this has not been easy.
During this term, we have had to manage unprecedented emergencies and navigate a very difficult international landscape, marked by unilateral decisions and events such as trade tensions, energy crises and the return of war to Europe and the Middle East.
We have had to work with a very acrimonious Parliament in which -absurdly- many confuse "making deals" with "giving in" and "blocking" with "winning."
We have had to contend with powerful economic and social elites who do not run for election yet seek to maintain control over our country.
And we have also had to deal with the worst opposition our democracy has ever known. It is an opposition lacking any sense of state responsibility - one that has ceaselessly questioned the legitimacy of our electoral system, blocked measures, voted against policies beneficial to the country and used its regional powers to sabotage policies that help ordinary people.
We have transferred more resources than ever to those regional governments so they could build housing and invest in healthcare. Yet, instead, they have bought up penthouses and privatised hospitals.
Even so, despite all these difficulties and hostility, the progressive coalition government has never stopped working. And, with it, Spain has never stopped moving forward.
Over these three years, our country has become the fastest-growing economy in the European Union, leading the bloc in job creation. The purchasing power of our citizens has grown three times as much as in France and Germany. And our levels of inequality and poverty - while still high - have fallen to their lowest point since records began.
Through effort and dialogue, we have succeeded in expanding scholarships, maternity and paternity leave, support for long-term care and the range of services provided by the National Health System.
We have also launched a profound modernisation of our industry by fully utilising European funds - specifically, the Next Generation funds.
We have tackled one of our country's major challenges - the lack of progress in energy transformation and the ecological transition - reaching the point where more than half of our energy comes from renewable sources. We have adopted bold measures to uphold the constitutional right to housing. And we have refused to sacrifice our welfare state on the altar of the 5% [defence spending target].
Ultimately, we have done everything within our power to defend the interests of the people of Spain.
At the same time, to the best of our ability, we have strived to build a better world for our fellow citizens and for humanity as a whole. We have supported Ukraine, the European Union and the United Nations during their darkest hours. We have denounced perpetrators of genocide while others remained silent. We have fought against tyrants, techno-oligarchs and the speculators who seek to destroy our children's future to line their own pockets. We have doubled our international development aid, while others boasted of slashing it with their "chainsaws" or sacrificing it on that military altar of 5% of GDP.
All of this has shaped our country; it has turned Spain into a global benchmark for peace, feminism and prosperity. It has enabled us to achieve the best economic, social and environmental results of any democratic government in our country's history. The very best.
And this is no exaggeration. Nor is it an opinion. It is a fact - verifiable data - made possible by the dedication of millions of workers, the self-employed and, of course, our country's business owners. It was also made possible by the generosity of other parliamentary forces - whom I wish to thank personally - who were able to look past their differences to forge agreements for the benefit of the social majority. And it was made possible by that very social majority, which has brought out the best in itself during every crisis we have had to face.
I know that part of that social majority feels dissatisfied today. I know that they are outraged to see how their interests are trampled upon in Parliament for the benefit of a few. I also know that we ourselves have made mistakes and have not managed to do everything we had set out to do. It is true that there are still many injustices to be corrected. Many social goals to be achieved. And many problems to be resolved, above all in the areas of inequality, public services and access to housing.
But the fact is that, in order to do more, we need to renew and expand people's support.
To undertake the pending reforms needed to reduce inequality, we must mobilise and secure a much broader, progressive majority in Parliament - one capable of overcoming the elites, achieving new social advances and continuing to transform Spain.
Therefore, after duly informing the Head of State, I have decided to convene an extraordinary Council of Ministers this very morning to dissolve the General Courts and call a general election for Sunday, 29 November , in accordance with statutory timeframes.
The time has come, then, for the Spanish people to decide what future you want for yourselves and for your country.
It is now up to you.
One need only look at the horizon to see that the world is facing a complex era - a time of transformation and transition. A time of great tension. Of climate emergency. Of social and - with artificial intelligence - highly disruptive technological changes
An era, therefore, of great dangers, but also, if we know how to make the most of it, of great opportunities.
You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play. Whether you wish to join the far-right wave that causes regression wherever it governs, or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility. Whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forward. Whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society. Or would you prefer to hand the reins of the country over to a far-right coalition that has proposed nothing - and whose sole objective is to repeal and curtail the rights and freedoms we have built up over these past eight years - in order to benefit the same old crowd, a privileged minority?
I have faith in my fellow countrymen and women. Because I know that you are a brave and supportive people, that you rise to challenges and that you have no qualms about being the only ones or the first to move in order to stand on the right side of history. That is why we are going to give it our all: to work hard to earn your trust, to inspire hope and to win again. Thank you very much.
(Transcript edited by the State Secretariat for Communication)
