The Republican consensus on Israel is starting to fracture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:05:47 UTC
19:05:47 KST

The Republican consensus on Israel is starting to fracture
Christian Zionism made Israel central to conservative politics. America First and younger Republicans are testing that consensus.
The Republican Party’s powerful alliance with Israel — repeatedly reaffirmed during President Donald Trump’s second term — is rooted in conservative Christianity’s rise as a political force more than half a century ago.
The Reverend Billy Graham’s relationship with President Richard Nixon helped bring evangelical politics into the White House. Graham later regretted his political entanglement, particularly after Watergate, but the opening remained. In the late 1970s, Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority mobilised conservative evangelicals into a potent Republican constituency that Ronald Reagan incorporated into his conservative coalition. Israel became increasingly central to that identity, with many evangelicals viewing support for the Jewish state through a biblical rather than purely strategic lens. Leaders such as televangelist John Hagee and Christians United for Israel later built an institutional network that translated religious conviction into political pressure. What began as evangelical access to Republican presidents became a durable political infrastructure.
For Christian Zionists, this alliance is about more than religious affinity. Many view Israel as central to biblical prophecy, including end-times interpretations and the anticipated return of Jesus Christ. These beliefs elevated support for Israel from a foreign-policy preference to a religious commitment. As evangelical voters became a core Republican constituency, politicians had strong electoral incentives to embrace that commitment, bringing theology, party loyalty and strategic interests into closer alignment.
The political heirs
Today’s Republican leaders inherited that system.
Mike Johnson of Louisiana, the speaker of the US House of Representatives, embodies its contemporary influence. He has invoked biblical passages to portray the relationship between the US and Israel as more than a conventional strategic partnership. His speakership gives him considerable influence over legislation, congressional spending and debates over US military assistance to Israel.
Senator Ted Cruz of Texas has repeatedly framed his support for Israel in explicitly Christian terms. Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas represents a more nationalist, hawkish version of the alliance. His effort to replace “West Bank” with “Judea and Samaria” in federal terminology illustrates how biblical language can enter government policy.
Former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee, now Trump’s ambassador to Israel, represents the same intersection of evangelical Christianity and Republican politics. His defence of Israeli settlements and rejection of conventional territorial terminology reflect a worldview in which biblical claims carry substantial political weight.
These figures did not create the alliance; they are its current custodians. Their influence extends beyond rhetoric. Congressional votes on military assistance, diplomatic protection and sanctions translate political commitments into policy. Christian Zionist organisations sustain that influence through church networks, lobbying, grassroots mobilisation and direct engagement with elected officials, keeping their priorities prominent even when other Republicans question overseas commitments.
Trump and the America First complication
President Donald Trump strengthened the evangelical alliance with Israel while introducing a competing force into Republican foreign policy: America First.
His administration’s recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and relocation of the US embassy fulfilled a longstanding Christian Zionist priority. Yet Trump’s coalition also includes voters sceptical of foreign entanglements, overseas military interventions and extensive foreign assistance. This creates a tension within the Republican consensus.
For Christian Zionists, support for Israel can constitute a biblical obligation. For some America First Republicans, the question is whether that commitment advances a clearly defined American interest. The positions overlap but are not identical.
The tension sharpens when support for Israel risks a wider war, additional deployments or prolonged US involvement in the Middle East. The Iran war has exposed precisely this contradiction, forcing Republicans to confront the point at which support for Israel collides with America First opposition to prolonged military involvement abroad. Religious conservatives may regard biblical commitments as decisive while more isolationist Republicans question the financial costs, potential American casualties and responsibilities Washington assumes on behalf of other countries.
Trump has sought to accommodate both constituencies, but their competing priorities have become increasingly difficult to reconcile.
The generational crack
A more consequential challenge may be emerging among younger Republicans.
A Pew Research Center March survey found that Republicans overall viewed Israel more favourably than unfavourably, by 58 percent to 41 percent. Among Republicans aged 18 to 49, however, 57 percent held unfavourable views. Older Republicans remained substantially more favourable. A separate Pew survey in May found that 42 percent of Republican-leaning Americans aged 18 to 29 viewed Israelis favourably, compared with 83 percent of those aged 65 and older. Although the surveys measured different populations and questions, both revealed a pronounced generational divide.
These findings do not mean younger Republicans have abandoned Israel or oppose the US-Israel relationship. They do suggest that the constituency underpinning the alliance is becoming less uniform.
The reasons extend beyond ideology. Younger Americans encounter the conflict through social media, reporting on Gaza and images of civilian suffering. Some question whether religiously grounded foreign-policy commitments serve American interests. Others support Israel while opposing particular Israeli government policies. Unfavourable views of Israel should not automatically be equated with hostility towards Israelis or rejection of the bilateral relationship.
Nevertheless, a generation increasingly divided over Israel may prove less receptive to appeals treating support for the country as an unquestionable test of conservative identity.
A changing Republican inheritance
Israel has developed into more than a foreign-policy priority. For millions of conservatives, support for Israel has been part of the Republican Party’s religious and moral identity.
That legacy remains powerful, but its foundations are shifting. Younger Republicans came of age during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, Trump’s nationalism, scepticism towards foreign intervention and Israel’s war on Gaza. Their questions increasingly concern not only theology but also national interests: What does US support for Israel accomplish, what does it cost and when should religious conviction yield to strategic considerations?
Such questions may reshape the coalition without immediately dismantling it. Evangelical organisations retain substantial resources, access to political leaders and the capacity to mobilise voters. Their congressional allies hold positions of considerable influence, and changing public opinion does not automatically translate into new party platforms or congressional votes.
Yet the growing divide between older evangelical voters and younger Republicans presents a longer-term challenge. Christian Zionism succeeded so thoroughly that its premises became Republican orthodoxy. But an alliance sustained by religious conviction, institutional influence and partisan loyalty becomes harder to preserve when a new generation questions those underlying assumptions.
For decades, support for Israel could be presented simultaneously as foreign policy and faith. Increasingly, younger Republicans may demand a different justification, one grounded in demonstrable US interests rather than religious obligation alone. Whether Republican support for Israel can survive that shift may become a defining test of the party’s evolving identity.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Nobel Prize for Medicine awarded to three scientists for their work in optogenetics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:05:01 UTC
19:05:01 KST

STOCKHOLM, October 5. /TASS/. The 2026 Nobel Prize for Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute announced on Monday.
The three scientists were selected as the winners for their work ‘concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics’, the Assembly explained in a press release.
"The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 is awarded for optogenetics - a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviors in the living brain. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. The Laureates have laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience," the press release reads.
According to Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, "optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
Optogenetics, a groundbreaking method for controlling nerve signals with light, has rapidly gained global impact and fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain, the Assembly continued. "Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works," it concluded.

Saudi Arabia sends 100 fighter jets into Yemen as Houthi war erupts again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:04:47 UTC
19:04:47 KST

A Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Monday that a major air campaign was underway along the country’s Red Sea coast, as fighting intensified following a series of Houthi territorial gains.
The announcement came shortly after the Houthis said they had captured additional territory in southwestern Yemen, including a strategically important town, dealing another blow to forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and bringing the rebels closer to the provincial capital of Taiz.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were providing support to Yemeni government forces battling the Houthis.
He said the coalition had secured “air protection” over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets during the ongoing campaign.
The claims and the scale of the campaign could not immediately be independently verified.
Houthis seize key town as fighting escalates
The Houthis captured the town of Turbah on Sunday, shortly before Yemen’s internationally recognized government announced a major military operation against the rebels.
The renewed fighting has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
Turbah lies on a major road linking Taiz with the southern port city of Aden, which serves as the interim seat of Yemen’s government. For years, the town served as an important position for government forces defending Taiz against the Houthis.
The rebels had already seized several villages and areas on the outskirts of Taiz, advances that could help them encircle Yemen’s third-largest city.
The latest Houthi gains follow a rapid offensive along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast that began in early September.
The rebels captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that allowed them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, through which roughly 12% of global trade passes.
In an announcement Sunday, the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said it was mobilizing troops throughout territory under its control.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operation was aimed at “recovering the remaining territories” held by the Houthis and called on the international community to support his government.
Hours later, al-Malki pledged “full operational support” for Yemeni government forces until the Houthis were “eliminated.”
He also said Saudi Arabia reserved the right to take all necessary measures against Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom during the nearly three-month escalation.
Saudi-backed forces launch counteroffensive
On Monday, factions aligned with the Saudi-backed coalition said they had begun offensives against Houthi positions east of coastal areas seized by the rebels.
The forces attacked Houthi positions in Dhubab, on the coast of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Col. Majed al-Nazili, a spokesman for the Saudi-backed forces.
The Giants Brigades, another government-aligned force, said it had launched a “decisive military operation against the Houthi militias” in the Bab el-Mandeb area.
Al-Alimi said in a post on X that the operation, dubbed “Yemen Dawn,” was intended to restore state institutions, “liberate” the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa and end what he called the Houthi “coup.”
The latest escalation began in mid-July, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa airport to prevent an unauthorized Iranian flight from landing.
The rebels responded with missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces and announced a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, later attacking several Saudi-linked vessels.
In September, the Houthis intensified their campaign, advancing rapidly down the Red Sea coast in their largest territorial push in years.
The capture of Turbah “will likely severely constrain Yemeni government-aligned forces’ ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions” across Taiz province and in the city itself, the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War said.
“Disrupting resupply has military value, of course, but controlling all the roads in and out of areas to the north of Turbah also prevents government forces from retreating out of the city,” the think tank wrote in an analysis Sunday.
Civil war flares again after four-year ceasefire
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis swept south from their northern stronghold, captured Sanaa and forced the internationally recognized government into exile in Saudi Arabia.
The conflict has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and killed more than 150,000 people.
The latest round of violence has killed more than 800 people and wounded more than 3,600, according to the United Nations.
More than 145,000 people have been displaced within Yemen, according to the U.N. migration agency, while more than 3,000 others have fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti.
Last week, the health ministry run by Yemen’s internationally recognized government warned that the renewed fighting was severely affecting medical services across Taiz province.
The ministry said health facilities in coastal, western and southern parts of the province had either closed or were operating only partially.

Raccoons taking over the Curonian Spit; hunting to be permitted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:03:31 UTC
19:03:31 KST

Raccoons on the Curonian Spit are being counted and monitored, and authorities are preparing a plan to combat this invasive species; hunting is likely to begin as early as spring.
Saulius Rumbutis, a staff member at the Tadas Ivanauskas Zoology Museum, noted that while there appears to be a significant number of raccoons on the Curonian Spit, it is difficult to determine exactly how many are present. He estimated the population to be between 50 and 100 individuals.
Raccoons are nocturnal animals that typically hide during the day. Rumbutis explained that they often choose large tree hollows or simply fallen trees—such as pines—for shelter; they climb up to sleep during the day and venture out at night in search of food.
The highest concentration of raccoons has been observed near Juodkrantė. As omnivores, these animals tend to stay near inhabited areas where food is more plentiful. Rumbutis noted that raccoons feed on mollusks and will also eat the eggs or chicks found in bird nests. If they happen to find something like a slice of pizza discarded in a trash bin, they will certainly eat that as well.

In the experimental short All-around Junior Male, the Inuk filmmaker Lindsay McIntyre documents a traditional Inuit game known as the one-foot high kick. Competitors attempt to leap from both feet to strike a suspended target, landing on the same foot used to kick, with the target rising after each successful round. The game was once used by hunters to indicate a successful hunt and demands extraordinary strength, balance and control. In her portrait, McIntyre captures the Nunamiut athlete Sean Uquqtuq in action with monochrome, hand-processed film that abstracts the landscape around him, focusing on his face and the movement of his body. Combined with an ambient score, these elements lend the piece an immersive, dreamlike quality.

Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual | Steven Greenhouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:53 UTC
19:00:53 KST

Donald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities, writing on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”
But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one that raised the possibility of cutting off all trade with dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according to a recent WSJ poll.
Responding to Trump’s reckless statements, one prominent advocacy group, Republicans Against Trump, derided him as “Dumbest. President. Ever.”
Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements. First, he wrote on Truth Social: “I’ll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Federal Reserve doesn’t cut interest rates.
The second disconcerting statement was: “If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.”
Not only is Trump’s arithmetic childishly silly here, but any college student who took Econ 101 knows that if a trade-dependent nation like the US suddenly ended all trade with dozens of countries, that would lead to economic disaster. What’s more, it was worrisome that Trump views himself as almighty emperor with the power to singlehandedly halt hundreds of billions of dollars in trade.
If Trump ordered the US to terminate all trade with every place with which it has a trade deficit – that includes China, Mexico, Taiwan and the European Union – many US manufacturers would quickly find themselves in desperate straits, unable to obtain critically needed computer chips, rare earths, auto parts, aluminum and much more. As a result, many factories would be forced to close. Not only that, many farmers would be crippled because they couldn’t import the fertilizer they need, while many homebuilders would have to stop work because they couldn’t import needed lumber.
Those were by no means Trump’s only recent mind-boggling statements.
Two days before the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% to combat inflation, Trump was on a tear, badgering and bullying the Fed, telling it not only not to raise interest rates, but to cut rates sharply. “We should be at 1% or half a percent,” Trump said. Again, anyone who took Econ 101 knows that cutting rates so sharply and so low will push prices skyward at a time when the Fed and consumers already think inflation is too high. And let’s not forget that Trump was the guy who promised to reduce prices on day one as president.
With that statement, the self-described “stable genius” president showed his utter failure to understand one of the most basic teachings of Econ 101 – when interest rates are extremely low, like 1%, that heats up the economy and that revved-up economic activity fuels inflation. The University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers called Trump’s demand for a 1% interest rate “the dumbest thing ever said by a president”.
Then there was this whopper. Trump said that if the Fed bowed to his demands and slashed interest rates, “we could have a GDP [growth] of 14, 15, 16 and 20.”
Those numbers are absurd, fantastical. Considering that the US economy grew at a moderate 2.2% rate in this year’s second quarter and rarely grows faster than 5%, talk of 20% growth is delusional. Since the second world war, the US economy has grown at a rate at 20% or higher just once. That happened in the third quarter of 2020 due to extraordinary circumstances – in that quarter, myriad businesses rushed to reopen after the worst pandemic in a century caused many to suddenly shut down during the previous quarter. (GDP plunged at a 28% rate that quarter.)
Then there was this colossally wrong-headed statement about trade: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS.” Trump coupled that assertion with his misbegotten statement that the US would magically be $1.5tn richer if it terminated all trade with every nation with which it has a deficit.
This shows an infantile understanding of trade – and a stunning blindness to its mutual benefits.
To explain how inane Trump is being here, let’s hypothesize for a second that in the US-France trade relationship, the only goods traded are wine and bourbon. Under Trump’s ludicrous logic, if the US buys $2bn of wine from France, and the French import $1bn worth of Kentucky bourbon, the resulting $1bn trade deficit means the US is simply giving away $1bn to France.
Trump bafflingly sees that as an outright $1bn loss. Blinded by ignorance, ideology or an idée fixe, Trump fails to see that that’s not a harmful $1bn “loss” – rather, Americans are getting $1bn worth of fine wine to enjoy. No doubt wine lovers across the US see that as a gain and certainly not as a $1bn loss.
Bottom line, Trump’s delusional statements on the economy show that he is becoming more detached from reality and from rational understanding of how the world works. One can’t help but wonder why his economic advisers don’t stop him from making such ridiculous and at times dangerous statements. If Trump turns his absurd economic notions into reality, as he has done in his ugly, unnecessary trade war with Canada, that will be more bad news for Americans.
Voters should realize that Trump, with his failure to grasp basic economics, is a danger to the economy. He has brought us higher prices, slower GDP growth, and constant economic chaos and uncertainty. His tariffs and disastrous war against Iran have hit the great majority of Americans in their wallets and pocketbooks.
Tragically, Trump’s Republican supporters in Congress either cheer him on or remain dismayingly silent while Trump does serious damage to the economy and to the finances of millions of struggling families. Americans shouldn’t forget this when they vote in November’s midterm elections.
- Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

MVRDV designs modular concrete street furniture to be occupied in "unexpected ways"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:46 UTC
19:00:46 KST

MVRDV designs modular concrete street furniture to be occupied in "unexpected ways"
Colourful concrete modules are combined to form impromptu hangout spots in the Barcode collection, designed by architecture studio MVRDV for Barcelona street furniture manufacturer Escofet.
The range consists of three basic building blocks – steps, slopes and a joint table and bench – that can be joined together to create an atlas of different topographies.
MVRDV founding partner Jacob van Rijs, who led the project, says he hopes the collection will encourage citizens to take ownership over their cities and appropriate urban infrastructure in a way that suits their needs.
"Too often, the design of urban spaces can feel formulaic – benches and other elements are selected from a catalogue and placed in the most predictable places," he says.
"This collection is built around a different approach: human occupation becomes the centrepiece of any design, with a creative collaboration between the individual elements, the arrangement made by an urban designer, and the unexpected ways that the public will occupy them," Van Rijs continued.
Barcode consists of three basic building blocks that can be adapted with add-ons like planters. They come in Escofet's eight different concrete colours, including red, green and yellow alongside more muted grey, white, beige and black.
The Tribune module consists of a set of broad steps for climbing and sitting, while the smooth slope of Dune invites lounging. Desk is a more traditional set-up of a table framed by two benches for al fresco eating or working.
All three modules have the same height and width, so they can be lined up to form a continuous surface. MVRDV envisions them being used in one long line – hence the name Barcode – or combined into more compact two-by-two "islands".
Considering all the different variations, MVRDV says the collection includes 72 different choices of elements that can be combined into nearly "infinite variations".
Previous adventures in street furniture from the studio, which was founded by Van Rijs alongside Winy Maas and Nathalie de Vries in 1991, include a giant woven floot mat that provided seating in Bangkok during the city's design week and bright-blue play areas for a 200-metre-long park beneath a Mumbai flyover.
All renders and photography courtesy of MVRDV.

European defence tech funding hits record levels
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:00:38 BST
19:00:38 KST

European defence technology startups have raised a record $7.4 billion in venture capital so far in 2026, nearly three times the $2.6 billion raised across the whole of 2025, according to Dealroom and Resilience Media.
The figures are contained in The State of Defence Tech 2026, which projects European defence-tech investment could reach $10.5 billion by the end of the year if current activity continues.
The report also records a marked increase in US involvement in European defence technology companies. American investors now account for 47 per cent of European defence-tech funding, compared with 17 per cent in 2020.
Much of the increase in investment has been concentrated in large funding rounds. Dealroom and Resilience Media said so-called mega-rounds, including Helsing’s $1.8 billion Series E, account for more than 85 per cent of European defence-tech funding recorded so far this year.
Across NATO members and allied countries, seven funding rounds of at least $1 billion have involved Anduril, Helsing, Saronic, Shield AI, Quantum Systems, ICEYE and Castelion. Defence startups across NATO countries have raised $27.1 billion in venture capital during 2026, around 1.9 times the amount raised during the whole of 2025.
Defence technology now accounts for 11.1 per cent of European venture capital investment, according to the report, rising to 15 per cent when considering the 27 European Union member states.
The pool of investors participating in the sector is also expanding. Dealroom identified 455 investors involved in at least one European defence deal during 2026 to date, compared with 408 during 2025 and 114 in 2020.
Specialist defence investment funds participated in 25 per cent of European defence funding rounds this year, up from 18 per cent in 2025 and 12 per cent in 2024. The report said private equity, project finance, debt and grants contributed a further $2.4 billion to defence companies across NATO and allied countries during 2025.
Germany is currently the largest European market for defence-tech venture funding, driven in part by investment in Helsing, Quantum Systems and Stark. German startups have raised $3.5 billion during 2026 and $5.9 billion since 2020, while Munich is identified in the report as Europe’s leading defence-technology hub.
According to a news update accompanying the report, Leslie Hitchcock, co-founder and publisher of Resilience Media, said: “National security, defence and technological innovation are now inseparable. Across NATO alliance countries, there is an urgent need to strengthen the infrastructure underpinning our collective security and resilience. For Europe, technological sovereignty must mean building together in the face of common threats.”
She added: “This is both a strategic imperative and a major economic opportunity: to build companies that protect peace and democracy while transforming defence, cybersecurity, energy and other critical infrastructure.”
US investors have become increasingly prominent within that European market. The report identifies Axon, Accel, Founders Fund, Y Combinator, General Catalyst and Lightspeed among the most active American investors in European defence technology during 2025 and 2026.
Among European investors, the NATO Innovation Fund recorded 12 defence-tech funding round participations since 2025, while Lakestar recorded ten, making them the two most active investors identified in the report over that period.
Klaus Hommels, Founder and Chairman of Lakestar, said: “Europe’s military leaders have been clear with us: if we want to build and retain critical defence capabilities in Europe, we also need sovereign European financing. The demand for these technologies is there and now the capital must follow. This record investment shows that Europe is beginning to recognise defence technology as a strategic necessity, not a passing investment trend.”
Despite the increase in funding, the report identifies areas where European companies remain behind global competitors. It describes Europe as relatively strong in quantum technology, photonics, space and drones, while identifying gaps in areas including AI chips and processors, launch vehicles, humanoid systems and communications satellites.
European quantum startups alone have raised $2.1 billion so far in 2026, with investment projected to reach $2.9 billion by the end of the year.
The value of European venture-backed defence startups has reached a combined $44 billion, according to the report, with companies founded since 2020 accounting for 77 per cent of that total.
Exit activity is also expected to increase. Across NATO and allied countries, defence-tech exits are projected to rise to 31 during 2026, compared with an annual average of around eight between 2021 and 2024. Exit value reached $18.6 billion during 2025, although the report said activity remained heavily concentrated in the United States.
The study also examined the movement of personnel between government, the military and the defence technology investment sector. Sixteen per cent of commercial leaders at European defence-tech companies were found to have military or defence ministry experience, while the proportion rises to 34 per cent among investors working at specialist defence funds.
Harry Mead, co-founder and CEO of Augur, said: “It’s reassuring to see European investment responding to the current threat environment. But this isn’t turning into deployed capability fast enough. The enemy are at the gates: Europe can’t afford to wait for new systems and legislation.”
“Our adversaries know this and are adept at exploiting the lag between identifying the problem, funding a solution and deploying it. We already have the infrastructure. What we urgently need is to make our sensors and systems more intelligent, so that operators can always stay a step ahead of our adversaries.”
The report is being presented at the Resilience Conference in London on 5 October, bringing together defence technology companies, investors and military and government representatives from the UK, NATO, Ukraine and other European countries.

Celebrity admiration is linked to submission to authority, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

People who strongly admire celebrities tend to be more deferential to authority and more attached to traditional norms, according to new research published in Psychological Reports. The findings suggest that strong emotional attachments to famous figures relate to a preference for established social order and conventional norms, even after accounting for a person’s general political orientation.
People often form one-sided emotional connections with famous actors, musicians, and social media influencers. While these parasocial relationships are common and can sometimes provide a sense of community, intense celebrity admiration involves spending excessive time and effort focusing on a favorite public figure. This level of absorption is sometimes linked to negative outcomes. For instance, a 2021 study covered by PsyPost indicated that higher obsession with celebrities was associated with lower performance on tests of vocabulary and fluid intelligence.
The idea that celebrity admiration might be tied to authoritarianism is not new. Researchers proposed in 2001 that people inclined to defer to authority might gravitate toward celebrities, who are often treated as authorities on a range of topics, but their study of British participants found no association between the two.
Since then, the understanding of authoritarianism has shifted. The authors of a 2010 paper argued that right-wing authoritarianism is better understood as three related but distinct sets of attitudes: authoritarianism (which involves aggression and strict control), conservatism (which focuses on submission to authority and preserving the status quo), and traditionalism (which centers on adhering to old-fashioned lifestyles and morality).
Nearly 25 years after that first study, and amid shifts in celebrity culture and politics, the researchers sought to test which specific dimensions of authoritarianism are actually associated with celebrity admiration, especially once general political ideology and demographic factors are taken into account. The team was led by Ho Huynh, a senior lecturer in the School of Medicine and Psychology at the Australian National University.
“We know that celebrities have undue influence over people and that celebrities typically endorse liberal-leaning causes (e.g., climate change, immigration, abortion),” Huynh told PsyPost. “We were surprised to learn through our previous work that people who admire celebrities tend to self-identify as more politically conservative.”
“In the current work, we wanted to see if celebrity admiration would extend to right-wing authoritarianism,” Huynh continued. “This work might help to explain the contradiction of why politically conservative people in the United States might be more attracted to celebrities despite the stereotype that celebrities tend to hold liberal views.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 331 adults living in the United States through the online crowdsourcing platform Prolific. The sample was deliberately balanced during recruitment to contain an equal mix of self-identified liberals, moderates, and conservatives, meaning it is not nationally representative. About 54 percent of the participants were women, and all were 18 or older, with an average age of about 40.
Participants completed the brief seven-item version of the Celebrity Attitude Scale, a questionnaire that asks people to indicate their agreement with statements about their favorite famous person. This scale measures two levels of admiration. The first is a lighter, entertainment-social level, which includes enjoying keeping up with news about the celebrity or discussing them with friends. The second is a more intense, pathological level, characterized by feelings that the celebrity is a soulmate or that the fan shares a special, indescribable bond with them.
The participants also completed a survey assessing the three dimensions of right-wing authoritarianism. For example, participants rated their agreement with statements like “Obedience and respect for authority are the most important virtues children should learn.” Finally, they provided demographic information, including their education level, socioeconomic status, and their overall political orientation on an 11-point scale ranging from completely liberal to completely conservative.
The initial results showed that both forms of celebrity admiration were linked to higher scores on all three dimensions of authoritarianism. The links were strongest for conservatism (correlations of 0.32 for the lighter form and 0.45 for the intense form, on a scale where 0 means no relationship), moderate for traditionalism (0.19 and 0.32), and weak for authoritarian aggression (0.15 and 0.13). Only the intense form was linked to political conservatism, and modestly so (a correlation of 0.19).
To see if these links held up under closer statistical scrutiny, the researchers ran a series of models that controlled for the participants’ age, gender, education, socioeconomic status, and general political orientation. This step helped rule out the possibility that the connection simply reflected factors like political conservatism, which was linked to authoritarian attitudes and to intense admiration.
After accounting for these factors, celebrity admiration consistently predicted right-wing conservatism and right-wing traditionalism. Demographics and political orientation explained about 24 percent of the variation in conservatism scores; celebrity admiration added 9 percent (lighter form) or 13 percent (intense form) on top of that. For traditionalism, it added only about 2 to 4 percent.
“The association between celebrity admiration and authoritarian submission seems to be robust and reliable, indicating that people who worship their favorite celebrity tend to prefer more dominant authorities,” Huynh explained. Asked what the average person should take away, he said: “People who report admiring their favorite celebrity are more likely to submit to authority and prefer traditional norms. These trends might help explain why people who admire celebrities may self-identify as more politically conservative.”
However, the relationship between celebrity admiration and the third dimension, authoritarianism (the demand for strict punishment of rule-breakers), did not remain robust. Once demographics and political orientation were factored in, intense admiration no longer predicted authoritarian aggression. The lighter form remained a statistically detectable predictor, but it accounted for only about 1 percent of the variation, and the authors do not consider this strong evidence of a link. The authors suggest this may be because people who heavily admire celebrities tend to see the world as fair, with people getting what they deserve, and so may feel less need to support harsh punishment for rule-breakers.
Huynh sees this boundary as an encouraging sign. “Celebrity admiration was not related to authoritarian aggression, which involves strictness and social control,” he noted. “This finding showed the limits of celebrity admiration, which is positive and worthy of optimism.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study measured these traits at a single point in time, so the direction of the relationship is unknown. Intense absorption in celebrity culture might lead someone to adopt more authority-respecting and traditional views, or people who already hold such views might be more drawn to celebrity culture. When the researchers flipped their statistical model, higher authority-submission scores also predicted more celebrity admiration, a pattern consistent with either direction.
The list of control variables was also limited, missing related traits like narcissism and a preference for social hierarchies. Additionally, the survey asked participants to focus on their favorite celebrity but did not distinguish between typical entertainers and political figures. Because modern politics has become heavily focused on personalities, admiring a politician might function differently than admiring a musician or actor.
“This research was not about political celebrities, but celebrities generally,” Huynh said. “Some people may want to view these findings through the Trump presidencies, but only 5 out of 331 people in the study listed Donald Trump as their favorite celebrity. As such, these findings represent the associations between celebrity admiration and endorsement of different aspects of right-wing authoritarianism more broadly.”
Finally, the study only included participants from the United States. Cultural values, political structures, and the nature of fame vary widely around the world, so these connections might operate differently in other countries.
Huynh suggested another direction for future work. “An interesting next step would be to examine the associations between celebrity admiration and left-wing authoritarianism (e.g., hostility toward people in power, support for censoring opposing views, and rejection of traditional values and norms),” he said.
The study, “Idols and Ideologies: Examining Associations Between Celebrity Admiration and Right-Wing Authoritarianism,” was authored by Ho Phi Huynh, Joshua L. Williams, Marla F. Jorgensen, Amy Dicke-Bohmann, and Lynn McCutcheon.

Chinese ‘Coffee Grandma’ learns brewing to save son’s cafe, inspires female independence

An 86-year-old grandmother in China has become a social media sensation for operating a coffee shop for over a decade – a business she took over from her son in 2015, despite having no experience with coffee at the time.
Zhao Qiying, affectionately known as the “Coffee Grandma,” revealed that the shop, located in downtown Qingdao in eastern China’s Shandong province, was nearly bankrupt due to her son’s lack of business acumen, according to the Peninsular Metropolis News.
At that time, Zhao was disheartened by the passing of her husband. Her son suggested she manage the coffee shop to help distract her, advising her to merely serve as a doorkeeper since few customers visited the outlet.
Despite her initial reservations, Zhao wanted to learn how to make coffee for customers. However, no institution was willing to accept her as a student due to her age, prompting her to take matters into her own hands.
She taught herself through coffee-making books and received tips from her son, gradually honing her skills.

Gambling Is Sending More People to the ER
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

Legalizing gambling can come with big health problems.
That’s the conclusion of a recent study out of Ontario, published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, which found that after the Canadian province legalized betting on individual sports events in 2022, emergency department visits for gambling disorders doubled. Most of the people who landed in the emergency department were men, and almost one third of the visits led to hospitalizations.
“This rise in severe presentations might be a bit of a warning signal of a wider increase in harms across the general population,” says Ryan Forrest, a public-health doctoral student at the University of Toronto and one of the authors of the study. “We think about things like financial distress, family and relationship problems, worsening mental health—and those things are not captured in the emergency department data.”
The authors of the Ontario study projected how many people would normally end up in an emergency department every year, and then compared that to what they saw after online betting on single sporting events became legal in Ontario. Emergency department visits were 154% higher than they would have been had the law not been changed, Forrest says. The visits were concentrated among men aged 10-44.
Many of the patients showed up at the emergency room with major depression and suicidality, and some had other mental-health or substance-abuse diagnoses, Forrest said. Doctors at the emergency department noted in patients’ records that gambling had contributed to those other issues.
A separate study by some of the same researchers also found that calls to ConnexOntario, Ontario’s free 24-hour mental health and addictions helpline, were 200% higher than they would have been had the law not been changed. That study found that the people reaching out for help were almost exclusively boys and men aged 15 to 44.
“There’s two data sources telling us there is a real health signal happening here,” Forrest says.
The mental-health consequences of expanding betting
The study is a warning to the U.S., which has seen sports gambling proliferate since 2018 after the Supreme Court struck down a law barring most state-authorized sports gambling, allowing states to decide for themselves whether to allow sports betting. Since then, dozens of states, including New Jersey, Tennessee, and New York, have legalized sports betting. Many states also allow online casino games. Gambling has spread in Canada, too, after the country legalized betting on single sports events in 2021.
Therapists in the U.S. say they are already seeing the mental-health consequences of the legalization of sport betting across the U.S., along with the results of more exposure to prediction markets. Birches Health, the largest provider specializing in the treatment of gambling disorder in the U.S., has seen the number of 18-to-34 year old clients grow more than twofold since 2024, according to Cynthia Grant, vice president of clinical for Birches Health.
“There’s more people gambling,” she says, “and when you have more people gambling, it simply means that there’s more people who are going to develop a problem.”
Grant says that clients are mentioning prediction markets 200% more often than they did last year, according to the company’s analysis of its initial clinical assessments. Prediction markets allow people as young as 18 to place wagers; sports betting is restricted to people over 21.
“It’s just not a regulated environment out there,” she says. “People’s lives are being ruined; their relationships are being destroyed, their retirement accounts are gone.”
One of the reasons younger people are seeking treatment may be that they are starting to gamble earlier, she says. It’s not just prediction markets: some kids are given lottery scratch tickets for gifts, she says, or they’ll participate in family fantasy sports wages. “Those are the memories that people talk about” in therapy, she says. Kids are also exposed to gambling with online games that encourage them to chase a reward, or through hobbies like collecting Pokemon cards, in which they are betting that they’ll get a valuable card in an anonymous pack.
The standard treatment for gambling disorder is cognitive behavioral therapy, Grant says, because people with a gambling addiction often have distorted thinking and believe that they can beat the system. But often, she says, people don’t even know that gambling disorder is a mental-health condition and that insurance can cover care. Studies show that suicidal ideation and suicide risk is 5 to 10 times higher in people with gambling disorders than in the general population.
An under-regulated betting landscape
Both Grant and Forrest say that the unregulated nature of gambling in both Canada and the U.S. leads to more people ending up with mental-health problems—but that there is little investment in tracking those problems. There has been no money set aside by the Canadian government to track whether it leads to more public-health problems, Forrest says.
“You compare that to something like when cannabis was legalized, there were huge amounts of grants given out to monitor these kinds of policy changes,” Forrest says.
Most apps don’t have automatic spending limits that prevent people from losing too much money gambling, and most take a hands-off approach to users who act in a way that suggests they have an addiction. In a recent ProPublica story, a reporter posed as a problem gambler and found that rather than flagging his behavior, the app tried to incentivize him to keep going.
“The way that online systems work right now do not protect people at all who are prone to behavioral addictions,” Grant says, “and that, to me, is very dangerous for my clients.”
“Bartenders have rules about how much they can serve someone,” Grant says. “Police can issue a DUI—there are efforts to stop people who are potentially causing harm. But that does not happen in the gambling space.”

The Case Against Wearing Headphones in Public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

I keep losing my wireless headphones. When I do have them with me, they’re often out of battery. So one day earlier this summer, I decided to ditch them.
It felt like a huge step, as I’d long used in-ear tech as a shield from the auditory chaos of London. But what happened felt transformative. I was surprised at how present I was without them.
During my first headphones-free commute, I smiled at strangers. I noticed the stops on the train line, something I never do when I rely on an app to tell me when to get off the train through my earphones. That one journey made me wonder if I had accidentally outsourced the joys of my city life to my phone.
In 2026, we have become remarkably good at filling every quiet moment: Spotify on the train, podcasts while walking, Google Maps telling us where to go, our phones providing something to look at whenever there’s a lull.
The scale of this is striking. Ofcom’s latest research found that 93% of U.K. adults listen to some form of audio every week, and more than a quarter listen to podcasts weekly. Hundreds of millions of people worldwide listen to podcasts.
There’s also a fascinating social angle. Research published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology found that people often avoid talking to strangers because they underestimate how enjoyable those interactions will be. And research into constant smartphone connectivity published in Current Directions in Psychological Science suggests that our devices can cause us to miss the emotional benefits of casual interactions by effectively replacing them.
It turns out that there might be a psychological reason why being without headphones has felt so unthinkable. Psychotherapist Jack Worthy tells me that our earliest impulses as newborns are approach and avoidance. “We approach what feels interesting, exciting, or otherwise potentially rewarding. We avoid whatever feels dangerous, disgusting, or boring.” Our emotional life proceeds from these drives, and these drives evolved to promote our survival and success.
Our headphones give us the power to dial in to highly appealing experiences and tune out everything we’d rather avoid in the environment. If our homes serve as refuge from the outside world, our headphones create a tidy micro-environment inside our heads.
I decided to continue my experiment, spending a month commuting without earphones at all.
After a week without them, I started observing fascinating new details about streets that I had walked countless times. One seismic discovery was that the nearest train station to my flat is a two-minute walk away. Google Maps had shown me the longer route, hauling me around the local houses for more than double as long, which in London may as well be wasted hours.
Without headphones, I found myself overhearing bizarre conversations. Like the girl next to me on the train, who had found a Rhode lip gloss in her boyfriend’s car when she is a Rare Beauty girl. She assured her friend that it could not have been her lip gloss because she would never buy anything from Hailey Bieber—after all, she is a long-time Selena Gomez fan. “I can’t believe how Hailey Bieber stole Justin Bieber from Selena Gomez, and now someone else is stealing my man!” she wailed with her head held between her knees and her friend rubbing her back.
Another time, I witnessed a man nearly lose his mind after a stranger accidentally smeared dirt onto his white shoes. The man exploded, yelling at this innocent stranger. It was a captivating fight, and I was absolutely glued. How could this man be fuming about a simple mistake? Imagine if I’d missed the spontaneous subterranean soap opera because I was listening to a podcast.
My absolute favorite eavesdropping moment was when two women in leather outfits and cowboy boots boarded the train and sat opposite me. The woman next to the window said her stressed boyfriend Keith had just bought the couple a flat, so she didn’t feel she could pressure him for an engagement ring. I was glued to their ridiculous conversation and, when they got off, sad that I couldn’t listen in anymore, as her requests were getting more and more ludicrous with every outburst.
“I don’t see him proposing to that nutter!” said the old man next to me, and we shared that rarest of joyous things: a communal laugh.
“Good luck to Keith! Lots going on, poor fella.”
I couldn’t believe I had been missing out on so much drama. Looking back, I realized how rarely I let myself be bored, instead always reaching for distraction.
Psychoanalysis uses the term “reverie” to define a particular kind of constructive, necessary daydreaming, points out Worthy. “In therapy, reveries refer to the daydreams, memories, and associations occurring to the analyst during a session.” A sensitive, attuned analyst interprets those reveries to understand what’s happening between themself and the patient.
If you’ve ever experienced a sudden moment of inspiration in the shower or on a run, if the solution to a sticky problem revealed itself to you spontaneously, you know something of what it means to use reverie. You let your mind unfold in unintentional directions, and your unconscious mind showed you what your conscious mind was missing.
If we’re always moving through the world with headphones in, listening to music or podcasts or books, we’re compromising our mind’s space for revery, says Worthy. There’s less room for the constructive daydreaming our mental processes use for creativity, problem-solving, and synthesizing.
By the end of the month, I had no desire for headphones. When the train got too loud, I would put them on just to cancel the screeching sounds of the metal wheels. But when it got calmer, off they came, and I was ready for the next drama. Now I’m excited for spontaneous comedy to pepper my commute and give me unexpected pick-ups throughout my day.
My friends complain about how people rarely approach each other in London. During my no-headphones experiment, there have been some headlines for me, too: I got asked out on the streets as well as on the tube. Not that it led to anything romantic, but it wouldn’t have happened if I had my headphones on.

Press review: White House names AI czar as Greece, Germany seek Ukraine aid audit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. The latest threats from Vladimir Zelensky could provoke a tougher response from Russia, while the White House appoints an AI czar. Meanwhile, Greece and Germany call for an audit of assistance to Ukraine. These stories topped Monday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Zelensky’s decisions could doom Ukraine to tougher response from Russia
The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine were a direct result of recent statements from Vladimir Zelensky and his actions, Russian authorities explained. In particular, the Kiev regime has announced plans to attack Russian refineries again and plans to acquire the FP-9 missile, which is capable of reaching Moscow. In response, the Russian Armed Forces will increase strikes targeting "military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kiev and other Ukrainian regions," the Russian Defense Ministry warned. The Russian Foreign Ministry said the goal would be to deprive Zelensky of the ability to escalate the conflict or harm the Russian economy. Meanwhile, the United States has taken a wait-and-see approach before the congressional elections.
Since the EU itself is unable to meet all Kiev's demands for increased financial assistance, the issue of seizing frozen Russian assets is being raised once again, Fernand Kartheiser, a member of the European Parliament from Luxembourg, told Izvestia. "All this indicates that the EU's policy regarding Ukraine is untenable even in the medium term, for Ukraine is a money pit. Voters in EU countries will never agree to further cuts in spending on social needs and other important budget items in order to continue to channel funds into this `black hole’ - Ukraine," the MEP said.
Disagreement about the forms, sequence and pace of support for Ukraine persists in Europe. A number of EU countries, for example, have refused to expedite the allocation of funds from a €90 billion loan for Kiev. This increases the likelihood of individual countries acting through bilateral agreements with Kiev, said Ivan Loshkarev, associate professor at the Department of Political Theory at MGIMO University. Apart from Germany, Nordic countries, primarily Sweden and France, may take a more proactive position. The latest escalation by Kiev is also meant to demonstrate that Russia is also suffering losses from the conflict, Loshkarev emphasized. This will probably allow Ukraine to demonstrate some fragmented progress in its attempts to delay peace. Zelensky rather views the idea of launching talks as an undesirable scenario that will again raise questions about the prospects of his tenure as president, the political scientist noted, and his term of office expired back in May 2024.
Zelensky’s calls to escalate the conflict further pose a direct security threat to which Moscow could respond with tough and exhausting military-technical measures, experts interviewed by Izvestia argued. According to them, today, Russia has a major arsenal of high-precision weapons enabling it to immediately increase the intensity and pace of combined attacks on key enemy targets.
Russia’s retaliatory measures are long-term and systemic, military expert Vasily Dandykin emphasized, with the list of targets also expanding. The West and Kiev should not expect to protract the conflict for another 18 to 24 months, for their defense capacities are designed for a much shorter period, so experts expect radical changes on the front line within the next few months already.
Kommersant: White House installs new authority to mitigate AI risks
US President Donald Trump has decided to appoint National Intelligence chief Jay Clayton as AI czar. A Clayton-led working group will have to present a report on the risks and potential of advanced AI technology within the next 120 days and recommendations to the government regarding potential regulation in this sphere. Russian President Vladimir Putin last week called imposing limits on the use of AI technology in security an existential issue facing humanity. However, neither the US nor Russia is currently ready to place major limits on their AI potential in defense.
Artificial Intelligence was among the key topics discussed at a recent summit between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington. The two leaders agreed to launch a regular interdepartmental dialogue on AI, including a separate communication channel for emergency discussions of major incidents related to the uncontrollable behavior of AI systems. However, no restrictions on the development of AI technology were discussed as there is fierce competition between the US and China in this sphere, and neither of them intends to hold its potential in check for the time being.
However, neither the US nor Russia is seemingly ready for outside-imposed restrictions. The Washington Post reported recently, citing sources, that the two countries’ delegations succeeded in having the requirement that AI-based systems must operate predictably and reliably removed from a document currently being drafted as they joined efforts at a UN debate. The clause made the consideration of ethical factors in using lethal autonomous systems and the stipulation requiring human verification of military targets selected by AI algorithms prior to a strike mandatory.
Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities, a US-based think tank, who took part in the latest meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, called the approaches of both Washington and Moscow quite logical in an interview with Kommersant. The US decision to refrain from imposing restrictions on AI stems from the fact that it views AI as a sphere of advantage over China, she explained. It is reluctant to restrict itself in order to prevent China from catching up with it, she noted. Meanwhile, Russia is facing different threats, mostly amid the continued Ukraine conflict and rearmament in Europe. In both cases, the benefits of using AI can help offset the disadvantages faced by Russia, the expert added. Against this backdrop, Kavanagh said, it is logical that both the US and Russia are seeking to avoid committing themselves to restricting what they view as their areas of advantage.
As Kommersant reported earlier, the only actual restriction lately agreed by P5 or the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, namely, Russia, the US, China, France and Britain, is that the decision to use nuclear weapons amid the widespread adoption of AI technology, including in the military and military-nuclear sphere, will always be made by humans. Even though the P5 members have not issued joint statements on this matter, they have expressed individual views on the subject.
Izvestia: Greece, Germany demand audit for assistance to Ukraine
The opposition in Germany and Greece is calling for an audit of how the financial and military aid delivered to Kiev has been used, Izvestia has learned. According to them, the money ends up in the pockets of Ukrainian officials, while the weapons are resold to other countries. Berlin has been a main donor, and Greece has Patriot interceptor missiles needed by the Ukrainian army.
Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kiev on an unannounced visit with a pledge of another €1.3 billion in support. Experts believe that due to corruption scandals in Kiev, control over the use of European funding will be tightened further.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party could establish committees at the next Bundestag to investigate the use of financial and military aid transferred to Ukraine, Steffen Kotre, a member of the German parliament from AfD, told Izvestia. "It is well known that money from Germany and other countries ends up in the pockets of corrupt Ukrainian politicians. It is also known that weapons intended for Ukraine have surfaced in Serbia and other countries. As soon as the AfD enters the new Bundestag with 25% support or more, investigative committees will surely be established that will deal with these issues," Kotre announced.
In Greece, the Greek Solution parliamentary faction made a similar demand to audit weapons supplies to Kiev, its leader Kyriakos Velopoulos told Izvestia. "Any military supply to Ukraine is tantamount to high treason. <...> We will give every bullet sent to Zelensky a check, holding everyone who has harmed the Greek economy, Greece’s national interests or Greek defense capabilities responsible," he warned.
According to Yegor Sergeyev, a senior researcher at the Institute of International Studies of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), a German audit will be more dangerous for Kiev. Berlin is not only one of its main donors, but it can also influence broader EU decisions. Control over the use of financial aid could be somewhat tightened, he said. However, the financial flow from Europe will not stop completely as the EU needs Ukraine mostly as a political instrument, he argued.
European countries are increasingly discussing audits of the use of resources supplied to Kiev even as this idea has not materialized anywhere yet. This would require political changes that may happen very soon, with a parliamentary election expected in Greece next year as France will elect a new president, while the German parliament could possibly be dissolved ahead of time.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: India, Pakistan balancing on the brink of war
There is a dangerous tension in relations between India and Pakistan. Two people were killed near the Bedian strategic border sector. India blamed the incident on Pakistani saboteurs or Islamist terrorists, while Pakistan claimed that locals who had lost their way there were to blame. The incident took place in an area disputed by the two countries over the use of the Indus River. However, there is no information on whether the October 2 shooting was somehow related to that dispute.
Islamabad and New Delhi again accused each other of an armed provocation as envoys were summoned to the two countries’ foreign ministries. Pakistan claimed that Indian border guards had opened fire on three unarmed Pakistani civilians, killing two of them and injuring one. India rejected these accusations as biased and groundless. The Indian Foreign Ministry told the Pakistani charge d’affaires that the Pakistani side had continued to send terrorists and drug traffickers across the border.
On the face of it, India has an advantage over its long-time opponent: it has a larger Army, and Pakistan is embroiled in a conflict with Afghanistan. The actual situation is more complicated. India, which has traditionally pursued the policy of non-alignment, has no close military allies. True, it is a member of QUAD, a US-led alliance with Japan and Australia, but the United States has shown no desire to get involved in the dispute between India and Pakistan.
Meanwhile, Pakistan, for one, has a close military partner, if not a true ally - China, formally a neutral party. However, Beijing has actually provided military assistance to Pakistan, Alexander Lukin, academic director of the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia at the Russian Academy of Science, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "As usual, China says disputes should be resolved in line with UN decisions. And it actually supports Pakistan which has signed a strategic partnership with China. The two countries maintain broad contacts, including military ones. China has established an `economic corridor’ toward the Indian Ocean on Pakistani soil. This corridor runs through a Pakistani-controlled area of Kashmir. However, India considers the whole of Kashmir to be its part. Consequently, the territorial conflict is in effect trilateral, given China controls an area in Kashmir under the 1963 agreement with Pakistan regarding border demarcation. Since India regards all of Kashmir as its own land, it does not recognize this agreement between Pakistan and China. In short, while China is formally neutral, in reality, it sides with Pakistan," Lukin concluded.
Vedomosti: Russian coal prices at Baltic ports reach three-year high
In September, export prices of Russian coal at Baltic ports rose to a more than three-year high, according to data from PBS Index, seen by Vedomosti. On September 25, Free-on-Board (FOB) prices of thermal coal with a calorific value of 6,000 kcal/kg at Baltic ports climbed to $89/metric ton. The last time a higher price was recorded was in April 2023. The prices increased by 13% last month, or were up 31% from January.
The rise in export prices is driven by the increased cost of coal on the global market, high demand in Turkey, and rising dry-bulk freight rates resulting from the reorientation of shipments from terminals in the country's south to Baltic ports, a PBS Index representative explained to Vedomosti.
Active purchases by China and the risk of reduced exports from Indonesia are also driving up the export price of Russian coal, said Yegor Vershinin, an analyst at the Finam financial group. Another factor behind the rise is the escalating political crisis in the Middle East, which has affected global energy prices, Boris Krasnozhenov, Head of Investment and Sector Analysis at Alfa-Bank, added.
Rising gas prices globally will help sustain demand for coal at least until the end of this year, therefore Russian fuel export prices will continue to increase, Alexander Kotov, a partner in consulting at NEFT Research, argued. According to him, thermal coal prices at Baltic ports will rise to $100/metric ton, given favorable market conditions.

Omega Has New Bond Watches Even if There Isn’t a New James Bond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

It's been five years since James Bond was on the silver screen in No Time to Die. For fans of the secret agent, the wait has been arduous, made even harder by the fact that Amazon, which now owns the franchise, still hasn't chosen a successor to Daniel Craig, let alone started filming Bond's resurrection.
But if it's seemed like a long haul for fans, just think how it has felt for Omega, which counts on a steady stream of Bond action to regularly inject lots of lovely cash into the company via watch releases linked directly to the films. Omega's last official Bond film tie-in watch was the titanium No Time to Die Seamaster prematurely launched back in 2019, ahead of the film’s then Covid-delayed release in 2021.
Considering that Swatch Group’s net profit collapsed by almost 90 percent to $32 million in 2025 (though, thankfully, things look rosier so far this year), we shouldn't be surprised that Omega isn't bothering to wait for Jeff Bezos to put his white cat down and proceed with world domination. As there's no new Bond or Bond film to work with, Omega has decided to launch 007-themed watches anyway—not just one, but an entire collection totaling six Seamaster Divers.
You can hardly blame the brand. When Omega first strapped a Seamaster to Pierce Brosnan's wrist in 1995's GoldenEye, it reportedly saw a 20-fold sales increase. In 2012, Omega's then-president Stephen Urquhart even told Variety that Omega’s sales “look like a stock market chart” that peaks during promotion of Bond films, then sinks afterward. “The films have had a very marked influence on sales,” Urquhart conceded.
The new “James Bond and Spectre” collection is themed around good and evil, with three watches bearing the “007” symbol of James Bond, and three the octopus-like motif of Spectre, the fictional global terrorist organization in the series.
The six Seamaster Diver 300M watches share the same movement. However, the two non-limited stainless-steel editions are the core pieces, available individually at $8,600 each—one with a blue aluminum dial dedicated to James Bond, and the other black for dastardly Spectre fans. Both come on a brushed mesh bracelet.
The James Bond edition has a grade 5 titanium bezel, while the Spectre edition boasts a black ceramic bezel ring to match the dial's blackened grained finish.
The remaining four Seamasters are split across two limited-edition numbered sets—one dedicated to Bond, the other to Spectre—capped at 77 boxes each. At a cool $89,800 per pair (Omega won't sell them individually), you get one stainless-steel model on a brushed mesh bracelet, and a second in platinum-gold on leather.
Each set comes in a presentation box with an additional NATO strap, strap-changing tool, cuff links, a cord bracelet, a loupe, a leather travel pouch and card holder, and papers. In the James Bond set, the strap keepers are engraved with 007; in the Spectre set, the strap keepers carry the Spectre emblem.
This collection is not the first time Omega has sought to leverage its Bond connection without a film peg. Back in May of this year, Omega unveiled the Seamaster Diver 300M Chronograph “007 First Light,” a new 44-mm chrono tied to 007 First Light, a James Bond game developed by the same studio responsible for the Hitman franchise. Originally designed as an in-game gadget, Omega turned it into a production model.
Back in 2012, there was the Seamaster James Bond 007 50th Anniversary watch with a red number 50 on the bezel. In 2019, there was an On Her Majesty's Secret Service edition Seamaster to mark 50 years of the 1969 film, limited to 7,007 pieces. Then, in 2022, Omega released a Seamaster to coincide with 60 years of Bond movies.
