Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Environmental groups and climate experts are challenging the Danish government’s claim that it has demonstrated a path to meeting its 2035 climate target.
Climate Minister Samira Nawa has said the government considers the path to an 85% emissions reduction by 2035 to be demonstrated, even though current measures are projected to deliver only an 80% reduction.
“It is demonstrated because there is enough time to make the decisions, and because there is enough time to handle the risks that may arise on the way towards 2035,” Nawa said.
Greenpeace and green think tank Concito argue that this differs from how the term has previously been used in Danish climate policy.
“That is stretching the definition of demonstrated,” Concito chief economist Torsten Hasforth said.
Greenpeace political campaign lead Christian Fromberg said additional policy would be needed before the target could be considered demonstrated.
“Of course, that target has not been demonstrated yet. That will require new policy,” he said.
The Climate Council has previously assessed possible pathways toward an 85% reduction target, while stressing that reaching a higher target would require additional measures beyond policies already adopted.
The government has proposed an 85% target for 2035, which would go beyond Denmark’s current 2030 target of a 70% reduction.
Enhedslisten climate spokesperson Rasmus Vestergaard Madsen also said the final 5 percentage points still needed to be backed by concrete measures.

Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.

Danish prisons are more overcrowded than ever, with 4,650 inmates currently held in facilities designed for 4,300 people, according to Fængselsforbundet, the Danish prison officers’ union.
The average occupancy rate has reached a record 105.4%, up from 102.7% last year.
Overcrowding means prisons have to create additional capacity by installing bunk beds in cells or converting hobby rooms, visiting rooms and offices into accommodation.
Vejle Arrest, a remand prison, has recorded an average occupancy rate of 135% this year.

Half of the increased penalties for violence and rape came into force in February, while further increases are due to take effect in January.

Denmark’s cyber hotline will remain open until midnight in the coming days following unauthorized access to 8.8 million records in the national CPR system.
The hotline will operate from 8 a.m. to midnight. It normally closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays, the Agency for Societal Security said.
The hotline advises residents and businesses on digital security, fraud and cyberattacks. It can also help people whose identities have been misused.
Residents with a specific suspicion that their CPR number is being used fraudulently can receive help creating a credit warning.
A credit warning alerts companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving loans or credit, making financial identity theft more difficult.
Authorities detected irregular activity in the CPR system on October 2.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information during September.
The records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority, said automated searches appeared intended to identify valid CPR numbers.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating. Authorities have not identified those responsible.
Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates urged residents to remain vigilant.
Authorities advised people never to provide passwords or other confidential information to unsolicited callers or message senders.

Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.
The affected records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.

Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.

The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”
EU countries to discuss coordinated response to rising fuel prices after US pressure
European Union countries will meet Friday to discuss a coordinated response to rising fuel prices, a European Commission spokesperson said, according to AFP.
The meeting follows pressure from the United States for Europe to help increase diesel supplies and lower prices.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News he was “very confident” that Europe would cooperate.
“Now is the time for a coordinated release of diesel stocks,” Wright said, citing the coming harvest and winter seasons.
The US government particularly wants France and Germany to release diesel from strategic reserves, AFP reported.
Washington has also threatened to ban diesel exports if European countries do not act, three unnamed sources told Reuters.
Europe has become more dependent on fuel imports from the United States since it banned Russian fuel following the invasion of Ukraine. The war involving the United States, Israel and Iran has also disrupted supplies from the Middle East.
US President Donald Trump has considered an export ban to reduce American fuel prices before the November midterm elections.
However, Trump said Wednesday that such a ban could instead push prices higher.
The average US diesel price has reached $6.39 per gallon, equal to about 42.52 DKK. A gallon is approximately 3.7 liters.
Diesel cost an average of $3.70 per gallon one year ago, according to AFP.

Legislation for departure centers outside the EU is now in place, says Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov
European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.
Bødskov said the five countries had made progress during talks Thursday morning.
EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.
Bødskov said Spain partly contributed to the situation by offering legal residence to undocumented migrants. Spain originally expected about 500,000 applications, but more than 1.1 million people applied by the June 30 deadline, according to Euronews.
He said the EU remained vulnerable to sudden large arrivals and needed stronger external borders.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Danish prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and temporary nightlife ban for a 31-year-old Danish man accused of punching a 32-year-old Swedish man who died three days later.
The incident occurred around 8:45 p.m. on June 30 during a public screening of the football World Cup at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen.
According to the indictment, the defendant stood on a bench and threw two beer cans toward a group, hitting one person. He then allegedly punched the Swedish man on the left side of his head or neck.
The victim fell and suffered a ruptured artery. He died on July 3.
The defendant is charged under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence. Prosecutors also cited Section 247 because he has previous convictions for crimes endangering others, including attempted murder.
That provision can increase a sentence by up to half.
A prosecutor previously said the Danish man could face eight to 10 months in prison. The indictment does not specify the requested sentence.
The nightlife ban would prevent him from entering bars and designated nightlife areas between midnight and 5 a.m. for a set period.
The trial begins October 7 at Copenhagen City Court. The defendant has been held since early July and denies guilt. His identity is protected by a court order.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Green groups challenge government claim that 2035 climate target is on track
Environmental groups and climate experts are challenging the Danish government’s claim that it has demonstrated a path to meeting its 2035 climate target.
Climate Minister Samira Nawa has said the government considers the path to an 85% emissions reduction by 2035 to be demonstrated, even though current measures are projected to deliver only an 80% reduction.
“It is demonstrated because there is enough time to make the decisions, and because there is enough time to handle the risks that may arise on the way towards 2035,” Nawa said.
Greenpeace and green think tank Concito argue that this differs from how the term has previously been used in Danish climate policy.
“That is stretching the definition of demonstrated,” Concito chief economist Torsten Hasforth said.
Greenpeace political campaign lead Christian Fromberg said additional policy would be needed before the target could be considered demonstrated.
“Of course, that target has not been demonstrated yet. That will require new policy,” he said.
The Climate Council has previously assessed possible pathways toward an 85% reduction target, while stressing that reaching a higher target would require additional measures beyond policies already adopted.
The government has proposed an 85% target for 2035, which would go beyond Denmark’s current 2030 target of a 70% reduction.
Enhedslisten climate spokesperson Rasmus Vestergaard Madsen also said the final 5 percentage points still needed to be backed by concrete measures.
4 years on, Danish-Greenland history projects unveiled
More than four years after Denmark and Greenland agreed to examine their historical relationship, researchers have presented the first four subprojects in the investigation.
The projects will focus on adoptions, people who were legally registered without a father, school and language policies, and settlement and working conditions, Greenlandic broadcaster KNR reported.
“We are beginning with four important projects, which each shed light on concrete decisions and their consequences,” research leader Tenna Jensen said in a press release cited by KNR.
The Danish government and Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, agreed to launch the investigation in June 2022.
The decision came after reporting by Danish broadcaster DR on the so-called IUD case, in which thousands of Greenlandic women and girls had contraceptive devices fitted without their knowledge or consent.
The investigation will examine major decisions and events since World War II and their consequences for Greenland’s population. Its stated purpose is to provide a basis for reconciliation with the past.
Possible areas of research mentioned earlier included the closure of Greenlandic settlements, adoptions and Greenlandic children sent to Denmark.
The investigation is based at Ilisimatusarfik, the University of Greenland, and citizens are expected to be involved in the work.
Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.

Danish prisons reach record overcrowding as inmate numbers exceed capacity
Danish prisons are more overcrowded than ever, with 4,650 inmates currently held in facilities designed for 4,300 people, according to Fængselsforbundet, the Danish prison officers’ union.
The average occupancy rate has reached a record 105.4%, up from 102.7% last year.
Overcrowding means prisons have to create additional capacity by installing bunk beds in cells or converting hobby rooms, visiting rooms and offices into accommodation.
Vejle Arrest, a remand prison, has recorded an average occupancy rate of 135% this year.
Jan Bruun, a union representative at the prison, said the situation is putting pressure on the facility as cells fall increasingly into disrepair.
“We spend a lot of time finding room for inmates, swapping around when a double cell does not work between two inmates, and moving again when some have letter and visiting controls lifted,” he said in the union’s statement.
Hillerød Arrest has had an occupancy rate of 140% in recent months, placing additional demands on staff. At Randers Arrest, occupancy has averaged 115% this year, with the local union representative reporting more conflicts among inmates.
The pressure could increase further as tougher sentences introduced under Denmark’s penal reform take effect.
Half of the increased penalties for violence and rape came into force in February, while further increases are due to take effect in January.

Three politicians facing criminal charges have been elected to Latvia’s 15th Saeima, and once their mandates are approved, parliament will have to decide whether to consent to the continuation of criminal proceedings against them, LETA has found.
The Saeima Rules of Procedure state that parliament’s consent is also required for the continuation of criminal proceedings in cases where criminal prosecution began before the mandate of a Saeima member was approved.
The Rules of Procedure also stipulate that an MP who has committed a criminal offence is considered expelled from the Saeima from the day a conviction enters into force.
Ainārs Šlesers (LPV), a current Riga City Council member who has been elected to the Saeima, is charged in the so-called second digital television criminal case. Several other people have also been charged in the case, including former Prime Minister Andris Šķēle.
The Supreme Court previously overturned an acquittal handed down by Riga Regional Court in the criminal case and sent the case back to Riga Regional Court for a new hearing.
Rūdolfs Brēmanis (SV/AJ), another current Riga City Council member elected to the Saeima, is accused of defrauding and embezzling 102,721 euros
 belonging to the Latvian state during his diplomatic career. The case is still before a court of first instance.
Former Rēzekne mayor Aleksandrs Bartaševičs (Together for Latvia/LPV), who has also been elected to parliament, is facing charges in two separate criminal cases.
The prosecutor’s office recently referred a case to Latgale District Court in which Bartaševičs is accused of exceeding his official authority during the implementation of a recreation centre project in Rēzekne.
Meanwhile, Vidzeme District Court in Gulbene is hearing another criminal case in which Bartaševičs is accused of disclosing restricted-access information and of deliberately failing for 16 years to declare information about property acquired abroad and other substantial income in his public official declarations.

Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:57:01 UTC
18:57:01 KST

Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country.
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.
“We have to start from the border and win from the first battles,” Kundla said, explaining that the move will help the army to fight with a posture of "active defense," allowing immediate return strikes on targets deeper in Russian territory in the event of an invasion.
Although Moscow has failed to achieve any of its strategic aims in almost five years of full-scale war against Ukraine, Russia's war has led many countries on NATO's eastern flank to amp up defense spending and reassess military doctrine, as the nature of warfare itself has undergone a paradigm shift.
In recent years, the Trump administration's open questioning both of the United States' status as Europe's security guarantor, and of Article 5 itself, has unnerved NATO members on the eastern flank.
In 2026, Estonia announced a record 42% increase in defense spending, reaching 2.4 billion euro ($2.69 billion), or around 5.4% of the small country's GDP.
With the extra spending also came procurement of new weapons systems, including U.S.- and South Korean-built rocket systems that could strike St. Petersburg.
“We are in the process of changing everything,” said a military policy official at Estonia’s defense ministry quoted by the Financial Times.
“The reality is that the [Estonian defense planning] has been the same for the last 10 years. But Russia is already planning to double its forces across our border.”

Overnight, a “Geran” missile struck a grain silo in a settlement in the Sedniv community of the Chernihiv district. The fire was extinguished, Chaus added.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 30 in the Chernihiv region, a Russian UAV struck a facility in Novhorod-Siverskyi. Two civilian men were injured and taken to the hospital.

After years of displacement, Syrian Christians return home as children go back to schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:56:09 UTC
18:56:09 KST

After years of displacement, Syrian Christians return home as children go back to schools
Christian schools resume role after some were seized by former regime, others used as shelters for displaced families
Ahmet Karaahmet, Hisam Sabanlioglu and Lina Altawell
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
IDLIB, Syria / ISTANBUL
‘The school was renovated over nearly two years and is now ready to resume education,’ Father Lucas Bashrafa tells Anadolu
Christian schools in Syria are resuming their educational role after years of disruption, as families displaced by the war return to their hometowns following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime.
Some of the schools had been seized by the former regime, while others were transformed into shelters for people displaced from their homes by bombardment and security crackdowns.
Children from Christian families returning to their communities have also begun re-enrolling in schools where they studied before years of displacement interrupted their education.
Christian clergy members say the reopening of the schools can help restore their role in promoting peaceful coexistence, education and development, while expressing hope for a Syria where freedoms and rights are protected.
‘Rights returned to their owners’
Father Lucas Bashrafa, priest of the church in Qunaya village in the Idlib countryside, said the village school belongs to the Franciscan friars and has resumed its role after years of closure.
“Rights have returned to their owners. The school was renovated over nearly two years and is now ready to resume education,” Bashrafa told Anadolu.
“The school was seized by Syria’s now-dissolved Baath Party in 1971, placing the building under the control of the former regime,” he said.
During the years of war, the building was turned into a shelter for displaced people forced to flee their communities because of bombardment by the former regime’s forces in Idlib and its countryside, he said, adding that it remained in use as a shelter for 10 years.
“I hope the school will once again become a center for peaceful coexistence, education and development,” Bashrafa said.
“The fundamental mission of the Franciscan friars in the region is to promote love and peace among people and villages,” he said.
“The school had previously been an important educational center for residents of surrounding villages,” he added.
“Some of the teachers who are teaching at the school today were once students here,” Bashrafa said.
He expressed hope that Syria would return to days “when education, development, freedom and rights are protected and restored to their owners.”
“We thank God for this blessing and for this new step in our lives,” he added.
Qunaya was among several Christian villages that experienced widespread displacement during the war waged by the Assad regime from 2011 to 2024.
Around 20,000 people lived in the predominantly Christian villages of Ghassaniyeh, Yacoubiyah, Jdeideh and Qunaya in western Idlib before the war began.
Between 2013 and 2015, amid some of the harshest years of the conflict, intensive bombardment by former regime forces and accompanying clashes forced most residents to flee, reducing the remaining Christian population to around 500.
Students return to classrooms
Hanna Jalf, a student from Qunaya, told Anadolu that she and her family fled to the central city of Hama after the war began before returning to their village following the fall of the former regime.
She said she resumed her education after returning home.
“I studied ninth grade here and passed. I got a good result and moved on to 10th grade,” she said.
Jalf said conditions in Qunaya are good now and encouraged other families who have not yet returned to come back to their homes.
Syria’s new government is also working to rehabilitate Christian schools across the country to restore their educational role.
Last month, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh announced the reopening of the Holy Land School in the Jisr al-Shughur area of Idlib countryside after it had been closed for nearly 60 years.
“This scene is part of the Syria we dreamed of … a Syria for all its people,” Saleh said at the time.
The reopening was part of a series of school openings in Idlib province amid efforts to rehabilitate educational infrastructure in the country.
On Dec. 8, 2024, Syrian opposition forces entered Damascus and announced the overthrow of Assad’s regime, ending his rule from 2000 to 2024. Assad had inherited power from his father, Hafez Assad, who ruled from 1970 to 2000.

Geran-4 Gets Russian Engine and New Navigation System — DIU

09:54:56 UTC
18:54:56 KST

Russia’s Geran-4 jet-powered drone has received a locally produced engine and a new optical navigation system.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine reported this on the War&Sanctions portal.
Russian forces began using an upgraded version of this UAV in the fall of this year.
A new MOKH module based on the high-precision PNI5GA magneto-inductive sensor manufactured by U.S. company PNI Sensor has been integrated into the Geran-4 design.
The sensor operates together with the SADRA inertial module, reducing gyroscope drift and improving the accuracy of autonomous navigation.
In addition to satellite and inertial navigation, the enemy has added the Susanin electro-optical correlation system.
It compares images from an optical sensor with a reference image stored in the computer’s memory to adjust the route from the launch point to the target.
Instead of the Chinese Telefly TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, Russians installed a locally produced equivalent manufactured in Alabuga.
According to Oboronka, engines assembled in Russia undergo additional testing and modifications due to poor manufacturing quality in China. Among the debris, investigators found a turbocharger impeller with Russian markings and drilled holes for weight balancing. Such modifications reduce the centrifugal force acting on the component at high rotational speeds and lower vibrations that can lead to engine failure.
To effectively strike bridge structures and power transmission line towers, the enemy has equipped the drone with a new KRSN shaped-charge cutting warhead.
The remaining electronic modules and components of the UAV remain identical to those used in previous versions of the Geran drones.
The Geran-4 jet-powered attack UAV features a flying-wing aerodynamic configuration and is designed to strike targets at medium and long ranges. The fuselage is approximately 3 meters long, the wingspan exceeds 2.5 meters, and the launch weight is estimated at 200–250 kg, with a warhead weighing up to 50 kg.
The drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that enables it to reach a flight speed of 400–500 km/h and provides an effective range of 400–600 km. Its onboard control system combines satellite navigation, an inertial module, a magnetometric unit, and an electro-optical correction system for autonomous guidance to the target.

Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:54:19 UTC
18:54:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
As Iran and the US take tentative steps towards a deal to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, there may be signs that Tehran's biggest source of leverage is being eroded.
Iran has long viewed its ability to paralyse the strategic chokepoint as its own version of a nuclear bomb, a Trump card which, if used, could trigger a global energy crisis of historic proportions.
Immediately after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) did just that, moving decisively to block the strait and trapping a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas inside the region.
But its ability to apply the thumbscrews to the global economy has been threatened in recent weeks as the US military facilitates covert oil shipments through the strait and Arab producers reconfigure export routes.
More oil is now leaving the region than at any point during the seven-month war, weakening Tehran's hand as it tries to negotiate permanent control over the strait.
Arab oil exports are rebounding
Middle Eastern crude exports excluding Iran returned to pre-war levels in September despite Iran and its allies escalating attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure.
Estimates by data tracking platform Kpler indicate that Arab countries shipped at least 16.5 million barrels of oil out of the region per day during the month.
Much of the rise was powered by Saudi Arabia, which responded to the attack on its Red Sea pipeline last month by surging exports through the strait.
Shipping data tracked by Bloomberg shows that the kingdom's Hormuz shipments rose to more than three million barrels per day in the first three weeks of September, more than triple the amount in August.
Exports through Hormuz have slowly ticked up since June, when the Pentagon launched a coordinated effort to get energy supplies onto the global market. Backed by US air cover, Gulf states have snuck millions of barrels of oil through the narrow stretch of water by using shadow fleets to evade Iranian fire.
The US attempt to prise open the waterway has dovetailed with moves by Arab states to find new ways of getting their oil out of the region. Saudi Arabia has re-routed its crude to the Red Sea via its East-West Pipeline while the UAE has relied on its terminal at Fujairah on the other side of the strait. Iraq has trucked millions of barrels of oil across the Syrian desert to the Mediterranean.
"Iran appears to have lost significant leverage over the Strait of Hormuz," said Ria Reddy, Iran team deputy lead at the American Enterprise Institute's Critical Threats Project.
"If commercial vessels can continue to transit the strait at high rates despite Iranian threats, Iran has less ability to use the strait to compel the US and other states to accept its demands," she told The New Arab.
The rise in Arab oil exports isn't the only way in which Tehran's control has slipped. The US blockade has turned the tables on Iran, trapping its oil in the region and depriving it of billions of dollars of vital revenues.
Dozens of its ships have been struck by US forces, in what the Trump administration has described as a "tanker for tanker" policy aimed at deterring IRGC attacks on maritime traffic.
Energy crunch continues
With no end in sight to the war, the millions of barrels of oil now making their way out of the region have had little impact on global prices, which continue to be influenced by heightened geopolitical risk and spiralling freight rates.
The unlocking of Hormuz has coincided with a 57% surge in the price of Brent, which peaked at $110 in mid-September following the Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Neither has it helped to curb shortages of fuels such as gasoline and diesel, whose prices have surged to record highs due to ongoing bottlenecks at refineries worldwide.
The US-led effort also appears not to have had the same success with raising gas shipments from Qatar, which remain far below pre-war levels. Last month, gas prices in Europe and Asia climbed to their highest levels since 2022 amid supply fears ahead of the winter.
All of this means that Iran continues to have a large say over the trajectory of the global economy, despite millions of barrels of crude now transiting the strait every day.
"Resumed oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz is not synonymous with stabilisation," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
"Iran still retains the capability to resume retaliatory drone and missile strikes on Gulf critical infrastructure and oil production sites," she said.
Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), said that although the US has weakened Iran's control of the strait, it has so far failed to achieve its overarching goal of stabilising the global energy market.
"Iran retains the ability to target tankers, threaten commercial shipping, and make passage through the strait increasingly difficult and expensive," he said.
"As a result, Washington's operational achievements have yet to produce the economic outcome it ultimately needs. Oil prices remain elevated, in part because of higher insurance premiums, tanker shortages, and the continuing risk to commercial shipping."
Tanker war
Iran's sporadic attacks on ships have prevented a normalisation of maritime traffic in the strait, keeping freight rates at record highs, extending the freeze in the insurance market, and maintaining pressure on oil prices.
September saw a notable uptick in attacks on tankers, with 21 vessels confirmed hit by Iranian projectiles, up from 12 the month before, according to data collected by conflict monitor ACLED.
"September has seen the largest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial ships since March, when the war was at its peak," Valentin d'Hauthuille, ACLED's Middle East regional team lead, told The New Arab.
Washington has for the moment gained the upper hand in the strait, but Iran's continued ability to threaten ships raises questions about the long-term viability of its escort operation, he said.
That said, the US's destruction of its coastal radars and surveillance systems is making it increasingly hard for it to use them. There are signs that the damage is forcing it to resort to cruder means of disrupting maritime traffic.
"Iran appears to have adopted less effective methods of tracking and attacking vessels, including the use of fast attack craft to visually identify targets and shore-based rocket launchers to deploy mines," the Critical Threats Project's Reddy said.
"These adaptations suggest that Iran faces greater difficulty identifying, targeting and consistently disrupting shipping at scale."
Widening the battlefield
Iran's say over the future of the strait extends beyond what happens in its immediate neighbourhood to other parts of the region, where its allies have been able to further tighten global energy markets.
Oil and gas prices spiked last month after Houthi forces and Iraqi paramilitaries mounted a one-two punch on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea exports, in the same day taking over the Bab al-Mandeb strait and disabling Aramco's East-West oil pipeline.
Since the ceasefire in Yemen collapsed in July, the group has struck several refineries on the kingdom's Red Sea coast and closed the chokepoint to Saudi-linked ships.
However, horizontal escalation has had limited success for the Axis of Resistance, with Arab producers proving resilient to these multi-pronged attacks and swiftly finding new export routes when one is closed down.
Oil traders may have been spooked by September's attack on the Saudi pipeline, but, in the end, it made little impact on the kingdom's ability to export. Aramco was able to quickly divert flows to Hormuz and brought the pipeline back online in only two weeks.
It also involves a degree of risk which Iran has thus far not been willing to fully take on. Iran has refrained from targeting the UAE since signing the ill-fated peace deal in June, allowing shipments to Fujairah to continue. Neither has it tried to disrupt Iraq's overland shipping route through Syria, a move which would only anger Baghdad and risk pushing it further into America's orbit.
War of attrition
Despite the intense US bombing campaign, the IRGC is believed to still possess thousands of drones and a sizeable missile inventory. There are also signs that China is shipping components to Iran's military to help it maintain production lines and replenish its stockpiles.
This means that, unless there is an end to the war or the US can accomplish the unlikely feat of fully destroying its offensive capabilities, Iran will likely be able to disrupt shipping for many months to come.
The sustainability of the US's operation is less certain. It may be succeeding in getting more oil through the strait at the moment, but it remains an open question about how long it can keep this up.
Months of deployment are putting US forces under increasing strain, with commanders recently warning that continuing the war is unsustainable. Missile interceptor stockpiles are dangerously low, naval forces are fatigued, and the concentration of assets in the region is harming the military's readiness elsewhere around the world.
Moreover, the cost of the operation is currently running at around $2 billion every month, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The Pentagon has put the total cost of the war at more than $45 billion up to the middle of September - and that's without factoring in the costs of replenishing missile inventories and repairing the damage at US bases.
Despite this, the Pentagon appears to be preparing to resume the full-scale war following November's midterm election, last week dispatching another carrier strike group and up to 10,000 additional troops to the region.
The Trump administration is hoping that economic pressure will push Tehran into accepting its conditions for an agreement and recently renewed its attempts to collapse Iran's economy.
The new wave of sanctions dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, together with the naval blockade, has piled more pressure on Iran's economy, sending inflation surging to 73% year-on-year in September and the Iranian rial plunging to a record low of 2.7 million to the dollar.
Meanwhile, the economy shrank more than 10% year-on-year between 21 March and 20 June, while the vital oil and gas sector contracted more than 26%.
RUSI's Ozcelik said that, while large portions of the Iranian public appear to be backing the government's twin calls for resilience and resistance, that may change in the coming months as the economic crisis continues to intensify.
"Tehran may find it harder to convince large segments of the public that they are winning the war and that resistance against the US is worth the heavy toll on the cost of living, hyperinflation, and shrinking economic opportunities," she said.
Matthew Hoare is a journalist at The New Arab
Follow him on X: @matt_h_9

Oil exports from the Middle East, excluding Iran, exceeded their pre-war average last week, Kpler data showed, as pipelines helped bypass the Strait of Hormuz despite continued attacks on shipping.
Despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil exports from the Middle East Gulf region, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. The recovery followed changes to the region’s export routes.
"At least 16.5 mbd (million barrels a day) left the region between 1 and 28 September, matching the pre-war average excluding Iran. That is 10.5 mbd above March's monthly average," said the firm.
However, 40% of those exports now bypass the Strait of Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, with pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates providing key alternative routes. Most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore.
The figures cover crude oil and condensate.
The export figures include shipments via the Red Sea, which exporters increasingly use to bypass Iran’s attempted blockade of Hormuz. Around a fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed through the strait before the conflict.
Oil prices remain well above their pre-war levels. International benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery traded at $102.25 a barrel on Monday morning, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded at $90.50 a barrel.
Brent futures were around $72 before the war. The disruption to shipping through the strait has sent shock waves through the global economy, prompting countries to scramble for alternatives and sending fuel prices soaring.
Iran continues to claim control over the waterway, and ships travelling without its authorisation risk attack. Nevertheless, more vessels are getting through, while alternative routes are operating at full capacity.
Despite the recovery in exports, experts warned that conditions remained far from normal. A US blockade of Iranian ports continues to restrict a large share of Iran’s own oil exports.
Saudi Arabia has benefited from the reopening of its East–West pipeline, which connects its main oil fields in the east to the Red Sea terminal at Yanbu, bypassing Hormuz.
The pipeline shut down on 11 September after strikes launched from Iraq and resumed operations on 22 September, Kpler analyst Amena Bakr said last week.
The UAE also has a route around Hormuz through its pipeline linking Abu Dhabi’s oil fields to Fujairah, a terminal on the Gulf of Oman outside the strait.
The recovery in exports comes as the seven core members of OPEC+, which comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, including Russia, agreed on Sunday to leave their production targets unchanged for November, in line with expectations.
The seven countries produced about 25 million barrels of crude oil a day in August, up 630,000 barrels a day from July, according to OPEC’s September report.

Eurozone business activity grows at fastest pace in 41 months in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:53:03 UTC
18:53:03 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Eurozone private sector activity expanded at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years in September, with the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) rising to a 41-month high, S&P Global said on Monday.
The final composite PMI output index climbed to 53.1 from 52.0 in August, while the services business activity index increased to a 10-month high of 53.0 from 51.6.
Readings above 50 indicate expansion, while those below that threshold signal contraction.
Output growth accelerated across both manufacturing and services, rounding off a robust third quarter as demand improved and employment increased.
All five countries covered by the composite survey recorded growth for the first time since November. Spain led the expansion, followed by Ireland, while Germany’s upturn accelerated. Italy and France registered more modest growth.
New orders increased at their fastest pace in 41 months, supported by the strongest rise in orders from foreign clients in more than 4 1/2 years.
Outstanding work increased for the first time since June 2022, prompting companies to hire additional staff, although employment growth remained marginal.
“The collective signal from the PMI surveys is one of GDP growing at a 0.4% quarterly rate, with momentum accelerating as we head into the fourth quarter,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
He said IT-related services showed particularly strong growth, supported by artificial intelligence investments, while consumer-oriented services remained resilient despite higher energy prices.
Inflationary pressures also intensified, with input costs and selling prices rising at their fastest rates since May. Services firms increased their charges at the sharpest pace since February 2024.
“A renewed upturn in price pressures signalled by the survey meanwhile hints at eurozone inflation running closer to 4% than the ECB’s (European Central Bank's) 2% target,” Williamson said.
Combined with accelerating growth, the figures would fuel speculation about more aggressive monetary policy tightening, he added.

Kuwait strips 415 of citizenship, including billionaire

Breadcrumb
Kuwait strips hundreds more of citizenship under six new decrees, including billionaire businessman
Kuwait has issued six decrees revoking the citizenship of 415 people, including prominent billionaire businessman Mahmoud Haider, as well as those who obtained nationality through them as dependants.
According to the decrees published in Kuwait's official gazette, citizenship certificates were withdrawn from six people and their dependants under Article 21 bis (A) of the 1959 Kuwaiti Nationality Law and its subsequent amendments.
A second decree revoked the citizenship of 286 people and their dependants, while a third stripped 14 people of their nationality.
A fourth decree revoked the citizenship of 25 people and their dependants, while a fifth affected another 41 people. A sixth decree stripped a further 43 people and their dependants of Kuwaiti nationality.
Kuwait began its nationality review campaign in 2024, saying it aimed to tackle fraudulent citizenship claims, including cases involving dual nationality or citizenship acquired through marriage. Kuwaiti law also allows nationality to be revoked on grounds of national interest and state security, provisions that rights organisations say have been applied broadly and with little public explanation.
The campaign has expanded significantly this year, with citizenship revoked from politicians, footballers, musicians and other public figures, including 1982 World Cup goalkeeper Ahmed al-Tarabulsi, singer Abdulmohsen Al Muhanna and composer Yousef Al Muhanna.
Rights groups estimate that at least 50,000 people have lost their Kuwaiti citizenship since 2024, warning that the campaign has raised growing concerns about due process, transparency and the risk of statelessness.

Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:52:07 UTC
18:52:07 KST

The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain.
Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.
The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists.
In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off.
Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more.
“Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said.
The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly.
Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse.
Further work by the pair revealed that when the genetic instructions for one of the proteins were inserted into human or mouse kidney cells, those cells became light sensitive.
Deisseroth took the discovery even further, using rats to demonstrate that by introducing the gene for a channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, it was possible to produce electrical signals in them using light.
He and his colleagues later applied the approach to nerve cells in the motor cortex of the brains of mice, allowing them to use light – delivered by tiny optic fibres passed through their skull – to trigger movement in the rodent’s whiskers.
Subsequent work in mice showed the approach could also be used to investigate which networks of nerve cells were involved in the formation of particular memories, including fear.
While rooted in basic science, the team’s work has already had real-world implications, opening up a field of medicine known as optogenetic therapy.
In one trial it was used to partially restore the sight of a man who went blind as a result of retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that results in damage to light-sensitive cells in the retina.
In that case, the genetic instructions for making a channelrhodopsin were delivered by means of a harmless virus into retinal ganglion cells in the man’s eyes.
He was then kitted out with light-stimulating goggles that captured pictures of the world around him and converted them into single-wavelength images that were projected on to his retina using pulses of light.
Prof Botond Roska, the director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel who co-led the study, welcomed the announcement of the Nobel laureates.
“This is truly wonderful news. I hope this helps to boost all efforts on optogenetic vision restoration to bring back vision to blind patients,” he said.
Anna Wedell, a professor at Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology or medicine, said the laureates’ work had provided new possibilities to map which cells were responsible for which functions, and which cells communicated with each other, opening up a new understanding of the function of the brain.
“We’ve had anatomical maps and correlations, but now we have a tool that can provide cause-and-effect relationships so we can get a functional map of the brain, exactly pinpoint which cells do what, which cells are responsible for creating behaviours or even emotions and memories in the brain,” she said.
Wedell said that by studying animals to understand how a normal, healthy brain worked, it was then possible to explore what happened when thing went wrong – for example in the case of diseases such as dementia, epilepsy and addiction.
“By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in the mouse, we can also understand where to look in the human,” she said.

Student protests continued across France on Monday, with classes fully or partially suspended at between 400 and 500 high schools amid demonstrations over education conditions and a rise in related incidents, according to broadcaster BFMTV.

The Interior Ministry and Education Ministry have reported a significant rise in arrests and injuries since the mobilisation began.
Authorities said around 5,000 people had been arrested since the start of the movement, about 85 percent of them minors in the Ile-de-France region.
Twenty-four schools have been “burned or ransacked,” while 78 Education Ministry staff members and around 600 police officers and gendarmes have been injured, according to the education minister.
The minister also said 170 students had been injured since the protests began.
Five investigations have been opened by France’s General Inspectorate of the National Police into incidents linked to the mobilisation.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is seeking to ease the crisis by putting forward five proposals and has called for decisions to be reached before the end of October.

Japanese leader calls woman's murder, allegedly by U.S. Marine in Okinawa, "heinous crime" as outrage spreads
