Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving incidents by U.S. personnel have long sparked protests on the island, which bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of U.S. military facilities in Japan. 
The new case involves Lance Cpl.     Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station in Okinawa, who was arrested on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
A patrolling police officer then found a 20-year-old man, later identified as Ballard, who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. The officer asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.
His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told lawmakers the government has lodged a strong protest with the United States, urging its "full cooperation with the investigation" and "strict discipline among U.S. military personnel."
"The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said.
Emotions run high
Around 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, holding up placards stating their "strong protest" against the murder, Japanese media reported.
Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organized a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman's death.
"We couldn't protect her. That made me so angry and sad," the university student told AFP, adding that she was planning to organize another protest in front of the U.S. Embassy for Tuesday evening.
"I want to ask them — what are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by their own?"
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that "the government will work with the United States to thoroughly make sure there will be no recurrence, and reduce burdens on local residents."
News of the Marine's arrest immediately prompted Japan's foreign affairs and defense ministers to summon senior U.S. officials to convey their "extreme disappointment" and "lodge strong protests," Kihara said.
The incident came just a few weeks after Okinawa elected Genta Koja as its new governor, ending the eight-year rule of his predecessor, who had long pushed for a major U.S. military base to be moved off the island.
Koja, 42, accepts a central government plan to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but to move it to a less populated location.
Calling the murder-robbery "extremely malicious in nature," Koja told reporters on Sunday it had "hugely shocked residents here who are forced to live side-by-side with the bases, and instilled new fear in them."
"I am infuriated," Koja said.
He said the incident showed U.S. efforts to "educate soldiers and improve their behavior have not been functioning at all."
Koja said he will travel to Tokyo "soon" to lodge a protest with top government officials, including Takaichi.
On Monday, U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass said on social media that he is telling U.S. military commanders this week they need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity." He also said that he and Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan.
There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

'Form 6 has not been approved by us': What SC said on EC's SIR decision - top quotes

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to pass order on plea seeking suspension of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations that he took decisions on the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls without the consensus of the two other election commissioners.A bench led by CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also issued notice to the Centre, Election Commission of India and its three commissioners on a plea that alleged that the powers vested in the poll panel as a multi-member constitutional body were being exercised without following the collective decision-making mechanism mandated by law.The bench also rejected the poll body's claim that the top court had upheld the declaration attached to Form 6, making it clear that it had not approved any modification to the form.
What the top court said
Justice Suryakant said that any modification of Form 6 - the application citizens use to register as new electors - had not been approved by the top court. “Any modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When record is produced, we would like to see who has modified. But, your prayers appear jumbled up,” the CJI said.
The top court said that the transaction of business within the poll panel “has to be unanimous” and if it finds that certain decisions were taken by CEC without the required unanimity, it could reconsider or recall those decisions. “They are expected to take unanimous decisions. If there is no unanimity, it has to be by majority. If records show some decision was not unanimous, etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra vires. Can we ex parte come to a decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner.”
“Let's first have authenticated information on that. We can always annul any decision,” the bench added.
“We presume that decisions are taken by Election Commission as per law,” the court said.
What is the controversy
A report by the Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that some were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
The report said the poll panel's software added a requirement for ancestral details and a link to the previous SIR in Form 6, the voter registration form, without the legal amendment required under election rules.
The poll panel however rejected the charges and said changes in the form were upheld by the Supreme Court . "The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used," it had said.The poll panel had also said that differences of opinion are normal in institutional deliberations and maintained that all its orders are legally valid and follow the prescribed procedures.

His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Eyal Zamir ordered a halt to all training exercises involving grenade throwing in built-up areas until the investigation was completed.

How to select, clean, and store fresh button mushrooms safely
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:48:34 EEST
18:48:34 KST

How to select, clean, and store fresh button mushrooms safely
Kyiv • UNN
Fresh button mushrooms should be firm, dry, and free of spots and unpleasant odors. Store them in a paper bag in the refrigerator for 3–5 days.
Champignons are often used for soups, salads, pizza, sauces, and other dishes; however, before cooking, the mushrooms need to be properly prepared. UNN explains in more detail what to look for when buying champignons and how to prepare them for cooking.
How to choose fresh champignons
First of all, you should inspect the mushrooms. Fresh champignons should be firm, dense, and uniform in color, with white or cream-colored caps. Also pay attention to the mushroom’s surface — if it has become shiny or slimy, or is covered with a sticky coating, it is better to avoid such mushrooms. You should also not buy champignons if they have dark, yellow, or black spots. Another important detail is the stem: its cut should be fresh, not dark and dried out. The smell is also important, as fresh champignons have a characteristic mushroom aroma. However, if they smell musty, rotten, chemical-like, or damp like a basement, it is better not to eat them.
How to clean champignons before cooking
Before cooking, champignons should be inspected and any remaining soil or other dirt should be removed. If the mushrooms are small, young, and almost clean, it is not necessary to peel them. Instead, it is enough to wipe the cap and stem with a clean napkin or brush, and cut off the bottom part of the stem, where particles of soil may remain.
Large champignons can, if necessary, also be cleaned of the thin skin on the cap and any dirt on the stem. If the mushrooms are heavily soiled, they can be cut into several pieces to make it easier to inspect the surface and remove the soil.
For quick cleaning, you can also use flour: place the champignons in a deep bowl or saucepan, sprinkle them with several spoonfuls of flour, cover the container, and carefully shake it. After that, the mushrooms should be wiped with a clean napkin, and some of the dirt should come off together with the flour.
If only a small amount of soil remains on the mushroom’s surface, you can simply wipe the champignons with a clean napkin instead of washing them.
Do champignons need to be washed?
Champignons should not be left in water for a long time, as they quickly absorb moisture, which can make the mushrooms watery and affect their texture and, consequently, their taste during cooking. If the mushrooms need to be washed, they can be quickly rinsed under cold running water. After that, the champignons should immediately be placed on a paper towel and dried.
How to store champignons
Fresh mushrooms are recommended to be kept in the refrigerator. A paper bag is suitable for storage, as it helps prevent excess moisture. Fresh champignons should not be left for too long after purchase. They should be used within 3–5 days.
Before cooking, the mushrooms should be inspected once again. If their smell, color, surface, or firmness has changed during storage, such champignons should not be eaten.

carry-over effect for 2026 stands at 0.8%.

final national consumption and gross fixed capital formation
grew by 0.2%," Istat said.

contribution of 0.2 percentage points to GDP growth, entirely
attributable to the performance of final consumption expenditure
of households and non profit institutions serving households.

percentage points, offset by an equally large negative
contribution from net foreign demand.

agriculture, forestry and fishing and in industry, by 0.1% and

🔴 Nobel Prize in Medicine jointly awarded to ​Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann ​and Georg Nagel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:47:22 UTC
18:47:22 KST

Nobel Prize in Medicine jointly awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel
The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.
Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based at universities in Germany and the United States.
The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method “is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries”.
The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Wurzburg in Germany.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobel week.
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

MPs actively use AI to submit spam amendments to 2026 budget draft – committee chair
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:44:29 EEST
18:44:29 KST

Technological development, especially artificial intelligence (AI), is one of the reasons for the surge in amendments to the state budget draft, posing a challenge compounded by the traditional submission of expenditure-increasing amendments without specified funding sources, Budget Committee Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Roksolana Pidlasa stated in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
"While previously MPs' assistants spent days and nights writing these spam amendments, like increasing or decreasing every single line in Appendix 3 of the state budget by UAH 1, now an AI like Claude or Gemini can write 2,000 amendments in 3 minutes," Pidlasa said.
She recalled that the trend toward an increasing number of amendments to the government's draft state budget has been growing in recent years, with a 19-year record broken previously at 3,339 amendments.
"I think there could be even more this year. Technological development is strongly facilitating the submission of amendments," the committee chair said.
According to her, AI-generated amendments are indistinguishable from those written by humans, whereas these amendments must still be processed by actual people rather than artificial intelligence.
Pidlasa stated that the use of AI has not led deputies to search for realistic sources of additional revenues to balance proposals for increased expenditures.
"This year is the same as always: deputies have many ideas on how to spend money, but not very many on where to get that money, and even fewer of those ideas are realistic. Many amendments regarding additional expenditures are submitted without any coverage sources. Or it is written that 'coverage will come from increased VAT revenues next year.' But how that increase in VAT revenues will happen remains unknown to anyone," the Budget Committee Chair said.

Ethiopian troops retake regional capital from rebels (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:43:30 UTC
18:43:30 KST

Ethiopian troops retake regional capital from rebels (VIDEO)
Ethiopian government forces and allied fighters have retaken the capital of the northern Tigray region, which rebels seized less than two weeks ago.
Fighters from the pro-government Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) announced in a post on Facebook on Sunday that they had “completely taken control” of Mekelle.
Footage shared by the TPF and dated October 3 shows armed men in military uniforms and vans moving through the streets, with horns sounding as people cheer. The forces entered the city center on Saturday afternoon, followed by federal troops, Reuters reported, citing a source close to the militia.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which governs the region, acknowledged its retreat in a statement posted on Facebook. It said the regional administration “has decided to temporarily leave Mekelle and operate from another location, while our forces continue carrying out their military operations.”
Residents reported looting of government offices during the withdrawal, while internet and cellphone disruptions have hampered verification of developments, AP reported.
Federal troops also recovered Mekelle’s airport, which TPLF fighters seized on September 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the city and two other Tigrayan destinations.
The East African country has struggled to secure lasting stability since an African Union-mediated peace agreement signed in November 2022 ended the two-year Tigray war, which killed hundreds of thousands. The conflict grew out of a power struggle between the federal government and the TPLF, whose decades of dominance in national politics ended when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018. Disputes over disarmament, territory, and the return of displaced people remain unresolved.
The latest escalation followed the formation of an opposition alliance between the TPLF and six other armed groups, including former battlefield enemies, seeking to oust Abiy. On September 24, the Ethiopian National Defense Force said it had killed 272 TPLF fighters and wounded another 260 in a counteroffensive. Tigray’s regional authorities said their troops entered a “defensive battle” after federal forces attacked them with aircraft, drones, and artillery.
The fighting has also deepened a regional diplomatic crisis, with Ethiopia accusing Egypt, Eritrea, and Sudan of supporting the rebels. All three deny the allegations. Ethiopia announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats on Thursday, citing Asmara’s “direct and indirect acts of hostility.” Eritrea responded by severing ties, claiming Addis Ababa was plotting to take its ports and backing Eritrean opposition groups to pursue regime change. Addis Ababa also ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave within 48 hours. Cairo retaliated by giving an Ethiopian Embassy counselor the same deadline.

====================================================================================================

UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:43:22 UTC
18:43:22 KST

The UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals.
It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely. Brussels believes the UK would have to introduce tariffs to create a level playing field to qualify for inclusion in the scheme and match the tariffs of up to 45% it has levied on Chinese cars since October 2024.
Imposing tariffs on Chinese cars would probably prompt a hostile response from Beijing and test Andy Burnham’s desire for a reset in the post-Brexit relationship with the EU.
It would also involve a lengthy World Trade Organization process. It took the EU 13 months between the launch of the investigation into state subsidies in production and transport lines and finally imposing tariffs in October 2024.
The UK has been lobbying hard to be included in the legislation, which will require manufacturers to procure components from the continent to protect against the growing presence of China in supply chains, particularly the auto and chemicals sector.
A government source pointed to comments from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, last week, saying tariffs on Chinese EVs were “always kept … under close review”.
If tariffs were to be imposed, the move would be a break with the previous government policy. Keir Starmer’s government positioned itself as a strong ally to China, viewing it as an important source of economic growth rather than a risk to British manufacturing.
The UK has consistently argued it does not need trade barriers in the way Brussels does because it does not have the huge trade deficit – now running at more than £1bn (€1.18bn) a day – that the EU is struggling to contain.
China’s increasing trade with the EU – not only in finished products such as cars but also in components – is causing deep concern about cannibalisation of native industries in European capitals. The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, is visiting Beijing this Wednesday for talks over a reset in trade relations.
Experts said last week the UK car industry faced a “difficult trade-off”, with Chinese investment a potential “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
However, Nissan’s chair in Europe, Massimiliano Messina, recently said Europe “cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market” through imports via Great Britain.
Nissan is in talks with the Chinese company Chery to manufacture cars in its Sunderland plant, but this would still align with the EU’s Made in Europe policy.
The EU views Chinese manufacturers based in Europe, employing EU staff, as less of a threat to its indigenous industries. Chinese brands made by BYD in Hungary, for example, will not be subject to import duties.
Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said any consideration of tariffs needed to be based on “robust evidence” and maintain a rules-based open and competitive market, adding: “Trade restrictions can have unintended consequences. 
“The immediate priority is a pragmatic agreement recognising the UK as a trusted ‘Made in Europe’ partner as the exclusion of UK-built vehicles would severely damage both our highly integrated industries, jeopardising the €80bn trading relationship.”
Brands such as BYD, Leapmotor and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to the latest industry figures.
BYD has almost doubled its share of the UK market in September 2026 compared with September 2025, with 5.75% of the market, according to figures from the SMMT released on Monday.
In the year to date, BYD’s share has gone up from 2.2% to 3.93%, with 68,000 BYD cars sold up to the end of September, closing in on BMW, which shifted 91,000.
Jaecoo’s share has rocketed, increasing by 223%, with 58,000 new cars sold in the year so far, while Leapmotor sales have soared by a phenomenal 765% – up from about 1,500 cars sold in 2025 to more than 13,000 in the year so far.
A UK government spokesperson said: “We have not put tariffs on Chinese EVs. We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”

Commander-in-Chief Drapatyi moves away from predecessor Syrskyi's micromanagement – UP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:43:00 EEST
18:43:00 KST

Commander-in-Chief Drapatyi moves away from predecessor Syrskyi's micromanagement – UP
Mykhailo Drapatyi, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, has chosen to move away from the micromanagement practised by his predecessor Oleksandr Syrskyi, opting instead to decentralise command.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda article (English translation to be available soon)
Quote: "The first word brigade and corps commanders use to describe the first few months of Drapatyi's tenure is 'freedom'. Unlike his predecessor, who would tell some brigade commanders how and where to fight – even specifying the coordinates where a position should be set up – Drapatyi has chosen a different approach. He has opted to decentralise command, moving away from the 'micromanagement' that has already become widely known to the public."
Details: Ukrainska Pravda understands that the commander-in-chief no longer commands troops directly but does so through the troop groupings of the relevant operational commands, in line with the military chain of command. This means that soldiers receive their orders from their immediate commanders.
After taking office, Drapatyi also somewhat reorganised the system of troop groupings. In particular, he disbanded the Skhid (East) Grouping of Forces, commanded by Viktor Nikoliuk – presumably because he was dissatisfied with Nikoliuk's performance – and merged Dmytro Voloshyn's Kursk Grouping of Forces into Mykhailo Shandar's Pivnich (North) Grouping of Forces.
There are now six troop groupings operating across the entire front: Pivnich (North), Pivden (South), Zakhid (West), the Joint Forces Grouping, and two recently established by Drapatyi – Centre, commanded by Andrii Biletskyi, and Azov, commanded by Denys Prokopenko.
Ukrainska Pravda sources say the move away from hands-on management of brigades and corps has brought another change: Drapatyi no longer spends several hours every day hearing reports from all commanders, as Syrskyi did.
"Syrskyi would hear reports from everyone every day and could give specific instructions on how to respond to developments, including where troops should advance… Drapatyi doesn't do that; that's the job of the troop grouping commanders. Drapatyi focuses on strategic and systemic issues. And when commanders do speak to the commander-in-chief, he isn't interested in a standard report on 'what happened', but in statistics, analysing problems and finding solutions – in other words, what conditions need to be created for a particular commander to accomplish their mission. And that's the right approach," a senior military officer told Ukrainska Pravda.

Head of German intelligence warns of the threat of an "armed conflict" with Russia
Kyiv • UNN
BND chief Martin Jäger said there is a real threat of an armed conflict between Germany and Russia. The intelligence service sees no signs of a large-scale attack on NATO.
The President of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Martin Jaeger, considers the threat of a military confrontation between Germany and Russia to be real. Die Welt reports this, UNN writes.
Details
"The confrontation in which we are engaged with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous quality: Germany is at risk of being drawn into an armed conflict with Russia," Jaeger said on Monday during an open hearing of the Bundestag’s Parliamentary Oversight Committee.
According to Jaeger, Russian intelligence services are operating "highly professionally and ruthlessly." "The threat of attacks on targets in Germany remains real and current. We must counter it."
As an example of this escalation, he cited an attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, for which Berlin blamed Russia.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany. We did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on us, seeing us as its main adversary. Because we do not accept Russia’s revisionist, expansionist policy and its aggressive war against Ukraine," Jaeger said.
According to the official, the Russian leadership seeks "to ensure for the future that political decisions directed against Moscow are not made in Berlin or other European capitals." This results in "increasingly aggressive actions by Russian intelligence services" against Germany and other states.
"Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war cannot be described using traditional military or legal categories. We are not in a state of defense, yet we are still under attack—that is precisely what a shadow war is," the official said.
"Russia seeks to undermine Europe’s political support for Ukraine. We must be prepared for attempts at intimidation and further interference. Nuclear threats will likely be heard again," the head of the BND added.
However, according to Jaeger, at present the intelligence agency sees no signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory. Nevertheless, "Russian military action on a limited scale" is possible, particularly in the Baltic states, the head of Germany’s intelligence service уточнив.

The world must call on Iran to release Zeynab Jalalian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:41:39 UTC
18:41:39 KST

Breadcrumb
The world must call on Iran to release Zeynab Jalalian
Imagine that you criticise the government and are arrested for it. You end up in prison not for a day, a month, or even a year. You are in prison for 18 years, and you do not know if you will ever be released. You are deemed too dangerous because you are not broken, and you are not famous enough to garner the public attention that would force the regime to let you go.
In 1982, the same year that I was arrested in Iran, a girl was born in a small village in West Azerbaijan Province. Her family called her Zeynab, and she became a women’s rights activist. In 2008, aged 27, while visiting a girls’ high school to talk about International Women’s Day, she was arrested. She was subsequently tortured and sentenced to execution for “enmity against God”.
Zeynab Jalalian and I belong to two different generations of Iranian women who fight against misogynistic laws. I did not reveal the names and addresses of friends who criticised the regime. So I was tortured severely and sentenced to death. My father’s unrelenting fight was what changed my fate.
Zeynab’s death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment in 2011. During her imprisonment, she has not been given any leave and has only been permitted a small number of visits from her family.
Writing to her mother a few years ago, Zeynab depicted the torture she was forced to endure:
My pen is unable to describe my pain and distress. They blindfolded me, tore off my clothes, chained me to an iron bed and lashed my feet with a cable. My feet became black and swollen under torture. Eventually, I felt nothing. My entire body became numb. Under torture, I held my beliefs and my hope for women who are struggling for a better future. How can I witness the execution of my friends and say nothing? They are asking me to confess to wrongdoing in order to receive medical treatment. How can I regret struggling against them?
Many prisoners died behind bars because they did not receive medical treatment. When my stomach bled, I was told that they would take me to hospital if I signed a letter of repentance. This is a different kind of execution.
Despite her life sentence, she is denied any peace in her cell, and her health has deteriorated due to the torture inflicted on her.
Zeynab was permitted fibroid embolisation surgery after Redress Trust, a global organisation that supports survivors of torture, wrote an open letter in September 2025. However, she was not even allowed to recover in hospital and was sent back to prison the following day.
Her health is still of extreme concern, as she has asthma, pterygium, kidney disease, digestive problems, and she is currently at risk of losing her eyesight as a result of injuries from torture.
Since the US-Israel war on Iran
The war on Iran has made conditions worse for prisoners. While bombs were killing people and flattening essential infrastructure, prisoners have not received enough food and care due to a lack of personnel.
Furthermore, activists who have had nothing to do with the war, and who were imprisoned years before the attacks started, have been executed for the crime of being Israeli or American spies. In reality, the regime has always weaponised the accusation of activists serving as informants for Western countries in order to repress and silence them.
Indeed, the war on Iran has only made the regime stronger than ever before. This leaves many of us asking what this will mean for those who have been trying to topple it for the past 47 years.
This war has been waged against the people of Iran and its prisoners.
The negotiations between the US and the Islamic Republic demonstrated where all the interests lie: oil and resources, not the innocent lives and well-being of Iranian citizens. American forces are certainly not pressing the demands that Iran’s prisoners should be released and that the death sentence should be cancelled.
Throughout the war, I was worried that prisons would be bombed again; after all, Israel already targeted Evin Prison, where many were killed. The victims were locked up by one regime and murdered in their cells by another.
Resilience despite everything
Yet despite all that has taken place in recent years, Iran’s prisoners haven’t lost their resilience.
The ‘No to Execution’ movement began on 30 January 2024 at Ghezel Hesar prison. Death row inmates released a statement condemning the rise in executions, revealing that they faced imminent death without a fair trial or adequate legal representation. To urgently rally public support and awareness, they pledged to begin a hunger strike every Tuesday, a day associated with the transfer of inmates to solitary confinement before execution.
Over 2100 people were hanged in 2025. Iran’s regime is the leading executioner in the world per capita. But even as the regime continues to escalate its executions, over 62 prisons across the country are taking part in the hunger strike.
Zeynab also joined the strike and kept going, even after she was made to pay a heavy price. 18 years behind bars have not stopped her from speaking out about those oppressed and killed at the hands of brutal regimes, including the cases of Verisheh Moradi and Pakhshan Azizi, both women activists who were sentenced to death for supporting the Mahsa Amini protests. Jalalian asked the world not to be silent.
Now it is our turn to stand up for Zeynab, and help secure her release. That includes all the Western intellectuals who ignorantly echoed the regime’s so-called anti-imperialist slogans. After all, if anyone knows about the impact of imperialism, it is certainly Zeynab.
Her case risks being forgotten on the global stage; it is our duty to keep raising her name and story, and to pressure the regime at every opportunity. We have seen how the Islamic Republic has released prisoners following vocal campaigning and solidarity, so we know an act as simple as speaking up about Zeynab Jalalian can impact change.
We must #FreeZainabJalalian.
Nasrin Parvaz is an activist and author. Her works include ‘One Woman's Struggle in Iran, A Prison Memoir’ (Award-Winner in the Women’s Issues category of the 2019 International Book Awards), and ‘The Secret Letters from X to A’. Nasrin has also written for The Guardian, The Morning Star, and Huck magazine, among others.

Japan has no plans for a new release from its petroleum reserves following a G7 agreement to coordinate a 100-million barrel drawdown, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said.
In a post on US social media company X, Takaichi said Japan had already been releasing supplies from its reserves and would not undertake additional release measures on this occasion.
Her remarks followed an emergency virtual G7 meeting held on Oct. 2 amid surging diesel prices.
Takaichi said the discussions focused particularly on responses to diesel prices in Europe, the US and elsewhere against the backdrop of delays in European strategic reserve releases.
France, which holds the G7 presidency, convened the meeting at short notice and permitted representatives to attend on behalf of leaders, she said.

Takaichi also said she understood that British Prime Minister Keir Starmer was represented by a proxy, while European Council President Antonio Costa was absent.
Japan would continue working to support global economic stability, energy security and markets, she added.
According to the G7’s joint statement, the coordinated release through the International Energy Agency will begin immediately and run for four months, including a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by members and partners.
The group also pledged to coordinate refinery maintenance, temporarily increase utilization where feasible and refrain from restricting energy exports between G7 countries.

Yemeni forces reclaim Dhubab, key positions near Bab al-Mandeb from Houthis

Saudi Arabia says three people wounded in attacks on southern airports
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority confirms 3 wounded in attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near Yemen border.
Saudi Arabia’s civilian aviation authority has said at least three people were wounded in attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemen border, as fighting with Yemen’s Houthis rages.
“The attacks resulted in three minor injuries and material damage,” the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on Tuesday.
Yemen’s Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), said late on Monday that their forces targeted sites across southern Saudi Arabia including airports and military sites.
Earlier on Monday, Yemen’s internationally recognised government said that its forces retook the strategic port city of Mocha and key positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait as they pursue a major counteroffensive against the Houthis.
The Saudi-backed government’s military said that a “strategic offensive” has also been launched on Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, which the Houthis have held since 2014.
The Houthis denied that Mocha had fallen.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the battlefield claims.
In a post on X, the Yemeni government’s military said it took control of Mocha after “fierce fighting with the Houthis” and that battles there resulted in several Houthi casualties.
The Saudi-led military coalition backing the government also said on Monday that it had begun an air campaign against the Houthis.
The coalition’s spokesman, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said 100 fighter jets were supporting Yemeni government forces and that the coalition had secured “air protection” over Bab al-Mandeb. Hundreds of Houthi targets were destroyed, he added.
Houthis dismiss response
Earlier on Monday, Yemeni government forces said they had reclaimed control of the Taiz governorate’s Dhubab district and key positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, as they seek to oust the Iran-aligned Houthis from control of the strategic waterway – a key route for global energy supplies.
The government-aligned Saba news agency reported that “forces from the Homeland Shield Forces and the Giants Brigades” were involved in the fighting in Dhubab.
“During the operation, they advanced and seized important positions – cutting off supply lines and roads leading to Bab al-Mandeb,” an unnamed army source told Saba.
Government forces are “continuing to comb and secure the liberated areas and cut off supply routes to the Houthi terrorist militia”, Saba reported.
The Houthis have dismissed the claims, with the group’s deputy governor of Taiz, Fuad Sinan, issuing a video statement from Mocha city on Monday evening.
“We are currently roaming around in the streets of Mocha city… negating any reports in the media about the occupation of Mocha city,” Sinan said in the video statement shared by Houthi officials on social media.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said that amid the conflicting claims, “what we do know for sure is that intense fighting is currently occurring in the south of Bab al-Mandeb, and also near the city of Taiz”.
He added, “We have to wait and see how the news is going to unfold in the coming hours so we can confirm 100 percent who’s in control.”
The Houthis have also claimed an attack on the King Khalid International airport in Riyadh and the Aramco refinery in coastal Rabigh. The group also said it hit a series of sites, including an airport, an airbase and other critical locations.
There was no confirmation from Riyadh on the Houthi claim.
‘Turning point’
The fighting is the latest turn in a conflict that has widened amid the United States and Israel’s war on Iran and Tehran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis relaunched hostilities against the Saudi-backed government and, in a rapid offensive in mid-September, they seized Mocha as well as islands and territory around Bab al-Mandeb.
The advance choked off a second major oil passageway.
Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines.
On Sunday, Rashad al-Alimi, the chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced the start of operations to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory.
Hisham al-Omeisy, a senior Yemen researcher at the European Institute of Peace, told Al Jazeera that a lot of observers were focused on the Red Sea “because that’s what basically triggers the attention of the international community because of the maritime routes”.
But, he said, “a turning point would be for the Yemeni government to take territories in the heartland, in the centre of the country; places like Taiz, places like al-Bayda, places like Ibb.”
The claims over Mocha on Monday came as defence and foreign ministers from Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh and agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to Saudi Arabia to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures, within the framework of the Alliance, in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, said in a social media post.
He said the alliance had “reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries, in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom, and holy sites”.

New molecule restores memory in animals with Alzheimer's' disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:40:25 UTC
18:40:25 KST

The molecule RSQ-020 targets the Tau protein, which, when it folds incorrectly and forms clumps, is implicated in many severe neurodegenerative diseases.
A Greek research team led by Giorgos Skretas has developed an innovative pharmaceutical molecule that, in preclinical tests, restored learning and memory capacity in animal models with characteristics of Alzheimer’s disease.
The discovery is the result of collaboration between scientists at the Alexander Fleming Biomedical Sciences Research Centre, the National Hellenic Research Foundation and the spin-off company ResQ Biotech. The molecule, RSQ-020, acts by targeting the Tau protein which, when it folds abnormally and forms aggregates, is linked to the onset and progression of serious neurodegenerative disorders.
The development of RSQ-020 relied on a new technological platform created by the same research group. The method uses modified bacteria which can produce an enormous number of different candidate molecules while simultaneously indicating which of them have genuine biological activity. The aim is to pinpoint substances capable of repairing the malfunction of proteins that have lost their normal structure.
This approach differs markedly from the traditional route to drug discovery, said Giorgos Skretas, director of the Institute of Bioinnovation at the Alexander Fleming Biomedical Sciences Research Centre and collaborating researcher at the Institute of Chemical Biology of the National Hellenic Research Foundation.
According to him, classical drug development is based on finding a molecule that “fits” a specific protein target, like a key in a lock. However, the proteins involved in misfolding diseases do not have a stable shape but change constantly, which makes it particularly difficult to develop effective treatments.
“Instead of simply looking for a molecule that will bind to a specific site on the protein, we look directly for one that delivers the desired effect. Our technology allows us to see when a faulty protein is restored, because the bacteria we use emit a green signal when that happens,” the researcher said.
How it works in practice
In practical terms, the scientists inserted a human protein they are studying into a bacterium and programmed it to light up only when this protein returns to a more normal state. At the same time, the same cells produce billions of different small molecules, each representing a potential solution to the misfolding problem.
When a bacterium emits light, this is a sign that it contains a molecule which has achieved the desired objective.
In this way, instead of relying on lengthy tests carried out exclusively under laboratory conditions, researchers can, within a short period of time, identify molecules that are already working inside living cells – an environment that more closely mirrors the real conditions of a human disease.
The technology was initially developed with a focus on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and the SOD1 protein, but its potential applications extend to many other neurodegenerative conditions. Protein misfolding is a common hallmark of diseases such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and other serious disorders of the nervous system.

﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? | Michael Jacobs

09:39:04 UTC
18:39:04 KST

Among the many crucial decisions Andy Burnham has to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year.
Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities.
The last time the UK chaired the forum was in 2009, when Gordon Brown presided over the rescue of the global economy after the financial crash. Before the London summit in April 2009, the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, had wrung his hands, saying that “none of us has a plan”. Barack Obama had a quick response to this: “Gordon has a plan.”
He did. Brown got the G20 to agree to a $5tn fiscal stimulus among its member states, increase International Monetary Fund lending to developing countries and create a new global coordinator for financial regulation, the Financial Stability Board.
But 2009 was a rare year for the G20, in that it actually achieved something. In general, the long communiques issued at its annual leaders’ summits reflect only the lowest-common-denominator agreement on broad principles. The G20 rarely commits its members to doing anything they were not planning to do anyway, and only occasionally makes genuinely collective decisions. One of the most consequential was the suspension of developing countries’ debt during the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the subsequent establishment of a “common framework” for debt treatment.
Indeed, for what is meant to be the effective executive committee of the global economy, the G20 is an oddly weak institution. Its 19 members (plus the EU and the African Union) have no HQ or staff and do not even have a standing website: if you want to know what the G20 has agreed over the past 20 years you need to go to a set of unofficial webpages hosted by some enterprising academics at the University of Toronto.
For most countries, hosting the G20 summit is a chance to impress its domestic audience by showing that its head of government bestrides the world stage. Last year Donald Trump boycotted it; the South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, was glad simply to get any kind of agreed communique. This year, the US is the host, with one of Trump’s own properties near Miami the summit venue in December: expect a show of personal and US power and very little attempt to achieve anything by way of multilateral cooperation.
But that makes Burnham’s task next year even more critical. The UK needs to show that it is still possible for the world’s leading nations – including the US and China – to work together to meet the key challenges facing the world.
So what should the UK’s presidency priorities be?
First, agreement on the need for, and a process towards, a global treaty on the regulation of artificial intelligence. After the recent alarm over the existential risks of AI, the UK has a chance to lead the world towards a global agreement on its control. Even if Trump is unwilling to sign up, getting the rest of the world to do so, seeking a form of global “technological security”, would be a vital achievement. A future US president might well wish to accede later.
Second, acknowledgment of the growing risk to food security and a plan to deal with it. The incoming “supersized” El Niño weather pattern is combining with the climate crisis, soil and biodiversity loss, and the impact of the war in the Middle East on diesel and fertiliser costs to create a perfect storm for the world’s food system. Agricultural yields are falling and food prices rising, leaving millions of people at risk of hunger. The G20 needs to act to prevent it.
Third, acknowledgment of accelerating climate insecurity – the severe risks posed by the climate emergency to all countries’ economies and societies – and agreement on coordinated measures to improve climate resilience. Though the Trump administration does not support emissions reduction, it does accept the need to adapt to climate change, and this year’s extreme weather events have impressed on all governments how urgent this is. The G20 should agree to provide more support to the most vulnerable countries.
Fourth, agreement on a debt restructuring programme for low- and middle-income economies whose debt – through no fault of their own, but because of rising global interest rates – has now become unsustainable. For too many countries the compounding of debt burdens with rising energy and food prices has made sustainable economic growth all but impossible.
What connects these issues is that all are global problems that can only be tackled through international cooperation. They each address aspects of national and global security – technological, food, climate and economic. Importantly, the first three address problems that are highly visible and politically salient to the British public, enabling the government to demonstrate how international action benefits people at home. (And the fourth represents a vital contribution to global economic growth.) And all have a good chance of being agreed in the G20, despite the conflicts and tensions that in other areas divide the world’s leaders.
G20 host countries always invent a slogan to express their presidency ambitions. In other contexts Burnham has said he wants to give people a sense of hope. That is something people all over the world need. For the G20 he might wish to try “national security through international cooperation”. It would not be a bad legacy to aim for.
- Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime minister

Yemen war: What’s the latest, as government forces claim advances?
After launching major military offensive to reclaim Houthi-held areas, Yemen’s government says it has retaken a key district.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has announced a major military campaign to retake all territory controlled by the Houthis, marking a new escalation in a civil war that had largely been frozen for several years before battles intensified in recent weeks.
The announcement by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of the Yemeni government, comes after weeks of heavy fighting and major Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important city of Taiz.
On Monday, Yemeni government forces said they were launching a “strategic” offensive on the country’s capital, Sanaa, which the Houthis have held since 2014.
Earlier in the day, the Yemeni forces — who are backed by Saudi Arabia — said they had regained control of the Dhubab district on the country’s west coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, though the Houthis denied the announcement. The Yemeni government later said it had also captured the port city of Mocha.
The fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic – and Yemeni government forces has expanded since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing more than 100,000 people since then.
Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid offensive that captured about 150km (93 miles) of Red Sea coastline and areas around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which is a critical route for international shipping.
On Monday, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally recognised government requested more support from the international community to defeat the Houthis, saying it is “in the world’s interest” for the country to be stable.
“We call upon our brothers, friends and the international community to support the Yemeni people, their state, and their national institutions in confronting the terrorist Houthi militia, which seizes their will by force of arms and lays waste to the lives of their sons – after exhausting all opportunities for de-escalation and peace,” Afrah al-Zouba said in a post on X.
So what is the latest on the fighting, and what does Yemen’s government hope to achieve?
What is the latest on the fighting?
The Yemeni government army said on Monday 1,747 Houthi fighters had been “neutralised” in 1,122 military operations in the Saada, al-Jawf and Taiz governorates and along Yemen’s western coast.
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the attacks targeted artillery and rocket positions, fortifications, supply lines, reinforcements and command centres.
Al-Nuzaili said warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers were involved and 364 military and logistical vehicles had been destroyed or disabled. The casualty and equipment figures could not be independently verified.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government also announced that its forces had taken control of Dhubab and Mocha on the Red Sea coast and were launching a major offensive on Sanaa.
Elsewhere, the front line in Marib governorate in northeastern Yemen witnessed an escalation in fighting on Monday.
A military source told Al Jazeera that government forces launched an attack on Houthi positions on the Raghwan front in the north of the governorate, coinciding with air raids on Houthi positions and reinforcements.
The source said the raids targeted Houthi positions near Mount Helan as well as an arms depot and military reinforcements northwest of Marib.
On Sunday, a Saudi-led coalition said its forces carried out 97 attacks against Houthi reinforcements around Taiz and the Tor al-Baha front using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
On the developments in Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau chief, Saeed Thabet, said Houthi operations in the rural areas around the strategic city are based on guerrilla tactics aimed at easing pressure on the coastal front and tightening the blockade of the road to Aden.
What has Yemen’s government announced?
Al-Alimi said on Sunday that government forces had been ordered to launch military operations to regain Houthi-controlled territory and restore state authority across Yemen.
“We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” al-Alimi said.
Military sources told the Reuters news agency that over the previous 48 hours, the Houthis advanced against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Taiz, pushing forward along the last remaining road linking the city with Aden on Yemen’s southern coast. The AFP news agency quoted four security sources as saying the Houthis had cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the Yemeni government’s interim capital.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen’s populous northwest since 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily the following year at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government but failed to dislodge the group.
A United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 brought years of relative calm before fighting intensified again this year. The latest round of fighting has focused heavily on the Red Sea coast and Taiz.
Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemeni defence analyst, said he believes the government and its allies face a formidable rival in the Houthis.
The missile arsenal of the Houthis, the precision of their drones and military “capabilities have grown” with support from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), he told Al Jazeera.
Having joined the US-Israel war on Iran on their own timeline, the Houthis have reinforced their place in Tehran’s “axis of resistance” and given the IRGC a way to shift pressure from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandeb in the Red Sea, he said.
What has Saudi Arabia said?
Saudi Arabia has pledged continued support for the internationally recognised government.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said Saudi Arabia and its allies would continue supporting Yemen until state institutions were restored and the Houthi threat to shipping in the southern Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb was ended.
Al-Maliki said Saudi Arabia had an “inherent right” to defend its sovereignty and take military measures to deter Houthi offensives, citing attacks in Riyadh, Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, Najran, Taif and Yanbu in recent weeks.

2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded for discoveries in optogenetics
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

18:38:16 KST

2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded for discoveries in optogenetics
Kyiv • UNN
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the prize for the discovery of light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." The Nobel Committee announced this on October 5, UNN reports.
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries that led to the development of optogenetics, which makes it possible to switch the activity of individual nerve cells on or off in the living brain. This method is now used in laboratories around the world to uncover the secrets of the brain
Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel — the 2026 medicine laureates — reportedly discovered the remarkable protein channelrhodopsin in single-celled algae.
"Hegemann wondered how Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, is able to swim toward a source of light. In the early 2000s, he and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, an algal protein with unique properties located on the cell surface. When illuminated with blue light, a channel opens in the protein. Charged ions then enter the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that regardless of which cell they inserted the protein into, those cells became light-sensitive," the statement said.
This year's Nobel Prize in Medicine laureate Karl Deisseroth, as noted, transformed the channelrhodopsin protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells.
Deisseroth introduced the channelrhodopsin gene into the nerve cells of rats. By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal. He published this discovery in 2005. Two years later, he made this light-controlled switch for nerve cells work in the brains of living mice.
The 2026 Nobel laureates in Physiology or Medicine have laid the foundation for a new era in neuroscience, the Nobel Committee emphasized.
"Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to identify neural circuits that control certain memories, feelings and behaviors associated with neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using this method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairments," the statement said.
"Optogenetics has fundamentally changed our understanding of how the brain works. Every day brings new discoveries that help unravel one of humanity's greatest mysteries: how our incredible brain works," the statement noted.
For reference
Nobel Week 2026 began on October 5 and will run until October 12. During it, laureates in six categories are announced.

As rising seas threaten low-lying Pacific Islands, regional leaders call on the world to take climate more seriously
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:37:00 UTC
18:37:00 KST

Pacific Islands urge world leaders to act on climate crisis
October 5, 2026
For Pacific islanders, the ocean is a source of food, livelihoods and cultural identity. But a changing climate is turning that lifeline into a threat, as rising global temperatures drive sea levels higher.
"When there's a low tide, you'll actually see foundations of homes, you see burial grounds of your ancestors...," said Anne Rasmussen, lead climate negotiator for the Association of Small Island States (AOSIS), adding that higher seas are making some land uninhabitable.
This week, a handful of world leaders are in Fiji with ministers and climate negotiators from around 60 countries to discuss the outstanding issues surrounding the UN-led international climate conference that kicks off in Turkey next month.
Pacific leaders see these talks ahead of COP31 as an opportunity to highlight the increasing urgency facing their low-lying islands.
"It's actually to bring the people who are continuing to turn a blind eye and deaf ears to the communities of the vulnerable islands to these effects," Rasmussen told DW, emphasizing the importance of holding these talks in the Pacific.
"It showcases the vulnerability. It showcases the impacts that are already happening. And it also brings the community, the real people at the front line, to participate in these pre-COPs," she added.
On the frontlines of climate change
Leaders attending the event will first travel to the island of Tuvalu, which scientists predict could be one of the first countries to become inhabitable due to rising sea levels caused by human-driven climate change.
At the UN General Assembly last month, Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told delegates that sea level rise is a "present reality."
"Tuvalu's message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come."
At an average of just two meters above sea level, the archipelago has faced more frequent and severe flooding as water levels have risen.
"Having back-to-back hurricanes and storms, having back-to-back significant floods...it really sets back countries and affects communities," Rasmussen, who comes from the Pacific island of Samoa, told DW. "People are losing their homes."
She also said rising sea levels are contaminating freshwater sources with salt, which threatens crops. In addition, hotter oceans mean corals lose the algae they rely on to survive, causing them to bleach and become less able to accommodate the diverse marine life that local populations rely on for their income.
Overshooting agreed limits on temperature rise
Although only few leaders from outside the region are expected at the conference, negotiators from countries including Germany, Mexico and South Korea will be present. Efforts to limit planetary heating are expected to be high on the agenda.
Pacific leaders are pushing for a renewed commitment to keep global temperature rise capped to 1.5 degrees (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a limit that was agreed on by world leaders at the Paris climate conference in 2015.
A UN report released in September said under a best-case scenario, temperatures were likely to reach at least 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels. The study added that it is still possible to "bring temperatures down."
Natasha Green, Australia country lead for climate think-tank E3G , said small island and least developing states are calling for countries to work together to enable vulnerable nations to "adapt and build resilience to the worsening impacts of climate change."
Tricky questions of climate finance
A key issue at this week's talks will be climate finance. Poorer nations, which have done little to contribute to rising global temperatures, yet are feeling some of the worst impacts, have long called on richer, higher-emitting countries to provide more money to help them adapt to a hotter world.
Laura Schäfer, international climate policy head of division at environment and human rights nonprofit, Germanwatch, said she would like to see Australia, who holds the COP presidency, "address tricky questions." 
Such as "how to include carbon majors, including the big fossil [fuel] industry in paying for climate damages like the ones we have just seen in Nepal." 
Also on the agenda will be a the non-use of fossil fuels for creating energy. At the 2023 climate conference, countries agreed for the first time to move towards a future that doesn’t rely on oil, gas and coal. Since then, however, there has been little progress.
Earlier this year just under 60 states took part in the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.
Scientists say an end to burning these polluting sources of energy is the only way to bring global temperature levels back under agreed limits. And thereby prevent some of the worst impacts of climate change — like the rising sea levels affecting island states and coastline communities.
"It's really important that the COPs continue to progress and elevate the commitment [...] to transition away from fossil fuels," said Green.

German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine for research on brain activity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:37:00 UTC
18:37:00 KST

German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine
October 5, 2026
The Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has gone to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, the academy announced on Monday.
The trio won the award for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, which combines the methods of optics and genetics to create a form of noninvasive stimulation of neurons.
The Nobel Assembly said that optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain, as researchers have been "able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders."
"The impact of optogenetics extends far beyond understanding the healthy brain, it has also helped revealed how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia," Abdel El Manira, Nobel committee member and professor of neuroscience, said after the announcement was made.
In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. Researchers hope that the field could lead to treatments for neurological and sensory disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
Who are the winners?
Hegemann is considered to be the leading expert in photobiology and one of the founding fathers of optogenetics. He is a professor of neuroscience at the Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany.
Georg Nagel is a biophysicist and professor at of neurophysiology at the University of Würzburg, Germany. Karl Deisseroth is a professor of bioengineering and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University in the US.
The trio came togther as Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae could swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.
Deisseroth then joined in to work with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
Medicine is the first of Nobels announced this week
The award for medicine is the first Nobel prize to be awarded this week, with laureates set to be named in physics, chemistry, literature and peace in the days up to Friday.
Last year's prize was awarded jointly to Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell of the United States and Shimun Sakaguchi of Japan for "for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance."
The prizes will be presented at ceremonies in Stockholm, Sweden on December 10.
Each prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.

Teen With Bulgarian Citizenship Held in France Over Alleged Police Murder Attempt During the Student Protests
A 17-year-old Bulgarian national has been remanded in custody after allegedly attacking a police commander during protests in Belfort, France, with prosecutors charging him with violence against a law enforcement officer, an offense punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
Belfort prosecutor Paul-Édouard Lallois announced the detention at a briefing, with NOVA and other Bulgarian media reporting on the case. A second minor, aged 15, has been placed under judicial supervision.
The incident occurred on October 2 near the Gustave Courbet High School, where a protest blockade was taking place. The demonstrations had begun the previous week over dissatisfaction with the quality of education and spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school students and other citizens have protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and the poor condition of school facilities. Twenty-four schools have been set on fire or looted, while more than 5,000 people have been taken into custody.
The police commander, who was in plainclothes, tried to detain a young person near the Savoureuse River but was attacked by several youths and knocked to the ground.
“Witness testimonies and video footage from the scene establish that one of the youths approached the police officer from behind and struck him hard with his fist, knocking him to the ground and thereby freeing the person who had just been detained,” Lallois said.

According to the prosecution, acquaintances later helped him remove the handcuffs by cutting them with pliers.
During questioning, the teenager acknowledged taking part in the assault and admitted that he had thrown stones at police officers earlier that day.

The teenager was born in Russia, but he and both of his parents hold Bulgarian citizenship. The family moved to France in 2020 and has four children in total. The teenager attends Gustave Courbet High School in Belfort and has no criminal record.

SC seeks EC response on changes during SIR: Why has Form 6 become a flashpoint — explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:34:32 UTC
18:34:32 KST

Chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar with election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday raised questions over changes made to Form 6, the application used for registering a voter, during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The issue came up while the court was hearing petitions alleging that several decisions linked to the SIR exercise were taken without the approval of all three election commissioners, particularly Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, who were at odds with poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar on multiple occasions.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from the Election Commission, the Centre, the CEC and the other two election commissioners before examining whether the poll panel's statutory procedure was followed.The bench, however, refused to pass an immediate order seeking the suspension of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, while considering the controversy over Form 6, which was one of the central issues raised in the petitions.
What is Form 6
Form 6 is the application through which an eligible person seeks inclusion of their name in the electoral roll. The Election Commission's guidelines states the application is addressed to the Electoral Registration Officer of the constituency where the applicant ordinarily resides.
The form requires basic details such as the applicant's name, details of a relative, Aadhaar information, gender, date of birth and present ordinary residence. Applicants are also required to complete a declaration, with the guidelines warning that making a false statement in it is punishable under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.The Election Commission's instructions also mandates that an applicant can fill the form either in English or in the official language of the state. Also, an applicant who does not know the number or name of the relevant constituency cannot have the application rejected merely for that reason.For age verification, applicants can submit a self-attested copy of one of the documents specified in the form. The guidelines also provide for verification by the Electoral Registration Officer in cases where the prescribed documents are unavailable.
The Form 6
The dispute over Form 6
The petitions allege that additional requirements connected with the SIR were introduced into Form 6 through the Election Commission's software.One of the allegations is that details concerning an applicant's ancestry (details of father or grandfather) and a link to the previous SIR were incorporated into the process without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.The petitioners have further alleged that Election Commissioner Vivek Joshi objected to the modification and that Election Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu subsequently endorsed the objection. Therefore, the issue therefore goes beyond the information sought from voters.
Chagnes were made to Form 6 without amending the electoral rules.
At the heart of the dispute is whether the Election Commission could alter the form and introduce SIR-linked requirements through its software without following the legal process required for changing the relevant electoral rules. During the hearing, the CJI specifically flagged the question of who authorised the modification.“Any modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When record has produced, we would like to see who has modified. But, your prayers appear jumbled up,” the CJI noted, as quoted by LiveLaw.The court, however, did not accept the petitioners' allegations as established facts at this stage as Justice Bagchi said the court would first need responses from the concerned authorities and records before deciding whether any decision was taken contrary to the statutory framework.Also Read | 'Form 6 has not been approved by us': What SC said on EC's SIR decision - top quotes"If records show some decision was not unanimous etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra-vires. Can we ex-parte come to decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner," Justice Bagchi added.
EC retracts on From 6
Amid the raging controvery, the Election Commission withdrew the additional SIR-related declaration from Form 6 in states where the electoral roll revision exercise had been completed.In states where the SIR was concluded, the EC removed additional declaration from the ECINET app and portal, as well as the respective Chief Electoral Officer portals. This meant that applicants in states where SIR is over will only need to fill the regular statutory Form 6 to enrol as voters.Just days before this action and as the controvery over dissent in the poll body emerged, the EC in a press note had, however, said that "the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used."
The larger SIR controversy
The Form 6 dispute forms part of a broader challenge to how the Election Commission has allegedly handled the SIR exercise. The petitions rely on claims that the two other Election Commissioners formally raised objections on at least 14 occasions over several months to decisions and orders concerning the revision of electoral rolls.The allegations include changes to electoral-roll software, communications issued in the name of the Election Commission and other decisions allegedly taken without the approval of all members of the multi-member poll panel.The petitioners have invoked Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023. The provision states that the Commission's business should, as far as possible, be transacted unanimously and that where the members differ, the matter is to be decided according to the majority view.The pleas argue that this framework means powers vested in the Election Commission cannot be exercised individually by the CEC where the law requires the Commission to act collectively.The petitioners have sought several forms of relief, including suspension of Gyanesh Kumar as CEC until the matter is decided, preservation of electoral-roll data and audit trails, and restrictions on further substantive changes to Form 6.
Another plea has sought criminal proceedings against the CEC and other officials and argued that decisions, guidelines and software changes allegedly made without the full Commission's agreement should be declared unconstitutional, ultra vires and void ab initio.The Supreme Court has therefore, at this stage, not ruled on whether the alleged changes to Form 6 or other SIR-related decisions were unlawful. The immediate question before the court is whether the Election Commission followed the statutory decision-making process.The court will consider the records and responses of the respondents before deciding whether any particular decision can be struck down.
