Israeli lecturer indicted for planning mass terror attack against Palestinians, Arab Israelis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:33:11 UTC
18:33:11 KST

The State Attorney’s Office on Monday indicted a mathematics lecturer at Bar-Ilan University for allegedly planning a series of mass terrorist attacks, motivated by nationalist ideology, against hundreds of Palestinians and Arab Israelis.
The defendant, a Petah Tikva resident in his 60s, cannot be named under a court-issued publication ban.
The goal, according to the prosecution, was forced mass transfer. The defendant called the plan AY”T, a Hebrew acronym for “Am ya’aseh transfer,” or “The people will carry out transfer.”
He was charged in the Central District Court in Lod with preparing to commit an act of terrorism under the Counterterrorism Law, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors asked the court to keep him in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings against him.
According to the indictment, the suspect developed his plan from early February 2023 until his arrest about two weeks ago. The prosecution said it was initially fueled by the May 2021 riots during Operation Guardian of the Walls and intensified after the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas War, which was first called Operation Swords of Iron.
His idea was to activate terrorist cells simultaneously in different locations. The prosecution said the defendant had also conducted a reconnaissance tour around Tuba-Zanghariya, a Bedouin town near Safed in the North, to examine possible access and attack routes.
The alleged plan envisioned 72 Jewish attackers, including the defendant, at least half of whom would have firearms licenses. They were to be divided into 12 cells of six people each and use a variety of weapons, including handguns, rifles, axes, and hammers.
The intended targets were mixed cities and Arab communities throughout Israel, including Tuba-Zanghariya, which the indictment describes as a primary target.
The plan also called for the terrorist cells to receive assistance and support coordinated in advance with subversive elements who would be recruited from within the IDF, including the bombardment of Arab population centers by the IAF, Artillery Corps, and Armored Corps.
According to the indictment, the practical section of the plan instructed members of the public to join in “carrying out mass killings and rapidly seizing areas of friction, roads, entrances to and exits from Arab communities, mixed cities, and hospitals… Do not show mercy even to the women or their cruel and repulsive children; do not stop in the face of pleas; harden your hearts. Any pause will lead to an intolerable state of chaos, followed by the massacre of Jews.”
The simultaneous mass terrorist attacks, amplified and publicized on social media in real time, were intended to cause all Arab citizens of Israel, including Bedouin, as well as Palestinians living in east Jerusalem and the West Bank, to flee or be permanently expelled to Jordan, Lebanon, and the Gaza Strip, according to the indictment.
Attempted recruitment of Moshe Feiglin
The defendant tried for about a year and a half to recruit supporters to join him, but none agreed, the indictment states.
In particular, he allegedly sought to recruit Zehut chairman Moshe Feiglin, who is No. 2 on the joint Religious Zionist Party-Zehut electoral list. He intended to enlist Feiglin and, with his help, recruit additional activists to take part in the plan.
The defendant attended two of Feiglin’s public events and tried to arrange a meeting with him and give him a summary of the plan, but Feiglin did not respond to any of his approaches, according to the indictment.
About a month ago, the defendant allegedly wrote a letter addressed to Feiglin in which he threatened to distribute it and, in his view, damage Feiglin’s public standing ahead of the election unless Feiglin cooperated and helped advance the plan.
About two days later, he allegedly went to Feiglin’s home, gave the letter to a passing neighbor, and asked her to deliver it. He later attended a Zehut event at Jerusalem’s Mahaneh Yehuda market and, through another woman, delivered several copies of the letter and a second letter containing a similar threat to the party’s director-general.
Feiglin’s team said it had filed a police complaint as soon as the letter was received.
The indictment further alleges that the defendant tried to conceal his activities and prevent the plan from being discovered. Among other measures, he allegedly wrote his documents by hand rather than on a computer, wore a protective mask, hat, and sunglasses when meeting prospective recruits, used a false name, and borrowed cellphones from passersby to contact others.
In response, Bar-Ilan University said it “condemns in the strongest possible terms and is deeply appalled” by the attributed acts to the lecturer. It called on the authorities to “pursue the matter to the fullest extent of the law, should the allegations be substantiated.”
“The university has, and will continue to have, zero tolerance for conduct of this nature – conduct that is fundamentally incompatible with the values we share as Jews, as Israelis, and as human beings, and that stands in clear opposition to the values of Bar-Ilan University,” it said.
“The lecturer will be suspended from his duties with immediate effect, pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings,” Bar-Ilan University said.

Of the 6,000 people who crossed the border from Gaza and infiltrated Israel on October 7, 4,000 have been killed, an Israeli source told The Jerusalem Post on Monday, citing data shared by Maj.-Gen. Shlomi Binder, head of the IDF's Military Intelligence, during a security cabinet meeting on Sunday evening.
"There are 2,000 remaining, and we will get to every last one of them," Binder said.
In the latest strike on Sunday, the IDF announced that it had killed Saqr Nabil Musa Qaisi, a Nukhba terrorist from Hamas who was posing as the director of a humanitarian aid organization called Deniz Feneri.
Earlier on Friday, the military killed Ibrahim Mustafa Suleiman Abu Oweimer, a Nukhba platoon commander in Hamas’ military wing and one of the terrorists who infiltrated Israel on October 7.
During the weekend, the military killed two Islamic Jihad rocket array commanders and reportedly attempted to kill Ali al-Amoudi, Yahya Sinwar’s successor as Hamas’s leader in the Gaza Strip.
There was no confirmation by the IDF that Amoudi was killed in the strike, with conflicting reports in Israeli media about his status.
The Post learned in July that the military had killed at least 420 Hamas terrorists since the 2025 ceasefire was established, while it has continued to target Hamas commanders ever since.
According to these estimates, from October 2025 til July 2026, Hamas reportedly has killed dozens or more of its own population since the ceasefire in order to retake control of all areas of the Gaza Strip where the Palestinian population lives.
UN estimates that around 1,000 Gazans have been killed during this time, meaning that, since the ceasefire, the percentage of Gazans killed by the IDF has likely been less than 50% civilians.
Defense Ministry says 1,318 Israeli security personnel killed since October 7
Since the start of the Israel-Hamas War on October 7, 2023, 1,318 members of Israel's security forces have fallen in the conflict, according to data published by the Families, Commemoration, and Heritage Department of the Defense Ministry on Sunday.
The number includes fallen personnel from the IDF, Israel Police, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Fire and Rescue Services, security coordinators, and local response team members.
The numbers account for the fallen across all fronts, including the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and the West Bank.
More than 7,150 people have been officially recognized as relatives who lost someone in service since the start of the war, including 2,143 bereaved parents, 355 widows, and 880 orphans. 3,772 people lost a sibling in the war.
Despite the ceasefire that took effect in the Gaza Strip on October 10, 2025, a number of Israeli soldiers have been killed in incidents along the Yellow Line that delineates the buffer zone within the strip.

German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:31:00 EEST

German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has stated that he sees the danger of a violent conflict with Russia, noting that the confrontation between the countries has acquired a "new, dangerous quality".
Source: European Pravda, citing Jäger's remarks during a hearing in the Bundestag, quoted by Die Welt
Details: The German intelligence head warned that the war in Ukraine, marked by increasingly brutal Russian attacks, is entering a "new, very dangerous phase", while the threat of hybrid attacks against Germany remains real.
Jäger stated that the risk involves Germany being dragged into a conflict with Russia.
The intelligence head emphasised that Russia is visibly escalating the conflict in Ukraine and continues to step up pressure on Europe and Germany. The confrontation Germany is in with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous character. The country risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia.
As an example of this escalation, he cited the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, responsibility for which Berlin attributed to Russia.
Jäger noted that no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany. Germany did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on the country, seeing it as its main adversary because Germany does not tolerate Russia's revisionist, expansionist policy and its war of aggression against Ukraine.
According to Jäger, the Russian leadership seeks to "ensure for the future that no political decisions directed against Moscow are made in Berlin or other European capitals". The consequence of this is "increasingly aggressive actions by Russian intelligence services" against Germany and other states.
Jäger stated that Russia is waging a shadow war against Germany. This undeclared war cannot be characterised using traditional military or legal categories. Germany is not in a state of defence, yet they are still under attack – that is precisely what a shadow war is.
The intelligence head added that Russia sought to undermine Europe's political support for Ukraine and emphasised that they had to be prepared for intimidation attempts and further interference. He noted that nuclear threats would likely be voiced again.
However, according to Jäger, at this time the intelligence agency sees no signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory. Nevertheless, "Russian military actions on a limited scale" are possible, particularly in the Baltic states, specified the head of German intelligence.
Background:
- Chancellor of Germany Friedrich Merz declared that his country is "preparing for major hybrid attacks, including severe ones" and will respond to them "swiftly and very clearly".
- German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt planned a package of measures covering protection against drones and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time more than decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:30:52 UTC
18:30:52 KST

Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence from Canada within the next two years.
If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade.
A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return to pitched battles over questions of language and identity between Quebec and the federal government.
Long considered a declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positioned himself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttal to François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year.
Analysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independent Quebec – but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues.
He has blamed immigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists.
Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Increasingly, though, they are on the right when it comes to social issues like systemic racism and accommodation of religious behaviour. They’ve hardened on these issues, and don’t see themselves in the left’s recent fixation on identity issues,” Lagacé said.
The biggest drag on St-Pierre Plamondon’s popularity has been his oft-repeated promise to hold a referendum during the first mandate of a PQ government. An overwhelming majority of Quebecers don’t want such a thing any time soon – particularly with Canada locked in a trade war with the US. The province mostly voted for Liberal leader Mark Carney over the separatist Bloc Québécois in last year’s federal election, expressly because of Carney’s “elbows up” posturing against the Trump administration.
But for the PQ, Donald Trump was at first a curse, then a gift. Early in the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t hold a referendum as long as Trump was in power, defusing the issue and allowing St-Pierre Plamondon to concentrate on attacking immigration and immigrants.
The party has also benefited from a four-way race for the right-leaning nationalist vote beyond the reliably Liberal fiefdom of Montreal – particularly around Quebec city, where the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec has made significant inroads. “The Parti Québécois is benefiting from a massive vote split because those who don’t like the PQ don’t agree on who to vote for,” said poll analyst Philippe Fournier.
Though the PQ will probably form the next provincial government, it remains unclear what sort of mandate it will have. Polls have the party hovering at roughly 30%, somewhat below the likely threshold for a majority government.
In any case, St-Pierre Plamondon is laying the groundwork for confrontation with the federal government. He has mused about defunding the office of Quebec’s lieutenant-governor (the British Crown’s representative in the province) and promised to introduce a law to abolish the province’s ties with the monarchy, which separatists see as the ultimate symbol of oppression of Canada’s French minority.
St-Pierre Plamondon also tore into Carney, after the prime minister said the government will probably increase immigration rates in the country. Doing so, St-Pierre Plamondon said, was an “abuse of power” that would have further nefarious effects on French-language services in Quebec.
For a man who trades on his relative youthfulness, St-Pierre Plamondon’s attacks on the monarchy have the whiff of anachronism – the kind of thing the PQ did in its 1970-era heyday.
Attacking the federal government is similarly outdated, and potentially risky for St-Pierre Plamondon. Carney remains popular in Quebec, and is likely to remain so, at least until the existential threat of Trump recedes.

Kraken and Saab test autonomous drone-seeker vessel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:30:40 BST
18:30:40 KST

Kraken Technology Group and Saab UK have developed and tested an autonomous vessel carrying an air-surveillance radar, intended to provide a rapidly deployable counter-drone sensing capability at sea, the companies stated.
The prototype combines Kraken’s K3 SCOUT uncrewed surface vessel with Saab’s Giraffe 1X radar, placing the lightweight three-dimensional sensor inside the vessel’s modular payload bay to detect and track airborne targets from an uncrewed platform.
Kraken and Saab said the system was taken from concept to a working prototype in less than seven months, with sea trials subsequently carried out to assess the radar while operating in a maritime environment.
The concept is intended to extend air surveillance away from crewed warships by placing radar sensors aboard autonomous vessels which can operate independently or as part of a wider naval force. According to the companies, the configuration could provide early warning against drones and other airborne threats around shipping, ports, offshore energy infrastructure and other maritime sites.
Giraffe 1X is a compact radar from Saab’s wider Giraffe family of air-surveillance systems. Saab describes the radar as capable of detecting and tracking small airborne targets, while its size and weight allow it to be installed on a range of fixed and mobile platforms.
The K3 SCOUT is designed around a modular payload architecture, allowing different sensors and mission equipment to be fitted depending on the task. The latest trials use that payload space to turn the vessel into what Kraken and Saab describe as an autonomous “drone seeker”.
According to a joint news update from Kraken and Saab UK, Mal Crease, CEO and Founder of Kraken Technology Group, said: “Kraken and Saab UK’s prototype ‘drone seeker’ vessel is exactly what the K3 SCOUT was designed to do: integrate with mission-relevant payloads to then operate in austere maritime environments.”
The approach reflects growing interest in so-called hybrid fleets, where crewed warships operate with uncrewed vessels carrying sensors, weapons or other mission systems. In this case, the prototype is focused on sensing and early warning rather than carrying an effector to engage the targets it detects.
Moving radar coverage onto an uncrewed surface vessel could allow sensors to be positioned away from larger ships or fixed installations, although the companies have not presented the prototype as a replacement for conventional shipborne air-defence sensors.
Andy Fraser, Managing Director of Saab UK, said: “This is a pioneering, UK manufactured, deployable capability, that together with Kraken we’ve developed in less than seven months. This reflects the strength of our partnership, the maturity and flexibility of our respective technologies, and our ability to respond at pace to the evolving threat landscape and needs of our customers.”
Both systems involved in the prototype are produced in Fareham. Kraken manufactures the K3 SCOUT there, while Saab UK also produces the Giraffe 1X radar at its facilities in the area.
Kraken is expanding production following a $175 million Series B fundraising round which valued the company at $1 billion. The company says its new 35,000 sq ft manufacturing facility is being developed to support production of up to 1,000 vessels per year as demand for uncrewed maritime systems grows among allied armed forces.
The British company was founded in 2020 and produces a family of uncrewed maritime platforms including the K3 SCOUT, K5 KRAKEN and K7 SABRE surface vessels, along with the K4 MANTA surface and subsurface platform.
Saab UK employs more than 600 people across eight major UK facilities, with its activities ranging from radar and underwater systems to training, simulation and software development.
The K3 SCOUT and Giraffe 1X integration remains an experimental prototype, with the recent sea trials used to demonstrate that the radar could be fitted to the vessel and operated in maritime conditions while exploring how an autonomous surface platform could contribute to wider air-surveillance and counter-UAS networks.

A Prediction Market About the Past? Sure, Why Not!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth?
Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened?
When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.)
Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.”
In a regular prediction market, participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour.
Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit, or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power.
Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time.
According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.”
When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says.
Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model.
For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can. Like Polymarket’s decentralized product, Verifact Markets is “on-chain,” and participants can make trades with stablecoins, a class of cryptocurrencies tied to the price of the US dollar and other fiat currencies.
Verifact Markets is part of a wave of startups interested in resolving the facts about disputed news and historical events. One of the most recent entries was the short-lived Peter Thiel–funded project Objection (later rebranded as The Primary), which aimed to determine whether specific media stories were accurate. But before the truth-adjudication stuff really got off the ground, The Primary pivoted to publishing news and a scoreboard for ranking journalists.
For now, there are very few details about how Verifact Markets will ultimately determine whether something is true or false, even though its entire value proposition rests on the idea that it’s uniquely positioned to do so. It's an extremely tall order, made even taller by all the other details that haven’t been worked out yet, like how the project will make money—it doesn’t plan to charge fees at launch. Wokwicz isn’t focused on that sort of thing, at least not yet. “What I'm looking forward to most is just some of the very unique evidence that people are going to dig up,” he says. “We're going to bring out truth—what is true and false.”
Some prediction market veterans say they are intrigued by Verifact Markets, even if there are plenty of remaining questions about how it will work. “I'll probably join just so I can keep making money off of the 2020 election for the rest of my existence,” says prominent prediction market trader Caleb Davies.

Font size
Bulgarian police are taking part in a Europe-wide road traffic enforcement operation focusing primarily on the use of mobile phones while driving and the wearing of seat belts and other safety restraints, Chief Inspector Lachezar Bliznakov said. The international ROADPOL campaign is being held under the slogan “Focus on the Road”. 
Since the beginning of the year, more than 100,000 violations involving the failure to use seat belts, helmets and child restraint systems have been recorded. Bliznakov pointed out that passengers are also required to wear seat belts, including in the rear seats, and may be fined for failing to comply with the requirement.
If a driver is found using a mobile phone while driving, eight penalty points are deducted from their driving record, while failure to wear a seat belt results in the deduction of 10 points. Chief Inspector Bliznakov noted that passengers on buses equipped with seat belts are also required to wear them.
Just 20% of drivers in Bulgaria do not reach for the phone while driving
He added that with the end of the summer season, traffic is now increasingly concentrated in built-up areas, and police enforcement efforts are being focused there as well, BTA reports.

The level of illegal migration through Bulgarian border has fallen by 40% compared with last year, Border Police Director Anton Zlatanov said.
Migrants are primarily from Afghanistan, Syria and Morocco, while the authorities’ efforts are focused not only on detaining them but also on uncovering the trafficking networks behind their movement.
Efforts to curb irregular migration are continuing, and the level of such migration is currently negligible, Chief Commissioner Anton Zlatanov said. He also highlighted the role of the Turkish side in protecting Bulgaria’s border:
“When we tell you that we have detained 10 people, you can be sure that there were at least another 100 whom we prevented from crossing. Police catch drug couriers operating over 450 caches across Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:28:00 UTC
18:28:00 KST

Police catch drug couriers operating over 450 caches across Estonia
In mid-September, police in Rakvere detained two men, aged 21 and 24, on suspicion of drug offenses. Evidence gathered so far indicates that the men worked as couriers, placing drugs in caches across Estonia.
On September 15, police caught the two men in the act in Rakvere and detained them. According to information currently available, the suspects had driven from Tallinn to Rakvere that day. Their task was to weigh and package drugs into suitable quantities and then place nearly 200 grams of cocaine in an area in Rakvere designated by the people who had recruited them.
During the investigation, police have determined that the suspects may be linked to more than 450 drug caches in Lääne-Viru County, Tallinn, Rapla, Viljandi and Jõhvi.
In recent weeks, police officers across Estonia have checked possible cache locations and found drugs in more than 300 of them. In total, police have seized several kilograms of drugs from the caches and during searches, including cocaine, cannabis, amphetamine and MDMA.
Rainet Juuse, head of the criminal investigation bureau at the East Prefecture, said police began investigating how the men operated and the possible extent of their activities.
"We involved police officers across Estonia in locating the caches. We have now established that the suspects were recruited as drug couriers through the messaging app Telegram. The criminal investigation will determine exactly how and where the men obtained the drugs and who gave them their instructions," Juuse said.
District prosecutor Kalmer Kask, who is leading the proceedings, said neither man has a previous criminal conviction.
"We are seeing an increasing number of cases in which criminal networks recruit young adults or people with substance use disorders to hide drugs," Kask said.
The investigation is being conducted by the East Prefecture and led by the Viru District Prosecutor's Office.

Unknown Publisher

A major cybersecurity breach has exposed the personal data of 8.8 million people in Denmark.
Denmark has suffered a major data breach after hackers broke into the country's national population registry and accessed the personal information of millions of people.
The country's digital affairs minister announced the data breach on Monday, calling it "an extremely serious incident" that affected 8.8 million people.
"Unauthorised individuals obtained illegal access" to the names, addresses and CPR, including those who have died or emigrated, the ministry said in a press release, referring to Denmark’s social security numbers.
“This is an extremely serious incident,” Christina Egelund, digital affairs minister, was quoted as saying in the press release.
“Together with all the relevant authorities, we are in the process of mapping out the full extent of the incident,” she added.
Denmark has a population of around six million, but the national registry has information on 11 million, including data on those deceased and people who have emigrated from the country.
An investigation has now been launched into the incident. Authorities said they have no information on who carried out the breach.
They broke into the national registry by hacking into a Danish company that legally had access to it, the government said, adding that the access has not been revoked.

Development Road Project could generate $80 billion annually as energy corridor, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:27:05 UTC
18:27:05 KST

Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar (AA Photo)
The Development Road Project could generate around $80 billion in annual economic value if it is developed into an energy corridor carrying oil, natural gas and electricity, according to Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar.
The project is designed to connect the Persian Gulf to Türkiye and Europe through road and railway links while strengthening energy ties between Türkiye and Iraq and creating a major international trade corridor.
Speaking after a visit to Ankara by Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudhair, Bayraktar said the project should be viewed as more than a transportation link. Türkiye is determined to develop it as a strategic energy route supported by oil, natural gas and electricity transmission infrastructure along the corridor, he said.
Bayraktar noted that the route could eventually handle up to 2.5 million barrels of oil per day. He said Iraq currently produces around 4 million barrels per day, while Kuwait has production capacity of roughly 2 million barrels per day, creating significant potential for regional crude flows to be redirected through the corridor.
According to Bayraktar, transporting 2.5 million barrels of oil per day through the route could create annual economic value of approximately $65 billion-$70 billion.
He also highlighted the project’s natural gas potential, saying it could provide an alternative route for Qatari gas exports to reach Europe via Iraq and Türkiye. Qatar currently depends largely on LNG shipments and the Strait of Hormuz for its gas exports, he noted.
“If Qatari gas is transported through Iraq and the Development Road, with part of the gas remaining in Türkiye and part exported to Europe, the combined oil and natural gas trade could generate an annual economic value of around $80 billion,” Bayraktar said.

Nolo becomes typhoon after crossing International Date Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:25:05 UTC
18:25:05 KST

Merve Berker
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Nolo, which has been active for nearly three weeks, has changed from a hurricane to a typhoon after crossing the International Date Line in the Pacific Ocean, media reports said Sunday.
Nolo was a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph) Sunday morning Hawaii time before crossing the date line, according to NBC News.
By Monday morning Japan time, Typhoon Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (161 kph) and was moving west at 19 mph (31 kph), according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
"The good news is there's a large, vast ocean, so even though it is still going to be strong, it's not near any land," NBC quoted John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist with the US National Hurricane Center, as saying.
Nolo is forecast to continue moving west while gradually weakening.
The storm skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago before weakening into a tropical storm and regaining hurricane strength Friday.
Tropical cyclones with winds exceeding 74 mph are called hurricanes in the northern Atlantic and central and eastern Pacific, but are known as typhoons in the North Pacific.

Cancer-fighting t cells burn out. Scientists may have found a fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:24:29 UTC
18:24:29 KST

Cancer-fighting t cells burn out. Scientists may have found a fix
- Date:
- October 5, 2026
- Source:
- Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
- Summary:
- Cancer immunotherapy can lose its punch when tumor-fighting T cells become exhausted, but researchers may have found a way to keep them going longer. Scientists at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center identified a signaling molecule called MEK that can push T cells to burn through their energy while producing cancer-killing proteins. In animal and laboratory studies, blocking MEK helped the cells conserve energy, survive longer, and remain active even in the harsh environment around tumors.
- Share:
Cancer immunotherapy can unleash T cells, the immune system's specialized cancer killers, against tumors. But there is a major limitation: These cells can become worn down before the cancer is eliminated. This condition, known as T cell exhaustion, leaves the cells unable to maintain a strong attack or keep tumor growth under control.
That problem has been particularly important for checkpoint inhibitors, immunotherapy drugs designed to remove biological restraints that normally limit T cell activity.
"A tragic part of T cell exhaustion is that the immunotherapy seems to be working for patients, and then it fades," says Santosha Vardhana, MD, PhD, a physician-scientist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) who treats people with lymphoma. "Many of them experience a brief wisp of promise only to have it taken away."
Researchers in Dr. Vardhana's laboratory have now identified a signaling molecule called MEK as an important driver of this exhaustion process. Based on animal studies published in Immunity, the findings suggest that blocking MEK might slow T cell exhaustion and potentially make immunotherapy more effective.
"We're excited about applying this finding to enhance multiple forms of immunotherapy," Dr. Vardhana says. "FDA-approved MEK inhibitors are already available, so this approach could be tested in humans without much delay."
How MEK Pushes T Cells Toward Exhaustion
Scientists have only recently begun to understand the processes that cause T cells to become exhausted. In 2020, Dr. Vardhana's laboratory identified an important piece of the puzzle: the cells' metabolism, meaning the chemical processes they use to turn nutrients into energy.
When T cells are continuously exposed to tumor antigens (the cancer proteins the immune system sees as foreign), the mitochondria inside the cells can become overburdened. Mitochondria are responsible for transforming nutrients into energy that cells can use.
"There is a large metabolic demand being imposed as T cells encounter cancer cells and try to produce cancer-killing, or cytotoxic, proteins," Dr. Vardhana says. "It turns out that the decision to make high levels of these proteins is regulated by MEK."
If MEK becomes excessively active, it can eventually drive T cells into terminal exhaustion, a severely depleted state in which immunotherapy can no longer reactivate them.
"We realized T cell exhaustion isn't simply a loss of function -- it reflects an imbalance between what these cells are being asked to do and the energy they have available," says Tanmana Mitra, PhD, a student in the Vardhana lab and the study's first author.
Surprisingly, the team discovered that exhausted T cells were not metabolically sluggish. They were actually highly active. When researchers treated the cells with MEK inhibitors, the T cells multiplied more while consuming less energy.
"That paradox made us ask where all that energy was going, and we discovered that these cells were investing enormous resources into making proteins," Dr. Mitra explains. "It changed how we think about T cell exhaustion -- from a problem of too little energy to one of excessive energy demand."
Helping T Cells Pace Themselves
The findings suggested that reducing MEK signaling could lower the pressure on T cells to continuously manufacture cytotoxic proteins. That, in turn, allowed some of the cells to stay active and capable of renewing themselves for longer, potentially extending the effectiveness of immunotherapy.
The concept is similar to pacing yourself during a long road trip instead of driving at full speed from beginning to end. Reducing the intensity can help preserve enough fuel to keep going.
In laboratory models, blocking MEK signaling allowed T cells to persist even in the difficult conditions surrounding a tumor.
But the researchers caution that suppressing MEK is unlikely to be the right approach for every cancer patient.
T Cell Exhaustion Can Also Be Protective
Scientists now understand that T cell exhaustion is more complicated than simply having immune cells lose their strength. MSK immunologist Andrea Schietinger, PhD, previously found that T cells can enter an exhausted state as a survival mechanism. By reducing their activity, they avoid becoming overstimulated and dying.
"As we've learned more about T cell exhaustion," Dr. Vardhana says, "we've increasingly understood that it's not the case that exhausted T cells are bad, so let's try to reverse the process with a drug. Instead, exhaustion is more of an equilibrium state that lets the cells survive and keep going -- almost like a 'safe mode' for T cells."
When a T cell is actively attacking cancer and producing cytoxic proteins, its mitochondria must turn nutrients from food into adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATP is the molecule cells primarily use to store and transfer energy.
"Think of ATP as the currency in a fund that the cell spends down," Dr. Vardhana says. "If you spend ATP on one thing, you don't have enough to do something else. The exhaustion program is a sign that the cell's bank account is getting close to zero. MEK tells exhausted cells whether to conserve fuel or go for broke. What we found is that inhibiting MEK makes the cells more conservative -- helping them live longer while reducing the rate at which they produce the proteins that actually kill cancer cells."
That makes MEK both part of the problem and part of the solution. Strong MEK activity helps T cells attack at maximum intensity, but it can also push them toward complete burnout. Blocking MEK therefore involves a tradeoff: The immune attack may become less intense, but the cancer-fighting cells can survive longer.
Whether a short, powerful immune response or a slower, longer-lasting one is preferable may depend on the characteristics of an individual patient's cancer.
When T Cells May Need To Go Full Speed
According to Dr. Vardhana, MEK inhibitors would need to be used selectively. Two factors can indicate that a patient is likely to respond well to immunotherapy:
- The tumors are small.
- The patients have a high number of immune cells attacking the tumor -- usually because the tumor has many mutations that make it recognizable.
"In these patients, conservation of T cells is not that important," he says. "It's like being in a car with 1/8 of a tank left, but you can see the finish line. In these patients, you would just let the car keep burning the gas -- in other words, take the traditional immunotherapy approach. These are the patients in whom MEK inhibition is probably not needed."
The situation may be different for patients with large tumors or relatively few tumor-fighting immune cells. Their immune response may not be powerful enough to eliminate the cancer quickly.
In those cases, creating a slower, sustained response with a MEK inhibitor could help T cells remain present for longer, even if they are partly exhausted. That persistence may be especially important when either the task at hand (the tumor) is large or the workforce (the number of T cells) is small.
Potential Uses Across Cancer Immunotherapy
Dr. Vardhana says carefully applied MEK inhibition could potentially improve several types of immunotherapy.
Checkpoint inhibitors: MEK inhibition has already shown effectiveness in melanoma when combined with checkpoint inhibitors and a targeted treatment known as a BRAF inhibitor.
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy: "We think this approach could dramatically boost T cell persistence, which has been a big problem with CAR T cell therapy," Dr. Vardhana says.
Tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy: This treatment takes advantage of immune cells that have already been attacking a patient's cancer and expands their numbers. Using MEK inhibition before or after TIL therapy could potentially help the most effective tumor-fighting TILs survive longer.
Bispecific antibodies: These laboratory-made proteins are designed to attach to two different targets at the same time. They can strongly activate T cells, but that intense stimulation may also contribute to exhaustion.
"This study shows the importance of understanding core principles of T cell biology -- what sets the balance between conservation of energy and strong, cancer-fighting activity," Dr. Vardhana says. "Once we know the answer to that, the therapeutic possibilities really start to fan out."
Key Takeaways
- T cells can become exhausted as they continuously recognize and attack cancer, reducing their ability to keep tumors under control.
- The signaling molecule MEK appears to play an important role in pushing T cells toward exhaustion.
- Blocking MEK may slow that process by reducing the cells' energy demands, potentially helping them persist for longer during cancer treatment.
- The researchers suggest this strategy could be particularly useful for patients who respond poorly to traditional immunotherapy, including those with large tumors or relatively few immune cells capable of recognizing the cancer.
Additional authors on the study include Jahan Rahman, Madeline Hwee, Yan-Ting Chen, Ruben Jose Jesus Faustino Ramos, Hui Liu, Travis Hartman, Justin Cross, Miguel de Jesus, Morgan Huse, Valerie Longo, and Pat Zanzonico.

Housing Crisis Pushes Spain Into Early Election Showdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:23:02 UTC
18:23:02 KST

Housing Crisis Pushes Spain Into Early Election Showdown
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early general election for November 29 after Congress rejected his government’s housing measures, the Spanish leader announced Monday.
The vote will take place on Sunday, November 29, the earliest date allowed under the procedural timetable. Sánchez made the announcement at Madrid’s Moncloa Palace after spending the weekend consulting ministers, senior Socialist Party figures and his closest advisers.
The decision follows Friday’s parliamentary defeat of two emergency housing decrees proposed by Sánchez’s minority government. The measures included provisions to extend tenancy contracts automatically, restrict evictions of vulnerable tenants, ban evictions until 2030, and regulate temporary rentals and room rentals.
The conservative People’s Party (PP), far-right Vox and the right-wing Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against the decrees. The PP, which leads the polls and could need Vox’s support to form a government, said construction rather than regulation was the appropriate way to address the housing crisis.
The defeat came after Sánchez’s government failed to secure sufficient parliamentary backing despite last-minute negotiations. It highlighted the difficulties facing his minority coalition, which has had to negotiate much of its legislative agenda with its partners on a vote-by-vote basis and has suffered several defeats in Congress.
In his address, Sánchez presented the election as a decision over Spain’s future direction, contrasting what he described as a choice between “regressing” under a “far-right coalition” and continuing with his progressive government.
“It is time for Spaniards to decide what future you want,” Sánchez said.
He said the election would determine who should lead Spain through a period marked by political tensions, global instability, the climate emergency and uncertainty linked to the rise of artificial intelligence.
Sánchez also acknowledged shortcomings in his government’s record.
“I know that we have made mistakes and have failed to do everything we had set out to do. It is also true that there are still many injustices to correct, many social goals to conquer and many problems to solve, especially in the areas of inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said.
The prime minister said his minority government needed a stronger mandate to pursue its agenda.
“To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people,” Sánchez said, adding that his objective was “to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament”.
Spanish news agency EFE reported that Sánchez had informed King Felipe VI of his plans by telephone Sunday afternoon. The government was due to formally approve the decision to dissolve parliament at its meeting Monday morning.
The parliamentary defeat came after housing protests intensified across Spain. Tens of thousands of people demonstrated in Madrid and other cities over the weekend, demanding urgent action to make housing more affordable.
Authorities estimated that 70,000 people joined Saturday’s demonstration in Madrid, while organizers said the number was 500,000.
The protests gained momentum after the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not afford a 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought the apartment.
Her case prompted tens of thousands of people to demonstrate and led to the creation of a large tent camp in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol, recalling the 2011 indignados movement. The housing issue has since become a major source of pressure on Sánchez’s government.
The housing demonstrations also produced an angry reaction outside Congress when lawmakers rejected the government’s decrees, with protesters shouting “shame” and “Your profits; our misery”.
Sánchez may be seeking to use the issue to mobilize left-wing voters despite polls consistently showing the PP well ahead of his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), while support for Vox has also been increasing.
Current polling places the PP at about 32-34%, compared with 26-27% for the Socialists. Vox is estimated at 18-19%, followed by Sumar at 5-6% and Podemos at 2-3%.
The figures point to a potential government led by the PP with Vox support. Such an outcome would put a far-right party in Spain’s central government for the first time since the country returned to democracy following the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
A Sánchez defeat would end one of the few remaining left-leaning governments in Western Europe at a time when conservative and populist parties are gaining ground across the continent.
The election also brings forward a contest that had been expected in 2027, when major elections were also scheduled in France, Italy and Poland.
The announcement was welcomed by the opposition PP, which posted “At last” on X alongside an election video set to the EU anthem “Ode to Joy”.
Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, is one of Europe’s longest-serving leaders. He has never won enough votes to establish a majority government but has remained in office through a succession of fragile coalitions involving parties ranging from the far left to the separatist right.
His government has passed relatively little legislation during its third term because of growing divisions among its parliamentary partners and has failed to approve a national budget since 2023. Spain’s economy, however, has continued to be among the strongest-performing in the developed world.
The election decision also follows months of pressure over a migration crisis in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta and corruption cases involving people close to the PSOE.
Around 70,000 people crossed into Ceuta from neighboring Morocco over a 48-hour period at the end of July, creating unprecedented pressure on the enclave. The government subsequently deployed additional resources and later declared a “situation of interest for national security” for the first time in Spain’s democratic era.
The government’s response has triggered a political dispute, with the PP and Vox accusing Sánchez of responding too slowly and questioning his policy toward Morocco. Sánchez has defended both the security forces and his government’s handling of the situation.
Several corruption cases and other legal proceedings involving members of Sánchez’s political circle have also increased pressure on the government.
Sánchez has nevertheless built a reputation as a political operator capable of recovering from setbacks. His government has survived three successive terms, covering eight years, despite repeated difficulties in maintaining parliamentary support.
He has also stood out internationally for his positions on progressive issues, including Palestinian statehood, defending multilateral institutions and action against “tech oligarchs”.
The early election represents a risky move because the Socialists are behind the PP in opinion polls. An election defeat could bring an end to one of Europe’s remaining left-leaning administrations while far-right parties are gaining support across the continent.
Sánchez’s decision also comes after he had repeatedly said in recent months that his government would serve out the full four-year parliamentary term.
The PP has said its preference is to address the housing crisis through increased construction rather than tighter regulation.
The party’s rejection of the housing decrees came as long-standing anger over high rents and insecure tenancies reached a peak following Abascal’s eviction. Her case and the resulting protests have kept housing at the center of the political debate.
The government’s housing proposals had sought to respond to the crisis through measures ranging from restrictions on evictions to changes affecting temporary and room rentals.
The failure to pass the decrees was the latest setback for Sánchez’s minority administration, whose parliamentary majority has become increasingly difficult to manage.
The election was called as Sánchez weighed whether to continue governing until the scheduled end of the parliamentary term or seek a new mandate from voters on November 29.

The vehicle was damaged and a border guard sustained minor injuries.
Source: TV8, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Traffic from the junction of the R-30 and R-31 roads in the Ștefan Vodă district towards Palanca has been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an investigation at the scene.

According to Moldova's Border Police, the incident occurred at approximately 09:38 on 5 October.
"The Border Police, together with the Customs Service, is continuously monitoring the situation in order to keep it under control and remains in contact with the competent Ukrainian authorities," the statement said.
People are strongly advised to refrain from travelling to the area. If they hear drones or explosions near the border, the authorities advise them to remain calm, take shelter indoors and rely exclusively on official sources for information.
People are also urged not to approach debris from aircraft, ammunition or other suspicious objects and to call the 112 emergency service immediately.
Background:

13th-century Christ mural in Ghent’s St Nicholas Church to undergo extensive restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:21:51 UTC
18:21:51 KST

A 13th-century mural of Christ in the St Nicholas Church in Ghent is undergoing a thorough restoration. The painting depicts Christ on a throne, surrounded by kneeling figures. The work was discovered by chance in the late 1990s, by which time it was already in a poor state of repair.
13th-century Christ mural in Ghent’s St Nicholas Church to undergo extensive restoration
The mural came to light in 1998 when the Baroque altar of the Chapel of the Sweet Name of Jesus in the lower church was dismantled. Christ suddenly appeared on a throne, surrounded by kneeling figures. The mural was in a pitiful state.
“The condition of the mural was a cause for concern,” city authorities say. “The underlying layers of plaster were crumbling and showed cracks. That is why, immediately after its discovery, the work was given a protective layer of Japanese paper.”
Some of the Japanese paper has already been removed for preliminary investigations. The restorers will remove all the paper in the spring. In doing so, there is a chance that further parts of the work will come to light. The actual restoration is scheduled for the spring of 2027.
Organ restoration too
Bressers Architecten is overseeing the restoration of the mural in the St Nicholas Church. Further restoration work in the church in the centre of city is planned over the coming years. The 19th-century organ, built by the French organ builder Aristide Cavaillé-Coll, is also due for a refurbishment.
The instrument dates from the 19th century and has not been played for 60 years. The Flemish Government has earmarked around 1.94 million euros for the restoration work, alongside restoration work at St James’s Church in Ghent.

Yemeni government forces seize district by Bab el-Mandeb, military sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:18:58 UTC
18:18:58 KST

Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Oct 5 - Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces staged a lightning advance on Monday to retake the coast around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait up to the city of Mocha, the government said, pushing the Iran-backed Houthis out of most of the areas they seized last month.
The forces of the internationally recognised government, backed by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha late on Monday and Houthi fighters were retreating into the highlands, four government sources said. The Defence Ministry said the city had fallen.
The government forces had already taken key positions including an airstrip in the Dhubab district at the mouth of the strait, a vital Red Sea oil route whose seizure by the Houthis last month sent shock waves through energy markets.
Reuters could not independently verify the extent of the government gains. The Houthis, who have controlled many of Yemen's more populous areas including the capital Sanaa since 2014, said the Saudi-backed government's claims were baseless.
While recapturing the coastal area around the strait would make it harder for the Houthis to disrupt shipping between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, they could still attack vessels with drones from positions further up the coast and inland.
Meanwhile, the Houthis themselves made important advances near the city of Taiz, gaining sections of a mountain road to leave government forces there besieged, according to five military sources with the Yemeni government. One government source denied the road had been cut.
The group also threatened to attack air traffic in Saudi airspace.
The escalating conflict has prompted Riyadh's allies to act. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia under their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement.
The war in Yemen resumed this summer after a ceasefire that had held since 2022 collapsed. The conflict has raged on and off since Saudi Arabia launched an air campaign against the Houthis in 2015, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in what was already the poorest Arab state.
KEY ENERGY EXPORT ROUTE AT CENTRE OF FIGHTING
Fighting has raged along several front lines in Yemen for weeks since a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.
With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the fighting in Yemen has pushed up global prices and raised new risks in a region already aflame.
It has worsened a humanitarian crisis in Yemen; the UN migration agency said on Monday that 184,000 people had been displaced since the war resumed.
Yemen's internationally recognised president, Rashad al-Alimi, swore on Sunday to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia".
Saudi Arabia said on Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets to provide air cover for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces. The Yemeni government said it had launched attacks on several fronts including in Sanaa province.
The Houthi-run health ministry said two people had been killed and seven wounded in strikes on the province's Sanhan and Sa'wan districts.
HEAVIEST FIGHTING IS IN SOUTHWEST YEMEN
While the war has raged on several fronts, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz.
Last week, Houthi attacks damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable.
On Sunday night, the group's fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, atop a promontory on the road, five government military sources said, though another government source denied this.
A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council.
The advances left Taiz, Yemen's third city with a population of over half a million and a garrison of thousands of government fighters, surrounded by Houthi forces, the government military sources said.
Taiz, nestled among Yemen's southern highlands, has been on the frontlines since early in the civil war, often under Houthi shell and sniper fire.
In al-Mudhaffar area, just outside Taiz but within the area besieged by the Houthis, a long queue formed outside a petrol station on Monday as people waited for fuel and cooking gas canisters.
"This is the daily state in Taiz," said one man queuing, Shehab Hazaa.
MECCA ALLIANCE AGREEs TO DEPLOY MILITARY FORCES IN SAUDI
In their statement, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan accused the Houthis of attempting to target Islam's holiest sites, Mecca and Medina, as well as cities and civilian infrastructure in the kingdom.

Details

Up to 16 hours without electricity: should Kyiv residents expect prolonged outages in October, and what does this depend on
Kyiv • UNN
An expert warned of prolonged outages in Kyiv due to new Russian strikes on the energy infrastructure. At temperatures as low as +5°C, they may last 14–16 hours.
This month, Kyiv may experience prolonged power outages if russia continues its strikes on energy facilities. Under certain conditions, there may be no electricity for 14–16 hours a day. Oleg Popenko, head of the Union of Utility Consumers, said this in a comment to UNN.
russia continues to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
According to the expert, Ukraine already had a similar experience last winter.
We have already been through this last winter, when we were without electricity for 20 or even 22 hours, and in the Kyiv region there was no electricity at all for five to seven days. Therefore, this is a real possibility. But there are certain factors that affect this. The main factors that could influence the continuation of the restrictions are attacks by the Russian Federation and damage to our energy facilities. Given that last week there were strikes on practically all components involved in supplying electricity to consumers, including the main generation facilities—namely the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant, and Thermal Power Plant No. 5. These facilities were hit
According to Oleg Popenko, further attacks could cause new damage to energy infrastructure, in which case restoring individual facilities could take a long time.
If the shelling continues, the destruction of energy facilities that russia has already struck in the past may await us. And all this will simply lead to a halt in electricity supplies, and we could simply be left without power for a long time
Oleg Popenko also explained that it is impossible to fully protect generating facilities from strikes.
"All facilities have different owners, but in most cases it is simply physically impossible to systematically prepare protection. We cannot fully protect generating facilities," Oleg Popenko emphasizes.
According to the expert, if the attacks continue, prolonged restrictions could begin as early as October. In addition, weather conditions will also affect their duration.
A drop in temperature is a decisive factor
If in February, amid low temperatures, we were without electricity for 20–22 hours, the situation in October could be different because the month is not yet as cold. But it is unknown what the weather will be after October 15. If the temperature falls to at least +5 °C, outages could last 14–16 hours
It is impossible to determine in advance exactly which districts of the capital may be affected most. This will depend on which facilities are damaged.
"There is no specific priority—it depends on where they strike. We have facilities supplied with electricity through Thermal Power Plant No. 5, others through the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, and others through the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant. In other words, depending on where the strikes occur, that is where there will be problems with electricity supplies. It also depends on the quality of our energy infrastructure—I mean DTEK in the city—which is capable of transmitting a particular amount of electricity to a particular district. This will also have an impact," Oleg Popenko concluded.
Thus, possible prolonged outages in the capital will depend primarily on further Russian strikes, the condition of energy facilities, and weather conditions.

Fake “I’m not a robot” verification — hackers are infecting Ukrainians’ PCs with a dangerous virus

Hackers have replaced Cloudflare CAPTCHA on more than 100 websites and are tricking Windows users into running dangerous PowerShell commands. The virus steals passwords and provides remote access to PCs.
Hackers are massively targeting Ukrainians, disguising malware as an “I’m not a robot” check. Attackers replace Cloudflare CAPTCHA on compromised websites and force users to execute dangerous commands, after which the LUNEXSTEALER virus is installed on the computer. The State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection reports this, UNN writes.
Details
CERT-UA reports a new large-scale infection campaign: in September, attackers hacked more than 100 websites and replaced the Cloudflare check on them with a fake page. Windows users who visited such pages from Google or other search engines were instructed to copy text and execute a command in PowerShell. Following the instructions led to the LUNEXSTEALER virus being installed on the computer.
It is noted that the malware disguises itself as legitimate files, exploits vulnerable drivers, and covertly embeds a fake “Microsoft Office Word Editor” extension in the browser. The consequences include the theft of passwords and browsing history, and even full remote control over the PC.
The State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection warned that no genuine CAPTCHA or Cloudflare will ask users to open Win+R or PowerShell or paste commands.

Writer Jeffrey Archer, author of a NYT bestseller, dies at 86
Kyiv • UNN
Jeffrey Archer died in London at the age of 86. The author of "Kane and Abel" sold hundreds of millions of books and left behind more than 40 works.
British writer, politician and former convict Jeffrey Archer died at his home in London at the age of 86. His death was announced by publisher HarperCollins. The New York Times reports, UNN reports.
Details
According to the publication, Archer became famous for thrillers and novels about wealthy and influential people. His books have sold hundreds of millions of copies worldwide. One of his best-known works was the 1979 novel "Kane and Abel," which has sold more than 50 million copies since its publication and topped The New York Times bestseller list. Archer's first novel, "Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less," was published in 1976. Before becoming a writer, he worked in public relations and was a politician.
"Where I come from, in Western Australia, we say: 'Tell them a story, (...) and make them turn the pages, and you can't go wrong,'" Archer explained about his approach to writing books.
Jeffrey Archer was a Member of the House of Commons and deputy chairman of Margaret Thatcher's Conservative Party. He later took a seat in the House of Lords with the title of Baron Archer of Weston-super-Mare.
In 2001, he was convicted of perjury.
"A political Houdini, he survived many twists and turns, including a 2001 conviction for perjury, when he was found guilty of fabricating diaries and inventing a story to win a court case over whether he had slept with a prostitute whom he had paid to keep silent," the publication writes.
Despite the political scandal, Archer continued his writing career and published more than 40 books.
"Storytellers are very rare, but they arouse a great deal of envy. The people who survive are storytellers," he told writer Anthony Horowitz in an interview in 2011.
Jeffrey Archer died on Monday in London. His final novel, "Adam and Eve," was due to be released the following day.

Letter from Mideast: Teaching children non-stop amid war in Yemen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
17:18:52 CST
18:18:52 KST

by Fatima Al-Huraibi
TAIZ, Yemen, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- When the war in Yemen forced me to flee Taiz city for the countryside some 11 years ago, I felt like I was going back to the life I had once tried to leave behind.
At the time, I was focused on finding a safe place for my children and keeping their education going.
I did not know then that returning home would lead me back to teaching and eventually to building an educational center for children in the rural area where I grew up.
The sixth of 11 children, I was born and raised in As Silw, a rural district in Yemen's southwestern Taiz province.
Although my mother had never received a formal education, she always encouraged me to study. She often told me how important education was and how much a teacher could mean to a child.
Her words stayed with me, and I began to dream of becoming a teacher.
That dream took me to Taiz University. In 2014, I graduated from its Faculty of Education and began teaching in Taiz city.
At that time, I had separated from my husband and was raising my two daughters, Haya and Saba, on my own.
Then war came. Schools were shelled, and some were turned into military barracks as fighting spread. Families fled their homes, livelihoods disappeared, and keeping children in school became increasingly difficult.
In 2015, I took my daughters to my home district, hoping to find somewhere safe.
But reaching safety raised another question: What would happen to my daughters' education?
The war had overturned the life my education had helped me build, but it had not taken away my ability to teach.
So I began with Haya and Saba. Soon, other children from nearby villages joined. I cannot remember which child came first. What I remember is how far some of them traveled. Some walked four or five kilometers along rural roads to reach our small classroom. They arrived tired, sat down, and began their lessons.
The room had a leaking roof. We used an old wooden door as our writing board. Sometimes, the children traced letters on the floor with sticks.
At first, I simply wanted to keep my own daughters learning after we were displaced. But as more children came, I began to wonder: If they were willing to walk several kilometers to reach a room like this, why shouldn't they have a proper place to learn closer to home?
That was when I began thinking about building a permanent educational center.
In As Silw, I got to know the women around me and their daily lives. I worked alongside them in the terraced fields, carrying crops, firewood, and water, and listened as they talked about their families and the futures they wanted for their children.
I also met girls who wanted to learn but lived far from schools. For some families, sending a daughter to the city was too expensive. For others, letting a young girl live away from home was simply not an option.
But distance was only part of the problem.
Years of war had also pushed teachers and students away from education. Around me, I saw teachers earn less than 60 U.S. dollars a month, and sometimes wait for months to be paid. Some choose to abandon teaching for other work, including military service, as fighting was seen as a quicker way to earn a living.
I have seen how war can empty a classroom without destroying the building itself.
I wanted a place where a boy could hold a book instead of being drawn toward a battlefield, and where a girl could continue learning rather than have poverty, distance or early marriage decide her future.
Wanting such a place was one thing. Building it was another.
There was no suitable building to rent. I had little money, and some people doubted that a woman could establish an educational center in a remote rural area in the middle of a war.
Others mocked the idea. My mother believed in me.
I spent my savings, sold my jewelry, and borrowed money from my brother. The construction began in 2016. In our mountainous area, getting cement and other materials to the site was difficult, and the war made transportation and supplies more uncertain.
There were days when I looked at the unfinished building and wondered whether I could really do it. But the walls kept rising.
Then came a day I still remember clearly: the children walked into a classroom built for them.
There were chairs to sit on, whiteboards to write on, and colorful pens to use. We even had computers where they could begin learning basic skills. These were ordinary classroom items, but to us, they felt anything but ordinary.
I looked at the whiteboards and remembered the wooden door. I watched the children use the computers and remembered them tracing letters on the floor with sticks.
I called the center "Non-Stop." War had interrupted our lives. I did not want the children's education to stop with it.
As word spread, more children came from nearby communities. Among them was Arwa, a 10-year-old primary-school student who had lost her father in the war.
When she first came to the center, she was frightened. I remember her holding tightly to my hand as we began reading together. So we went slowly, letter by letter and word by word.
Today, Arwa can read and is learning English. Most importantly, she wants to stay in school.
I could not undo what the war had done to her family. But I could sit beside her and teach her to read.
Nowadays, the center serves primary- and secondary-school students. About 10 teachers offer English, mathematics, chemistry, and physics, along with basic computer skills.
For rural girls, having these opportunities close to home can make a difference. Families that cannot afford to send their daughters away, or are unwilling to have them live alone in cities, can still keep them in school within their own communities.
Now, at 41, I sometimes stand in the center and think about how I got here. The education that once opened up a wider world for me is now something I can share with other rural children.
I still do not know what Yemen will look like when my students grow up. But I know what I want them to remember.
Not just the war, but a classroom, a book in their hands, and a teacher who kept telling them: their future is not defined by the war around them.
Editor's note: Fatima Al-Huraibi is a Yemeni teacher and founder of the Non-Stop educational center in the As Silw district of Taiz province.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

"The project is so huge that it's basically hard to really grasp it, even though we're right here on the sidelines. But so far, I have been fairly positive: that we're getting life, and this kind of large-scale business activity, to the countryside. That might, and hopefully will, attract other businesses around it as well. And of course, for a small municipality like this, it feels like a real boost."
As construction continues, Muhos faces a difficult balancing act between the economic opportunities offered by Google's investment and concerns over forests, environmental rules and future energy demand.

British aircraft carrier ‘opens fire’ at night
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:16:14 BST
18:16:14 KST

British aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth has conducted night-time gunnery training as the warship continues work to restore full operational and warfighting readiness following its recent docking period, according to the ship.
The carrier released imagery of its gunners firing during darkness, describing the serial as part of the routine training required to keep weapons crews prepared to operate the ship’s defensive systems at sea.
In an update from HMS Queen Elizabeth, the ship said: “HMSQNLZ’s gunners breathe fire into the night! Night shoots are essential training exercises ensuring our gunners maintain their operational readiness.”
@HMSQNLZ‘s gunners breathe fire into the night! Night shoots are essential training exercises ensuring our gunners maintain their operational readiness.#NightShoot #OperationalReadiness #NavalTraining pic.twitter.com/Yf1eJkEqUg
— HMS Queen Elizabeth (@HMSQNLZ) October 4, 2026
The firing forms part of a broader programme of activity aboard the 65,000-tonne carrier as its crew progressively rebuild the range of skills required for front-line operations after a recertification docking period. Recent weeks have seen the ship conducting a series of training milestones covering aviation, replenishment at sea and the routine work required to bring both the vessel and its company back towards operational readiness.
On 24 September, the carrier reported that a Wildcat AH1 helicopter from 847 Naval Air Squadron had landed aboard, describing the event as the beginning of the return of aviation operations after the docking period. The ship said at the time: “The process of integrating aircraft into operations at sea is a complex one, but landing a Wildcat AH1 from @847NAS marked the start of our return to Warfighting readiness after our recent recertification Docking Period.”
That aviation milestone followed the carrier’s first replenishment at sea since 2024 earlier in September, when HMS Queen Elizabeth worked with Royal Fleet Auxiliary tanker RFA Tidespring. During a replenishment at sea, ships manoeuvre in close formation while fuel or other supplies are transferred between vessels, requiring bridge, seamanship and engineering teams to work together while both ships remain underway.
HMS Queen Elizabeth said following the serial: “@HMSQNLZ carried out its first replenishment at sea (RAS) since 2024! @RFATidespring provided fuel and our bridge and seamanship teams gained experience as we contjnue on our journey to warfighting readiness.”
The carrier has been rebuilding several core areas of activity in parallel, ranging from aviation integration and replenishment to shipboard weapons training.
HMS Queen Elizabeth is one of two Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carriers operated by the Royal Navy alongside HMS Prince of Wales. The ships were designed primarily around carrier aviation, with F-35B Lightning aircraft providing their principal offensive capability, while helicopters and shipboard systems support surveillance, anti-submarine warfare, logistics and force protection.
