‘We had 20 guns guarding 250 people’: Givati trainees recall fighting in Sderot on Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:16:10 UTC
18:16:10 KST

The prayers that morning, Oct. 7, 2023, were interrupted by gunfire from the street. Three soldiers from hesder yeshivas, religious institutions that combine Torah study with IDF service, were just three weeks away from completing their combat training in the Givati Brigade when they sprang into action.
Armed with their personal rifles and still wearing white shirts for the Simchat Torah holiday, they fought their first battles in the streets of Sderot. Nearly three years later, they returned to a short video that captured only a fraction of the fighting they experienced that day.
Lt. B., 23, from Sha’arei Tikva, Lt. Matan, 23, from Be’er Sheva, and reserve Staff Sgt. Nehorai, 23, from Haifa, enlisted in March 2023 in Givati’s hesder track.
Their original plan was to return to the army after Simchat Torah for another 21 days of training, culminating in the march marking the end of their combat course.
“Before we went home, we asked our platoon commander, just this once, to let us leave without our weapons,” Nehorai recalled. “We knew we would be at the yeshiva celebrating Simchat Torah. We wanted to dance and celebrate properly without carrying them.”
But the commander refused.
“He said, ‘No chance, because of the tiny possibility that you might encounter a terrorist,’” Nehorai said.
On the morning of Oct. 7, they understood just how consequential that decision had been.
‘There are gunshots outside’
The three met as planned at the Afikei Da’at yeshiva for early Saturday morning prayers.
“Then there was a siren,” B. recalled. “We weren’t particularly alarmed. In Sderot, we were used to sirens.”
But when the alerts kept coming, they began to suspect something was different.
“It became very intense,” Matan said. “We saw huge numbers of launches from Gaza, quantities we had never seen in Sderot. We understood that something strange was happening.”
The three readied their weapons. Then a civilian burst into the synagogue and shouted: “There are gunshots outside.”
They immediately ran out.
“We advanced about 200 meters and encountered 15 armed terrorists wearing headbands,” Matan said.
“The pickup stopped right in front of me, outside the police station,” B. recalled, referring to the vehicle whose images became some of the first indications for many Israelis that terrorists had penetrated deep into Israeli territory.
“Nothing in training can prepare you for a moment like that,” Nehorai said. “When we opened fire, for a moment I still felt like I was at a shooting range on a training base.”
At first, they hoped that street battle would be the only fighting they encountered that day.
“Hours later, when we returned to the yeshiva, someone from our platoon mentioned terrorists at the party near Re’im and said something extreme was happening,” Nehorai recalled.
“Until then, I thought it was one pickup truck with 15 terrorists at the police station. That was the first time I got a slightly broader picture of what was happening. The switch happens very quickly.”
‘We had weapons, Shabbat clothes and 30 rounds’
After the initial battle, the soldiers split up to carry out different missions across Sderot.
“At the end of the day, we had weapons, Sabbath clothes and 30 rounds. We didn’t have much,” B. said. “After the intense part of the fighting at the police station, before the terrorists barricaded themselves inside and larger forces arrived, we began to understand what was happening.”
Some of the soldiers moved to secure one side of the city. Others helped evacuate families from homes hit by mortar fire, guarded the yeshiva or directed police officers and soldiers toward locations in a city they knew well.
“In everything we did, we already felt the meaning of it, how important we were,” B. said.
He remembers one yeshiva student approaching him in tears because his wife and baby were near the market, where terrorists had been reported.
“I ran with him to his house while carrying my weapon,” B. said. “After he went inside, I realized I was alone. I saw people still walking around outside, so I pushed them back into their homes while moving wounded people and bodies out of the way.”
B. eventually returned to the yeshiva, where he reunited with Matan and Nehorai.
“The head of the yeshiva called our company commander and asked him to let us stay there for the time being,” Nehorai said. “We couldn’t leave the city anyway, and they needed someone to protect them. We had maybe 20 guns guarding around 250 people.”
The following day, Oct. 8, the three reported back to their base and, together with the rest of their unit, moved farther south, closer to Gaza.
“Suddenly we had commanders again. We weren’t each fighting on our own,” Matan said. “I felt safer, like part of an army. We were fighting the way we had been taught.”
As they waited in staging areas ahead of the ground offensive in Gaza, B. remembers a sense of anticipation among the soldiers.
“This is what we enlisted for,” he said. “Throughout training, they talked to us about combat, and now it was becoming real. I was waiting to join the fighting, especially after what we had experienced and seen the terrorists do while we were fighting in Sderot.”
Matan said he did not feel afraid at the time.
“I was waiting for it,” he said. “But when I went in again later as a commander, with my own soldiers, that’s when I was afraid, mainly for them, because I was responsible for bringing them home healthy and safe.”
Seeing the battle from the outside
Before they entered Gaza, the three came across footage showing the first moments of their fighting in Sderot.
The short video, which circulated widely online, had been filmed by a civilian they did not know who ran toward them that morning.
“Do you see terrorists?” Matan can be heard shouting from a crouched position, with Nehorai covering him and the terrorists’ pickup truck ahead of them.
“Every time I watch that video, it brings back a lot,” Nehorai said. “Suddenly you see everything in a tangible way. I connected the puzzle from all the moments I remembered before: who was hit by a bullet at which point, which direction the police officer ran.”
“It’s interesting to look at my face and expression too, to see how I reacted in that situation, when the stress and adrenaline were extremely high,” he added. “Those are things you don’t notice while it is actually happening. Only when you look back do you understand what was going on there.”
‘There was no other option’
Nearly three years have passed since that day.
B. is nearing the end of his role as a platoon commander in Givati’s Shaked Battalion. He said the war played a decisive role in his decision to remain on the command track.
“That was the major factor,” he said. “It was obvious that we would stay as long as there was a war and contribute whatever we could.”
Throughout his command role, he said, the responsibility for his soldiers remained constantly on his mind.
“At the end of the day, your mission is to bring them home healthy and safe to their families,” he said. “It isn’t simple, but because of that responsibility, you have to succeed. There is no other option.”
Matan completed his service as deputy company commander in a squad-commanders course at the IDF’s School for Infantry Professions and Squad Commanders. He is now in the final stage of the hesder program and is expected to return soon to his yeshiva for three months of study.
“The war played a large part in my decision to become a commander, and even more so the friends who were killed and the feeling that I needed to continue their path,” he said.
“I trained the next generation of commanders. I wanted them to finish their training with the feeling that we are part of something bigger: a people, an army, 2,000 years of history. When you see things that way, the small difficulties look different.”
Nehorai has already completed his regular service and last served as a platoon commander’s radio operator.
“Since Oct. 7, we were fighting nonstop,” he said. “During our platoon’s last entry into Gaza, the force hit an explosive device. Four friends were wounded: the platoon commander, the sergeant and two other soldiers.”
Afterward, the unit spent much of its final month on base, giving the soldiers an opportunity to begin processing what they had experienced.
“Suddenly we had time to digest everything we had been through,” Nehorai said. “We understood our mission. It’s an incredible feeling to be part of something so enormous.”

Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te condemned the incident and slammed China for its blatant disregard of human rights and suppression of personal freedoms, in what he labelled a “barbaric” act.
The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president's family for China.
Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while she was in the United States, according to the FBI.
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges of working for China as an unregistered agent, Assistant US State Attorney Bill Essayli announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he added.
She was arrested as she was departing the country for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and an attorney who represents her could not be determined. She is due to appear in federal court in Los Angeles on Monday.
Taiwan’s Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te’s relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression.”
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts, which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families, as such behaviour should not be tolerated in the civilised world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory.
Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the “People's Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan.”
China considers him a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace.”
While in office, Lai has dramatically ramped up defence spending for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defence expenditure from 3% to 5% of GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defence system.

European Muslim group expresses concern over anti-Muslim incidents in Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

The European Muslim League has expressed concern over recent incidents targeting Lithuania’s Muslim community and Islamic religious symbols, calling on authorities and society to stand against hatred and intimidation.
In a statement released over the weekend, the organisation cited two incidents: the possible public burning of a Quran in Vilnius and an incident in which bikers disrupted Muslim prayers near a mosque in Kaunas’ Ramybės Park by making noise, displaying a pig’s head and playing loud music.
The league welcomed the response from Lithuanian authorities, including a warning from the State Security Department about increased incitement to hatred against Muslims in the public sphere.
It also cited President Gitanas Nausėda’s statement that the incidents could be more than isolated acts and may have been commissioned.
Further reading
“When institutions act to defend religious freedom, they are not protecting only one community, but the fundamental values of society as a whole,” European Muslim League Chairman Alfredo Maiolese said.
The organisation said combating Islamophobia should not be confused with restricting legitimate debate in a democratic society. At the same time, it said issues including immigration, integration and security should not be used as tools for intimidation, humiliation or incitement to hatred.
The statement comes amid a broader debate in Lithuania over immigration policy.
Several hundred people gathered Saturday in Vilnius’ Kudirkos Square to protest what organisers described as “mass immigration”. More than 100 people held a counterprotest across the street, expressing opposition to the rally.
Further reading
According to Lithuania’s Migration Department, 226,999 foreign nationals held residence permits in the country in September. The largest groups were citizens of Ukraine, with 80,300 residents, followed by Belarus with 47,800, Russia with 13,200, Uzbekistan with 12,600 and India with 9,400.
The European Muslim League is a nongovernmental organisation founded in Italy in 2010. It says its aims include presenting Islam as a religion of peace, respect and coexistence, promoting intercultural and interfaith dialogue, and helping prevent religious conflicts.

The United States confirmed on Oct. 4 that it has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from the British airbase of RAF Fairford, with officials telling U.S. media that the move was linked to “new threats.”
Police were called to the base in southwest England on Sept. 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.
The scare prompted a counter-terrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but “a quantity of petrol was recovered,” according to counter-terrorism police.

An unidentified U.S. official told CNN that the bombers were moved after “an unspecified new threat,” with the source calling the latest threat a “real world incident.”
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the U.K. hit record highs this week.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.

Kyiv Rolls Out 12+ .50-Cal Turrets to Hunt Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:15:25 UTC
18:15:25 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kyiv Rolls Out 12+ .50-Cal Turrets to Hunt Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones
Ukraine has deployed more than 12 automated gun turrets in Kyiv to counter Russian jet-powered drones, with another eight systems set to be installed across the Kyiv region as Russia increasingly uses faster UAVs in attacks on the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the deployment on October 4 during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
“We have started installing turrets. More than 12 have already been installed in the capital, and now another eight ‘fifties’ will additionally be installed in the Kyiv region,” Zelenskyy said. The systems are automated combat modules designed for .50-caliber machine guns.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is developing a combined approach to air defense as Russia adjusts its strike tactics and increases the use of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles alongside conventional Shahed-type UAVs.
According to the Ukrainian president, Ukrainian forces currently intercept approximately 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed-type drones. The interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is lower, at roughly 50% to 70%.
Aircraft are also being used against the faster drones, including Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine is currently working to secure additional weapons suitable for those interception missions.
Jet-powered drones pose a different challenge from propeller-driven Shahed-type UAVs because of their higher speed, reducing the time available for detection, tracking, and engagement.
The announcement came during Merz’s visit to Kyiv on October 4. During the visit, Germany also announced a new support package for Ukraine worth more than €1.3 billion, including funding for weapons and energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

Russia Builds Giant Hangars Near Moscow. Here’s What They Could Hide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:15:16 UTC
18:15:16 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Builds Giant Hangars Near Moscow. Here’s What They Could Hide
Russia is nearing completion of several large aircraft hangars at the Ramenskoye airfield near Moscow, with their dimensions and location suggesting they could support testing, maintenance, or modernization of Russia’s Tu-160, Tu-95, and Tu-22M3 strategic bombers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
New satellite imagery published by the AviVector analytical group on October 4 shows significant progress on several large aircraft hangars under construction at the Ramenskoye airfield near Moscow. The structures were first identified under construction in March 2026.
The largest building measures approximately 100 by 230 meters (328 by 755 feet) and stands about 33 meters (108 feet) high. It is divided into three hangar sections, each roughly 77 meters (253 feet) wide. An adjoining structure measures about 17 by 220 meters (56 by 722 feet), while a second major building covers approximately 90 by 220 meters (295 by 722 feet).
The scale of the main structure exceeds what would normally be required simply to shelter aircraft. Each of its three sections is around 21 meters (69 feet) wider than the maximum wingspan of a Tu-160, Russia’s largest operational bomber, while the building’s depth exceeds the aircraft’s length by roughly 46 meters (151 feet).
The 33-meter height is also about 2.5 times the height of the Tu-160, potentially providing sufficient space for cranes, elevated work platforms, and other equipment used during aircraft maintenance, testing, or modernization.
The construction site is connected by road to the Gromov Flight Research Institute, although satellite imagery currently shows no direct taxiway linking the new buildings to the airfield’s runway.
The imagery also shows lighter metal-framed hangars nearby. Unlike reinforced aircraft shelters, these structures would provide little protection against potential drone or missile strikes.
Ramenskoye, located in Zhukovsky in the Moscow region, is part of the Gromov Flight Research Institute’s aviation testing complex and hosts experimental, state, and civilian aviation operations. Zhukovsky International Airport, which opened in 2016, operates from the same airfield.
The site is also used by Russian aircraft manufacturers for flight-testing programs. Sukhoi facilities at Zhukovsky have supported testing of the Su-57 fighter, while Yakovlev uses the complex for certification work involving the MC-21 airliner and the Russian-built version of the Superjet.
Tupolev also maintains testing and research facilities at the site. Its programs include experimental and upgraded versions of the Tu-160M, Tu-95MS, and Tu-22M3—the same bomber families that the dimensions of the new hangars could accommodate.
However, the buildings’ purpose has not been independently confirmed. Another possibility is that the construction is connected to the expansion of the permanent exhibition complex previously used for the MAKS International Aviation and Space Salon.
The MAKS exhibition grounds are located immediately next to the construction site. The complex covers more than 42 hectares, including over 40,000 square meters of indoor exhibition space and more than 45,000 square meters dedicated to outdoor aircraft displays.
The proximity of the new buildings to those facilities leaves both aviation testing and exhibition-related use as possible explanations for the construction. Satellite imagery alone does not establish the final purpose of the structures.
Earlier, Russian Tu-160, Tu-95MS, and Tu-22M3 strategic bombers were spotted at Ramenskoye alongside major new construction, with the activity assessed at the time as more likely linked to testing, modernization, and exhibition preparations than to a permanent bomber deployment.

Another appeal against shutdown of ex-ILVA furnaces rejected
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:14:36 CEST
18:14:36 KST

A Milan court on Monday rejected a
second petition against an order for the furnaces of the
troubled former ILVA steelworks in Taranto to be shut down by
the end of this month.
                                    
The government-appointed administrators of the plant and AdI
S.p.A., the company that owns it, had requested a suspension
pending a decision by the supreme the Court of Cassation on the
appeal against the closure of the facility's hot area.
                                    
The Cassation is set to hold a hearing on the case on October
20.
                                    
The original decision was made in July, when a Milan court
upheld a motion presented on health grounds by members of a
parents' association and a child with a rare genetic mutation
and said that activity at the hot area must stop within three
months unless all the asbestos on the site is removed and
measures to bring particulate emissions within safe limits are
taken.
                                    
The ruling ramped up existing uncertainty about the future of
the plant and implementation of a plan to decarbonize it and
make it electric, with fears thousands of jobs could be lost.
                                    
Italy's steel federation Federacciai said in August that its
board has tasked its president, Antonio Gozzi, to express an
interest in taking over the former ILVA steelworks with the
authorities on behalf of a consortium of Italian companies.
                                    
Premier Giorgia Meloni's government has not ruled out State
involvement.
                                    
Indian group Jindal, Czech group CE industries, and US-based
private investment group Flacks have also expressed interest in
buying the plant.
                                    
The Taranto factory, once Europe's biggest steelworks, has been
dogged by economic problems in recent years and linked to high
cancer rates in the Puglia port city.
                                    
ADI was put into State-controlled administration early in 2024
after ArcelorMittal's ownership of the group ended
acrimoniously.

German spy chief warns of violent conflict risk with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:14:27 UTC
18:14:27 KST

Ayhan Simsek
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia, the head of the country’s foreign intelligence service warned Monday, saying Moscow now treats Berlin as a main adversary.
 
Martin Jaeger, president of the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, told parliament’s intelligence committee that the confrontation with Russia has taken on a new and more dangerous quality.
 
“Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia. The attempted attack in Leipzig is only one example of that,” he said, referring to an attempted drone strike on a Ukrainian cargo plane in August.
 
“No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany,” Jaeger said. “We did not seek this confrontation. Russia is forcing it upon us and sees us as a main adversary, because we refuse to accept its revisionist, expansionist policies and its war of aggression against Ukraine.”
 
His remarks came a day after Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv and announced new measures to support Ukraine. Only hours before that trip, Russia’s Foreign Ministry had urged foreign diplomats and other visitors to stay clear of the Ukrainian capital, above all military sites and government buildings. Drone attacks on Kyiv continued during the visit.
 
Russia’s ‘shadow war’ against Germany
 
Jaeger told lawmakers that, according to the BND’s assessment, Germany has become a main obstacle to “Russian hegemonic power projection in Europe” and therefore a prime target for Russian operations.
 
He accused Moscow of stepping up increasingly aggressive covert activities by its services in and against Germany.
 
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us,” Jaeger said, referring to sabotage attempts and other hybrid attacks. “This undeclared war cannot be grasped in conventional military or legal categories. Germany has not declared a constitutional state of defense, and yet we are under attack.”
 
Jaeger said the intelligence services need new powers, and that a government draft law would strengthen the BND as Germany’s first line of defense.
 
“Russian intelligence agencies operate with a high degree of professionalism and ruthlessness,” he said. “The threat of attacks against targets in Germany remains real and present. We must counter this. That also requires a fundamental change in the Federal Intelligence Service.”
 
Russia has not issued an immediate statement in response to the BND chief’s warnings. Moscow has in the past dismissed allegations of hybrid attacks in Europe as baseless, accusing Western governments of using such claims to justify higher military spending and sustain support for Ukraine.

European Diplomats Defy Russian Warning and Stay in Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

The German, Italian, Spanish and Swedish embassies in Ukraine said on social media that they would remain in Kyiv despite warnings issued by the Russian Foreign Ministry against foreign diplomats.
The four diplomatic missions said they and other heads of diplomatic missions in Kyiv had taken note of the Russian MFA’s threat toward diplomats and foreign citizens in Ukraine.
“Russia is bound by the Vienna Convention and international humanitarian law. We stay in Kyiv,” the embassies said in their social media posts.
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová said all European Union member state embassies would continue operating in Kyiv despite the Russian threats. The Polish and Estonian foreign ministries issued the same message.
The European Commission also responded to the Russian warnings, saying the EU would continue supporting Ukraine and increase pressure on the aggressor country.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on September 30 that debris had been discovered on the grounds of an embassy belonging to one of the Western countries in the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district following Russian strikes on Kyiv.
Russia has also struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, with the attack taking place as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital on an unannounced visit to demonstrate Germany’s support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit the key crossing, marking the fourth straight day of Russian attacks on bridges used by tens of thousands of people traveling between the two banks of the city. Video showed vehicles crossing the bridge when the drone struck the roadway and exploded, while Klitschko said two people were injured.
The attack occurred shortly after Merz reached Kyiv, as Ukraine enters one of its most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s largest provider of military aid since Merz took office in May 2025, overtaking the United States as American support has declined.
Kyiv has faced almost continuous Russian attacks involving new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, with the intensifying campaign increasingly disrupting daily life and threatening the city’s power supply this winter.
During his visit, Merz announced that Germany would finance joint production of drones intended to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, saying recent technical advances were allowing production to move faster.
“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” Merz said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”
Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly while Merz was in Kyiv, including during a visit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building. A Russian drone attack on the building killed two people the previous week.
Zelenskyy told Merz that residents of Kyiv were enduring “terrible nights and days” because of the continuing attacks and called Russia’s adversaries “absolute barbarians”.
Merz said the destruction he saw demonstrated the futility of the war and stressed the need for continued support for Ukraine.
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” Merz said, adding that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. He also warned, “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us.”
Russian forces had previously damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly attacked the Southern Bridge. Although both crossings remain standing, the repeated strikes and possibility of further attacks have led city authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of Kyiv’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, resulting in temporary closures and major traffic jams.
Severe damage to the bridges could produce a logistical crisis for Kyiv, a city of 3 million people whose Dnipro crossings were last destroyed on a large scale when Nazi German forces withdrew in 1943. More than one-third of Kyiv’s residents live on the left bank, while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is located on the right bank.
The bridge strikes are part of a wider Russian campaign targeting civilian and industrial infrastructure across Ukraine. Recent attacks have hit logistics centers, railway lines, data centers, medical storage facilities and steel plants, while Russia has also maintained a sustained assault on Ukraine’s energy system that is expected to intensify during the winter.
“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference with Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”
Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel on Saturday against staying in or traveling to Ukraine, saying those who ignored the warning would bear responsibility for any consequences.
A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.
“The EU delegation is staying,” Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”
Some pro-war commentators in Moscow reacted positively to the continuation of Russian strikes after Merz arrived. Prominent pro-war commentator Sergei Markov wrote that Russia had previously paused attacks on Kyiv during visits by European politicians but no longer did so.
The visit was Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been one of Kyiv’s most vocal European supporters and has repeatedly warned about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other countries.
Germany formally accused Moscow last month of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a major logistics hub for Western military aid to Ukraine.
At home, however, Merz is facing increasing opposition to his support for Ukraine as his approval ratings decline. Germany’s far left and far right have questioned continued assistance to Kyiv and called for Berlin to reduce its aid.
The pressure has increased as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made major electoral gains.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel criticized Merz in a social media post over his visit and additional financial support for Ukraine, while arguing that Germany was facing a severe energy crisis and lacked money for pension and health insurance funds.
“Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis,” Weidel wrote.

Estonia to Move Troops to Russian Border Under “Active Defense” Strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:12:54 UTC
18:12:54 KST

Estonia is moving some of its troops closer to the Russian border as part of a new “active defense” strategy.
The Financial Times reports that the main units of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade, the country’s main combat force, will be permanently stationed in Jõhvi instead of Tapa.
Jõhvi is located about 50 km from the Russian border, while Tapa is approximately 130 km away.
To accommodate the troops in Jõhvi, Estonia is building new military facilities. The country is also constructing a military base in Narva that will be able to accommodate up to 1,000 troops.
Around 200 troops are expected to be stationed there in peacetime, with up to 800 more deployed in the event of war.
The changes are part of a broader review by Estonia’s Ministry of Defense of its military strategy, as the country shifts to an “active defense” concept introduced in May 2026.
The concept calls for defending the country directly from the border and attempting to stop an enemy at the earliest stage of an attack. As part of this approach, Estonia is acquiring modern weapons and long-range artillery, including HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems.
Militarnyi previously reported that, after four months of training, Estonian troops carried out their first live-fire exercises using the country’s own HIMARS rocket systems.
The wartime structure of the Estonian Defense Forces includes more than 43,000 positions. About 4,200 are assigned to active-duty personnel, while the rest are reservists and members of the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit).
As of 2026, the Estonian Division forms the core of the land component of the Estonian Defense Forces. It is the country’s largest land formation, reports directly to the Commander of the Defense Forces, and is integrated into NATO’s command structure.
The division includes the 1st and 2nd Infantry Brigades, a headquarters and signals battalion, an ISTAR reconnaissance battalion, and artillery, engineering, and logistics battalions.
The division’s main maneuver unit remains the 1st Infantry Brigade. It comprises the Scouts Battalion, the Kalev and Viru infantry battalions, an air defense battalion, a combat support battalion, headquarters and signals companies, and an anti-tank company.
The brigade also trains conscripts, who are later transferred to the reserve.
The 2nd Infantry Brigade is primarily responsible for the southeastern part of the country. In peacetime, it consists of a headquarters in Tartu, the Kuperjanov Battalion in Võru, a combat support battalion, and a support and communications company. In wartime, the brigade is expanded with reserve units.
In addition to the division, the Estonian Defense Forces include the Cyber Command, Support Command, Military Police, Special Operations Forces, and other units.

South Korea says North deliberately planted mines in demilitarized zone that wounded 3 soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:12:18 UTC
18:12:18 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
South Korea said Monday that North Korea had "deliberately planted" two mines inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that exploded last month and wounded three South Korean soldiers, reiterating its demand for an apology from Pyongyang.
Pyongyang has denied involvement in the Sept. 21 incident and slammed Seoul over what it called “cheap tricks,” urging South Korea to stop attempts to “tarnish the image” of North Korea.
“The military strongly calls on North Korea to offer a sincere apology to the South Korean soldiers injured in the mine blast and immediately remove the mines it planted in violation of the armistice agreement,” Lt. Gen. Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), told a news conference.
The Korean Peninsula has remained divided since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
The JCS said a joint operation with the UN Command (UNC) successfully removed additional mines planted near the blast site.
It added that the mines involved in the explosion “contained TNT and thermosetting resin components consistent with North Korean mines” and that fragments “recovered from the injured soldiers have also been found to be identical to North Korean plastic antipersonnel mines previously recovered from the Imjin River.”
The JCS said the mines were discovered about 10 meters (33 feet) south of the Military Demarcation Line, suggesting they had been “planted” there rather than swept into the area, Yonhap News reported.

Spain's prime minister has called early elections amid the housing crisis
Kyiv • UNN
Pedro Sánchez has called early elections in Spain for November 29 following protests over the housing crisis. Polls predict an advantage for the center-right.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced early elections for November 29 on Monday. The vote could mark the end of the last major socialist government in the EU and remove one of U.S. President Donald Trump’s leading European critics from the political forefront. Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Sánchez was prompted to call early elections by the housing crisis, which sparked nationwide protests after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in Madrid from the apartment where she had lived since 1956. On Friday, lawmakers rejected two bills intended to resolve the problem.
Sánchez’s standing had already been weakened by corruption scandals that undermined the position of his Socialist Party. This summer, the prime minister faced harsh criticism over the migration crisis in the enclave of Ceuta.
According to polls, Spaniards may elect a government led by the center-right People’s Party, which is currently supported by 34% of voters, compared with 26% for the Socialist Party. The People’s Party will likely be forced to form a coalition with the far-right Vox party, which, according to the publication, could win 18% of the vote.
In his address to the nation, Sánchez warned about the growing popularity of far-right forces.
You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you want to play in this era and what role Spain should play. You must decide whether to join the far-right wave, which leads to regression everywhere it comes to power, or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility
Over the past year, Sánchez has gained recognition on the international stage as one of the Western leaders who most strongly criticized U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over their policies regarding the conflicts in Gaza and Iran.

Spanish PM calls early election after housing crisis defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:10:48 UTC
18:10:48 KST

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez arrives to attend the EU Summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on June 18, 2026. (AFP File Photo)
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Oct. 5 called a snap election for Nov. 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
The defeat on Oct. 2 was just the latest political setback for the Socialist premier, one of the few European prime ministers from the left still in power.
“To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people,” Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was “to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament.”
Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Oct. 3 to demand affordable housing.
The government’s proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain’s parliament.
The defeat infuriated those protesting the country’s increasingly expensive housing market and underscored the difficulties his minority coalition government faces in passing legislation.
Spain has been operating under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan passed by Sanchez’s government, for several years.
The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.
Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up more than a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.
Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the European Union.
Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent, according to real estate website Idealista.
Abascal’s eviction catalyzed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.
The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 percent, say housing campaigners.
The backlash led the new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.
The housing bills Sanchez’s leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts, on whose support the government relies, voted against them, arguing they were hastily drawn up and would make the housing crisis worse.
Sanchez defended his government’s record in his address, pointing out that under his leadership Spain’s economy has grown faster than those of its main European peers.
But after eight years in power, Sanchez is also under pressure from corruption scandals involving people close to him, including his wife and top figures in his Socialist Party.
While polls put the PP ahead, they suggest the party would fall short of an absolute majority in parliament and would need the support of far-right Vox to govern.

Leaders in California have denounced Donald Trump as “reckless” and “deranged” after the US president suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego – two liberal cities in the blue state that has been a frequent target of his administration.
At a rally in ruby red Nebraska on Monday night, Trump told supporters that he hoped to see a “tremendous victory” in the fast-approaching November midterm elections. He then suggested high prices due to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”.
“They can take out a city,” Trump said in Grand Island. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded.
“It’ll be over very soon,” Trump said of the war.
The governor and the cities’ mayors quickly condemned the comments. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.”
Newsom, a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump over his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal. None of this is. And we will continue to remind folks of that every day.”
Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, assailed the president for making what she called “irresponsible threats” that “could potentially compromise” the safety of America’s second-largest city.
“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” she said in a statement.
Todd Gloria, the mayor of San Diego, said his city was “not collateral damage” in the president’s war. “We are not expendable. And we are never a “small price to pay,” he wrote on X “Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”
San Diego, the nation’s eighth-largest city, is home to critical US military infrastructure.
Online, the comments – part of a rambling, nearly hour-and-a-half speech – set off a debate about what the president actually meant. Was it a crude joke about two blue cities or had he, accidentally perhaps, disclosed confidential intelligence about potential Iranian targets?
Some conservative activists argued that Trump, in his elliptical way of speaking, was referring to high gas prices when he argued that it was a “small price to pay”, and not the capacity of Iran to “take out” a US city.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US defence officials have previously stated that Iran currently lacks the capability to launch a direct missile attack on the US mainland.
Trump has argued in previous speeches that allowing Iran to develop a nuclear weapon would threaten US cities. In his last state of the union speech he claimed that Iran was working to build missiles that would “soon” reach US soil.
In Nebraska, where an unexpectedly close Senate race has rattled Republicans, Trump insisted that he was “doing great” and urged supporters to pretend like his name was on the ballot when the vote in November. But in California, where Steve Hilton, the Republican gubernatorial candidate endorsed by Trump, is seeking an upset, the president’s comments were unwelcome.
“Thirteen million Californians call LA and San Diego counties home,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor who has sought to take up the anti-Trump mantle carried by the outgoing Newsom. “Their lives are not a ‘small price to pay’ or a punchline for Donald Trump.”

'New pace, new height': PM Modi-Parmelin talks put India-Switzerland ties on fast track
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:06:29 UTC
18:06:29 KST

File photo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss President Guy Parmelin at Hyderabad House for bilateral talks, in New Delhi on Monday
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss Confederation president Guy Parmelin held wide-ranging talks in New Delhi on Monday, with the two sides discussing ways to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, mobility, infrastructure, defence, nuclear energy and critical technologies.The talks came as India and Switzerland seek to build on the India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), which entered into force last October and is set to complete a year of implementation this week.
Addressing a joint press statement after the talks, PM Modi said the relationship between India and Switzerland had gained fresh momentum and highlighted the two countries' cooperation in innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology.“India-Switzerland friendship is centuries-old... Innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology are strong pillars of our foundation today. With the Summit today, we are going to give a new pace and height to our partnership,” PM Modi said.
India eyes $100 billion investment under TEPA
PM Modi said TEPA was an ambitious blueprint for investment, innovation, jobs and shared prosperity and set out a target of attracting $100 billion in investment into India and creating 1 million direct jobs over the next 15 years.
“I am very happy to welcome the president of Switzerland to India. First of all, I would like to appreciate his commitment to India-Switzerland relations. With his personal support, last October we implemented a historic Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement between India and the European Free Trade Association, or EFTA, countries,” PM Modi said.
“This is India's first FTA with any economic bloc in Europe,” he added.The Prime Minister said India and Switzerland had also taken decisions to increase market access for Indian exports to Switzerland and facilitate investment between the two countries.He said the measures would support exports of Indian agricultural products, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods, while encouraging Swiss investment in sectors including biotechnology, life sciences, banking, insurance, food processing and sustainability.
Defence, nuclear energy and infrastructure on agenda
The talks also expanded beyond trade and investment, with PM Modi saying the two countries had identified new opportunities for military exchanges and defence production cooperation.“We also agreed to further deepen nuclear energy cooperation,” he said.PM Modi pointed to projects such as the Varanasi ropeway, Noida's Jewar airport and railway and tunnelling projects in mountainous regions as examples of India-Switzerland infrastructure cooperation.The two sides also signed an agreement covering transport, mobility and infrastructure, with PM Modi inviting Swiss infrastructure companies to increase investment in India and participate in capacity-building, design and manufacturing.People-to-people ties were another focus of the discussions. PM Modi said the Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement and Young Professionals Agreement signed during the visit would create new opportunities in Switzerland for Indian students, researchers, professionals and young people.
Parmelin calls visit a ‘stepping stone’
Parmelin, who is on a three-day State visit to India, described the trip as an opportunity to further strengthen the long-standing relationship between the two countries.He said India and Switzerland shared democratic values as well as trust and mutual respect, and described his visit as a “stepping stone” towards deepening their partnership.The Swiss president's visit is also significant for TEPA, which was signed in March 2024 after nearly 16 years of negotiations and came into force in October 2025. The EFTA countries — Switzerland, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — have committed to investing $100 billion in India over 15 years under the agreement.Parmelin is scheduled to attend the second India-EFTA Prosperity Summit on October 7, marking the first anniversary of TEPA's implementation.
Swiss business delegation accompanies Parmelin
Parmelin arrived in New Delhi earlier on Monday and was accorded a ceremonial reception at Rashtrapati Bhavan before visiting Rajghat to pay tribute to Mahatma Gandhi. He was accompanied by a delegation of senior officials and business representatives.External affairs minister S Jaishankar also met Parmelin and said he appreciated the Swiss president's commitment to deepening the India-Switzerland partnership and building on the promise of TEPA.
According to the ministry of external aaffairs, Switzerland is India's largest trade and investment partner among the four EFTA countries.More than 330 Swiss companies currently operate in India across sectors including engineering, services, precision instruments, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, while Indian companies in Switzerland have a presence in areas including IT, pharmaceuticals and machinery.Parmelin will also meet President Droupadi Murmu, who is scheduled to host a banquet in his honour. The visit is his first State visit to India and his second trip to the country this year, after his participation in the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February.

Qatar partners with Euroclear to widen foreign access to government debt market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:05:03 UTC
18:05:03 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Qatar’s central bank and Euroclear, a Brussels-based provider of securities settlement and custody services, announced Monday a collaboration to establish an international settlement link aimed at widening foreign investor access to the country’s domestic government debt market.
The initiative will allow international investors to access Qatari government bonds and sukuk, or Islamic bonds, through Euroclear’s infrastructure, while giving issuers access to a broader and more diversified pool of capital.
The collaboration is expected to boost liquidity, improve market efficiency and deepen international capital flows into Qatar. It aligns with the country’s Third Financial Sector Strategy and Third National Development Strategy for 2024-2030.
The link will cover eligible Qatari riyal-denominated conventional government bonds and sukuk.
Euroclear Bank will act as the issuer central securities depository, while Edaa, Qatar’s central securities depository, will serve as the investor depository for local investors. Qatar Central Bank will act as issuer and paying agent.
Euroclear Chief Executive Valerie Urbain said the collaboration would “simplify market access, enhance liquidity and strengthen Qatar’s appeal to global investors.”

German defense company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian company Roboneers have entered into a strategic partnership to jointly develop and integrate unmanned ground systems.
The agreement was signed in Kyiv on October 4 in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
That same day, Zelensky and Merz attended the Ukrainian-German Business Forum, where the two sides reached several agreements covering the defense industry, unmanned systems, air defense, and energy.
The new agreement between ARX Robotics and Roboneers provides for deeper technical integration of the two companies’ systems, as well as joint research and development activities.
“Together with Roboneers, we are providing Ukrainian forces with a powerful yet intelligent fleet of unmanned ground systems at scale,” Witfeld said.
Under the partnership, the combat experience gained from operating robotic platforms in Ukraine will also be used to develop future ground systems for the armed forces of Western countries.
ARX Robotics supplies Ukraine’s Defense Forces with GEREON-family unmanned ground systems. In May, the company signed a contract to supply Ukraine with several hundred more of these systems, which is expected to increase the Defense Forces’ fleet fivefold. According to the company, its systems constitute the largest fleet of Western-made unmanned ground systems deployed in Ukraine.
The current agreement expands cooperation between ARX Robotics and Roboneers, which already includes the joint production of the Ukrainian Lynx Pro unmanned ground system. In June 2026, the companies announced the establishment of a joint venture, ARX Industries, as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative.
In July, soldiers from the 123rd Brigade deployed an unmanned ground system from a maritime unmanned platform onto the occupied Kinburn Spit. The operation is believed to have involved a Roboneers-produced Lynx unmanned ground system equipped with a PKT machine gun.
In September 2026, the company also codified the combat version, the ShaLynx PRO Mk.19 (M), which combines the Lynx PRO platform with the remotely controlled Shablya weapon station and a 40 mm automatic grenade launcher.
Earlier, Roboneers also integrated the Shablya MK-19 combat module onto the Volya-E unmanned ground system, transforming the logistics platform into a remotely controlled fire-support system.
The companies’ cooperation comes amid a rapid increase in the number of unmanned ground systems in the Ukrainian Defense Forces. In April, the Ministry of Defense announced plans to contract 25,000 unmanned ground systems during the first half of 2026. In July, the ministry reported that it had contracted more than 22,000 Ukrainian-made unmanned ground systems for 2026.

Ministry of Defence Sanctuary Awards
The annual Sanctuary Awards recognise outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the Ministry of Defence (MOD) estate.
The Sanctuary Awards have been recognising outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the MOD estate since 1991.
The awards celebrate and encourage group and individual efforts that benefit sustainable development, environmental and heritage conservation, utilities and resource-saving measures, sustainable construction and procurement or community awareness on land or property that the MOD owns or uses in the UK and overseas.
35th Sanctuary Awards 2026: Shortlisted entries
Winners will be announced on 17 November 2026. You can sign up for the free Sanctuary Awards 2026 live feed online.
Many congratulations to the 14 projects that have been shortlisted for the 35th Sanctuary Awards 2026:
- 507 Specialist Team Royal Engineers – A1 Steam trust, Darlington Railhead Construction Project (A1 Steam Locomotive Trust, Darlington)
- AA Wick Marsh Ranges (AA (Wick Marsh) Ranges, Fingringhoe, Colchester)
- Aldershot’s Training Area – sustaining military capability (Aldershot Military Fieldcraft Training Areas)
- Barton Stacey Flyfishing Club (Barton Stacey Training Area)
- Beckingham Cadet Training Centre – sustainable construction (Army HQ, Andover)
- Devonport Open Days (HMNB Devonport)
- Group Captain Maurice Dixon (RAF Leeming and RAF High Wycombe)
- Sq Ldr Don Earl (RAF High Wycombe)
- Exercise Druid Sacrifice (RAF Valley)
- Find it in Plymouth – supply chain resilience at Devonport (HMNB Devonport)
- FuelActive – cleaner fuel for Team Leidos’ fleet (Defence Fulfilment Centre, DM Beith, MOD Bicester, JHC FS Aldergrove, MOD Kineton, MOD Longtown, DM Gosport, HMNB Portsmouth)
- Lydd Ranges Sea Defence Project (Lydd Ranges)
- Project Life (National Armaments Director Group Bicester)
- SPINNERET – microgrids for operational energy (MOD Bovington Camp)
Nominations were sought in the following categories:
- Climate Change Resilience Award – projects or activities focused on taking action to enhance climate resilience through adaption.
- Energy Award – for energy of fuel projects that decrease energy demand, increase energy efficiency and/or increase energy resilience through sustainability.
- Environmental Enhancement Award – projects focused on wildlife, biodiversity, environmental research, or tackling pollution or contamination issues.
- Heritage Award – projects focused on archaeology, historic buildings, historic parks or gardens, landscape preservation, museum collections, or heritage education or public engagement.
- Individual Achievement Award – any individual who has made a significant personal contribution to MOD’s sustainability or conservation ambitions.
- Social Impact Award – grass-roots sustainability projects focusing on community engagement, green spaces, wellbeing or facilitating public access.
- Sustainability Improvement Award – for projects that demonstrate sustainability improvements through implementation of circular economy principles (including reducing resource consumption or waste and recycling), sustainable procurement, sustainable construction or refurbishment projects, and improvements in equipment or systems through eco design.
The Operational Capability Award will be chosen from the shortlisted nominations and awarded to the project which best delivers enhanced operational capability through sustainability and climate considerations.
And the Silver Otter Trophy will be chosen from the category winners and awarded to the best Establishment, Conservation Group or community led project or individual conservation effort on the MOD estate.
For queries please email: DIO-Sanctuary@mod.gov.uk

Swiss government backs VAT increase to fund 13th pension

Swiss government backs VAT increase to fund 13th pension
The Swiss government has supported an increase in Value-Added Tax (VAT) to pay for the 13th payment of the Swiss old-age and survivors' (AHV/AVS) pension.
On Monday, the government advocated a rise of 0.4 percentage points, from 8.1% to 8.5%, ahead of the referendum on November 29. A double majority will be required for the vote.
To fund the 13th AHV/AVS pension, which will be paid from December 1, CHF4.2 billion ($5.06 billion) will be required in 2026. This figure is expected to rise to around CHF4.5 billion in 2030 and CHF5.4 billion in 2040.
Parliament has opted for funding solely through VAT, rejecting a parallel 0.2-point increase in employees’ contributions. The 0.4-point rise in VAT will generate CHF1.5 billion per year.
+ Swiss Senate backs mixed financing for 13th pension
The reduced rate will remain at 2.6%. The VAT increase for the accommodation sector will be 0.2 percentage points, rising from 3.8% to 4%.
This change will not be sufficient in the long term. In its AHV2030 reform proposal, the government has included a scenario for additional funding for the 13th pension. Both the left and the right have voiced criticism.

British cavalry tests horses for battlefield patrols
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:01:42 BST
18:01:42 KST

The British Army has been experimenting with the use of horses for reconnaissance, patrol and security tasks in terrain where military vehicles may struggle to operate, according to imagery released by the Ministry of Defence.
Soldiers and Military Working Horses from the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took part in a mounted combat capability experiment on the Barossa training area at Sandhurst, exploring how mounted troops could support battlefield activity beyond the Regiment’s familiar ceremonial duties.
The training was conducted across difficult terrain and focused on environments where conventional vehicles could face restrictions, giving soldiers an opportunity to examine how horses might provide an alternative means of moving personnel during reconnaissance and security operations.
Images from the exercise show Household Cavalry soldiers conducting mounted patrols in pairs while using the SA80 sighting system to locate and track simulated enemy positions. The experiment focused on reconnaissance, patrol and security roles, with troops required to operate from horseback while maintaining observation of the surrounding terrain and identifying potential enemy activity.
The use of horses gives mounted personnel a different mobility profile from troops operating in vehicles, particularly across ground where access routes may be narrow, broken or otherwise unsuitable for conventional platforms. The Sandhurst activity was specifically intended to examine their use in such environments rather than establish a new Army-wide mounted combat role.
According to the MOD caption accompanying the imagery, the activity drew on lessons from international partners while exploring how mounted troops could contribute to patrol and security missions.
Military horses have historically been used for reconnaissance, transport and mounted patrols, although mechanisation removed them from most frontline roles during the 20th century. The Sandhurst experiment examined whether some of those characteristics could still have relevance in specific modern operating environments where access, terrain and mobility create problems for vehicles.
The mounted patrol serial took place on 23 September at the Barossa training area, with soldiers and horses working together to test reconnaissance and security techniques in terrain selected to challenge conventional movement.

Euro hits 17-month low as French debt fears mount and Spain heads for snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:01:38 UTC
18:01:38 KST

The euro slid to its weakest level against the US dollar since May 2025 on Monday, as France's debt troubles and Spain's political turmoil, capped by a snap election call, fuelled fears of a fresh eurozone crisis and of contagion across the bloc's bond markets.
The euro fell to a 17-month low against the US dollar at the start of the week, as fiscal and political risks in Paris and Madrid revived memories of the eurozone debt crisis.
The euro touched $1.1161 during Asian trading, after four consecutive weekly losses, and stood at around $1.12 at the European open, recovering slightly.
Analysts at Dutch bank ING warned in a note on Friday that the market could "easily add another 2% in risk premium to the euro" if the bond sell-off extended.
The spread between French and German 10-year bond yields stands at roughly 146 basis points, after the largest weekly increase in 17 years last week, according to data provider LSEG.
France's 10-year yield rose to 4.917% in early trading on Monday, close to last week's 24-year high, after closing Friday at around 4.856%.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure insisted last week that France remained a solid borrower, unveiling a 2027 budget that aims to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP to 5%, ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Spain added to the political uncertainty on Monday, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November, after the parliament rejected two of his minority government's housing decrees on Friday.
Spain's 10-year yield was mostly steady between 4.07% and 4.09% on Monday morning, leaving its premium over German debt at around 65 basis points, less than half of France's current gap.
Against this backdrop, European stocks were mixed at the open.
The Euro Stoxx 50 fell 0.4%, and the broader Stoxx 600 rose 0.6%.
France's CAC 40 fell more than 1%, while Spain's IBEX 35, which slipped into the red after Sánchez's announcement, was 0.4% higher.
Meanwhile, Germany's DAX, Italy's FTSE MIB, the UK's FTSE 100 and the Netherlands' AEX traded between 0.1% and 0.3% higher.
Contagion fears test the ECB
Last week's sell-off also hit Italian, Belgian and Greek bonds, while German debt drew safe-haven demand. Italy's premium over Bunds neared 110 basis points on Thursday.
Analysts at Belgian bank KBC wrote in a note on Monday that there had been "clear contagion towards the likes of Belgium or Italy" since then.
The turmoil leaves the European Central Bank in a bind.
It has raised rates twice since June to tame inflation, which hit 3.8% in September, but traders have pared bets on more hikes.
Its Transmission Protection Instrument, a bond-buying backstop created in 2022, has never been used.
Speaking at a think tank event on Thursday, Joachim Nagel, head of Germany's Bundesbank and a likely candidate for the ECB's next presidency, said the central bank's focus was price stability, not "certain spread levels".
Asked about France, ECB President Christine Lagarde told French daily La Croix last week that "when your debt is close to 120% of GDP and not on course to be brought under control, it's a serious matter".
However, Lagarde asserted that "it's not 2008 or 2011".
Wall Street rallies after weak jobs data
US stocks climbed on Friday after the American economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, far fewer than expected, prompting traders to pare bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in October.
The S&P 500 rose 0.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.5% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.2%.
US futures were mostly flat on Monday, except for the Nasdaq-100, which was about 0.5% lower.
The minutes from the Fed's September meeting are due on Wednesday.

Confrontations between Yemen's internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis have escalated since early July following years of relative calm.
The country has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, before a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

Ex-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to appear at New York City hearing on AI
NEW YORK – Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that artificial intelligence could become too powerful for humans to control, will testify on Oct 5 at a New York City Council hearing, alongside representatives of some of the world’s biggest AI companies.
Coxon will appear at the request of Council Speaker Julie Menin, who has urged AI whistleblowers to testify as city lawmakers weigh a package of bills aimed at establishing safeguards around the technology, according to people familiar with the matter.
Coxon quit Anthropic in September and issued a stark warning about the race to develop increasingly powerful AI, accusing his former employer and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives”. He confirmed he plans to testify on Oct 5.
The hearing will put some of the industry’s most vocal critics in the same room as representatives of Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and Meta.
Former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner and Daniel Kokotajlo, executive director of the AI Futures Project and a former OpenAI researcher, are also expected to testify, according to one of the people. Turner confirmed he plans to attend the hearing. Kokotajlo could not be reached for comment.
Menin’s office said Anthropic will be represented by Logan Graham, head of its Frontier Red Team, which tests advanced AI models for their capabilities and risks.
OpenAI will send Morgan Dwyer, head of policy development and operations; Meta will send Shane Cahill, an AI policy director; and Google will be represented by AI policy executive Alice Friend.
A spokesperson for Google declined to comment. Representatives for the other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
The hearing is part of an effort by New York officials to play a larger role in regulating an industry that has expanded rapidly in the city, even as much of AI regulation remains the province of federal and state governments.
One proposal before the council, sponsored by Menin, would give whistleblowers a portion of fines or penalties recovered from AI companies following reported violations.
Other legislation under consideration would allow people harmed by AI systems to sue developers under certain circumstances and require third-party validation of some systems before they can be deployed in the city.
OpenAI, Anthropic and Google agreed to appear after Menin’s office warned that they could be subpoenaed, while Meta had committed to attending earlier, Bloomberg News previously reported. The council subpoenaed SpaceX’s artificial intelligence unit after it failed to respond to requests to appear.
Officials from Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration will also testify, including Samuel Levine, commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, and Sarah Milstein, deputy commissioner at the Office of Technology and Innovation. BLOOMBERG

Bulgarian National Television Ends the Ukrainian-Language News Program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

The Bulgarian National Television (BNT) has ended its Ukrainian-language news broadcast, presenter and editor Maria Plachkova, a Bessarabian Bulgarian, said in a Facebook post.
The program was launched in 2023 for Ukrainian citizens who came to Bulgaria and began building new lives there after the outbreak of the war.
“The Ukrainian-language news on Bulgarian National Television is ceasing broadcast,” Plachkova wrote, describing it as a great honor to have worked as the program’s presenter and editor since it began.
She said the broadcasts covered developments in Ukraine as well as Ukrainians living in Bulgaria, focusing on their lives, stories and experiences between the two countries.
Plachkova began her journalism career in Ukraine by producing a Bulgarian-language program for the Bulgarian community there. She later described the Ukrainian-language program in Bulgaria as a continuation of that connection.
“And in Bulgaria, from the very beginning, we spoke about Ukraine - about what was happening there, about Ukrainians in Bulgaria, and about our shared history and culture,” Plachkova wrote.
She also expressed gratitude for Bulgaria’s support for Ukraine since the beginning of the full-scale war and said Bulgarians in Ukraine had a role connecting the two countries, cultures and peoples.
“Bulgaria has supported Ukraine since the very first days of the full-scale war, and I am sincerely grateful for that—especially today, when this support matters so much. We, the Bulgarians of Ukraine, have the distinct honor and responsibility of serving as a bridge between two states, two cultures, and two peoples,” Plachkova said.
For her, she added, the program went beyond reporting news because each broadcast involved people and their personal experiences and hopes. She described the broadcasts as a form of support and assistance that gave Ukrainians an opportunity to be heard, while thanking everyone who had contributed to the program.
In an earlier social media post, Plachkova had indicated that the Ukrainian-language broadcast could be discontinued.
She said she had worked at BNT for four and a half years and had spent the last three as editor and presenter of the Ukrainian-language news. She said she first learned about the program’s low viewership and the conclusion that there was insufficient interest when the issue was presented to the Council for Electronic Media (CEM).
“I have been working at BNT for four and a half years, and for the last three, I have served as the editor and presenter of the Ukrainian-language news. I learned about the low viewership figures and the conclusion regarding a lack of interest only during the presentation before the Council for Electronic Media (CEM). Prior to that, I had not been made aware of any such analysis or any decision concerning the format's future,” Plachkova stated.
She said she had repeatedly raised the issue with BNT management and submitted letters with questions and proposals for developing the program but received no response.
Plachkova also said the broadcasts were mainly posted on BNT’s website rather than YouTube, while business trips and opportunities to produce reports on location had been suspended.
“The news broadcasts were published primarily on the BNT website without being uploaded to YouTube, and business trips and opportunities for on-site filming were suspended. Therefore, I believe that the assessment should take into account not only viewership figures but also the way the content was produced and distributed,” she said in a statement on September 25.
She argued that the Ukrainian-language news was part of BNT’s public service role and was important for people living, working or staying in Bulgaria.
“To me, the Ukrainian-language news is part of BNT’s public service mandate and is significant for people living, working, or staying in Bulgaria. Consequently, I believe that before a final conclusion is reached regarding the necessity of this information product, it is important to consider all circumstances surrounding its creation, distribution, and viewership,” Plachkova stated on September 25.
The latest broadcast currently listed in the Ukrainian-language section of BNT’s website was published on July 17, 2026.

Shortages of crucial HIV medicines due to aid cuts are a ‘warning’, say experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:52 UTC
18:00:52 KST

Aid cuts have affected HIV drug and test supplies across the world, with some providers reporting they are out of stock of key medicines, according to a survey of 40 countries.
Organisations providing HIV care revealed that more than half (55%) had run out of stock within the past year, with a critical scarcity of HIV tests and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – a prescription medicine that people take to reduce the risk of getting HIV.
The survey by the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF), a network of organisations in more than 170 countries dedicated to sexual and reproductive health, rights and justice, showed that at the time of questioning, 40% of its members reported they had run out of all stock of a product and 60% had at least one product at low stock levels.
Mallah Tabot, a senior adviser at IPPF Africa’s regional office, said: “These shortages are a warning of what happens when funding becomes uncertain and the supply systems communities depend on grow fragile.
“We cannot let decades of progress against HIV be undone simply because products aren’t available. This is not a distant risk – it is already happening.
“HIV infections are rising in a number of countries around the world and lives are being lost,” she added.
Findings from the 40 member associations that responded to the survey revealed that HIV rapid diagnostic tests were the most critically affected product across all respondents.
Testing is provided by almost every responding member association, yet 17 reported low stock and a further five reported no availability, meaning that more than half cannot offer sustained HIV testing at the point of care.
Oral and injectable PrEP were also scarce, with 12 member associations reporting low stock or none at all. Without reliable access to these basic commodities, there will be gaps and interruptions in care for people seeking healthcare from IPPF member associations.
In general, respondents from the Arab world, Asia and Oceania, Europe, the Americas and the Caribbean said supplies, including condoms and antiretroviral therapy, were unreliable.
Lori Miller, an HIV adviser for IPPF, said: “Our partners already have what it takes to deliver integrated HIV prevention, testing and treatment – the clinic networks, digital infrastructure, health workforce and community trust to reach people with care – but unreliable supplies are letting them down.”
An estimated 40.9 million people were living with HIV worldwide last year, when there were 570,000 Aids-related deaths recorded, alongside 1.2 million new HIV infections.
In 2025, HIV responses around the world were disrupted by cuts that threatened to stall years of progress. That year, there was a fall in aid spending of about 23% compared with 2024, leading the UN to warn in June of the risk of a resurgence of the HIV epidemic.
