NATO state preparing to strike St. Petersburg – FT
Estonia is preparing to deploy weapons capable of striking the Russian city of St. Petersburg, the Financial Times has reported.
Amid unprecedented mis- and dis-information from NATO’s European members, Tallinn has presented the proposed buildup as a form of deterrence, should Moscow “test” NATO. However, Russia’s leadership has repeatedly stressed that it has no intention of attacking the US-led military bloc. Moscow has also warned that any direct conflict with NATO would likely escalate into nuclear war.
The British newspaper reported on Monday that Estonia is deploying additional troops along the Russian border and acquiring tactical missile systems capable of reaching St. Petersburg. They include US-made HIMARS and South Korean Chunmoo launchers, both of which can fire longer-range projectiles.
Estonia also trained with the UK during this year’s Spring Storm exercise using Nyan kamikaze jet drones, which can likewise reach Russia’s second-largest city from Estonian territory, according to the report.
The Baltic state has a standing army of just 4,200 troops, but plans to reinforce it with tens of thousands of reservists if tensions with Russia escalate.
Last month, Defense Minister Martin Herem said during a public lecture that Tallinn could not afford to keep mobilized troops in the field for long.
“I have jokingly said that if we get to the orange zone there and carry out mobilization, but Russia does not attack, then it would be economically more correct to attack ourselves,” he said. “Then at least we will know when it will start, and we will not waste food and air in vain”
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to the remark with an idiom: “The circus has left, but the clowns remain.” He added that Moscow has no plans to attack Estonia or any other NATO member.
Commenting on the FT report, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova echoed the president, saying it belongs in the funny pages.
Russian diplomats previously cited Herem’s remarks as examples of what they described as aggressive rhetoric by senior officials in NATO countries. The Russian Foreign Ministry has formally warned the bloc against attacking Russian territory or imposing a blockade on the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, saying the country’s response could involve “all weapons” in its arsenal.
While NATO poses as a purely defensive organization, it has a history of military interventions on foreign soil and does not rule out preemptive attacks. Last week, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said European members of the bloc should have been capable of attacking Iran themselves to eliminate what was described as a nuclear threat from Tehran. He argued that Europe’s military buildup should eventually allow it to conduct such operations without relying on the US.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have all sharply increased military spending in recent years and are reportedly seeking additional procurement funds from the EU budget. According to Finnish newspaper Iltalehti, the three Baltic states have asked Brussels to urgently provide €500 million ($570 million) in additional funding, citing the scenario of Russia seeking to “test NATO.”

Lukoil’s foreign asset sale becomes part of U.S.–Russia talks on ending Ukraine war, NYT reports
The sale of Lukoil’s foreign assets has become part of Russia–U.S. talks on ending the Russia–Ukraine war, sources told The New York Times.
Vladimir Putin personally raised the issue of selling Lukoil’s assets on September 5 during talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys handling negotiations over the the Russia–Ukraine war, the NYT said.
Putin proposed seeing the deal through to completion, saying it would confirm that Russians and Americans can do business together, one of the newspaper’s sources said.
The Financial Times reported that a group of investors seeking to buy Lukoil’s foreign assets includes former Chelsea co-owner Todd Boehly, Sheikh Tahnoon, brother of the president of the UAE, and the Qatari Al-Khayyat family. All of them have ties to the Trump and Witkoff families.
Boehly donated $2 million to Trump’s political projects. The Al-Khayyat brothers are building a resort in Albania with Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, the president’s daughter. Sheikh Tahnoon has invested in projects involving Kushner, Witkoff, and Trump’s sons.
Kushner and Witkoff’s ties to the parties involved in the Lukoil deal raise questions about a conflict of interest and clearly show why Trump’s friends and family members should not serve as his foreign policy advisers, Hui Chen, a former U.S. Justice Department prosecutor, told the NYT.
The Trump administration imposed sanctions on Lukoil in the fall of 2025. The company then began looking for a buyer for its foreign assets, worth about $20 billion. It remains unclear how much the assets might ultimately sell for.
The Russia-linked trading company Gunvor was the first to try to acquire Lukoil’s foreign business, but U.S. authorities called it a “puppet” of the Kremlin and refused to approve the deal. The American investment fund Carlyle became another contender, but the U.S. Treasury Department has yet to approve its application either.

US defence experts to work inside Taiwan military HQ under reported pact

According to Taiwanese media reports at the weekend, the Pentagon plans to send one official from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Policy and one expert from the Institute for Defence Analyses (IDA) to work on a long-term basis at the defence ministry’s headquarters in Taipei.
The two would aid policy coordination and combat capability assessments under an expanded “Taiwan-US Defence Ministry Joint Cooperation Assessment” programme that would run from this year to 2028, according to the reports.
The programme has a total budget of more than NT$471 million (US$14.8 million), including NT$152.5 million this year for expenses such as US personnel and consultancy costs, travel, research equipment and data collection, and interpreting for classified-level meetings.
If confirmed, the arrangement would mark a significant change from the existing US military presence in Taiwan, where American personnel have generally worked as trainers or through the American Institute in Taiwan, Washington’s de facto embassy on the self-ruled island.

Farhadi criticizes Hollywood’s perspective at Rio Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:44:43 UTC
17:44:43 KST

Farhadi criticizes Hollywood’s perspective at Rio Film Festival
TEHRAN – Renowned Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi discussed the perceived dominance of American cinema and cautioned against viewing Hollywood as a reliable source for authentic portrayals of foreign cultures.
Farhadi, who is in Brazil for the presentation of his latest film “Parallel Tales” at the Rio Film Festival, made the remarks during a panel, ISNA reported.
The two-time Oscar winner was asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A Separation” won Best International Film at the Oscars. “I watched the film at the time it came out and felt it was a ‘Hollywood thing’,” Farhadi said.
In “Argo,” loosely based on a true story, director Ben Affleck plays a Latino exfiltration specialist who masquerades as a Hollywood producer to rescue six Americans held captive in Tehran during the US hostage crisis in Iran.
“The problem with these kinds of films in Hollywood [and] some people in the United States [is that] they look at the world from up to down,” he added. “Someday you should ask them: Why do you feel you’re up and we’re down? I don’t understand why they have this ego that they’re up.” The Iranian director then said Americans often claim to “have democracy,” but they don’t. “You don’t have democracy. It’s a lie.”
Farhadi then recalled spending time in the US a few years ago when working on a project and, during research, travelling to San Francisco to speak with incarcerated men. “I met some people in prison who are Black, [some who come] from other countries, and the real America was there. But people in the world don’t see that part of the United States.”
“I have this problem when they feel they are up and they think, ‘[others] should be like us,’” he continued. “Even if it’s in a good way and they want to be kind to you, they wish ‘one day you’ll become like us,’ and no, I don’t want to.”
Still on “Argo,” the director said movies like that “are not deep.” “They make these movies for money; it’s a business. And in these films, it’s always a white guy from the United States saving others. My question is: Why? Why does an American go to Cuba or Iran to save people? People understand they can save themselves. Who asked you to come and save us?”
Asked about how he broaches politics in his films, the renowned filmmaker said that, whenever “you talk about society, you are talking about politics.” “Even when you talk about family life, their relationships, their difficulties and problems, indirectly you are talking about politics. In my films, I always try not to talk about politics directly because, to me, that is a bit far from cinema. The cinema that I believe is the kind of cinema that gives space to audiences to discover things about themselves.”
The director then brought up Abbas Kiarostami’s “Fellow Citizen” as Iran’s “most political film.” The 1983 documentary heavily trails drivers across the streets of the Iranian capital. “He made a documentary about car drivers in Tehran, but when you see people, the way they talk to the police, the layers are very political.”
“Media and cinema don’t give you a complete image of people’s ordinary life,” he added. “But the thing about empathy is that, all around the world, people are similar to each other. Cinema is based on hate and love. And [when it comes to] hate and love, everywhere is the same. A love between a mother and child in Brazil and in Tehran is the same. The way they express it is different, but the core is the same.”
Farhadi said that when he watches a Brazilian film, he soon forgets he is watching a story from another place in the world, and feels it is a “film about us” as people. “If one day people can travel to other countries, and if they shake hands, that’s the best way to know people, not through media. I don’t believe media can give us the whole image.”
On this, the filmmaker emphasized how his last two films, “A Hero” and “Parallel Tales,” are about how we see others and how we are seen in return. They are also heavily influenced by “how social media has shaped our lives.”
“When we see something in the media, we should be careful,” he continued, adding that most information replicated by mainstream media about Iran, for example, comes from “very simple knowledge” of real life in the country. When a singular discourse is perpetuated, the director implied, it means people are “ready to accept” when someone says “they are the enemy.” “This is something the media is doing, because the most powerful media belongs to powerful people. This is the problem.”
Farhadi spoke very briefly about his next film, reiterating it will be shot in Persian. Enquired as to whether the film might deal with the current war in Iran and the conflict in Palestine, the director said: “Not directly,” suggesting the current political climate might have an underlying effect on the story despite not being the subject of his project.
“The Salesman” helmer also recalled how “Parallel Tales” was supposed to be shot in the US: “I stayed there for three years, writing, searching, casting. I did casting in the US with American actors, very big names. But every day that I came back to my home, I told myself: I cannot connect with this. Something is wrong. It was a big problem. One night I decided to change.”

According to the Border Police, one agency employee sustained a minor injury, and operations at the "Palanca–Maiaki–Udobne" checkpoint were suspended. NewsMaker reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred as a result of Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure.
The Border Police clarified that the shell fell at approximately 09:38. According to preliminary data, the bus and the control booth were damaged. There are no other casualties.
The Border Police and Moldova’s Customs Service are monitoring the situation and maintaining contact with the competent Ukrainian authorities.
Citizens were urged to avoid traveling to this area. If residents hear the characteristic sound of drones or explosions near the border, they are advised to remain calm, take shelter in a safe place indoors, and follow information from the authorities.
Citizens are also asked not to approach possible fragments of aircraft, ammunition, or other unidentified objects and to immediately report them by calling 112.
At 10:50, traffic in the direction of Palanca was temporarily blocked from the intersection of the R-30 and R-31 roads in the Ștefan Vodă district. Three years on: Israel is asphyxiating Gaza and dismantling the means of survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:41:58 UTC
17:41:58 KST

- Israel is continuing its genocide in Gaza, Palestine, where the space in which people can live is shrinking and the conditions for survival are being systematically destroyed.
- Governments must act now to ensure that Israel stops the destruction and killing, and prevents ethnic cleansing, in Palestine.
Amman / Jerusalem – Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that Israel is progressively asphyxiating Gaza, Palestine, and continuing its genocide: the space in which people can live is vanishing, while the conditions people need to survive are being systematically destroyed through continued violence, the deliberate blockade of essential supplies, and the destruction of healthcare and vital infrastructure.
In the past year, the physical trapping of people in Gaza has been made increasingly definitive by the establishment of Israel’s Yellow Line. Originally presented as a temporary, first-phase military withdrawal position and a key part of maintaining the so-called ceasefire – it is now reinforced by military positions, berms and ongoing demolitions and has continued to move west, squeezing people into a smaller and smaller area. Israeli forces now occupy approximately 65 per cent of Gaza, using the line to draw a clear border around this area.
As the Yellow Line moves, the threat to people living nearby becomes increasingly immediate, compounded by the uncertainty of approaching a line that is not clearly or consistently demarcated. People risk being shot by Israeli forces when they approach it, and MSF teams continue to treat people with gunshot wounds sustained nearby. Its encroachment is also disrupting the delivery of essential assistance: MSF water trucking has had to stop when shooting occurs near communities living close to the Yellow Line.
“The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map,” says Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza. “It has become a mechanism of encirclement and ethnic cleansing, while cutting communities off from the infrastructure, healthcare, water and other essentials they need to survive.”
The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map.
Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza
Violence is not confined to the areas around the Yellow Line. In June and July alone, despite a so-called ceasefire, MSF teams treated more than 1,200* cases of violent trauma across Gaza, including blast injuries, burns, gunshot wounds and injuries resulting from physical assault.
Over the past three years, our teams have treated more than 200,000 trauma cases*, including injuries resulting from intentional physical violence, while Israel’s military offensive has killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 20,000 children.
As Israel confines Palestinians into increasingly limited areas, families are being pushed into overcrowded and unlivable conditions, without sufficient access to clean water, sanitation services, shelter, or healthcare. These conditions are contributing to the spread of disease.
MSF teams have treated more than 11,000 cases of skin diseases, such as scabies, this year alone, while seeing more than 1,500 cases of chickenpox in June and July. MSF distributed around 2.1 million litres of drinking water per day in August, yet the scale of need remains far beyond what can be met under these restrictions. 
“Most people have less than six litres of domestic-use water per day and limited access to basic hygiene items such as soap and detergent,” says Dr Murad Asaliyya, medical activities manager in Gaza. “We are treating gastroenteritis, acute respiratory infections, a lot of skin conditions, hepatitis, bacterial skin infections, scabies and lice.”
“At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies,” says Dr Asaliyya. “Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.”
At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies. Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.
Dr Murad Asaliyya, medical activities manager in Gaza
Over the past three years, access to healthcare has deteriorated dramatically, with hospitals increasingly running out of basic supplies and patients unable to access essential medicines and treatment. Restrictions on essential supplies, such as engine oil and spare parts, are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances and water systems running, with generators already breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced.
The destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system and damage to more than 80 per cent of all structures in the Strip, alongside the lifelong physical and mental health impacts of repeated violence and displacement, will extend far beyond the present and prevent any meaningful recovery for years to come.
Nor is this crisis limited to Gaza. Since 2023, violent settler attacks, military operations and raids on homes, displacement camps and agricultural land, illegal settlement expansion, displacement, home demolitions and movement restrictions have rapidly escalated across the West Bank and East Jerusalem, particularly this year. Patients at MSF clinics tell teams about homes being demolished by Israeli forces, attacks by settlers, and livestock being stolen. The policies of violence, harassment and forced displacement affecting Palestinians extend beyond Gaza, causing further fragmentation of Palestine.
“It will take generations to recover from the harm that has already been done over the past three years, and in the preceding decades, while the excruciating consequences of Israel's ongoing genocide are still being felt every day,” says Bazerolle. 
“Destruction, displacement and deprivation have become normalised — practices Israel is carrying out with impunity,” says Bazerolle. “Governments must act now to ensure Israel stops the destruction and killing, prevents ethnic cleansing, and stops denying Palestinians the means of survival.”
*This refers to cases not patients, including new or follow-up consultations.

Iran says it disabled Starlink terminals during January protests

Sahin Demir
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Iran claimed Monday that it had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during nationwide protests in January and has other tools to counter the satellite internet service.
According to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, head of Iran’s National Cyberspace Center, said Tehran had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during the protests.
“For the first time, Iran managed to successfully disable Starlink terminals during the coup in January,” Aghamiri said, using the Iranian authorities’ description of the protests.
He claimed that Western media had also reported at the time that Iran had successfully carried out an operation to disable Starlink terminals.
“That important technical operation, which was completely successful, is one of our tools, and we also have other tools at our disposal to counter Starlink,” he added.
Aghamiri’s comments came in response to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who displayed a Starlink terminal during his address to the UN General Assembly in New York on Sept. 24.
Netanyahu said the device allowed Iranians to access information, accusing Tehran of spending large sums of money on internet censorship.
Iran witnessed widespread anti-government protests in January, with demonstrations intensifying on Jan. 8 and 9 amid clashes between protesters and security forces.
Iranian authorities imposed a nationwide internet blackout on Jan. 8 as the protests intensified.
Starlink remained one of the few ways for Iranians to access the internet during the blackout, although reports at the time indicated that the satellite service was also experiencing significant interference and disruptions.
Aghamiri said the disruptions were caused by an Iranian operation targeting Starlink terminals.
Starlink, operated by US space technology company SpaceX, provides internet connectivity through a network of satellites.

Bar-Ilan lecturer indicted over plot to kill hundreds of Arabs in coordinated attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:39:42 UTC
17:39:42 KST

A Bar-Ilan University mathematics professor accused of planning coordinated terrorist attacks intended to kill hundreds of Arabs has asked to be released to house arrest, telling a court that he does not pose a danger and has “exams to grade” at home.
The professor, around 60 and from Petah Tikva, has been in custody since Sept. 17. The investigation began after the Shin Bet domestic security agency received initial information about his alleged plan, after which the case was transferred to the Central District police’s major-crimes unit.
Prosecutors have asked that he remain in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings. He is charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism under Israel’s Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice.
At a hearing Monday at the Lod District Court, the defendant’s attorneys also asked that the gag order preventing publication of his name remain in place. They argued that the indictment “could harm the State of Israel internationally” and said members of his family in Australia could also suffer if he were identified.
The judge extended the gag order until noon on Oct. 7.
The indictment alleges that the professor spent years developing a detailed plan he called “Ayit,” a Hebrew acronym for a phrase meaning “The People Will Carry Out Transfer.”
Under the plan, prosecutors say, he intended to recruit 71 additional Jewish attackers and divide a total of 72 participants, including himself, into 12 six-person terrorist cells. At least half were supposed to hold firearms licenses.
The cells were allegedly to arm themselves with pistols, rifles, axes and hammers and launch simultaneous surprise attacks in mixed Jewish-Arab cities and Arab and Bedouin communities, with the goal of killing hundreds of people and driving Arabs and Palestinians permanently toward Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
Alleged plan included help from within the IDF
The indictment describes an even broader element of the alleged plan: assistance from people the defendant hoped to recruit from within the IDF.
Prosecutors say he envisioned sympathetic military personnel providing coordinated support to the attacking cells, including Air Force strikes on Arab population centers and assistance from artillery and armored forces.
In written instructions described in the indictment, the professor allegedly called for mass killings and the rapid seizure of friction points, roads, entrances and exits to Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals.
One passage allegedly instructed participants not to show mercy, including toward women and children, and not to stop in response to pleas.
According to prosecutors, the professor believed simultaneous mass attacks, amplified in real time on social media, would prompt Arab citizens of Israel, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians in east Jerusalem and the West Bank, to flee.
The alleged preparations stretched from February 2023 until his arrest last month and included reconnaissance trips, detailed handwritten documents and repeated attempts to recruit others.
Prosecutors say his thinking began after the May 2021 intercommunal violence and intensified following the Oct. 7 attack and subsequent war.
‘I don’t see who I am dangerous to’
During the court hearing, the professor argued that he should be allowed to return home.
“In my opinion, I am not currently dangerous to anyone. I can be released to house arrest,” he told the court.
“My life has been completely turned upside down. I have so many things to do and financial matters to take care of,” he said.
He also expressed fear for his safety in custody.
“I don’t see who I am dangerous to. If they want to publish this, do it without my name,” he said. “All the prison guards are Muslim and I am afraid. Israel is a small country. Some of them tell me they know what I am accused of. I am alone there.”
“I am a professor at Bar-Ilan and I worked until my arrest. I have exams to grade at home,” he added.
The professor also said he had developed the plan “because of Oct. 7, not for myself,” although the indictment alleges that his preparations began months before the Hamas attack.
“I didn’t do anything for myself. I buried my life for three years,” he said. “I don’t think I should be punished.”
Disguises, reconnaissance and failed recruitment attempts
According to the indictment, the defendant spent roughly a year and a half attempting unsuccessfully to recruit supporters and partners.
He allegedly conducted reconnaissance around the Bedouin community of Tuba-Zangariyye in northern Israel to study access routes and determine how it could be attacked. Prosecutors say he intended the community to be one of the plan’s central targets.
Investigators also allege that he went to considerable lengths to conceal his identity during his recruitment efforts.
He is accused of wearing a face mask, hat and sunglasses, identifying himself under the false names “Menachem” or “Menachem Livneh,” and using the phones of passersby to contact people connected to his recruitment efforts.
He allegedly wrote his documents by hand instead of using a computer and prepared instructions explaining how participants should avoid detection.
Alleged attempt to recruit Feiglin
The indictment also says the professor sought to involve Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin in his plans.
According to prosecutors, he intended first to recruit Feiglin and then, with his help, identify additional participants.
The professor allegedly planned to invite preselected activists to a Zehut election gathering without initially telling them why. At the event, prosecutors say, the participants would be informed that they had been recruited for a terrorist attack scheduled for the following day and would be given detailed operational instructions.
He attended two public events held by Feiglin and attempted to arrange a meeting and deliver a summary of his plan, but Feiglin did not respond to any of his approaches, according to the indictment.
About a month ago, prosecutors allege, the professor wrote Feiglin a threatening letter criticizing him for refusing to cooperate and warning that he would publish the letter if Feiglin did not assist him, in what the defendant allegedly believed would cause political damage ahead of the election.
Two days later, he allegedly went to Feiglin’s home and handed the letter to a neighbor, asking her to deliver it.
He later attended a Zehut event at Jerusalem’s Mahane Yehuda market and, through another woman, delivered several copies of the letter to the party’s director-general along with another letter containing a similar threat.
Zehut said after the indictment was published that Feiglin and the party leadership contacted police immediately after receiving the threatening and extortion letters and filed a formal complaint.
Feiglin thanked police for handling the case and called for the legal process against the professor to be pursued fully.
Bar-Ilan suspends professor immediately
Bar-Ilan University said the professor would be suspended immediately pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings.
“Bar-Ilan University condemns in the strongest possible terms and is deeply appalled by the acts attributed to the lecturer in the indictment. The University’s leadership calls upon the police and the prosecution to pursue the matter to the fullest extent of the law, should the allegations be substantiated.
“The University has, and will continue to have, zero tolerance for conduct of this nature, conduct that is fundamentally incompatible with the values we share as Jews, as Israelis, and as human beings, and that stands in clear opposition to the values of Bar-Ilan University.
“The lecturer will be suspended from his duties with immediate effect, pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings.”
Prosecutors argue that the alleged conduct, which they say extended over several years, reflects an extremist ideology that led the defendant to formulate a detailed, multi-stage plan for mass killing.
In their request to keep him detained until the end of proceedings, prosecutors said the alleged nationalist and ideological motivation, the extensive preparations and the heightened security tensions during the period demonstrate what they described as an immediate danger to individuals, the public and the state.

One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:39:26 UTC
17:39:26 KST

One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
“Your mind follows the thread, one by one, row by row. You know? It’s like meditation. I don’t like machines.”
Weo, a prisoner at the Central Women’s Correctional Institution in Bangkok, prefers to sew by hand. She tried the sewing machine, but noticed that her mind was calmer when threading with her fingers directly. By not using a machine, she can produce a unique pattern that is hard to find in conventional shops.
She is explaining this to a group of design students who, sketchbooks in hand, are walking through the rows, observing the women who sew.
As time passes, some lose their initial apprehension and sit across from them, picking up fabric samples. Others ask about the products they are making. Some borrow their needles and, with the women’s guidance, try a bit of sewing themselves. A few sit on the floor in the basket-weaving corner with the women who have, by now, mastered the skill.
Today, the students have left the classroom behind to spend their morning at Thailand’s first women’s prison, where approximately 150 women learn weaving, knitting and machine sewing to make marketable products.
The students’ task is to design a product that these women can manufacture during their sentences.
Through the wall
The initiative, launched in November 2025 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the Thailand Institute of Justice (TIJ) pairs design students with incarcerated women to create modern, sustainable products that can be sold outside prison.
Earlier this year, 22 students visited the prison and interacted with the women who are now manufacturing new products. Their designs had to appeal to modern consumers, be practical and tell a story linked to rehabilitation that would raise awareness of the critical role vocational training plays in reducing recidivism.
“The stigma surrounding those who have made mistakes has long been a wall in our society. To help them cross that barrier, we must restore their human dignity,” said TIJ’s Chontit Chuenurah.
“By weaving their stories into these products, we use the creativity of the youth to build a bridge between the prison and the outside world, replacing fear with understanding.”
Under the theme Through the Wall, the initiative seeks to dismantle physical and social barriers, helping incarcerated women return successfully to society, she added.
“The project aims to create prison-made goods that appeal to modern consumers while equipping correctional officers with essential marketing skills,” said Aki Okanan, former prison reform expert at UNODC.
The project also raises international awareness of the role of rehabilitation and vocational training in reducing re-offending she added.
Time well spent
A panel of judges evaluated nine projects from 19 students in a competition earlier this year.
The winner was Time-Made, featuring intricately smocked watch straps.
For the students behind the design, time has a two-fold meaning: the sentence that prisoners can reduce by working in prison, and the time that people outside value, a privilege sometimes taken for granted.
“We wanted our product to remind people that we can use time carefully and meaningfully. That we can watch our time,” says Game, 21, co-winner of the competition.
First steps
All designs received support for product development and marketing, and the winning product, together with a selection of others, will be produced in collaboration with partner correctional facilities.
Natty, also 21, has been studying lifestyle products for three years. She had expected the prison to look gloomy and scary and was surprised to find the workroom bright and airy. Still, she noticed that most prisoners used dark colours.
“I want to take the skills they have and show them brighter fabrics and see what happens,” she said.
Sitting by Weo’s side, Ana*, from Latin America, tells the story of how she was caught attempting to smuggle cocaine into Bangkok. After four years in prison, she can produce perfect stuffed animals and is fluent in Thai, although she has never seen Thailand outside prison.
“I heard it’s beautiful here, but it doesn’t matter. After this, when I manage to get back to Brazil, I will start an import business and sell stuffed animals from Thailand. I know how to do it. I have the connections, and I speak the language.”
As the students pass through the gates and security controls to leave, their enthusiasm wanes. Although the prisoners cannot leave, this collaboration connects them to the outside world, the first step in reintegration.

Israel marks October 7 anniversary as national memorial day

Two state ceremonies are being held at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, where President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other senior officials are expected to attend, The Jerusalem Post reported.
More memorial events, rallies and ceremonies are planned across the country with schools, municipalities and communities also holding events throughout the day.
Flags at state institutions, police stations, prisons and military bases were lowered to half-mast, reports said. The memorial fell on October 5 this year due to the Hebrew calendar, which is lunisolar.
October 7 terror attacks set of chain of events
The Hamas terror attack on October 7 killed some 1,200 people in Israel, with the Palestinian militant also taking another 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.
The October 7, 2023, attacks had massive consequences not only for Israeli society but also for Palestinians in Gaza, where Hamas had maintained power since the territory last held elections in 2006.
Following the Hamas attacks, the Israeli military began a war targeting Hamas in Gaza. The European Union, as well as the United States, Germany, and other countries, classify Hamas as a terrorist organization.

E3G, a climate change thinktank, has made the argument on the basis that, without the rule, which requires new homes to have low-carbon heating, owners will pay at least £25,000 more in running costs over 25 years.
The UK’s shadow chancellor will announce today that the Conservative party would axe the Future Homes Standard if elected. This policy cuts energy bills and emissions in new build homes by requiring builders to fit new homes with heat pumps and solar panels instead of gas boilers. Heat pumps and solar panels offer dramatically lower running costs than homes fitted just with gas boilers, to the tune of around £1,000 a year in a 3-bed house.
The small additional upfront cost is quickly recovered by homeowners and protects them from price shocks on the volatile fossil fuel market. If the government builds all its promised 1.5 million new build homes to the Future Homes Standard, this will save bill payers around £35bn on their energy bills over 25 years, and stops 41m tonnes of dangerous carbon dioxide from being released into the atmosphere.

School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Consumer watchdog ACM has criticised educational publishers for pricey and poor-quality textbooks, calling on the industry to change its practices.
The ACM says that for the past seven years, prices for educational materials have been rising faster than those of other products and schools say the publications are not meeting their needs.
In a statement, the watchdog said it “calls on educational publishers to stop mandatory tied selling of licences and textbooks, and to better align product supply with demand.”
One major problem the organisation highlighted is that textbooks and the licences for e-materials are bundled together, which drives up costs. The ACM wants them to be sold separately.
The organisation also calls on schools to do more research into the textbooks they purchase.
“Pressure on publishers starts with schools’ willingness to switch to other learning materials,” board member Martijn Snoep said in a statement.
Secondary schools buy around €280 million worth of learning materials every year.

Expert warns of continued ‘earthquake storm’ after tremors hit southern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:35:34 UTC
17:35:34 KST

A potential “earthquake storm” could continue in southern Türkiye, according to an expert, after magnitude 4.9 and 5.2 earthquakes struck Adana and Osmaniye within minutes of each other, causing panic but no reported damage.
The earthquakes occurred on Oct. 4 in the districts of Saimbeyli in Adana and Sumbas in Osmaniye. Türkiye’s Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) said a magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Saimbeyli at 2:19 p.m., followed by a magnitude 4.9 quake in the same district at 2:36 p.m. and a magnitude 5.2 earthquake in Sumbas at 2:43 p.m. The earthquakes occurred at depths of about 7-9 kilometers.
AFAD’s preliminary assessment of the magnitude 5.2 earthquake recorded at least 16 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 1.0 to 2.4. Overall, 113 earthquakes were recorded in the region during the following 24 hours.
The authority noted that 32 earthquakes of magnitude 4 or greater have occurred in the area since 1900, with the strongest reaching magnitude 5.7.
Seismologist Hasan Sözbilir said the latest activity occurred between the Saimbeyli and Savrun faults, which have been considered areas of accumulated seismic energy following the February 2023 earthquakes.
“Earthquakes of similar magnitude may continue their activity in the form of an earthquake storm at this stage,” Sözbilir said, urging residents not to panic.
Hakan Güneyli, a member of AFAD’s Earthquake Science Board, said the available data indicated that the sequence would gradually weaken.
“Based on the data so far, we can say that these earthquakes will diminish in magnitude and occur at increasingly longer intervals,” Güneyli said. He added that smaller aftershocks could continue for some time.
Güneyli linked the activity to the transfer of elastic deformation energy generated by the February 2023 earthquakes toward the west and southwest. He also warned that seismic activity could continue for years following the 2023 disaster.
He further warned that recent tremors, combined with heavy rainfall and steep terrain, could increase the risk of landslides and rockfalls in the region.

Share of Ukrainians who approve country's direction drops to 40% – survey

Unknown Publisher

Share of Ukrainians who approve country's direction drops to 40% – survey
According to a survey, 40% of Ukrainians believe that affairs in the country are developing in the right direction, compared to 44% in February 2024.
Source: a survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), conducted September 12–21, commissioned by Forum NGO
Details: According to survey data, 40% of Ukrainians believe that affairs in the country are developing in the right direction, while 45% believe they are going in the wrong direction. Another 15% were undecided.
Compared to February 2024, the share of those who consider the direction right decreased by four percentage points – from 44% to 40%. The share of those holding the opposite view remained virtually unchanged – 46% then versus 45% in September 2026.
At the same time, the share of undecided respondents rose from 10% to 15%.
KIIS notes that overall indicators have stayed largely stable and the shift in the share of those who consider the direction wrong is not statistically significant.
For reference: KIIS conducted the Omnibus survey from 12–21 September 2026, via telephone interviews among 1,002 adult citizens of Ukraine in government-controlled territory. Questions regarding the direction of the country's development and attitudes towards the current authorities were added at the request of Forum NGO.
Respondents were selected based on a random sample of mobile numbers and the results were statistically weighted. Residents of occupied territories and citizens who went abroad after 24 February 2022, were excluded from the sample. However, internally displaced persons from occupied territories were included among the respondents.
Under normal circumstances, the statistical margin of error with a 95% probability and accounting for the design effect would not exceed 4.1 percentage points for indicators close to 50%, 3.5 for indicators close to 25%, 2.5 for indicators close to 10% and 1.8 for indicators close to 5%.
In wartime conditions, additional systematic deviations are possible. Nonetheless, KIIS believes the results maintain high representativeness and allow for reliable analysis of public sentiment.
Background: According to a KIIS survey conducted 5-10 February 2024, the share of Ukrainians who believed affairs in the country were developing in the right direction fell from 54% in December 2023 to 44% in February 2024.

US Pulls B-1 Bombers From RAF Fairford After Security Scare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

The United States has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain following a security incident that triggered a counter-terrorism investigation, the Pentagon confirmed Sunday.
Police were called to the airbase in southwest England on September 27 after a local farmer reported several vans and a group of men behaving in a “suspicious” manner. The incident led to the evacuation of 85 homes near the base, which has been used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
The farmer, who lives in the village of Whelford near the airbase, had reported seeing three vans blocking a road while masked men fled the area. Aerial footage showed that the vans appeared to contain barrels, with at least one carrying a fake logo and phone number intended to make it appear to belong to a legitimate diesel delivery company.
Counter-terrorism investigators found no explosives in the vehicles. Instead, “a quantity of petrol was recovered,” National Counter Terrorism Policing head Lawrence Taylor said.
A Pentagon official said the US bombers had now been returned to their bases in the United States. “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” the official said.
At least 10 of the 12 B-1 bombers at Fairford left the base Sunday, including aircraft that had arrived less than a week earlier as part of a rotation, highlighting the speed of the withdrawal and the importance Washington appeared to attach to the threat.
The Pentagon official who spoke about the redeployment was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity. The UK Ministry of Defence had not immediately commented.
US media reports said the withdrawal appeared to have been prompted by new or renewed concerns over security at the base. The New York Times reported that US officials declined to identify the information that led to the rapid departure, while one US official said it was connected to threat warnings that had emerged three weeks earlier and that specific details and the level of urgency had increased sharply over the previous 24 hours.
The motives behind the incident remained the subject of speculation, ranging from a potential terror threat to fuel theft as energy prices in Britain reached record levels this week.
Six London-based Britons were arrested during the investigation and later released on bail, including a dual British-Iranian national. One account said five of those arrested were men in their mid-20s. British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran, while Iran has denied any involvement.
Donald Trump criticized the decision to release the suspects. “I wouldn't have done that,” the US president told reporters, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a “foreign actor” was involved.
Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved.
Security at RAF Fairford had reportedly been increased recently. Britain gave Washington permission in March to use the base for “specific defensive operations into Iran,” and US bombers and other aircraft have since been seen arriving and departing from the facility.
RAF Fairford is the only airbase on mainland Britain used for that purpose. Located 100 miles (160km) west of London, it has been used by US bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Its recent use followed permission from then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer for Washington to conduct “defensive” strikes against Tehran from British bases.
The US military continues to maintain a sizeable presence in the Middle East. A US official said Thursday that the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group were heading toward the region. Together, the ships carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines, and the move could result in three US carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.

Majority of Ukrainians express disappointment with current authorities – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:34:09 EEST
17:34:09 KST

A majority of Ukrainian citizens, when asked about their attitude toward the current authorities, reported feelings of disappointment and shame, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
According to the report released on Monday, sociologists asked respondents about their feelings regarding the current government. Respondents were given a list of 12 feelings/emotions from which they could choose up to three answers or provide their own option.
"The largest number of respondents spoke about disappointment (44% of all respondents, an increase from 36% in December 2025) and shame (33%, up from 20%). These were followed by hope (23%, unchanged), anger (20%, up from 14%), sympathy (16%, unchanged), hatred (14%, up from 11%), and indifference (12%, up from 7%)," the report states.
Relatively fewer respondents mentioned sympathy (4%, unchanged), amusement/laughter (4%, unchanged), and pride (7%, unchanged).
It is noted that even among respondents who stated they trust incumbent President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a considerable number harbor negative feelings toward the authorities.
The survey was conducted from September 12 to 21, 2026, using computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all regions of Ukraine under government control. A total of 1,002 respondents aged 18 and older living in government-controlled territory were interviewed. The survey did not include residents of temporarily occupied territories or citizens who left abroad after February 24, 2022.
Under normal circumstances, the sampling error for this sample does not exceed 4.1% for indicators close to 50%, 3.5% for indicators close to 25%, 2.5% for indicators close to 10%, and 1.8% for indicators close to 5%. Under wartime conditions, certain systematic biases are added to the formal margin of error.

Hundreds of French schools stay closed ahead of nationwide day of student protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Hundreds of French schools stay closed ahead of nationwide day of student protests
PARIS – Hundreds of French high schools will begin a second week of closures on Oct 5 as protests over dilapidated schools and classrooms, overcrowding and teacher shortages precede a nationwide day of demonstrations on Oct 6.
The nationwide demonstrations and blockades underline a fraught social atmosphere as France’s government embarks on trying to pass a deficit-narrowing 2027 budget.
France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5% last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded investor concerns over the country’s fiscal outlook.
About 400 to 500 high schools are expected to remain completely or partially closed on Oct 5 in France, out of a total of 3,700, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on the evening of Oct 4.
The protests began in late September at a high school in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages before spreading nationwide.
“Our priority is to restore order,” government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Oct 5.
Geffray said that 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and that 78 employees of the national education system had been injured since the beginning of the demonstrations.
Police and students clash, tear gas used
On Oct 5, BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille in northern France, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the south-west and of a fire being lit as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in the 13th district of Paris, said her school had been attacked by a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks who tried to break through the school’s entrance door and then lit a fire.
Police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated and classes suspended.
“It was very violent and happened very quickly,” she said, adding that the attack lasted 15 to 20 minutes.
“It was terrible for students who witnessed this outburst of violence,” she said, adding those behind the attack on her school were not students of the school.
Since Sept 28, around 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested nationwide and dozens injured.
Teachers and members of the public have been attacked, while damage to property is estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
Bregeon said the French government would fast-track a Bill in Parliament on Oct 27 to make those found to have damaged property during protests financially liable.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure, in an open letter published on social media platform X on Oct 3, said those who had launched the protests no longer controlled them and called on students to abandon blockades in favour of peaceful protest.
Student unions have nevertheless called for a national day of demonstrations on Oct 6.
Security officials fear that an organised protest in central Paris in particular could see further violence amid concerns that far-left and anarchist groups could try to take over the protests.
CGT union head Sophie Binet told TF1 television on Oct 5 that CGT union members will attend the demonstrations on Oct 6 “to protect high school students”.
“We’ve been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students,” she said. REUTERS

Nationalists eye win in Bosnia elections marked by low turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:33:00 UTC
17:33:00 KST

Preliminary results from Sunday’s election show a Bosniak moderate, a pro-Russian Serb nationalist and a Croatian nationalist leading races for Bosnia’s tripartite presidency, the election commission said early Monday.
The results were largely in line with expectations and with projections by the Poliwave tracking platform, although voter turnout was low at a combined 42.02% in Bosnia's two entities, the Bosniak-Croat Federation and the Bosnian Serb republic (Republika Srpska). Voters also cast ballots for the national parliament, alongside regional races in the two entities.
Voter frustration has grown over an economic slowdown, the slow pace of EU entry talks and a lingering political crisis in which ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities have repeatedly stalled decisions by the weak central government that links them.
Denis Becirovic, a Bosniak of the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH) and part of the current tripartite presidency, garnered 26.78% of votes in the Bosniak-Croat Federation, ahead of the candidate for the center-right Muslim Party of Democratic Action (SDA). The two had been considered favorites in the election.
Also leading in the Bosniak-Croat Federation was newcomer Darijana Filipovic of the nationalist and pro-European Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ-BiH), with 13.89% of the vote.
In the Bosnian Serb republic, Zeljka Cvijanovic, an existing member of the tripartite presidency from the Serb and pro-Russian nationalist Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), secured 55.41% of votes, the election commission said.
Voting continued in some polling stations after the 7 p.m. (5 p.m. GMT) deadline Sunday due to delays related to a new electronic balloting system, Bosnia's Central Election Commission head Jovan Kalaba told reporters in Sarajevo.
The election commission redesigned ballots and introduced new biometric voter identification and electronic scanners, which it said were aimed at curbing voting fraud.
Speaking in Banja Luka, the largest Bosnian Serb city, Milorad Dodik, a separatist and pro-Russian leader of the SNSD who visited Moscow and met Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, said his party's candidate Savo Minic won the most votes for president of the entity.
"We have won the member of the (Bosnian) Presidency, and the president of the Republika Srpska. An unexpectedly high result," Dodik said.
Since the Bosnian war ended in 1995 under the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord, the country has been split along ethnic lines into two entities linked by the weak central government and tripartite presidency.
Bosnia, which has struggled to recover from the 1992-95 war, secured EU candidate status in December 2022 and approval to open accession negotiations in 2024.
Actual talks have not started, however, because the domestic legislatures have yet to enact core requirements such as bolstering judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.
Borjana Kristo, the deputy head of the Croat HDZ-BiH, said that overall progress could be made through dialogue after the elections.
"Bosnia must make progress solely on the principle of consensus, dialogue, and mutual respect," she told party supporters, cautioning against rhetoric that would drag the country backward.
Many voters in the country of 3.4 million people say they want to move beyond divisive rhetoric but its politics have become deadlocked.
The EU and Russia have been vying for influence over Bosnia, with the EU seeking to expand its membership across the Balkans while Russia wants to slow that process down and preserve its influence over the Bosnian Serb entity.
The U.S. has also sought to bolster its influence in Bosnia, pushing for a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import U.S. liquefied natural gas.
The EU has said, however, that the selection of the company for the project lacked competitive transparency, while Washington and Brussels have also clashed over the role of the High Representative, the international peace overseer for the country.

Imran Khan supporters head for Islamabad demanding his release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:31:00 UTC
17:31:00 KST

Over 5,000 supporters of imprisoned former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan began a dayslong march toward Islamabad Monday to demand his release following failed talks between the government and opposition.
The looming showdown threatens to deepen Pakistan’s political uncertainty at a time when the country is also grappling with a surge in terrorist attacks.
Khan is current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s main political rival and has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his party say are politically motivated.
Despite his imprisonment, he retains a substantial and passionate support base, keeping him at the center of Pakistan’s turbulent political landscape.
The demonstrators, traveling in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars, departed from Lakki Marwat district in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where Khan’s party holds power.
Organizers have planned overnight stops along the route as the caravan makes its way toward the capital. Sohail Afridi, the province’s chief minister, and a staunch Khan supporter is leading the march.
Speaking from a specially designed container truck emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, he expressed confidence in the movement’s ability to press its demands and bring the political standoff into the heart of the capital.
Authorities have erected roadblocks , using containers, at the entrance to Islamabad and inside the city.
Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, and the federal government were in talks to postpone the march but failed to reach a resolution. Gohar Khan, the party’s chairman, said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.
Sharif's government urged postponement of the march, citing a surge in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban in the northwest. His government has accused PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.
The organizers now vow to reach the capital after rallying with hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters.
Besides Khan’s release, protesters are demanding his transfer to a hospital and permission for his family to visit him. Officials say he is in good health and receives regular family visits but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former leader cannot be used for political purposes.
The march was originally scheduled for Sept. 27 but was postponed after party leaders said authorities blocked key approaches to Islamabad, including Attock Bridge, a major crossing for convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Previous protests by Khan’s supporters have turned violent, including one in 2024 in which security personnel and civilians were killed.
Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Sharif returned to office after the February 2024 election, which Khan’s party says was rigged to deny it victory. The government denies the allegation.

Why protecting home values is Beijing’s new priority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

Why protecting home values is Beijing’s new priority
With resale transactions outpacing new home sales for the first time, stabilising the existing housing stock has become vital
Official figures published by the National Bureau of Statistics in September reveal that secondary market home transactions have surpassed new residential builds in volume. Nationwide registered resales reached 549 million square metres, signalling that housing demand in China has not vanished. Rather, it appears to have structurally migrated.
This marks a departure from the previous growth model. For a quarter of a century, following the end of the old welfare housing system in 1998, China’s property market operated on a high-velocity loop: developers acquired municipal land, pre-sold unfinished apartments, collected buyer cash and funnelled those advances into their next projects. That mechanism turned residential construction into the primary economic engine of the country.
That engine is now losing momentum. What is emerging is not merely a smaller version of the old market but a different market altogether. The centre of gravity is shifting – from developers selling a promise of tomorrow to households trading the homes of today.

Dutch government considers nationwide mobile phone ban in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:29:52 UTC
17:29:52 KST

Melike Pala
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The Dutch Cabinet has called on primary and secondary schools to ban students from using mobile phones throughout the school day, including during breaks and on school grounds, broadcaster NOS reported Monday.
Under the proposed measure, students would be required to keep their mobile phones away for the duration of the school day, including in classrooms, assembly halls, during breaks and elsewhere on school premises, from Jan. 1, 2027.
The Cabinet currently does not have the legal authority to impose a nationwide ban on mobile phone use in schools but can issue recommendations to the education sector.
The proposal is part of a broader government strategy aimed at protecting children from risks associated with excessive and potentially harmful online activity.
Officials warned that addictive algorithms, autoplaying videos and social media can make it difficult for young people to reduce their screen use.
The government previously reached national agreements in 2024 aimed at restricting mobile phone use during lessons.
The Cabinet is also calling for stronger measures to protect children online, including a possible age limit for access to social media platforms.
The European Commission is considering an age threshold of 13, while the Dutch government has proposed setting the minimum age at 15.
The government is also preparing tighter regulations for family vloggers and child influencers.
Under the proposed rules, online content produced by children under 15 could be classified as child labor and subject to penalties.

Ukraine Hits Russian Buk-M3, Drone Launch Hub, and EW Station in Coordinated Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:28:58 UTC
17:28:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian Buk-M3, Drone Launch Hub, and EW Station in Coordinated Strikes
Ukrainian forces launched retaliatory strikes against Russian military targets on October 3 and overnight into October 4.
A Russian Buk-M3 air defense system, a strike-drone storage and launch site, an electronic warfare station, and several other military facilities were targeted during the operation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 4, the Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system was hit near Kuroshany in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.
Ukrainian forces also struck a site near temporarily occupied Donetsk where Russian forces stored, prepared, and launched attack drones.
The General Staff described such facilities as priority targets because of their role in Russian drone operations against Ukraine. “Systematic strikes on such facilities are aimed at reducing the Russian Federation’s ability to use strike drones against Ukraine’s civilian population,” the General Staff said.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian electronic warfare station near Klimovo in Russia’s Bryansk region. Russian telecommunications nodes were also hit near Hirnyk, Yasynuvata, and Donetsk in the Donetsk region, according to the General Staff.
In the temporarily occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces targeted Russian repair units near Vesela Tarasivka and Lysychansk.
Earlier on October 4, drones targeted Russia’s Khanskaya military airfield in the Republic of Adygea, where Su-34 and Su-35 fighter jets are based, with open-source footage showing a fire near the facility.

Germany Unveils €1.35 Billion Ukraine Package as Merz Arrives in Kyiv to Finalize Drone Deal
Germany is preparing to provide Ukraine with €1 billion in new military assistance and another €350 million to repair damaged energy infrastructure, as Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv for talks on expanding bilateral defense cooperation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on October 4, German government officials said Merz is expected to announce the funding package during his visit, while Germany and Ukraine are also set to finalize an agreement covering the joint production of several types of drones.
“I travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said. “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us.”
Reuters reported that Merz traveled to Kyiv alongside German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation that includes executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems, and other companies. The German chancellor is also expected to discuss reforms requested by Ukraine’s European Union partners, including anti-corruption measures.
A major part of the visit is expected to focus on expanding Ukrainian-German defense production. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week, following a phone call with Merz, that the two countries were preparing to finalize an agreement covering drones, missiles, and related software, Reuters reported.
One of the priorities is the rapid production of interceptor drones designed to counter high-speed jet-powered attack drones. German defense company Quantum Systems has tested technology for this role.
The planned cooperation extends beyond drone interceptors. According to Reuters, Germany and Ukraine are also working on the joint development and production of weapons with ranges exceeding 1,000 kilometers, giving Ukraine additional domestically and jointly produced options for long-range strikes against military targets inside Russia.
Merz arrived as Russia continued large-scale attacks on Kyiv. Air raid alerts and explosions were reported across the Ukrainian capital on October 4, while one Russian strike damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River and nearby infrastructure, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Germany has significantly expanded its military support for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The German government says it has provided or committed around €57.6 billion in bilateral military assistance for Ukraine, while Berlin has also financed energy repairs, air defense capabilities, and other infrastructure support.

The Yemeni army said Monday that government forces had seized the Dhubab district and strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait following clashes with the Houthis. 
Yemen’s official Saba news agency said forces from the Nation’s Shield and the pro-government Southern Giants Brigades, backed by the Popular Resistance, took control of Dhubab in western Taiz province.

FACTBOX: Incumbent president, senator to advance to runoff in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:26:46 UTC
17:26:46 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 5. /TASS/. Brazil’s first round of the presidential election ends without any candidate receiving the 50% of votes needed to win.
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro will compete in the runoff election on October 25.
TASS summarizes key results.
First-round results
- Official results from the Superior Electoral Court, which serves as Brazil’s election authority, show Senator Flavio Bolsonaro leading the first round with 47.09% of the vote after 99.70% of electronic voting records were processed. More than 56 million votes were cast for him.
- Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva finishes in second with 45.09%, receiving more than 53.6 million votes.
- Bolsonaro leads Lula da Silva by 2 percentage points, a difference of nearly 2.39 million votes.
- The other candidates do not seriously challenge the two frontrunners, dividing the remaining votes among themselves.
- Writer Augusto Cury finishes third with 2.89%, receiving 3.44 million votes.
- Mission movement activist Renan Santos comes in fourth with 2.25%, receiving 2.67 million votes.
- Goias Governor Ronaldo Caiado receives 2.19%, or 2.60 million votes.
- Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema wins the support of 0.27% of voters, or 325,900 votes.
- Candidates from small parties collectively receive slightly more than 0.2%.
- The first round leaves the right-wing camp with a significant advantage going into the runoff.
- Center-right and libertarian candidates who exit the race receive a combined 7.60%, or more than 9 million votes, with most of their voters historically opposing left-wing forces.
- The governing coalition loses ground after Lula da Silva falls behind in the strategically important state of Minas Gerais in southeastern Brazil, where victory has traditionally been seen as a guarantee of a national win.
Turnout
- Voter turnout exceeds 78.93% in the general election, with more than 124.9 million citizens voting out of nearly 158.7 million registered voters.
- The abstention rate reaches about 21.1%, with more than 33.3 million people not voting.
- Valid votes total 118.8 million, or 95.23%, while blank ballots account for 1.84%, or 2.29 million votes, and spoiled ballots account for 2.93%, or 3.66 million votes.
Runoff
- Brazil will hold the runoff of the presidential election on October 25.
- Both finalists will participate in a series of in-person debates and work to mobilize undecided voters in the largest metropolitan areas of southeastern Brazil over the next three weeks.
Statements by runoff candidates
- Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Brazil’s presidential race is entering its decisive phase and that efforts to mobilize voters will resume immediately.
- The incumbent president acknowledged that his campaign had anticipated a first-round victory.
- Lula da Silva also called the vote a "lesson in democracy" and personally thanked millions of Brazilians for fulfilling their civic duty by going to the polls.
- Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing Liberal Party candidate, expressed confidence that he would win the presidential runoff and said the country’s decades of left-wing rule were drawing to an end.
- Bolsonaro promised to run a "clean campaign" and noted that he is the only presidential candidate to have officially committed to ending presidential reelection.
Impact of results on relations with Russia
- Brazil’s policy toward Russia is unlikely to undergo significant changes regardless of the presidential election outcome, international affairs journalist, translator and Latin America expert Oleg Yasinsky told TASS.

Majority of Ukrainians believe Zelenskyy should not run for second term – survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:25:00 EEST
17:25:00 KST

Majority of Ukrainians believe Zelenskyy should not run for second term – survey
More than half of Ukrainians believe that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should serve only one term as president and should not run for a second term in the next election.
Source: a poll conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on 12-21 September
Quote: "Now 53% believe he should be limited to one current term (up from 46% in December 2025). Meanwhile, 42% believe he should participate in the next election (down from 45%). The remaining 5% were undecided."
Details: KIIS notes that there is a clear correlation between the level of trust in the president and support for him running in the election.
"If among those who completely trust the president, 85% support his participation in the elections, then this indicator decreases to 53% among those who rather trust and to, respectively, 20% and 7% among those who rather or completely do not trust," the sociologists said.
For reference: The survey was conducted on 12-21 September. A total of 1,002 respondents aged 18 and over living in all regions of Ukraine under Ukrainian government control were interviewed by telephone based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers. The sample did not include residents of territories temporarily outside the Ukrainian government's control (although some respondents were internally displaced persons who had moved from occupied territories). The survey also did not include Ukrainian citizens who left the country after 24 February 2022.
Under normal circumstances, the statistical margin of error for a sample of this size (with a 95% confidence level and a design effect of 1.3) would not exceed 4.1% for figures close to 50%, 3.5% for figures close to 25%, 2.5% for figures close to 10% and 1.8% for figures close to 5%.
In wartime conditions, there is a certain systematic deviation in addition to the formal margin of error mentioned above. However, the sociologists believe that the results remain highly representative and allow for a fairly reliable analysis of public opinion.

India in talks with Russia and Ukraine to end conflict – FM
India has moved “beyond advocacy” in the Russia-Ukraine conflict and is now holding talks with both Moscow and Kiev on Black Sea shipping, grain, and energy exports, as well as possible non-attack arrangements, Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has said. 
New Delhi has become more directly involved in recent months after years of calling for dialogue and diplomacy, Jaishankar said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. India is trying to help first on the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, while discussions have expanded to other immediate concerns shared by the two sides.
“We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard,” he said, describing talks over grain and energy exports and “non-attack possibilities” as ongoing. 
Ukraine separately acknowledged India’s increased involvement. Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga said last week that New Delhi had submitted the most comprehensive of four ceasefire proposals being considered by Kiev, alongside initiatives from Türkiye, Egypt, and the US. 
Kiev is prepared to consider an energy and Black Sea ceasefire if it includes a halt to attacks on energy facilities and port infrastructure, Sibiga said. Ukraine says it is also open to an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact.
Russia has also welcomed India’s efforts. President Vladimir Putin said last week that Prime Minister Narendra Modi raises the Ukraine conflict at every meeting and has “very good ideas” aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. Modi urged Putin in August to move from “endless war” to an “end of war.”
India’s diplomatic engagement is unfolding as New Delhi also faces increased US pressure over its purchases of Russian energy. A recently passed US law would allow Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major purchasers of Russian oil, including India and China. New Delhi has warned that such measures could damage bilateral relations and disrupt global energy markets.
Russian crude, which accounts for more than 40% of India’s oil supplies, is crucial for the energy security of the world’s most populous nation. However, New Delhi is also seeking to preserve its commercial relationship with Washington amid prolonged trade negotiations.
India has maintained that the Ukraine conflict will ultimately be resolved through diplomacy and negotiations rather than restrictions on trade. Jaishankar said last month that New Delhi was in continuous contact with both sides and was looking for ideas that could help mitigate or end the fighting.

Swiss divided on early foreign language education
The reform of language teaching in primary schools is stirring debate in Switzerland. Left-wing parties defend early language teaching for national cohesion, while the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party defends federalism.
On June 12, the Swiss government submitted two proposals for the new Languages Act for consultation. This consultation period ended on Monday. The debate centred on whether to introduce one national language and English in primary school, or a second national language from primary school through to the end of lower secondary education.
+ Young Swiss must learn second national language, says government
The Green Party supports the first option, while the Social Democratic Party favours the second should a revision prove necessary. The Radical-Liberals reject both options.
Swiss teachers support the second option, subject to adjusted objectives and sufficient funding. Cantons are also divided. Canton Fribourg, fore example, supports the first option, as does Valais.
Several cantonal parliaments in German-speaking Switzerland wish to postpone French lessons until secondary level.

Germany denies Russian art student a visa citing ‘security threat.’ Rights advocates call it a dangerous precedent.
The German Embassy in Moscow has denied a study visa to a graduate of the Design program at the Higher School of Economics (HSE) who had been accepted into a similar program at a German art university. Molnia, a human rights project for students, reported the refusal after reviewing the letter denying the visa.
In the letter, the embassy cited the risk that knowledge gained at the German university could be misused and pose a threat to Germany’s security and interests. “When weighing your personal interest in entering the country against the public interest in preventing a threat, it was determined that the public interest carries greater weight,” the embassy wrote in its response.
European universities could previously deny admission to students in technical fields over the risk of “knowledge being used for unintended purposes.” “This is the first time we have seen the phrase ‘security threat’ applied to a graduate of an arts program with no ties to government structures or military developments,” Molnia said.
Molnia called the case a dangerous precedent and promised to continue helping the student.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in early September that German authorities would tighten control over the entry of Russians in response to the sabotage at Leipzig Airport. He did not specify how the entry rules would change.
